App Feature Area 1: Screen-by-Screen App Experience

Purpose of this feature area

This section begins the long-form detail of the Verivae design brief toward the requested large target. The goal is not to inflate the document with filler. The goal is to expand the design brief in professional feature areas so the final document becomes genuinely useful for building, testing, designing, explaining, and improving the app later.

This section stays in product-design language. It defines expected app behavior, user-visible screens, decision support, permission boundaries, and safety outcomes so later design and engineering work have a clear product target.

This first feature area focuses on screens because screens are where users experience the product. A function like Quick Scam Check is useful only when the user knows where to tap, what to enter, what warnings they see, what result they receive, and what the app tells them to do next.

Long-form design brief growth strategy

The design brief should stay useful by deepening each app feature with real product detail. Each section should answer questions a future designer, developer, tester, or product reviewer would actually need answered.

Advised detail path:

App Feature Area 1 detail: Screen-by-screen specification foundation. This section defines the main screens, their purposes, interface behavior, user emotions, wording needs, safety rules, and first-version states.

App Feature Area 2: Detailed function specifications. This section should deeply expand each function: Quick Scam Check, Guided Review, Payment Request Review, Rule-Based Risk Engine, Warning Sign Detector, Safer Next Step Guide, Education Center, Settings, Feedback, Notes, and Already-Sent-Money Flow.

App Feature Area 3: User flows and edge cases. This section should describe every major user path, including confused users, users who paste sensitive info, users who already sent money, users helping someone else, users who do not know the scam category, and users who abandon the flow halfway through.

App Feature Area 4: Interface writing and exact copy. This section should write the actual button labels, helper text, warnings, result messages, privacy reminders, empty states, error states, and plain explanations.

App Feature Area 5: Visual design and aesthetic system. This section should define layout, spacing, color use, typography direction, risk-level styling, icon style, accessibility, and what the app should visually avoid.

App Feature Area 6: Privacy, data, and security feature system. This section defines what the app collects, what it avoids collecting, how linked-device review works, how weekly checks protect privacy, and how sensitive info stays under user control.

App Feature Area 7: Scam detection logic and risk explanation system. This section defines warning sign categories, risk weights in plain text, decision rules, result logic, confidence limits, and how the app explains its reasoning.

App Feature Area 8: Feature-by-feature deep feature specifications. This section deepens the app's main features, including manual checks, payment review, evidence storage, trusted helper support, device security checks, weekly checks, scam-category review, and future phone integrations.

Related Feature Area: Accessibility and inclusive design. This area covers older users, stressed users, users with low technical confidence, mobile readability, plain text, color-blind accessibility, motor accessibility, and screen-reader-friendly structure.

Related Feature Area: User understanding and safety validation. This area defines how the app experience should prove that users understand risk, avoid sensitive-data entry, and choose safer next steps.

Screen specification format

Each screen should eventually be described with the same structure:

Screen name: The plain name of the screen.

Purpose: Why the screen exists.

User mindset: What the user may be feeling when they reach the screen.

Primary action: The main thing the user should do.

Secondary actions: Other useful options that should not distract from the main action.

Required content: The text, labels, warnings, and choices that must appear.

Interface behavior: How the screen should respond when the user taps, types, skips, backs out, or makes a mistake.

Safety rules: What the screen must avoid asking, implying, or promising.

Aesthetic direction: How the screen should look and feel.

Accessibility notes: How the screen should remain usable for people with different needs.

first app version decision: Whether this screen belongs in the first version.

Screen 1: Opening Home Screen

Purpose:

The Opening Home Screen is the user's first contact with Verivae. It must explain the app quickly without feeling like a marketing page. The user should immediately understand that the app helps review risky situations before acting. The screen should make starting a check easy, but it should also set the app's limits carefully.

User mindset:

A user may open the app while worried, embarrassed, rushed, confused, or risky. Some users may have received a text saying a bank account is locked. Others may be helping a parent who is about to send money. Others may simply be curious. The Home Screen must work for all of those states without becoming cluttered.

Primary action:

Start a check.

Advised label:

Start a check

This is better than Detect scam because detect sounds too absolute. It is better than Protect me because that sounds like a guarantee. Start a check is simple, honest, and action-oriented.

Secondary actions:

\- Learn about scams  
\- What this app does  
\- Privacy basics

Required content:

The Home Screen should include the app name Verivae, a short explanation, the Start a check button, a Learn about scams option, and a small safety note for users who already sent money or lost account access.

Advised short explanation:

Review risky messages, payment requests, and online situations before you act.

Advised safety note:

If money was already sent or an account is compromised, contact your bank, payment service, or official support right away.

Interface behavior:

When the user taps Start a check, the app should go to Situation Selection. When the user taps Learn about scams, the app should go to the Education Center. When the user taps What this app does, the app should show a plain explanation of the app's purpose and limits.

The Home Screen should not require sign-in. Requiring an account too early would create friction and reduce trust. The user should be able to get help first.

Safety rules:

The Home Screen must not say guaranteed protection, scam-proof, certified fraud detection, bank-level security, or official scam prevention. It should say that the app helps review warning signs, helps the user pause before acting, and helps the user choose safer next steps.

Aesthetic direction:

The Home Screen should look calm and spacious. It should not look like an emergency siren. Use a neutral background, strong readable text, and one clear main button. The design should feel serious but not frightening.

A good Home Screen should feel like opening a careful checklist, not like entering a panic room.

Accessibility notes:

Main text should be large enough to read on a phone. The primary button should be easy to tap. The screen should not rely only on color to communicate meaning. Avoid tiny legal text. Keep sentences short.

first app version decision:

Must build in the first version.

Screen 2: Situation Selection Screen

Purpose:

The Situation Selection screen helps the user choose what kind of risky situation they want to review. This is important because scam situations vary. A payment request has different warning signs than a job offer. A family emergency scam has different emotional pressure than a marketplace listing.

User mindset:

The user may not know what category their situation belongs in. The screen must support both confident users and unsure users. The category labels should match real-life language, not expert language.

Primary action:

Choose a situation type.

Advised choices:

\- Message or email  
\- Payment request  
\- Marketplace listing  
\- Job or money offer  
\- Relationship or romance situation  
\- Family emergency request  
\- Account warning or login alert  
\- Not sure

The Not sure option is important. A confused user should never feel blocked because they do not know the right category.

Required content:

The top of the screen should say:

What do you want to check?

Helper text:

Choose the closest option. If you are not sure, pick Not sure and the app will guide you.

Each option should be short, with optional helper examples beneath it. Message or email can include texts, emails, DMs, support messages, delivery messages, and bank alerts. Payment request can include gift cards, crypto, wire transfers, payment apps, deposits, and refunds. Marketplace listing can include buying, selling, renting, shipping, deposits, and fake payment proof.

Interface behavior:

Selecting a category should move the user forward to the Privacy Reminder screen. The app should remember the selected category so later questions can be tailored. If the user selects Not sure, the app should use a general guided review path.

Safety rules:

The screen should not ask the user to paste message text yet. First, the app should show the privacy reminder. This ordering matters because users may paste sensitive info without thinking.

Aesthetic direction:

Use simple stacked choice cards or large list buttons. Each option should have a clear label and one short example line. Avoid dense grids on small screens because longer labels may become cramped.

Accessibility notes:

Each option should be readable without needing icons. Icons may help but must not be the only cue. The Not sure option should be visible without scrolling too far.

first app version decision:

Must build in the first version.

Screen 3: Privacy Reminder Screen

Purpose:

The Privacy Reminder screen protects the user before they enter info. Scam-related situations often involve private messages, financial details, login codes, and emotional pressure. The app must teach users what not to enter before asking for input.

User mindset:

The user may be rushed and may want to paste everything immediately. They may not understand that a message contains sensitive data. They may also be embarrassed and want the app to solve the problem quickly. The privacy reminder needs to be short enough to read but strong enough to matter.

Primary action:

Continue after reading the reminder.

Advised button:

I understand, continue

Secondary action:

Back

Required content:

Advised reminder:

Before you continue, do not enter passwords, one-time login codes, full card numbers, bank account numbers, Social Security numbers, government ID numbers, or private account details. You can summarize the situation instead.

Short helper text:

Verivae reviews warning signs. It does not need your most sensitive info.

Interface behavior:

The user should see this reminder before any free-text input. The reminder should appear in a calm content block. It should not be hidden in terms and conditions. The app should let the user go back if they realize they are not ready.

Safety rules:

The app must not encourage users to paste everything. It should explicitly say they can summarize. The app should treat less data as better.

Aesthetic direction:

This screen can use a subtle caution color, but it should not look like a severe error. The message should feel protective, not accusatory.

Accessibility notes:

Do not use small legal text. Use short paragraphs. Key sensitive items should be easy to scan. The continue button should be clearly separate from the warning text.

first app version decision:

Must build in the first version.

This feature area connects to Quick Message Input, Guided Review, Already-Sent-Money, Review Before Result, and Result Screen detail.

Screen 4: Quick Message Input Screen

Purpose:

The Quick Message Input screen lets the user type, paste, or summarize a risky message. This is the fastest useful check in the app. It should support texts, emails, direct messages, fake bank alerts, delivery notices, marketplace messages, job messages, and other risky written communication.

User mindset:

The user may want an answer immediately. They may feel time pressure because the message says an account will be locked, a package will fail delivery, a payment must happen now, or a loved one needs help. The screen should help them move quickly while still reminding them not to enter sensitive info.

Primary action:

Paste or summarize the risky message.

Advised input label:

Paste or summarize the message

Helper text:

Remove passwords, login codes, account numbers, card numbers, and private details before entering anything.

Primary button:

Review warning signs

Secondary actions:

\- Use guided questions instead  
\- Clear text  
\- Back

Required content:

The input area should be large enough for a full message or short summary. It should not feel like a tiny search field. The screen should also ask where the message came from because the same words may mean different things depending on the source.

Source choices:

\- Text message  
\- Email  
\- Social media or direct message  
\- Marketplace app  
\- Dating app  
\- Phone call summary  
\- Website pop-up  
\- Not sure

The screen should also ask whether the message involves risky requests:

\- Money or payment  
\- Gift cards  
\- Crypto  
\- Password or login code  
\- Bank or card details  
\- Identity info  
\- Clicking a link  
\- Downloading a file  
\- Keeping it secret  
\- Acting urgently

Interface behavior:

If the user enters text, the Review warning signs button should become available. If the user leaves the input blank, the app should offer a helpful prompt instead of an error that feels harsh:

Add a short message summary, or use guided questions instead.

The app should allow short input. A user might write, “Someone says my bank account is locked and wants me to click a link.” That is enough to identify important warning signs. The app should not require the full private message.

Safety rules:

This screen should repeat the privacy warning in shorter form. Users may have forgotten the previous screen. The app should never say “paste the whole conversation.” It should say “paste or summarize.”

If the user appears to include a one-time code, password, full card number, or account number, the app should warn them to remove sensitive details before continuing. The first design version does not need to define exactly how that detection works. It only needs to define the intended user protection.

Aesthetic direction:

The screen should feel like a calm review form. It should not look like a casual chat with an unknown bot. The user should feel in control of what they enter.

Accessibility notes:

The input label should remain visible. Placeholder text should not be the only instruction. The text field should work with larger text sizes. The Review warning signs button should be easy to reach on mobile.

first app version decision:

Must build in the first version.

Screen 5: Guided Review Intro Screen

Purpose:

The Guided Review Intro screen prepares users for a stepwise review. This path is for users who are unsure, overwhelmed, helping someone else, or dealing with a situation that cannot be explained well by pasted text.

User mindset:

The user may be stressed and may not know how to describe the problem. A guided review can feel easier because it asks one question at a time. The screen should reassure the user that they can skip questions and that general answers are enough.

Primary action:

Start guided review.

Advised button:

Start guided review

Secondary actions:

\- Use quick message check instead  
\- Back

Required content:

Intro copy:

Answer a few simple questions. You can skip anything you do not know. The app will look for warning signs and suggest safer next steps.

Reassurance copy:

You do not need to enter private account details. General answers are enough.

Interface behavior:

The screen should briefly preview the process. A simple progress preview can help:

Step 1: What happened  
Step 2: What they asked for  
Step 3: Warning signs  
Step 4: Safer next steps

The app should not call this a quiz or test. The user is not being graded. The app is helping them think clearly.

Safety rules:

The guided review should ask about categories, not exact secrets. For example, ask whether someone requested a login code, not what the login code is.

Aesthetic direction:

This screen should feel structured and reassuring. It should use simple spacing, short text, and a clear start button. It should not look like a long form before the user even begins.

Accessibility notes:

The user should be able to go back. The progress preview should be readable as text. The Start guided review button should be visually obvious.

first app version decision:

Must build in the first version.

Screen 6: Guided Review Question Screen

Purpose:

The Guided Review Question screen is a reusable screen pattern for the stepwise review. Instead of creating a different interface for every question, the app should use a consistent question screen so the user learns the pattern quickly.

User mindset:

The user may be nervous or impatient. They may want the app to “just tell me if this is a scam.” The design must make each question feel useful. Helper text should explain why a question matters without overwhelming the user.

Primary action:

Answer the current question.

Common answer choices:

\- Yes  
\- No  
\- Not sure  
\- Skip

Some questions may need multiple-choice choices, such as sender type or payment method.

Required question examples:

Question:  
Is anyone asking you to send money?

Why this matters:  
Scammers often create pressure around payments, especially methods that are hard to reverse.

Question:  
Is anyone asking you to keep this secret?

Why this matters:  
Secrecy is a warning sign because it prevents you from getting help before acting.

Question:  
Is anyone rushing you or threatening consequences?

Why this matters:  
Urgency can pressure people into acting before they verify.

Question:  
Are they asking for gift cards, crypto, wire transfer, or payment through friends and family?

Why this matters:  
Some payment methods are difficult to reverse and are often used in scams.

Question:  
Are they asking for a password, login code, bank detail, card number, or ID doc?

Why this matters:  
Legitimate organizations usually do not ask for passwords or one-time login codes through random messages.

Question:  
Have you verified the request through a trusted channel you already had before this message?

Why this matters:  
Using contact info inside a risky message can lead you back to the scammer.

Interface behavior:

Each question should have a clear title, optional helper text, and large answer buttons. After the user answers, the app moves to the next question. The user should be able to go back and change an answer.

The app should show progress, such as Question 3 of 8\. Progress helps users understand that the review is limited and will end soon.

Safety rules:

Questions should not request exact private data. The question screen should never ask “What is the code?” or “What is your account number?” It should ask whether that type of info was requested.

Aesthetic direction:

The question screen should be uncluttered. The current question should be the visual focus. Helper text should be available but not dominate the screen.

Accessibility notes:

Yes, No, Not sure, and Skip must be easy to tap. The current question should be the largest text on the screen. Helper text should be readable and not too faint. Progress should be understandable without relying only on a visual progress bar.

first app version decision:

Must build in the first version.

Screen 7: Already Sent Money or Shared Info Screen

Purpose:

This screen handles the most urgent user state: the user already sent money, shared a password, gave a code, clicked a risky link, downloaded something, or provided account info. This path must be different from prevention. The user needs response guidance, not a normal warning-sign check.

User mindset:

The user may be scared, embarrassed, angry, or panicked. The app must avoid blame. It should move quickly to practical action.

Primary action:

Identify what happened at a high level.

Advised question:

Have you already sent money or shared sensitive info?

Answer choices:

\- No, I have not acted yet  
\- Yes, I sent money  
\- Yes, I shared a password or login code  
\- Yes, I shared bank, card, or identity info  
\- I clicked a link or downloaded something  
\- Not sure

Required response logic:

If the user has not acted yet, continue the normal prevention flow.

If the user sent money, show response steps:

\- Contact your bank, card company, payment app, or payment service right away.  
\- Do not send more money to recover the first payment.  
\- Save records if you can do so safely.  
\- Report the account or message through the platform if appropriate.

If the user shared a password or login code, show response steps:

\- Change the password from the official app or website.  
\- Turn on two-factor auth if available.  
\- Review recent account activity.  
\- Contact official support if you cannot access the account.

If the user shared bank, card, or identity info, show response steps:

\- Contact the bank, card issuer, or official organization immediately.  
\- Watch for unauthorized activity.  
\- Follow the official institution's instructions.

If the user clicked a link or downloaded something, show response steps:

\- Do not enter more info.  
\- Close the page or app if it seems risky.  
\- Use official support channels if account access may be affected.  
\- Consider device security help if something was downloaded.

Safety rules:

The app must not promise money recovery. It must not say it can reverse payments. It must not tell the user to delay contacting official support. It must not shame the user.

Aesthetic direction:

This screen can be more urgent than other screens, but it should still be calm. Use direct text and clear action blocks. Avoid panic-heavy design.

Accessibility notes:

The response steps should be short and scannable. Critical actions should appear near the top. Buttons and next steps should be obvious.

first app version decision:

Must include a basic version in the first release.

Screen 8: Review Before Result Screen

Purpose:

The Review Before Result screen lets the user confirm the info they provided before the app generates the final risk explanation. This helps reduce mistakes and gives the user one more chance to remove sensitive details.

User mindset:

The user may want an immediate answer, so this screen should not feel like a barrier. It should be short and useful.

Primary action:

Continue to result.

Advised button:

Show result

Secondary actions:

\- Edit answers  
\- Remove sensitive details  
\- Back

Required content:

The screen should summarize:

\- situation type  
\- whether money is involved  
\- whether sensitive info is involved  
\- major warning signs selected  
\- whether the user already acted

It should not display a full pasted message if that makes the screen too sensitive. A future version could show a collapsed summary instead.

Safety reminder:

Before continuing, make sure you did not include passwords, login codes, full card numbers, bank account numbers, Social Security numbers, or private identity details.

Interface behavior:

If the user taps Edit answers, they should return to the relevant screen. If they taps Show result, the app should generate the risk explanation based on the info provided.

Safety rules:

Do not force users to confirm exact sensitive details. The screen is for review and cleanup, not for collecting more private info.

Aesthetic direction:

Use a simple summary layout. Avoid long paragraphs. The screen should feel like a final checkpoint.

Accessibility notes:

Summary labels should be clear. Edit buttons should say what they edit. The Show result button should be easy to find.

first app version decision:

Should build if time allows. If skipped in the earliest prototype, the privacy reminder must be strong enough to compensate.

Screen 9: Result Screen Foundation

Purpose:

The Result Screen is the most important screen in the app. It is where the user decides what to do next. It must be clear, honest, useful, and careful.

User mindset:

At this point, the user needs a clear answer. They may be hoping the app says everything is fine, afraid the app will confirm their suspicion, or under pressure to make a decision quickly. The screen should reduce confusion and help them act more safely.

Required structure:

1\. Risk level  
2\. One-sentence summary  
3\. Warning signs found  
4\. What not to do yet  
5\. Safer next steps  
6\. Why this matters  
7\. Optional trusted-person summary  
8\. Start another check

Risk level labels:

Low concern  
Needs caution  
Risk  
Stop and verify

Risk level explanation:

Low concern means few warning signs were found, but the user should still use normal caution.

Needs caution means some warning signs are present and the user should verify before acting.

Risk means multiple serious warning signs are present. The user should avoid sending money or sharing info until verified.

Stop and verify means the situation includes strong warning signs such as secrecy, urgent payment, gift cards, crypto, one-time codes, account access requests, threats, or an unverified sender.

Example result for a risky payment request:

Risk level: Stop and verify

Summary: This request has strong scam warning signs.

Warning signs found: urgent payment, secrecy, gift card request, and unverified sender.

Do not do yet: Do not buy gift cards, send card codes, or send more money.

Safer next step: Contact the person or organization through a trusted phone number or official app you already had before this request.

Why this matters: Gift card payments are difficult to reverse, and secrecy prevents other people from helping you check the situation.

Interface behavior:

The result should appear quickly and should not be hidden behind animation or marketing. The user should be able to read the main answer at the top of the screen without scrolling. The app should let the user expand explanations if they want more detail. The first view should be concise, with deeper explanations available below.

Safety rules:

The result must not say safe as a final guarantee. Even Low concern should include a reminder to verify if anything feels wrong. The result should not accuse a real person by name. It should describe the situation and warning signs.

Aesthetic direction:

Risk levels can use color, but the words must carry the meaning. Do not rely on color alone. Red should be reserved for Stop and verify. The screen should feel serious but readable.

Accessibility notes:

Risk level must be text, not only color. Warning signs should be listed plainly. Important next steps should be near the top. Buttons should be large and clearly labeled.

first app version decision:

Must build in the first version.

App Feature Area 1 design notes for screen and aesthetic direction

The app's aesthetic should support trust without copying banks, police, or government agencies. It should feel like a practical safety tool made for normal people.

Advised visual personality:

\- calm  
\- steady  
\- plainspoken  
\- protective without being dramatic  
\- modern but not flashy  
\- serious but not cold  
\- simple enough for stressed users

The interface should avoid decoration that makes the app look less serious. It should also avoid security-theater visuals. Security theater means design that looks protective but does not actually make the product safer, such as fake badges, dramatic shields, glowing locks, or official-looking seals.

The best design direction is a calm checklist style. The user should feel guided through a careful review, not judged by a machine.

App Feature Area 1 accept rules

App Feature Area 1 is acceptable when:

\- it keeps the design brief in planning mode only  
\- it avoids coding  
\- it does not start launch instructions  
\- it starts the feature-based path toward the requested large goal  
\- it defines a repeatable screen specification format  
\- it details the Home Screen in detail  
\- it details Situation Selection in detail  
\- it details the Privacy Reminder in detail  
\- it details Quick Message Input in detail  
\- it details Guided Review screens in detail  
\- it details the Already-Sent-Money path in detail  
\- it details the Result Screen foundation in detail  
\- it connects interface design to safety and privacy  
\- it preserves Harborwake as the company name and Verivae as the app name

Additional feature area to define

The design brief should also include App Feature Area 2: Detailed Function Specifications.

\---

App Feature Area 2: Detailed Function Specifications

Purpose of this feature area

App Feature Area 2 explains the app functions in deeper professional detail. App Feature Area 1 described the main screens. App Feature Area 2 describes what each function is supposed to accomplish, why it matters, how it should behave for users, what info it needs, what result it should produce, what safety rules apply, and whether it belongs in the first version.

This section still contains no coding. It should not explain how to program the app. It should explain what the app must do from a product, design, safety, and user-experience point of view. A future builder should be able to read this section and understand the intended behavior before any technical work begins.

The main principle for all functions is that the app is a careful review assistant. It helps users slow down, notice warning signs, and choose safer next steps. It does not replace a bank, payment service, police department, lawyer, financial advisor, family member, or official support channel.

Function specification format

Each function should be described using a consistent structure:

Function name:  
The plain name of the function.

Purpose:  
Why the function exists.

User need:  
What problem this function solves for the user.

Inputs:  
What info the function may need from the user.

Outputs:  
What the function gives back to the user.

User experience behavior:  
How the function should feel and behave inside the app.

Safety and privacy rules:  
What the function must avoid asking, storing, implying, or promising.

Interface notes:  
How the function should appear in the interface.

First-version decision:  
Whether the function should be part of the first app version, delayed, or partially included.

Function 1: Quick Scam Check

Purpose:

Quick Scam Check is the fastest path through the app. It exists for users who have a risky message, request, or situation and want a quick review before they act. This function should be useful when the user has a text message, email, direct message, marketplace message, job message, fake bank alert, fake delivery notice, or short summary of a phone call.

The purpose is not to produce a perfect answer. The purpose is to quickly identify warning signs and give the user a safer next step. In a scam situation, speed matters, but careless speed is dangerous. Quick Scam Check should feel fast while still being cautious.

User need:

The user may be asking:

\- Is this risky?  
\- Should I click this link?  
\- Should I send money?  
\- Should I reply?  
\- Should I trust this person?  
\- What should I do before acting?

The user may not know the right scam category. They may not know whether the message is fake. They may simply feel that something is off. Quick Scam Check should meet the user at that level of uncertainty.

Inputs:

Quick Scam Check may use:

\- pasted message text  
\- user-written summary  
\- source type, such as text message, email, marketplace app, dating app, phone call summary, or website pop-up  
\- whether the request involves money  
\- whether the request involves a link  
\- whether the request involves a password or one-time code  
\- whether the request involves bank, card, or identity info  
\- whether the sender is known or unknown  
\- whether urgency, secrecy, or threats are present

The app should not need highly sensitive details. It should not ask for full card numbers, bank account numbers, login codes, passwords, Social Security numbers, or government ID numbers.

Outputs:

Quick Scam Check should produce:

\- risk level  
\- short summary  
\- warning signs found  
\- what not to do yet  
\- safer next steps  
\- optional explanation of why the signs matter

Advised output structure:

Risk level: Stop and verify

Summary: This message has strong warning signs.

Warning signs found: urgency, risky link, request for account verification, and unverified sender.

Do not do yet: Do not click the link or enter login info.

Safer next step: Open the official app or type the official website yourself instead of using the link in the message.

User experience behavior:

Quick Scam Check should be short, calm, and direct. It should not feel like a long form. It should not make users answer unnecessary questions before giving help. However, it should ask enough context questions to avoid giving a vague answer.

The function should support both pasted messages and summaries. This is important because privacy-conscious users may not want to paste a full message. A summary should be accepted as a valid input.

The function should let users move to Guided Review if they need more help. Quick Scam Check and Guided Review should not feel like separate products. They should feel like two paths inside the same safety tool.

Safety and privacy rules:

Quick Scam Check must show a privacy reminder before the input area. It must warn users not to enter passwords, login codes, account numbers, card numbers, Social Security numbers, government ID numbers, or private account details.

The result must not say that a message is definitely safe. Even if few warning signs appear, the app should say something like:

Few warning signs were found from the info provided, but verify through a trusted channel if anything feels unusual.

Quick Scam Check should not make legal claims, financial claims, or official fraud determinations.

Interface notes:

The interface should include:

\- a large message input box  
\- source type selector  
\- simple checkboxes or toggles for risky requests  
\- privacy reminder text  
\- Review warning signs button  
\- Use guided questions instead option

The function should avoid dense language. The screen should feel like a clear review form, not a technical scanner.

First-version decision:

Quick Scam Check must be part of the first app version. It is the core fast path and likely the first function many users will try.

Function 2: Guided Review

Purpose:

Guided Review is the slower, more supportive path. It exists for users who do not know what to type, do not want to paste a message, are helping someone else, or are dealing with a situation that is more complicated than one risky message.

Guided Review turns scam awareness into a sequence of simple questions. It helps users examine the situation piece by piece: what happened, who contacted them, what was requested, what pressure was used, what payment method was involved, and whether the request was verified.

User need:

The user may need structure. A scam situation can be emotionally confusing. A user may know something feels wrong but may not know why. Guided Review helps the user think through the situation without needing scam expertise.

This function is especially useful for:

\- users who are stressed  
\- users who are not confident with technology  
\- users helping parents or family members  
\- users dealing with phone-call scams  
\- users facing romance, family emergency, job, or marketplace scams  
\- users who have only a partial description of what happened

Inputs:

Guided Review should ask about:

\- situation type  
\- sender or requester type  
\- whether money is involved  
\- payment method  
\- urgency  
\- secrecy  
\- threats  
\- emotional pressure  
\- links or downloads  
\- passwords or login codes  
\- bank, card, or identity details  
\- whether the sender was verified independently  
\- whether the user already acted

The app should include Not sure and Skip options. Forcing exact answers can make stressed users quit. It can also lead users to guess. Not sure is a valid answer and should be handled thoughtfully.

Outputs:

Guided Review should produce the same basic result structure as Quick Scam Check:

\- risk level  
\- summary  
\- warning signs found  
\- what not to do yet  
\- safer next steps  
\- explanation of important warning signs

Because Guided Review has more structured info, the result can be more specific than a quick check. For example, if the user answers yes to secrecy, urgency, gift cards, and unverified sender, the app can explain how those signs work together.

User experience behavior:

Guided Review should ask one question at a time. This keeps the experience manageable. The user should see progress, such as Question 4 of 9\. The user should be able to go back and change an answer.

Each question should be short. When a question might be unfamiliar, the app can include a small “Why this matters” explanation. The explanation should be optional or visually secondary so the screen does not become overwhelming.

Good question style:

Is anyone asking you to keep this secret?

Why this matters:  
Scammers may ask for secrecy so you do not check with someone who could help.

Less effective question style:

Has the adversarial actor attempted to isolate the target from external verification?

The second version is technically meaningful but wrong for the user experience. The app must speak normal human language.

Safety and privacy rules:

Guided Review should never ask for exact secrets. It should ask whether a type of secret was requested. For example:

Good:  
Are they asking for a login code?

Bad:  
What login code did they ask for?

Good:  
Are they asking for bank or card details?

Bad:  
Enter the card number they requested.

Guided Review should also avoid blame. If a user answers that they already sent money, the app should shift into response mode, not scold them.

Interface notes:

Guided Review should use large answer buttons:

\- Yes  
\- No  
\- Not sure  
\- Skip

For payment method questions, use a list of common payment types:

\- Gift cards  
\- Crypto  
\- Wire transfer  
\- Bank transfer  
\- Payment app  
\- Cash  
\- Friends-and-family payment  
\- Check  
\- Not sure

The interface should use repetition to reduce mental load. Once users learn how to answer one question, the next question should feel familiar.

First-version decision:

Guided Review must be part of the first app version. It is the main accessible path for users who need more support than a pasted-message check.

App Feature Area 2 continues with Payment Request Review, Warning Sign Detector, Rule-Based Risk Engine, Safer Next Step Guide, Education Center, Settings, Feedback, Notes, and Future Function Boundaries.

Function 3: Payment Request Review

Purpose:

Payment Request Review focuses on the moment when harm can become immediate: the user is being asked to send money. Many scams are built around getting the user to pay quickly, secretly, or through a method that is hard to reverse. This function should help users pause before sending money and think through the request carefully.

This function is one of the most important parts of Verivae because money movement is often the point of no return. The app should not wait until after the user sends money to provide guidance. It should make the review feel urgent enough to matter, but calm enough that the user can think.

User need:

The user may be asking:

\- Should I send this payment?  
\- Is this payment method risky?  
\- Why are they asking for gift cards or crypto?  
\- Is this deposit normal?  
\- Is this refund request risky?  
\- What should I verify before paying?

Payment Request Review should help the user understand that the payment method, pressure, and verification path matter as much as the story itself. A scammer may have a convincing story, but the payment request may reveal the danger.

Inputs:

Payment Request Review should ask:

\- Who is asking for payment?  
\- How do you know them?  
\- What payment method are they asking for?  
\- Is the payment urgent?  
\- Are they asking you to keep it secret?  
\- Are they threatening consequences?  
\- Are they asking you to pay outside a normal platform?  
\- Have you verified the request through a trusted channel?  
\- What happens if you wait one hour?  
\- Have you already sent money?

Payment method choices should include:

\- gift cards  
\- crypto  
\- wire transfer  
\- bank transfer  
\- Zelle or instant payment service  
\- Cash App, Venmo, PayPal, or similar payment app  
\- friends-and-family payment  
\- prepaid debit card  
\- money order  
\- check  
\- cash  
\- platform checkout  
\- not sure

Outputs:

Payment Request Review should return a result that explains:

\- why the payment method may be risky  
\- whether the request includes urgency or secrecy  
\- whether the requester is verified  
\- what the user should avoid doing yet  
\- what safer verification step should happen next

Example output:

Risk level: Stop and verify

Summary: This payment request has strong warning signs.

Warning signs found: gift card payment, urgency, secrecy, and unverified requester.

Do not do yet: Do not buy gift cards or share gift card codes.

Safer next step: Contact the person or organization through a trusted phone number, official app, or known contact method before sending anything.

Why this matters: Gift card payments are difficult to reverse, and scammers often ask for secrecy so no one else can help you check the request.

User experience behavior:

Payment Request Review should feel more direct than general education. When money is involved, the app should not bury the practical warning. The result should appear clearly and should prioritize action.

The function should allow the user to say “I already paid.” If that happens, the app should move to the already-sent-money response flow. It should not continue acting like prevention is still possible.

Safety and privacy rules:

The function should not ask for exact amounts unless a future design reason exists. It can ask for a general amount range later if useful, but the first version does not need it. The function should not ask for card numbers, account numbers, transaction IDs, bank login info, or screenshots.

It must not promise that a payment can be recovered. It can say that some payment methods are difficult to reverse and that the user should contact the payment provider or bank quickly if they already sent money.

Interface notes:

This function should use simple payment-method choices rather than making the user type everything. Payment methods should be easy to scan. Risky methods can be explained after selection, not before, so the screen does not become too long.

First-version decision:

Payment Request Review must be part of the first app version. If the app can only do two core reviews at first, they should be Message Check and Payment Request Review.

Function 4: Warning Sign Detector

Purpose:

The Warning Sign Detector is the app's internal pattern-recognition function. It identifies categories of risky behavior from the user's answers or message summary. The purpose is not to secretly judge the user. The purpose is to support clear explanations.

The detector should help the app say, “This has warning signs because...” instead of giving vague advice. Users are more likely to trust and learn from the result if the app explains its reasoning.

User need:

The user needs to understand why something is risky. A vague warning like “be careful” is not enough. The app should name the pattern:

\- urgency  
\- secrecy  
\- unusual payment method  
\- request for login code  
\- unverified sender  
\- emotional pressure  
\- fake authority  
\- risky link

Inputs:

The Warning Sign Detector can use:

\- message text or summary  
\- user-selected checkboxes  
\- guided review answers  
\- payment method choice  
\- source type  
\- whether sender is known  
\- whether request was independently verified  
\- whether the user already acted

Warning sign categories:

Urgency:  
The situation pressures the user to act quickly.

Secrecy:  
The requester tells the user not to tell anyone.

Threats:  
The requester says something bad will happen if the user does not act.

Unusual payment:  
The requester asks for gift cards, crypto, wire transfer, instant transfer to a stranger, prepaid cards, or friends-and-family payment.

Sensitive info request:  
The requester asks for passwords, login codes, card details, bank details, Social Security number, ID docs, or private account details.

Risky link or download:  
The user is asked to click a link, download a file, open an attachment, or enter info on a page reached through a message.

Impersonation:  
The sender claims to be a bank, government agency, delivery company, employer, platform support, police, family member, romantic partner, or authority figure.

Too-good-to-be-true offer:  
The situation promises easy money, guaranteed profit, unusually high pay, unusually cheap rent, or a reward that does not match normal reality.

Emotional manipulation:  
The requester uses fear, guilt, romance, emergency, shame, loyalty, or pressure to keep the user from thinking clearly.

Unverified contact:  
The request comes from a new number, new account, unusual email, or contact method that the user has not independently verified.

Outputs:

The detector should output warning sign labels and plain explanations. It should not output only hidden scores. The user should see the meaningful parts.

Example warning sign explanation:

Urgency: The message pressures you to act quickly. Scammers often use urgency so people act before verifying.

Secrecy: The requester says not to tell anyone. Secrecy is risky because it prevents someone else from helping you check the situation.

Gift card payment: Gift cards are difficult to reverse once the code is shared. Legitimate organizations usually do not ask for payment through gift cards.

User experience behavior:

The detector should work quietly in the background, but its findings should be visible in the result. The user should not feel like the app is making mysterious judgments. The app should show enough reasoning to be understandable.

Safety and privacy rules:

The detector should not accuse a named person of being a scammer. It should describe the situation and warning signs. For example, say “This request has warning signs” rather than “Your friend is a scammer.”

It should not promise that no warning signs means safety. It should say that no obvious warning signs were found from the info provided.

Interface notes:

Warning signs can appear as simple labels in the result screen. Each label can expand to a short explanation. The first version should avoid overly technical categories.

First-version decision:

A simple Warning Sign Detector must be part of the first app version. It can start with clear categories and grow over time.

Function 5: Rule-Based Risk Engine

Purpose:

The Rule-Based Risk Engine turns warning signs and user answers into a risk level. It is called rule-based because it follows defined rules rather than relying on paid AI or hidden judgment. This is the right starting point because it is easier to explain, easier to test, cheaper to run, and safer for a first version.

The engine should help the app decide whether the result should be Low concern, Needs caution, Risk, or Stop and verify.

User need:

The user needs a clear summary of how concerned they should be. A long list of warning signs can be helpful, but the user also needs a simple top-line answer. The risk level gives the user that top line.

Inputs:

The engine uses:

\- warning signs found  
\- payment method risk  
\- whether the sender is verified  
\- whether urgency is present  
\- whether secrecy is present  
\- whether sensitive info is requested  
\- whether money was already sent  
\- whether the user is being threatened  
\- whether the situation involves known risky scam patterns

Outputs:

The engine outputs one of four risk levels:

Low concern:  
Few warning signs were found from the info provided. The user should still use normal caution.

Needs caution:  
Some warning signs are present. The user should verify before acting.

Risk:  
Multiple serious warning signs are present. The user should not send money or share info until verified.

Stop and verify:  
The situation includes strong danger signs, such as gift card payment, crypto request, secrecy, threats, login code request, urgent payment to an unverified person, or bank/account access request.

Plain-language rule examples:

If a message includes urgency and a risky link, the risk should increase.

If a requester asks for gift cards, the risk should become Risk or Stop and verify depending on the rest of the situation.

If a requester asks for a one-time login code, the result should strongly warn the user not to share the code.

If a requester asks for secrecy and money, the result should be high concern.

If a user already sent money, the app should switch to response guidance rather than only assigning a risk level.

If there are few warning signs, the app should still recommend independent verification if the situation feels unusual.

User experience behavior:

The engine should not be visible as a complicated scoring system. Users do not need to see math. They need a clear result and a reason. The app should not show fake precision, such as “86.4 percent scam risk.” That can create false confidence.

Safety and privacy rules:

The engine should not say “safe” as a final conclusion. It should avoid percentages in the first version. It should not act like official fraud detection.

Interface notes:

The risk level should be visible at the top of the Result Screen. The explanation should connect the risk level to the warning signs.

Example:

Risk level: Risk

Why: This request includes urgency, an unverified sender, and a payment method that may be difficult to reverse.

First-version decision:

The Rule-Based Risk Engine must be part of the first app version. It is the safest and most practical starting point.

App Feature Area 2 continues with Safer Next Step Guide, Education Center, Settings, Feedback, Notes, function boundaries, and accept rules.

Function 6: Safer Next Step Guide

Purpose:

The Safer Next Step Guide is the function that turns the app from a warning tool into a practical helper. A user does not only need to know that something is risky. They need to know what to do next. This function should appear in every result and should adapt to the situation.

A warning without a next step can leave the user stuck. If the app says “Risk” but does not explain what to do, the user may still reply, click, pay, or panic. The Safer Next Step Guide should give users one or more clear actions that reduce risk.

User need:

The user may be asking:

\- What do I do now?  
\- Should I reply?  
\- Should I call someone?  
\- Should I contact my bank?  
\- Should I ignore this?  
\- Should I ask a family member?  
\- What if I already acted?

Inputs:

The guide should use:

\- risk level  
\- situation type  
\- warning signs found  
\- whether money is involved  
\- whether a link is involved  
\- whether sensitive info is involved  
\- whether the user already acted  
\- whether the sender is verified

Outputs:

The guide should give specific next steps. Examples:

For risky bank message:

Do not click the link. Open your bank's official app or type the official website yourself. You can also call the number on the back of your card.

For payment request:

Do not send money yet. Verify the request through a trusted contact method you already had before this message.

For gift card request:

Do not buy gift cards or share card codes. Legitimate organizations usually do not ask for payment through gift cards.

For one-time code request:

Do not share the code. Login codes can give someone access to your account.

For already-sent-money situation:

Contact your bank, card company, payment app, or payment service right away. Do not send more money to recover the first payment.

User experience behavior:

The guide should appear near the top of the result, not buried at the bottom. It should use plain action language. The user should be able to act on the advice immediately.

The guide should avoid too many steps at once. For high-stress situations, three clear next steps are better than fifteen. Extra detail can appear below if needed.

Safety and privacy rules:

The guide must not tell users to ignore banks, payment services, official support, or emergency services. It must not promise recovery. It must not provide legal advice. It should encourage official verification when appropriate.

Interface notes:

Next steps should be shown as clear action blocks or a short checklist. The design should make the first step obvious. If the user already acted, response steps should replace normal prevention advice.

First-version decision:

Must build in the first app version. The app is not complete without practical next steps.

Function 7: Education Center

Purpose:

The Education Center helps users learn scam patterns before or after a risky moment. It should support prevention, confidence, and plain understanding. It should not feel like a textbook or a fear-based article collection.

User need:

The user may want to understand:

\- why gift cards are risky  
\- why secrecy is a warning sign  
\- what fake bank alerts look like  
\- how job scams work  
\- what romance scams often do  
\- why one-time codes should not be shared  
\- how to verify a risky request

Inputs:

The Education Center does not need sensitive user data. It can use the warning signs from a result to suggest relevant lessons, but it should also be browsable from the Home Screen.

Outputs:

Each lesson should include:

\- what the scam pattern looks like  
\- why it works  
\- warning signs  
\- safer response  
\- example message or situation  
\- what not to share

Example lesson structure:

Lesson: Gift card payment requests

What it looks like:  
Someone asks you to buy gift cards and send the numbers from the back.

Why it is risky:  
Once the code is shared, the value can be used quickly and may be difficult to recover.

Warning signs:  
Urgency, secrecy, threats, unusual payment method, unverified requester.

Safer response:  
Do not buy gift cards or share card codes. Verify the request through a trusted channel.

User experience behavior:

Lessons should be short and scannable. Users should not need to read long articles during a stressful moment. The Education Center can grow over time, but the first version should include a small set of high-value lessons.

Safety and privacy rules:

Lessons should not include instructions that help scammers improve. The app can explain warning signs without teaching harmful tactics in operational detail.

Interface notes:

The Education Center should use simple categories:

\- Payment scams  
\- Message scams  
\- Account and login scams  
\- Marketplace scams  
\- Job scams  
\- Relationship scams  
\- Family emergency scams

First-version decision:

A basic Education Center should be part of the first app version, but it can start small.

Function 8: Settings and App Info

Purpose:

Settings gives users a place to understand the app, manage basic preferences, and read privacy and safety info. It should not hide critical warnings. Important warnings must still appear in the flow. Settings is for reference and control.

User need:

The user may want to know:

\- what the app does  
\- what the app does not do  
\- whether the app stores info  
\- how to clear local notes if notes exist  
\- how to send feedback  
\- what version they are using

Inputs:

Settings should require little or no user input in the first version.

Outputs:

Settings should show:

\- What this app does  
\- What this app does not do  
\- Privacy basics  
\- Clear local data, if local data exists  
\- Send feedback, if feedback exists  
\- App version  
\- Contact or support info later

User experience behavior:

Settings should be simple. It should not become a cluttered technical control panel. The most important content is clarity and trust.

Safety and privacy rules:

Settings must not be the only place privacy warnings appear. Users may never open Settings. The app must show privacy reminders before sensitive input.

Interface notes:

Use plain labels. Avoid vague items like Advanced unless there is a real need. In the first version, Settings can be a simple info screen.

First-version decision:

A basic Settings page should be part of the first app version.

Function 9: Feedback Function

Purpose:

The Feedback Function helps Harborwake learn whether the app's explanations are useful. It should let users report confusion, missing warning signs, or overly cautious results without collecting private info.

User need:

The user may want to say:

\- this helped  
\- this was confusing  
\- this missed something  
\- this felt too cautious  
\- I needed a different kind of help

Inputs:

Feedback choices should be simple:

\- This helped  
\- This was confusing  
\- I think this missed a warning sign  
\- I think this was too cautious  
\- I needed different help

If free-text feedback exists, it must include a privacy warning:

Please do not include passwords, login codes, bank numbers, card numbers, Social Security numbers, or private financial details.

Outputs:

The app can thank the user and explain that feedback helps improve the product. It should not promise a personal response unless Harborwake is ready to provide one.

User experience behavior:

Feedback should be optional. It should not block the user from finishing a check. It should appear after the result, not before the user gets help.

Safety and privacy rules:

Feedback must not ask for sensitive examples. It should not encourage users to paste full scam messages into a feedback box.

Interface notes:

Use quick buttons first. If free text exists, make it optional and include a privacy reminder.

First-version decision:

Feedback is useful but not required for the earliest first app version. It should be included if easy and if privacy handling is clear.

Function 10: Local Notes

Purpose:

Local Notes lets the user save a short record of a situation for their own reference. This may help if they need to contact a bank, payment service, platform, or trusted person later. However, notes create privacy responsibility, so this function should be handled carefully.

User need:

The user may want to remember:

\- what type of situation happened  
\- what warning signs were found  
\- what safer next step they chose  
\- whether they already acted  
\- what they need to do next

Inputs:

Possible note fields:

\- situation type  
\- risk level  
\- warning signs found  
\- safer next step  
\- short user note

Avoid collecting:

\- full private conversations  
\- passwords  
\- login codes  
\- full card numbers  
\- account numbers  
\- Social Security numbers  
\- ID docs  
\- private bank details

Outputs:

The app could show a saved note summary. Example:

Situation: Payment request  
Risk level: Stop and verify  
Warning signs: gift cards, urgency, secrecy  
Next step: Verify through a trusted contact before sending money

User experience behavior:

Notes should be optional. The app should not save by default. If notes are included, the user should clearly choose to save them.

Safety and privacy rules:

The first version should avoid cloud-saved notes. Local-only notes are safer, but still need clear wording. If the app cannot handle local privacy well yet, notes should wait.

Interface notes:

If included, Notes should be simple and private-feeling. The app should include a Clear local data option in Settings.

First-version decision:

Delay unless easy and privacy-safe. Notes are useful but not essential for the first first app version.

Function 11: Future Function Boundaries

Purpose:

Future Function Boundaries define what the app should not build yet. This prevents the product from becoming too large, expensive, risky, or legally complicated too early.

Functions to delay:

Accounts:  
Accounts create privacy, security, support, and password-reset responsibilities. The first version should work without accounts.

Cloud sync:  
Cloud sync means storing user info on servers. This should wait until privacy rules are clear.

AI analysis:  
AI may be useful later, but it can cost money, make mistakes, and require more privacy planning. Start rule-based first.

Screenshot uploads:  
Screenshots may include private names, phone numbers, account details, and conversations. Delay until privacy handling is stronger.

Bank integrations:  
Bank connections are complex, sensitive, and not needed for the first version.

Automatic inbox scanning:  
This requires deep access to private messages or email and should not be part of the early product.

Payment processing:  
The app does not need paid plans or payments inside the core safety experience.

Browser extension:  
A browser extension could be useful later, but it adds platform and review complexity.

Official reporting integrations:  
Official reporting links may be useful later, but they should be researched carefully before inclusion.

First-version decision:

All of these should wait. The first version should focus on manual checks, guided questions, warning signs, risk results, and safer next steps.

App Feature Area 2 function priority map

Must build in first app version:

\- Quick Scam Check  
\- Guided Review  
\- Payment Request Review  
\- Warning Sign Detector  
\- Rule-Based Risk Engine  
\- Safer Next Step Guide  
\- Basic Education Center  
\- Basic Settings  
\- Already-Sent-Money Flow  
\- Privacy Reminder  
\- Result Screen

Should build if easy:

\- Feedback Function  
\- Trusted-person summary  
\- Review Before Result screen

Delay until later:

\- Local Notes, unless privacy-safe  
\- Accounts  
\- Cloud sync  
\- AI analysis  
\- Screenshot uploads  
\- Bank integrations  
\- Automatic inbox scanning  
\- Payment processing  
\- Browser extension  
\- Official reporting integrations

App Feature Area 2 accept rules

App Feature Area 2 is acceptable when:

\- it stays in design/planning mode only  
\- it includes no coding  
\- it avoids launch instructions  
\- it details core app functions in detail  
\- it explains each function's purpose and user need  
\- it defines inputs and outputs for major functions  
\- it describes safety and privacy rules for each function  
\- it explains which functions belong in the first app version  
\- it identifies functions that should wait  
\- it keeps the app realistic, calm, and beginner-friendly  
\- it preserves Harborwake as the company name and Verivae as the temporary app name

Additional feature area to define

The design brief should also include App Feature Area 3: User Flows and Edge Cases.
