App Feature Addendum: Detailed Function Detail and Behavioral Depth

Purpose of this addendum

This addendum adds more depth to the function work already completed in App Feature Area 2\. It does not replace the previous section. It builds on it by adding more detail about purpose, user behavior, interface decisions, exact in-app wording patterns, safety boundaries, fallback behavior, and the kinds of mistakes the product must expect from real users.

This section clarifies app behavior before build work begins. It describes the intended user experience, expected screens, safety boundaries, permission behavior, and decision-support logic in enough detail that later design and engineering choices can stay aligned with the product.

The app should be designed as if the user is not calm, not technical, and not reading carefully. This is not because users are careless. It is because scams usually reach people during pressure, distraction, fear, urgency, loneliness, hope, or confusion. A professional app builder should design the product for that real human state.

Extreme detail principle

Every function in the app should answer five deeper questions:

1\. What exact moment in the user's life does this function support?  
2\. What mistake is the user most likely to make at that moment?  
3\. What should the interface do to reduce that mistake?  
4\. What should the app say without overpromising?  
5\. What should the app avoid collecting, saying, or implying?

If a function cannot answer those questions, it is not ready to be built.

Deepened Function 1: Quick Scam Check

Real-life moment supported

Quick Scam Check supports the moment when the user has something risky in front of them and wants help quickly. The user may be holding their phone, reading a text, looking at an email, listening to a voicemail, chatting with someone online, or reading a marketplace message. They may already be halfway convinced that the request is real. They may be afraid that ignoring the message will cause harm.

Examples of real-life moments:

\- A text says the user's bank account will be locked unless they verify immediately.  
\- A message says a package cannot be delivered unless the user pays a small fee.  
\- A marketplace buyer sends a fake payment screenshot and asks for a refund.  
\- A dating app contact asks for money because of an emergency.  
\- A job contact says the user must deposit a check and buy equipment.  
\- A caller says a family member is in trouble and money is needed now.  
\- A pop-up says the user's device is infected and they must call support.

Quick Scam Check must support these situations without needing the user to know the scam name. The user may not know whether it is phishing, smishing, romance fraud, fake check fraud, impersonation, or account takeover. They only know something feels urgent or strange.

Most likely user mistakes

Mistake 1: Pasting too much private info.

A stressed user may paste a full message that includes names, phone numbers, account fragments, or codes. The app should warn them before input and remind them that summaries are acceptable.

Mistake 2: Asking the app for certainty.

Users may expect the app to say “scam” or “safe.” The app must resist false certainty. It should give risk language and verification steps.

Mistake 3: Skipping context.

A user may paste only “is this real?” or a very short message. The app should ask for context instead of failing harshly.

Mistake 4: Treating a low-risk result as permission.

If the app says Low concern, the user might assume the action is safe. The result must still say that the app is not a guarantee.

Mistake 5: Continuing the risky action after seeing the warning.

The app cannot control the user, but the interface can make the safer next step more visible than the risky action.

Interface behavior to reduce mistakes

The input area should be preceded by a short warning:

You can summarize. Do not include passwords, login codes, full card numbers, bank account numbers, Social Security numbers, or private ID details.

The app should include a secondary link or helper line:

Not sure what to enter? Write what happened in your own words.

If the user enters very little text, the app should respond with a gentle prompt:

I need a little more context to review this. You can summarize who contacted you, what they want, and whether they asked for money, codes, links, or private info.

If the user enters a message but skips all context questions, the app should still produce a cautious result, but it should say:

This review is based only on the info provided. Add more details for a stronger check.

Exact microcopy patterns

Input label:

Paste or summarize the risky message

Helper text:

Remove private details first. A short summary is enough.

Context prompt:

What kind of message is this?

Risk request prompt:

Does it ask you to do any of these?

Review button:

Review warning signs

Empty input prompt:

Add a short message or choose guided questions instead.

Sensitive detail warning:

This may include sensitive info. Remove passwords, login codes, full card numbers, account numbers, or government ID details before continuing.

Result transition text:

Checking for common warning signs...

The transition text should be brief. The app should not pretend to perform official fraud detection. “Checking for common warning signs” is better than “Scanning for fraud.”

Purpose detail by input type

Text message:

Text messages often create urgency and include links. The app should look for language about locked accounts, failed deliveries, missed payments, bank alerts, verification, prizes, and unusual sender numbers.

Email:

Email scams may include sender impersonation, attachments, fake invoices, account warnings, fake job offers, or business-looking language. The app should ask whether the email address looks familiar, but it should not require the user to understand email headers.

Direct message:

Social media messages may involve impersonation, romance pressure, giveaways, investment offers, or hacked friend accounts. The app should ask whether the message came from a known person and whether the request feels normal for that person.

Marketplace message:

Marketplace messages often involve deposits, overpayment, fake shipping, fake payment confirmation, or moving off-platform. The app should ask whether the other person wants to avoid normal platform protections.

Phone call summary:

A phone call summary may not have text to paste. The app should let the user summarize what the caller said and what they wanted. This is critical for family emergency and fake support scams.

Design detail

Quick Scam Check should feel fast, but not casual. It should not look like a search engine. It should look like a structured safety check. The main input should be centered in the task, but the privacy helper text should be visible. The button should be clear and stable.

The screen should use plain labels rather than clever branding. In a safety product, cleverness can reduce clarity.

Deepened Function 2: Guided Review

Real-life moment supported

Guided Review supports users who cannot easily summarize the situation or do not know what matters. It is the app's most beginner-friendly path. It should work for a person who says, “I do not know if this is a scam, but something feels off.”

The function should be designed for users who may be embarrassed. A user may worry that they should already know the answer. The app should normalize uncertainty. It should make the user feel that checking is a smart action, not a sign of weakness.

Most likely user mistakes

Mistake 1: Guessing instead of choosing Not sure.

The app should make Not sure feel acceptable. If Not sure looks like a failure, users may guess and get a less accurate result.

Mistake 2: Quitting because there are too many questions.

The guided flow should show progress and keep each question short.

Mistake 3: Misunderstanding terms.

Words like crypto, wire transfer, two-factor code, and platform checkout may be unfamiliar. The app should explain terms simply when they appear.

Mistake 4: Feeling judged by the questions.

Questions must avoid blame. For example, “Did you already send money?” is better than “Why did you send money?”

Mistake 5: Answering for someone else without context.

Family-helper users may not know every answer. The app must still let them proceed.

Guided Review question strategy

Questions should move from general to specific:

1\. What kind of situation is this?  
2\. What is the other person asking for?  
3\. Is money involved?  
4\. Is private info involved?  
5\. Is pressure involved?  
6\. Is the sender verified?  
7\. Has the user already acted?  
8\. What safer step should happen next?

This order matters. If the app begins with very specific questions, the user may feel lost. Starting broad helps the user settle into the review.

Detailed question examples

Question:  
What happened?

Answer choices:

\- I got a message or email  
\- Someone asked me for money  
\- Someone sent a job or money offer  
\- Someone contacted me about buying, selling, or renting  
\- Someone online is asking for help or money  
\- Someone says a family member is in trouble  
\- I got an account warning or login alert  
\- I am not sure

Helper text:

Choose the closest option. You can still continue if you are not sure.

Question:  
What are they asking you to do?

Answer choices:

\- Send money  
\- Click a link  
\- Share a password or code  
\- Share bank, card, or identity info  
\- Download something  
\- Move to another app or website  
\- Keep it secret  
\- I am not sure

Helper text:

Many scams involve a request. This helps the app understand what action they want from you.

Question:  
Are they rushing you?

Answer choices:

\- Yes  
\- No  
\- Not sure  
\- Skip

Helper text:

Urgency is a warning sign because it can pressure people to act before verifying.

Question:  
Have you verified this through a trusted channel?

Answer choices:

\- Yes, through a contact method I already had  
\- No  
\- I used the link or phone number they gave me  
\- Not sure

Helper text:

A trusted channel means a phone number, app, website, or contact method you already knew before this message.

Interface behavior in detail

Each Guided Review screen should show only one main question. Secondary text should be shorter than the question. Buttons should use ordinary language. The app should avoid dropdowns for simple yes/no questions because large buttons are easier under stress.

The progress indicator should not create pressure. It should say something like Question 3 of 8 rather than showing a countdown. A countdown could increase anxiety.

The user should be able to back up. If the user changes an earlier answer, later risk logic should adjust. The design brief does not need to define implementation; it only needs to state that changed answers should be reflected in the final result.

Guided Review tone rules

Use:

\- It is okay if you are not sure.  
\- Choose the closest answer.  
\- You can skip this.  
\- General answers are enough.  
\- This helps identify warning signs.

Avoid:

\- You should know this.  
\- This answer is required.  
\- Prove the sender is real.  
\- Enter the exact code.  
\- Why did you trust them?

Guided Review design detail

The visual design should feel like a calm stepwise checklist. Each question screen should have generous spacing. The current question should be visually dominant. Helper text should be available but not visually louder than the answer choices.

Answer buttons should be consistent in shape and placement. A stressed user should not have to relearn the screen each time. If Yes is first on one screen and in a different place on another, the experience may feel unstable. Consistency creates trust.

Guided Review output detail

The result from Guided Review should explain which answers mattered most. For example:

Your answers showed three important warning signs: the request involved gift cards, the person asked you to keep it secret, and you have not verified them through a trusted contact method.

This is better than:

Risk score: 91\.

The first version teaches the user and supports action. The second version gives fake precision without context.

Addendum continuation marker: continue with Payment Request Review, Warning Sign Detector, Rule-Based Risk Engine, Result behavior, visual/aesthetic details, and deeper function boundaries.

Deepened Function 3: Payment Request Review

Real-life moment supported

Payment Request Review supports the moment immediately before financial harm may happen. This is one of the highest-stakes areas of the app. The user may be deciding whether to send gift card codes, transfer money, pay a deposit, send crypto, refund an overpayment, pay a fake fee, or help someone who claims to be in trouble.

This function should treat money movement as a special category. A risky message is concerning, but a risky payment request can cause immediate loss. The interface should therefore make payment-related warnings more direct while still staying calm.

Most likely user mistakes

Mistake 1: Believing the story because it feels emotional.

The story may involve a family emergency, romantic partner, job opportunity, landlord, buyer, seller, bank issue, or delivery problem. The app must help the user separate the story from the payment method.

Mistake 2: Thinking a small payment is harmless.

Many scams begin with a small fee. A small delivery fee, app fee, verification fee, or deposit can be used to test whether the user will comply.

Mistake 3: Using the contact method provided by the requester.

If the message says “call this number,” the number may lead back to the scammer. The app should teach independent verification.

Mistake 4: Sending more money to recover the first payment.

Recovery scams often ask victims to pay more to get money back. The app must warn against this in already-sent-money flows.

Mistake 5: Assuming a payment screenshot proves payment.

Marketplace and overpayment scams often use fake payment confirmations. The app should warn users to verify inside the actual payment account or platform, not from a screenshot.

Detailed payment method behavior

Gift cards:

Gift card requests should be treated as a serious warning sign. The app should explain that once a code is shared, the value can be used quickly and may be difficult to recover. The app should say that legitimate banks, government agencies, police departments, tech support teams, employers, and delivery services usually do not ask for payment through gift cards.

Crypto:

Crypto requests should be treated as risk for ordinary users. The app should explain that crypto transfers can be difficult to reverse and are often used when scammers want fast, final payment. The app should avoid technical crypto explanations unless the user asks for education content.

Wire transfer:

Wire transfer requests should trigger caution, especially when the requester is unverified, urgent, secretive, or newly contacted. The app should suggest verifying directly through a trusted institution or contact method.

Payment apps:

Payment apps vary, but instant payments to strangers should be treated carefully. The app should warn users not to assume a payment can be reversed. If a buyer or seller asks to move outside normal platform checkout, that should increase concern.

Friends-and-family payment:

This should be treated as a warning sign when used for purchases from strangers. The app should explain that this type of payment may reduce buyer protection.

Deposits:

Deposits should be reviewed in context. A deposit is not automatically a scam, but apartment, pet, ticket, vehicle, and marketplace scams often use pressure for deposits before proof. The app should ask what proof the user has and whether the platform provides protection.

Checks:

Checks should trigger caution when paired with overpayment, equipment purchases, refund requests, or instructions to send money elsewhere. The app should explain fake-check risk simply: a check may appear available before it is fully verified, and the user may still be responsible if it later fails.

Payment Review microcopy examples

Payment method question:

How are they asking you to pay?

Helper text:

Some payment methods are harder to reverse than others.

Urgency question:

Are they pressuring you to pay right now?

Helper text:

Pressure can make it harder to verify before acting.

Verification question:

Have you verified this request through a trusted contact method?

Helper text:

A trusted contact method is one you already had before this message, not one the requester just gave you.

Risky result copy:

This payment request has strong warning signs. Do not send money yet. Verify the request outside this conversation before taking any action.

Already-paid result copy:

If you already sent money, contact the payment provider, bank, card company, or platform right away. Do not send more money to recover the first payment.

Deepened Function 4: Warning Sign Detector

Warning sign relationships

The app should not treat every warning sign as equal in the user's mind. Some warning signs are mild alone but serious together. The design brief should describe these relationships clearly.

Urgency alone:

Urgency can be normal in some real situations, but it becomes more concerning when paired with payment, secrecy, links, account access, or threats.

Secrecy alone:

Secrecy is rarely necessary for legitimate financial action. Secrecy should be treated as a strong warning sign, especially when money or personal info is involved.

Unverified sender plus payment:

A new contact asking for money should increase risk. The app should ask whether the user verified the person through a separate trusted channel.

Link plus account warning:

A message that says an account is locked and includes a link should trigger caution. The safer step is to open the official app or type the official website manually.

Romance plus investment:

A romantic or relationship contact introducing investment or crypto should be treated as a risky pattern, especially if there is urgency or secrecy.

Job offer plus check:

A job offer involving a check, equipment purchase, or money forwarding should be treated as a risky pattern.

Marketplace plus off-platform payment:

A buyer or seller pushing the user away from platform protections should trigger caution.

Warning sign explanation rules

The app should explain warning signs in normal language. Each explanation should answer:

\- What did the app notice?  
\- Why can that be risky?  
\- What should the user verify?

Example:

What the app noticed: The requester wants payment through gift cards.

Why this can be risky: Gift card codes can be used quickly once shared and may be difficult to recover.

What to verify: Confirm the request through a trusted contact method before buying or sharing any codes.

This structure helps the result feel educational, not mysterious.

Deepened Function 5: Rule-Based Risk Engine

Risk level design philosophy

Risk levels should help users decide how cautious to be. They should not pretend to be scientific certainty. The app should avoid percentages because percentages can create false precision. A user might treat “20 percent risk” as permission or “95 percent risk” as official proof. Neither is appropriate for the first version.

The four risk levels should be easy to understand:

Low concern:  
The app did not find clear warning signs from the info provided. This does not mean guaranteed safe.

Needs caution:  
The app found some warning signs or missing verification. The user should slow down and verify before acting.

Risk:  
The app found multiple warning signs or one serious warning sign involving money, private info, or pressure. The user should avoid acting until verified.

Stop and verify:  
The app found strong danger signs. The user should stop the risky action, avoid payment or sharing info, and verify through a trusted channel.

Risk escalation examples

Low concern example:

A user receives an expected message from a known contact with no link, no money request, no urgency, and no private info request. The app can say few warning signs were found, but it should still recommend checking through normal trusted channels if anything feels unusual.

Needs caution example:

A user receives a delivery message with a link but no payment request and no private info request. The app should recommend not using the link directly and checking through the official delivery website or app.

Risk example:

A marketplace seller asks for a deposit outside the platform before the user has verified the item or seller. The app should explain off-platform payment and deposit risk.

Stop and verify example:

A person asks the user to buy gift cards urgently and keep it secret. This should trigger Stop and verify because gift cards, urgency, and secrecy together form a strong risk pattern.

Risk engine explanation behavior

The result should not simply say:

Stop and verify.

It should say:

Stop and verify because this request includes gift cards, secrecy, and urgency. Those warning signs often appear when someone is trying to get money before you can check with anyone else.

This wording helps the user learn. It also makes the app feel transparent.

Deepened Result Behavior

The result is where the product earns or loses trust. If the result is vague, users may ignore it. If the result is too dramatic, users may panic. If the result is overconfident, users may rely on it in unsafe ways.

Every result should include:

\- a clear risk level  
\- a short summary  
\- the top warning signs  
\- what not to do yet  
\- the safest next step  
\- a reminder of uncertainty when appropriate  
\- a path for users who already acted

Result wording should use direct verbs:

\- Pause  
\- Verify  
\- Do not click  
\- Do not send money yet  
\- Do not share codes  
\- Contact official support  
\- Ask someone you trust

Result wording should avoid weak vagueness:

\- Be careful  
\- Consider whether this might be problematic  
\- Exercise caution in relation to the interaction

The weak versions are not wrong, but they are not useful enough in a stressful moment.

Result layout detail

The result screen should prioritize info in this order:

1\. What is the risk level?  
2\. What should the user avoid doing right now?  
3\. What should the user do next?  
4\. Why did the app say this?  
5\. What can the user learn from this?

The result should not begin with a long explanation. A stressed user needs the action first.

Aesthetic detail for results

Low concern should not look celebratory. Do not use party-like visuals or “You're safe\!” language. It should remain calm.

Needs caution should feel like a yellow light, not a red alarm.

Risk should feel serious and clear.

Stop and verify should be visually distinct, but not panic-inducing. Red can be used sparingly for the risk label or key warning area, but the whole screen should not become aggressive red.

Deeper Function Boundaries

The product should be intentionally limited at first. A professional app builder should protect the product from becoming too broad too early.

Do not build account creation yet because the user should receive value before trusting the app with identity.

Do not build AI-first analysis yet because privacy, cost, and reliability need more planning.

Do not build screenshot upload yet because screenshots often contain private names, phone numbers, account details, and message history.

Do not build bank connections yet because financial account access creates major trust and security responsibilities.

Do not build automatic message scanning yet because it requires sensitive inbox or alert access.

Do not build paid subscriptions yet because the product has not proven its core usefulness.

Do not build official reporting integrations yet because incorrect or outdated reporting guidance could mislead users.

Do not build a launch flow yet because the user explicitly asked for no launch work at this stage.

Addendum accept rules

This addendum is acceptable when:

\- it adds meaningful detail to prior function work  
\- it stays in design and planning mode  
\- it includes no coding  
\- it includes no launch instructions  
\- it explains real-life moments supported by each function  
\- it identifies likely user mistakes  
\- it adds interface behavior and microcopy examples  
\- it deepens payment review logic  
\- it deepens warning sign relationships  
\- it deepens risk level behavior  
\- it details result screen expectations  
\- it reinforces the app's calm, nonjudgmental aesthetic  
\- it strengthens boundaries around what should not be built yet

Additional feature area to define

The design brief should also include App Feature Area 3: User Flows and Edge Cases, but it should be written with the same extreme-detail standard used in this addendum. App Feature Area 3 should walk through full user journeys from beginning to end, including stressed users, unsure users, family-helper users, users who already sent money, users who paste sensitive info, users who misunderstand a result, and users who abandon the flow before completion.

\---

App Feature Area 3: User Flows and Edge Cases

Purpose of this section

App Feature Area 3 explains how real users should move through Verivae from beginning to end. Earlier sections defined screens and functions. This section connects those pieces into full journeys. A user flow is the path a person takes through the app to accomplish something. An edge case is a situation that is not the clean, easy version of that path, but still must be handled thoughtfully.

This section is still design and planning only. It includes no coding, no technical implementation, no launch instructions, no app store work, and no website work. The goal is to make the design brief more realistic by describing how users actually behave when they are worried, rushed, confused, embarrassed, helping someone else, or already dealing with harm.

Why user flows matter

A feature can look good in isolation and still fail in real use. For example, a Quick Scam Check feature may sound simple, but the actual user may paste too much private info, provide too little context, misunderstand a result, close the app halfway through, or use the app after money has already been sent. A professional design brief must account for those messy realities before building begins.

The main product design rule for App Feature Area 3 is this:

The app must help users recover from confusion without making them feel punished.

If a user chooses the wrong category, the app should still guide them. If a user is not sure, the app should offer Not sure. If a user already acted, the app should switch to response guidance. If a user enters sensitive info, the app should help them remove it. If a user misunderstands a result, the app should clarify the limits.

User flow specification format

Each major flow should be described using the following structure:

Flow name:  
The plain name of the journey.

User scenario:  
What is happening in the user's life.

User emotional state:  
What the user may be feeling.

Entry point:  
Where the user starts in the app.

Step-by-step path:  
The screens and decisions the user moves through.

Required app behavior:  
What the app must do at each point.

Possible user mistakes:  
What the user may do wrong or misunderstand.

Recovery behavior:  
How the app helps the user recover without shame.

Result behavior:  
What kind of result or next step the app should provide.

Safety and privacy notes:  
What the app must avoid collecting, saying, or implying.

first app version decision:  
Whether this flow must be fully supported in the first version.

Flow 1: Risky Text Message Before User Acts

User scenario:

The user receives a text message that appears to come from a bank, delivery company, payment service, government agency, or familiar brand. The message says something urgent: an account is locked, a package cannot be delivered, a payment failed, risky activity occurred, or the user must verify their identity. The message includes a link or phone number.

Example scenario:

The user receives a text saying their bank account has been locked and they must click a link to verify their identity within 30 minutes.

User emotional state:

The user may feel worried, hurried, and uncertain. They may not want to lose access to their bank account. They may be tempted to click the link because the message sounds official. They may also feel embarrassed for needing help with something that looks simple.

Entry point:

Home screen, then Start a check.

Step-by-step path:

1\. User opens Verivae.  
2\. User taps Start a check.  
3\. User selects Message or email.  
4\. App shows Privacy Reminder.  
5\. User taps I understand, continue.  
6\. User pastes or summarizes the message.  
7\. User selects Text message as the source.  
8\. User marks that the message includes a link, urgency, and account verification.  
9\. User taps Review warning signs.  
10\. App shows Result Screen.

Required app behavior:

The app should first protect privacy. It should remind the user not to enter login codes, passwords, account numbers, or full card details. It should accept a summary instead of requiring the full text.

The app should recognize the pattern of urgency plus link plus account warning. The result should not say the bank message is definitely fake because the app may not have enough proof. Instead, it should say the message has warning signs and should be verified through a trusted channel.

Advised result behavior:

Risk level: Stop and verify

Summary: This message has strong warning signs because it creates urgency and asks you to use a link to verify account access.

Do not do yet: Do not click the link or enter login info through the message.

Safer next step: Open the official bank app, type the official website yourself, or call a trusted number such as the number on the back of your card.

Why this matters: Scam messages often use urgency and links to send people to fake login pages.

Possible user mistakes:

The user may paste the full message including partial account info. The user may click the link before finishing the check. The user may think the app can confirm whether the specific bank message is real. The user may see Low concern or Needs caution in a different case and assume that means full safety.

Recovery behavior:

If the app sees likely sensitive info, it should warn the user to remove it before continuing. If the user says they already clicked the link or entered info, the app should switch to already-acted guidance. If the user asks for certainty, the wording should emphasize verification instead of pretending to know.

Safety and privacy notes:

The app should not ask the user to enter bank login details. It should not ask for the link destination in the first version unless privacy handling is clear. It should not claim to officially verify the bank.

first app version decision:

This flow must be supported in the first app version. Risky message review is one of the app's core use cases.

Flow 2: Payment Request Before User Sends Money

User scenario:

The user is asked to send money through a payment method that may be difficult to reverse. This could be gift cards, crypto, wire transfer, payment app, friends-and-family payment, deposit, refund, or off-platform marketplace payment. The request may include urgency, secrecy, emotional pressure, or threats.

Example scenario:

A person claiming to be tech support tells the user to buy gift cards and read the codes over the phone to fix an account issue.

User emotional state:

The user may feel frightened, pressured, or obedient toward the person claiming authority. They may believe they are solving a problem. They may be on the phone while using the app, which means the interface must be extremely clear and fast.

Entry point:

Home screen, then Start a check, then Payment request.

Step-by-step path:

1\. User opens Verivae.  
2\. User taps Start a check.  
3\. User selects Payment request.  
4\. App shows Privacy Reminder.  
5\. User confirms they understand.  
6\. App asks how the person wants payment.  
7\. User selects Gift cards.  
8\. App asks whether the request is urgent.  
9\. User selects Yes.  
10\. App asks whether the requester wants secrecy.  
11\. User selects Yes or Not sure.  
12\. App asks whether the user verified through a trusted channel.  
13\. User selects No.  
14\. App shows Result Screen.

Required app behavior:

The app should treat gift cards plus urgency as a serious warning. If secrecy is also present, the result should be Stop and verify. The result should explain that legitimate organizations usually do not ask for gift card codes as payment.

Advised result behavior:

Risk level: Stop and verify

Summary: This payment request has strong scam warning signs.

Warning signs found: gift cards, urgency, possible secrecy, and no trusted verification.

Do not do yet: Do not buy gift cards or share card codes.

Safer next step: End the conversation and verify the issue through an official phone number, official app, or trusted contact method.

Why this matters: Gift card codes can be used quickly once shared and may be difficult to recover.

Possible user mistakes:

The user may say “but they sound official.” The app should not argue. It should separate official-sounding language from unsafe payment method. The user may believe a small payment is safe. The app should explain that scams often begin with small requests. The user may be afraid to hang up. The app should calmly recommend pausing and verifying.

Recovery behavior:

If the user says they already bought cards but did not share codes, the app should say not to share the codes and to contact the gift card issuer or store if appropriate. If the user already shared codes, the app should shift to response guidance and avoid promising recovery.

Safety and privacy notes:

The app must not ask for gift card codes. It must not ask for card photos. It must not ask for transaction receipts in the first version. It should never offer to recover the money.

first app version decision:

This flow must be supported in the first app version. It is one of the highest-value prevention flows.

Flow 3: User Already Sent Money

User scenario:

The user opens the app after sending money. They may have sent gift card codes, crypto, a wire transfer, payment app transfer, bank transfer, deposit, or friends-and-family payment. They may suspect something is wrong only after the payment is complete.

User emotional state:

The user may feel panic, shame, anger, denial, or desperation. They may be searching for a way to reverse the payment. They may also be vulnerable to recovery scams that promise to get money back for another payment.

Entry point:

The user may enter through Home, Quick Scam Check, Payment Request Review, or Guided Review. The app should provide an already-acted path from multiple places.

Step-by-step path:

1\. User opens Verivae.  
2\. User taps Start a check.  
3\. User chooses Payment request or Not sure.  
4\. App asks whether money or sensitive info was already sent.  
5\. User selects Yes, I sent money.  
6\. App asks what type of payment at a high level.  
7\. User selects gift cards, crypto, wire transfer, payment app, card payment, bank transfer, or not sure.  
8\. App shows response guidance.

Required app behavior:

The app should immediately stop acting like prevention is still the only goal. It should shift to response. The first guidance should be practical and calm.

Advised response behavior:

Summary: Since money may already have been sent, act quickly through official channels.

First steps:

\- Contact your bank, card company, payment app, or payment service right away.  
\- Do not send more money to recover the first payment.  
\- Save messages, usernames, receipts, or records if you can do so safely.  
\- Report the account or transaction through the platform if available.

Important limit:

the app cannot recover money or guarantee reversal. Acting quickly through official channels may give you more options.

Possible user mistakes:

The user may search for recovery services and fall into another scam. The app should explicitly warn against paying anyone who promises guaranteed recovery. The user may keep talking to the scammer. The app should advise not to send more money and to verify through official channels. The user may enter transaction details into the app. The app should avoid collecting those details.

Recovery behavior:

The app should provide calm, immediate steps. It should not shame the user. It should not say “you were scammed” as the first message. It should say something like:

This is stressful, but there are still practical steps you can take. Start with the official payment provider or bank.

Safety and privacy notes:

The app should not ask for account numbers, card numbers, transaction IDs, screenshots, or receipts in the first version. It should not promise recovery.

first app version decision:

A basic version of this flow must be supported in the first app version.

App Feature Area 3 continuation marker: continue with family-helper flow, unsure-user flow, sensitive-info edge case, abandoned-flow edge case, misunderstood-result edge case, and App Feature Area 3 accept rules.

Flow 4: Family Helper Reviews a Situation for Someone Else

User scenario:

The user is not the person being targeted. They are helping a parent, grandparent, sibling, friend, partner, or other trusted person review a risky situation. The targeted person may be on a phone call, texting with someone, or feeling pressured to act. The helper may have incomplete info.

Example scenario:

A daughter is helping her father check a message from someone claiming to be tech support. The father is worried and does not understand why gift cards would be risky.

User emotional state:

The helper may feel protective, frustrated, worried, or rushed. The targeted person may feel embarrassed, defensive, scared, or convinced the request is real. The app must support the helper without making the targeted person feel insulted.

Entry point:

Home, Start a check, then Not sure, Payment request, Message or email, or Guided Review.

Step-by-step path:

1\. Helper opens Verivae.  
2\. Helper taps Start a check.  
3\. Helper chooses the closest category or Not sure.  
4\. App shows Privacy Reminder.  
5\. Helper chooses Guided Review because they do not have the full message.  
6\. App asks general questions about what is being requested.  
7\. Helper answers Not sure where needed.  
8\. App identifies warning signs from available info.  
9\. App gives a result and a calm explanation the helper can share.

Required app behavior:

The app should support partial info. It should not require the helper to know every detail. It should allow Not sure and still produce cautious guidance when major warning signs are present.

The app should include wording that helps the helper communicate respectfully. A trusted-person summary can eventually support this. The app should avoid language that would make the targeted person feel foolish.

Advised helper-friendly output:

This situation has warning signs worth checking before anyone sends money or shares info. The safest next step is to pause and verify through an official or already-known contact method.

Possible user mistakes:

The helper may become too forceful and alienate the targeted person. The helper may not have enough details. The helper may answer incorrectly because they are guessing. The helper may paste someone else's private info.

Recovery behavior:

The app should make Not sure acceptable. It should say:

It is okay if you do not know every answer. The result will be based only on what you can provide.

If the helper lacks details, the app can suggest questions to ask the targeted person:

\- What are they asking you to do?  
\- Are they asking for money?  
\- Are they asking you to keep it secret?  
\- Did you verify them through a contact method you already had?

Safety and privacy notes:

The app should not ask the helper to enter someone else's private account details. It should avoid escalating family conflict. It should provide calm language that can be shared.

first app version decision:

This flow should be supported through Guided Review and Not sure options in the first app version. A polished family-helper mode can wait.

Flow 5: Unsure User Does Not Know What Category Fits

User scenario:

The user knows something feels wrong but does not know whether it is a payment scam, message scam, job scam, romance scam, marketplace scam, or account scam. They may not know the right words to describe it.

User emotional state:

The user may feel confused or technically insecure. They may worry that choosing the wrong category will make the app useless. The design must make wrong-category anxiety disappear.

Entry point:

Home, Start a check, Situation Selection, Not sure.

Step-by-step path:

1\. User opens the app.  
2\. User taps Start a check.  
3\. User sees situation options.  
4\. User selects Not sure.  
5\. App shows Privacy Reminder.  
6\. App starts a general Guided Review.  
7\. App asks broad questions first.  
8\. App identifies likely category or warning signs from answers.  
9\. App shows result with plain explanation.

Required app behavior:

The app should not force category selection. It should guide the user from broad questions to specific risks. It should not say “invalid category” or “choose the correct type.”

Advised wording:

Not sure is okay. Answer a few simple questions and the app will guide you.

Possible user mistakes:

The user may choose a category that is close but not perfect. The app should still work. For example, a fake job offer may involve a payment request. A romance scam may involve crypto. A marketplace scam may involve a fake payment message. Categories overlap.

Recovery behavior:

The app should allow category switching or continue with general warning signs. It should never dead-end because the first category was imperfect.

Safety and privacy notes:

The Not sure flow should still include privacy warnings before text input.

first app version decision:

Must support Not sure in the first app version.

Edge Case 1: User Pastes Sensitive Info

Scenario:

The user pastes a full message that includes a login code, account number, card number, address, or other sensitive detail.

Required app behavior:

The app should warn the user before continuing. The warning should be calm and specific:

This may include sensitive info. Remove passwords, login codes, full card numbers, account numbers, Social Security numbers, or government ID details before continuing.

The app should offer choices:

\- Go back and edit  
\- Clear text  
\- Continue with a safer summary

The app should not shame the user. It should not say they made a dangerous mistake. It should frame the warning as protection.

Design reason:

A scam-safety app must teach privacy by behavior, not just policy. If the app silently accepts sensitive data, users will assume it is okay to provide it.

first app version decision:

The first version should at minimum show privacy warnings before input. More advanced sensitive-data detection can wait, but the design intent should be documented now.

Edge Case 2: User Abandons the Flow Halfway Through

Scenario:

The user starts a check but closes the app, goes back, stops answering questions, or becomes overwhelmed.

Required app behavior:

The app should make re-entry easy. If no sensitive data is stored, the app may simply restart. If future versions save progress, that must be privacy-safe and optional.

The flow should be short enough that abandonment is less likely. The app should also make progress visible so the user understands they are close to the result.

Possible message if user tries to leave:

You can stop anytime. If you are about to send money or share info, pause and verify through a trusted channel first.

Safety note:

The app should not use manipulative retention patterns. It should not trap the user in the flow. The goal is safety, not engagement metrics.

first app version decision:

The The first app version should allow users to leave freely. Saving abandoned progress can wait.

Edge Case 3: User Misunderstands a Low Concern Result

Scenario:

The app returns Low concern because few warning signs were found, but the user interprets that as “the app says this is safe.”

Required app behavior:

Low concern must include a limit statement:

Few warning signs were found from the info provided. This does not guarantee the situation is safe. If anything feels unusual, verify through a trusted channel before acting.

Design reason:

Low concern is useful, but dangerous if interpreted as permission. The result must preserve uncertainty.

first app version decision:

Must include cautious Low concern wording in the first app version.

Edge Case 4: User Disagrees With the Result

Scenario:

The user thinks the app is too cautious or not cautious enough.

Required app behavior:

The app should not argue. It should explain its reasoning and offer a path to review answers.

Advised copy:

This result is based on the info provided. You can review your answers or use guided questions for a more detailed check.

If feedback exists, the app can ask:

Was this result helpful?

Choices:

\- Helpful  
\- Too cautious  
\- Missed something  
\- Confusing

Safety note:

Feedback should not ask for sensitive details.

first app version decision:

Review answers is useful but optional. Basic explanatory reasoning is required.

Edge Case 5: User Is On a Live Call With a Possible Scammer

Scenario:

The user is using the app while someone is pressuring them on a phone call or video call.

Required app behavior:

The app should provide very direct guidance if urgency, payment, secrecy, or remote support is involved.

Advised copy:

If someone is pressuring you while you use this app, pause the conversation. Do not send money, share codes, install software, or give account info until you verify through an official channel.

Design reason:

Live pressure reduces the user's ability to think. The app should help interrupt the pressure without escalating fear.

first app version decision:

This can be handled through Guided Review and result copy in the first app version.

Edge Case 6: User Is Embarrassed

Scenario:

The user suspects they may have been fooled or nearly fooled. They may feel ashamed and avoid answering honestly.

Required app behavior:

The app should normalize checking. It should say:

Scams are designed to create pressure and confusion. Checking before acting is a smart step.

The app should never use mocking language. It should not say “obvious scam” or “you fell for it.”

Design reason:

Shame makes users hide info and delay help. A respectful tone improves safety.

first app version decision:

Must apply across all flows.

App Feature Area 3 flow quality rules

Every flow in the app should:

\- let users continue when they are not sure  
\- avoid requiring sensitive info  
\- provide a safer next step  
\- explain uncertainty  
\- avoid blame  
\- support users before and after action  
\- make verification easier to understand  
\- avoid trapping users in the app  
\- avoid fake certainty  
\- preserve calm design

App Feature Area 3 accept rules

App Feature Area 3 is acceptable when:

\- it stays in design/planning mode only  
\- it includes no coding  
\- it includes no launch instructions  
\- it maps complete user flows from start to result  
\- it includes risky-message flow  
\- it includes payment-request flow  
\- it includes already-sent-money flow  
\- it includes family-helper flow  
\- it includes unsure-user flow  
\- it documents sensitive-info handling  
\- it documents abandoned-flow handling  
\- it documents misunderstood-result handling  
\- it documents disagreement with result handling  
\- it accounts for users under live pressure  
\- it accounts for embarrassed users  
\- it keeps the app calm, practical, and nonjudgmental  
\- it keeps Harborwake as the company and Verivae as the app name

Additional feature area to define

The design brief should also include App Feature Area 4: Interface Writing and Exact Copy.
