These include passwords, one-time codes, full card numbers, full Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, ID docs, private addresses, login links, account recovery details, crypto wallet recovery phrases, private keys, seed phrases, medical details, intimate photos, threats, extortion material, and private family info.

The app should discourage users from submitting these details. The Privacy Redaction Helper should detect likely sensitive patterns and ask the user to remove or mask them before checking.

The app should never ask users to paste a crypto seed phrase, private key, bank password, email password, one-time code, full Social Security number, or full card number. If a scam message asks for these, the app can review the request without the actual sensitive value.

Safer replacement language should be encouraged. A user can write "they asked for my bank password" instead of pasting the password. A user can write "they asked for a one-time code" instead of pasting the code. A user can write "I sent $500 through a payment app" instead of pasting full account details.

Privacy Redaction Helper rules

The Privacy Redaction Helper should appear before the app processes risky content when likely sensitive info is present. It should not shame the user. It should explain that the app can usually help without private details.

Redaction means removing or hiding private info. The helper should support three patterns: remove, replace, and mask. Remove means deleting the sensitive detail. Replace means using a general phrase such as "my card number." Mask means showing only partial details, such as "card ending in 1234" if needed for the user's own notes.

The helper should not show sensitive values in large warning text. If the app detects a possible card number, the warning should say "This may include a full card number" rather than repeating the number. If the app detects a possible one-time code, it should say "This may include a one-time code" rather than showing the code.

The helper should operate before saving too. A user may paste sensitive details into a case note. The app should warn before saving if the note appears to include passwords, codes, full card numbers, identity numbers, or seed phrases.

User consent system

Consent should be specific. The user should know what they are allowing. A broad prompt like "Allow access to protect you" is not acceptable. A better prompt says exactly what feature is asking for access and what the app will do with it.

Consent should be optional where possible. The manual check should work without Gmail, messages, contacts, device files, or linked-device sharing. If the user declines a permission, the app should offer a manual alternative.

Consent should be reversible. The app should include settings where users can disconnect Gmail, remove a trusted helper, turn off weekly deep-check reminders, delete saved cases, stop sharing a device summary, or disable history.

Consent should be repeated when the context changes. If the user gave permission to share one case with a helper, that does not mean the helper can see all future cases. If the user allowed weekly reminders for one device, that does not mean the app can share those reminders with family members.

Consent should be understandable to beginners. The app should avoid legal language in permission screens. It can still link to a full privacy policy later, but the in-app explanation should be plain.

Future Gmail and email data rules

If Verivae later supports Gmail or other email integration, the email feature should be narrow and user-controlled. The user should be able to manually paste an email without connecting Gmail. Connecting Gmail should be optional.

The app should explain what email access means. It should say whether the app can see selected emails only, scam-report emails only, user-forwarded emails, or broader mailbox info. The safest direction is selected-email review, where the user chooses what to send to Verivae.

The app should avoid reading all emails by default. It should not scan a user's entire mailbox without a very clear need, strong controls, and explicit permission. Even then, the design should prefer limited access.

Email review should avoid saving message content unless the user chooses to save a case. If email content is processed temporarily, the app should say so. If it is saved, the app should say where and why.

Email integration should include a disconnect option. Users should be able to revoke access from inside the app and through their account provider where supported.

Future messages and SMS data rules

If Verivae later supports message review, it should respect phone platform rules and user consent. On some platforms, message access may be limited or unavailable. The app should not secretly read messages.

The safest first design is share-to-app or copy-and-paste review. The user chooses a risky message and sends it to Verivae. This keeps control with the user and avoids hidden monitoring.

If future message filtering is supported on a platform, the app should explain exactly what it can see, what it filters, what it saves, and how the user can turn it off. Message filtering should not expose private message content to trusted helpers or paid features without clear consent.

Message data should be treated as highly sensitive. Messages may include family matters, romance conversations, passwords, codes, financial details, health details, workplace info, or private conflict.

Linked-device privacy rules

Linked-device features should be opt-in. The user should add devices intentionally. The app should not silently scan a home network, discover devices, or create device profiles without user action.

A linked-device record should use a nickname instead of a permanent hardware identifier whenever possible. "Mom's phone" is usually enough for the user. The app should avoid collecting serial numbers, hardware IDs, advertising IDs, or other device identifiers unless a future feature truly requires them.

Weekly Deep Check should save a simple summary by default. Example: "Family laptop: action advised, full scan suggested." It should not automatically save full scan logs, file paths, app lists, browser history, or detected filenames unless the user chooses to attach them.

Device sharing with trusted helpers should be summary-based by default. A helper can see "Needs review" or "Weekly check missed" only if the device owner allows it. Detailed device notes should require separate sharing.

Device-security alerts should not reveal private details on the lock screen. A safe alert says: "Weekly security check from Verivae." An unsafe alert says: "Dad's laptop may have malware from a bank scam." The second version could embarrass or expose the user.

Trusted Helper privacy system

Trusted Helper should be designed around case-by-case sharing. A trusted helper is not a hidden monitor. The user chooses what to share, who receives it, and when sharing stops.

The app should show a share preview before sending anything. The preview should list included content: risk result, message text, warning signs, next steps, notes, screenshots, device summary, timeline, or evidence items. The user should be able to remove items before sharing.

A helper should not automatically see all saved cases. If a family plan later allows broader sharing, it should use explicit controls and clear labels. The default should be private.

The app should show sharing status on saved cases. A case card can say "Private" or "Shared with trusted helper." If multiple helpers exist, the case should show who can see it.

Removing a helper should stop future access inside the app. The app should explain that removing a helper may not delete screenshots, exports, or info the helper already saved outside the app.

Evidence Vault security rules

Evidence Vault will likely contain sensitive scam details. It should be treated as one of the most sensitive areas of the app. The app should support clear organization, deletion, and sharing controls.

Evidence should be private by default. A screenshot, transaction note, phone number, email, link, username, wallet address, or case timeline should not be shared unless the user chooses to share it.

Evidence Vault should support masking. If a user saves a payment detail, the app should encourage partial details rather than full private numbers. Example: "payment app transfer to username" is often safer than saving full bank account details.

The app should distinguish app storage from external exports. If a user exports a report, the exported file may live outside Verivae. Deleting the case inside the app may not delete the exported file. The interface must explain this.

Evidence Vault should also support recovery notes. The user may record that they contacted a bank, changed a password, filed a report, called official support, or asked a helper. These notes should be protected because they can reveal private financial or identity issues.

Account and sign-in security

If the app supports accounts, account security should be simple and strong. Users should be able to protect their Verivae account because saved cases may contain sensitive info.

The app should support strong passwords or secure sign-in methods. It should support multi-factor auth if accounts and cloud storage are used. Beginner explanation: multi-factor auth means the user needs more than just a password to sign in, such as a code, passkey, or device confirmation.

The app should support sign-out from other devices if cross-device sync exists. If a user thinks someone else has access, they should be able to review active sessions and remove unknown ones.

The app should use plain warnings for account security. Example: "If someone else can access this account, they may see saved cases. Change your password and sign out of other devices."

The app should avoid sending sensitive details in email alerts. Account emails should be generic: "A saved case was shared" or "Your password was changed," not full scam content.

Cloud sync privacy

Cloud sync means saved cases can appear across multiple devices. This can be useful, but it increases privacy responsibility. The app should not require cloud sync for basic manual checks.

If cloud sync is offered, the app should explain what is synced: saved cases, notes, evidence, device summaries, helper settings, reminders, and account preferences. The user should know whether quick checks are synced or only saved cases.

Cloud sync should have a clear off option where possible. A user may prefer local-only use. Local-only means info stays on the device unless the user exports or shares it. This can be an important privacy option.

If paid plans include detailed cloud history, the app should still provide basic free safety checks without sync. Paid cloud features should pay for convenience and organization, not basic protection.

Data deletion feature

The app should give users ways to delete sensitive info. Deletion should be understandable and not hidden. Users should be able to delete a single check, delete a saved case, delete all saved cases, remove a linked device, delete device-check history, remove a trusted helper, disconnect integrations, and close an account if accounts exist.

Deletion screens should explain what deletion does and does not remove. It may remove data inside Verivae, but it may not remove original emails from Gmail, original text messages, screenshots saved in Photos, exported reports, bank records, payment app records, or copies already shared outside the app.

Deletion confirmation should not be manipulative. The app can warn that deletion cannot be undone, but it should not guilt the user into keeping sensitive data.

The app should avoid dark patterns around deletion. A dark pattern is a design trick that makes it hard for users to do what they intend. Deleting data should not require unnecessary steps, confusing wording, or paid support.

Privacy settings screen

The privacy settings screen should be one of the clearest parts of the app. It should show what is saved, what is linked, what is shared, and what reminders are active.

Suggested sections: Saved data, Linked features, Trusted helpers, Device security checks, Alerts, Account security, Exports, and Delete data.

Saved data can show check history, saved cases, evidence items, detailed reports, and local versus cloud status.

Linked features can show Gmail, messages, contacts, alerts, device security checks, and share-to-app settings if those features exist.

Trusted helpers can show who can see what. Device security checks can show linked devices and weekly check reminders. Account security can show password, multi-factor auth, active sessions, and sign-in alerts.

The privacy settings screen should use plain labels and short explanations. It should not require the user to read a privacy policy to understand app controls.

Data use for app improvement

The app may eventually need feedback data to improve scam detection and product quality. This should be handled carefully. User-submitted scam content should not be used for improvement without clear disclosure and appropriate controls.

The safest default is to separate personal content from product analytics. Product analytics can count general events such as feature usage, error rates, or whether users complete a check. It should avoid storing full scam messages, emails, screenshots, device logs, or case notes by default.

If the app asks users to contribute examples to improve scam detection, it should ask clearly and allow refusal. The app should explain whether examples are reviewed, stored, anonymized, or used for model improvement. Beginner explanation: anonymized means details that identify a person are removed or reduced, but anonymization is not always perfect.

The app should not pressure users to donate scam examples. A scared user should not feel that helping the product is required to get safety guidance.

AI review privacy

If Verivae uses AI to review messages or situations, the app should explain that submitted content may be processed to produce a result. It should explain whether the check is temporary, whether content is saved, and whether saved cases are separate from temporary review.

AI review should avoid overcollection. The app should not ask for more context than needed. It should ask for the message, request, payment method, contact method, and relevant behavior rather than full private account details.

AI outputs should include uncertainty. The app should not claim perfect detection. Privacy and safety both improve when the app is honest about limits.

If a user deletes a saved case, the app should explain what happens to the saved content. If the system uses temporary processing, the app should explain that separately in user-friendly language.

Payment and monetization privacy

Paid features should not require selling sensitive data. The monetization model should be user-paid value, not data resale. The app should never sell private scam messages, email content, SMS content, evidence items, device notes, contact lists, account details, or financial details.

Payment processing should be separated from scam content. If the app uses Apple or Google in-app purchases, the app should not need to handle full payment card details directly. If web billing ever exists for allowed cases, payment data should be handled by a trusted payment provider rather than stored by Verivae.

Premium features should not unlock basic privacy. Privacy should not be a paid feature. Free users should still get basic redaction warnings, deletion controls for their saved data, and clear permission settings. Paid plans can offer detailed organization, sync, storage, and family controls, but not basic privacy protections.

Alerts privacy

Alerts should be privacy-preserving by default. Scam and device-security alerts can accidentally reveal embarrassing or sensitive info on a lock screen.

Good alert: "Safety reminder from Verivae."

Bad alert: "You may have sent money to a romance scammer."

Good alert: "Weekly device check ready."

Bad alert: "Dad's phone may have malware."

Users should be able to choose alert detail level. Options can include private, standard, and detailed. Private should be the default. Detailed alerts should require clear user choice.

Official reporting and privacy

The Reporting Guide should explain that saving a case in the app is not the same as filing an official report. If the app later helps users prepare reports, it should show what info will be included.

If the user follows an external reporting link, the app should explain that the user is leaving Verivae and entering another organization's site. The other organization will have its own privacy practices.

The app should avoid automatically sending reports without user review. A user should see the info before it goes to a bank, payment provider, marketplace, platform, agency, or helper.

Security model for sensitive areas

Sensitive areas should include saved cases, Evidence Vault, trusted helper settings, linked-device details, reports, exports, account settings, and integration settings. These areas should have extra care.

The app can support app lock or re-auth for sensitive areas. Re-auth means asking the user to confirm their identity again before opening private content, such as with device unlock, passcode, fingerprint, face unlock, or password.

The app should avoid showing sensitive previews in recent-app switchers or alerts where possible. This matters if someone else can see the user's screen.

If the app is used by families, the security model should recognize shared-device situations. A parent, child, spouse, or caregiver may use the same device. Private cases should not be casually visible to everyone who opens the app.

Security incident behavior

The app should include a simple user-facing incident concept. If Verivae ever detects risky account access, unusual sign-in, unexpected helper changes, or integration changes, it should notify the user in a privacy-safe way.

Security alert copy: "Important account change in Verivae."

Alert detail inside app: "A trusted helper was added," "A linked feature was turned on," "A new device signed in," or "Your password was changed."

The app should help users respond. Response options can include review activity, remove helper, disconnect feature, sign out other devices, change password, and contact support.

Beginner-friendly privacy explanations

The app should explain privacy concepts simply. It should not assume users know terms like encryption, cloud sync, local storage, permissions, data sharing, or analytics.

Encryption explanation: "Encryption helps protect info so it is harder for someone else to read."

Local storage explanation: "Local means the info stays on this device unless you share, export, or sync it."

Cloud sync explanation: "Cloud sync means your saved cases can appear on your other devices after sign-in."

Permission explanation: "A permission is access you allow, such as alerts, contacts, or selected email review."

Data sharing explanation: "Sharing means info leaves your private app space and is sent to a helper, service, platform, or other organization."

Privacy accept rules

The privacy, data, and security feature system is acceptable only if manual checks can work without connecting Gmail, messages, contacts, phone, device files, or payment accounts.

The system is acceptable only if the app collects the least info needed for each feature.

The system is acceptable only if temporary checks are clearly different from saved cases.

The system is acceptable only if sensitive data redaction is visible before checking and before saving.

The system is acceptable only if users can delete saved cases, device records, helper sharing, reminders, and linked integrations.

The system is acceptable only if trusted helper sharing is case-based, previewed, and consent-based by default.

The system is acceptable only if linked-device checks are opt-in and do not secretly scan or profile devices.

The system is acceptable only if weekly deep-check reminders are private, optional, and easy to turn off.

The system is acceptable only if paid features do not weaken privacy for free users.

The system is acceptable only if the app does not sell private scam content, message content, email content, evidence, device notes, contact lists, financial details, or identity details.

The system is acceptable only if future integrations explain access, saving, sharing, and disconnect options in plain text.

Source notes for privacy, data, and security feature

[Source: FTC Protecting Personal Info](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/protecting-personal-information-guide-business). FTC business guidance emphasizes collecting only what is needed, keeping it only as long as necessary, protecting what is kept, and disposing of data securely.

[Source: FTC Start with Security](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/start-security-guide-business). FTC security guidance emphasizes building security into decisions from the beginning and avoiding unnecessary data collection.

[Source: NIST Privacy Framework](https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework/getting-started-0). NIST describes privacy outcomes around identifying, governing, controlling, communicating, and protecting privacy risks.

[Source: Apple App Privacy Details](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/app-privacy-details/). Apple's App Store privacy guidance requires developers to explain app privacy practices, including data types collected and whether data is linked to users or used for tracking.

[Source: Google Play Data safety](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10787469?hl=en-EN). Google Play requires developers to declare how apps collect, share, and protect user data, including security practices such as encryption and whether users can request deletion.

Additional feature area to define

The design brief should also include App Feature Area 7: Scam Detection Logic and Risk Explanation System. That section should define how Verivae evaluates risk signals, assigns risk levels, explains confidence, handles uncertainty, separates scam risk from device risk, avoids false guarantees, and gives safer next steps based on message, payment, device, account, and behavior signals.

## App Feature Area 7: Scam Detection Logic and Risk Explanation System

Purpose of this feature area

This feature area defines how the app should evaluate scam risk and explain that risk to users. It describes the product rules for risk logic: what warning signs matter, how those warning signs combine, how confidence is explained, how uncertainty is handled, how device risk stays separate from scam risk, and how the app gives safer next steps without pretending to know more than it can know.

The app should be built around transparent risk explanation. A user should not only see a label like "Risk." They should understand why the app is concerned, what evidence created the concern, what the app does not know, and what safer action to take next. A result without explanation may feel mysterious. A mysterious result may be ignored, misunderstood, or overtrusted.

The detection system should be conservative, calm, and honest. Conservative means the app should prioritize preventing harm when money, account access, identity info, one-time codes, remote access, crypto, gift cards, wire transfers, fake checks, threats, secrecy, or urgent payment are involved. Calm means the app should avoid panic language. Honest means the app should not claim certainty when the situation is incomplete.

Beginner explanation: scam detection logic means the way the app decides what warning signs are present. A risk level means how concerning the situation looks. Confidence means how much info the app has to support that result. Uncertainty means the app may need more details before giving a stronger answer.

Core detection promise

the app should promise to look for scam warning signs, organize them, explain them, and suggest safer next steps. It should not promise to detect every scam, verify every sender, identify every criminal, guarantee recovery, guarantee safety, or replace banks, law enforcement, lawyers, cybersecurity tools, or official reporting agencies.

User-facing promise: "Verivae reviews the situation for scam warning signs and explains safer next steps."

User-facing limit: "This is a risk review, not a guarantee. Scams can be hard to confirm from one message or screenshot."

This promise-and-limit pair should appear throughout the product. It protects users from overtrusting the app while still making the app useful.

Risk source categories

The app should evaluate risk across several categories. Each category represents a different type of warning sign. A strong result should explain which categories were involved rather than giving a vague warning.

Contact risk: how the person or message reached the user. Unexpected contact, unknown sender, spoofed number, risky email, social media message, marketplace message, dating app message, private chat invitation, or movement to another platform can all matter.

Identity risk: who the sender claims to be. Claims involving banks, government agencies, law enforcement, employers, delivery companies, tech support, family members, romantic partners, celebrities, investment experts, recruiters, or marketplace buyers can change risk.

Urgency risk: pressure to act quickly. Scammers often want users to move before they verify. Words about immediate action, account closure, arrest, missed delivery, limited opportunity, expiring offer, frozen funds, emergency, or final warning should raise concern.

Payment risk: how money is requested. Gift cards, crypto, wire transfer, payment apps, bank transfer, fake checks, upfront fees, delivery fees, loan fees, equipment fees, taxes, release fees, recovery fees, or unusual payment instructions can raise risk.

Info risk: what the sender wants from the user. Requests for passwords, one-time codes, account numbers, full card numbers, Social Security numbers, ID docs, bank login, crypto seed phrases, private keys, remote access codes, or screenshots of accounts should raise concern.

Device risk: whether the user is asked to click links, download files, install apps, approve permissions, disable security, share a screen, allow remote control, scan a QR code, install a profile, add a browser extension, or follow fake tech-support instructions.

Secrecy and isolation risk: whether the sender tells the user not to tell anyone, not to contact the real company, not to talk to family, not to call the bank, not to use official support, or to keep the transaction private.

Story risk: the emotional or practical story used to influence the user. Romance, family emergency, fake job, investment success, account threat, refund promise, delivery problem, government penalty, tech-support alert, business invoice change, or fake marketplace sale can each create different risk patterns.

Channel-switching risk: whether the sender moves the user to WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, email, phone, fake support chat, remote-access software, crypto wallet, payment app, or another channel where protections may be weaker.

Recovery-scam risk: whether someone promises to recover lost money, unlock frozen funds, return crypto, punish a scammer, or reverse a transaction if the user pays a fee or shares more info.

Risk levels

The app should use plain risk levels. The advised levels are Lower risk, Use caution, Risk, Stop before acting, and Not enough info.

Lower risk means the app did not find strong scam warning signs from the info provided. It does not mean the situation is guaranteed safe. The result should still encourage official-channel verification if money, login, identity, or account access is involved.

Use caution means some warning signs are present or the situation is incomplete enough to require careful verification. The app should explain what is unclear and what the user should verify before acting.

Risk means the app found strong warning signs that commonly appear in scams. The app should tell the user not to send money, share codes, click links, download files, install apps, or provide account access until verified through an official channel.

Stop before acting means the situation may put money, accounts, identity, or device access at immediate risk. This should be used for serious combinations such as urgent gift card requests, crypto investment pressure, one-time code requests, remote-access requests, bank login requests, fake check return-payment requests, or threats demanding fast payment.

Not enough info means the app cannot provide a useful risk review yet. It should not default to safe. It should ask for specific missing details: exact request, payment method, contact method, sender claim, link, device action requested, or whether money or codes are involved.

Confidence levels

Risk level and confidence level should be separate. Risk says how concerning the situation looks. Confidence says how much info supports that conclusion.

High confidence means the app has enough specific evidence to explain the result clearly. Example: a message asks for gift card codes urgently while claiming to be a government office. The warning signs are strong and specific.

Medium confidence means the app has meaningful warning signs but some details are missing. Example: the user says someone asked for payment through a link, but does not provide the exact message or payment method.

Low confidence means the app has too little info or the content is too vague. Low confidence should not be presented as safe. It should prompt the user for more details.

Confidence copy should be plain. Example: "The app is more confident because the message includes urgent payment pressure and an unusual payment method." Another example: "The app is less certain because the sender, link, and payment method were not included."

Scam risk versus device risk

The app should separate scam risk from device risk. A situation can be a scam without device compromise. A situation can involve device risk even if the message itself is unclear. The result should show both when relevant.

Scam risk means the request, story, sender claim, payment method, or info request looks risky. Device risk means the user's phone, computer, browser, account, or linked device may need review because the user clicked a link, downloaded a file, installed an app, approved remote access, shared a screen, or entered credentials.

Example: "Scam risk: High. Device risk: Needs review." This could happen if the user clicked a fake bank link and entered a password. The scam pattern is risk, and the device/account situation needs follow-up.

Example: "Scam risk: Use caution. Device risk: High concern." This could happen if the message is unclear but the user installed remote-access software at someone's request.

Device risk should not be called a virus result unless the app has a real antivirus or platform-supported scan result. Safer wording is "device-security warning signs" or "device review advised."

Weighted warning signals

The app should treat some warning signs as stronger than others. A single mild warning sign may lead to Use caution. Multiple strong warning signs should push the result higher. Certain critical warning signs should trigger Stop before acting even if the rest of the message looks normal.

Critical warning signs include requests for one-time codes, passwords, remote access, crypto seed phrases, private keys, gift card codes, urgent wire transfers, urgent crypto transfers, fake check return payments, bank login details, screen sharing during banking, or secrecy around sending money.

Strong warning signs include unexpected contact, urgent payment pressure, threats, unusual payment method, movement to private messaging, investment promises, romance-based money requests, fake job fees, fake delivery fees, fake tech-support claims, account closure threats, and request to install software.

Moderate warning signs include vague sender identity, risky link, grammar or formatting problems, mismatched sender domain, unfamiliar marketplace request, pressure to continue off-platform, new contact asking for help, and unusual personal info request.

Context warning signs depend on the situation. A delivery fee might be normal in one context and risky in another. A job equipment purchase might be legitimate in some cases and a scam in others. The app should explain the context instead of treating every keyword as proof.

Payment risk logic

Payment method should heavily influence risk. The app should treat gift cards, crypto, wire transfers, payment apps, fake checks, and upfront fees as risky when combined with unexpected contact or pressure.

Gift cards should be a major warning sign when requested by someone claiming to be a company, government office, bank, law enforcement agency, employer, tech support agent, family member in trouble, romantic partner, or prize organization. The result should say that real organizations usually do not demand gift cards as payment.

Crypto should be risk when linked to investment promises, romance, wrong-number texts, online groups, celebrity endorsements, fake platforms, withdrawal fees, tax fees, recovery services, or pressure to move money quickly. The app should warn that crypto transfers can be very hard or impossible to reverse.

Wire transfers should be risk when tied to urgent invoices, changed bank instructions, property transactions, business email requests, government threats, family emergencies, or investment opportunities. The app should encourage separate-channel verification.

Payment apps should be concerning when someone contacted the user unexpectedly, is asking for fast payment, wants payment outside a marketplace platform, or claims the user must pay to unlock funds, delivery, a prize, a job, or a refund.

Fake checks should be risk when the user receives a check and is asked to send money back, buy equipment, pay a fee, forward funds, or return an accidental overpayment before the bank confirms the check fully cleared.

Identity and impersonation logic

The app should evaluate who the sender claims to be and whether the claimed identity matches the request. A bank asking for a password through text is risky. A government office demanding gift cards is risky. A tech-support agent asking for remote access after an unexpected popup is risky. A family member asking for urgent secrecy and money should be verified separately.

Impersonation risk should rise when the message uses authority, fear, or familiarity. Authority includes banks, government offices, police, courts, employers, tech companies, delivery services, app platforms, and payment providers. Familiarity includes family members, friends, romantic partners, coworkers, bosses, and trusted community members.

AI and deepfake impersonation should be included. If a voice, video, or image seems convincing but the person asks for money, secrecy, one-time codes, account access, or urgent action, the app should still recommend verification through a separate known contact method.

The app should teach that realistic content is not proof. A believable video, cloned voice, professional website, friendly romance message, or polished investment dashboard can still be part of a scam.

Urgency, threats, and secrecy logic

Urgency is one of the strongest cross-scam signals. The app should flag language that pressures the user to act before verifying. Examples include immediate, today only, final notice, last chance, account closing, warrant, penalty, emergency, frozen funds, missed delivery, job expires, investment window, and limited time.

Threats should raise risk. Threats may involve arrest, account closure, public embarrassment, job loss, missed benefits, family harm, legal penalties, immigration consequences, delivery failure, or financial loss. The app should explain that threats are often used to force fast action.

Secrecy should raise risk strongly when combined with money or account access. A sender who says not to tell family, not to call the bank, not to contact official support, not to tell a manager, or not to discuss the transaction is isolating the user.

The app should not assume every urgent message is a scam. Some real messages are urgent. But the app should say urgency increases the need to verify through an official channel before acting.

Link and website logic

Risky links should raise caution, especially when the message involves banking, delivery, account access, payment, government claims, job offers, marketplace transactions, or identity info. The app should not need to prove a link is malicious before recommending safer behavior.

The safest advice is usually to avoid the link and go to the official app or website directly. If the app later includes URL analysis, it should explain that link checks are imperfect and can miss new or disguised threats.

The app should treat shortened links, misspelled domains, lookalike domains, unusual subdomains, unexpected login pages, and links sent through urgent messages as warning signs. It should also flag QR codes used for payment, login, crypto, or account changes when received unexpectedly.

The app should avoid showing link safety as guaranteed. A link can be safe at one time and unsafe later, or a scam can happen on a professional-looking site. The result should say "This link has warning signs" or "Use the official site instead" rather than "This link is definitely safe."

Remote access and device-control logic

Requests to install remote-access software, screen-sharing tools, device-management profiles, browser extensions, unknown apps, or security tools from a risky message should raise device risk and scam risk.

If the user is asked to open a banking app, payment app, crypto wallet, password manager, email account, or identity account while someone else is viewing or controlling the screen, the app should treat the situation as high concern.

If someone says they need access to fix a refund, remove a virus, reverse a bank charge, unlock crypto funds, recover a hacked account, or protect the user from fraud, the app should flag tech-support or recovery-scam risk.

The result should route to Device Security Check and Already Acted guidance. The user may need to stop the remote session, disconnect, use a safe device for important accounts, change passwords, and contact official support.

Account and code-request logic

One-time code requests should be treated as critical. A one-time code is meant to prove the user's identity. If someone asks the user to read or send a code, they may be trying to access the user's account.

Password requests should be treated as critical when coming through a message, phone call, social media chat, marketplace chat, dating app, fake support page, or unexpected link. The app should tell users that legitimate support should not ask for their password.

Account recovery requests should be treated carefully. Scammers may ask for recovery codes, backup codes, identity screenshots, security answers, or device approvals. These should trigger risky guidance.

The app should distinguish between the sender asking for a code and the user receiving a normal security code after trying to sign in themselves. The context matters. If the user did not initiate the sign-in, the code is more risky.

Scam type classification

The app should classify likely scam patterns in beginner language. Classification should help explanation and next steps. It should not be presented as a legal conclusion.

Possible scam types include bank impersonation, government impersonation, delivery fee scam, gift card scam, crypto investment scam, romance scam, fake job scam, fake check scam, marketplace scam, tech support scam, remote-access scam, business email compromise, fake invoice, family emergency scam, AI/deepfake impersonation, recovery scam, prize or lottery scam, charity scam, loan fee scam, subscription refund scam, account takeover attempt, phishing, spoofing, and unknown pattern.

If the app is unsure, it can say "This may match more than one scam pattern." For example, a fake job asking for crypto could involve both fake job and crypto-payment risk.

Classification should never override immediate safety. If a user is asked for a one-time code, the app should prioritize code safety even if the exact scam type is unclear.

False positives and false negatives

A false positive means the app flags something as risky when it is actually legitimate. A false negative means the app misses a scam or treats it as lower risk. Both matter.

The app should reduce false positives by explaining uncertainty and encouraging verification rather than simply declaring scams. If a message looks risky but might be legitimate, the app should say what to verify.

The app should reduce false negatives by being cautious with high-harm signals. If money, codes, passwords, crypto, remote access, or identity info are involved, the app should lean toward pausing and verifying.

The app should avoid the phrase "safe" as a final answer. A lower-risk result should say "No strong warning signs found from the info provided" and still recommend official-channel verification for sensitive actions.

Result explanation structure

Every result should explain risk in the same order: risk level, confidence level, main reason, warning signs found, missing info, safer next steps, and limits.

Risk level answers "How concerning is this?" Confidence answers "How much info supports this result?" Main reason answers "What mattered most?" Warning signs answer "What did the app notice?" Missing info answers "What could change the result?" Safer next steps answer "What should I do now?" Limits answer "What can the app not guarantee?"

This structure should be consistent across manual checks, Before You Pay, Already Acted, Device Security Check, Evidence Vault, Trusted Helper, and Reporting Guide.

The app should avoid vague explanations like "Risky activity detected." A better explanation is "The message asks for a one-time code and says your account will close today. Urgency plus code requests are strong warning signs."

Next-step matching

The app should match next steps to the specific risk. A gift card request should not receive only generic advice. It should say not to buy or share gift card numbers. A code request should say not to share codes and to secure the account if a code was shared. A remote-access request should route to device-security guidance.

For bank impersonation, next steps should include using the official banking app or the number on the card. For delivery scams, use the official delivery app or website. For government impersonation, use official government websites or phone numbers. For family emergency scams, contact the family member or another trusted relative through a known number.

For crypto investment scams, stop sending money, do not pay withdrawal or recovery fees, preserve evidence, and report through appropriate channels. For fake checks, do not send money back until the bank confirms the check fully cleared.

For business invoice or payment-change requests, verify through a separate known channel before changing payment details or sending funds.

Already Acted risk logic

If the user already acted, the app should stop focusing only on prevention and shift to response. It should ask what happened, identify urgent categories, and show recovery steps in priority order.

Urgent categories include sent money, shared password, shared one-time code, clicked link and entered info, installed remote access, shared ID docs, gave bank or card details, sent intimate content under threat, or moved crypto to a scam platform.

The app should not shame users. Result language should say "Focus on the next safest step" rather than "You made a mistake." Shame can prevent users from asking for help.

If money was sent, payment method should determine the response. Contact bank, card company, payment app, wire service, crypto platform, marketplace, or other payment source through an official channel. Save evidence. Report where appropriate.

Trusted Helper explanation logic

When a case is shared with a trusted helper, the helper view should show the same risk explanation but include helper-specific guidance. The helper should see what warning signs were found, what the user may need help verifying, and what not to do.

The helper should not receive an overly technical score. The helper should receive plain reasoning: "This looks risky because it asks for crypto after a romantic conversation and says the opportunity will disappear today."

The helper view should include emotional guidance: help calmly, do not shame, verify through official channels, and help preserve evidence if needed.

Evidence Vault risk history

Saved cases should keep risk history. If a case changes over time, the app should show what changed. A message that started as Use caution may become Risk after a payment method, link, or remote-access request appears.

The app should support case updates. Users may add new messages, screenshots, transaction notes, device notes, or reporting updates. The risk explanation should be able to update without losing the previous context.

The app should label old results. If a case was checked earlier, the app should show when that result was produced. Scam situations can change, and old results may not reflect new messages.

Confidence and missing info should also update as the case grows. More details may raise or lower confidence.

Premium and risk logic boundary

Risk logic should not be worse for free users. The app should not create weaker basic safety results in order to sell premium. Basic scam checks, risky warnings, basic next steps, privacy redaction, and already-acted guidance should remain available.

Premium can add deeper reports, saved case history, family sharing, cross-device sync, advanced education, detailed device check history, and organized evidence summaries. Premium should not unlock the basic answer to "Is this risky?"

Upgrade prompts should never say "Pay to see your risk." A better prompt is "Save this case and create a detailed report." The free result should already show the basic risk and next steps.

Quality and review rules

The app's detection logic should be reviewed against real scam patterns. It should be tested with examples from common scam categories: bank texts, delivery fees, gift cards, crypto investments, romance requests, fake jobs, fake checks, marketplace messages, tech support, government threats, family emergencies, business invoices, AI impersonation, recovery scams, and remote access.

Testing should include benign examples too. The app should not label every payment, every bank message, every delivery message, or every job offer as a scam. It should explain what to verify.

The app should include a way for users to say whether a result helped. Feedback can improve the product, but it should not require users to donate private scam content without clear consent.

The app should track whether explanations are understandable. A result that is technically accurate but confusing is not good enough for this product.

Scam detection accept rules

The scam detection logic is acceptable only if it explains why a result was produced.

The logic is acceptable only if risk level and confidence level are separate.

The logic is acceptable only if lower-risk results do not promise complete safety.

The logic is acceptable only if risky results clearly show what not to do next.

The logic is acceptable only if payment methods such as gift cards, crypto, wire transfers, payment apps, and fake checks receive specific handling.

The logic is acceptable only if one-time codes, passwords, private keys, seed phrases, remote access, and bank login requests are treated as critical warning signs.

The logic is acceptable only if device risk and scam risk can be shown separately.

The logic is acceptable only if already-acted situations shift from prevention to response.

The logic is acceptable only if trusted helpers receive clear, calm, non-shaming explanations.

The logic is acceptable only if paid features do not hide basic scam-risk results or urgent safety guidance.

The logic is acceptable only if the app avoids false guarantees, legal conclusions, and unsupported claims of certainty.

Source notes for scam detection logic

[Source: FTC signs of a scam](https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2025/03/what-are-signs-scam). FTC consumer guidance emphasizes common scam patterns such as unexpected contact, hurry pressure, and demands to pay through methods such as cash, gift cards, wire transfers, crypto, or payment apps.

[Source: FBI common frauds and scams](https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/common-frauds-and-scams). FBI guidance identifies common fraud categories including business email compromise, crypto investment fraud, romance scams, spoofing and phishing, tech support scams, and other scams.

[Source: FBI 2025 IC3 report notice](https://www.fbi.gov/news/press-releases/cryptocurrency-and-ai-scams-bilk-americans-of-billions). The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report notice highlights major reported losses from cyber-enabled crime, including investment fraud, crypto complaints, business email compromise, tech support fraud, and AI-related complaints.

[Source: FBI crypto investment fraud](https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/victim-services/national-crimes-and-victim-resources/cryptocurrency-investment-fraud). FBI guidance describes crypto investment fraud patterns including social media contact, wrong-number texts, dating sites, private chat groups, fake platforms, and pressure to invest through crypto.

Additional feature area to define

## The design brief should also include Current Feature Alignment Note

The design brief is now organized around app features rather than a build plan. Harborwake remains the company name, and the app name remains Verivae until a separate naming decision is made.  
The current structure is: scope note, screen experience, function specs, user flows, integration addendum, monetization addendum, interface copy, professional success features, visual interface system, device security and weekly checks, privacy/data/security, scam detection logic, and next feature-by-feature deep specifications.  
Device security now fits in three places: the device-security addendum defines the user-facing feature; Area 6 defines consent, data limits, and privacy boundaries; Area 7 separates scam risk from device risk so warnings stay honest and understandable.  
The app specification should stay centered on product behavior: what the app can do, how screens behave, what users see, what privacy limits apply, what is free, what may be paid, and what safety boundaries prevent overclaiming.  
Next app-only section to expand: App Feature Area 8 should deeply define each major feature one by one, including Manual Scam Check, Payment Review, Evidence Vault, Trusted Helper, Device Security Check, Weekly Deep Check, Privacy Redaction Helper, Reporting Guide, Scam Pattern Library, and phone integrations.

## App Feature Area 8: Feature-by-Feature Deep Feature Specifications

Purpose of this feature area  
This feature area defines each major feature in full operational detail. It should cover what the feature does, who uses it, what info it needs, what the user sees, what privacy limits apply, how free and paid boundaries work, and what safety claims the app must avoid. It should include Manual Scam Check, Before You Pay, Already Acted, Evidence Vault, Device Security Check, Weekly Deep Check, Trusted Helper, Scam Pattern Library, Reporting Guide, Privacy Redaction Helper, and future phone integrations.

### Area 8 Part 1: Core Protection Feature Specifications

This part of Area 8 defines the core protection features that make Verivae useful before, during, and after a risky situation. These features are written as product features, not coding instructions. Each feature description explains what the feature is supposed to accomplish, what the user sees, what info the app may need, what privacy boundary must be respected, what free version behavior should exist, what paid upgrade behavior may exist, and what the app must avoid promising.

### Feature 8.1: Manual Scam Check

Manual Scam Check is the central feature for users who want to ask, "Is this a scam?" It should let a person paste, type, summarize, or upload info from a message, email, phone call, payment request, social media chat, marketplace listing, job offer, rental listing, investment pitch, romantic conversation, family emergency request, fake bank alert, fake delivery notice, or other risky situation. The feature should be built for people who are stressed and uncertain. It should not assume the user knows the scam category before starting.

The main purpose of Manual Scam Check is to slow the situation down. Many scams depend on urgency, fear, embarrassment, or excitement. The app should create a calm pause between the risky request and the user's next action. The feature should treat the user's concern as legitimate without making them feel foolish. The first screen should make the action simple: paste the message, describe what happened, add a screenshot, or choose a guided review. The user should not have to understand technical security language before getting help.

Manual Scam Check should accept different input styles. A user may paste exact text from a risky message. Another user may type a summary such as, "Someone said my bank account will close unless I click a link." Another user may add a screenshot from Messages, Gmail, WhatsApp, Facebook Marketplace, Instagram, or another service. Another user may describe a phone call from memory. The app should handle all of those inputs, but it should clearly explain that better details can lead to a clearer review. If the user gives very little info, the app should still provide a cautious result and ask follow-up questions instead of pretending to know more than it does.

The feature should separate the situation from the evidence. The situation is what the user says is happening. The evidence is the actual message, link, payment request, sender info, screenshot, phone number, email address, profile name, requested payment method, and timing. The result should never be based on one clue alone unless that clue is extremely strong. For example, a request for gift cards is a serious warning sign, but the app should still explain why it is risky and what safer action to take. A link that looks strange may be risky, but the app should avoid saying it is definitely malicious unless it has a reliable reason.

The Manual Scam Check flow should begin with an input screen, then a context screen, then a review screen, then a result screen. The input screen collects the risky material. The context screen asks what the person wants the user to do. The review screen lets the user confirm what they are comfortable sharing. The result screen gives a risk level, confidence level, warning signs, safer next steps, and optional evidence saving. This structure helps avoid accidental overcollection of personal info.

The app should warn users before they paste private data. If the user appears to paste a Social Security number, bank number, card number, password, login code, address, medical detail, or other sensitive item, the app should pause and say that private info is not needed for a scam check. The app should offer to redact the sensitive part before continuing. Redact means hide or remove private details so the review can focus on the scam pattern instead of storing unnecessary personal info.

Manual Scam Check should explain results in plain text. The app should not just show "High Risk" and stop. It should say why the situation looks risky, what behavior matched common scam patterns, what info is missing, and what action the user should take now. A useful result might say that the request is risk because the sender created urgency, asked for payment through an unusual method, told the user not to contact anyone else, and used a link that does not match the claimed company. The explanation should be direct, but not frightening.

The feature should produce one of several result types. Low Risk means the app found no strong scam signs, but the user should still be careful. Medium Risk means the situation has warning signs and should be verified outside the conversation. High Risk means the user should stop, avoid paying, avoid clicking, and verify through an official channel. Urgent Risk means the user may be about to send money, share login access, give a login code, or install something dangerous. Unknown Risk means there is not enough info to decide. Unknown should not feel like failure. It should tell the user what details would help.

Manual Scam Check should include a confidence level separate from the risk level. Risk means how dangerous the situation appears. Confidence means how sure the app is based on the info provided. A situation can be risk but low confidence if the user only provides a vague summary. A situation can be medium risk but high confidence if several clear warning signs are present but no immediate money transfer is requested. Separating these two ideas makes the app more honest and more professional.

The free version of Manual Scam Check should include enough value to protect users. Basic scam checks, plain results, core warning signs, and safer next steps should be free. The app should not lock basic safety behind payment. Paid features may include deeper history tracking, advanced evidence organization, family monitoring controls, detailed device checks, richer scam pattern comparisons, priority report preparation, or larger monthly review limits. The paid version should improve convenience and depth, not make the free version unsafe.

Manual Scam Check should avoid several harmful claims. It should not say, "This is guaranteed safe." It should not say, "This is definitely fraud" unless the product has a legally and technically defensible reason. It should not promise to recover money. It should not tell users to confront a suspected scammer. It should not advise users to send test payments. It should not encourage users to click risky links for investigation. It should not ask users to share passwords, one-time codes, full bank credentials, or full identification numbers.

The feature should support users who already feel embarrassed. Many scam victims hesitate because they think they should have known better. Manual Scam Check should use language that removes shame. It should say things like, "Scams are designed to feel believable," and "It is smart to check before acting." This tone matters because a user who feels judged may close the app and continue the risky conversation alone.

The feature is acceptable when a beginner can use it without knowing scam categories, when sensitive info is reduced before review, when risk and confidence are separate, when each result gives a safe next step, when the app avoids certainty it cannot prove, and when free users still receive meaningful protection.

### Feature 8.2: Before You Pay Review

Before You Pay is the feature for moments when the user has not sent money yet but is being pressured to act. This is one of the most important prevention features in Verivae because stopping a payment before it happens is usually easier than fixing the damage afterward. The feature should be built around one simple question: "Should I pause before sending this money?"

Before You Pay should recognize that payment pressure can appear in many forms. A scammer may ask for gift cards, wire transfers, crypto, peer-to-peer payment apps, bank transfers, prepaid cards, mobile deposits, payment links, marketplace deposits, rental app fees, job equipment fees, fake invoice payments, fake shipping fees, fake bank unlock fees, or family emergency payments. The app should treat payment method as a major clue because many scam payment methods are hard to reverse.

The feature should start with a short payment-context screen. It should ask who is requesting money, how the user met them, what payment method they want, how urgent it feels, whether the user has met the person in real life, whether the requester told the user not to tell anyone, whether the requester changed payment methods, whether the user is being promised money back, and whether the user is being threatened with account closure, arrest, embarrassment, legal trouble, missed delivery, lost job opportunity, or family harm. The questions should be written plainly and should not feel like a police report.

Before You Pay should use stronger warnings when the payment method is difficult to reverse. If a user says the requester wants gift cards, crypto, wire transfer, or payment through a stranger's account, the app should raise the risk level and explain why. It should say that some payment types are commonly used by scammers because they are fast, hard to reverse, or difficult to trace. It should not claim every such payment is a scam, but it should strongly recommend independent verification before sending anything.

The result screen for Before You Pay should be action-focused. It should not only explain risk. It should give the user a direct pause step. Examples include: call the organization through a number from the official website, contact the family member through a known phone number, visit the bank app directly instead of using the link, ask the marketplace seller to use platform-protected checkout, avoid paying with gift cards, avoid sending crypto to a stranger, wait and talk to a trusted person, or refuse to share login codes. The app should make the safer next step feel easier than continuing the risky payment.

Before You Pay should support a quick "pressure check." This check should ask whether the person is rushing the user, threatening consequences, demanding secrecy, changing the story, refusing normal verification, asking for unusual payment, or telling the user the payment must happen immediately. If multiple pressure signs are present, the app should highlight manipulation risk. Manipulation risk means the danger comes not only from the payment request, but also from the way the requester is pushing the user to ignore normal caution.

The feature should include a "pause script" that users can copy or read. A pause script is a short message the user can send without arguing. For example, it can say, "I do not send money under pressure. I am going to verify this another way first." Another version can say, "I need time to confirm this request. I will not send payment until I verify it independently." The app should not encourage long debates with risky people. Short refusal language is safer.

Before You Pay should be especially careful with family-emergency scams. If someone claims a loved one is in trouble, the app should guide the user to contact that person or another known family contact directly. It should recommend using a known number already saved in the user's contacts, not a number provided by the risky requester. It should also remind the user that real emergencies can be verified without secrecy or unusual payment methods.

The feature should be free for basic payment checks. Because payment prevention is central to user safety, the app should not block core payment-risk warnings behind a subscription. Paid enhancements may include detailed transaction history notes, trusted-helper sharing, automatic recurring payment-risk reminders, advanced scam-pattern comparisons, and printable evidence summaries. The free experience should still protect users in the moment they need help.

Before You Pay must avoid giving financial, legal, or banking guarantees. It should not promise that a bank can stop a payment. It should not promise that a payment app will refund money. It should not say the user will definitely recover money if they report quickly. It should instead use careful wording such as, "Contact your bank or payment provider as soon as possible," and "Ask what options are available." The feature should guide the user toward official support without pretending to control the outcome.

The feature is acceptable when it helps users pause before irreversible payments, clearly explains risky payment methods, gives safe verification steps, supports short refusal language, handles emotional pressure, and keeps core prevention available for free.

### Feature 8.3: Already Acted Recovery Guide

Already Acted is the feature for users who may have already clicked a link, sent money, shared a code, installed an app, gave remote access, provided personal info, or continued a risky conversation. This feature must be calm, practical, and nonjudgmental. Its purpose is not to make the user panic. Its purpose is to help the user take the next safe action in the right order.

The entry screen should ask what already happened. The user should be able to choose from simple options: I sent money, I shared a password, I shared a login code, I clicked a link, I downloaded something, I gave remote access, I shared personal info, I shipped an item, I received a risky check, I deposited money, I talked on the phone, I am not sure what happened, or something else. The app should allow more than one option because scams often involve several actions.

Already Acted should organize guidance by urgency. If the user shared a password, the app should recommend changing that password through the official site or app and enabling stronger account security if available. If the user shared a one-time code, the app should recommend securing the account immediately because login codes can allow account takeover. If the user sent money, the app should recommend contacting the payment provider, bank, card issuer, or platform through official channels. If the user installed software or allowed remote access, the app should recommend disconnecting from the risky session and using device security tools or trusted technical help.

The feature should include a "do this first" section. Users in distress need order, not a wall of info. The app should rank actions based on the user's answers. For example, if the user shared a banking password and sent money, securing the bank account may come before writing a full report. If the user installed remote access software, disconnecting and checking the device may come before continuing to chat with the risky person. If the user shared a Social Security number or ID doc, the app should suggest identity-protection steps in careful, non-alarmist language.

Already Acted should distinguish between immediate safety actions and documentation actions. Immediate safety actions protect accounts, devices, and payments. Documentation actions preserve screenshots, receipts, usernames, phone numbers, email addresses, links, transaction IDs, dates if known, and conversation history. The app should help users do both, but not in a confusing order. It should never ask users to keep engaging with a suspected scammer just to collect more evidence.

The feature should connect strongly to Evidence Vault. After giving first steps, it should ask whether the user wants to save related details. Evidence Vault can organize screenshots, notes, payment details, contact info, and report-ready summaries. The user should be able to skip evidence saving if they are too stressed or if saving evidence would require collecting sensitive info they do not want stored.

Already Acted should support a "trusted helper" option. If the user is overwhelmed, the app should let them share a summary with someone they trust, such as a family member, friend, caregiver, financial counselor, or support person. The app should avoid exposing sensitive info automatically. The user should preview what will be shared and remove details before sending. This matters because users may need help but still deserve control over their privacy.

The tone of Already Acted must be especially careful. The app should never say, "You made a mistake," "You were scammed," or "You should have known." It should say, "You still have useful steps you can take," and "Focus on securing accounts and payments first." The language should reduce shame because shame can delay action. The feature should be designed for users who may be scared, embarrassed, angry, confused, or exhausted.

The feature should include realistic limits. It should explain that the app can organize next steps, help identify likely risks, and prepare info for official support, but it cannot cancel payments, reverse transfers, recover funds, remove malware by itself, or guarantee law-enforcement outcomes. The app should not pretend to be a bank, lawyer, police department, antivirus company, or government agency.

The free version should include immediate recovery guidance for common situations. Users who already acted are often in the highest-stress moment, so basic help must be free. Paid enhancements may include extended evidence storage, organized timelines, report templates, family-helper collaboration, and scheduled follow-up reminders. Paid features should reduce effort, not withhold essential safety guidance.

The feature is acceptable when it gives calm next steps, organizes actions by urgency, avoids blame, connects to evidence saving, supports trusted helpers, explains limits honestly, and keeps emergency-style guidance available to free users.

### Feature 8.4: Evidence Vault

Evidence Vault is the feature that helps users collect and organize useful info without turning the app into a place that stores unnecessary private data. It should exist because scam situations can become confusing quickly. A user may have screenshots in one place, payment receipts in another place, phone numbers in call history, email addresses in Gmail, links in Messages, and notes in their memory. Evidence Vault should bring order to that info while keeping user control at the center.

Evidence Vault should store evidence as cases. A case is one risky situation. A case might be called "Marketplace sofa deposit," "Fake bank alert," "Job equipment fee," or "Unknown text about delivery." The app should allow the user to rename a case in plain text. It should not force legal wording or technical labels. Each case should contain optional items such as screenshots, pasted text, sender names, phone numbers, email addresses, links, payment method, amount if the user chooses to enter it, date if known, notes, risk result, safer next steps, and report status.

The feature should make evidence saving optional. Manual Scam Check and Before You Pay should work even if the user does not save anything. Some users will want maximum privacy and will prefer not to keep records in the app. Other users will want organized documentation because they need to contact a bank, payment app, marketplace platform, employer, school, family member, or official reporting channel. The app should respect both choices.

Evidence Vault should include privacy redaction before saving. If a screenshot or pasted text contains sensitive info, the app should offer to hide private details. The user should be able to blur, remove, or replace sensitive parts such as account numbers, passwords, codes, full addresses, identification numbers, and unrelated personal messages. The app should explain that evidence is often still useful without exposing every private detail.

Evidence Vault should separate raw evidence from report summaries. Raw evidence is the original screenshot, message, receipt, or note. A report summary is a cleaner version that explains what happened. The summary can say who contacted the user, what they requested, how they pressured the user, what payment method was involved, what warning signs appeared, and what the user did next. This separation helps the user share a clean report without accidentally sending private screenshots to someone who does not need them.

The feature should include an evidence timeline. A timeline is a simple ordered list of what happened first, second, third, and so on. The user should be able to add events manually, such as "Received text," "Clicked link," "Entered email," "Sent payment," "Called bank," or "Blocked sender." If the app can safely infer a timeline from imported messages or screenshots, it should still let the user confirm before saving. The app should not silently build a detailed history without consent.

Evidence Vault should help users prepare for reporting without telling them where they must report. Depending on the situation, a user may need to contact their bank, card issuer, payment app, marketplace platform, email provider, phone carrier, employer, local police, or a government reporting site. The app should organize the details that these groups commonly ask for: amount, payment method, transaction ID if available, sender contact, risky link, screenshots, timing, and what the user already tried. It should avoid promising that reporting will recover money.

The feature should include export options. Export means creating a shareable copy of selected evidence or a summary. The user should be able to export a plain summary, a detailed summary, or selected attachments. Before exporting, the app should preview what will be included and warn if sensitive data appears. Export should never automatically include everything by default. The safest default is to share less and let the user add more.

Evidence Vault should have strong deletion controls. Users should be able to delete a case, delete individual items, remove attachments, clear summaries, and turn off future saving. The app should use plain text such as "Delete this case from the app" instead of confusing technical words. If deletion has limits because of backups or device storage rules, the app should explain those limits clearly in beginner-friendly wording.

The free version should include basic case saving for a small number of cases, basic notes, and basic export summaries. Paid enhancements may include more storage, richer timelines, family-helper collaboration, advanced redaction tools, organized report packets, and longer history. The app should never force users to pay in order to delete evidence or protect their privacy.

The feature is acceptable when it keeps evidence organized, makes saving optional, supports redaction, separates raw evidence from summaries, gives users export control, provides deletion controls, and avoids collecting more sensitive info than needed.

### Feature 8.5: Trusted Helper

Trusted Helper is the feature that lets a user involve another person without giving that helper unnecessary access. This feature matters because many people avoid asking for help when they are embarrassed, but a trusted person can help them pause, verify, and recover. The app should make asking for help feel normal, private, and controlled.

A trusted helper can be a family member, friend, caregiver, financial coach, school staff member, workplace support person, or another person the user trusts. The app should not assume every user has the same support structure. It should allow the user to choose who helps, what they can see, and whether access is temporary or ongoing. The safest default is limited, case-by-case sharing.

Trusted Helper should include two sharing modes. The first mode is one-time share. In this mode, the user sends a selected summary or case snapshot to a helper. The helper does not get ongoing access. The second mode is ongoing helper access. In this mode, the user allows the helper to see selected cases, alerts, or summaries over time. Ongoing access should require clear consent, easy review, and easy removal.

The app should never secretly share private scam checks. If the user connects a helper, the app should clearly show what will be shared. For example, the user may share only the risk result, only the safer next step, a redacted summary, selected screenshots, or a full case packet. The app should not automatically share full messages, bank details, payment amounts, account names, passwords, login codes, identification numbers, or unrelated personal content.

Trusted Helper should include a helper invitation flow. The user should be able to invite someone by entering an email address or phone number if the app supports it, but the app should explain what the helper role means before the invitation is sent. The helper should receive a plain explanation that they are there to help review possible scam situations, not to control the user's account, approve every decision, or access unrelated personal info.

The helper view should be simple. A helper should see a short summary, risk level, confidence level, warning signs, advised next steps, and any evidence the user explicitly shared. The helper should be able to respond with support such as "Pause before paying," "Call the bank using the official number," or "Let's verify this together." The helper should not be able to change the user's results, delete evidence, or take over the account unless the user separately grants a very specific permission.

Trusted Helper should include emergency-style sharing without panic language. If the app detects that the user may be about to send money or share a code, it can ask, "Would you like to check this with someone you trust first?" It should not force the user to involve another person. It should not shame them. The feature should make help available at the right moment while respecting independence.

The feature should be designed carefully for older users and users with low technical confidence. Some users may not understand permission settings. The app should use plain labels such as "Can see this one case" and "Can see future cases I choose to share." It should avoid confusing account-management words. It should show a simple review screen before any sharing happens.

Trusted Helper should include revocation controls. Revocation means taking access back. The user should be able to remove a helper, stop sharing a case, stop future sharing, or change what the helper can see. The app should display these controls in Settings and inside each shared case. If a helper has already received an exported copy outside the app, the app should explain that it cannot take back copies already sent outside the app.

The free version should include one-time redacted sharing because asking for help is a basic safety need. Paid enhancements may include multiple trusted helpers, shared family dashboards, recurring check-ins, caregiver workflows, more detailed collaboration, and detailed case-history sharing. The paid model should never trap a user in unwanted sharing or charge for removing a helper.

The feature is acceptable when users control exactly what is shared, helpers receive useful but limited info, one-time sharing is available, ongoing sharing is clearly optional, revocation is easy, and the feature increases safety without reducing privacy.

### Area 8 Part 1 accept rules
