Area 8 Part 1 is acceptable when the core features are understandable without technical knowledge, each feature explains its purpose and boundaries, free users receive meaningful protection, paid features add convenience rather than blocking safety, privacy controls appear inside the feature descriptions, and the app avoids guarantees it cannot prove. These specifications should also align with Area 6's privacy rules and Area 7's risk-explanation rules. Manual Scam Check, Before You Pay, Already Acted, Evidence Vault, and Trusted Helper should feel linked rather than separate tools. The user should be able to move from checking a risky message, to pausing a payment, to taking recovery steps, to saving evidence, to asking a trusted person for help without feeling lost.

### Area 8 Part 2: Device Protection and Integration Feature Specifications

Area 8 should have four total parts. Part 1 defines the core protection features. Part 2 defines device protection, weekly checks, linked-device review, permission review, and phone integration safety. Part 3 should define reporting, scam education, scam pattern library behavior, and privacy redaction in deeper detail. Part 4 should define cross-feature behavior, limits, paid/free boundaries, user settings, and final Area 8 accept rules.

This part exists because the app is not only a message checker. The app should also help users understand whether risky activity may involve their phone, email account, messages, linked devices, app permissions, account connections, or unsafe settings. The app must handle this carefully. It should be useful without pretending to have unlimited access to the user's device. It should explain what it can check, what it cannot check, and when the user should use built-in phone security tools, official account settings, or trusted technical help.

### Feature 8.6: Device Security Check

Device Security Check is the feature that helps a user review whether their phone or linked device may have been affected by a scam. The feature should be especially useful after the user clicked a risky link, downloaded an unknown file, installed an app, allowed remote access, shared a login code, signed into a fake page, changed security settings, or noticed unusual behavior. It should not be described as a magic virus scanner. It should be described as a guided device safety review that helps identify warning signs, risky permissions, risky settings, and next steps.

The word virus can be confusing for beginners. In the app, the safer beginner-friendly wording is harmful software. The app can explain that harmful software means an app, file, setting, or tool that may let someone spy, steal info, control part of the device, show fake screens, redirect links, or trick the user into giving more info. The app can still mention viruses because users use that word, but it should not make false promises that it can find every virus on every device.

Device Security Check should start by asking what happened before the user became worried. The app should ask whether the user clicked a link, downloaded a file, installed an app, gave screen-sharing or remote-control access, scanned a QR code, entered a password, entered a login code, allowed a browser alert, installed a profile, allowed a VPN, changed accessibility settings, changed alert settings, or noticed pop-ups. These questions should be phrased as simple choices. The app should avoid technical terms unless it immediately explains them.

The feature should then ask what device is involved. The user may be using an iPhone, Android phone, iPad, Android tablet, Windows computer, Mac, Chromebook, or another device. The app should avoid pretending that every platform works the same way. A phone is different from a laptop. An iPhone is different from an Android phone. Some systems limit what outside apps can inspect. Those limits are a privacy and safety feature of modern devices, not just a weakness of Verivae. The app should say this plainly so users understand why some checks are guided rather than fully automatic.

Device Security Check should include a visible feature boundary. The app should say that it can guide the user through risky settings, risky apps, risky permissions, dangerous links, risky alerts, and account-safety steps. It should also say that it may not be able to inspect every file, read every app's private data, prove that a device is clean, or remove every harmful program by itself. This boundary protects user trust because it avoids overclaiming.

The main check should be organized into categories. The first category is risky apps. The app should help users review recently installed apps, apps they do not recognize, apps installed around the time of the scam, apps with strange names, apps that look like security tools but were advised by a stranger, and apps that request broad control. The app should never delete apps automatically. It should guide the user to review and remove risky apps through the device's normal settings.

The second category is permissions. A permission is an allowance the user gives an app, such as access to contacts, photos, camera, microphone, location, alerts, files, accessibility controls, screen recording, or account info. Device Security Check should explain permissions in plain text. It should help the user notice when an app has more access than it reasonably needs. For example, a flashlight-style app usually should not need contact access. A scam-related remote support app may request screen sharing, accessibility access, or device administration. The app should flag unusual permission patterns without claiming every unusual permission is malicious.

The third category is browser and link safety. If the user clicked a risky link, the app should help them check whether they entered info, downloaded anything, allowed alerts, saved a password, or stayed signed in to a fake page. The app should recommend safer actions such as closing the risky page, avoiding the link, clearing risky browser alerts if needed, changing passwords through the official app or website, and using official account security settings. The app should not tell users to revisit risky links to gather evidence.

The fourth category is remote access and screen sharing. If the user allowed a stranger to view or control their device, Device Security Check should treat this as risk. The feature should explain that remote access can let another person see screens, guide actions, or control parts of the device depending on the tool used. The app should recommend disconnecting from the session, closing the remote tool, reviewing installed apps, changing important passwords from a trusted device if possible, contacting banks or account providers if financial accounts were shown, and using built-in security scans or trusted technical support.

The fifth category is account security. Many scams affect the user's accounts more than the physical device. The app should guide the user to review email accounts, bank accounts, payment accounts, social media accounts, marketplace accounts, cloud storage, phone carrier accounts, and password managers if relevant. It should ask whether the user shared a password, shared a one-time code, approved a login prompt, added a new recovery email, changed a phone number, or gave access to Gmail or another account. The app should recommend reviewing account security through official settings.

The sixth category is alert and profile abuse. Some scams trick users into allowing browser alerts, installing configuration profiles, or approving tools that make fake warnings appear. Device Security Check should explain that a fake alert can look scary but does not always mean the device is infected. The app should guide users to remove risky alerts, profiles, or settings through official device controls. It should not ask the user to install a random cleaner app from an advertisement.

The Device Security Check result should show three layers: device concern, account concern, and scam concern. Device concern means the phone or computer may have risky apps, permissions, downloads, or settings. Account concern means the user's login, email, bank, payment, or social account may be at risk. Scam concern means the situation itself looks like a scam even if the device is probably fine. Separating these layers helps users understand what to do. A risky bank text may be high scam concern but low device concern if the user did not click. A remote access incident may be high device concern and high account concern even if no money was sent.

The result should include a clear next-step order. The app might say: disconnect from risky remote access first, stop communicating with the requester, secure important accounts, contact financial providers if money or banking data was exposed, review risky apps and permissions, run built-in security tools, save evidence if safe, and ask a trusted person for help. The order should change based on what the user selected. The app should avoid giving the same generic checklist to everyone.

Device Security Check should include built-in safety copy for anxious users. If the user reports pop-ups or fake warnings, the app should say that scammers often use alarming messages to make people act quickly. It should tell the user not to call phone numbers shown in risky pop-ups, not to install suggested cleaner apps from the risky page, and not to grant remote access to strangers who claim they are support agents. This language should be calm and direct.

The free version of Device Security Check should include basic guided checks for recent scam incidents, risky apps, permissions, links, account exposure, and remote access. Paid enhancements may include weekly checks, linked-device summaries, detailed device-history notes, family-helper alerts, detailed account-connection monitoring, and longer device-security history. The app should not make users pay to see immediate safety steps after a likely device compromise.

Device Security Check is acceptable when it helps users review risky device behavior, explains platform limits, separates device concern from account concern and scam concern, avoids claiming to find every virus, gives safe next steps, and never encourages risky investigation.

### Feature 8.7: Weekly Deep Check

Weekly Deep Check is a scheduled review that helps users catch risks they may have missed. It should not be a scary weekly alarm. It should feel like a calm safety maintenance routine, similar to checking locks, reviewing bank alerts, or cleaning up account settings. The purpose is to help users notice risky patterns before they become bigger problems.

Weekly Deep Check should be optional. Users should choose whether to turn it on. The app should not enable deep checks without clear permission. A weekly check may touch sensitive areas such as app permissions, linked accounts, recent scam checks, evidence cases, device-security reminders, and account-safety tasks. Because of that, the feature must be transparent and user-controlled.

The setup screen should explain what a weekly check is. It should say that the app can review selected safety areas once per week and show a simple summary. The user should be able to choose which areas are included: scam-check history, risky links saved in cases, device-permission reminders, recently added trusted helpers, evidence cases with unfinished next steps, linked Gmail review if enabled, message-review integration if enabled, linked-device status if enabled, and account-security reminders. The user should be able to leave some areas off.

Weekly Deep Check should avoid collecting new private info unnecessarily. If the user has not linked Gmail, Messages, or another service, the weekly check should not pressure them to connect it. If the user has linked a service, the check should use the least info needed. Least info needed means the app should review only what is necessary for the safety purpose and avoid storing full message contents unless the user explicitly saves them to a case.

The weekly summary should be short and understandable. It should not bury the user in technical logs. A good summary might say: no urgent issues found, two unfinished safety tasks remain, one app permission needs review, one saved case has not been exported, and one linked account should be checked because the user reported sharing a code. If nothing important is found, the app should say so calmly. It should not invent warnings just to feel useful.

Weekly Deep Check should prioritize open safety tasks. If the user previously marked that they shared a password but never confirmed changing it, the app should remind them. If the user started an Evidence Vault case but never exported a summary, the app can ask if they still need it. If the user linked a trusted helper but has not reviewed sharing settings in a long time, the app can suggest reviewing access. These reminders should be helpful, not nagging.

The feature should include risk aging. Risk aging means older unresolved issues can remain visible but become less urgent depending on context. For example, an old risky text that the user never clicked may not need weekly warnings forever. But an unresolved shared password or unknown remote-access app may remain important. The app should avoid making every old issue feel equally urgent.

Weekly Deep Check should include a quiet mode. Some users may not want security alerts on the lock screen because a family member, coworker, or stranger might see them. The app should allow private alert wording such as "the app has a weekly review ready" instead of "Possible scam or device risk found." Sensitive details should stay inside the app after auth.

The feature should include snooze and stop controls. Snooze means delay the reminder. Stop means turn off the weekly check. The user should be able to snooze one reminder, skip a week, change the day, change the time, remove a check category, or turn off weekly checks completely. These controls should be easy to find. The app should not make weekly checks feel like a trap.

Weekly Deep Check should support trusted-helper summaries only with consent. If the user has a trusted helper, they may choose to share a limited weekly summary. The summary should not automatically include private screenshots, message contents, payment amounts, full contact details, or sensitive account data. A safe summary might say, "One unresolved payment-risk case needs review" rather than exposing the full story. The user should approve what is shared.

Weekly Deep Check should not be marketed as a complete antivirus replacement. It can help with scam-related device safety, account reminders, risky permissions, and unresolved risk tasks. It may work alongside built-in device protections and other security tools. It should not claim that running a weekly check guarantees the device is clean, guarantees account safety, or prevents every future scam.

The free version should include a basic weekly review for active scam cases and unresolved safety steps. Paid enhancements may include more linked services, linked-device summaries, family-helper weekly reports, detailed storage, richer historical trends, and more advanced permission reminders. The free version should still include enough weekly support to help a user remain safer after a scam scare.

Weekly Deep Check is acceptable when it is optional, easy to understand, easy to turn off, respectful of privacy, focused on unresolved risks, calm in tone, and honest about what it can and cannot verify.

### Feature 8.8: Linked Device Review

Linked Device Review helps users understand whether the app is protecting only the current phone or also helping them review other devices. A linked device can mean another phone, tablet, computer, or family device that the user chooses to include. This feature should be designed carefully because linked devices can involve other people's privacy.

The feature should never scan another person's device without that person's consent. If the user wants to help a parent, child, partner, roommate, friend, or employee, the app should require permission from the person who owns or uses the device unless the legal and account context clearly allows management. The app should explain this in simple terms: checking another device should be something the device owner agrees to.

Linked Device Review should have two modes. The first mode is personal device list. This lets the user record and review their own phone, tablet, or computer. The second mode is helper-supported device review. This lets a user help someone else through a guided check, but it should still require the other person to participate or approve what is shared. The app should not create hidden monitoring.

The device list should be simple. A user should be able to add a device name such as "My iPhone," "Work laptop," "Dad's tablet," or "Old Android phone." The app should avoid forcing technical identifiers unless needed. Each device can show basic status such as last reviewed, open safety tasks, linked account concerns, recent scam-related incident, weekly check status, and whether the user has enabled reminders.

Linked Device Review should distinguish manual review from automatic review. Manual review means the user follows guided steps and confirms what they see. Automatic review means the app can check supported data through approved permissions or platform-supported tools. The app should clearly label which is happening. If a platform does not allow certain automatic checks, the app should provide guided manual steps instead of pretending the check is automatic.

The feature should support common linked-device situations. A user may have clicked a risky link on a phone but later changed passwords on a laptop. A user may have installed a risky app on an old device. A user may have a parent who receives scam texts on a tablet. A user may use Gmail on multiple devices and worry that one login exposed the account. Linked Device Review should help organize these situations without assuming every device is infected.

Linked Device Review should include account-spread awareness. Sometimes a scam affects multiple devices because the same account is signed in everywhere. For example, if an email password was shared, the risk may follow the email account across the phone, laptop, and tablet. The app should explain that changing the password and reviewing account sessions may matter more than checking only one device. This distinction helps users focus on the right fix.

The feature should include linked-device privacy boundaries. The app should not show another device's personal messages, photos, browsing history, contacts, or full app list to a helper unless the device owner clearly chooses to share that info. Most linked-device summaries should be high level: needs review, last checked, open task, account concern, or no urgent issue found. Detailed data should require explicit user action.

Linked Device Review should support family use without becoming surveillance. The app can help a family protect an older relative from scams, but it should avoid designs that let one person secretly watch another person's private messages. A safer model is consent-based review, shared alerts, trusted-helper summaries, and user-approved case sharing. The app should focus on protection and education, not control.

The free version may include a basic personal device list and manual review steps for one or two devices. Paid enhancements may include multiple linked devices, family helper summaries, recurring review schedules, multi-device case linking, and detailed history. The app should not charge users to remove a linked device or stop sharing device status.

Linked Device Review is acceptable when it clearly separates personal review from helping someone else, requires consent for shared or helper-supported review, avoids hidden monitoring, explains account-spread risk, and gives users control over device status and shared summaries.

### Feature 8.9: Permission and Account Connection Review

Permission and Account Connection Review helps users understand what the app is allowed to access and what other apps or services may be linked to their accounts. This feature matters because scams often involve more than a single message. A user may have granted a risky app permission, approved an account connection, signed into a fake page, accepted a third-party login, or allowed alerts that continue the scam.

Inside Verivae, this feature should show the app's own permissions first. It should tell the user whether the app can access alerts, screenshots, photos selected by the user, Gmail if linked, messages if supported and linked, contacts if ever requested, files selected by the user, device status signals if supported, and trusted-helper sharing. Each permission should have a plain explanation. For example, "Photos access is used only when you choose a screenshot for review" is clearer than technical permission wording.

The user should be able to disconnect permissions from inside Settings where possible. If the OS requires the user to change permissions in system settings, the app should guide them there with plain instructions. The app should not hide permission controls. If a permission is needed for a feature, the app should explain what will stop working when the permission is removed.

The feature should also guide users through reviewing account connections outside Verivae. Many services let users connect third-party apps, grant account access, or stay signed in on multiple devices. If a user reports that they signed into a risky page or shared a login code, the app should recommend checking official account-security pages for unfamiliar sessions, recovery methods, linked apps, forwarding rules, filters, saved payment methods, and password changes. The app should not ask for the user's full account password.

For Gmail integration, the feature should be especially conservative. If the user connects Gmail, the app should explain exactly what type of email access is requested and why. The safest design is to ask for the narrowest useful permission and to review only user-selected risky emails unless the user clearly enables broader monitoring. The app should avoid reading the whole mailbox by default. It should not store full email contents unless the user saves a specific item to Evidence Vault.

For Messages integration, the app must respect platform limits and user consent. The app should support user-selected message review where possible, such as sharing a risky message into Verivae or pasting a message manually. If automatic message monitoring is not allowed or not appropriate, the app should say so plainly. It should not claim it can read all messages on every phone. It should also avoid collecting private conversations unrelated to scam checks.

Permission and Account Connection Review should include a permissions dashboard. The dashboard should show linked services, last review time, what each connection is used for, what data may be reviewed, whether data is saved by default, and how to disconnect. The dashboard should use simple status labels: Not Linked, Linked for Manual Review, Linked for Weekly Review, Needs Attention, or Dislinked. It should avoid vague labels that hide what is really happening.

The feature should include risky permission warnings. If the user reports installing an app during a scam and that app has broad access, the app should flag that as a device-security concern. It should explain why certain permissions are sensitive. Accessibility access can allow powerful interaction with the device. Alert access may reveal messages. Screen recording can expose private info. Location can reveal where the user is. Contacts can expose other people. The app should explain these risks without overwhelming the user.

The feature should also include account-recovery reminders. If the user says they shared a password or code, the app should recommend checking for account changes such as new recovery email, new phone number, unknown login session, risky forwarding rule, unfamiliar linked app, or changed security settings. It should encourage using official account settings and avoiding links from the risky message.

The free version should include the app's own permission dashboard, basic account-connection guidance, and manual review steps. Paid enhancements may include weekly permission review, linked-account reminders, multiple-service summaries, family-helper permission reports, and longer history. The user should never have to pay to disconnect a permission or remove the app's access.

Permission and Account Connection Review is acceptable when users can understand what access exists, why it exists, how to remove it, what risks broad permissions create, and how account connections relate to scam recovery. It should make access visible instead of hiding it behind technical settings.

### Feature 8.10: Phone, Gmail, and Message Integration Guardrails

Phone, Gmail, and Message Integration Guardrails define how the app should integrate with everyday communication tools without becoming invasive. The app should be useful because scams often arrive through text messages, email, phone calls, social media chats, marketplace conversations, and payment apps. At the same time, the app must not treat private communication as an unlimited data source.

The safest starting model is user-initiated review. User-initiated means the user chooses what to send into Verivae. A user can paste a message, upload a screenshot, use a share sheet if supported, forward a risky email if supported, select a Gmail message if linked, or summarize a phone call. This model respects privacy because the user decides what is reviewed.

A more advanced model is opt-in monitoring. Opt-in means the user clearly turns it on. Monitoring should be limited to specific safety purposes, such as identifying likely scam patterns in risky messages, reviewing selected folders, or checking new messages that match clear risk categories. The app should not silently read every message forever. If monitoring exists, the app should show what is monitored, how often, what is saved, and how to stop it.

Gmail integration should focus on risky email review, not general inbox reading. The app can help users check risky sender names, email addresses, links, attachment warnings, urgency language, fake invoices, fake account alerts, fake delivery notices, fake job offers, fake bank warnings, and impersonation attempts. If linked, the app should still avoid storing full emails unless the user saves them. It should also give users a manual alternative so Gmail connection is not required for basic protection.

Messages integration should focus on user-selected risky texts where possible. The app should support copying, pasting, screenshot upload, share-sheet import, or manual summary. If a platform allows deeper integration, the app should still use clear permission language and privacy controls. If a platform blocks deeper access, the app should provide practical alternatives rather than making false promises.

Phone-call support should focus on after-call review and call-note capture. The app should not claim it can listen to every phone call unless the user has explicitly enabled a supported feature and local law, platform rules, and consent requirements are handled. A safer first version is manual call summary: the user chooses "I got a risky call" and describes what was said. The app can ask whether the caller claimed to be a bank, government agency, tech support worker, family member, delivery company, employer, romantic partner, investor, or marketplace buyer.

The integration guardrails should define what the app should never do. It should never secretly read private conversations. It should never sell message contents. It should never share full messages with helpers by default. It should never train public-facing examples on a user's private scam messages without explicit permission. It should never ask users to forward sensitive codes, passwords, full account numbers, or private documents unless there is a clear redaction and consent flow. It should never require account integration for basic manual checking.

The app should include a simple integration settings screen. Each integration should have a plain explanation: what it does, what it can see, what it saves, what it does not save, whether it participates in weekly checks, whether trusted helpers can see summaries, and how to disconnect. The app should show linked services in one place so the user does not have to hunt through hidden menus.

The app should also include integration fallback paths. If Gmail is not linked, the user can paste email text or upload a screenshot. If Messages integration is not available, the user can copy and paste the message. If call recording or call analysis is unavailable, the user can summarize the call. If automatic device scanning is limited, the user can follow guided manual review. These fallback paths make the app useful even when platform limits exist.

Phone and message integrations should also avoid creating false urgency. The app should not send constant alerts for every risky phrase. Too many alerts can make users ignore warnings. The app should prioritize strong warning signs, user-selected review, unresolved risky cases, and direct user requests. The goal is useful protection, not noise.

The free version should include manual input, screenshot upload if supported, basic Gmail or email review alternatives, message paste review, and call-summary review. Paid enhancements may include more linked integrations, weekly linked-service summaries, trusted-helper sharing rules, detailed integration history, and advanced filtering. The app should never require paid integration for a user to manually check a risky message.

Phone, Gmail, and Message Integration Guardrails are acceptable when integration is optional, clear, privacy-controlled, useful without full account access, honest about platform limits, and supported by manual fallback options.

### Area 8 Part 2 accept rules

Area 8 Part 2 is acceptable when device-related features are helpful without overpromising, when weekly checks are optional and easy to stop, when linked-device review requires consent, when permissions are visible and removable, when Gmail and Messages integrations stay user-controlled, and when Verivae clearly separates scam risk, account risk, and device risk. The app should help users check for harmful software or risky settings, but it should not claim to replace every security tool or prove that every device is clean. Part 2 should strengthen Area 6's privacy rules and Area 7's risk-explanation rules while staying focused on what the app can actually do for users.

### Area 8 Part 3: Reporting, Education, Pattern Library, and Privacy Redaction Feature Specifications

Part 3 defines the features that help Verivae turn scam confusion into organized understanding. Part 1 covered direct protection and recovery. Part 2 covered device protection and integrations. Part 3 covers what happens when the user needs to understand the scam, prepare info for official support, learn from the situation, compare the situation to known scam patterns, and remove private details before sharing or saving evidence. These features should make the app more useful without making it noisy, invasive, or overly confident.

### Feature 8.11: Reporting Guide

Reporting Guide is the feature that helps users understand where and how they may report a risky situation. It should not force the user to report. It should not claim that reporting guarantees recovery. It should not pretend that Verivae itself is a bank, police department, payment app, marketplace platform, email provider, or government agency. Its purpose is to organize the user's next steps so they can contact the right official channel with clearer info.

The feature should begin by asking what kind of situation happened. A payment scam needs different reporting guidance than a fake job offer, fake bank alert, fake delivery message, account takeover, marketplace deposit, romance scam, fake investment pitch, fake tech support call, or risky email. The user should not need to know the official category name. The app should ask plain questions such as: Did money move? Was an account accessed? Was a password shared? Was a phone number or email used? Was a marketplace involved? Was a package or delivery mentioned? Was a bank, government agency, employer, or family member impersonated?

Reporting Guide should turn the user's answers into a practical reporting path. A reporting path is a suggested order of places to contact. For example, if money was sent, the first path may involve the payment provider, bank, card issuer, or platform used for the transaction. If an account was accessed, the first path may involve the official account-security page. If a marketplace listing was involved, the path may include the marketplace platform. If identity info was shared, the path may include identity-protection steps. The app should phrase this as guidance, not legal or guaranteed recovery advice.

The feature should include a report readiness screen. This screen should show what info the user has already saved and what may still be missing. Useful fields may include the risky sender, phone number, email address, username, profile link, website link, requested payment method, amount if the user chose to save it, transaction ID if available, screenshots, dates if known, what the scammer asked for, what the user already did, and what action the user wants help with. The app should label missing info as optional unless it is truly necessary for the selected report type.

Reporting Guide should connect directly to Evidence Vault. If the user has a case saved, the app should be able to build a clean summary from that case. The summary should not automatically include every raw screenshot or private message. Instead, it should separate key facts, timeline, warning signs, money or account exposure, and selected attachments. The user should preview the report packet before using it. Preview matters because the user may need to remove private details before sharing the packet outside the app.

The feature should include plain reporting scripts. A script is a prepared explanation the user can copy, read, or use as a checklist when contacting a bank, payment provider, platform, or support channel. A script should be short enough for a stressed user to understand. It may say: "I believe I was targeted by a scam. I need help securing my account and checking whether this transaction can be stopped or disputed." Another script may say: "Someone contacted me pretending to be your company and asked me to click a link. I did not use the link and want to verify whether this message was real." The app should allow the user to edit scripts before use.

Reporting Guide should distinguish urgent reporting from normal documentation. Urgent reporting means the user may need to contact a bank, card issuer, payment app, account provider, or platform quickly because money, access, or personal info is at risk. Normal documentation means the user may want to report the scam attempt or save info for future reference, but there is no immediate account or payment emergency. The app should use this distinction to prioritize actions.

The feature should also include "do not do this" guidance. Users should be told not to use phone numbers, links, or email addresses from the risky message as their official reporting route. They should be encouraged to use the official app, official website typed manually, a known phone number, or support contact already saved from a trusted source. The app should explain this plainly: scammers often put fake support links inside the scam itself.

Reporting Guide should avoid overwhelming users with too many destinations. If the app suggests ten places at once, the user may do nothing. The result should focus on the most relevant first contact, then the second contact, then optional additional reporting. The app can label them as "Start here," "Also consider," and "Optional record." This keeps the flow practical.

The free version should include basic reporting guidance, report readiness, and copyable scripts for common scam situations. Paid enhancements may include richer report packets, longer saved report history, multi-case report summaries, trusted-helper review before reporting, and more organized export formats. The app should not make users pay to learn the first place they should contact after a likely scam.

Reporting Guide is acceptable when it helps users decide who to contact, prepares useful info, avoids guarantees, reduces confusion, does not replace official support, and gives users control over what evidence is included.

### Feature 8.12: Report Packet Builder

Report Packet Builder is the feature that turns a messy scam situation into a clear packet the user can use when contacting official support, a trusted helper, a bank, a payment app, a platform, or another relevant party. A report packet is not a legal document by default. It is a structured summary that helps the user explain what happened without forgetting important details.

The packet should have selectable sections. The user should be able to include or exclude a case summary, timeline, payment details, account details, risky sender details, links, screenshots, user notes, app risk result, app warning signs, safer next steps, and selected attachments. The app should not assume that more info is always better. Some support contacts need only a short summary. Others may need more details. The user should control the level of detail.

Report Packet Builder should include three packet sizes. The first size is Quick Summary. This is a short paragraph or small set of facts for fast support conversations. The second size is Standard Packet. This includes the main facts, timeline, warning signs, and selected evidence. The third size is Detailed Packet. This includes more complete evidence and notes for cases where the user needs a stronger record. The app should clearly show what each size includes before the user exports or shares it.

The packet should include a plain timeline when available. A timeline helps support staff understand the sequence of events. It may include when the risky message arrived, when the user clicked a link, when money was sent, when a password was shared, when the user contacted support, and when the user changed settings. If exact dates or times are missing, the app should allow approximate wording such as "earlier today," "last week," or "not sure." The app should not invent exact times.

Report Packet Builder should include a risk explanation section, but it must be careful. The app can say what warning signs it detected and why they matter. It should not state that a person committed a crime unless that has been confirmed by an appropriate authority. It should use language such as "The situation matched warning signs commonly seen in scams" rather than making legal conclusions. This protects the user and the company from overclaiming.

The packet should be redaction-aware. Before the user exports or shares anything, the app should scan the packet for obvious sensitive details and ask whether to remove or hide them. Sensitive details may include passwords, login codes, full bank numbers, full card numbers, full identification numbers, home address, private messages unrelated to the scam, photos of children, medical details, or other unrelated personal data. The app should explain that redaction helps protect privacy while preserving useful facts.

The feature should support different sharing destinations without deeply integrating with all of them at first. A user may want to copy text, save a file, share to email, send to a trusted helper, or keep the packet inside Evidence Vault. The first version can focus on copyable summaries and exportable text. Later versions may add richer exports. The app should avoid promising direct submission to every agency or platform unless that connection is actually supported.

Report Packet Builder should preserve user dignity. The summary should avoid shaming phrases such as "victim fell for scam." It should use neutral wording such as "User received a risky request" or "User reports sending payment after receiving a message that appeared to impersonate a known organization." The app should help the user sound clear and credible without making them feel blamed.

The packet should include a review screen before final output. This screen should show: who can see this, what details are included, what sensitive items were detected, what attachments are included, and whether the packet includes app-generated analysis. The user should be able to edit text, remove attachments, change the packet size, or cancel.

The free version should include Quick Summary and basic Standard Packet creation. Paid enhancements may include detailed packet templates, multi-case packet building, richer formatting, family-helper review, long-term packet storage, and platform-specific packet organization. The user should never have to pay to remove sensitive data from a packet.

Report Packet Builder is acceptable when it produces useful summaries, keeps user control over included evidence, supports redaction, avoids legal overclaiming, and helps users communicate clearly with official support or trusted helpers.

### Feature 8.13: Scam Pattern Library

Scam Pattern Library is the feature that helps users understand what type of scam pattern their situation resembles. A pattern is a repeated structure scammers use, such as fake urgency, impersonation, unusual payment, secrecy, fake refund, fake job equipment purchase, marketplace deposit, fake bank alert, fake delivery issue, romance pressure, fake investment return, fake tech support, account verification trick, or family emergency request. The library should teach patterns without making the user memorize technical names.

The feature should connect to scam-check results. When Manual Scam Check or Before You Pay detects warning signs, the result can link to relevant pattern explanations. For example, if the app finds urgency, secrecy, and gift-card payment, it can show a short explanation of payment-pressure scams. If the app finds a fake delivery link and request for a small fee, it can show a delivery-fee impersonation pattern. This helps the user understand why the situation is risky instead of simply trusting a score.

The pattern library should be organized by user-facing situations, not only by expert categories. Categories may include money requests, account alerts, job offers, marketplace buying and selling, romance and friendship pressure, family emergencies, tech support warnings, delivery messages, investment offers, prize or refund claims, rental listings, check deposits, and login codes. A beginner should be able to browse by what happened to them.

Each scam pattern should have a consistent layout. The app should explain what the pattern looks like, why it works emotionally, common warning signs, what the scammer wants, what the user should avoid doing, safer verification steps, and what to save if the user needs evidence. The layout should be predictable so the user does not have to relearn the screen every time.

The library should include emotional manipulation explanations. Scams are not only technical tricks. They often use fear, urgency, shame, excitement, loneliness, authority, scarcity, or trust. The app should explain this without blaming the user. For example, a family emergency scam works because people care about loved ones and want to act quickly. A fake job scam works because people need work and may feel pressure to secure an opportunity. These explanations can make users more resilient.

Scam Pattern Library should include pattern comparison. If a user's case matches several patterns, the app should show the top matches and explain the difference. A fake bank alert and a fake delivery alert may both include risky links, but the claimed organization, requested action, and risk may differ. Pattern comparison helps avoid oversimplified labels.

The feature should include examples, but examples must be carefully handled. Example messages should be clearly labeled as examples, not real user messages. If the app uses real reports or user-submitted material in the future, it should require explicit permission and strong redaction. The design brief should assume that private user messages are not automatically used as public examples.

The library should include safe verification guidance for each pattern. Verification means checking through a separate trusted route. For a bank alert, the user should use the bank's official app or a known number. For a family emergency, the user should contact the family member or another known contact. For a marketplace deal, the user should stay inside platform-protected payment and messaging where possible. For a job offer, the user should verify the company through official channels and avoid paying upfront fees to a stranger.

Scam Pattern Library should also include "why this might be legitimate" context where appropriate. Not every odd message is a scam. Some legitimate messages are poorly written, urgent, or confusing. The app should explain what legitimate verification looks like. This makes the product more trustworthy because it does not label everything as dangerous.

The free version should include the core pattern library and links from scam-check results. Paid enhancements may include deeper pattern comparisons, personalized learning history, family education packs, printable guides, detailed examples, and advanced case-to-pattern mapping. Basic scam education should remain free because education is a core safety feature.

Scam Pattern Library is acceptable when it teaches scam patterns clearly, connects to real user situations, avoids blame, supports safe verification, protects private examples, and helps users understand risk rather than merely obeying a warning.

### Feature 8.14: Learning Center

Learning Center is the feature that teaches users how to become safer over time. It is different from Scam Pattern Library because the pattern library explains types of scams, while Learning Center teaches habits, concepts, and decision skills. The goal is to make users more confident without overwhelming them.

The Learning Center should be organized into short lessons. A lesson should take only a few minutes. Topics may include: how to pause before paying, how to verify a message outside the conversation, why gift cards and crypto are risky for strangers, why login codes should not be shared, how fake urgency works, how account takeover happens, how remote access scams work, how to check official links, how to talk to a trusted helper, and what to do if money was already sent.

Lessons should be written for beginners. The app should not assume the user knows cybersecurity terms. When it uses a term, it should explain it immediately. For example, account takeover means someone gets into an account that belongs to you. Two-step verification means an account asks for a second proof that it is really you. A recovery email is an email address used to regain access to an account. These explanations make the app useful for people with low technical confidence.

The Learning Center should be linked to live app moments. If a user is reviewing a risky payment request, the app can offer a short lesson on payment pressure after the result. If a user shared a login code, the app can offer a lesson on account takeover. If a user installed remote access software, the app can offer a lesson on screen-sharing scams. Lessons should be offered at helpful moments, but they should not block urgent safety actions.

The feature should include calm progress tracking. The app can show completed lessons, saved tips, or advised next lessons. It should avoid turning scam education into a game that makes users rush through important safety info. The tone should be steady and practical. The user should feel more prepared, not tested or judged.

Learning Center should support different user groups. Some users may be young adults dealing with marketplace scams, job scams, and payment app requests. Some may be older adults targeted by fake tech support or family emergency scams. Some may be parents helping children understand online safety. Some may be caregivers helping relatives. The app can recommend lessons based on user needs, but it should avoid stereotypes. Age alone should not determine what the app assumes.

The feature should include shareable learning cards. A learning card is a short tip that can be shared with a trusted person. For example: "Never share a login code with someone who contacted you first." Another card might say: "If someone asks for gift cards as payment, pause and verify." These cards should not include private case details unless the user chooses to attach them.

Learning Center should avoid fear-based education. Scare tactics can make people anxious and less able to think clearly. The app should teach practical decisions: pause, verify through official channels, protect codes, avoid unusual payment, ask for help, save evidence, and secure accounts. The app should repeat these habits across lessons so they become memorable.

The free version should include core lessons and situation-based advices. Paid enhancements may include family lesson packs, longer courses, quizzes, caregiver education, printable guides, and personalized learning plans. Basic education should remain free because it supports prevention.

Learning Center is acceptable when lessons are short, beginner-friendly, linked to real app moments, calm in tone, useful for different user groups, and focused on practical safety habits.

### Feature 8.15: Privacy Redaction Helper

Privacy Redaction Helper is the feature that helps users hide sensitive info before checking, saving, exporting, or sharing scam-related material. Redaction means removing, masking, blurring, or replacing private details so the user can get help without exposing unnecessary info. This feature should appear throughout Verivae, not only as a standalone tool.

Privacy Redaction Helper should work with pasted text, screenshots, report packets, evidence cases, shared summaries, and trusted-helper messages. If a user pastes a risky message that includes a login code, password, bank number, card number, address, medical info, identification number, or unrelated private conversation, the app should warn them before saving or sharing it. The warning should be calm and specific: "This looks like it may include a login code. You usually do not need to share that for a scam check."

The feature should support automatic suggestions and manual control. Automatic suggestion means the app identifies possible sensitive details and offers to hide them. Manual control means the user can select info themselves and choose to hide it. The user should always remain in control because automatic redaction can make mistakes. The app should allow the user to undo redaction before final saving or exporting.

Privacy Redaction Helper should use plain replacement labels. Instead of leaving a blank space, the app can replace sensitive text with labels such as \[code hidden\], \[account number hidden\], \[address hidden\], \[name hidden\], \[phone hidden\], or \[private message hidden\]. These labels preserve the story while protecting the exact private value. For example, a report can still say that a scammer asked for a login code without showing the actual code.

The feature should avoid storing the original unredacted version unless the user explicitly chooses to keep it. The safest default is to save the redacted version for review and evidence summaries. If the user decides to keep original evidence, the app should explain why that may be useful and what the privacy risk is. This choice should be visible, not hidden in settings.

Privacy Redaction Helper should be integrated into Manual Scam Check. Before the app reviews pasted text or screenshots, it should scan for obvious sensitive items and ask whether to redact them. The user should not be blocked from checking a scam because redaction is imperfect. Instead, the app should say which items it found and let the user decide. If the user skips redaction, the app should still avoid asking for sensitive data in future steps.

The helper should also be integrated into Evidence Vault. When a user saves a screenshot or message, the app should offer to save a redacted copy. For some cases, keeping the original may be important, but the app should not assume that by default. The user should know whether they are saving a redacted copy, original evidence, or both.

The helper should be integrated into Trusted Helper and Report Packet Builder. Before anything is shared outside the user's private app space, the app should show a redaction review screen. This screen should list possible sensitive items, attachments, and summaries. The user should be able to remove or hide details before sending. The app should never automatically share full unredacted evidence with a trusted helper.

Privacy Redaction Helper should include screenshot redaction. Screenshot redaction may allow the user to blur or cover parts of an image. The app should provide simple controls such as tap to hide, drag to cover, undo, preview, and save redacted copy. The app should warn that redaction should be applied before sharing externally. If the first app version cannot perform advanced image redaction, it should still support a basic manual crop or clear warning that the screenshot may include private info.

The feature should include redaction limitations. It should explain that automatic detection may miss private details or mark harmless text by mistake. The user should review before sharing. The app should not claim that redaction is perfect. It should not promise that once something was shared externally, the app can remove it from other people's devices or services.

The free version should include basic text redaction suggestions and sharing warnings. Paid enhancements may include advanced screenshot redaction, batch redaction, custom redaction labels, report-packet redaction review, and helper-sharing redaction tools. The app should not charge users for basic privacy protection before sharing sensitive material.

Privacy Redaction Helper is acceptable when it appears before risky sharing moments, gives users control, supports both automatic suggestions and manual edits, avoids storing unnecessary originals, explains limitations, and protects privacy without blocking urgent safety checks.

### Feature 8.16: Saved Safety Notes

Saved Safety Notes is the feature that lets users keep personal notes about scam situations, safety decisions, trusted contacts, account-security reminders, and lessons learned. It should not replace Evidence Vault. Evidence Vault stores case materials. Saved Safety Notes stores the user's own thoughts and reminders. This distinction matters because users may want to remember a lesson without saving an entire case.

A safety note might say, "I will call my bank through the app, not through text links," or "My son said to call him directly if someone claims he needs emergency money," or "I removed the unknown remote access app from my laptop." These notes can help users turn a stressful event into a future safety habit. The feature should be private by default.

Saved Safety Notes should support linking to a case, but not require it. A user may create a note after a scam check, after reading a lesson, after talking with a trusted helper, or after securing an account. The note should optionally connect to a case in Evidence Vault. If linked, the user should still control whether the note appears in report packets or helper summaries.

The feature should include reminder options. A user may want to be reminded to change a password, check a bank statement, verify a marketplace buyer, talk to a family member, review linked devices, or finish a report. Reminders should be private on the lock screen by default. The app should avoid revealing sensitive scam details in alerts.

Saved Safety Notes should support simple organization. Notes can be grouped by account safety, payment safety, family safety, device safety, reporting, or general reminders. The app should not become a complicated note-taking app. It should stay focused on scam safety and money safety.

The feature should include deletion and export controls. The user should be able to delete a note, export selected notes, or include a note in a report packet. The app should never include a personal note in a shared report without the user's approval. Some notes may contain private feelings, family details, or financial concerns that do not belong in external reports.

The free version should include basic saved notes and simple reminders. Paid enhancements may include longer note history, recurring reminders, shared family safety notes, richer organization, and cross-device note sync. The app should not charge users to delete notes or keep them private.

Saved Safety Notes is acceptable when notes are private by default, easy to create, optionally linked to cases, useful for future safety habits, and never shared without clear approval.

### Area 8 Part 3 accept rules

Area 8 Part 3 is acceptable when reporting support is practical but not overpromising, report packets are user-controlled, scam education is beginner-friendly, pattern explanations reduce confusion, privacy redaction appears before saving or sharing, and safety notes remain private by default. These features should help the user understand what happened, explain it clearly, protect private details, and become more prepared in the future. Part 3 should strengthen the full Area 8 system by connecting Evidence Vault, Reporting Guide, Scam Pattern Library, Learning Center, Privacy Redaction Helper, Trusted Helper, and Saved Safety Notes into one coherent app experience.

### Area 8 Part 4: Cross-Feature Behavior, Free and Paid Boundaries, Settings, and Final Area Accept Rules

Part 4 closes Area 8 by defining how the major features work together as one app experience. Parts 1, 2, and 3 described individual features in detail. Part 4 defines the rules that should apply across those features: how users move between features, how free and paid access should behave, how settings should work, how alerts should stay private, how the app should recover from unclear inputs, and how the full feature area should be judged.

### Feature 8.17: Cross-Feature Case Continuity

Cross-feature case continuity means the app should remember that one scam situation may move through several features without forcing the user to start over. A user may begin with Manual Scam Check, then move into Before You Pay, then use Evidence Vault, then open Reporting Guide, then ask a Trusted Helper for input. The app should treat those steps as linked parts of one case when the user chooses to save or continue the case.

The user should never feel like each feature is a separate app. If they check a risky payment request and the result says risk, the app should offer natural next actions: save to Evidence Vault, open Before You Pay, create a pause script, ask a Trusted Helper, start a report packet, or learn about the scam pattern. These actions should appear as helpful choices, not as a confusing wall of buttons.

Case continuity should be optional. A user may want a quick one-time check without saving anything. The app should allow that. If the user does not save the check, the app can still show results and safer next steps, but it should not create a permanent case without permission. If the user does save the check, the case should keep relevant context, such as the risk result, warning signs, selected evidence, user notes, next steps, and whether follow-up tasks remain open.

A saved case should have a clear status. Status labels should be beginner-friendly. Examples include New Check, Needs Review, Waiting to Verify, Payment Paused, Already Acted, Evidence Saved, Report Prepared, Shared with Helper, Closed, or Archived. The app should avoid technical workflow labels. A user should know what the status means without reading documentation.

Cross-feature continuity should also protect privacy. Moving from one feature to another should not automatically share all info. For example, opening Trusted Helper from a case should not automatically share the full case. Opening Report Packet Builder should not automatically include every screenshot. Opening Learning Center should not publish or reuse the user's private message as an example. Each transition should preserve user control.

The app should include a case summary panel that appears consistently across features when a case is active. The panel can show the case name, risk level, confidence level, main warning signs, open safety tasks, evidence status, and sharing status. It should be compact and not visually overwhelming. The user should be able to open the full case details when needed.

The app should support returning users. If a user leaves the app after a risky result and comes back later, the app should help them continue. It can show open cases, urgent tasks, unresolved account actions, device checks, or saved notes. The tone should be calm. The app should avoid implying that the user failed because they did not finish everything immediately.

Case continuity is acceptable when users can move between features without retyping the same situation, saving remains optional, privacy does not weaken during transitions, open tasks remain visible, and the app feels like one linked protection system.

### Feature 8.18: Free and Paid Boundary System

The free and paid boundary system defines what must remain free and what can reasonably become paid. Because the app is a safety-focused app, the free version must provide real protection. The app should be able to make money, but it should not make basic scam safety feel trapped behind a paywall.

The free version should include the core safety loop. The core safety loop means the user can check a risky message or situation, understand the risk result, see warning signs, receive safer next steps, pause before paying, get basic already-acted guidance, use basic privacy redaction, save limited evidence, and access basic scam education. If the free version cannot protect someone during a common scam moment, the product will feel exploitative and less trustworthy.

Paid features should add convenience, depth, scale, collaboration, and long-term organization. Convenience means fewer manual steps. Depth means richer explanations and more complete summaries. Scale means more saved cases, more linked devices, more integrations, or more history. Collaboration means trusted-helper dashboards, family sharing, or caregiver workflows. Long-term organization means weekly checks, recurring reminders, advanced report packets, and richer evidence timelines.

Paid upgrades should never block emergency-style guidance. If a user says they sent money, shared a password, shared a login code, allowed remote access, or installed something risky, the app should show immediate basic next steps for free. It can offer paid organization afterward, but the first safety response should not be locked.

The upgrade screen should use trust-safe language. It should not say or imply that a user is unsafe unless they pay. It should not use fear, countdown timers, fake urgency, or manipulative security warnings. The app's own business model must not copy the emotional tactics used by scammers. Upgrade prompts should be quiet and clear: paid plans give more storage, deeper reports, more linked devices, more helper options, and more weekly review features.

The free version can have reasonable limits. It may limit the number of saved cases, report packet exports, linked devices, weekly check categories, helper slots, or history length. These limits should be explained plainly before the user hits them. When a user reaches a limit, the app should still let them delete old items, export their own info, remove permissions, disconnect helpers, and protect privacy without paying.

The app should include a free-safety guarantee inside the design philosophy. This does not mean a legal promise of perfect protection. It means a product rule: basic scam checking, basic payment pause guidance, basic already-acted guidance, basic redaction warnings, and basic education should stay available without subscription. This rule protects Harborwake's brand trust.

Paid features should be framed as support for power users, families, and long-term protection. A single user who checks a message once should not feel forced to subscribe. A family helping an older relative, a user with many scam attempts, or someone who wants ongoing device and account review may see more value in a paid plan. This distinction makes the business model more ethical and more sustainable.

The paid boundary system should include cancellation and downgrade safety. If a user cancels, they should not lose access to critical safety records without warning. The app should explain what happens to saved cases, evidence history, weekly checks, linked devices, and helper access. Users should be able to export their own data before losing paid storage. Privacy controls should remain available after downgrade.

The free and paid boundary system is acceptable when basic protection remains free, paid upgrades add value without fear pressure, privacy controls are never paywalled, emergency-style guidance is available to free users, and cancellation does not trap user data.

### Feature 8.19: Settings and Control Center

Settings and Control Center is the place where users manage permissions, integrations, privacy, alerts, saved data, trusted helpers, weekly checks, paid plan status, and accessibility preferences. The settings area should be simple enough for beginners but complete enough for a professional app.

The main Settings screen should be organized by user question. Instead of only using technical categories, the app can use plain sections: What the app can access, What the app saves, Who can see my info, Weekly checks and reminders, Linked accounts, Linked devices, Privacy and redaction, Alerts, App appearance, Accessibility, Plan and billing, Export and delete data, and Help. This structure helps users find controls by intent.

The settings area should make permissions visible. If Gmail is linked, the user should see that. If message review is manual only, the user should see that. If photo or screenshot access is used only when the user selects an image, the app should say so. If trusted-helper sharing is active, the app should show who can see what. Hidden access creates distrust.

Each permission should have a plain explanation and a remove option or removal instructions. If the OS controls a permission outside the app, the app should guide the user to the right system area. It should not pretend it can remove permissions that only the device settings can remove. Honest instructions are better than fake convenience.

Settings should include a data controls area. Users should be able to see saved cases, evidence storage, saved notes, redacted and original evidence choices, report packets, weekly check history, device lists, linked accounts, and helper sharing. They should be able to delete items individually. They should also be able to request broader cleanup, such as deleting all cases or removing all local evidence, depending on how the app stores data.

The Control Center should include privacy status. A simple privacy status can show whether the user has linked accounts, enabled weekly checks, shared with helpers, saved original evidence, or enabled lock-screen alerts. This helps users understand their privacy posture without reading every setting. It should be infoal, not shaming.

Settings should include accessibility controls. Users should be able to increase text size if supported, choose clearer contrast, reduce motion, use simpler language mode if offered, adjust alert style, and access screen-reader-friendly layouts. Scam protection often matters most when users are stressed, older, distracted, or low on confidence. Accessibility is therefore part of safety, not decoration.

The Plan and billing section should be clear but not dominant. It should show whether the user is on a free or paid plan, what limits apply, what paid features are available, and how to manage or cancel the plan. The settings area should not hide cancellation or make the user contact support for basic account control if the platform allows self-service.

Settings should include help and explanation. If users do not understand a feature, they should be able to tap simple explanations. For example, "What is redaction?" should explain that redaction hides private details. "What is a trusted helper?" should explain that a helper can review selected info only when the user chooses. These explanations should be short and practical.

Settings and Control Center is acceptable when users can understand access, remove access, review sharing, control alerts, manage data, change weekly checks, adjust accessibility, understand paid status, and delete or export their own info without needing technical confidence.

### Feature 8.20: Alert and Alert Behavior

Alert and alert behavior defines how Verivae communicates outside the main app screen. Alerts can be useful, but they can also expose private info or create anxiety. The app should treat alerts as sensitive.

The app should use private alert wording by default. A lock-screen alert should not say, "Risky scam found in your bank message" or "Your device may be compromised." Someone else could see that. Safer wording might be, "the app has a safety review ready" or "A private safety reminder is available." Details should appear only after the user opens the app and passes the device's normal unlock protection.

Alerts should be tied to user choices. A user may want weekly check reminders, unresolved safety task reminders, trusted-helper replies, report packet reminders, device review reminders, or saved note reminders. The user should be able to turn categories on or off. The app should not use security alerts as marketing messages.

Urgent alerts should be rare and justified. If everything is urgent, nothing is urgent. The app should reserve urgent-style alerts for situations where the user may be about to send money, share a code, continue remote access, or ignore an unresolved risky account task. Even then, the alert should be calm and private.

The app should include alert previews. In Settings, users should be able to see examples of alert wording. This helps them decide whether lock-screen privacy is sufficient. A user who lives with others may choose very private wording. Another user may want more detail. The app should make the tradeoff understandable.

Trusted-helper alerts require special care. If a helper sends feedback, the alert should not reveal sensitive case info. A safe version is, "Your trusted helper responded." The app should not put message contents or case facts on the lock screen by default. The user can open the app to read details.

Alerts should avoid shame and fear. They should not say, "You ignored a dangerous scam" or "Your money is at risk unless you act now." Even when the situation is serious, the app should use controlled language: "A saved safety task still needs review" or "Review this before sending money." The app should not sound like the scammers it is trying to protect against.

Alert and alert behavior is acceptable when alerts are private by default, user-controlled, rare when urgent, not used for fear marketing, understandable in settings, and linked to real safety needs.

### Feature 8.21: Error, Unknown, and Low-Info Handling

Error, unknown, and low-info handling defines what the app does when it cannot give a strong answer. This is important because many scam checks will begin with incomplete info. A user may paste one sentence, describe a call from memory, upload a blurry screenshot, or say only that something feels wrong. The app must handle uncertainty professionally.

The app should treat unknown results as legitimate outcomes. Unknown does not mean the app failed. It means the app does not have enough info to make a confident assessment. The result should explain what is missing and what the user can do safely. For example, if the user only says "Someone wants money," the app can ask who asked, how they contacted the user, what payment method they requested, and whether there is urgency or secrecy.

Low-info results should still give protective advice. The app can say, "There is not enough info to judge this clearly, but do not send money or share codes until you verify through a separate trusted route." This is useful without pretending to know the answer. The app should avoid false confidence.

The app should have recovery paths for bad screenshots, unsupported files, dislinked integrations, expired permissions, unavailable Gmail access, missing message access, and interrupted checks. It should explain the problem in plain text and offer alternatives. If a screenshot is unreadable, the app can ask the user to crop it, type the key message, or summarize what it says. If Gmail is dislinked, the app can offer paste or screenshot review.

Error messages should not blame the user. Instead of "Invalid input," the app can say, "I could not read this clearly. Try pasting the message text or uploading a clearer screenshot." Instead of "Permission denied," it can say, "The app does not currently have access to this. You can connect it in Settings or use manual review." The tone should keep users moving.

The app should avoid dangerous troubleshooting. If a link cannot be checked, the app should not tell the user to open it. If a file cannot be scanned, the app should not tell the user to download it again. If a risky account cannot be verified, the app should not tell the user to log in through the risky message. Safe fallback paths matter.

Unknown handling should connect to confidence scoring. The app should show when confidence is low and why. It can say that the result is based only on the user's summary, that no screenshot was provided, that the sender could not be checked, or that the payment method is unknown. This helps users understand the limits of the result.

Error, unknown, and low-info handling is acceptable when the app gives useful next steps without pretending certainty, offers safe alternatives, avoids blaming users, explains missing info, and never encourages risky investigation.

### Feature 8.22: Final Area 8 System Accept Rules

Final Area 8 accept rules define when the feature-by-feature specifications are strong enough to support future design and build work. Area 8 should be considered complete only when its features form one coherent product system, not a pile of dislinked ideas.

Area 8 is acceptable when a beginner can understand the purpose of every major feature. Manual Scam Check should answer whether something looks risky. Before You Pay should help users pause before sending money. Already Acted should help users take recovery steps. Evidence Vault should organize info. Trusted Helper should support consent-based help. Device Security Check should guide device review without overclaiming. Weekly Deep Check should support ongoing review. Linked Device Review should handle multi-device concerns with consent. Permission and Account Connection Review should make access visible. Reporting Guide and Report Packet Builder should organize official-support preparation. Scam Pattern Library and Learning Center should teach users. Privacy Redaction Helper should protect private details. Saved Safety Notes should help users remember decisions. Settings should give control.

Area 8 is acceptable when every feature has privacy boundaries. The app should not collect private info just because it can. It should not automatically save every check. It should not secretly share with helpers. It should not read Gmail, Messages, screenshots, photos, or linked-device data without clear user action or permission. It should give users ways to disconnect, delete, redact, export, and review what is saved.

Area 8 is acceptable when every feature has honest limits. The app should not guarantee that something is safe, guarantee recovery, guarantee that a device is clean, guarantee that reporting will work, or guarantee that every scam can be detected. It should separate risk from confidence, scam risk from device risk, and account risk from payment risk. Honest limits make the app more trustworthy.

Area 8 is acceptable when the free version protects users in the most important moments. A free user should be able to check a risky situation, pause before payment, get basic already-acted guidance, see basic warning signs, use basic redaction warnings, read core education, and understand basic reporting options. Paid features can expand storage, depth, history, linked devices, helper collaboration, weekly reviews, and report organization.

Area 8 is acceptable when the app can support profit without weakening trust. The product can charge for organization, scale, collaboration, advanced summaries, detailed storage, family workflows, linked-device history, and richer weekly review. It should not charge for deletion, disconnection, basic privacy protection, or immediate safety guidance. It should not use fear-based upgrade prompts.

Area 8 is acceptable when the feature system can support future screens. A designer should be able to turn these specifications into screens for home, manual check, result, before-you-pay, already-acted, evidence case, trusted helper, device check, weekly check, linked devices, permissions, integrations, reporting, packet builder, pattern library, learning center, redaction review, safety notes, settings, alerts, and plan controls.

Area 8 is successful when it clearly defines what the app can do for users and how those features should behave. The section should keep the user's in-app needs at the center: understanding risk, choosing safer actions, saving useful evidence, involving trusted help, and recovering from suspicious or harmful situations.

### Area 8 final closure note

Area 8 completes the feature-by-feature feature specifications for the current design brief stage. The next area should build from these features rather than restart them. Future sections should deepen user scenarios, accessibility, testing expectations, screen states, trust language, or operational rules while preserving the boundaries defined here: user control, beginner-friendly explanations, privacy-first behavior, free core safety, paid convenience and depth, no false guarantees, and no hidden monitoring.

## App Feature Area 9: Scam Category Deep Dives

Purpose of this feature area  
Area 9 defines how the app should understand and respond to specific scam categories. This area is functional because each category includes the situation type, common user inputs, detection clues, questions the app should ask, result behavior, safer next steps, privacy boundaries, free and paid boundaries, and unacceptable claims.
