The goal is not only to list scam types. The goal is to make each category usable inside Manual Scam Check, Before You Pay, Already Acted, Evidence Vault, Reporting Guide, Scam Pattern Library, Learning Center, and future integrations.

A scam category is a practical label that helps the app reason about what might be happening. A category should never be treated as a final legal conclusion. The app should say a situation matches warning signs commonly seen in a category. It should not say a person is definitely a criminal, a company is definitely fake, or money is definitely recoverable. The category should help the user pause, verify, protect accounts, save useful evidence, and choose safer next steps.

Area 9 should use a consistent functional structure for every category. First, the app identifies the likely situation. Second, it asks the minimum useful follow-up questions. Third, it separates scam risk, payment risk, account risk, and device risk. Fourth, it shows warning signs in plain text. Fifth, it gives safer next steps that do not require risky investigation. Sixth, it offers evidence saving and reporting support only after the user understands the immediate safety action. Seventh, it explains what the app cannot prove.

Every scam category should support low-info input. A user might paste a full message, upload a screenshot, describe a call, summarize a conversation, or only say that something feels wrong. The app should still be useful. When info is missing, the result should say what is unknown and ask for safe details. It should not pressure the user to click risky links, continue talking to a risky person, download files, or provide private info just to improve the result.

### Category 9.1: Text Message and Email Impersonation Scams

Text message and email impersonation scams happen when someone pretends to be a real organization, person, service, employer, bank, delivery company, payment app, government office, school, marketplace, or support team. This category should be one of the most common entry points for Verivae because many users will begin by pasting a message, sharing an email, or uploading a screenshot.

The app should recognize that impersonation does not always look obvious. A fake message may use a real company name, a copied logo, official-looking wording, a familiar sender name, or a link that looks close to the real domain. It may also be short and messy. The detection system should not depend only on grammar mistakes. A professionally written fake message can still be risky if it creates urgency, asks for login, requests payment, sends the user to a risky link, or asks for sensitive info.

The app should ask functional follow-up questions: Who does the sender claim to be? Did the message ask the user to click a link? Did it ask the user to sign in? Did it ask for a login code, password, payment, document, or personal info? Did it threaten account closure, missed delivery, legal action, lost money, or account suspension? Did the user expect this message? Does the sender address, phone number, or link match an official source the user already knows? These questions should be optional and beginner-friendly.

Warning signs should include mismatch between claimed identity and contact details, urgent deadlines, risky links, unexpected attachments, requests to bypass normal login, pressure to respond through a different channel, sender secrecy, unusual payment requests, and requests for codes or passwords. The result should explain each warning sign plainly. For example, it can say that a message claiming to be a bank is riskier when it asks the user to sign in through a link rather than using the official bank app.

The app should provide category-specific safer next steps. It should tell the user not to click links from the risky message, not to reply with private info, not to call phone numbers shown in the message, and not to forward passwords or login codes. It should recommend verifying through a separate trusted route: open the official app, type the official website manually, use a known phone number, or contact the person through a saved contact. If the user already clicked, the app should move them toward Already Acted and Device Security Check.

Privacy boundaries matter for this category because emails and messages may contain unrelated private conversations. The app should support redaction before saving or sharing. It should avoid saving full inbox content by default. If Gmail or message integration is linked, the app should still prefer user-selected review unless the user has clearly enabled broader monitoring.

The free version should include basic text and email impersonation checks, warning explanations, safe verification steps, and basic redaction reminders. Paid enhancements may include deeper sender-pattern comparisons, saved organization lookups, detailed email review history, family-helper summaries, and weekly checks for unresolved impersonation cases. Basic impersonation protection should remain free.

This category is functional when the app can help a user decide whether to pause, verify separately, protect accounts if they clicked, save only useful evidence, and understand that the result is based on warning signs rather than guaranteed identity proof.

### Category 9.2: Payment Pressure and Unusual Payment Scams

Payment pressure scams happen when someone pushes the user to send money quickly, secretly, or through a payment method that is difficult to reverse. This category should connect strongly to Before You Pay because the best outcome is stopping the payment before it happens.

The app should recognize payment pressure across many payment methods: gift cards, crypto, wire transfer, peer-to-peer payment apps, prepaid cards, bank transfer, mobile deposit, payment links, marketplace deposits, fake invoice payments, fake shipping fees, fake account unlock fees, job equipment fees, rental deposits, and emergency money requests. The specific payment method matters because some methods offer fewer protections than others.

The app should ask: Who is asking for payment? How did they contact the user? Has the user met or verified them outside the conversation? What payment method do they want? Are they rushing the user? Are they asking for secrecy? Are they threatening consequences? Are they promising a refund, prize, job, investment return, delivery release, account unlock, or emergency solution? Did the requester refuse safer payment methods? Did they change payment instructions unexpectedly?

The app should treat urgency, secrecy, unusual payment, and irreversible transfer as major risk signals. The result should show the difference between ordinary payment risk and scam-style pressure. For example, paying a known utility bill through the official website is different from buying gift cards because a stranger says the utility account will close immediately. The app should help users identify the pressure pattern.

The result should be very action-oriented. It should say: pause before sending money, verify through an official channel, do not use gift cards or crypto for strangers, do not send screenshots of gift card codes, do not send a small test payment, do not keep negotiating under pressure, and talk to a trusted person if unsure. If the user already sent money, the app should route to Already Acted and Reporting Guide.

The app should include a payment pause script. The script should be short, non-confrontational, and reusable. It might say, "I do not send money under pressure. I am going to verify this another way first." The app should avoid long arguments with risky requesters. It should help the user stop the momentum.

Privacy boundaries include payment amounts, account names, transaction IDs, receipts, and screenshots. The app should allow the user to save payment details only if they choose. It should explain that some info may help official support, but full financial details should be protected and redacted when not needed.

The free version should include payment pressure detection, safer next steps, pause scripts, and already-acted routing. Paid enhancements may include organized payment timelines, report packets, trusted-helper review, and longer evidence history. The app should not make payment-pause guidance paid.

This category is functional when it helps the user stop, verify, avoid irreversible payment, understand payment-method risk, and move to recovery guidance if money was already sent.

### Category 9.3: Marketplace Buying and Selling Scams

Marketplace scams happen when a buyer, seller, renter, shipper, or platform impersonator uses a marketplace situation to steal money, goods, account access, or personal info. This category should cover online selling platforms, local pickup groups, resale apps, social media marketplace posts, rental listings, ticket sales, and peer-to-peer item exchanges.

The app should understand both sides of a marketplace transaction. A buyer can be scammed by a fake seller who demands a deposit, shipping fee, off-platform payment, or payment before inspection. A seller can be scammed by a fake buyer who sends a fake payment confirmation, asks for a login code, overpays with a check, asks the seller to refund extra money, sends a fake courier link, or claims the platform needs the seller's email or phone number to release payment.

The app should ask: Is the user buying or selling? What platform is involved? Is the other person asking to leave the platform? Are they asking for a deposit, shipping fee, gift card, crypto, wire transfer, or payment app transfer? Are they sending screenshots of payment instead of using platform checkout? Are they asking for the user's email, phone number, login code, or banking details? Is there a story about a courier, mover, family member, military deployment, urgent pickup, or overpayment?

Warning signs should include off-platform payment, refusal to meet safely or use platform protections, fake payment screenshots, pressure to mark an item as sold before payment clears, requests for login codes, risky courier arrangements, overpayment, refund requests, and emotional urgency. The app should explain that legitimate marketplace transactions usually do not require giving a login code or sending money back from an overpayment.

The result should recommend safer marketplace behavior: stay inside the platform when possible, use platform-protected checkout, avoid sending deposits to unverified strangers, avoid refunding overpayments, verify that payment appears inside the official app rather than a screenshot, meet safely when local pickup is chosen, and avoid sharing codes or banking info. The app should avoid giving physical safety instructions beyond basic caution unless a separate safety feature is defined later.

Marketplace scams often need evidence organization. Evidence Vault should save listing screenshots, profile names, chat messages, payment requests, payment confirmations, shipping claims, and platform names. Reporting Guide should prepare platform-specific summaries without claiming the app can force the platform to refund money.

Privacy boundaries include the user's address, phone number, email, payment app handle, and photos of their home or item. The app should warn before sharing or exporting these details. If a user uploads a listing screenshot, the app should offer to redact home address or personal contact info.

The free version should include basic marketplace scam checks and safer transaction advice. Paid enhancements may include marketplace case packets, seller/buyer history notes, trusted-helper review, and detailed evidence storage. The app should not charge for warning users about off-platform payment or verification-code requests.

This category is functional when the app handles both buyer and seller risks, identifies common marketplace pressure patterns, supports evidence saving, and gives safer transaction steps without pretending to guarantee platform outcomes.

### Category 9.4: Job, Task, and Fake Employment Scams

Job and task scams happen when someone offers work, remote income, secret shopper tasks, package forwarding, fake equipment reimbursement, fake check deposits, app fees, training fees, investment tasks, app-review tasks, or commission work that is designed to take money or personal info from the user. This category matters because job scams can target users who urgently need income.

The app should avoid shaming language. A user looking for work may be financially stressed and hopeful. The app should say that fake job offers are designed to look professional and exciting. It should help the user verify without making them feel foolish.

The app should ask: Where did the job offer appear? Did the user apply, or did someone contact them unexpectedly? Is the interview only by chat? Is the pay unusually high for simple work? Is the employer asking the user to buy equipment, deposit a check, send money to a vendor, receive packages, move money, use personal accounts, pay for training, or provide sensitive documents early? Does the email domain match the real company? Is the user being rushed to accept?

Warning signs should include upfront fees, fake checks, equipment purchase requests, reimbursement promises before funds clear, interviews only through messaging apps, requests to receive and reship packages, requests to move money, requests for banking details before formal hiring, unrealistic pay, and pressure to keep the job process secret or fast. The app should explain why each sign matters in plain text.

The result should recommend verifying the employer through official company channels, checking whether the job is listed on the official company website, avoiding payment to get hired, avoiding depositing risky checks, avoiding sending money to a vendor from a check deposit, and avoiding using personal accounts to move company money. If ID docs were shared, the app should route toward Already Acted and identity-safety steps.

Job scams may involve sensitive personal info such as resumes, addresses, phone numbers, Social Security numbers, bank details, tax forms, ID docs, and direct deposit forms. Privacy Redaction Helper should warn users before saving or sharing these details. Report Packet Builder should allow a summary that excludes unnecessary identity data.

The free version should include fake job offer review, upfront-fee warnings, fake-check warnings, and safe verification guidance. Paid enhancements may include organized job-scam case history, document redaction support, trusted-helper review, and deeper pattern comparisons. Basic job-scam safety should remain free.

This category is functional when it helps users verify employment claims, avoid paying for a job, avoid fake check traps, protect identity info, and understand that a professional-looking job process can still be risky.

### Category 9.5: Romance, Friendship, and Social Trust Scams

Romance, friendship, and social trust scams happen when someone builds an emotional relationship, friendship, romantic connection, mentorship, fan relationship, gaming friendship, social media bond, or long-distance connection before asking for money, gifts, account access, investments, travel help, emergency support, private images, or secrecy. This category must be handled with extra care because the user may feel emotionally attached.

The app should never mock the relationship or call the user gullible. It should explain that emotional scams work because trust and care are real human strengths. The app should focus on the behavior pattern, not judging the user's feelings.

The app should ask: How long has the user known the person? Have they met in person or verified through a separate trusted route? Is the person avoiding video calls or in-person meetings? Are they asking for money, gift cards, crypto, phone cards, travel funds, medical help, customs fees, investment deposits, or account help? Are they creating secrecy? Are they saying they love the user quickly? Are they using emergencies repeatedly? Are they asking for private images or threatening exposure?

Warning signs should include fast emotional intensity, repeated emergencies, inability to meet, excuses around video calls, requests for unusual payment, investment pressure, secrecy, guilt, isolation from friends or family, requests for private photos, and sudden financial needs. The app should explain that one warning sign alone may not prove a scam, but multiple warning signs create serious risk.

The result should recommend pausing financial help, talking to a trusted person, verifying identity outside the relationship channel, avoiding sending private images, avoiding investments suggested by the person, refusing secrecy, and not sending money to third parties. If the user has already sent money or shared private content, Already Acted should provide nonjudgmental next steps.

Trusted Helper is especially useful here, but the app must respect privacy. The user may not want to share intimate details. The app should offer a redacted summary that focuses on behavior: money requests, secrecy, urgent claims, and refusal to verify. The user should control what is shared.

The free version should include romance and social trust scam checks, emotional manipulation explanations, safe pause scripts, and trusted-helper redacted sharing. Paid enhancements may include long-term case notes, repeated pattern tracking, family-helper collaboration, and deeper education. The app should not charge for basic help in emotionally manipulative scam situations.

This category is functional when it reduces shame, identifies relationship-based pressure, supports confidential help, protects private content, and helps the user pause without requiring them to reject their feelings immediately.

### Category 9.6: Family Emergency and Loved-One Impersonation Scams

Family emergency scams happen when someone claims that a child, parent, grandparent, sibling, spouse, friend, or other loved one is in trouble and needs money, secrecy, bail, medical help, travel support, ransom, or urgent assistance. The scam may involve voice calls, text messages, social media accounts, email, or someone pretending to be an authority figure.

The app should treat these cases as emotionally urgent. The user may be scared. The app should not slow them down with a long lesson before giving a safe verification step. The first useful action should be: contact the loved one or a known trusted person through a separate known number, not through the contact info provided by the risky requester.

The app should ask: Who is supposedly in trouble? How did the user receive the message? Did the requester demand secrecy? Did they ask for gift cards, wire transfer, crypto, payment app transfer, courier pickup, bail money, or medical payment? Did they prevent the user from calling other family members? Did the voice or writing style seem unusual? Is the phone number, account, or email known to the user?

Warning signs should include secrecy, pressure, unusual payment, refusal to let the user verify, claims involving law enforcement or hospitals without verifiable contact, changed phone numbers, vague details, emotional panic, and requests to stay on the phone while paying. The app should explain that real emergencies can usually be verified without secret payment to a stranger.

The result should give a safe emergency verification sequence. First, pause payment. Second, contact the loved one using a known number. Third, contact another family member or trusted person. Fourth, call an official organization through independently found contact info if needed. Fifth, save evidence if the situation appears risky. The app should not tell users to confront the caller or keep them on the line.

This category should support older users and stressed users. Text should be large, direct, and calm. The app should allow a one-tap trusted-helper share that says only, "I received an urgent request about a loved one and need help verifying it," without exposing private details by default.

The free version should include family emergency detection, safe verification steps, pause scripts, and trusted-helper sharing. Paid enhancements may include family safety plans, saved trusted contacts, recurring education, and caregiver workflows. Emergency verification guidance should always be free.

This category is functional when it helps users verify loved-one claims through a separate route, pause unusual payment, involve trusted support, and act calmly without ignoring the possibility of a real emergency.

### Category 9.7: Fake Bank, Payment App, and Account Alert Scams

Fake bank, payment app, and account alert scams happen when a message, email, call, or pop-up claims that the user's bank, card, payment app, shopping account, cloud account, email account, or social media account has a problem. The scammer may claim there is fraud, a locked account, risky transaction, failed payment, refund, chargeback, security issue, or urgent verification need.

The app should ask: What account is mentioned? Did the user expect a message from that service? Is there a link? Is there a phone number? Does the message ask for login, password, code, card number, bank info, payment, remote access, or ID doc? Did the user already click, call, or enter info? Does the message threaten account closure or money loss?

Warning signs should include links to login pages, requests for login codes, requests to move money to a safe account, pressure to call a number in the message, claims that support needs remote access, unusual refund instructions, requests for full card or bank details, and instructions not to contact the bank normally. The app should explain that real banks and payment services generally do not need users to share passwords or one-time codes with a person who contacted them.

The result should recommend opening the official bank or payment app directly, using a known support number, checking recent transactions through official channels, refusing to share codes, and not moving money because someone on the phone says it is safer. If the user shared credentials or codes, the app should route to Already Acted, account-security steps, and Permission and Account Connection Review.

The app should distinguish account risk from device risk. If the user only received a message and did not click, the account risk may be low but scam risk may be high. If the user entered credentials, account risk increases. If the user installed remote access software, device risk increases. The result should make these layers clear.

Privacy boundaries are important because bank messages and payment screenshots can expose transaction details. The app should offer redaction before saving or report packet export. It should never ask for full passwords, full card numbers, or one-time codes.

The free version should include bank and payment app alert checks, account-risk guidance, and safe verification steps. Paid enhancements may include account-safety reminders, evidence timelines, trusted-helper summaries, and weekly unresolved-task checks. Basic bank-scam safety should remain free.

This category is functional when it helps users avoid fake login pages, fake support numbers, code theft, unsafe money movement, and account takeover while using official account channels for verification.

### Category 9.8: Fake Delivery, Package, and Shipping Scams

Fake delivery and shipping scams happen when a message claims that a package is delayed, a delivery fee is due, an address must be confirmed, customs payment is required, a label failed, or a shipping company needs urgent action. These scams often use familiar delivery brand names and small payment amounts to make the request feel harmless.

The app should ask: Is the user expecting a package? Does the message include a link? Does it ask for a small fee, card number, address, login, or personal info? Does the link match the official delivery company? Did the message arrive by text, email, social message, or marketplace chat? Did the user already enter payment or address info?

Warning signs should include unexpected delivery alerts, shortened links, pressure to pay a small fee, request for full card details, mismatch between sender and claimed shipping company, vague package details, and links that require login or payment before showing the package. The app should explain that small-fee scams can still expose card data or lead to fake login pages.

The result should recommend checking delivery status through the official shipping app, official website typed manually, or order page from the original store. It should tell the user not to use links from risky messages. If the user entered card details, the app should route to Already Acted and suggest contacting the card issuer through official channels.

Evidence Vault should save the risky message, link, claimed delivery company, requested fee, and whether the user was expecting a package. Privacy Redaction Helper should warn before saving address details or card info.

This category is functional when the app helps users avoid fake delivery links, verify through official tracking routes, protect payment details, and understand that a small fee can still be a serious warning sign.

### Category 9.9: Fake Tech Support, Virus Warning, and Remote Access Scams

Fake tech support scams happen when a pop-up, call, email, ad, search result, or message claims the user's device has a virus, security breach, expired subscription, hacked account, or urgent technical problem. The scammer may ask the user to call a number, install remote access software, pay for support, share screen control, or give account credentials.

The app should ask: Did the warning appear in a browser, message, email, phone call, search result, or app? Did it show a phone number? Did someone ask to control the device? Did the user install anything? Did the user share a password, code, payment info, or screen access? Is the warning still visible? Did the user pay for support?

Warning signs should include alarming pop-ups, phone numbers inside warnings, claims that the device is locked, instructions to call immediately, pressure to install remote access tools, requests for payment, requests for gift cards, claims to represent a major technology company without verification, and threats that files or money will be lost. The app should explain that scary pop-ups are often designed to make users act before thinking.

The result should recommend closing the risky page if possible, avoiding the phone number shown in the warning, not installing suggested tools, disconnecting remote access if already allowed, reviewing installed apps and permissions, changing important passwords from a trusted device if credentials were exposed, and using built-in device security tools or trusted local technical help. It should connect strongly to Device Security Check.

The app should avoid claiming it can remove every virus. It should say it can guide the user through scam-related safety steps and risky settings, but it may not replace dedicated device security tools. This distinction is essential for trust.

This category is functional when it helps users recognize fake security pressure, stop remote access, avoid fake support numbers, review device exposure, and take account-safety steps without panic.

### Category 9.10: Investment, Crypto, and Get-Rich-Quick Scams

Investment and crypto scams happen when someone promises unusually high returns, secret strategies, guaranteed profit, fast wealth, trading signals, account management, mining opportunities, recovery services, or investment access through a person or platform the user cannot independently verify. This category should be handled carefully because users may already be emotionally and financially invested.

The app should ask: Who introduced the investment? Was it a stranger, romantic contact, social media account, influencer, group chat, fake advisor, or friend of a friend? Are returns guaranteed? Is the user being asked to send crypto, wire money, pay taxes or fees before withdrawal, install a trading app, use a specific exchange, or keep the opportunity secret? Has the user tried to withdraw money? Did the platform ask for more money to unlock funds?

Warning signs should include guaranteed returns, pressure to invest quickly, screenshots of large profits, romance or friendship leading into investing, unfamiliar platforms, requests to deposit more before withdrawal, fake account dashboards, tax or unlock fees, and claims that only a special advisor can help. The app should explain that a dashboard showing profit does not prove money can be withdrawn.

The result should recommend pausing deposits, not sending additional unlock fees, verifying the platform independently, avoiding investment advice from strangers, saving evidence, and contacting financial institutions or official support if money was sent. If the user cannot withdraw, the app should treat requests for more money as a risky warning sign.

The app must avoid financial-advice claims. It should not tell users what to invest in. It should not evaluate legitimate investment performance. It should focus on scam-warning behavior, pressure, payment method, platform verification, and safer next steps.

This category is functional when it identifies investment-pressure patterns, explains fake profit dashboards, warns about withdrawal-fee traps, avoids giving investment advice, and helps users stop sending additional money.

### Category 9.11: Verification Code and Account Takeover Scams

Login code scams happen when someone asks the user to share a one-time code, login approval, password reset code, two-step login code, device approval, or account recovery link. Account takeover means someone may gain access to an account that belongs to the user. This category should be treated as high priority because sharing a code can quickly lead to account loss.

The app should ask: What code was requested? Who asked for it? Did the requester claim to be support, a buyer, a friend, a bank, an employer, or a platform? Did the user already share it? Did the user receive login alerts, password reset messages, new-device messages, or account recovery emails? Did the user approve a login prompt?

Warning signs should include any request from another person for a login code, pressure to read a code aloud, claims that a code proves identity for a marketplace sale, requests to screenshot a code, or instructions to approve a login prompt the user did not start. The app should explain simply: a login code is usually meant for the account owner only.

The result should be direct. If the user has not shared the code, the app should say not to share it. If the user already shared it, the app should route to Already Acted and recommend securing the account through official settings, changing passwords if needed, reviewing recovery methods, checking active sessions, and contacting official support if locked out.

Privacy Redaction Helper should automatically warn before saving or sharing actual codes. Evidence can say \[code hidden\] instead of showing the real number. The app should never ask users to provide active login codes.

This category is functional when it helps users understand that codes are private, stop code sharing before it happens, and recover account safety if a code was already shared.

### Category 9.12: Rental, Housing, and Deposit Scams

Rental and housing scams happen when someone advertises a home, apartment, room, vacation rental, or sublease and asks for deposits, app fees, background-check fees, viewing fees, wire transfers, gift cards, or personal documents before the user can verify the property or landlord. This category can cause serious financial harm because housing decisions are urgent and emotional.

The app should ask: Where was the listing found? Has the user seen the property in person or through a trusted platform? Is the price unusually low? Is the landlord unavailable? Are they asking for money before a viewing? Are they asking for a deposit by wire, gift card, crypto, or payment app? Are they requesting ID docs, Social Security number, pay stubs, or bank statements through an unofficial channel?

Warning signs should include low price, pressure to pay quickly, refusal to show the property, claims of being out of town, requests for unusual payment, copied listing photos, vague lease details, and requests for sensitive documents before verification. The app should explain that real rental processes can involve apps, but users should verify the property and landlord before sending money or private documents.

The result should recommend verifying the property through official listings, public records if appropriate, platform protections, in-person or trusted virtual viewing, written lease review, and safer payment channels. The app should advise against sending deposits to an unverified stranger.

Privacy boundaries include ID docs, income info, pay stubs, addresses, and bank statements. The app should strongly encourage redaction before saving or sharing rental documents and should avoid storing originals unless the user chooses.

This category is functional when it helps users identify fake rental pressure, verify housing claims, avoid unsafe deposits, and protect ID docs.

### Category 9.13: Check Deposit, Overpayment, and Refund Scams

Check deposit and overpayment scams happen when someone sends a check or payment that appears to be too large, then asks the user to send back the difference, buy supplies, pay a vendor, forward money, or refund part of the amount before the original payment is truly safe. This can happen in job scams, marketplace sales, rental situations, prize scams, and fake refunds.

The app should ask: Did the user receive a check, mobile deposit image, payment screenshot, or notice of overpayment? Who sent it? Why was it sent? Is the user being asked to return money, buy gift cards, pay a vendor, ship an item, or send funds elsewhere? Has the bank confirmed final payment status, or does the user only see a temporary balance?

Warning signs should include overpayment, pressure to refund quickly, instructions to use part of a check for equipment or fees, fake payment screenshots, promises that the check has cleared immediately, and requests to send money before the payment is final. The app should explain that seeing money appear temporarily does not always mean the payment is safe.

The result should recommend waiting, contacting the bank through official channels, avoiding sending money back under pressure, not buying gift cards or equipment from risky funds, saving evidence, and using Reporting Guide if money was already sent. The app should avoid giving banking guarantees or timelines.

This category is functional when it helps users recognize overpayment traps, avoid returning money from risky funds, and contact official financial support before acting.

### Category 9.14: Government, Legal, Utility, and Authority Threat Scams

Authority threat scams happen when someone claims to represent the government, police, court, tax agency, immigration office, utility company, school, healthcare office, or other authority and threatens arrest, fines, deportation, service cutoff, account closure, legal action, or public embarrassment unless the user acts immediately. These scams rely on fear and obedience.

The app should ask: What authority does the person claim to represent? How did they contact the user? Are they asking for payment, gift cards, crypto, wire transfer, personal info, login codes, or remote access? Are they threatening arrest, legal action, shutoff, deportation, public exposure, or account closure? Did they tell the user not to contact anyone else?

Warning signs should include immediate threats, unusual payment methods, secrecy, refusal to allow independent verification, claims that law enforcement or government accepts gift cards or crypto, pressure to stay on the phone, and instructions to ignore normal official channels. The app should explain that legitimate authorities usually provide official ways to verify claims and do not require secret payment through unusual methods.

The result should recommend pausing, ending the risky conversation if needed, using official contact info found independently, contacting a trusted person, and avoiding payment under threat. If the user already paid or shared info, the app should route to Already Acted and Reporting Guide.

The app should be careful with legal wording. It should not give legal advice or tell the user to ignore real notices. It should say to verify through official channels and seek appropriate professional help when needed.

This category is functional when it helps users separate fear-based authority pressure from verifiable official communication, avoid unusual payment, and verify safely.

### Category 9.15: Prize, Refund, Subscription, and Recovery Scams

Prize, refund, subscription, and recovery scams happen when someone claims the user won money, is owed a refund, has an expiring subscription, can recover lost funds, or must pay a small fee to receive a benefit. These scams often look positive rather than threatening. They may ask for fees, bank details, card numbers, remote access, gift cards, or personal info.

The app should ask: Did the user enter a contest? Is a refund expected? Is there a real subscription involved? Is the person asking for payment before release? Are they asking for card or bank details? Are they claiming they can recover money lost in a previous scam? Did they contact the user unexpectedly?

Warning signs should include upfront fees for prizes, unexpected refund offers, fake subscription renewal warnings, requests for remote access to process a refund, claims that money can be recovered for a fee, pressure to act quickly, and requests for unusual payment. Recovery scams should be treated as especially risky because they target people who may already have been harmed.

The result should recommend verifying through official accounts, avoiding upfront fees, not granting remote access for refunds, not paying recovery agents who contacted the user unexpectedly, and saving evidence. If the user already paid a recovery fee or shared financial info, the app should route to Already Acted.

This category is functional when it helps users recognize positive-pressure scams, avoid fake refunds and recovery-fee traps, verify subscriptions through official channels, and protect financial details.

### Area 9 Cross-Category Functional Rules

Area 9 should not treat categories as isolated boxes. Many real scams combine categories. A romance scam can become an investment scam. A marketplace scam can become a verification-code scam. A fake bank alert can become a remote-access scam. A job scam can become a check-deposit scam. The app should allow multiple category matches and explain which warning signs belong to which category.

The result system should show primary category, secondary category, and risk layers when useful. Primary category means the strongest pattern. Secondary category means another relevant pattern. Risk layers include scam risk, payment risk, account risk, device risk, privacy risk, and emotional pressure risk. This helps the app give more accurate next steps.

The app should avoid category tunnel vision. If a user selects "delivery message" but the message asks for a bank login, account risk should still be considered. If a user selects "job offer" but the process includes a fake check, payment risk and banking risk should be raised. If a user selects "romance" but the person asks for crypto investment, investment risk should be included.

Area 9 should support a category-specific question bank. A question bank is a set of optional questions the app can ask when a category is likely. The app should ask only the most useful questions first. It should not overwhelm a stressed user with every possible question. The app can offer "answer more questions for a clearer result" after the initial result.

Area 9 should support category-specific safer next steps. The next step for a fake delivery text is not the same as the next step for a remote access incident. The next step for a code-sharing scam is not the same as a rental deposit scam. Functional category design means the result points the user toward the right action quickly.

Area 9 should support category-specific Evidence Vault templates. A marketplace case needs listing details. A bank alert case needs account-safety notes. A job scam case may need employer name, email domain, check details, and document-sharing status. A romance scam case may need privacy-sensitive redacted summaries. The app should not force one evidence template onto every scam type.

Area 9 should support category-specific education links. After a result, the app can offer a short lesson or pattern explanation. Education should not block urgent action. If the user is about to pay, the app should prioritize pausing the payment before offering a lesson.

Area 9 should support category-specific report preparation. Reporting Guide and Report Packet Builder should adapt based on the category. A payment scam packet should highlight payment method and transaction details. A job scam packet should highlight employer identity and check/payment requests. A fake delivery packet should highlight risky link and requested fee. The user should still control what is included.

### Area 9 Free and Paid Boundaries

Basic category detection should be free. Users should be able to identify common scam patterns, see warning signs, get safe next steps, and access basic education without paying. Paid features may deepen category comparison, save more category history, generate richer report packets, support family dashboards, provide advanced weekly review, and organize larger evidence sets. The app should not charge users just to learn that a payment request or verification-code request is risky.

### Area 9 Accept Rules

Area 9 is acceptable when each scam category is functional enough to guide product behavior. Each category should define what the situation looks like, what the app should ask, what warning signs matter, what risk layers apply, what safer next steps should appear, what privacy boundaries matter, what evidence may be saved, and what the app must avoid promising.

Area 9 is acceptable when categories support combined scams. The app should handle mixed patterns such as romance plus crypto investment, job offer plus fake check, marketplace sale plus login code, fake bank alert plus remote access, delivery message plus card theft, and authority threat plus gift card payment.

Area 9 is acceptable when the app remains beginner-friendly. The user should not need to know terms like phishing, social engineering, malware, chargeback, or account takeover before getting help. When those terms appear, the app should explain them plainly.

Area 9 is acceptable when the app is useful in real moments. A user should be able to paste a risky message, select a category if they know it, skip category selection if they do not, answer a few clear questions, receive a category-aware result, take a safe next step, save useful evidence, and move to reporting or recovery if needed.

Area 9 is acceptable when the app avoids false certainty. The app should say that a situation matches warning signs, not that every suspected person is definitely a scammer. It should give practical guidance without guaranteeing safety, recovery, device cleanliness, legal outcomes, or account recovery.

### Area 9 completion note

Area 9 completes the scam category deep-dive layer for the current design brief stage. Future areas should build on these categories when defining accessibility, testing, screen states, trust language, and final product requirements. Area 9 should remain app-only: it defines how the app should behave for users, not how Harborwake should market, launch, or code the product.

## App Feature Area 10: Accessibility and Inclusive Design

### Purpose of this feature area

Area 10 defines how the app must work for people who are stressed, scared, older, disabled, overwhelmed, tired, distracted, low on technical confidence, using assistive technology, or trying to protect someone else. This area is not a marketing section and it is not a development schedule. It is a functional design section that explains how the app should behave so its protection remains usable when the user is under pressure.

A scam-protection app cannot only be accurate. It must also be understandable at the exact moment when the user is least able to think clearly. Many scams succeed because the user is rushed, embarrassed, confused, or afraid of losing access to money, family, employment, housing, accounts, or legal standing. the app should therefore treat accessibility as part of safety, not as optional polish. If a user cannot read the result, understand the next step, use the controls, hear the warning, enlarge the interface, or share the issue with a trusted helper, the app has failed that user even if the detection model was technically correct.

The core accessibility rule for the app is simple: every important protection action must be clear, reachable, reversible where possible, and understandable without expert language. The app should never depend on color alone, tiny text, hidden settings, fast reaction time, complex menus, or the user's ability to remember earlier instructions. The interface should assume the user may be panicking, may have limited vision, may be using a screen reader, may have hand tremors, may speak English as a second language, may not know what phishing means, may be embarrassed, or may be acting on behalf of a parent, grandparent, child, partner, friend, client, or coworker.

Accessibility in the app must also protect privacy and dignity. The app should not make the user feel foolish for asking whether something is a scam. It should not display loud, humiliating, or overly dramatic language in a public setting. It should not expose sensitive scam content in alerts where other people can see it. It should not pressure the user into paid features when they are already afraid. The product should be designed around calm interruption, plain explanation, and confident next steps.

### Area 10.1: Accessibility Philosophy for Scam Protection

The accessibility philosophy of the app should be built around the idea that scam safety is only useful if a normal person can act on it. The app's job is not to impress the user with security vocabulary. The app's job is to help the user pause, understand the risk, decide what to do, and preserve evidence if needed.

This means every major feature should support three layers of understanding. The first layer is the immediate answer: safe, risky, risky, or needs review. The second layer is the reason: what pattern made the app concerned. The third layer is the action: what the user should do next. A user should not have to read a long explanation to find the next step, but the explanation should be available when they want it.

For example, if the app reviews a text message that says a bank account will be closed unless the user clicks a link, the accessible result should not only say risk. It should explain that the message is using urgency, an account threat, and a link that may not belong to the real bank. The primary action should be clear, such as do not tap the link, contact the bank using the official app or card number, and save this message if money or account access is involved.

The app should avoid treating accessibility as a separate mode that makes the product feel weaker. Large text, clear labeling, voice support, simple language, confirmation prompts, and privacy-safe alerts should be part of the normal design. Advanced controls can exist, but the basic protective experience should work without the user hunting through settings.

The app should also understand that users have different needs at different times. A technically confident user may want detailed evidence and risk scoring. A scared user may only want to know whether to stop. An older user may want larger text and stepwise verification. A blind user may need the same flow to work through a screen reader. A caregiver may need a consent-based way to help. The system should serve all of these users without making one group feel like an afterthought.

### Area 10.2: Stressed User and Panic-Safe Interaction Design

the app must be designed for moments of stress. Scams often create artificial urgency: send money now, verify now, call now, download now, give the code now, deposit this check now, reply before the offer disappears, or act before a loved one gets hurt. The app's interface should interrupt that pressure by slowing the moment down without making the user feel trapped.

When a user opens the app from a risky message, email, screenshot, phone call note, or manual check, the first screen should be calm and direct. It should not flash warnings, use aggressive countdowns, or bury the user under choices. The first task should be obvious: check this, scan this, paste this, upload screenshot, review message, or start a safety check. If the app already has context from a share sheet or system integration, it should show that it is reviewing the item and give the user an easy cancel option.

Panic-safe design requires a clear exit. The user should always know how to go back, stop the review, close the result, or save it for later. The app should never use manipulative patterns such as blocking the user from leaving a warning screen, making paid upgrade buttons look like the only safe action, or hiding the free next step under a paywall. When the risk is high, the app can strongly recommend caution, but it should still explain the reason and give the user practical actions.

The result screen should be structured around one primary action at a time. If the app says something is risk, the primary action might be stop and verify. Secondary actions can include save report, share with trusted helper, learn why, block sender, report scam, or open official contact checklist. The user should not have to choose from ten similar buttons while already nervous.

The language should avoid blame. The app should not say you fell for a scam, you made a mistake, or obviously fake. It should say this looks risky, this matches common scam behavior, the safest next step is to pause, or do not send money yet. The app should treat asking for help as normal. A person who feels judged is more likely to hide the problem and continue interacting with the scammer.

If the user indicates they already sent money, shared a code, installed remote access software, deposited a check, or gave account info, the app should shift from prevention mode to response mode. The interface should show calm triage: what happened, what accounts may be affected, what to secure first, what evidence to save, and what official channels to contact. It should not show a giant failure message. The goal is to help the user recover and limit harm.

### Area 10.3: Older Users and Low Technical Confidence

the app should work especially well for users who do not consider themselves technical. This includes older adults, first-time smartphone users, people who only use a few apps regularly, people who are uncomfortable with security settings, and people who understand money and relationships but not digital threat patterns.

The app should avoid assuming users know terms such as phishing, malware, spoofing, two-factor auth, account takeover, device permission, remote access, encryption, redaction, or credential theft. These words can appear when necessary, but the app should define them in plain text beside the action. For example, instead of saying possible credential theft, the app can say this may be trying to steal your password or login code.

The main protection flow should use familiar steps. The user should be able to send a message into the app, take a screenshot, paste text, or tap a button that says check this. The app should not require the user to understand file systems, email headers, raw URLs, account tokens, browser certificates, or developer-style permissions before receiving basic help.

Older and low-confidence users need visible reassurance that they are still in control. If the app asks for permission to read messages, emails, screenshots, contacts, alerts, calendar events, or device security signals, it should explain what is being requested, why it helps, what is not being collected, and how to turn it off. Permission screens should not use vague copy such as enable full protection without explaining the tradeoff.

The app should include a simplified mode that keeps the interface focused on core tasks: check a message, check an email, check a call or voicemail summary, check a link, check a payment request, check device safety, and ask a trusted helper. This mode should not remove protection. It should reduce visual complexity and hide advanced analysis unless the user asks for it.

A trusted-helper feature should support older users without taking away independence. The user should be able to choose a helper, control what gets shared, revoke access, and send a specific scam check result without giving the helper full account access. The helper should see a clean explanation, the risky content if the user allows it, and advised steps. The helper should not automatically gain access to all past checks, private messages, or device scans.

### Area 10.4: Plain Language and Reading-Level Rules

Every important explanation in the app should be written in plain text. Plain language does not mean childish language. It means the app should tell the user what matters, why it matters, and what to do next without unnecessary terms.

The app should prefer short sentences in urgent screens. It should use direct verbs such as pause, do not send, verify, call the official number, save this, block, report, change password, remove access, and ask for help. The app should avoid long security paragraphs on the first result screen. Detailed explanations can appear below the summary or behind a learn why control.

The app should explain unfamiliar terms when they are first used in a flow. Redaction should be explained as hiding private details before sharing. Remote access should be explained as software that lets another person control or view the device. Login code should be explained as a code meant only for the user, not for a caller, buyer, employer, or support agent. Account takeover should be explained as someone trying to get into the user's account.

Risk labels should be understandable without training. Risk should mean the app found strong scam signals and the user should not continue without verification. Medium risk should mean there are concerning signals but the app needs more context. Low risk should mean the app did not find obvious scam patterns, while still reminding the user that no scan is perfect. Needs review should mean the app needs another screenshot, more text, or manual context before giving a useful result.

The app should avoid confusing probability language. A normal user may not understand what 82 percent scam probability means or how to act on it. If a score is shown, it should be paired with a plain label and explanation. The score should never be the only guidance. A user needs the action more than the math.

The interface should also avoid shame-based language. Words like foolish, obvious, ridiculous, careless, or gullible should not appear. The app can be firm without being cruel. It can say this request is dangerous because it asks for gift cards and creates urgency. That is more useful than saying this is clearly a scam.

### Area 10.5: Visual Accessibility, Color, Contrast, and Risk Signals

the app should never communicate risk through color alone. Color can help users scan quickly, but every status must also include text, icons, and plain explanation. A red warning alone is not enough for color-blind users, low-vision users, older users, users in bright sunlight, or users with display settings that reduce color differences.

Each risk level should have a stable visual pattern. Risk should include a clear label, a warning icon, a concise reason, and an action. Medium risk should include a caution label, the missing context, and suggested verification. Low risk should include a calm confirmation label and a reminder to stay cautious with money, codes, passwords, and remote access. Needs review should show what the app needs next.

Text should remain readable when the user increases system text size. The app should not clip labels, overlap buttons, or force important info off-screen when text is enlarged. Long labels should wrap cleanly. Buttons should grow vertically if needed. Result cards should preserve the order of info instead of shrinking text until it becomes unreadable.

The visual hierarchy should prioritize action over decoration. Scam protection is not a place for dense visual effects, tiny badges, low-contrast text, or decorative backgrounds that compete with warnings. The app can still look professional, but the user's safety instruction must be the strongest visual signal.

The app should support dark mode and light mode without weakening risk clarity. Risky warnings should remain legible in both modes. Links should be visibly distinct. Disabled controls should look disabled without becoming invisible. Error text should be readable and should not depend on red color alone.

Screens that show sensitive content should use readable spacing. Risky messages, email excerpts, phone numbers, names, links, payment amounts, login codes, and screenshots should be displayed in a way that users can review without accidentally tapping a dangerous link. When possible, risky links should appear as text first, with opening disabled or guarded until the user confirms they understand the risk.

### Area 10.6: Screen Reader, VoiceOver, TalkBack, and Keyboard-Friendly Behavior

the app should be usable with screen readers such as VoiceOver and TalkBack. Every button, tab, switch, warning, result label, and permission control should have a meaningful accessible name. An icon-only button should not be announced as button. It should be announced by what it does, such as share result, save report, start scan, close result, copy official checklist, or remove helper access.

Screen reader order should match the visual order. When a result screen opens, the user should hear the risk level, the core explanation, and the primary next step before hearing optional details. The app should not force screen reader users through a long navigation list before reaching the warning. If the result is risk, the screen reader should announce that status clearly but calmly.

Dynamic scan updates should be announced in a controlled way. If a scan changes from checking to complete, the screen reader should announce the completion and result. It should not announce every internal processing step. If the app finds urgent risk, it should announce the risk and next action. If a deep device check takes longer, the app should provide progress updates without overwhelming the user.

Screenshot-based review needs special handling. A blind or low-vision user may upload a screenshot but not know whether the screenshot captured the important part. The app should describe what it detected in the screenshot: sender name if available, visible link if available, amount if available, request type, deadline language, and any missing info. If the screenshot is blurry or incomplete, the app should explain what to recapture.

Keyboard and external-control support should be respected where platform rules allow it. Users with motor disabilities may use switch controls, external keyboards, voice control, or assistive touch. All important flows should be reachable without requiring a precise swipe pattern, drag gesture, long press, or tiny tap target. Gesture shortcuts can exist, but they should not be the only way to complete a safety task.

### Area 10.7: Touch Targets, Motor Accessibility, and One-Handed Use

The app should use touch targets that are easy to hit, especially during stressful moments. Primary actions such as check this, stop and verify, save evidence, call official number, share with helper, block sender, and start device check should not be cramped. The user should not have to tap tiny text links to protect themselves.

Dangerous or irreversible actions should have confirmation steps. If the app offers to delete a message, remove a trusted helper, clear scan history, disable monitoring, remove a device connection, or open a risky link for review, it should confirm the action and explain the consequence. Undo should be available where possible.

One-handed use matters because users may be walking, holding a phone during a call, sitting in a car, helping a family member, or switching between apps. The most important actions should be reachable without awkward hand movement. The bottom area of mobile screens should carry common actions when it fits the platform pattern.

The app should avoid time-limited controls unless they are required for security. A user with motor difficulty should not lose the chance to review a warning because a banner disappears too quickly. Toast messages should not carry critical safety instructions by themselves. Critical instructions should remain on the page until the user dismisses them or completes the action.

Forms should be forgiving. If the user is describing a scam manually, the app should not require perfect grammar, exact timestamps, full URLs, or exact sender names. It should accept partial info and ask follow-up questions one at a time. Long forms should save progress automatically so a user can stop and return later.

### Area 10.8: Cognitive Accessibility and Step-by-Step Flow Control

Cognitive accessibility is central to Verivae because scams often attack attention, memory, fear, and decision-making. The app should reduce cognitive load by organizing info into clear steps rather than presenting everything at once.

A review result should answer four questions in order: what is the app seeing, why could it be risky, what should the user do now, and what can the user do next if they need help. This order should stay consistent across scam categories so users build confidence over time.

The app should chunk complex safety tasks. For example, if a user has shared a banking password, the app should not show a wall of instructions. It should guide the user through immediate account protection, official bank contact, password change, account activity review, evidence saving, and reporting. Each step should have one clear action and one short reason.

The app should remember context within a case. If the user already told the app that they sent money through a payment app, later steps should not ask as though nothing happened. The case summary should track what the user reported, what the app advised, what steps are completed, and what remains. This reduces repetition and helps users who are stressed or forgetful.

The app should avoid false certainty. Saying definitely safe can create dangerous overconfidence. Saying definitely a scam may be appropriate only when the evidence is extremely strong, but the safer default is to describe the pattern and action. The app should say no scan is perfect in low-risk situations where the user is about to send money, share a code, install software, or disclose personal info.

Educational content should be integrated carefully. A user checking a scam does not need a lecture first. The app can teach through the result explanation and offer deeper learning after the immediate decision. For example, after warning about a verification-code scam, it can explain why real support agents should not ask for codes.

### Area 10.9: Alert Privacy and Sensitive Context Accessibility

Alerts from the app should protect privacy. Many users share lock screens with family, coworkers, classmates, roommates, or strangers nearby. A alert that says possible romance scam from Alex or bank scam involving $2,000 could expose sensitive info. The default alert wording should be private and general, such as review advised, safety check ready, or action needed in Verivae.

Users should be able to choose alert detail level. A private mode can show minimal text. A detailed mode can include more context for users who prefer direct reminders. The app should explain the difference clearly. Privacy-safe alerts should be the default for sensitive categories such as romance, family emergency, banking, explicit threats, legal threats, ID docs, and device compromise.

Alert timing should be respectful. Weekly checks should notify the user when the scan is done, when attention is needed, or when a linked device has a meaningful issue. The app should not create frequent vague alerts that train the user to ignore it. If there is no issue, the app can summarize calmly without sounding alarming.

If an urgent warning appears while the user is in another app, the alert or overlay should be careful. It should interrupt risky behavior when needed, such as before opening a risky link or sending a login code, but it should not reveal sensitive content in public. The user should be able to open the full explanation inside Verivae.

Accessibility settings should include alert controls in plain text. Instead of only offering technical categories, the app can let users choose options like keep alerts private, show more detail, remind me to finish safety steps, notify my trusted helper only when I approve, and quiet hours for non-urgent reminders.

### Area 10.10: Trusted Helper and Caregiver Accessibility

The trusted-helper system should be designed for consent, clarity, and limited access. Many users will want help from a parent, adult child, partner, friend, mentor, financial coach, or caregiver. The app should support that without turning the helper into an owner of the user's private life.

A user should be able to share one specific case, one specific result, or a summarized safety report. The app should clearly show what will be shared before sending it. Sensitive details such as full account numbers, private messages, addresses, ID docs, or intimate content should be redacted by default unless the user intentionally includes them.

The helper view should explain the situation in plain text. It should say what the app reviewed, what risk patterns were found, what the user is considering doing, what the safest next step is, and what the helper can do. The helper should not receive complicated internal model scores as the main message. The helper needs practical context.

The app should prevent helper abuse. A helper should not be able to secretly monitor everything, receive all future scam checks by default, disable protection, view private history, or change payment settings without the user's consent. If the user chooses ongoing helper access, the app should show that status clearly and make revocation easy.

For older users or users with cognitive challenges, the app can support guided helper setup. The setup should explain the relationship in plain terms: this person can help you review risky messages when you choose to share them. It should not imply that the helper can control the phone, money, email, or accounts.

The app should also support emergency sharing in limited form. If a user is actively being pressured, they should be able to send a short alert to a trusted helper, such as I need help reviewing a possible scam. The message should not include sensitive details unless the user approves them.

### Area 10.11: Inclusive Monetization and Access Boundaries

Because the app is intended to make money eventually, accessibility and monetization must be designed carefully. The app should not withhold basic accessibility features behind a paid plan. Screen reader support, readable text, privacy-safe alerts, plain text explanations, core scam checking, core safety warnings, and basic trusted-helper sharing should remain available to free users.

Paid features can add convenience, scale, advanced monitoring, detailed device checks, family dashboards, deeper history, priority review, advanced reporting exports, or broader integrations. But the app should not make a scared user pay just to understand a warning, enlarge text, hear a result, redact private details, or learn the safest next step. Charging for basic safety comprehension would weaken trust.

Upgrade prompts should be calm and separate from urgent safety decisions. If the user is on a risky warning screen, the app should prioritize the protective action first. It can mention paid features after the immediate safety step is clear, but the upgrade prompt should not look like the only way to avoid harm. The free path must remain visible.

The app should also consider users with limited money. Scam victims may already be under financial pressure. A protection product that feels predatory would damage credibility. The free tier should be useful enough to genuinely help people, while paid tiers should add durable value for users who want more coverage.

Accessibility settings should sync across free and paid experiences. If a user chooses large text, private alerts, simplified mode, screen reader-friendly labels, or trusted-helper safeguards, those choices should not reset when the user changes plans, cancels, upgrades, downgrades, or reinstalls.

### Area 10.12: Accessibility Behavior by Feature

Manual check should support paste, screenshot, share-sheet input, typed summary, and voice-dictated text where platform support allows it. The app should not punish users for incomplete info. It should identify what it can review and ask for only the missing details that matter.

Email and message integration should present results in a way that does not require users to understand the technical difference between email, SMS, chat, alert, and screenshot. The app can explain the source, but the safety instruction should remain consistent: this message is asking for money, this message is asking for a code, this link may be unsafe, or this sender may not be who they claim to be.

Call and voicemail review should support users who cannot remember the full call. The app should let the user summarize what was said, select common prompts such as they asked for a code or they said I owed money, and add details later. If transcription is used, the app should warn that transcriptions can be imperfect and let the user correct important parts.

Device security and weekly checks should explain findings in ordinary terms. Instead of saying risky sideloaded package with elevated permissions, the app can say an app installed outside the normal app store has access that could be risky. The detailed technical explanation can be available for advanced users, but the first action should be understandable.

Redaction should be accessible. When the app hides personal info before sharing a report, the user should be able to review what was hidden. The labels should be clear: hidden phone number, hidden address, hidden bank name, hidden code, hidden email address. Users should not have to understand data privacy vocabulary to control what gets shared.

Reports should support both short and detailed versions. A user may need a short version for a helper and a detailed version for a bank, platform, employer, school, marketplace, or law-enforcement-style report. The app should make the difference clear and let the user choose.

### Area 10.13: Failure States and Accessibility Recovery

When the app cannot complete a scan, the failure message should be useful. It should not simply say error. It should explain what happened in plain text and give the user a next step. For example, if a screenshot is unreadable, the app should say the text in the screenshot is too blurry to review and suggest retaking it with the message fully visible.

If a permission is missing, the app should explain the effect. It should say that message monitoring is off, but manual checks still work. It should not imply the whole app is useless. This helps users who choose privacy over automation.

If the app loses connection, cannot reach a server, or cannot complete an advanced check, it should preserve the user's input where possible. The user should not have to retype a stressful story. Offline or limited-connection states should still provide basic safety reminders for obvious risky scenarios such as never share a login code, do not send gift cards, do not install remote access tools for unknown callers, and verify payment requests through official channels.

If an accessibility setting causes layout problems, that is a product defect, not the user's fault. The design brief should treat large text, screen readers, reduced motion, high contrast, and assistive control support as normal product conditions that must be tested.

Error recovery should never shame the user. The app should not say invalid input when the user describes a confusing scam. It should say I need a little more info to check this well, then ask a focused question.

### Area 10.14: Accessibility Accept Rules

Area 10 should be considered functionally satisfied only if the product design meets these conditions.

Every critical action can be understood without expert security vocabulary. If technical terms are used, the app defines them in the same flow.

Every risk result includes a plain label, a reason, and a next step. Color is never the only signal.

Every urgent safety screen has one primary action and does not hide the free protective path behind a paid upgrade.

Every risky flow avoids shame, blame, panic language, and manipulative pressure.

Every permission request explains what access is requested, why it helps, what is not being accessed, and how the user can turn it off.

Every core feature remains usable with larger text, screen readers, and accessible touch targets.

Every sensitive alert has a privacy-safe default and user-adjustable detail level.

Every trusted-helper flow shows what will be shared before sharing and allows access to be revoked.

Every device scan result explains the issue in normal language before showing technical detail.

Every failure state gives the user a practical next step instead of only an error message.

Every monetization boundary protects basic accessibility and basic safety comprehension for free users.

Every completed scam check can be saved, reviewed, shared, or dismissed without requiring the user to remember earlier instructions.

### Area 10 completion note

Area 10 completes the accessibility and inclusive-design layer for the current design brief stage. Future areas should build on these rules when defining testing, screen states, onboarding, privacy settings, family/helper behavior, paid-tier boundaries, and final product requirements. Area 10 should remain app-only: it defines how the app should behave for users in real situations, not how Harborwake should market, launch, or code the product.

## App Feature Area 11: Screen States, System Responses, and Recovery Behavior

### Purpose of this feature area

Area 11 defines how the app should behave when the app is checking something, waiting for input, missing permission, unsure, offline, blocked by a platform limitation, showing a risky result, showing a low-risk result, handling a failed scan, guiding the user after harm already happened, or helping the user return to a case later. This area is app-only. It is about what the product is capable of showing and doing in real usage conditions.

A scam-protection app must be functional in more than the ideal successful scan. Real users will paste incomplete messages, upload blurry screenshots, deny permissions, lose connection, switch apps, misunderstand a result, try to open risky links, receive new scam messages while reviewing old ones, or come back days later after something has already happened. the app should be designed for all of those states, not only for the clean path where the app receives perfect data and gives a perfect answer.

Screen states matter because users judge safety tools by how they behave under uncertainty. If the app freezes, gives a vague error, repeats the same warning for everything, or fails to explain what is missing, users will stop trusting it. If the app is calm, specific, recoverable, and clear about what it knows and does not know, users are more likely to pause before making a risky decision.

The product should treat every state as part of the user experience. Loading is a state. No data is a state. Permission denied is a state. Partial evidence is a state. Risk is a state. False alarm is a state. Already harmed is a state. Helper requested is a state. Weekly check complete is a state. Each one needs a predictable interface, plain text, and a safe next step.

### Area 11.1: Global State Design Principles

the app should follow a consistent state model across the entire app. The user should be able to tell what the app is doing, what it needs, what it found, and what the user can do next. The app should avoid mysterious processing, vague warnings, and dead ends.

Every major state should answer four basic questions. First, what is happening right now? Second, why is this happening? Third, what can the user do? Fourth, what happens if the user does nothing? These questions should be answered with plain text and visible controls.

For example, if the app is scanning an email, the screen should say that it is checking the email for impersonation, risky links, payment pressure, code requests, and urgent language. If the scan takes longer than expected, it should say that the check is still running and the user can leave the screen without losing the case. If the scan cannot complete, it should explain whether the issue is connection, permission, unsupported content, or unreadable input.

The app should avoid silent states. A silent state is when the user taps something and receives no visible response. In Verivae, every tap on a critical action should create a visible result: progress, confirmation, explanation, error, saved state, or next-step guidance. Scam-protection users are often stressed, so silence can feel like failure.

State language should remain consistent. The app should use the same meaning for terms such as checking, reviewing, scanning, monitoring, protected, paused, blocked, saved, shared, reported, and needs review. If checking means manual review in one screen and background monitoring in another, users may misunderstand what protection is active.

### Area 11.2: Loading, Checking, and Processing States

Loading states in the app should reduce anxiety rather than increase it. When the app starts checking a message, email, link, screenshot, call summary, device signal, or weekly deep-check result, it should show a clear progress state that tells the user what is being reviewed.

The app should not use fake precision. If it cannot truly know that a scan is 73 percent complete, it should not show a detailed percentage. A simple progress label is better: checking the message, reviewing the link, checking for payment pressure, comparing known scam patterns, preparing your result. These labels should be short and truthful.
