For fast checks, a simple loading indicator may be enough. For longer checks, the app should display a short explanation and an option to keep working later. If a weekly check is running, the user should be able to close the app and receive a privacy-safe alert when the result is ready. The user should not feel trapped staring at a screen.

The app should show protective guidance during longer checks. For example, while reviewing a payment request, the loading state can say do not send money while this check is running. While reviewing a verification-code request, it can say do not share login codes with anyone who contacted you first. These temporary reminders should be calm and short.

If the user leaves during processing, the case should be preserved. The app should show the case in a recent checks area with a status such as checking, ready, needs more info, or failed to complete. A user should not lose their input because they took a phone call, switched to Gmail, answered a family member, or locked the phone.

Processing states should not overpromise. If the app is checking only the text supplied by the user, it should not imply it has checked the sender's full identity, the real bank account, the user's phone account, or the user's financial institution. The state label should match the actual scope of the scan.

### Area 11.3: Empty States and First-Use States

The first time a user opens Verivae, the app should not feel empty or confusing. The first screen should show the core protection actions immediately: check a message, check an email, check a link, check a screenshot, check a payment request, check a call or voicemail, review device safety, or set up protection. The user should understand that the app is usable even before connecting integrations.

Empty states should teach through action, not through long explanations. If there are no recent checks, the app can say no checks yet and offer check something now. If no trusted helper is set up, it can say no helper added and offer add trusted helper. If no weekly check has run, it can say no deep check yet and offer start first check. The empty state should always contain a useful next step.

The app should avoid making first-time users feel behind. It should not say complete setup to be protected unless the user truly has no protection. Manual checks should work before optional integrations. A better message is manual checks are ready; connect messages or email for more automatic protection.

When a feature depends on permission, the empty state should explain the dependency. For example, the email protection area can say Gmail protection is not linked yet. You can still check emails manually by sharing or pasting them. This makes the free and permission-light experience feel legitimate.

First-use states should prioritize the highest-value safety behavior. The app should encourage the user to check risky messages before responding, avoid sending money under pressure, and never share login codes. It should not start with business-style dashboards or advanced settings that only make sense after the user has history.

### Area 11.4: Permission Missing, Permission Denied, and Limited Access States

the app should handle missing permissions with respect. A user may deny access to messages, email, alerts, contacts, photos, files, device info, or background activity for privacy reasons. The app should explain what still works instead of treating the user as wrong.

A permission-missing state should include three parts. First, what is off. Second, what that means. Third, what the user can do next. For example: message monitoring is off; the app cannot automatically warn you about new texts; you can still check texts manually by sharing or copying them into the app.

The app should avoid manipulative permission wording. It should not say you are unsafe unless you allow full access. It should say more automatic protection requires access, but manual checking remains available. This protects trust and supports privacy-conscious users.

If the user previously allowed permission and later revoked it, the app should show a clear changed-state message. It should not silently fail. A protection status area can show email protection paused, message monitoring off, device check limited, or alerts disabled. Each status should include a simple restore option and a plain explanation.

The app should distinguish between user choice and platform limitation. If the phone OS does not allow a certain integration, the app should say that direct scanning is not available on this device, then offer alternatives such as share to Verivae, screenshot review, paste text, or manual case creation. Users should not be blamed for platform restrictions.

Permission screens should be accessible. They should explain why access is requested before the system dialog appears, and they should explain what to do if the user says no. Users should never be stranded after denying a permission.

### Area 11.5: Partial Input and Needs-More-Info States

Many scam checks will start with incomplete info. A user may paste only part of a message, upload a screenshot that cuts off the sender, summarize a phone call from memory, or forward an email without headers. the app should still help.

When input is partial, the app should identify what it can review and what it cannot. It should not pretend to know more than it does. For example, it can say the message contains urgency and a payment request, but the sender identity is not visible. That is more trustworthy than forcing a complete risk score.

The needs-more-info state should ask focused questions. It should not show a long form with every possible field. The app can ask one or two important questions based on the scam category: did they ask for money, did they ask for a code, did they send a link, did they ask you to install an app, did they claim to be family, did they say your account would close, did they ask you to move the conversation elsewhere.

The app should allow the user to continue without perfect info. A user may not know whether the link is official or whether the phone number is real. The app can still recommend safer behavior, such as do not use the link from the message; open the official app or type the known website yourself.

Partial input should be saved as part of the case. If the user later adds a screenshot, call note, payment receipt, sender name, email address, or transaction detail, the app should update the case rather than creating unrelated fragments. This makes the app useful during real incidents that unfold over time.

### Area 11.6: Low-Risk, Medium-Risk, High-Risk, and Unclear Result States

Risk result states should be consistent across the app. A user should quickly recognize the difference between low risk, medium risk, risk, and unclear. Each state should have a label, reason, and next step.

Low-risk states should be careful. Low risk should not mean guaranteed safe. It should mean the app did not find strong scam signals in the reviewed material. If the user is about to send money, share a code, give a password, install software, or disclose private info, the app should still encourage verification through official channels.

Medium-risk states should explain uncertainty. The app might detect pressure, unusual payment method, a risky link, an unfamiliar sender, or missing context. The next step should focus on verification, not panic. The app can suggest contacting the person or company through a known official method.

Risky states should be firm but calm. The app should say that the content matches strong scam patterns and the safest action is to stop before sending money, sharing codes, opening links, installing software, or giving private info. The risky state should include evidence and next steps, not only a warning.

Unclear states should be honest. If the app cannot determine risk because the screenshot is unreadable, the message is too short, the situation is outside supported categories, or important context is missing, it should say so. Unclear should not be treated as safe. The default behavior should be cautious: pause, verify externally, and provide more info if possible.

Each result state should include an optional details area. Advanced users can see signal breakdowns, but non-technical users should see plain reasons first. Details should support understanding, not overwhelm the main decision.

### Area 11.7: High-Risk Interruption and Safe-Stop States

Risky interruption is one of the most important behaviors for Verivae. When the app detects a dangerous pattern, especially during link opening, code sharing, payment, remote access, or money transfer preparation, it should help the user stop safely.

A safe-stop screen should be direct. It should say what action is risky and why. For example, this request asks you to send money by gift card, or this person is asking for a login code, or this link may not belong to the company it claims to represent. The screen should then give the safest next step.

The app should not physically trap the user, but it can add friction before risky actions. If the user tries to open a risky link from inside the app, the app can require an extra confirmation that explains the risk. If the user tries to share a code, the app can warn that codes are for the user only. If the user tries to continue after a risky payment warning, the app can recommend verifying through official contact first.

Safe-stop states should include an emergency exit from the scam conversation. The app can suggest stop replying, block the sender, save evidence, contact the real company, or ask a trusted helper. The app should not tell users to confront the suspected scammer. Confrontation can increase pressure or cause the scammer to change tactics.

If the user dismisses a risky warning, the app should not harass them, but it may save the warning in the case history and offer a reminder. The product should respect user control while still making the risk clear.

### Area 11.8: Already-Happened and Damage-Control States

the app must support users after something has already happened. A user may have sent money, shared a login code, revealed a password, clicked a link, installed remote access software, deposited a fake check, shipped an item, paid a rental deposit, shared ID docs, or given a scammer access to an account.

The app should shift from prevention to damage control. The screen should not say prevention failed. It should say let us secure what we can now. The first step should be triage: what happened, when it happened, what was shared, what accounts or devices may be affected, and whether money is still pending.

The damage-control state should prioritize actions by urgency. If a login code or password was shared, account security may come first. If money was sent, contacting the payment provider or financial institution may come first. If remote access software was installed, removing access and checking the device may come first. If a fake check was deposited, avoiding spending the funds and contacting the bank may come first.

The app should generate a case summary from the user's answers. The summary should include the risky contact, scam category, money or account risk, evidence saved, steps completed, and advised next steps. The user should be able to use this summary when contacting official support, a bank, a platform, or a trusted helper.

Damage-control states should support emotional reality. The user may feel embarrassed, scared, angry, or ashamed. The app should stay calm and practical. It should avoid language that increases shame. It should keep the user focused on what can still be done.

### Area 11.9: Device Scan and Weekly Deep Check States

Device scan states should be understandable to ordinary users. When Verivae checks a linked device for risky apps, risky permissions, unknown profiles, unsafe settings, or signs that a scammer may have gained access, the app should show what it is checking in plain text.

A quick device check can show immediate items such as risky recently installed apps, remote-control tools, risky permissions, alert-access changes, and settings that affect protection. A weekly check can review broader patterns, stale permissions, unusual app behavior, linked devices, browser risk signals where supported, and protection status across linked areas.

The app should separate findings by severity. Critical findings need immediate action. Important findings need review soon. Infoal findings help the user understand device health. The app should not label everything as dangerous. Too many severe warnings will make users ignore real danger.

For each device finding, the app should explain the issue, why it matters, what the user can do, and whether the app can help directly. If the app cannot remove an app or change a setting due to platform rules, it should provide stepwise guidance. The app should distinguish between scan result and completed fix.

Weekly check completion states should be calm. If nothing concerning is found, the app can say no urgent issues found. If something needs attention, it should list the top issues and advised order. The user should be able to schedule reminders, share a summary with a trusted helper, or review detailed findings.

### Area 11.10: Background Monitoring and Alert State Changes

If Verivae supports background monitoring for messages, email, links, device signals, or scam patterns, the app should show whether monitoring is active. Users should not have to guess whether protection is running.

A protection status area should show active, paused, limited, needs attention, or unavailable. Active means the feature is working within current permissions. Paused means the user or system disabled it. Limited means some protection works but not all. Needs attention means a permission, account connection, update, or setting must be fixed. Unavailable means the device or platform does not support that feature.

When monitoring status changes, the app should explain what changed. For example, email protection paused because account connection expired, or message monitoring limited because alert access is off. The app should offer a restore path, but it should also say what still works manually.

Background warnings should be privacy-safe by default. They should not expose full scam content on the lock screen. They should draw the user back into the app for details. If the warning is urgent, the app can say review before responding or possible risky request detected, then reveal the details only inside the app.

Monitoring should not create constant noise. The app should group low-priority updates and reserve interruptions for risky moments. A security app that interrupts too often becomes less protective because users learn to dismiss it.

### Area 11.11: Case History, Saved Evidence, and Return-Later States

the app should let users return to a scam case later. Scam situations often unfold across hours, days, or weeks. A user may first receive a message, then a call, then a payment request, then a threat, then a request to move platforms. The case history should connect these events.

A saved case should include the reviewed content, risk result, reasons, user notes, evidence attachments, completed steps, remaining steps, shared-helper status, and report/export options. The user should be able to rename a case with a simple label such as marketplace sale, bank text, rental deposit, job offer, or family emergency.

The return-later state should show what has changed since the user last viewed the case. If a scan finished, a helper replied, a weekly check found a related issue, or the user added evidence, the case should show that update. The user should not have to reread everything to understand the status.

Evidence should be preserved carefully. The app should save messages, screenshots, links, phone numbers, emails, payment notes, and user explanations in a way that helps later review. It should also support redaction when sharing. The user should control whether sensitive details remain visible.

Case history should not become a confusing archive. It should support search, filtering, and status labels. Useful statuses include checking, needs info, risk, resolved, evidence saved, shared with helper, reported, and follow-up needed.

### Area 11.12: Error, Failure, and Retry States

Errors in the app should be specific and recoverable. The app should not rely on generic labels such as something went wrong. It should explain the likely cause and the next useful action.

If a screenshot cannot be read, the app should say the screenshot text is blurry, cut off, too dark, or missing the key part. If a link cannot be checked, it should say whether the link is incomplete, blocked, expired, or unsupported. If email connection fails, it should say whether the account needs reconnecting. If a device scan cannot finish, it should say whether permission, battery setting, connection, or platform limitation is involved.

Retry should be available when retry makes sense. The app can offer retry scan, upload clearer screenshot, paste text instead, reconnect account, check manually, or save for later. It should not make the user restart from the beginning unless there is no alternative.

The app should preserve user-entered info during errors. If the user typed a long scam story and the connection fails, the text should stay. If a payment case fails to submit, the app should preserve the case draft. Losing info during a stressful moment would make the product feel unreliable.

Error states should distinguish between safety advice and technical completion. If the app cannot complete a full scan, it can still offer universal safety guidance: do not send money under pressure, do not share login codes, do not install remote access tools for unknown callers, verify through official channels, and save evidence. This is not a replacement for the scan, but it is better than leaving the user with no guidance.

### Area 11.13: Offline and Low-Connection States

the app should remain useful when the device has poor connection. Scam situations may happen while traveling, at work, in a store, during a phone call, or in a place with weak service. The app should not become useless just because the full online scan cannot run.

Offline mode can provide basic static safety checks. The app can ask whether the request involves gift cards, wire transfer, crypto, login codes, account passwords, remote access software, urgent threats, secrecy, fake family emergency, marketplace overpayment, or a link from an unknown sender. If the user selects one of these, the app can recommend pausing and verifying before continuing.

Offline states should be clearly labeled. The app should say that full analysis is unavailable until connection returns. It should not pretend that offline guidance is the same as a complete scan. The user should be able to save the case and run a full check later.

When connection returns, the app should offer to finish pending checks. It should not silently ignore them. Pending checks should appear in case history with a status such as waiting for connection.

Offline safety guidance should be short and conservative. It should focus on actions that are broadly protective: pause, do not send money, do not share codes, do not install tools, do not use links from risky messages, and contact the real person or company through a known official method.

### Area 11.14: State Consistency Across Phone, Email, Messages, and Device Integrations

The app should behave consistently across integrations. A risky email, risky text, risky marketplace message, and risky call summary should all share the same result structure: risk label, reason, next step, save option, share option, and detail option.

Integration-specific differences should be explained without changing the mental model. For email, the app may check sender, links, attachments, and impersonation language. For messages, it may check sender patterns, links, payment pressure, and code requests. For calls, it may rely on transcription or user summary. For device scans, it may check apps and settings. But the user-facing structure should remain familiar.

If an integration is not available on a user's device, the app should offer an equivalent manual path. For example, if direct message integration is limited, the user can share a message, paste text, or upload a screenshot. If email connection is unavailable, the user can forward or paste the email. If device checks are limited, the app can guide the user through manual settings review.

Cross-integration cases should merge intelligently. If a risky email leads to a phone call and then a payment request, the app should let the user connect those events. The case should become stronger because the pattern is clearer.

The app should also avoid duplicate warnings when the same scam appears in multiple places. If the same link is in a text and email, the app should recognize the connection where possible and show a combined case summary rather than confusing the user with separate unrelated warnings.

### Area 11.15: State Accept Rules

Area 11 should be considered functionally satisfied only if the product design meets these conditions.

Every major action has a visible state: ready, checking, complete, needs info, failed, saved, shared, blocked, or paused.

Every loading state tells the user what is being checked and preserves the case if the user leaves.

Every empty state offers a useful next action instead of only saying nothing is available.

Every permission-missing state explains what is off, what still works, and how to restore protection.

Every partial-input state says what the app can review, what is missing, and what question matters next.

Every risk result state includes a label, reason, and next step.

Every risky state gives a safe-stop action without hiding basic protection behind payment.

Every already-happened state shifts into damage control with prioritized recovery steps.

Every device scan result explains findings in normal language and separates severity levels.

Every background monitoring state makes active, paused, limited, needs attention, and unavailable conditions visible.

Every saved case can be returned to later with evidence, status, next steps, and sharing controls intact.

Every error state gives a cause and a practical recovery path.

Every offline state gives conservative safety guidance and saves pending checks for later full review.

Every integration uses a consistent result structure while respecting platform-specific limits.

### Area 11 completion note

Area 11 completes the screen-state and recovery-behavior layer for the current design brief stage. Future areas should build on these rules when defining onboarding, user testing, quality assurance, account setup, subscription behavior, settings, and final product requirements. Area 11 should remain app-only: it defines how the app should behave across real product states, not how Harborwake should market, launch, or code the product.

## App Feature Area 12: Onboarding, Setup, Permissions, and Personalization

### Purpose of this feature area

Area 12 defines how the app should introduce itself, help a new user start safely, explain protection options, request permissions, connect phone and account integrations, configure device checks, add trusted helpers, personalize risk sensitivity, and keep the free experience useful. The area focuses on onboarding and setup behavior inside Verivae, including what the user sees, what choices they make, and how the app protects trust from the first session.

Onboarding is not just the first few screens. For a scam-protection app, onboarding is the first trust test. The user needs to know what the app can do, what it cannot do, what info it may access, what remains private, how to get protection without paying, and how to start checking risky messages immediately. If onboarding is confusing, pushy, overly technical, or too focused on permissions, users may quit before receiving any protection.

the app should treat setup as a guided safety path rather than an account-registration chore. The app should let users get value quickly through manual checks, then gradually invite them to connect deeper protection. A user should be able to open the app for the first time, check a risky text or email, and understand the result before deciding whether to connect Gmail, messages, device checks, alerts, or trusted helpers.

The onboarding system should also support different user types. Some users will install Verivae because they already received a risky message. Some will install it for a parent or grandparent. Some will install it after being scammed. Some will install it because they want ongoing monitoring. Some will be privacy-conscious and avoid integrations. Some will want the strongest automatic protection possible. The app should handle all of these starting points without forcing everyone through the same rigid flow.

### Area 12.1: Onboarding Philosophy and First Trust Moment

The first trust moment happens before the app detects any scam. The user is deciding whether the app is safe enough to use. The app should therefore introduce itself with clarity, restraint, and practical value. It should not exaggerate protection, promise that scams can always be detected, or imply that the user must connect everything before the app helps.

The opening experience should communicate three things. First, the app helps users check risky messages, emails, links, calls, payment requests, and device risks. Second, the user controls what gets linked and shared. Third, manual checking works even before optional setup. These points should appear in normal language, not legal language.

The app should avoid fear-based onboarding. It should not start by saying scammers are everywhere, your phone is probably compromised, or you are unsafe unless you complete setup. Scam protection is serious, but panic is not a good product strategy. A better opening tone is calm and capable: check risky requests before you respond; connect optional protection when you are ready; keep control of your info.

The first trust moment should include an immediate action. A user should be able to tap check something now without making an account if the product model allows it, or with minimal account setup if accounts are required. The app should not force a long tutorial before the user can review a risky message.

The onboarding philosophy should also make limitations clear. the app can review patterns, guide safer decisions, and help preserve evidence, but it cannot guarantee that every message is safe or unsafe. It cannot recover money by itself. It cannot access accounts the user does not connect. It cannot replace official financial, platform, or law-enforcement processes. Honest limitation language increases trust.

### Area 12.2: First-Run User Paths

the app should support several first-run paths. The app should not assume that every new user has the same reason for installing it. The first-run screen can ask a simple question: what do you want to do first? The choices should be practical and user-centered.

One first-run path is check something risky. This path should take the user directly to manual input options: paste text, upload screenshot, share from another app, check a link, summarize a call, or describe a payment request. This is the fastest path for users who are currently under pressure.

Another path is set up ongoing protection. This path can explain message protection, email protection, device checks, alerts, weekly checks, and trusted-helper options. It should sequence setup in small steps instead of asking for every permission at once.

Another path is help someone else. This path should explain trusted-helper support, case sharing, consent, privacy redaction, and how the user can assist a family member or friend without taking over their accounts. The app should be careful not to enable secret monitoring or coercive control.

Another path is I already got scammed or I already shared something. This path should move directly into damage-control triage. It should ask what happened and prioritize recovery actions. The user should not be forced through normal setup before receiving urgent guidance.

Another path is just exploring. This path should let the user see examples, learn core safety rules, and try a sample check. The product can demonstrate value without requiring sensitive permissions immediately.

### Area 12.3: Account Creation and Sign-In Experience

If Verivae requires an account, account creation should be simple and explain why the account exists. The app should not ask for unnecessary info. It should collect only what is required to keep cases, settings, trusted-helper relationships, subscription status, and linked devices consistent.

The app should explain account value in normal terms. An account can let the user save scam checks, return to case history, sync settings across devices, receive helper replies, manage subscriptions, and restore protection after reinstalling. The explanation should not sound like data collection for its own sake.

The sign-in process should support users who are stressed. If the user opens the app from a risky message, the app should avoid making them complete a long profile before getting basic guidance. If possible, the app can allow a temporary check first, then ask whether the user wants to save the result by creating an account.

If passwords are used, the app should encourage strong password practices without turning onboarding into a security lecture. If passkeys, social sign-in, or email sign-in are supported, the app should explain them simply. The user should know what happens if they lose access to the account.

Account recovery must be designed carefully. A scam-protection account may contain sensitive case history. Recovery should be secure enough to protect private info, but clear enough that normal users can regain access. Recovery screens should never ask users to share login codes with support agents. The app should teach that codes are for the user only.

### Area 12.4: Permission Request Sequencing

Permission sequencing is one of the most important parts of setup. the app should not ask for every permission on the first screen. That can feel invasive and confusing. The app should ask for permissions when the user understands the feature that needs them.

The app should use just-in-time permission requests. If the user chooses message protection, the app explains message access. If the user chooses email protection, it explains email connection. If the user chooses weekly device checks, it explains device signals or settings review. If the user chooses alerts, it explains what alerts will look like and how privacy is protected.

Each permission request should include four pieces of info before the platform dialog appears. The app should say what access is being requested, why it helps, what is not being accessed or shared, and how to turn it off later. This should be written in plain text.

Permission prompts should be separate enough that users can make informed choices. Bundling message access, email access, alerts, contacts, photos, and device info into one setup moment would make consent weaker. The user should be able to choose one protection layer without accepting all of them.

If a user declines a permission, the app should continue gracefully. It should explain what still works and offer alternatives. For example, if message monitoring is denied, the app can still support sharing a message into Verivae, pasting text, or uploading screenshots. Declining permission should not make the user feel locked out.

### Area 12.5: Manual Protection Before Full Setup

Manual protection should be available early because it proves the app's value. A user who is unsure about permissions should still be able to check a risky message, email, link, screenshot, call summary, or payment request. This supports free-first trust and privacy-conscious users.

The manual check flow should be included during onboarding. The app can say you can start with manual checks and connect automatic protection later. This helps users who are not ready to link accounts. It also helps users who are installing the app during an urgent situation.

Manual protection should not feel like a weak demo. It should provide real guidance, risk explanations, next steps, save options, and trusted-helper sharing if the user has enough account state to support it. Some advanced automation can remain optional, but the core manual safety check should be meaningful.

The app should make manual input flexible. Users can paste text, upload screenshots, share content from another app, type a summary, check a link, describe a phone call, or identify what the other person is asking them to do. The app should not require perfect formatting.

Manual protection should also teach the user's mental model. After checking something manually, the app can explain that connecting email, messages, alerts, or device checks can help detect similar risks sooner. This is a better upgrade path than asking for access before the user sees value.

### Area 12.6: Email, Messages, and Phone Integration Setup

Integration setup should be broken into clear modules. The app should not treat phone, email, messages, calls, screenshots, and alerts as one vague protection package. Each module should have a name, benefit, permission explanation, setup status, and manual alternative.

Email setup should explain that the app can help review risky emails, links, sender claims, payment requests, attachment warnings where supported, and impersonation patterns. It should also explain any limits. If the app cannot read every email automatically due to platform or provider limits, it should say what is supported and offer manual forwarding, sharing, or paste options.

Message setup should explain how text or chat review works on the user's device. If direct message monitoring is limited by the OS, the app should present screenshot, share-sheet, copy-paste, or alert-based review as alternatives. The app should avoid promising background access that the platform does not permit.

Phone and call setup should be careful. Users may expect the app to listen to calls, record calls, block callers, or read voicemail. The setup should explain what is actually supported. If the feature relies on call summaries, transcripts, user notes, caller ID signals, or voicemail review, the app should say that plainly.

Each integration should have a test step. After connecting email, the app can show connection active and explain how to check an email. After enabling message sharing, it can show how to share a risky text. After enabling alerts, it can show a sample privacy-safe alert. A test step helps users feel that setup worked.

### Area 12.7: Device Check and Weekly Deep Check Setup

Device check setup should explain what the feature is and what it is not. Users may think a device scan means the app can detect every virus. the app should be careful. It can say it checks for signs that may increase scam or account risk, such as risky apps, risky permissions, remote-access tools, unsafe settings, stale access, or protection gaps where platform support allows.

The first device check should be optional but clearly useful. The setup can offer run a quick device safety check now. The app should explain how long it may take and what the user can do while it runs. It should also say that some checks may require permission or manual review of settings.

Weekly check setup should let the user choose timing, alert privacy, and whether results can be shared with a trusted helper. The default should be respectful. Weekly checks should not wake users at bad times with scary alerts unless there is an urgent issue.

The app should explain the difference between quick check and weekly check. A quick check is for immediate review. A weekly check is a regular review of broader protection status. The user should understand why both exist.

If device checks are limited on a platform, the app should offer a guided manual checklist. It can walk users through reviewing installed apps, remote access tools, alert access, browser extensions where relevant, linked devices, and account security settings. The app should mark platform-limited checks as guided rather than automatic.

### Area 12.8: Trusted Helper Setup

Trusted-helper setup should be simple, consent-based, and privacy-first. The user should understand exactly what a trusted helper can see and do. The helper is not the owner of the account, not a hidden monitor, and not someone who can silently access everything.

The setup flow should ask who the helper is and what type of access the user wants. Options can include share one case at a time, allow helper replies on shared cases, send urgent help request, or allow ongoing helper visibility for selected safety cases. Ongoing visibility should require clear consent and be easy to revoke.

The app should explain redaction before sharing. Redaction means hiding private details before someone else sees them. During helper setup, the app should show examples such as hidden phone number, hidden account number, hidden address, hidden login code, or hidden email address. The user should be able to review what will be shared.

Helper setup should include abuse-prevention boundaries. The app should not allow a helper to secretly monitor all messages, view all emails, disable protection, change payment settings, remove evidence, or pressure the user through the app. If the helper has any ongoing visibility, the app should display that clearly in settings and case screens.

For users helping a parent, grandparent, or friend, the app should explain that the protected person should stay in control whenever possible. The app can support family help without encouraging account takeover or privacy invasion.

### Area 12.9: Personalization and Risk Sensitivity

Personalization should make Verivae more useful without making it confusing. The app can ask users what they want extra help with: banking and payment alerts, marketplace scams, job scams, romance or social scams, family emergency scams, device safety, email impersonation, or all of the above.

Risk sensitivity settings should be understandable. A high-sensitivity setting can warn more often and may create more false alarms. A balanced setting can focus on clearer scam patterns. A quiet setting can reduce alerts but may miss weaker signals. The app should explain these tradeoffs in plain text.

The app should avoid giving users unsafe customization. Users should not be encouraged to turn off warnings for login codes, remote access tools, unusual payment requests, or risky money movement without understanding the risk. Some critical warnings should remain strongly advised.

Personalization can also include preferred language complexity, simplified mode, alert privacy level, trusted-helper sharing defaults, weekly check timing, and whether the user wants educational explanations after results. These settings should make the app feel respectful rather than overwhelming.

Personalization should not create unequal safety by payment tier. Paid users may get more automation or broader monitoring, but free users should still receive clear warnings and basic safety explanations. The user's ability to understand danger should not depend on paying.

### Area 12.10: Free-First Setup and Upgrade Boundaries

Because the app is intended to be free-first while still supporting future paid features, setup must define fair free and paid boundaries. The free setup path should help real users immediately. It should not feel like a locked demo.

The free onboarding path should include manual checks, plain risk results, basic next steps, basic case saving if account support allows it, privacy-safe alerts where supported, and limited trusted-helper sharing. The user should see that the app is useful before being asked to pay.

Paid setup can add advanced convenience. Examples include detailed monitoring, more linked accounts, family dashboards, deeper device checks, longer case history, more detailed export options, priority review features, or broader weekly protection reports. These should be framed as added coverage, not as the only way to be safe.

Upgrade prompts during setup should be placed carefully. A user who is trying to check an urgent message should not be blocked by a paywall before receiving basic guidance. If an advanced paid feature is relevant, the app can show the free path first and the paid enhancement second.

The app should explain plan status clearly. The user should know what is included, what is optional, and what changes if they upgrade, downgrade, cancel, or remain free. Confusing plan boundaries create distrust, especially for a safety product.

### Area 12.11: Setup Progress, Protection Status, and Completion

The app should show setup progress in a way that is useful but not guilt-inducing. A protection status screen can show manual checks ready, email protection active or not linked, message protection active or limited, device check ready or not set up, weekly check scheduled or off, trusted helper added or not added, and alerts private or disabled.

The status screen should avoid one oversimplified score that makes users feel unsafe unless everything is enabled. A completion percentage can be misleading because not every user needs every integration. A better approach is a protection map: core protection ready, optional protections available, and attention needed items.

Setup should be considered complete enough when the user has at least one useful way to check risky content and understands how to return. The app can then encourage optional layers without implying the user failed setup.

Protection status should remain visible after onboarding. Users need to know whether monitoring is active, paused, limited, or unavailable. The status should update when permissions change, accounts disconnect, alerts are disabled, device checks fail, or subscription status changes.

The app should support reminders for incomplete setup, but reminders should be respectful. It should not repeatedly nag users to connect sensitive accounts. Reminder frequency should be controlled and privacy-safe.

### Area 12.12: Onboarding for Users Who Already Experienced Harm

A user who already sent money, shared a code, installed remote access software, deposited a check, gave a password, shipped an item, or shared ID docs should not be forced through normal onboarding first. The app should recognize this path and move directly into response mode.

The first question can be practical: what happened? The user can choose from money sent, code shared, password shared, link clicked, app installed, check deposited, item shipped, identity info shared, or not sure. The app should then prioritize immediate next steps.

This onboarding path should still explain account creation and saving, but only after urgent guidance begins. For example, the app can say save this case so you can track recovery steps. The user should not feel that setup is blocking help.

The already-harmed path should include evidence preservation early. The app can ask the user to save messages, screenshots, payment notes, caller info, emails, tracking numbers, receipts, and account changes. It should also support redaction and helper sharing.

This path should be emotionally careful. The app should not say you made a mistake. It should say we will focus on what can still be protected. The interface should keep the user moving through concrete steps.

### Area 12.13: Onboarding Accept Rules

Area 12 should be considered functionally satisfied only if the product design meets these conditions.

A new user can check risky content before completing every optional integration.

The first-run experience supports multiple starting points: urgent check, ongoing setup, helping someone else, already-harmed response, and exploring.

Every account request explains why the account is useful and avoids unnecessary personal info.

Every permission request explains what access is requested, why it helps, what is not accessed or shared, and how to turn it off.

Every denied permission has a graceful manual alternative.

Every integration has a visible setup status and a test or confirmation step.

Device check setup explains the difference between quick checks, weekly checks, automatic checks, and guided manual review.

Trusted-helper setup is consent-based, redacted by default where appropriate, and easy to revoke.

Personalization improves usefulness without hiding critical warnings or creating unsafe defaults.

Free setup provides real safety value before upgrade prompts.

Paid setup boundaries are clear and do not block basic safety comprehension.

Protection status remains visible after onboarding and updates when permissions, accounts, monitoring, device checks, or plan status change.

Users who already experienced harm can enter damage-control mode immediately.

Setup language stays calm, plain, and app-only.

### Area 12 completion note

Area 12 completes the onboarding, setup, permissions, and personalization layer for the current design brief stage. Future areas should build on these rules when defining settings, account management, subscription behavior, testing, privacy review, family-helper workflows, and final product requirements. Area 12 should remain app-only: it defines how the app should guide setup and protection choices, not how Harborwake should market, launch, or code the product.

## Area 13: Complete App Function and Layout Blueprint

### Area 13 purpose

## This final main area defines the overall functional shape and layout logic of Verivae as an app. It describes what the app should contain, how its major surfaces should relate to one another, what users should be able to do inside each surface, and how the layout should support scam safety, device safety, recovery, trusted helper support, privacy, reporting, education, and paid feature boundaries.

## 

## The purpose of this area is to make the design brief feel complete as an app specification. Earlier areas define screens, functions, user flows, integrations, security rules, detection logic, scam categories, accessibility, states, onboarding, permissions, and personalization. This final main area ties those pieces into one coherent app structure so a future designer or builder can understand the whole product without turning the brief into a project schedule.

## 

## the app should feel like a calm protection workspace. It should not feel like a noisy antivirus dashboard, a bank app, a police report system, a social media app, or a generic chatbot. The app should feel focused, practical, private, and action-oriented. Its layout should help the user answer the same essential questions from many entry points: Is this risky? Why? What should I do now? What should I save? Who can help me? What can I safely ignore? What should I check later?

## 

### Area 13 \- Core App Shape

## The core shape of the app should be organized around five main user needs: check something risky, recover from something that already happened, review saved cases, protect the device and accounts, and manage trust settings. Every major screen should support one or more of these needs. The app should avoid adding decorative or unrelated areas that distract from safety.

## 

## The main app should have a persistent navigation structure that is simple enough for beginners. A advised bottom navigation model is Home, Check, Cases, Protection, and Settings. Home is the safety dashboard. Check is the fastest way to review a risky item. Cases is the saved history and case space. Protection contains device checks, weekly checks, account safety, and linked services. Settings contains privacy, helpers, subscriptions, accessibility, and app preferences. If the app uses a different navigation model later, it should still preserve these functional destinations.

## 

## The app should support deep links from external contexts. If a user shares an email, text, screenshot, link, or file into Verivae, the app should open the Check flow directly with the submitted item loaded. If a user taps a weekly check alert, the app should open the weekly check result. If a helper taps a case invitation, the app should open the helper review view. These entry points should respect privacy and auth before showing sensitive content.

## 

## The app should distinguish between active safety surfaces and reference surfaces. Active safety surfaces include manual check, result screen, recovery checklist, device check, helper review, report package, and account protection. Reference surfaces include education library, scam examples, privacy explanations, settings descriptions, and help center. Active safety surfaces should prioritize action. Reference surfaces can provide deeper learning.

## 

### Area 13 \- Home Screen Layout

## The home screen should be the user's safety dashboard. It should not be a marketing page or a decorative landing page. The first visible area should show the user's current protection status in plain text. Example summary states include: No urgent items, One case needs action, Weekly check due, Device check limited, Helper response waiting, or Critical case active. The summary should be calm and specific.

## 

## The primary action on the home screen should be a manual check. This action should be visually obvious and reachable with one tap. The label should be direct, such as Check something risky. Supporting actions can include Run device check, Review saved cases, Start recovery, Ask trusted helper, and View weekly check. The app should not bury manual check behind menus because manual check is the core free-first value.

## 

## The home screen should include an active cases area. This area should show only cases that need attention by default, not every old case. Each case preview should include risk level, short title, category, status, and next action. A case preview should avoid exposing sensitive content on the dashboard unless the user has chosen that setting. Sensitive case titles should be discreet.

## 

## The home screen should include a protection status area. This area should show device check status, weekly check status, linked services status, and helper status. Each status should be understandable: On, Off, Limited, Needs permission, Needs review, or Not set up. If something is limited, the app should explain why in one tap.

## 

## The home screen should include a small education prompt only when useful. Education should not dominate the dashboard. A good prompt might match the user's recent activity, such as marketplace safety after marketplace checks or login code safety after code-related checks. The prompt should be optional and easy to dismiss.

## 

### Area 13 \- Manual Scam Check Layout

## The manual check layout should support many input types without overwhelming the user. The first screen should ask what the user wants to check. Input options should include Paste text, Share or paste a link, Add screenshot, Describe a call, Upload or attach a file where supported, Check a payment request, Check a job offer, Check a marketplace message, and I am not sure. The app should allow the user to start broadly and refine later.

## 

## The input screen should include a short privacy note. It should explain whether the item will be saved automatically or only after the result. The default should make the user feel in control. The app should say that the user can delete saved cases later if they choose to save them.

## 

## The manual check flow should support guided questions. If the user gives limited info, the app should ask practical follow-ups: Did they ask for money? Did they ask for a code? Did they ask you to click a link? Did they ask you to install anything? Did they say it was urgent? Did they ask you not to tell anyone? Did you already respond? Did you already send money? These questions should appear only when useful.

## 

## The manual check layout should support progressive disclosure. A beginner should see a simple flow. A detailed user should be able to expand advanced fields such as sender address, phone number, link destination, payment method, attachment type, or account affected. The app should never require advanced fields before giving basic safety guidance.

## 

## The manual check screen should always preserve an exit path. The user should be able to cancel, save as draft, clear the input, or get basic safety guidance if they are not ready to submit. If the user is on a risky call or under pressure, a Stop-now guidance option should be visible.

## 

### Area 13 \- Result Screen Layout

## The result screen is one of the most important layouts in Verivae. It should show the risk level, the plain reason, and the next safest action above everything else. A result screen should never make the user scroll past a long explanation before seeing what to do.

## 

## The advised result structure is: risk label, one-sentence summary, immediate next step, key warning signs, safer verification path, optional recovery actions, save/share/report actions, and deeper explanation. This structure should work for Low concern, Caution, Risk, Critical risk, and Unknown results.

## 

## A Low concern result should still avoid overpromising. It should say that no major warning signs were found in the provided info. It should remind the user to use official apps or websites for sensitive actions. It should offer saving only if the user wants a record.

## 

## A Caution result should focus on verification. It should show what is unclear, what warning signs exist, and what the user should verify before acting. The main action might be Verify another way, Ask helper, or Add more details.

## 

## A Risk result should tell the user not to proceed until verified. The screen should emphasize the specific action to avoid, such as do not send money, do not share the code, do not click the link, do not install the app, or do not refund the overpayment. The app should provide a safer path immediately.

## 

## A Critical risk result should show stop-now guidance. It should include large clear actions, such as Stop responding, Contact bank through official route, Start recovery checklist, Remove remote access, Preserve evidence, or Ask trusted helper. It should avoid panic language while making urgency clear.

## 

## An Unknown result should be useful, not empty. It should explain what info is missing and offer next steps. The app should never use Unknown as a dead end. It should guide the user to add a screenshot, sender info, link, payment details, or context.

## 

### Area 13 \- Case Detail Layout

## A case detail screen should act as the full record for one risky situation. It should include summary, evidence, risk result, status, recovery checklist, helper activity, reporting package, audit trail, and privacy controls. The layout should make active next steps easy to find while preserving full detail for later.

## 

## The top of a case detail screen should show the case title, risk level, status, category, and next action. If the case is sensitive, the title can be discreet. The user should be able to rename a case because default titles may expose private details or be hard to recognize.

## 

## Evidence should be grouped by type. Message text, screenshots, links, call summaries, payment details, files, and notes should not be mixed into one confusing block. Each evidence item should show whether it is included in helper sharing or export. Sensitive evidence should have redaction and deletion controls.

## 

## The risk result should remain visible inside the case, but it should also show when it was generated and whether new evidence has been added since then. If new evidence changes the situation, the app should offer to review again. Old conclusions should not silently change without context.

## 

## Recovery steps should be shown as a checklist with clear states: Not started, In progress, Done, Skipped, Not applicable, or Need help. The checklist should adapt to what happened. Password exposure, money sent, code shared, link clicked, remote access installed, blackmail threat, and account takeover should each produce different recovery steps.

## 

## Helper activity should be clear. The user should see whether a case was shared, who it was shared with, what they could see, whether they responded, and what they said. Helper responses should not override the app's safety result without explanation.

## 

### Area 13 \- Recovery Workspace Layout

## The case space should be designed for users who already made a mistake or may already be harmed. It should not feel like a punishment screen. It should feel like an organized checklist for getting control back.

## 

## The case space should start by identifying the harm type. Harm types include clicked link, entered password, shared login code, sent money, sent gift cards, sent crypto, deposited check, installed app, gave remote access, shared ID doc, shared payment card, lost account access, received threats, or not sure. The user should be able to select multiple harm types.

## 

## Recovery modules should be shown in priority order. Urgent steps come first. For money loss, official bank or payment contact should appear early. For account compromise, password change and session review should appear early. For remote access, device access removal and device review should appear early. For blackmail threats, stop communication, preserve evidence, platform reporting, and trusted support should appear early.

## 

## The recovery layout should show progress without gamifying harm. A simple progress bar or completed-step count can help, but it should not celebrate a scam situation like a game. The tone should be calm and practical.

## 

## The case space should include helper sharing. The user should be able to share the checklist with a trusted person. The share preview should show exactly what will be visible. Sensitive details should be hidden by default.

## 

## The case space should end with a recovery summary. The summary should include what happened, what evidence is saved, what steps were completed, what remains unresolved, and what the user should monitor. This summary should be stored in the case.

## 

### Area 13 \- Protection and Device Safety Layout

## The Protection section should collect device checks, weekly checks, account protection, linked services, and safety reminders. It should not feel like a technical control panel for experts only. Each protection surface should explain what it does in simple words.

## 

## The device check screen should show what can be checked and what is limited. The app should separate device permission review, risky downloads, risky links, app permission concerns, security setting reminders, and unresolved scam-related device actions. It should not claim full virus scanning when platform limits prevent it.

## 

## The weekly check screen should show the most recent check result, unresolved findings, next scheduled check if scheduling exists, and what categories are included. If a check did not complete, the app should explain why. If weekly checks are off, the screen should still explain what they would do.

## 

## Account protection should be organized by account type: email, bank, payment app, social media, shopping, work, phone account, and not sure. Each account type should have guidance for password exposure, code sharing, risky login alerts, account takeover, and payment risk. The app should never ask for the user's password.

## 

## Linked services should show status and controls. Email review, message sharing, browser sharing, device permissions, helper contacts, alerts, and sync should each have a plain explanation. Disconnect and permission-change paths should be visible.

## 

### Area 13 \- Trusted Helper and Family Layout

## The helper and family layout should make support easier without allowing hidden monitoring. It should show who is linked, what they can see, what roles they have, and which cases are shared. The user's control should be visible at all times.

## 

## The helper dashboard should show helper status: No helper set up, Invite pending, Helper linked, Helper paused, or Helper removed. It should also show whether case-by-case sharing or urgent-risk sharing is enabled. The default should be case-by-case sharing.

## 

## The helper invite screen should explain the role before sending. It should say whether the helper can review selected cases, receive urgent alerts, comment, view summaries, or help with recovery steps. The app should avoid vague permissions like full access.

## 

## The helper case share screen should preview the exact content to be shared. It should include toggles for summary, message text, screenshot, app explanation, recovery steps, payment amount, sender details, and user's personal note. Sensitive content should be excluded by default unless needed and confirmed.

## 

## The family or trusted-circle view should show multiple helpers only when the user chooses that setup. It should make disagreements visible without turning helper feedback into a vote. The app should keep official verification and evidence-based safety guidance central.

## 

### Area 13 \- Privacy and Settings Layout

## Settings should be functional, not a dumping ground. The Settings section should include Privacy Center, trusted helpers, linked services, alerts, weekly checks, personalization, accessibility, subscription, account, help center, and delete data. Each settings row should have a short description.

## 

## Privacy Center should show saved data, linked services, helper access, export history, consent records, and deletion controls. The user should be able to manage privacy without reading a separate policy first.

## 

## Alert settings should be organized by purpose: critical risk, recovery reminders, weekly check, helper responses, permission issues, education tips, subscription notices, and account security. Lock-screen privacy controls should be visible for sensitive alerts.

## 

## Accessibility settings should include language, text size support, simple mode, reduced motion, contrast support, screen-reader-friendly labels, and haptic or sound preferences where supported. Accessibility should be presented as normal app control, not a hidden advanced feature.

## 

## Subscription settings should show the current plan, free features, paid features, renewal or billing status where available, cancellation path, and what changes if the plan ends. Paid feature prompts should never block critical safety guidance.

## 

### Area 13 \- Reporting, Export, and Evidence Layout

## The reporting and export layout should help users create useful summaries without accidentally oversharing. It should begin with the report destination or purpose: bank or card issuer, payment app, marketplace, social platform, email provider, employer or school, trusted helper, personal record, or not sure.

## 

## The report package builder should show selectable sections. These can include summary, original messages, screenshots, links, sender details, payment info, recovery steps, helper comments, audit trail, and app risk explanation. Each section should indicate whether it may contain sensitive info.

## 

## The export preview should be mandatory before creating or copying a package. The user should see what will be included and should be able to redact details. Redaction controls should be simple: hide names, hide phone numbers, hide email addresses, hide payment amounts, hide images, hide personal notes, or hide selected text.

## 

## The app should separate export from report submission. Export creates a package. Submission sends info somewhere else. the app should not submit anything externally without user confirmation. If direct submission is ever supported, the app should show the destination, contents, and consequences clearly.

## 

### Area 13 \- Education Library Layout

## The education library should be a reference area, not the main product. It should help users learn about scam patterns when they have time, while results and recovery screens teach in context. The library should be organized by situations rather than abstract technical terms.

## 

## Advised library categories include Bank alerts, Payment apps, Marketplace buying and selling, Job offers, Family emergency texts, Romance requests, Tech support calls, Delivery messages, Fake invoices, Investment pressure, Account takeover, Device safety, Login codes, Gift cards and crypto, Blackmail threats, and How to verify safely.

## 

## Each education page should include what it looks like, why it works, warning signs, safer action, false-alarm comparison, and what to do if it already happened. Pages should include example language without teaching scammers how to improve. Examples should be realistic but not unnecessarily detailed in a harmful way.

## 

## Education pages should link back to action. A page about login codes should include a Check a code request action. A page about marketplace scams should include Check a buyer or seller message. Education should support real app workflows.

## 

### Area 13 \- Universal Screen States

## Every important screen should support loading, empty, error, limited, offline, permission missing, sensitive, and completed states. These states should be designed intentionally because scam safety fails when unclear states leave users guessing.

## 

## A loading state should say what is happening. For example: Reviewing message, Checking link, Preparing report, Sharing case, Running device check, or Loading helper response. Loading states should not imply completion before work is done.

## 

## An empty state should explain what the user can do. If there are no cases, the app can say that saved checks will appear here. If no helper is linked, it can explain trusted helpers. If no weekly check exists, it can explain how weekly checks work.

## 

## An error state should explain what failed and what the user can do next. If review failed, the app should still show basic safety rules. If upload failed, the case should not be lost. If sharing failed, the app should say the helper did not receive it.

## 

## A limited state should be honest. Limited review means the app reviewed what was available but could not inspect everything. Limited device check means the phone or permission settings restrict the check. Limited email review means only selected content was reviewed. Limited should never look like safe.

## 

## An offline state should offer local guidance and queued actions where appropriate. The app should make clear what will happen when internet returns and whether sensitive content will be sent.

## 

### Area 13 \- Functional Completeness Standards

## the app should be considered functionally complete only when the major app surfaces work together coherently. Manual checks should create results. Results should become cases if saved. Cases should connect to recovery, helpers, reports, privacy controls, and history. Device checks should connect to recovery when risk is found. Weekly checks should connect to unresolved cases. Helper sharing should connect back to case records. Settings should control the behavior users experience elsewhere.

## 

## Every major feature should answer three questions: What is this for? What can the user do here? What happens next? If a feature cannot answer those questions, its layout is not clear enough.

## 

## Every major screen should have a primary action. The home screen checks something risky. The result screen gives a safe next step. The case screen advances or resolves the case. The recovery screen completes urgent steps. The protection screen reviews device and account safety. The helper screen manages support. The privacy screen controls data. The report screen prepares evidence.

## 

## Every sensitive flow should have a privacy checkpoint. Saving screenshots, sharing with helpers, exporting evidence, syncing cases, connecting services, and enabling ongoing checks should all show what will happen. The app should make privacy choices visible before action, not after.

## 

## Every risky flow should have a recovery path. If the app says a situation is risk or critical, it should not stop at warning. It should offer recovery, official verification, helper support, evidence saving, or reporting package creation depending on the situation.

## 

### Area 13 \- Final Main Area Accept Rules

## The final app layout is acceptable when a beginner can open Verivae, check something risky, understand the result, take a safe next action, save the case, start recovery if needed, ask a trusted helper, review device or account safety, manage privacy, and export a useful report without needing a separate instruction manual.

## 

## The navigation is acceptable when Home, Check, Cases, Protection, and Settings or equivalent destinations are clear, reachable, and consistent. External share entry points should land in the correct review flow.

## 

## The home screen is acceptable when it shows current safety status, urgent cases, manual check, protection status, and useful next actions without overwhelming the user.

## 

## The manual check flow is acceptable when it supports text, links, screenshots, call summaries, files where supported, and uncertain situations while preserving privacy and offering guided questions.

## 

## The result screen is acceptable when it shows risk level, summary, reason, next step, warning signs, safer verification, save/share/report actions, and recovery options when needed.

## 

## The case screen is acceptable when it organizes evidence, risk results, recovery steps, helper activity, report packages, audit trails, statuses, and privacy controls in one coherent record.

## 

## The case space is acceptable when it adapts to the harm type, prioritizes urgent steps, tracks progress, supports helper sharing, and creates a recovery summary.

## 

## The protection section is acceptable when device checks, weekly checks, account safety, and linked services are understandable and honest about limits.

## 

## The helper and family layout is acceptable when support is consent-based, role-based, previewed before sharing, privacy-preserving, and transparent to the primary user.

## 

## The privacy and settings layout is acceptable when users can manage saved data, permissions, helpers, alerts, personalization, accessibility, subscription, account, and deletion from clear settings.

## 

## The reporting layout is acceptable when users can build, preview, redact, copy, export, and understand report packages without accidentally oversharing.

## 

## The education library is acceptable when it supports real user situations, connects back to app actions, and teaches safer alternatives without replacing active protection flows.

## 

## Universal states are acceptable when loading, empty, error, limited, offline, permission-missing, sensitive, and completed states are clear and actionable.

## 

### Area 13 completion note

## Area 13 completes the main design brief areas by defining the app's complete app function and layout blueprint, including navigation, home, manual check, result screens, case details, recovery, protection, helper support, privacy settings, reporting, education, universal states, and functional completeness standards while keeping the document focused on the app rather than a timeline plan.

## 

## Design Brief Section 1: Deepening Areas 1-12 Toward the \-Word Target

### Detail pass purpose

This design section deepens the existing app design brief without adding the final area yet. The purpose is to increase the functional completeness of the current areas, add more implementation-ready product behavior, clarify user-facing decisions, and reduce gaps that could become confusing later. This section should be read as additive app design detail for Verivae. It does not replace earlier sections unless a later sentence explicitly clarifies a safer or more complete interpretation.

The detail approach is deliberately functional rather than decorative. The goal is not to add filler. The goal is to make the app more buildable later by defining more states, user expectations, examples, boundaries, warnings, and product rules. When this section mentions the app, it means Verivae. When it mentions Harborwake, it refers only to the company that may own or publish the app, not the app name.

### Section 1 \- Area 1: Screen-by-Screen App Experience

Area 1 should be detailed with a clearer understanding that each screen in the app has a safety job. The home screen is not only a menu. It is the user's first decision point and should reduce panic, not add pressure. The screen should make it obvious that the user can check something risky immediately, learn about common scam signs, review a saved case, or continue setup. The main visual structure should prioritize the fastest safety action, because many users will open the app while already being pressured by a message, caller, seller, romantic contact, employer, fake bank alert, or family emergency claim.

The home screen should include a strong but calm primary action such as Check something risky. Secondary actions can include Review saved case, Start device check, Set up protection, Ask trusted helper, and Learn scam signs. The app should avoid turning the home screen into a dashboard full of percentages, complex charts, and technical status badges. A simple protection status area is useful, but it should not dominate the first safety action. If a feature is inactive, the app should say what still works manually.

The manual check screen should support several input paths without making the user choose a technical category first. A user may not know whether something is a phishing email, marketplace scam, impersonation scam, or account-takeover attempt. The app can ask what they want to check in plain terms: message, email, link, payment request, screenshot, call or voicemail, job offer, marketplace situation, relationship request, family emergency, device concern, or not sure. The not sure option is important because real scam victims often know something feels wrong before they know the category.

The result screen should be consistent across input types. It should show the risk label, the main reason, what not to do yet, the safest next step, optional details, and saving or sharing options. If the result is risk, the result screen should not bury the next step under education content. If the result is unclear, the app should ask for the missing info rather than creating false confidence. If the result is low risk, the app should still warn users not to share codes, passwords, money, or identity details solely because one scan did not find obvious danger.

The case screen should become the user's safety record. It should hold the original checked content if the user saved it, the risk decision, warning signs, user notes, helper shares, evidence, device findings, and completed recovery steps. The case screen should not be designed like a social feed. It should be designed like a calm incident folder that helps the user keep track of what happened and what still needs attention.

### Section 1 \- Area 2: Detailed Function Specifications

Area 2 should further define the boundaries between major functions so future development does not merge every feature into one vague scanner. Quick Scam Check is for fast review. Guided Review is for structured thinking. Payment Request Review is for money-risk decisions. Device Check is for device-safety signals. Trusted Helper is for human review. Education is for learning outside an urgent moment. Case History is for continuity.

Quick Scam Check should be optimized for speed. It should accept messy input and produce a clear initial answer. The user should not need to know the scam type, platform, or technical sender info. The app should look for urgency, secrecy, emotional pressure, payment method, identity claim, link behavior, code requests, remote access requests, and whether the request pushes the user away from normal verification. The output should be cautious and action-oriented.

Guided Review should be optimized for uncertainty. It should ask one focused question at a time and explain why the answer matters only when needed. The guided flow should adapt based on answers. If the user says no money is involved but a login code is involved, the flow should shift toward account takeover. If the user says money was already sent, the flow should shift toward damage control. If the user says the contact is romantic or personal, the flow should use especially careful language.

Payment Request Review should treat payment method as a central risk signal. It should distinguish between reversible and hard-to-reverse payment methods in plain text. It should ask whether the person is rushing the user, asking for secrecy, refusing platform protections, using a new account, or claiming an emergency. The app should not simply say payment is risky. It should explain what makes this payment request different from a normal payment.

The Warning Sign Detector should be explainable. The app can use internal logic, AI, rules, or a mixture later, but the user-facing output should always translate signals into normal language. For example, instead of saying risky syntactic urgency, the app can say the message is pushing you to act before you can verify. Instead of saying sender mismatch, it can say the sender claims to be a company, but the contact info does not look official.

Trusted Helper should remain a support feature, not a surveillance feature. The app should let the user share a case, summary, or redacted report with someone they trust. It should not silently send private content. It should not let helpers take over the account. It should make the user's control visible before and after sharing.

### Section 1 \- Area 3: User Flows and Edge Cases

Area 3 should include more attention to interrupted and messy flows. A user may begin a scam check, switch to a bank app, answer a phone call, receive another message from the suspected scammer, close the app, return later, or ask a family member for help. the app should preserve context where possible. A half-finished review should not vanish because the user was interrupted.

The urgent check flow should be very short. The user opens the app, chooses check something risky, provides the content, and gets a clear result. If the app needs more info, it should ask the smallest useful question. If the user does not answer, the app should still give conservative safety advice based on what it has.

The already-happened flow should start differently. If the user indicates that they already sent money, shared a code, installed an app, gave a password, deposited a check, or shared identity info, the app should stop treating the case as a pre-decision warning and start treating it as response guidance. The next questions should identify what happened, what is still reversible, what accounts may be affected, and what evidence should be saved.
