The helper flow should include consent checkpoints. When the user shares with a helper, the app should show a preview of the message or report. It should clearly identify what is hidden, what is included, and whether the helper can reply. If a helper replies, the app should show the helper's message as advice from that person, not as official verification.

The abandoned flow should be recoverable. If the user starts a case but does not finish, the app can show it as draft, needs info, or incomplete. It should not create guilt-inducing reminders. A gentle reminder can say a safety check is unfinished if you still need it. If the app detects risky signals before abandonment, it can preserve the warning in the case.

Edge cases should include contradictory answers. A user might say no money is involved but then paste a message asking for gift cards. A user might say the sender is known but the message comes from a new number. The app should handle this by explaining the conflict calmly and asking one clarifying question. It should not accuse the user of inconsistency.

### Section 1 \- Area 4: Interface Writing and Exact Copy

Area 4 should eventually become one of the largest areas because exact app text matters in a scam-protection product. Users under pressure will read only what is clear. Every button, warning, helper note, permission explanation, result label, and error state should be written so a non-technical user can act immediately.

The app's tone should be calm, direct, and never mocking. The strongest warnings can still be respectful. Good warning copy includes phrases like this has strong scam signs, pause before sending money, do not share this code, verify through a method you already trust, and save this message before deleting anything. The app should avoid phrases like you almost got scammed, obviously fake, you should have known, or this is definitely safe.

Button labels should describe actions. Check this is stronger than submit. Stop and verify is stronger than continue. Save evidence is clearer than archive. Share with trusted helper is clearer than send. Review why is clearer than details. Turn on message protection is clearer than enable integration. Keep alerts private is clearer than privacy mode if the surrounding text explains what it does.

Permission copy should be specific. For email, the app can say: connect email protection to review risky emails and links. You can still check emails manually without connecting. For messages, it can say: message protection depends on what your phone allows. If automatic monitoring is limited, you can still share, paste, or screenshot messages. For device checks, it can say: device checks look for risky apps, permissions, and settings that may increase scam risk. They do not guarantee that every virus or threat will be found.

Result templates should use the same structure. Risk result copy can say: This has strong warning signs. Do not send money, share codes, click links, or install anything until you verify through a trusted source. Medium risk can say: This has some warning signs, but more context is needed. Pause and verify before acting. Low risk can say: No strong scam signs were found in what you shared, but still be careful with money, codes, passwords, and private info. Unclear can say: I need more info to check this well. Until then, treat the request cautiously.

Error copy should always give the next step. Instead of unable to process, the app should say: I could not read this screenshot clearly. Try uploading a clearer screenshot or paste the message text. Instead of connection failed, it can say: the full check could not finish because the connection was lost. I saved this case so you can retry when connection returns.

### Section 1 \- Area 5: Visual Interface System and Screen Layout Detail

Area 5 should expand the visual rules around trust. the app should look serious without feeling cold, alarming, or corporate in a way that distances the user. The app should be visually calm, readable, and organized. The most important info should appear first, with enough spacing for stressed users and older users to understand the screen quickly.

The result screen should use a strong hierarchy. The risk label should be visible, but the next action should be equally prominent. A warning without a next action can leave the user frozen. The layout should show: status, reason, action, evidence, optional details, and case controls. The user should not have to scroll past long analysis to see what to do.

Colors should support meaning without carrying meaning alone. Red or strong warning colors can signal risk, but the app must also show text labels and icons. Medium risk should not look almost identical to risk. Low risk should not look like a celebration. A low-risk state should feel calm, not like permission to trust everything.

Screenshots and risky messages should be displayed safely. Links in risky content should not be easily tappable by accident. The app can show links as reviewed text and require a deliberate action to open them. If a link is risk, the app should discourage opening it and suggest official verification instead.

Case history should be visually scannable. Each case card can show the label, date or relative time if available, risk state, source type, and next action. Sensitive previews should be hidden or privacy-safe by default. A saved case should not expose embarrassing or private scam details on a shared screen.

Device-check screens should separate urgent problems from infoal findings. Critical issues should appear at the top with specific action. Infoal findings should be lower and not styled like emergencies. If the app cannot complete a device check automatically, the layout should show guided steps instead of treating the feature as broken.

### Section 1 \- Area 6: Privacy, Data, and Security Feature System

Area 6 should be treated as a core product feature, not a background policy. Users will be asked to trust Verivae with sensitive messages, possible financial details, scam evidence, helper relationships, and device-risk signals. The app should therefore collect less by default, explain more clearly, and give users control over saving and sharing.

Data minimization should guide every feature. If Quick Scam Check can work from pasted text, it should not require full account access. If a report can be shared with private details hidden, redaction should be available. If device checks can be done through guided review rather than invasive access on some platforms, the app should offer that path. The safest data is data the app never collects.

The app should warn users not to submit secrets unnecessarily. Input screens can include a short reminder: do not paste passwords, full bank numbers, Social Security numbers, or one-time codes. If the app detects something that looks like a code or sensitive number, it can ask whether the user wants to hide it before saving or sharing. This should be done carefully to avoid showing the sensitive item more widely.

Saved cases should have clear retention behavior. The user should know whether a case is saved only on the device, synced to an account, shared with a helper, or included in reports. If the app later supports cloud accounts, it should explain what changes. A user who wants temporary help should be able to check something without creating permanent storage when the product model allows it.

Trusted-helper privacy should be explicit. Before sharing, the app should preview what the helper sees. After sharing, the case should show that it was shared. If helper access is ongoing, the app should show that status in settings and inside relevant cases. Revoking helper access should be easy and should explain what happens to already-shared reports.

Security language should remain understandable. The app can use encryption and strong auth internally, but the user-facing explanation should focus on control: your saved cases are private to your account unless you share them, you can delete saved cases, you can turn off linked protections, and you can hide sensitive details before sharing.

### Section 1 \- Area 7: Scam Detection Logic and Risk Explanation System

Area 7 should expand the detection model around explainability and humility. The app should detect patterns, not pretend to read intent. A scammer can imitate legitimate language, and a legitimate message can sometimes look risky. The app should therefore explain signals and avoid false certainty.

Risk explanation should separate evidence from interpretation. Evidence is what the app saw: a request for a login code, a gift card payment method, a link, urgency, secrecy, a new sender, a remote access request, or a threat. Interpretation is what that could mean: the request may be trying to take over an account, make money harder to recover, prevent verification, or impersonate authority. The app should show both in plain text.

Risk signals should carry different weight. A typo alone should not create risk. A bank threat plus a link plus a request to enter login details is much stronger. A romantic contact asking for emergency gift cards is stronger than a romantic contact simply messaging frequently. A job offer with a fake check and equipment purchase is stronger than a job offer with one awkward phrase.

The app should ask follow-up questions when the risk depends on missing context. If the user says the sender is their bank, the app should ask whether they used the official app or a number they already had. If the user says a family member needs help, the app should ask whether they called that person through a known number. If the user says a buyer overpaid, the app should ask whether the payment is fully cleared and protected by the platform.

False positives should be handled with care. If a user says the app is too cautious, the app can let them provide feedback, but it should not remove critical warnings too easily. False negatives should be treated as serious. Feedback should help improve patterns without asking users to reveal private details.

### Section 1 \- Area 8: Feature-by-Feature Deep Feature Specifications

Area 8 should continue to serve as the detailed feature catalog. The detail should clarify dependencies between features. Manual Scam Check is the foundation. Guided Review improves decision quality. Payment Review handles money-specific risk. Message and email integrations improve convenience. Device checks extend protection beyond content. Trusted Helper adds human support. Case History preserves continuity. Education improves future judgment.

Manual Scam Check should be available across the product. It should not be buried after setup. Any user should be able to return to it from the home screen, share sheet, case screen, education examples, or helper flow. It should support quick entry and later enrichment with more details.

Guided Review should have category-specific branches. A payment branch asks about method, reversibility, urgency, and verification. A relationship branch asks about emotional pressure, secrecy, money, and refusal to meet or verify. A job branch asks about interviews, checks, equipment purchases, official company identity, and early personal info requests. A device branch asks about newly installed apps, remote access, permission changes, and risky support calls.

Education should be linked to real results. If the user checks a verification-code scam, the result can link to a short lesson on why codes are private. If the user checks a marketplace overpayment, the result can link to a lesson on fake payment confirmations and refund tricks. Education should not interrupt urgent action, but it should be available when the user is ready.

Settings should be treated as a safety feature. Users should be able to see linked accounts, monitoring status, alert privacy, helper access, saved case behavior, sensitivity level, weekly check timing, language or simplified mode, and plan boundaries. A user should never have to guess which protections are active.

### Section 1 \- Area 9: Scam Category Deep Dives

Area 9 should expand each scam category with scenario variations, not just definitions. Scammers adapt language across platforms, so the app should recognize patterns even when the wording changes. Each category should include common setup, pressure tactic, requested action, user risk, app response, and safe next step.

For bank impersonation, the app should recognize account-lock threats, risky-login alerts, fake fraud department messages, refund claims, and verification links. The safe next step is usually to avoid the provided link and contact the bank through an official app, card number, or known website.

For payment pressure scams, the app should recognize gift cards, crypto, wire transfers, instant transfers to strangers, friends-and-family payments for purchases, and requests to split or refund overpayments. The app should explain reversibility and platform protection in plain text.

For marketplace scams, the app should recognize moving off-platform, fake payment screenshots, overpayment refunds, shipping label manipulation, deposits before proof, unusually low prices, and refusal to meet safe marketplace norms. The app should help buyers and sellers because both can be targeted.

For romance and social trust scams, the app should use careful language. It should focus on behavior: fast emotional intimacy, refusal to verify identity, repeated emergencies, secrecy, money requests, investment pitches, and guilt. The app should not attack the relationship or insult the user.

For device and tech support scams, the app should recognize urgent virus warnings, unknown callers claiming support authority, remote access instructions, requests to download tools, and payment demands for fake cleanup. The safe next step is to stop remote access, avoid payment, and review device safety.

For job scams, the app should recognize fake checks, equipment purchase schemes, unrealistic pay, no real interview, unofficial email addresses, early requests for identity info, and pressure to move quickly. The app should explain that check funds appearing in an account does not always mean the check is legitimate.

### Section 1 \- Area 10: Accessibility and Inclusive Design

Area 10 should be detailed by treating accessibility as a safety requirement. A scam-protection app fails if stressed, older, disabled, low-confidence, or non-technical users cannot act on the warning. The warning must be readable, understandable, reachable, and usable with assistive technology.

Large text support should be tested conceptually across all critical screens. If text is enlarged, buttons should wrap and screens should scroll without hiding the next step. Risk labels, permission explanations, helper previews, and device findings should not be clipped. Long scam messages should be readable without forcing the user to pinch and zoom.

Screen reader behavior should be planned for every result. A screen reader user should hear the risk level, reason, and next step in the correct order. Icon-only controls should have meaningful labels. Dynamic scan completion should be announced calmly. Screenshot review should include a text summary of what the app detected in the image.

Cognitive accessibility should reduce choices during risky moments. A risky result should not show six equally weighted actions. It should show one primary safety action and optional secondary actions. Recovery flows should break complex steps into small pieces. Users should not have to remember instructions from earlier screens.

Privacy and accessibility should work together. Alerts should be private by default. Users who rely on spoken output should be able to understand sensitive content without exposing it unnecessarily in public. Helper sharing should be previewable in plain text.

### Section 1 \- Area 11: Screen States, System Responses, and Recovery Behavior

Area 11 should be detailed by making state behavior consistent across the app. Every feature should have ready, checking, needs info, result, saved, shared, failed, paused, limited, and unavailable states where relevant. These states should not be invented differently for every screen.

The checking state should always tell the user what is being checked. If the app is reviewing a link, it should say link. If it is reviewing a screenshot, it should say screenshot. If it is checking a device setting, it should say device safety check. This prevents the user from believing the app did more than it actually did.

Needs-info states should ask the fewest useful questions. The app should not require full sender data if a clear risky payment request is already visible. It should not require a full email header for basic user guidance. It can offer stronger analysis if more info is provided, but the user should still receive conservative guidance from partial input.

Paused and limited states should be visible in protection status. If message monitoring is off, the app should say so. If email connection expired, the app should say so. If device checks are limited by platform rules, the app should say guided checks are still available. A limited state is not failure if the app offers a clear manual path.

Recovery behavior should support continued use after errors. Failed screenshot review should offer retake or paste. Failed email connection should offer reconnect or manual check. Failed device scan should offer retry or guided settings review. Offline mode should save pending cases. The user should not lose work.

### Section 1 \- Area 12: Onboarding, Setup, Permissions, and Personalization

Area 12 should be detailed by defining onboarding as a continuing relationship rather than a one-time tutorial. A user can complete basic onboarding by learning how to check risky content, but deeper setup can happen later as trust increases.

First-run onboarding should not force account creation, full permissions, paid upgrades, or long lessons before the user gets value. The app should start with the user's immediate goal. If the user wants to check something risky, setup should get out of the way. If the user wants ongoing protection, setup should guide them through modules. If the user already experienced harm, onboarding should become response triage.

Permission onboarding should include examples. Email protection can show a sample risky email result. Message protection can show how to share a text into the app if automatic access is not available. Device check setup can show the difference between quick check and weekly check. Trusted-helper setup can show a redacted preview before sharing.

Personalization should be framed as control, not complexity. Users can choose alert privacy, sensitivity, weekly check timing, simplified language, trusted-helper defaults, and education depth. The app should not ask so many setup questions that users quit. It can start with defaults and let users adjust later.

Free-first onboarding should remain explicit. The app should show useful free features before upgrade prompts. Paid features can be introduced as additional coverage, automation, or convenience. A risky warning should never require payment to understand the risk or see the basic next step.

### Section 1 completion note

Section 1 adds cross-area depth to the existing design brief while preserving the final area for later. The brief still needs additional design sectiones to reach the large target without relying on filler. Future design sectiones should continue deepening scenarios, screen copy, edge cases, feature requirements, privacy behavior, device-check flows, helper flows, settings, monetization boundaries, and testable accept rules before the final area is written.

## Design Brief Section 2: Scenario Depth, Decision Rules, and Product Behavior Detail

### Detail pass purpose

This design section adds more scenario-level depth to the existing areas. It focuses on how the app should behave when the same core features are used in different real-life situations. The goal is to make the design brief more useful for later product decisions while continuing toward the large target. This section still does not add the final area. It details the areas already defined.

### Section 2 \- Area 1: Screen Experience Scenario Detail

A key screen-design scenario is the user who opens Verivae while actively receiving pressure from another person. The user might have a text thread open, a caller on speakerphone, a seller waiting for payment, or a fake support agent telling them to hurry. The app's first screen should therefore reduce the number of decisions. It should not ask the user to choose between many technical tools. It should offer a quick path: Check this now. The second screen can ask how the user wants to provide the risky content.

Another screen scenario is the user who opens the app after a family member asks for help. This user may not have the original message on their phone. The app should support a describe the situation path, allowing the helper to type what the protected person said. The app should not require direct access to the other person's messages. It should treat secondhand summaries as partial evidence and ask clarifying questions. The result should say that the app is reviewing the described situation, not the original message.

A third screen scenario is the user who is not currently in danger but wants ongoing protection. This user should see setup options, but the screen should still preserve access to manual checks. The app should make ongoing setup modular: email protection, message protection, device check, weekly check, trusted helper, alert privacy, and sensitivity settings. Each module should have its own status and plain explanation.

A fourth screen scenario is the user returning to a saved case. The case screen should show what happened, what the last result was, what steps were completed, and what remains. If the user saved evidence but did not finish recovery steps, the screen should show follow-up needed. If a helper replied, that reply should be visible in context. If the app learned new info from a later scan, the case should show that the risk assessment was updated.

### Section 2 \- Area 2: Function Scenario Detail

Quick Scam Check should support extremely short inputs. A user might paste only: your account is locked, click here. The app should still flag urgency, account threat, and link risk. It should say that more detail would improve review, but the user should avoid clicking the link and instead use the official app or known website.

Guided Review should support emotionally complex inputs. A user might say: my online friend says he is stranded and needs money, but I trust him. The app should not respond by attacking the relationship. It should ask whether the person has met the user in person, whether they are asking for secrecy, whether this is the first money request, whether they avoid video calls, and whether payment is being requested through a hard-to-reverse method.

Payment Request Review should support businesslike scams too. A fake invoice, fake vendor change, fake landlord deposit, or fake employer reimbursement can sound professional. The app should not rely only on emotional pressure. It should look for changed payment instructions, unusual urgency, new bank details, refusal to verify through normal channels, and pressure to ignore ordinary approval steps.

Device Check should support user-described device concerns. A user may say: someone told me to install an app so they could fix my bank account. The app should immediately treat remote access as risk and ask whether the app is still installed, whether the other person saw the screen, whether passwords were typed while linked, and whether banking or email accounts were opened during the session.

Trusted Helper should support the user who is embarrassed. The app should offer a short share message that does not include private details by default. It can say: I am checking a possible scam and would like a second opinion. The app found warning signs involving money pressure and urgency. Can you review this with me before I respond? This protects dignity and still gets help.

### Section 2 \- Area 3: Flow Scenario Detail

The flow for a fake bank alert should be direct. The user shares a message into Verivae. The app identifies that the sender claims to be a bank, the message includes a link, and the text creates urgency. The app returns a risky or stop-and-verify result depending on details. The safest next step is to open the bank's official app or call the number already known to the user, not the number in the risky message.

The flow for a marketplace seller should account for overpayment and fake confirmations. The user says they are selling an item and the buyer sent a screenshot showing payment. The app asks whether the payment appears inside the official platform or bank account, whether the buyer overpaid, whether the buyer wants a refund, and whether shipping is being rushed. The app should explain that screenshots can be fake and that refunds before confirmed payment are dangerous.

The flow for a job offer should ask about interview quality, company identity, early money movement, and personal info. If the employer sends a check for equipment and asks the user to forward money to a vendor, the app should explain fake check risk in plain terms. It should say that a check appearing in the account does not always mean the money is safe to spend.

The flow for a family emergency should prioritize independent contact. If the user receives a call claiming a grandchild is arrested or injured, the app should ask whether the caller demanded secrecy, whether the user called the family member through a known number, and whether payment is requested by gift card, wire, courier, or crypto. The app should recommend pausing and contacting family through known channels.

### Section 2 \- Area 4: Copy Scenario Detail

For fake bank messages, exact copy should be firm: This message claims there is an account problem and asks you to use a link. Do not use the link from this message. Open your bank's official app or use a phone number you already trust. This copy is useful because it gives a direct alternative.

For verification-code requests, exact copy should be stronger: Do not share this code. Login and login codes are meant for you only. A real support person should not need you to read a login code from your phone. If you already shared it, secure the affected account now. This copy should appear whenever the app detects code-sharing pressure.

For remote access requests, exact copy should focus on control: Do not install an app or give screen access to someone who contacted you unexpectedly. Remote access can let another person view or control your device. If you already installed it, stop the session, remove the app if possible, and review account security.

For payment pressure, exact copy should explain reversibility: This payment method may be hard to reverse. Pause before sending money. Verify the request through a method you already trust, not through the link, number, or account in the risky message.

For low-risk results, exact copy should avoid overconfidence: No strong scam signs were found in the info you shared. This does not guarantee the situation is safe. Be especially careful before sending money, sharing codes, entering passwords, or installing apps.

### Section 2 \- Area 5: Visual Scenario Detail

In a risky result, the screen should visually separate the warning from the evidence. The first block should say the risk and next step. The second block should explain warning signs. The third block can offer optional details, saving, sharing, and education. This prevents the user from reading a long explanation before seeing the safety action.

In an unclear result, the visual state should not look safe. A neutral color, question icon, or needs review label can signal that the app does not have enough info. The screen should show a missing-info prompt and conservative guidance. It should not use green styling for unclear results.

In a device-check result, the visual design should avoid panic. If one app has risky permissions, the app should show the finding, why it matters, and how to review it. If several findings appear, the app should group them into critical, important, and infoal. The user should not see a long undifferentiated list of warnings.

In helper sharing, the preview screen should be visually clear. Included content, hidden content, helper name, and sharing purpose should be visible. The user should know whether they are sharing a summary, full case, or redacted report.

### Section 2 \- Area 6: Privacy Scenario Detail

If a user pastes a login code into the app, the app should not save that code by default. The app can detect that the text looks like a code and warn the user before saving or sharing. It can offer to hide the code in the saved case. This protects the user from turning a safety action into a new exposure.

If a user uploads a screenshot with names, phone numbers, addresses, account balances, or identity details, the app should offer redaction before sharing. The app does not need to force redaction before analysis, but sharing should show a preview. The user should be able to choose whether private details are hidden.

If a user connects email, the app should explain whether it reviews selected emails, risky emails, user-shared emails, or broader mailbox signals. The user should not be left with the impression that every email is being read if the app only checks shared content. The opposite is also true: if broader access is enabled, the app should say so plainly.

If a user deletes a case, the app should explain whether deletion removes local data, cloud data, helper-shared copies, reports, or only the visible case. Deletion should be understandable and should not create false expectations.

### Section 2 \- Area 7: Detection Scenario Detail

Detection should handle impersonation without relying only on sender names. A scammer may use a name that looks legitimate. The app should focus on behavior: urgency, link pressure, request for secrets, unusual payment, refusal to verify, or pressure to move outside normal channels. A real company name inside the message does not automatically make it safe.

Detection should handle friendly language. A scam may sound polite, professional, romantic, or helpful. The app should not rely on aggressive wording only. A fake job offer can sound professional. A romance scam can sound loving. A fake support agent can sound calm. The app should detect requested actions and context, not just emotional tone.

Detection should handle multilingual or partially translated messages when possible. If the app cannot fully analyze language, it should still look for universal signals such as links, payment methods, code requests, urgency phrases, and contact changes. If language support is limited, the app should say that review may be incomplete.

Detection should handle evolving cases. One message may not look dangerous, but several messages together can reveal a pattern. The app should let users add messages to a case and update the risk explanation when pressure escalates.

### Section 2 \- Area 8: Feature Dependency Detail

Manual check should not depend on account creation. Case history may depend on saving. Trusted-helper sharing may depend on account state or device sharing tools. Email integration depends on provider connection. Message monitoring depends on platform permissions. Device scans depend on operating-system access. The design brief should keep these dependencies clear.

A feature should always define its fallback. If email integration is unavailable, use manual email check. If message monitoring is unavailable, use share, screenshot, or paste. If device automation is limited, use guided manual review. If helper sharing is unavailable, provide a copyable summary. If cloud saving is unavailable, provide local notes or temporary review.

Features should be layered. The app can begin as manual review plus education and later add automation. The design should support that growth without making the first version feel broken. A free or early version can still be valuable if the main safety actions work.

### Section 2 \- Area 9: Scam Category Scenario Detail

A fake delivery scam might say a package cannot be delivered until a small fee is paid. The app should flag the link, small payment pressure, and identity-info request if present. The safe next step is to use the official delivery company's website or app, not the link in the message.

A subscription refund scam might say the user is owed money or will be charged unless they call a number. The app should flag unexpected refund claims, remote access requests, and bank-login pressure. The safe next step is to check the account through the official service.

A recovery scam might target someone who was already scammed. The scammer may claim they can recover money for an upfront fee. The app should flag this as especially risky because the user may already be vulnerable. It should recommend caution before paying anyone who promises guaranteed recovery.

A fake authority scam might use court, tax, utility, or police language. The app should flag threats, payment urgency, secrecy, and unusual payment methods. It should advise verification through official publicly listed contact channels.

### Section 2 \- Area 10: Accessibility Scenario Detail

A stressed user may only read the first sentence. The first sentence of a risky result should therefore contain the main action. For example: Do not send money yet. This is clearer than a long explanation that eventually reaches the action.

An older user may not understand app permissions. Permission screens should compare automatic and manual options. For example: If you turn this on, the app can help warn you sooner. If you leave it off, you can still check messages manually.

A screen reader user should not be forced through decorative content before the result. The app should announce the result title, risk level, reason, and primary action first. Optional details can come later.

A user with motor difficulty should be able to recover from accidental taps. Destructive actions such as delete case, remove helper, disable protection, or clear history should require confirmation. Undo should be available where practical.

### Section 2 \- Area 11: State Scenario Detail

If a user starts a scan and connection drops, the state should say the full check could not finish and the case was saved for retry. The app should still show basic safety advice if the input involved money, codes, passwords, links, or remote access.

If a user denies message permission, the app should not show setup failed. It should show message monitoring off and manual message checks available. This preserves trust and keeps the user protected through a fallback path.

If a weekly check finds no urgent issues, the result should be calm. It should say no urgent issues found rather than all safe. It can also show what was checked and what was not checked due to platform limits.

If a helper invitation fails, the app should preserve the case and offer retry, copy summary, or choose another helper. A failed share should not lose the user's work.

### Section 2 \- Area 12: Onboarding Scenario Detail

A privacy-conscious user should be able to complete onboarding with manual checks only. The app should explain that linked protections are optional and can be added later. This user should not be punished with constant alarm language.

A user setting up for a parent should see a consent-focused helper path. The app should encourage the protected person to control sharing where possible. If ongoing helper access exists, it should be visible and revocable.

A user who already lost money should see recovery guidance before upgrade prompts, tutorials, or optional setup. The app can ask the user to save the case, but urgent triage should come first.

A user interested in paid features should see clear boundaries. The app should explain what free protection includes and what paid features add. Paid features should be presented as detailed coverage, not the only safe path.

### Section 2 completion note

Section 2 details the design brief through concrete scenarios, fallback paths, copy examples, privacy behavior, accessibility behavior, and cross-feature dependencies. More detail is still needed to approach larges. The next design section should go deeper into exact screen copy libraries, result templates, scam examples, device-check details, helper workflows, settings behavior, and accept rules while continuing to reserve the final area for later.

## Design Brief Section 3: Exact Screen Copy, Result Templates, and User-Facing Language

### Detail pass purpose

Section 3 deepens the design brief by creating a practical copy library for Verivae. Earlier areas define what the app does. This section defines more of what the app should actually say. The purpose is to make future screens easier to design by giving reusable labels, prompts, explanations, warnings, and state messages. The wording here should be treated as draft product copy, not final branding. It can be refined later, but it establishes the tone and content rules the app should follow.

This section continues to reserve the final area for later. It focuses on detail, not conclusion. The copy below should be app-only. Harborwake remains the company name. Verivae remains the temporary app name.

### Section 3 \- Copy Principles for All Screens

the app should use calm, direct, plain text. The user may be scared, embarrassed, rushed, angry, distracted, or helping someone else. The app should not write like a legal document, a cybersecurity manual, or a marketing page. The app should write like a careful safety assistant that knows the user needs a clear next step.

The app should prefer action-first copy. When risk is high, the first sentence should tell the user what not to do yet. For example: Do not send money yet. Do not share this code. Do not install that app. Do not use the link in this message. These sentences are useful because they interrupt the risky action immediately. The explanation can follow after the action.

The app should avoid blame. The app should not say you got tricked, you were careless, you should have known, or this is obvious. The app should also avoid playful language in serious moments. A scam warning is not the right place for jokes, exaggerated excitement, or shame. Good copy is serious without being cold.

The app should avoid false certainty. It should not say this is 100 percent safe or this is definitely not a scam unless future evidence standards justify that, and even then the safer posture is to describe patterns rather than claim perfect knowledge. Better wording is: this has strong scam signs, this needs caution, no strong warning signs were found in what you shared, or more info is needed.

The app should explain limits clearly. When it reviewed only a screenshot, it should say it reviewed the screenshot. When it reviewed only pasted text, it should say it reviewed the text provided. When it cannot verify a sender's real identity, it should say that. This protects user trust and keeps the app from overpromising.

### Section 3 \- Home Screen Copy Library

Primary home screen title options should be simple. The best default is: What do you want to check? This title works because it starts from the user's need, not the app's technology. Alternative titles can include: Check something risky, Review a possible scam, or Start a safety check. The app should avoid vague titles like dashboard or security center on the main starting screen.

Advised home screen subtitle: Paste a message, upload a screenshot, check a link, review a payment request, or get help after something happened. This subtitle communicates breadth without listing every feature.

Primary button: Check something risky. Secondary buttons: Review saved cases, Start device check, Set up protection, Ask trusted helper, Learn scam signs. These labels should remain short because home screen buttons must be easy to scan.

If the user has no saved cases, empty state copy can say: No saved cases yet. When you check something, you can save the result here if you want to review it later. Button: Check something now.

If protection setup is incomplete, status copy can say: Manual checks are ready. Optional protections can be linked when you are ready. This avoids making the user feel unsafe just because they have not linked every permission.

If a weekly check is available but not set up, copy can say: Weekly device checks are off. You can turn them on to review device safety signals on a regular schedule. Button: Set up weekly check.

If a risky case is unfinished, home screen copy can say: A risky case needs follow-up. Review the advised next steps before sending money, sharing codes, or continuing the conversation. Button: Review case.

### Section 3 \- Manual Check Input Copy Library

Manual check input title: What do you want to check? Helper text: Share as much as you feel comfortable sharing. Do not include passwords, full bank numbers, Social Security numbers, or one-time login codes.

Input options should use plain labels: Paste text, Upload screenshot, Check a link, Describe a call, Review payment request, Check an email, Check a job offer, Check marketplace situation, Check relationship request, Check device concern, Not sure.

Paste text field placeholder: Paste the message or describe what happened. You can remove private details first. This placeholder is better than enter text because it explains that summaries are allowed.

Screenshot upload helper text: Upload a screenshot that clearly shows the message, sender, link, or request. If the screenshot includes private details, you can hide them before sharing or saving. If the screenshot is blurry, the app should say: I could not read this screenshot clearly. Try a clearer screenshot or paste the text instead.

Link check helper text: Paste the link exactly as it appeared. Do not open it first if you are unsure. This matters because the user might otherwise click the risky link to copy it.

Call summary helper text: Describe what the caller said, what they wanted you to do, and whether they asked for money, codes, passwords, remote access, or secrecy. You do not need to remember every word.

Payment request helper text: Tell me who is asking, how they want to be paid, why they say payment is needed, and whether they are rushing you. Do not include full account numbers or card numbers.

Not sure helper text: That is okay. Describe the situation in your own words. I will ask a few follow-up questions if needed.

### Section 3 \- Result Template Copy Library

All result screens should follow a predictable language structure: risk label, immediate action, reason, do not do yet, safer next step, optional details, save/share controls, and limitations. This structure reduces confusion across scam categories.

Risky template:  
Risk level: Risk.  
Immediate action: Do not continue yet.  
Reason: This matches strong scam patterns, including \[warning signs\].  
Do not do yet: Do not send money, share codes, click links, install apps, or give private info until you verify through a trusted source.  
Safer next step: Use a contact method you already trust, such as an official app, known phone number, or saved contact.  
Limitation: I reviewed the info you provided. I cannot confirm the sender's real identity from this alone.

Stop-and-verify template:  
Risk level: Stop and verify.  
Immediate action: Pause before responding.  
Reason: This request includes signs that scammers often use, such as urgency, pressure, secrecy, or unusual payment.  
Do not do yet: Do not use the link, phone number, payment details, or instructions from the risky message.  
Safer next step: Verify through a separate official source.

Medium-risk template:  
Risk level: Needs caution.  
Immediate action: Verify before acting.  
Reason: Some warning signs are present, but more context would help.  
Do not do yet: Do not send money or share private details until you confirm the request independently.  
Safer next step: Add more info, ask a trusted person, or contact the person or company through a known channel.

Unclear template:  
Risk level: Needs more info.  
Immediate action: Treat this cautiously until it is clearer.  
Reason: I do not have enough detail to judge the risk well.  
What would help: Add the message text, sender info, payment method, link, screenshot, or what the person asked you to do.  
Safer next step: If money, codes, passwords, remote access, or ID docs are involved, pause and verify first.

Low-risk template:  
Risk level: Low concern based on what you shared.  
Immediate action: Stay cautious with money and private info.  
Reason: I did not find strong scam signs in the info provided.  
Important limit: This does not guarantee the situation is safe. Be careful before sending money, sharing codes, entering passwords, or installing apps.  
Safer next step: If anything changes or pressure increases, check the new message.

### Section 3 \- Warning Message Copy Library

Login code warning:  
Do not share this code. Login and login codes are meant for you only. A real support agent, buyer, employer, bank employee, or romantic contact should not need you to read a login code from your phone.

Password warning:  
Do not share your password. If someone needs your password to help you, pay you, refund you, verify you, hire you, or protect your account, that is a serious warning sign.

Gift card warning:  
Do not pay with gift cards. Gift cards are difficult to recover once the code is shared. Real banks, government agencies, employers, delivery companies, and support teams should not demand gift card payment.

Crypto warning:  
Be careful with crypto payments. Crypto transfers are usually hard to reverse. If someone is rushing you, promising guaranteed profit, or asking you to keep the payment secret, pause and verify.

Wire transfer warning:  
Wire transfers can be difficult to reverse. Do not send a wire transfer because of a message, call, job offer, rental listing, romantic emergency, or account threat until you verify through a trusted source.

Remote access warning:  
Do not give remote access to someone who contacted you unexpectedly. Remote access can let another person see or control your device. If you already installed a remote access app, stop the session and review your accounts.

Risky link warning:  
Do not use the link from this message. Open the official app or type the known website yourself. Scammers often make links look close to real company links.

Secrecy warning:  
A request to keep this secret is a warning sign. Scammers often isolate people so nobody else can help them slow down and verify.

Urgency warning:  
Pressure to act immediately is a warning sign. A legitimate issue should usually allow you to verify through official channels before sending money or private info.

### Section 3 \- Permission and Setup Copy Library

Email setup title: Connect email protection. Explanation: the app can help review risky emails, links, sender claims, and payment requests. You can still check emails manually without connecting email. Button: Connect email. Secondary button: Skip for now.

Email permission pre-prompt: This helps Verivae review emails you choose or connect for protection, depending on the setup you select. It does not mean you should share passwords, bank numbers, or login codes in the app.

Message setup title: Set up message protection. Explanation: Message protection depends on what your phone allows. If automatic monitoring is limited, you can still share, paste, or screenshot risky messages. Button: Set up messages. Secondary button: Use manual checks.

Alert setup title: Keep alerts private. Explanation: Private alerts avoid showing scam details on your lock screen. You can open Verivae to see the full result. Button: Use private alerts. Secondary button: Choose alert detail.

Device check setup title: Start device safety check. Explanation: This checks for signs that may increase scam or account risk, such as risky apps, remote access tools, risky permissions, and protection gaps where supported. It does not guarantee that every virus or threat will be found. Button: Start quick check.

Weekly check setup title: Schedule weekly checks. Explanation: Weekly checks can review broader protection status and device-safety signals. You choose the timing and alert privacy. Button: Schedule weekly check. Secondary button: Not now.

Trusted helper setup title: Add trusted helper. Explanation: A trusted helper can review cases you choose to share. They cannot secretly see everything, control your account, or turn off protection. Button: Add helper. Secondary button: Maybe later.

### Section 3 \- Helper Sharing Copy Library

Helper preview title: Review before sharing. Helper preview subtitle: You control what your trusted helper sees. Private details can be hidden before sharing.

Share summary option: Share short summary. Explanation: Best for asking for a quick second opinion without sending full details.

Share redacted report option: Share redacted report. Explanation: Hides private details such as codes, account numbers, addresses, or phone numbers where detected or selected.

Share full case option: Share full case. Explanation: Includes more context. Review carefully before sharing.

Default helper message:  
Can you help me review a possible scam? Verivae found warning signs and recommends that I pause before acting. I have not included private codes, passwords, or full account details.

Urgent helper message:  
I need help checking a possible scam before I respond. The situation may involve money, codes, links, or pressure. Please review this with me before I continue.

Already-happened helper message:  
I may have already shared something or sent money. the app is helping me organize next steps. Can you help me review what to do next?

Helper access status copy: This helper can only see what you choose to share. Ongoing access is off. If ongoing access is ever turned on, it should be clearly shown here and easy to revoke.

Remove helper confirmation: Remove this helper? They will no longer be available for new shares from Verivae. This does not delete anything you already sent outside the app.

### Section 3 \- Empty State and Error Copy Library

No cases empty state:  
No saved cases yet. When you check something risky, you can save the result here if you want to review it later.

No helper empty state:  
No trusted helper added. You can add someone you trust so it is easier to ask for a second opinion during a risky situation.

No device check empty state:  
No device check has run yet. A quick check can review device-safety signals that may increase scam or account risk.

No internet state:  
Full analysis is unavailable while you are offline. You can still save this case and review basic safety reminders. Do not send money, share codes, enter passwords, or install remote access tools while you are unsure.

Screenshot unreadable error:  
I could not read this screenshot clearly. Try uploading a clearer screenshot, zooming in on the message, or pasting the text instead.

Link unsupported error:  
I could not fully check this link. Do not open it just to test it. If the message claims to be from a company, use the official app or a website you already know.

Permission denied message:  
That permission is off. Manual checks still work. You can turn this permission on later if you want more automatic protection.

Connection expired message:  
This connection needs to be renewed. Until then, you can still check messages manually by sharing, pasting, or uploading screenshots.

Scan failed message:  
The scan could not finish. I saved the case so you can retry. If the situation involves money, codes, passwords, links, or remote access, pause and verify before continuing.

### Section 3 \- Education Snippet Copy Library

Login code lesson snippet:  
A login code is meant to prove that you control an account. If you give the code to someone else, they may be able to get into your account. Treat codes like passwords.

Gift card lesson snippet:  
Gift cards are a common scam payment because the money is hard to recover after the code is shared. Real companies and agencies should not demand gift cards as payment.

Remote access lesson snippet:  
Remote access tools can be useful when you choose a trusted support source, but they are dangerous when an unknown caller tells you to install one. They may be able to see your screen or control your device.

Fake check lesson snippet:  
A check can appear in your account before the bank fully confirms it is real. If someone sends a check and asks you to send money back or buy equipment, pause and verify before spending or forwarding funds.

Marketplace overpayment lesson snippet:  
If a buyer overpays and asks you to refund the difference, be careful. The original payment may be fake, reversed, or never fully cleared.

Romance money request lesson snippet:  
A caring relationship should still allow verification. If someone avoids verification, asks for secrecy, or repeatedly needs emergency money, pause before sending anything.

### Section 3 \- Settings Copy Library

Protection status label options: Active, Paused, Limited, Needs attention, Not linked, Manual only, Ready.

Manual checks status: Manual checks are ready. You can check risky messages, links, screenshots, calls, and payment requests without connecting accounts.

Email protection status active: Email protection is active for the connection you selected. Review what access is enabled at any time.

Email protection status limited: Email protection is limited. Manual email checks still work.

Message protection status limited: Message protection is limited by your current settings or device support. You can still share, paste, or screenshot messages.

Device check status: Device checks review safety signals where supported. Some checks may require manual review depending on your device.

Alert privacy status: Private alerts are on. Lock-screen alerts avoid showing scam details.

Risk sensitivity setting: Higher sensitivity may warn more often. Lower sensitivity may reduce alerts but can miss weaker warning signs. Critical warnings should stay on.

Saved cases setting: Choose whether checked cases are saved, saved only when you choose, or not saved after review. The safest option for privacy is to save only when you choose.

### Section 3 \- Acceptance Rules for Copy Quality

Every risky screen must include an immediate action in the first visible sentence.

Every result must include a limitation statement when the app reviewed only partial info.

Every permission request must explain what still works if the user says no.

Every paid-feature prompt must leave the free safety path visible.

Every helper-sharing flow must show a preview before sharing.

Every error message must include a recovery action.

Every empty state must offer a useful next step.

Every educational snippet must connect to a practical behavior.

Every device-safety message must distinguish between what the app checked and what it cannot guarantee.

Every low-risk result must avoid saying the situation is guaranteed safe.

### Section 3 completion note

Section 3 details the design brief with reusable product copy for home screens, manual checks, result templates, warnings, permissions, helper sharing, empty states, errors, education, settings, and copy-quality rules. More detail is still needed to approach the large target. The next design section should continue into larger scam example libraries, detailed device-check flows, trusted-helper workflows, settings behavior, and deeper accept rules while still reserving the final area for later.

## Design Brief Section 4: Scam Example Library, Device Check Flows, Helper Workflows, Settings Behavior, and Accept Rules

### Detail pass purpose

This design section deepens the design brief by adding more concrete examples and product behavior around the parts of Verivae that will decide whether the app feels useful in real life. Earlier sections describe the app's core experience, screen behavior, privacy rules, risk logic, category coverage, onboarding, and setup. This section adds larger example libraries, more detailed device-check behavior, trusted-helper workflows, settings requirements, and accept rules. The purpose is not to create a separate plan, launch checklist, or company document. The purpose is to make the app specification more complete so a future design, product, or engineering team can understand exactly what the app must be capable of.

This section keeps Harborwake as the company name and Verivae as the app name. It describes the app itself, the user's experience inside the app, the safety boundaries around its features, and the standards that determine whether each feature works correctly. This section adds detail to already established areas rather than replacing them.

### Section 4 \- Scam Example Library Overview

the app needs a broad internal scam example library because users will not describe scams in neat category names. A user may say, "Someone texted me about a delivery," "My bank called me," "A buyer wants to pay by check," "A recruiter sent me a task," or "My online friend needs emergency money." The app must translate messy real-world descriptions into structured review. The example library should help the app recognize patterns, ask better follow-up questions, explain risk in plain text, and avoid overreacting when the message is ordinary.

The example library should not be treated as a list of exact phrases only. Scams change wording quickly. The library should be treated as a set of behavior patterns. Each pattern should include the channel where it may appear, the user's goal, the other person's claimed identity, the requested action, the pressure tactic, the money movement, the data requested, and the safest next step. The app should compare a submitted message or scenario against these pattern fields rather than only searching for banned words.

The app should support at least four levels of example matching. First, exact language matching should identify common phrases such as urgent account lock warnings, refund prompts, fake security alerts, gift card requests, risky check deposits, and remote access demands. Second, intent matching should identify what the other person is trying to get the user to do, even when the wording is new. Third, sequence matching should identify risky multi-step behavior, such as building trust first and then moving the conversation to payment. Fourth, contradiction matching should identify claims that do not make sense together, such as a buyer overpaying by mistake and asking for a refund before the payment clears.

Every example in the library should include an app response template. That response should include a short risk label, a plain explanation, the specific details that triggered concern, a advised action, a safer verification path, and an optional deeper explanation. The user should never be left with only a scary warning. They should understand what to do next.

The library should also include false-alarm examples. A false alarm is a situation that may look risky but may be legitimate after verification. For example, a real bank alert may tell a user to review recent activity, but it should not pressure them to provide a password by text. A real delivery service may send tracking updates, but it should not need a card payment through a strange link for an unexpected package. A real employer may ask for ID docs after a formal hiring process, but not through casual messages before an interview. These comparisons help the app teach users how to separate normal inconvenience from fraud pressure.

### Section 4 \- Bank and Payment Alert Examples

Bank and payment alert scams are a core category for Verivae because they create panic and ask users to act fast. The app should recognize texts, calls, emails, pop-ups, and chat messages claiming that an account is locked, a payment failed, a transfer is pending, a card was used, a refund is available, or an unauthorized purchase needs confirmation. These scams often rely on urgency, authority, and fear. The app should slow the user down and give them a safer path.

Example: "Your bank account has been suspended due to risky activity. Verify immediately at this link." The app should classify this as risk if the message includes urgency, a link, and a request to verify account access. The app should explain that banks may send alerts, but a message pressuring the user to log in through a link is unsafe. The safest action should be to close the message, open the bank app directly, or call the number on the back of the card.

Example: "We detected a $942 transfer. Reply Y if this was you or N if not." The app should classify this as caution or risk depending on what happens next. The first message may resemble real fraud alerts. The app should advise the user not to provide codes, passwords, or account details if someone calls after they reply. If the message includes a link, odd sender, grammar problems, or a request for login, the app should increase the risk level. If the user already replied, the app should provide a recovery flow that says to stop responding and contact the bank through an official route.

Example: "A payment from PayPal, Cash App, Venmo, or Zelle failed. Click here to fix it." The app should evaluate whether the user expected a payment, whether the sender address is official, whether the link domain is recognizable, whether the message asks for sensitive info, and whether the message creates urgency. The app should not guarantee the brand is involved. It should say the message claims to be from a payment service and should be verified inside the official app.

Example: "Your account has received a refund. Pay a small release fee to unlock it." The app should classify this as risk. The explanation should be direct: legitimate refunds normally do not require the user to pay a separate fee to receive their own money. The app should recommend not paying, not sending ID docs, and not sharing account login info.

Example: "Someone accidentally sent you money. Please send it back right away." The app should treat this as a risk scenario, especially if the sender asks the user to return money through a different app, gift card, crypto wallet, wire transfer, or instant payment method. The app should explain that accidental payments can be reversed or disputed, and returning money separately can cause the user to lose funds twice. The safest next step is to contact the payment platform through the official app and wait for the platform to resolve it.

Example: "Your bank representative says your money is unsafe and must be moved to a safe account." The app should classify this as critical risk. The app should explain that a bank will not ask a customer to move money into a separate account controlled by another person for protection. The advised action should be to hang up, avoid sending money, contact the bank directly through official contact info, and consider placing a fraud alert or account lock if sensitive details were shared.

For bank and payment alerts, the app should show a review card with three decision layers. The first layer should say what the message is asking for. The second layer should say why that request is risky. The third layer should say what the user should do instead. The app should avoid technical phrasing like "phishing vector" unless the user asks for expert detail. A beginner-friendly result might say, "This message is trying to get you to open a link and prove who you are while you are worried. Use your bank's official app instead."

### Section 4 \- Marketplace and Selling Examples

Marketplace scams are important because users often feel they are doing normal buying and selling. the app should cover scams involving online marketplaces, local pickup, shipping, fake buyers, fake sellers, fake payment confirmations, overpayment, rental listings, ticket sales, and item deposits. The app should help users understand not only whether a message is risky, but also how money can be lost in the transaction.

Example: "I will buy your item, but I need your email to send a payment confirmation." The app should ask what payment method is being used and whether the marketplace has its own checkout. If the buyer sends a screenshot or email claiming payment was made, the app should tell the user to verify money inside the official payment account, not through a screenshot. The risk should increase if the buyer says the money is pending until the item ships or until the seller pays an upgrade fee.

Example: "Your payment is on hold because your account is not a business account. Ask the buyer to send extra money, then refund the difference." The app should classify this as risk. The app should explain that the message is trying to make the seller believe they owe money in order to receive money. The app should recommend not sending any refund or fee and checking the payment service directly.

Example: "I accidentally overpaid by $500. Please send the extra back to my mover." This is a classic overpayment pattern. The app should flag the combination of overpayment, urgency, third-party refund destination, and movement of money before payment clears. The result should tell the user not to send back funds through a separate method and to wait for the original payment to fully clear through the platform.

Example: "The seller wants a deposit before showing the apartment." The app should ask whether the user has toured the property, verified ownership or management, and used a secure rental process. The app should not say every deposit is fraudulent, but it should warn against sending money before verification. The app should suggest using official property management contact details, in-person or verified virtual tours, written lease review, and payment methods with records.

Example: "A buyer wants to use a courier, mover, shipping agent, or relative to pick up the item." The app should evaluate whether that arrangement is being used to justify strange payment steps. A courier pickup can be legitimate in some cases, but when paired with overpayment, account upgrade fees, or external communication pressure, the app should raise the risk level.

Example: "A ticket seller says the tickets will transfer after payment, but only accepts instant payment, crypto, gift cards, or friends-and-family payment." The app should classify the transaction as risk because the payment method gives the buyer little recourse. The app should recommend using the official ticket platform's transfer and payment protections.

Marketplace result cards should include a transaction timeline. The timeline should show what has happened, what the other person wants next, and what must be verified before the user proceeds. This is important because many marketplace scams are not risky at the first message. The risk becomes clear only after the payment story changes.

### Section 4 \- Job, Check, and Employment Examples

Job scams are important for Verivae because people looking for work may already be under financial pressure. The app should handle job offers, remote-work messages, task scams, fake recruiter messages, fake onboarding portals, check deposit requests, equipment purchase requests, and payment-before-work schemes. The app should be careful not to shame the user for hoping the opportunity is real.

Example: "You are hired after a short chat interview. Deposit this check and buy equipment from our vendor." The app should classify this as risk. The explanation should say that a real job may reimburse equipment, but a stranger sending a check before normal hiring steps and asking the user to spend money quickly is dangerous. The check can appear to clear before it is later reversed, leaving the user responsible for the spent money.

Example: "A recruiter contacted you on a messaging app and wants your personal info before a formal interview." The app should evaluate the requested data. Basic resume info may be normal, but Social Security numbers, banking info, ID docs, or account login details before a legitimate hiring process should be treated as risk. The app should suggest verifying the recruiter through the company's official website or established recruiting platform.

Example: "A remote assistant job asks you to receive packages and reship them." The app should flag this as risk because the user may become involved in moving stolen goods or fraudulent purchases. The app should recommend not accepting packages, not using personal addresses, and not providing ID docs.

Example: "A task app says you can earn money by completing simple product ratings, but you must deposit money to unlock more tasks." The app should classify this as risk. The pattern is not just the promise of easy money. The risk is the requirement that the user deposits their own money to continue earning or to withdraw earnings. The app should explain that legitimate work does not usually require paying to unlock wages.

Example: "A company sends a link to a payroll setup page." This may be legitimate after a real hiring process. The app should not automatically mark it as a scam. It should ask whether the user applied, interviewed, signed an offer, recognizes the company, and can access the payroll provider through official company communication. If the user cannot verify those steps, the app should recommend pausing.

For job scams, the app should include a hiring-process checklist. This checklist should not be framed as a business plan. It should be part of the app's user-facing scam review. The checklist should ask: Did you apply or were you contacted unexpectedly? Did you interview through a recognizable process? Did the company domain match the real company? Were you asked to pay money or deposit a check? Were you asked to share sensitive info before an offer? Were you pressured to act today? The app should convert these answers into a clear risk level.

### Section 4 \- Romance, Family, and Social Trust Examples

Romance, family, and social trust scams require a different tone because the user may feel emotionally attached, embarrassed, or afraid. the app should be able to review these situations without sounding cold or judgmental. The app should focus on behavior patterns, not insults toward the other person.

Example: "Someone I met online says they love me and needs money for an emergency." The app should ask how long the relationship has existed, whether the person has avoided video calls, whether they ask for secrecy, whether money is requested through irreversible methods, and whether emergencies repeat. The app should explain that the risk comes from urgent money pressure and limited verification, not from the user's feelings.

Example: "A family member texts from a new number and says they are in trouble." The app should classify this as caution or risk depending on the requested action. It should recommend calling the family member through a known number, using a family code word if one exists, or asking a question only the real person would know. The app should warn against sending money, gift cards, or login codes before confirming identity.

Example: "A person says they are overseas, cannot access their account, and needs a temporary loan." The app should look for repeated excuses, avoidance of direct verification, requests for unusual payment methods, and escalating amounts. The app should present a safe reply such as, "I cannot send money until I verify this independently." The app should also allow the user to save the situation and review it with a trusted helper.

Example: "A friend on social media sends an investment opportunity." The app should determine whether the friend's account may be compromised. If the message uses unusual language, pushes quick money, asks for crypto, or asks the user to move to another app, the app should recommend contacting the friend through another known channel.

Example: "Someone threatens to release private photos unless paid." The app should classify this as urgent harm risk and provide calm next steps. It should tell the user not to pay, not to continue negotiating if unsafe, to preserve evidence, to report through the platform, and to seek trusted help. If the user indicates they may be in immediate danger or at risk of self-harm, the app should encourage contacting emergency services or a trusted local person immediately. The design brief should mark this as a sensitive safety path that must be handled carefully.

For social trust scams, the app should provide an emotional-pressure meter. This is not a mental-health diagnosis. It is a simple product feature that shows which pressure tactics are present: secrecy, urgency, guilt, fear, romance, authority, shame, isolation, and repeated crises. The result should say, "These pressure signs make it harder to think clearly. Pause before sending money or info."

### Section 4 \- Device Check Flow Detail

The device check feature should be described realistically. the app should not promise unlimited virus scanning across every phone, email inbox, message app, and linked device without permission or platform support. Instead, the feature should be designed as a device safety review system with multiple layers. Where the OS allows direct scanning, the app can inspect permitted files, links, downloads, app metadata, risky permissions, configuration warnings, and risky behavior signals. Where the OS does not allow full scanning, the app should clearly explain what it can check and what it cannot check.

The device check entry point should be visible from the home screen and from manual scam results. A user who receives a risky link may wonder whether their phone is infected after tapping it. The app should offer a button such as "Check my device" or "Run a safety check." The first screen should explain the check in plain terms: the app can look for risky downloads, risky links, unsafe settings, unusual app permissions, and signs that the user may need to take action. The app should avoid promising that it can prove the device is perfectly clean.

The device check should begin with a short triage screen. The app should ask what happened: I tapped a risky link, I downloaded a file, I installed an app, I gave remote access, I entered a password, I shared a code, I sent money, or I am not sure. Each answer should route the user to the most relevant checks. If the user tapped a link but did not enter info, the app may recommend browser history review, password caution, and link analysis. If the user entered a password, the app should recommend changing that password through the official service and enabling additional security where available. If the user installed an app, the app should guide them through reviewing installed apps and permissions.

The device check should include a permissions review. This review should explain permissions simply. Camera permission means an app may use the camera when allowed by the system. Microphone permission means an app may access audio when allowed. Location permission means an app may see approximate or precise location depending on system settings. Contacts permission means an app may access saved contacts. Accessibility permission can be powerful on some devices and should be treated carefully. Alert access, SMS access, file access, VPN profiles, device administrator access, and screen recording access should be explained in user-friendly language.

The app should prioritize findings by actionability. A finding is actionable when the user can understand it and do something about it. For example, "Unknown app has alert access" is more useful than "Potential anomaly detected." Each finding should include what was found, why it might matter, what the user can do, and how urgent the action is. Findings should not be buried in technical language.

The device check should have a safe-mode behavior for uncertain results. If the app cannot determine whether something is harmful, it should say so clearly. For example: "I cannot confirm this file is dangerous from the info available, but it came from a risky message. Do not open it again. Delete it if you do not need it." The app should be comfortable saying "unknown" instead of pretending to know.

The device check should include a post-scam recovery route. If the user says they entered a password, installed a remote access tool, shared a login code, or sent money, the app should not only scan. It should open a recovery checklist. That checklist should include steps such as change the affected password, sign out of other sessions where the service allows it, contact the bank or payment app through official channels, remove risky apps, revoke risky permissions, preserve evidence, and monitor accounts. The app should adapt this checklist to the user's stated incident.

The device check should avoid creating panic. The interface should use calm severity labels such as Needs attention, Review soon, High concern, and Immediate action advised. It should avoid dramatic language unless the user is in immediate financial or personal danger. The app's tone should be protective and direct.

### Section 4 \- Weekly Deep Check Detail

The weekly check should be a recurring safety review that users can schedule. It should not feel like a meaningless alert. It should give the user a practical summary of what changed, what needs attention, and what is fine. The weekly check should be useful for people who are not technical and do not want to manually inspect their phone every day.

The setup screen should ask whether the user wants weekly checks. It should explain that a weekly check is a scheduled review of available safety signals, recent risky items saved in the app, risky links submitted to the app, device permission changes where available, security setting reminders, and unresolved scam cases. The app should state that weekly checks may require alert permission and may be limited by device permissions.

The weekly check should have a predictable structure. First, it should review unresolved alerts. Second, it should review recent manual checks and whether the user completed advised actions. Third, it should review device safety signals that the app is allowed to access. Fourth, it should suggest one or two next steps. Fifth, it should let the user mark items as resolved, snooze them, or ask a trusted helper for review.

A weekly check result should not dump a long list of raw warnings. It should provide a summary at the top: "No urgent issues found," "Two items need review," or "One risky item needs action." Then it should group findings by category. For example: Scam messages, Risky links, Device permissions, Account recovery, Trusted helper items, and Education reminders. Each group should be expandable so the user is not overwhelmed.

The weekly check should respect privacy. Users should be able to choose whether the app reviews saved scam cases only, device-level signals only, or both.
