If helper sharing is enabled, the app should ask whether weekly summaries can be shared with the helper. The default should avoid sharing sensitive message contents unless the user explicitly allows it.

The weekly check should include missed-check behavior. If the phone was off, the app was force closed, permissions were removed, or the weekly check could not run, the app should say so. It should not silently pretend everything is fine. A clear message could say: "This week's check was incomplete because device review permission is off. Turn it back on to review app permissions and risky downloads."

The weekly check should include improvement tracking. This should not be gamified in a childish way. It should simply show that the user is becoming safer: fewer unresolved alerts, stronger settings, fewer unknown links opened, helper reviewed, and recovery steps completed. The purpose is confidence, not entertainment.

The weekly check should also include a quiet emergency path. If the app detects unresolved critical-risk scenarios such as sent money, remote access installed, shared bank code, or active blackmail threat, it should bring those to the top. The user should see the most important next step immediately.

### Section 4 \- Trusted Helper Workflow Detail

Trusted helper workflows are central to Verivae because many users need a second opinion before sending money, responding to a message, or trusting a stranger. A trusted helper may be a parent, adult child, spouse, sibling, close friend, financial caretaker, or other person the user chooses. The app should make helper support easy while protecting the user's privacy and control.

The helper feature should begin with consent. The app should explain that a trusted helper can review selected scam cases only when the user chooses to share them, unless the user sets up a broader sharing preference. The app should avoid language that makes the user feel monitored. The user should stay in control of what gets shared.

The helper setup flow should let the user add a helper by contact, email, or invite link where supported. The app should explain what the helper can and cannot do. For example, a helper can see selected scam review summaries, add comments, suggest a next step, and mark whether they think the situation is safe or risky. A helper should not be able to see all messages, all accounts, full device contents, passwords, payment details, or private documents unless the user explicitly chooses a specific share action that includes them.

The app should support multiple helper levels. A basic helper can receive a share card for a single situation. A saved helper can be reused for future checks. A safety circle can include more than one person for users who want a broader support group. A high-trust helper may receive urgent alerts for critical-risk cases if the user enables that setting. Each level should be explained in ordinary language.

The case-sharing screen should show exactly what will be shared before sending. It should include the risk summary, selected message text or screenshot if included, the app's explanation, the user's question, and any sensitive fields that will be hidden. The app should offer controls such as Include message text, Include screenshot, Hide names, Hide phone numbers, Hide dollar amounts, and Add my note. The default should minimize sensitive sharing while preserving enough context for the helper to understand the risk.

The helper response screen should be simple. A helper should be able to choose: Looks risky, Looks safe after verification, Need more info, or I am not sure. They should be able to write a short note. The helper should not be positioned as the sole authority. The app should combine helper feedback with its own safety guidance and still recommend official verification for money, identity, or account issues.

The trusted helper workflow should include disagreement handling. If the app says risk but the helper says it seems safe, the app should not simply downgrade the risk. It should display both views and ask for verification steps. For example: "Your helper thinks this may be safe, but the message still includes a payment request and urgency. Verify through the official company website before sending money." If the helper says risky but the app score is low, the app should invite the user to review the details again.

The helper workflow should include an emergency pause. If a user is about to send money and the app identifies critical risk, the app should suggest contacting a helper before proceeding. This should be a prompt, not a lockout. The app should respect adult user autonomy while making the safer path easy.

The helper workflow should include user-friendly status tracking. A case can be Not shared, Shared, Waiting for helper, Helper responded, Resolved, or Archived. The user should be able to see what is still waiting. If a helper does not respond, the app should recommend independent verification rather than waiting indefinitely.

### Section 4 \- Settings Behavior Detail

Settings in the app should be practical, understandable, and privacy-centered. A user should not need to understand technical security language to configure the app. Settings should be organized around user needs: Protection, Privacy, Alerts, Linked services, Device checks, Trusted helpers, Scam education, Subscription, Accessibility, and Account.

Protection settings should let the user choose how active the app feels. A quiet mode should provide fewer alerts and rely on manual checks. A balanced mode should notify about saved cases, weekly checks, and unresolved risky items. A strong protection mode should use more reminders and helper prompts where the user has enabled them. The app should explain each mode clearly and avoid implying that stronger always means better. Some users may need fewer interruptions.

Privacy settings should be separate and easy to find. The user should be able to control saved history, screenshot storage, message text storage, helper sharing defaults, analytics, account data, and deletion. The app should provide plain explanations such as "Saved scam cases help you review patterns later" and "Deleting history removes your saved cases from this app." If some deletion requires backend processing, the app should explain the status without legalistic wording.

Linked service settings should show each connection and permission. If Gmail, messages, browser, contacts, or device signals are integrated in any version of the app, each connection should have a status. Possible statuses include Not linked, Linked, Permission limited, Needs attention, and Dislinked. The user should be able to disconnect a service from inside Verivae where technically possible, or receive exact instructions if the OS requires them to disconnect through system settings.

Device check settings should include weekly check schedule, check depth where supported, alert timing, scan history, and allowed review categories. The app should allow the user to choose a day and time for weekly checks. It should also allow the user to pause weekly checks without deleting history. If a scheduled check is missed, the settings area should show why if known.

Trusted helper settings should show who is linked, what each helper can see, what alerts they receive, and when they were last active. The user should be able to remove a helper, pause sharing, change helper permissions, or send a test share. The app should make it obvious if no helper is linked.

Alert settings should group alerts by purpose, not by technical channel. Examples include Scam result reminders, Weekly check, Unresolved risky case, Helper response, Permission issue, Education tip, Subscription update, and Account security. Each alert type should have a short explanation and an on/off control. Risky alerts should include a plain explanation of why the app recommends keeping them on.

Accessibility settings should allow larger text support, reduced motion, high contrast, simpler language, voice-friendly layout, and haptic feedback where available. These should not be hidden behind advanced menus. Scam protection must be usable by people under stress, older adults, people with low vision, people with cognitive load, and people who are not comfortable with technology.

Subscription settings should be trust-safe. If the app has paid features, the settings area should clearly show the user's current plan, renewal status, included features, and cancellation path. The app should not use confusing dark patterns. For a scam safety app, billing transparency is part of product trust.

### Section 4 \- Deeper Accept Rules

Acceptance criteria define what must be true before a feature can be considered complete. For Verivae, accept rules should measure usefulness, clarity, privacy, and safety. A feature is not complete just because a screen exists. It must work under realistic conditions and communicate clearly to a beginner.

Manual check accept rules: The user can paste text, upload or attach a screenshot where supported, summarize a call, or describe a situation in their own words. The app can identify the likely scam category or say that the category is uncertain. The app provides a risk level, trigger details, explanation, advised next step, and safer verification path. The user can save the result, share it with a helper, start recovery steps, or dismiss it. The result does not claim certainty when the evidence is incomplete.

Scam example library accept rules: Each major category includes realistic examples, false-alarm comparisons, risk triggers, safe actions, and user-facing explanations. The app can handle messy input that does not name the category. The app can explain why an example is risky without relying only on generic warnings. The app can update examples over time without changing the entire product design.

Bank and payment accept rules: The app warns against logging in through risky links, sharing login codes, moving money to a so-called safe account, paying release fees, refunding overpayments before clearing, and sending money through irreversible channels. The app recommends official verification paths. The app avoids pretending to be the bank or payment platform.

Marketplace accept rules: The app can identify payment confirmation screenshots, business-account upgrade fees, overpayment refunds, courier pickup manipulation, rental deposit pressure, ticket transfer risk, and off-platform payment pressure. The app explains the transaction step that creates the loss. The app provides seller-specific and buyer-specific guidance.

Job scam accept rules: The app detects check deposit equipment scams, fake recruiters, task scams, reshipping jobs, premature identity requests, and pay-to-work schemes. The app explains the risk without discouraging legitimate job searching. The app includes verification prompts for company identity, interview process, offer legitimacy, and payment requests.

Social trust accept rules: The app detects family emergency impersonation, romance emergency money requests, social media account compromise, blackmail threats, secrecy pressure, repeated crises, and unusual payment methods. The app uses a careful tone. It gives users practical verification steps and encourages trusted support when appropriate.

Device check accept rules: The app clearly states what it can check on the user's device. It reviews available risky downloads, risky links, unusual app permissions, security setting warnings, unresolved scam cases, and recovery actions where supported. It does not claim a complete virus scan if the OS does not allow one. It provides actionable findings and avoids technical noise.

Weekly check accept rules: The user can turn weekly checks on or off, choose timing, understand what will be reviewed, and see a clear weekly result. The check summarizes urgent issues, unresolved cases, device concerns, permission problems, and advised next steps. If a check cannot complete, the app says why. The weekly check respects privacy and does not share sensitive details by default.

Trusted helper accept rules: The user can add, remove, and manage helpers. The user can share a specific case with clear preview of what will be shared. The helper can respond with a simple judgment and note. The app handles helper disagreement without hiding its own risk warning. Sensitive info is minimized by default. The user can revoke helper access.

Settings accept rules: Settings are organized by understandable user purpose. Every linked service has a visible status and disconnect path or instructions. Privacy controls are easy to find. Alert categories are clear. Weekly checks can be paused or adjusted. Subscription info is transparent. Accessibility options are available without requiring technical knowledge.

Monetization accept rules: Paid features must not make the free version useless for basic scam safety. The free tier should allow meaningful manual checking, basic results, and basic safety education. Paid features may expand convenience, monitoring, weekly reports, helper support, deeper device checks, saved history, and advanced guidance. The app must never use fear-based billing language such as implying the user is unsafe unless they immediately pay. Upgrade prompts should be calm, factual, and easy to dismiss.

Privacy accept rules: The app collects only what is needed for the feature the user chooses. Sensitive message contents, screenshots, payment details, and personal identifiers are handled carefully. The app explains storage and sharing in plain text. The user can delete saved cases. Helper sharing is explicit. The app avoids unnecessary exposure of private content in alerts.

Recovery accept rules: When the user has already clicked, paid, shared a code, installed an app, or gave account info, the app opens a recovery path instead of only warning. Recovery steps are ordered by urgency. The user can mark steps complete. The app can recommend contacting official support, changing passwords, removing risky apps, preserving evidence, and monitoring accounts. The app should not provide legal or financial guarantees.

Interface accept rules: Every screen should answer the user's immediate question: Is this risky, why, and what should I do next? Buttons should be clear. Warnings should be calm. Technical terms should be explained. Important actions should be visible without searching. The app should work for users who are stressed, embarrassed, distracted, or inexperienced.

### Section 4 completion note

Section 4 details the design brief with scam example libraries, device-check behavior, weekly deep-check behavior, trusted-helper workflows, settings behavior, and deeper accept rules while continuing to reserve the final area for later.

## Design Brief Section 5: Integration Behavior, Account Protection, Evidence Handling, and Recovery Journeys

### Detail pass purpose

This design section deepens Verivae as a practical protection app that fits into the places where users actually encounter scams: email, text messages, calls, browsers, social apps, payment apps, banking alerts, device settings, and conversations with trusted people. It describes product capabilities, screen behavior, user decision support, permission expectations, safety boundaries, and cross-feature connections. Harborwake remains the company name. Verivae remains the app name until a final app name is chosen.

This section focuses on the product behavior that should exist around integrations, account safety, evidence preservation, and recovery after a mistake. Many scam safety apps fail if they only tell users that something is risky. A professional version of the app should help users prevent harm, understand what happened, save the right info, recover safely, and learn enough to avoid repeat harm. The app should be especially strong when the user is stressed, embarrassed, hurried, or confused.

### Section 5 \- Integration Principles

the app should treat integrations as permission-based bridges between the app and the places where risky activity appears. An integration is a connection that lets the app review or receive info from another service or area of the phone, such as email, messages, browser sharing, call history, device files, or linked accounts. The app should never make the user feel that it secretly watches everything. Every connection should explain what it can access, why it helps, what is stored, what is not stored, and how to turn it off.

The app should have a simple rule: the user must understand the tradeoff before turning on a connection. For example, connecting an email account may make scam review easier because risky emails can be forwarded or imported for review. The tradeoff is that email may contain private info. The app should explain whether it reviews only user-selected emails, only emails forwarded to a review address, or broader inbox signals if that version ever supports them. The most privacy-friendly option should be the default.

The app should support manual sharing even when a full integration is unavailable. On many phones, users can share a message, screenshot, email, link, or file into another app through the system share sheet. The share sheet is the phone's built-in menu that lets a user send something from one app into another app. the app should appear as a share destination where technically possible. This gives the app useful access without requiring always-on monitoring.

Integrations should be divided into three trust levels. Level one is manual review, where the user sends one item to Verivae. Level two is limited connection, where the user allows a specific kind of review such as saved risky emails or weekly device checks. Level three is active protection, where the app can monitor certain signals or notify the user when a risky pattern appears. The app should not push every user toward level three. Some users will be better served by manual review and strong education.

Every integration should have a status label. The label should be understandable: Off, Ready, Limited, Needs permission, Needs review, or Linked. The app should avoid vague labels like Active if the user cannot tell what is active. If a connection stops working, the app should say what changed and how to fix it.

### Section 5 \- Email and Gmail Review Behavior

Email review is one of the most important features because many scams begin with fake invoices, account warnings, job offers, refund notices, shipping notices, business messages, document-sharing links, or password reset alerts. the app should be able to help users review email content through forwarding, sharing, copy-and-paste, screenshot upload, or linked mailbox review where available and permitted.

The simplest email flow should be: the user opens an email, shares it to Verivae, and receives a result. The app should inspect visible sender info, subject line, body text, links, attachments, payment requests, urgency language, brand claims, and requested user action. The app should show the result in a way that separates evidence from conclusion. For example, it should say, "This looks risky because the sender claims to be a company, asks you to click a link, and says your account will close today." The user should be able to expand the result to see each risky detail.

For Gmail-style usage, the app should be designed to work with user-selected emails first. A user-selected model means the app only reviews emails the user chooses to send into the app. This is simpler, more private, and easier for beginners to understand. If a later version supports a deeper mailbox connection, that deeper connection should be optional and should have separate permission explanations.

The app should classify email links carefully. A link can be risky because it hides the real destination, uses a lookalike domain, uses a shortened address, claims to be a known company but sends the user elsewhere, asks for login info, or leads to a file download. The app should explain link risk in simple terms. A beginner-friendly explanation could say, "The words in the email look like a bank link, but the actual link points somewhere else." If the app cannot inspect the real destination safely, it should say that the destination could not be confirmed and recommend opening the official app or website manually.

Email attachments should have cautious handling. The app should not encourage users to open unknown files. It should label attachment review as limited if the app cannot scan the file contents. It should identify attachment warning signs such as unexpected invoices, password-protected files, executable files, archive files, fake delivery documents, fake legal notices, and files that ask the user to enable macros or special access. The app should tell the user when an attachment should not be opened.

Email impersonation should receive special treatment. If an email appears to come from a boss, coworker, bank, school, government office, customer support agent, family member, or known company, the app should ask whether the user expected the message and whether the request matches normal behavior. The app should teach users to verify through a separate known channel. A separate known channel means the user should not reply to the risky email or use contact info inside it; they should use a number, app, or website they already trust.

The email review result should support quick actions: Mark as risky, Save case, Share with helper, Start recovery, Copy safe reply, Delete guidance, and Report guidance where supported. The safe reply should be optional. In many cases, the safest reply is no reply. The app should not encourage engagement with scammers.

### Section 5 \- Text Message and Messaging Review Behavior

Text messages and chat apps create a different product challenge because scams often look short, casual, and urgent. the app should handle SMS, MMS, RCS, messaging apps, social app direct messages, and screenshots of conversations. The app should support one-message review and conversation review. One-message review is useful for quick checks. Conversation review is better when the scam pattern develops over time.

The message review flow should begin with the user's source. If the user shares text directly, the app can analyze the words, links, numbers, and requested action. If the user shares a screenshot, the app should extract visible text where supported and ask the user to confirm anything unclear. If the user summarizes a call or conversation, the app should ask follow-up questions instead of pretending it saw the full content.

The app should recognize short-message scam patterns. Examples include package delivery fees, bank lock warnings, unpaid tolls, fake missed payments, fake job offers, fake prize wins, fake family emergencies, fake login alerts, fake login code requests, and messages from unknown numbers asking the user to move to another app. These short messages should be scored by what they ask the user to do, not just by spelling or grammar.

Conversation review should include pattern memory within a case. If the first message is harmless but later messages request gift cards, crypto, wire transfer, bank codes, remote access, secrecy, or urgent action, the risk level should increase. The app should show the turning point. For example: "The earlier messages were friendly, but the risk increased when the person asked you to buy gift cards and send the codes."

The app should support safe response templates for messaging. These templates should help users pause without escalating conflict. Examples include: "I need to verify this another way before I send anything," "I cannot share codes or passwords," "I will contact the company directly," and "I am not comfortable continuing this conversation." The app should also say when no response is safer.

Message review should protect privacy. If a screenshot includes private names, phone numbers, account numbers, or personal photos, the app should offer to hide sensitive parts before saving or sharing with a helper. The app should make redaction easy. Redaction means covering or removing private info so someone else cannot see it. The app should explain redaction in beginner-friendly language.

### Section 5 \- Browser, Link, and Website Safety Behavior

Scam links are one of the most common ways users are pushed into danger. the app should provide a link review flow that can handle pasted links, shared links, links from screenshots, links from emails, and links from text messages. The app should be careful not to open dangerous content unnecessarily. Link analysis should prefer safe inspection methods and should warn the user before opening any unknown destination.

A link review result should explain the visible link, the actual destination if known, the claimed brand, the action requested, and the risk signs. If a message says it is from a bank but the link destination does not match what the user would expect, the app should highlight that mismatch. If a link is shortened, the app should say that shortened links can hide the real destination and should be treated carefully when attached to money, passwords, or account alerts.

The app should include a website lookalike explanation. A lookalike site is a website address or page that imitates a trusted company while being controlled by someone else. The app should teach users to watch for small spelling changes, extra words, strange endings, unnecessary login prompts, fake support chat, poor formatting, urgent banners, and payment requests that do not match the official service. The app should not rely only on appearance because fake pages can look polished.

If browser integration is available, the app should support a browser share action. The user should be able to share the current page or URL into the app. The app should then produce a link safety result. If browser integration is not available, the app should provide copy-and-paste instructions.

The app should include a post-click path. If a user already clicked a risky link, the app should ask what happened next: I only opened the page, I entered a password, I entered payment info, I downloaded a file, I installed an app, I gave a login code, or I am not sure. Each answer should route to a different recovery sequence. This is important because clicking alone is not the same as entering a password or installing software.

### Section 5 \- Call and Voicemail Safety Behavior

Phone calls are difficult because the app may not be able to hear or record calls depending on device rules, privacy laws, and permissions. the app should still help users review calls by letting them summarize the call afterward, paste voicemail text, upload a voicemail transcript where available, or answer guided questions. The app should be clear about what it did and did not review.

Call scam review should focus on the caller's claimed identity, requested action, pressure tactic, and money or data request. Common call patterns include fake bank support, fake government agent, fake tech support, fake police or court threat, fake utility shutoff, fake family emergency, fake refund department, and fake investment advisor. The app should not require the user to remember every word. It should ask simple prompts: Who did they claim to be? What did they want you to do? Did they ask for money? Did they ask for codes? Did they ask to install anything? Did they tell you not to tell anyone?

The app should include a call pause feature. If a user is currently on a risky call and can safely open Verivae, the app should provide a large, simple "What to do now" screen. This screen should say: do not share codes, do not move money, do not install apps, hang up if pressured, and contact the organization through a known number. The app should be written for a person under pressure, so the copy should be short and direct.

Voicemail review should inspect urgency, threat language, callback numbers, official claims, and requested action. The app should advise the user not to call back using a number from a risky voicemail if the message claims to be a bank, government office, delivery service, or major company. Instead, the app should recommend using official contact info.

### Section 5 \- Account Protection Behavior

Account protection is the part of Verivae that helps users after they suspect an account may be at risk. It should cover email accounts, banking accounts, payment apps, social media accounts, shopping accounts, work accounts, and device accounts. The app should not ask users to give it their passwords. It should guide them to secure accounts through official apps and websites.

The account protection flow should begin with a plain question: "Which account may be at risk?" The user can choose categories like email, bank, payment app, social media, shopping, phone account, work account, or not sure. The app should then ask what happened: password entered, code shared, card entered, risky login alert, unknown charge, account locked, account taken over, or risky message sent from the account.

For password exposure, the app should recommend changing the password through the official service, using a strong unique password, signing out of other sessions if the service allows it, enabling additional login protection where available, and checking recovery email and phone settings. The app should explain that changing a reused password on one account may not protect other accounts where the same password was used.

For login code exposure, the app should explain that codes are used to prove account access. If the user shares a code, someone else may use it to log in or approve a transaction. The app should recommend contacting the affected service, changing login settings, checking recent activity, and watching for unauthorized changes. The app should avoid blaming the user.

For payment info exposure, the app should recommend contacting the bank or card issuer through official channels, monitoring activity, freezing or replacing cards when appropriate, and saving evidence. The app should avoid promising refunds. It should say that outcomes depend on the financial institution, timing, payment method, and user actions.

For social account takeover, the app should guide the user through recovery: attempt official account recovery, change password if still logged in, check recovery email and phone, remove unknown sessions, warn contacts if scam messages were sent, and save evidence. The app should provide a short message the user can send to contacts: "My account may have been used to send risky messages. Please do not click links or send money from recent messages that looked like they came from me."

Account protection should include a priority system. Critical steps should appear first. If money could be moved, bank or payment contact comes before education. If an account is actively compromised, password and session recovery come before archiving evidence. If the user is safe but uncertain, education and monitoring can come later.

### Section 5 \- Evidence Handling and Case Records

Evidence handling should help users save the right info without turning the app into a confusing legal tool. A case record is a saved scam situation inside Verivae. Each case should contain the submitted message, screenshot, link, call summary, risk result, actions taken, helper comments if any, recovery checklist, and status. The app should allow the user to keep evidence organized in case they need to report the issue, explain it to a bank, or review it later.

The app should support evidence types such as message text, email text, screenshots, links, phone numbers, sender names, dates written by the user, transaction amounts, payment method, files, notes, helper responses, and app-generated risk summaries. If a piece of evidence contains private info, the app should label it as sensitive. Sensitive means the content could expose personal details if shared.

Case records should have simple statuses: Open, Needs action, Waiting, Shared with helper, Reported, Resolved, and Archived. The status should help the user remember what to do. The app should not bury active cases behind completed cases.

The app should include an evidence quality guide. This guide should explain what is useful to save: original messages, sender info, payment receipts, usernames, phone numbers, email addresses, links, screenshots, dates, and notes about calls. It should also explain what not to do: do not reply just to collect more evidence, do not click risky links to get more proof, do not threaten the scammer, and do not share passwords or private documents inside evidence notes.

Evidence export should be available for users who need to contact a bank, platform, trusted helper, or support organization. The export should allow the user to choose what to include. It should not automatically include everything. Export options should include summary only, summary plus messages, summary plus screenshots, recovery actions completed, and helper notes. The app should warn the user before exporting sensitive info.

The app should preserve clarity around app-generated conclusions. A case export should separate user-provided evidence from the app's interpretation. For example, the export can say, "User-submitted message" and then "App risk summary." This matters because banks, platforms, or helpers may need to distinguish original evidence from the app's analysis.

Evidence handling should include deletion and retention controls. Retention means how long info is kept. The user should be able to delete individual cases, delete attachments, delete helper comments if allowed by policy, and clear history. The app should explain whether deletion is immediate in the app and whether backup or server deletion has a processing delay. This should be written plainly.

### Section 5 \- Recovery Journey System

The recovery journey system should activate when prevention is no longer enough. A user may come to Verivae after they already clicked, paid, shared a code, installed a remote access tool, gave personal info, deposited a fake check, or sent private images. The app should not treat these users as failures. It should move directly into practical recovery.

The recovery journey should start with a calm intake screen. The screen should ask: What happened? What info or money was involved? Is the issue still happening? Is anyone threatening you? Did you install anything? Did you share a login code? Did you contact your bank or platform yet? The app should allow "I am not sure" because stressed users may not know.

Recovery journeys should be modular. A module is a small set of steps for one type of harm. Password shared should open the password module. Bank info shared should open the payment safety module. Remote access installed should open the device access module. Gift cards sent should open the payment evidence module. Blackmail threat should open the urgent support and evidence module. The app can combine modules when more than one thing happened.

Each recovery module should include three layers: do now, do next, and monitor later. Do now includes urgent actions such as stop responding, contact the bank, change password, remove risky app, or preserve evidence. Do next includes deeper actions such as review account recovery settings, notify contacts, report the account, or update settings. Monitor later includes watching statements, checking login activity, keeping evidence, and reviewing new messages.

The recovery system should include progress tracking. Users should be able to mark steps as done, skipped, not applicable, or need help. The app should not force every user through every step. It should explain why a step matters so the user can make an informed choice.

The recovery journey should support helper sharing. If the user is overwhelmed, they can share the recovery checklist with a trusted helper. The helper should see only what the user chooses to include. The app should let the helper suggest steps, but the user should remain in control.

The app should include a recovery summary at the end. This summary should say what happened, what was reviewed, what actions were completed, what remains unresolved, and what the user should watch for. It should be saved to the case record.

### Section 5 \- Reporting Guidance

Reporting guidance should help users understand where a scam might be reported without pretending that reporting always solves the problem. the app should distinguish reporting to a bank, payment app, marketplace, social platform, email provider, phone carrier, employer, school, or law enforcement. The app should not provide legal advice. It should provide organized, practical guidance.

The reporting screen should ask what kind of harm occurred. If money was sent, the app should prioritize the financial institution or payment platform. If an account was taken over, the app should prioritize the account provider. If a listing or seller was fraudulent, the app should prioritize the marketplace. If threatening content is involved, the app should prioritize platform reporting, trusted human support, and urgent safety steps.

The app should prepare a report summary. The summary should include the case title, what happened, date or approximate timing as entered by the user, amount if entered, payment method if entered, sender info, links, screenshots, and actions already taken. The app should let the user copy this summary or export it. It should not submit reports automatically without user confirmation.

Reporting guidance should include expectation setting. A beginner-friendly explanation might say, "Reporting creates a record and may help the platform investigate. It does not guarantee money will be returned." The app should be honest because false hope damages trust.

### Section 5 \- Integration Failure and Permission Loss Behavior

Professional apps handle failure clearly. the app should explain when integrations stop working, permissions are removed, internet access is unavailable, or the app cannot inspect an item. A connection failure should not look like safety. If a weekly check cannot review a linked area, the app should say so.

If email connection is removed, the app should say, "Email review is dislinked. You can still paste or share emails manually." If device review permission is off, the app should say, "Device check is limited because permission is off." If helper sharing fails, the app should say, "This case was not sent. Try again or copy the summary manually." If screenshot text cannot be read, the app should ask the user to type the important text or upload a clearer image.

The app should provide fallback paths for every major integration. Manual paste should exist when email connection fails. Screenshot upload should exist when direct message sharing is unavailable. Guided call summary should exist when call integration is unavailable. Link paste should exist when browser sharing is unavailable. This makes the product more resilient and keeps users protected even when a platform blocks deeper integration.

### Section 5 \- User Trust and Consent Requirements

Trust is not just branding for Verivae. It must be part of the interface behavior. Scam protection users are being asked to bring sensitive messages, money concerns, and private fears into the app. The product must be clear, restrained, and honest.

Consent should be specific. Instead of saying, "Allow access," the app should say what access means. For example: "Allow Verivae to review selected emails you choose to share" is clearer than "Allow email access." If broader access is ever supported, the app should explain the difference between selected review and ongoing review.

The app should avoid fear-based prompts. It should not say, "Upgrade now or you could lose everything." It should not make free users feel abandoned. It should not show repeated panic alerts to push paid conversion. A scam safety product that manipulates fear would violate the trust it is supposed to create.

The app should include confirmation before sensitive sharing. Before sending a case to a helper, exporting evidence, storing screenshots, or connecting a service, the app should preview what will happen. The user should have a clear cancel option.

The app should use plain privacy copy throughout. Examples include: "You choose what to share," "You can delete this case later," "This helper will see only this case summary," and "This check is limited because your phone does not allow full access." The product should earn trust through repeated clarity.

### Section 5 \- Future Feature Boundaries

The design brief should leave room for future versions without promising impossible behavior. the app may eventually support deeper email review, browser protection, device safety checks, account monitoring reminders, helper dashboards, report packages, and paid family protection features. Each future feature should be framed around user permission, platform limits, and privacy.

The app should avoid claims like "detects every scam," "guarantees virus removal," "prevents all fraud," or "protects every account automatically." Better claims are more honest: reviews risky messages, explains risk signs, helps users verify safely, guides recovery, and supports device safety checks where available. This difference matters because overpromising can create legal risk and user harm.

Future versions should preserve the free-first principle. Basic scam checking, basic education, and basic recovery guidance should remain useful without payment. Paid tiers can add convenience and depth, such as larger saved history, more helper features, deeper reports, enhanced weekly checks, or family-circle tools. The core safety promise should not be locked completely behind payment.

### Section 5 completion note

## Design Brief Section 6: Risk Decision Engine, Explanation Quality, Alert Behavior, Education, and Review Standards

### Detail pass purpose

This design section deepens the internal decision behavior of Verivae. The app should not simply say that something is safe or unsafe. It should explain how it reached the result, what signs mattered most, what is still unknown, what the user can do next, and how confident the result should feel. The section covers risk scoring, explanation quality, false-positive handling, alert behavior, education, review queues, and quality standards as product behavior inside the app.

The design goal is a product that can help a beginner make a safer decision under pressure. The user may be frightened by a bank warning, excited about a job offer, emotionally attached to an online relationship, embarrassed about being tricked, or confused by technical language. The decision engine and its explanations must be strong enough to support those moments without overstating certainty.

### Section 6 \- Risk Decision Engine Overview

The risk decision engine is the part of Verivae that turns an email, text, screenshot, link, call summary, device finding, or user description into a useful safety result. It should collect signals, weigh them, choose a risk level, explain the result, and recommend next steps. The engine should be designed around practical user safety rather than abstract scoring. A score is only useful if it helps the user avoid harm.

The engine should evaluate four broad questions. First, what is the other party asking the user to do? Second, what pressure tactics are being used? Third, what kind of money, account access, personal info, device access, or emotional leverage is involved? Fourth, what safer verification path exists? These questions should matter more than surface details such as spelling mistakes. Many scams have poor writing, but many professional-looking scams have clean writing. The app should not teach users that polished messages are automatically safe.

The engine should treat requested action as the strongest signal. A message that asks the user to send money, share a code, enter a password, install an app, open a file, move funds, buy gift cards, deposit a check, or keep the situation secret should receive more attention than a message that only provides neutral info. The app should identify the requested action and show it clearly in the result.

The engine should treat context as important but not absolute. If the user expected a delivery, a delivery notice is less risky than a completely unexpected notice, but it can still be dangerous if it asks for a strange payment or login. If the user applied for a job, a recruiter message may be normal, but it becomes risky if the recruiter asks for a check deposit or sensitive identity info before a real hiring process. Context should adjust the result, not override the risk signs.

The engine should support uncertainty. Some results should say "Not enough info" instead of forcing a high or low risk label. The app should ask follow-up questions when the result depends on missing context. Examples include whether the user expected the message, whether money has already been sent, whether a password was entered, whether the sender is known, whether the link was opened, or whether the user can verify through an official channel.

### Section 6 \- Risk Levels and Meaning

the app should use risk levels that are easy to understand. A advised set is Low concern, Caution, Risk, Critical risk, and Unknown. These labels should be paired with plain explanations so the user does not have to guess what they mean.

Low concern should mean that the submitted item does not show major scam signs based on the available info. It should not mean guaranteed safe. The app should still recommend basic caution for money, passwords, codes, and sensitive info. A Low concern result should include a small note such as, "No major scam signs were found here, but only use official apps or websites for payments and login."

Caution should mean that the item has one or more warning signs, but the available info does not prove a likely scam. The app should recommend verification before action. Caution is important because many real situations are mixed. A message can be from a real company but still require official verification. A buyer can be legitimate but still use a payment method that creates risk. The app should help the user slow down without claiming fraud too early.

Risk should mean that the app found strong scam patterns and the user should not proceed until they verify through a separate trusted channel. A Risk result should include specific triggers, such as a payment request, urgent threat, risky link, code request, overpayment story, remote access demand, or secrecy pressure. The result should provide a safe next action at the top.

Critical risk should mean the user may be in immediate danger of financial loss, account takeover, device compromise, blackmail, or active manipulation. Critical risk should be reserved for strong patterns such as moving money to a so-called safe account, sharing bank codes during a call, installing remote access at a stranger's direction, sending money under threat, paying blackmail, depositing a risky check and spending the funds, or providing credentials on a risky link. Critical risk should trigger a recovery or stop-now interface.

Unknown should mean the app cannot decide from the evidence. Unknown is not a weak result. It is an honest result. The app should explain what info is missing and ask for the next useful detail. For example, "I cannot tell whether this is your real bank because the sender info is missing. Do not click the link. Open your bank app directly to check."

### Section 6 \- Signal Categories

The decision engine should organize scam signs into signal categories. A signal is a detail that helps the app understand risk. Signal categories should include identity claims, requested actions, urgency, payment method, account access, device access, secrecy, emotional pressure, link behavior, attachment behavior, communication channel, transaction structure, and user history inside the case.

Identity claims include who the sender claims to be: bank, payment app, government office, employer, recruiter, romantic partner, family member, marketplace buyer, seller, tech support, delivery company, or investment contact. Identity claims matter because scammers borrow authority from names users already trust. The app should not trust the claim by itself. It should ask whether the user can verify independently.

Requested actions are the clearest risk signals. The app should detect requests to click links, scan QR codes, share passwords, share one-time codes, send money, buy gift cards, transfer crypto, wire funds, deposit checks, refund overpayments, install apps, give remote access, upload ID docs, share bank info, or keep the conversation private. Each requested action should have its own risk explanation.

Urgency signals include today-only deadlines, account closure threats, police or court threats, delivery failure warnings, bank suspension messages, limited job openings, emergency family stories, and investment opportunities that must be accepted quickly. The app should explain that urgency is risky because it reduces time to verify.

Payment method signals should distinguish reversible and hard-to-recover methods in beginner-friendly terms. The app should avoid complicated payment law explanations. It can say that some methods are difficult to reverse once sent. Gift cards, crypto, wires, instant transfers, friends-and-family payments, and cash deposits should generally raise concern, especially when requested by a stranger or under pressure.

Account access signals include password requests, login pages, login codes, security questions, recovery email changes, and prompts to approve a sign-in. Device access signals include remote access apps, screen sharing, configuration profiles, risky downloads, browser extensions, device administrator settings, and permissions that let another app see or control sensitive activity.

Emotional pressure signals include romance, fear, guilt, shame, secrecy, flattery, authority, family emergency, loneliness, and threats. These signals should be handled with care. The app should say the tactic is risky without insulting the user or the person they care about.

### Section 6 \- Scoring Behavior and Weighting

The app does not need to expose a complicated numeric score to the user. Internally, however, the decision engine should weigh signals so that serious danger signs matter more than minor clues. For example, a typo should not matter as much as a request to share a login code. A strange sender should not matter as much as a demand to install remote access software. The app should prioritize the harm that could happen if the user follows the request.

Signal weighting should consider severity, confidence, and immediacy. Severity asks how bad the harm could be. Confidence asks how strongly the evidence supports the interpretation. Immediacy asks whether the user is being pushed to act now. A critical device access request with high urgency should outrank a low-confidence risky wording pattern.

The app should allow multiple medium-risk signs to combine into a risky result. For example, a marketplace buyer asking to move off-platform, use a shipping agent, send a payment screenshot, and receive a refund may be risk even if no single message says something obviously fraudulent. The engine should notice the pattern across the case.

The app should also allow strong safe-context signals to reduce but not erase risk. If a user opened an email from a known service inside the official app, and no money, password, code, or link request is present, the risk may be lower. But if the same message asks for login through a link, the app should still recommend official verification.

The scoring system should produce both a visible result and an explanation package. The visible result is the user-facing risk card. The explanation package includes trigger details, missing info, safer actions, recovery actions if needed, and optional technical detail for advanced users. This separation lets Verivae stay simple for beginners while still being useful for people who want depth.

### Section 6 \- Explanation Quality Standards

Explanations must be specific. A weak explanation says, "This may be a scam." A strong explanation says, "This message says your account will close today and asks you to log in through a link. That combination is risky because it pushes you to act fast instead of opening your bank app directly." The app should always connect the warning to the user's evidence.

Explanations should use plain words before technical terms. If the app uses a term like phishing, spoofing, malware, remote access, or two-factor auth, it should explain it. For example, "Phishing means a fake message trying to get private info." The user should never need outside knowledge to understand the result.

Explanations should separate facts from advice. The app should say what it found, why it matters, and what to do. This prevents vague warnings. A useful structure is: Found, Meaning, Next step. Found: "The message asks for a login code." Meaning: "Codes can approve account access or payments." Next step: "Do not share the code. Contact the service through its official app."

Explanations should show uncertainty honestly. If sender info is missing, the app should say so. If a screenshot is blurry, the app should say the review is limited. If a link cannot be checked safely, the app should say that. The product should build trust by admitting limits.

Explanations should avoid blame. Instead of saying, "You should not have clicked that," the app should say, "Since the link was opened, the safest next step is to check whether any info was entered or anything was downloaded." This tone matters because users who feel judged may stop using the app.

Explanations should avoid panic language. Even in critical cases, the app should be direct and calm. A critical result can say, "Stop responding and contact your bank through the official number now." It should not say, "You are doomed" or "Your money is gone." Panic makes recovery worse.

### Section 6 \- False Positive Handling

A false positive happens when the app marks something as risky even though it is legitimate. the app should reduce false positives because too many unnecessary warnings will make users ignore the app. At the same time, the app should not become so cautious about false alarms that it misses serious scams. The design should balance safety and trust.

The app should handle possible false positives by asking clarifying questions. If a message claims to be from a company the user actually uses, the app should ask whether the user expected it, whether it appears inside the official app, whether the sender address matches known patterns, and whether the user is being asked for money, codes, passwords, or downloads. The app should never require the user to know technical email headers.

The app should include a "This seems legitimate" feedback option. When the user chooses it, the app should ask why: I verified in the official app, I expected this message, I know the sender, no money or login was requested, or other reason. This feedback can improve future design and helps the user document their verification.

The app should explain why it still recommends caution after a false-positive-like result. For example, "This may be a real delivery update, but the safest way to check is still through the official delivery app or website." That kind of explanation lets the app be useful even when it cannot prove fraud.

False positive handling should also protect paid trust. If a user receives too many warnings and then sees upgrade prompts, the app may feel manipulative. Upgrade prompts should not appear directly after an uncertain warning unless the paid feature is genuinely relevant and the free result remains useful.

### Section 6 \- False Negative Handling

A false negative happens when the app misses a scam or gives a result that feels too safe. This is more dangerous than a false positive because the user may proceed with a harmful action. the app should reduce false negatives by being conservative around high-harm actions. If the user is being asked to send money, share codes, install software, move funds, provide bank details, or keep secrets, the app should lean toward caution even if the message looks professional.

The app should not use a Low concern result when major evidence is missing and the requested action is high stakes. For example, if a screenshot only shows a short message saying "send the code now," the app should not say low concern just because the sender is unknown. It should say unknown or risk depending on context, and it should warn that login codes should not be shared.

The app should support user correction after harm. If a user says, "The app said caution but I got scammed," the app should allow them to update the case. The app should then open recovery guidance and save the user feedback. It should not argue with the user.

False negative handling should include follow-up warnings when a conversation changes. A case that starts as low concern can become risk after new messages. The app should encourage users to add new messages if the other person asks for money, codes, secrecy, or quick action.

### Section 6 \- Alert Timing and Alert Behavior

Alerts should be helpful, not noisy. the app should notify users when there is a meaningful reason to act: a critical risk result, an unresolved recovery step, a weekly check finding, a helper response, a permission issue, or a case that changed after new evidence. The app should not flood users with generic fear messages.

Critical alerts should be immediate and clear. If the user is in a critical-risk flow, the app should show the most important action first. A critical alert should say what to stop and what to do instead. For example, "Do not share the code. Open the official app or contact support directly." The alert should include a button to open the recovery flow or safe verification instructions.

Caution alerts should be softer. They should remind the user to verify before acting. For example, "This case still needs verification before payment." These alerts should be easy to snooze or mark resolved.

Weekly check alerts should summarize rather than alarm. A good alert might say, "Your weekly safety check found two items to review." A bad alert would say, "You may be in danger, open now," unless there is a genuinely critical unresolved case. The app should reserve strong language for strong evidence.

Helper alerts should preserve privacy. A lock-screen alert should not expose sensitive scam details, private relationship details, payment amounts, or embarrassing content. It can say, "Your trusted helper responded to a case" instead of displaying the message content.

### Section 6 \- User Education System

Education should be woven into the app at the moment the user needs it. the app should not rely only on a separate library of articles. Users under pressure will not stop to read long lessons. The app should teach through short explanations attached to real results.

Each scam result should include a small learning moment. If a message asks for a code, the learning moment explains why codes matter. If a buyer overpays, it explains why refunds before clearing are risky. If someone asks for gift cards, it explains why gift card codes are hard to recover. These explanations should be short by default and expandable for more detail.

The app should include a learning library for users who want to browse. The library should be organized by real situations: bank alerts, job offers, marketplace selling, romance requests, family emergency texts, tech support calls, package messages, fake invoices, investment offers, and device warnings. The library should not feel like a school textbook. It should feel like a safety reference.

Education should include examples and safe alternatives. Users learn better when they see the risky message and the safer behavior side by side. For example, the app can show: risky path, "Click the link from the text"; safer path, "Open the bank app yourself." The safer path should always be practical.

Education should adapt to user history without becoming invasive. If a user frequently checks marketplace messages, the app can surface marketplace safety tips. If a user often reviews job offers, it can surface job scam examples. The app should explain personalization and allow it to be turned off.

### Section 6 \- Review Queue and Case Prioritization

As users save more cases, the app should help them know what matters most. A review queue is a list of cases or findings that still need attention. The queue should prioritize by urgency and possible harm, not simply by newest item.

The top of the queue should show critical unresolved cases. These include active money requests, account compromise, device access concerns, blackmail threats, and urgent payment pressure. Next should come risky cases waiting for verification, then caution cases, then low concern or archived cases.

Each case in the queue should show a short reason for its position. For example: "Critical because a login code was shared," "Risk because payment is requested before verification," or "Caution because sender identity is unclear." This keeps the queue understandable.

The queue should allow filtering by status, risk level, category, helper state, and unresolved recovery steps. Filters should be written in plain text: Needs action, Waiting for helper, Money involved, Account involved, Device involved, and Resolved.

The app should prevent stale cases from becoming invisible. If a risky case remains unresolved, the app should remind the user gently. If the user marks it resolved, the app should ask what resolved means: I verified it was safe, I stopped responding, I contacted my bank, I changed my password, I reported it, or I no longer need this case. This creates cleaner records and better guidance.

### Section 6 \- Quality Review Standards

the app should have product quality standards for risk results before the app is considered professional. A result should be accurate enough to help, clear enough for a beginner, honest about uncertainty, and actionable. If a result does not tell the user what to do next, it is incomplete.

Every risk result should pass a clarity test. The user should be able to answer: What is the risk level? What detail caused the warning? What should I avoid doing? What should I do instead? What info is missing, if any? If the result fails any of these, the explanation needs improvement.

Every risk result should pass a calmness test. The result should make the user more capable, not more panicked. Strong warnings are allowed, but the tone must remain steady. The app should never use shame, ridicule, or fear-based upselling.

Every risk result should pass a privacy test. The result should not reveal sensitive message content in alerts, helper previews, exports, or summaries without user control. If the app stores a case, it should make that visible. If it shares a case, it should preview what will be shared.

Every risk result should pass an actionability test. A warning that says "be careful" is not enough. The app should recommend a concrete safer action: use the official app, call a known number, do not share the code, stop responding, change the password, remove the risky app, contact the bank, save evidence, or ask a helper.

### Section 6 \- Advanced Detail Mode

Some users will want more depth than a beginner result provides. the app should include an optional advanced detail mode. This mode should show more technical explanation without making the default experience harder. Advanced detail can include link structure, sender details, message pattern analysis, confidence notes, device permission details, and why the app weighted some signs more than others.

Advanced detail should be optional because most users need simple guidance first. The default result should always be understandable without expanding anything. Advanced detail should never hide the main action. If a case is critical, the app should still show the immediate safety step first.

Advanced detail should also help trusted helpers. A helper may want to see why the app marked something risky. The shared helper view can include a compact version of advanced detail if the user chooses to include it. The app should avoid sharing technical logs or private metadata by default.

### Section 6 \- Accept Rules for the Decision System

The risk decision engine is acceptable when it can identify requested actions, pressure tactics, money movement, account access, device access, and emotional manipulation across emails, messages, screenshots, links, and user descriptions. It must handle incomplete evidence by asking questions or using an Unknown result. It must not present certainty when certainty is not available.

Risk levels are acceptable when users can understand the difference between Low concern, Caution, Risk, Critical risk, and Unknown. Each level must have a clear meaning, a matching tone, and a advised next step. Critical risk must trigger immediate action guidance.

Explanations are acceptable when they identify the evidence, explain why it matters, and recommend a safer action. They must be beginner-friendly, calm, specific, and free of blame. They must explain technical terms when used.

False positive handling is acceptable when users can give feedback, verify through safer channels, and understand why the app advised caution. False negative handling is acceptable when users can update a case after harm, open recovery guidance, and add new evidence as a conversation changes.

Alerts are acceptable when they are timely, privacy-preserving, and tied to meaningful action. Alerts must not expose sensitive details on the lock screen. Critical alerts must be direct. Routine reminders must be gentle.

Education is acceptable when users learn in context, not only through long articles. The app should attach short lessons to real results and provide a browsable library for deeper learning. Education should reinforce safer alternatives.

The review queue is acceptable when unresolved cases are prioritized by harm and urgency. Users must be able to see why a case needs attention, filter cases, resolve cases, and return to recovery steps.

### Section 6 completion note

Section 6 details the design brief with the risk decision engine, risk levels, signal categories, scoring behavior, explanation quality, false positive handling, false negative handling, alert timing, education behavior, review queue behavior, quality standards, advanced detail mode, and accept rules while continuing to reserve the final area for later.

## Design Brief Section 7: Personalization, Family Protection, Vulnerable-User Modes, Subscription Boundaries, Offline Behavior, and Long-Term Safety History

### Detail pass purpose

This design section deepens how Verivae adapts to different users without becoming confusing, invasive, or manipulative. Scam protection is not one-size-fits-all. A young adult selling items online has different risk patterns than an older adult receiving bank calls. A person managing family safety needs different controls than a single user who only wants manual checks. A user who is embarrassed after a scam needs a different tone than a user casually checking a risky link. This section details the design brief around personalization, family and trusted-circle protection, vulnerable-user support, subscription boundaries, offline behavior, long-term safety history, and cross-device continuity.

The content remains about Verivae as an app. Harborwake remains the company name, and Verivae remains the temporary app name. This design brief detail should support product, design, and engineering decisions by clarifying how the app behaves, what the user sees, and which safety boundaries remain in place.

### Section 7 \- Personalization Principles

Personalization should make Verivae more useful without making the user feel watched. The app should learn from user choices, risk patterns, saved cases, selected categories, helper preferences, and accessibility needs, but it should always explain what is being personalized and let the user control it. Personalization should support safety, clarity, and convenience. It should not be used to pressure payment, increase fear, or hide important controls.

The app should allow users to choose a protection profile during onboarding or later in settings. A protection profile is a simple setup choice that adjusts the app experience. Example profiles include General protection, Marketplace seller, Job seeker, Family helper, Older adult support, Student protection, Small business owner, Frequent traveler, and Minimal manual mode. These profiles should not lock the user into a rigid path. They should adjust examples, reminders, education, and quick actions.

A General protection profile should show balanced scam categories and basic manual checks. A Marketplace seller profile should surface overpayment, shipping-agent, fake payment confirmation, and off-platform payment guidance. A Job seeker profile should surface fake recruiter, check deposit, equipment purchase, and task scam guidance. A Family helper profile should make trusted-helper setup more visible. Older adult support should emphasize phone calls, family emergency texts, bank impersonation, remote access, and simple language. Small business owner support should emphasize invoice scams, vendor impersonation, payroll changes, fake customer payments, and account access.

Personalization should also work inside individual cases. If a user says they already sent money, the app should stop focusing only on prevention and move into recovery. If a user says they only want to know whether a message is safe, the app should keep the first result short and offer deeper detail only if requested. If a user repeatedly reviews job offers, the app should make job-scam follow-up questions easier to reach.

The user should be able to reset personalization. A clear setting should say, "Reset app suggestions." Resetting should not delete saved evidence unless the user separately chooses to delete history. This distinction matters because users may want a fresh experience without losing case records.

### Section 7 \- User Profiles and Safety Modes

the app should support safety modes that change tone, depth, and reminder behavior. A safety mode is not a diagnosis and should not label the user. It is a product setting that helps the app present info in a way that works for the user.

Simple mode should use shorter sentences, fewer technical terms, larger actions, and fewer choices per screen. It should be useful for users under stress, users with low technology comfort, older users, or anyone who prefers direct guidance. Simple mode should still include all important safety info. It should simplify presentation, not reduce protection.

Detailed mode should provide more explanation, optional technical details, link info, signal breakdowns, and case history. It should be useful for users who want to understand why the app reached a result. Detailed mode should not replace the main advice with long analysis. The main action should remain at the top.

Quiet mode should reduce non-urgent reminders. It should still show critical risk warnings and user-requested reminders. Quiet mode is important because too many alerts can make users uninstall the app. A user who chooses quiet mode should not lose manual checking, recovery guidance, or case saving.

Strong protection mode should increase reminders, weekly check visibility, helper prompts, and unresolved-case follow-up. This mode should be useful for users who are actively worried, supporting a vulnerable family member, recovering from a scam, or dealing with repeated risky contacts. Strong protection mode should be transparent. The app should explain what extra reminders will happen.

Recovery mode should appear after a user reports that harm may have already occurred. This mode should prioritize recovery checklists, evidence, account protection, device review, bank or platform contact guidance, and helper support. It should reduce unrelated education until the urgent situation is handled.

### Section 7 \- Vulnerable-User Support

the app should be designed for users who may be more vulnerable to scams because of stress, age, isolation, disability, language difficulty, financial pressure, grief, cognitive load, lack of technical experience, or repeated targeting. The app should never label the user as vulnerable in a way that feels insulting. It should provide optional support features and respectful language.

The app should support low-pressure explanations. A user who is being manipulated may resist a harsh warning because they trust the person contacting them. Instead of saying, "This person is lying," the app can say, "This situation has several risk signs that are commonly used to pressure people into sending money. Verify outside the conversation before continuing." This helps the user pause without feeling attacked.

For users who may be isolated, trusted-helper prompts should be gentle and visible. The app can say, "Would you like a trusted person to review this with you?" It should not say, "You cannot handle this alone." The product should support independence while making help easier.

For users who may struggle with reading dense text, the app should provide short result summaries, optional audio readout where supported, high-contrast visuals, clear icons, and action-first layouts. A critical result should be understandable at a glance. The app should avoid tiny text, long paragraphs on urgent screens, and too many secondary options.

For users facing threats, shame, romance pressure, or blackmail, the app should provide privacy-sensitive support. Alerts should not reveal sensitive details. Helper sharing should require confirmation. Evidence saving should be clear. The app should recommend trusted human support when appropriate and should avoid making unrealistic promises.

For users facing financial pressure, the app should avoid judgment around desperation. Job scams, loan scams, investment scams, and refund scams often work because the user needs money. The app should explain the risk pattern without shaming the user's need. A result might say, "This offer is risky because it asks you to pay before you can earn. Legitimate work usually does not require paying to unlock wages."

### Section 7 \- Family and Trusted-Circle Protection

Family and trusted-circle protection should let users support one another without turning Verivae into surveillance. A trusted circle is a small group of people the user chooses for scam review support. It may include a parent, adult child, partner, sibling, friend, caregiver, or other trusted person. The app should treat trusted-circle support as consent-based collaboration.

The primary user should control what is shared. They should be able to share one case, share only a summary, share a redacted screenshot, share recovery progress, or enable urgent-risk sharing. The app should preview what each share option means. The default should be case-by-case sharing, not automatic full access.

Trusted-circle roles should be clear. A Review helper can comment on selected cases. An Emergency helper can receive alerts for critical-risk cases if the user enables it. A Family organizer can help manage a family protection plan if the user is part of a paid family tier. A View-only helper can see selected summaries but cannot comment. These roles should be explained in plain text.

The app should support helper invitations with safety checks. The invitation should say who is inviting the helper, what access is being requested, and how the helper can accept or decline. If a user receives a helper invite from someone they do not recognize, the app should tell them not to accept. Scam protection apps can themselves be impersonated, so the invite flow must be careful.

Trusted-circle alerts should be privacy-preserving. A helper should see that a case needs review, but sensitive content should remain hidden until the primary user chooses to share it. Lock-screen alerts should not include message text, payment amounts, romance details, blackmail details, or account names.

The app should handle family disagreement. If one helper says risky and another says safe, the app should show the disagreement and return to evidence and verification steps. It should not turn helper opinions into a popularity vote. The app should still prioritize clear scam signals and official verification.

Family protection should include boundaries for adults. The app should not let one adult secretly monitor another adult's private messages or accounts. Adult users should give explicit consent. If the app ever includes child or teen protection, that should be designed separately with age-appropriate privacy and legal requirements. The current design brief should focus on consent-based protection for general users unless future requirements say otherwise.

### Section 7 \- Caregiver and Older Adult Support

Caregiver support should be optional and respectful. Some older adults may want help reviewing risky calls, texts, emails, and payment requests. Others may not want family members involved. the app should provide a structure where support can be accepted, limited, paused, or removed.

The older adult support experience should emphasize phone scams, bank impersonation, fake family emergencies, tech support scams, Medicare-like or benefit-like impersonation patterns without making legal claims, prize scams, romance scams, delivery scams, and remote access pressure. The language should be calm and direct. The app should avoid infantilizing the user.

Caregiver view should prioritize active risks and unresolved actions. A caregiver should not need to read every case. They should see what needs review, what changed, what the app recommends, and whether the primary user has asked for help. The app should show the minimum useful info by default.

The primary user should see a caregiver activity log. This log should show when a helper viewed a case, commented, changed a status if allowed, or received an alert. Transparency helps prevent the support relationship from feeling hidden or controlling.

The app should allow temporary caregiver access. For example, a user recovering from a scam may want stronger support for a few weeks. The app should let them set a temporary sharing window. When the window ends, the app should ask whether to continue, reduce, or stop helper access.

### Section 7 \- Subscription and Free-Tier Boundaries

Because the user wants to profit from the app while keeping trust, the app needs careful subscription boundaries. The app can have paid features, but the free version must still provide meaningful protection. A scam safety app should not feel like it withholds basic safety to pressure payment.

The free tier should include manual checks, basic risk results, basic explanation, basic education, limited case saving, basic recovery guidance, and basic settings. Users should be able to paste a risky message or describe a situation and receive a useful answer without paying. This is the foundation of trust and public usefulness.
