Paid individual features can include detailed saved case history, deeper explanation mode, enhanced weekly checks, more device-check depth where supported, larger evidence exports, more helper sharing, advanced personalization, priority review features if human review ever exists, and richer recovery tracking. Paid features should add depth and convenience rather than making free safety useless.

A paid family tier can include multiple trusted helpers, family-circle dashboards, more shared case history, stronger urgent alerts, caregiver workflows, and household safety summaries. The app should explain exactly what a family tier includes. It should not imply that the user's family is unsafe unless they pay.

Subscription prompts should be contextual and calm. A good prompt says, "Advanced weekly summaries are included in the paid plan. Your current free result is still available." A bad prompt says, "Upgrade now before you lose money." Fear-based upselling should be explicitly prohibited in the design brief.

The app should have a transparent subscription screen. It should show the current plan, included features, renewal status where applicable, cancellation path, billing platform, and what happens if the plan expires. If a feature is paid, the app should label it before the user invests time setting it up.

### Section 7 \- Offline and Low-Connectivity Behavior

the app should work gracefully when the user has weak internet, no internet, airplane mode, or limited service. Scam situations often happen while a user is away from home, traveling, shopping, or under pressure. The app should not become useless when connection is poor.

Offline mode should support locally available guidance. The app should be able to show saved education, basic scam warning signs, emergency stop-now guidance, saved cases, and locally stored recovery checklists. It may not be able to perform full link review, cloud-based analysis, email import, helper sharing, or updated device checks while offline. The app should explain these limits plainly.

If the user submits a scam check offline, the app should offer a limited offline review if supported. A limited review can inspect the user's typed description against built-in safety rules such as do not share codes, do not send gift cards, do not move money to a safe account, do not install remote access for a stranger, and verify through official channels. The result should clearly say that a fuller review will run when connection returns.

When the connection returns, the app should ask before uploading sensitive content if the user has not already agreed to cloud review. A queued review should show status: Waiting for connection, Ready to review, Review complete, or Failed. The user should be able to delete a queued item before it is sent.

Helper sharing should queue carefully. If a user tries to share a case while offline, the app should say it has not been sent yet. It should not pretend the helper received it. When connection returns, the app should either send it with confirmation based on the user's settings or ask the user to confirm.

### Section 7 \- Cross-Device and Account Continuity

Some users will use Verivae on more than one device. Cross-device continuity should allow saved cases, settings, helper relationships, subscription status, and recovery progress to follow the user where appropriate. It should also avoid exposing sensitive data on a device the user does not trust.

The app should explain account sync. Sync means keeping selected info the same across devices. The user should be able to choose whether case history syncs, whether attachments sync, whether helper settings sync, and whether device-check history stays local. Sensitive attachments should require clear storage choices.

If the user signs in on a new device, the app should protect them from accidental exposure. It can ask whether this is a personal device, shared device, or temporary device. On shared or temporary devices, the app should recommend limited sync, no sensitive attachments, and automatic sign-out reminders.

Cross-device recovery should be useful after phone loss or compromise. If a user thinks one device may be unsafe, the app should help them continue recovery on another device while warning that device-local checks from the unsafe device may not be available. It should separate account-level case history from device-local findings.

The app should show active sessions where supported. A session means a device or browser where the user is signed in. Users should be able to sign out of other sessions, especially after account compromise. The app should explain this in simple language.

### Section 7 \- Long-Term Safety History

Long-term safety history should help users and helpers understand patterns over time without creating a creepy surveillance feeling. The app should show saved cases, categories, outcomes, repeated senders, repeated scam types, unresolved actions, and improvement trends. It should not shame the user for having many cases.

The history screen should be organized by usefulness. The user should be able to view All cases, Open cases, Resolved cases, Money involved, Account involved, Device involved, Helper reviewed, and Education learned. Each case should show risk level, category, status, date entered by the app or user where available, and the next action if unresolved. If dates are uncertain, the app should avoid inventing precision.

The app should provide pattern summaries. A pattern summary could say, "Most of your recent checks involved marketplace payments," or "You have two unresolved account-safety cases." These summaries should be factual and calm. They should not say, "You are bad at spotting scams." The goal is awareness.

Long-term history should support privacy controls. The user should be able to hide sensitive cases, lock the app, delete cases, export selected history, and choose whether helpers can see history summaries. Sensitive categories such as romance, blackmail, family conflict, or financial hardship should be especially protected.

The app should allow users to mark outcomes. Outcomes include Verified safe, Stopped responding, Reported, Money sent, Account secured, Device cleaned, Helper reviewed, Lost access, No longer relevant, or Unsure. Outcomes help future guidance and make history more meaningful.

### Section 7 \- Personal Safety Insights

Personal safety insights should be simple, useful observations from the user's own cases. They should help users recognize repeated situations and improve habits. Insights should not feel like a scorecard judging the user.

Examples of useful insights include: "You often check links from delivery messages," "You have several cases where the other person asked for secrecy," "Most risky cases involved payment before verification," or "You completed three recovery steps this week." These insights should be written in a neutral tone.

The app should avoid manipulative insight wording. It should not say, "You are at risk because you keep making mistakes." It should say, "Several recent cases involved urgent payment requests. Consider verifying payment requests through official channels before acting." The difference is important.

Insights should include a practical next step. If the pattern is marketplace risk, the next step may be reading marketplace examples or turning on marketplace-specific reminders. If the pattern is job scams, the next step may be enabling job-offer checks. If the pattern is device concerns, the next step may be weekly checks.

Users should be able to turn insights off. Some users may not want pattern summaries. Turning insights off should not delete case history unless the user separately deletes it.

### Section 7 \- Safety Settings for Personalization

Personalization settings should be grouped in a way that users understand. A Personalization area can include Protection profile, Safety mode, Scam categories to emphasize, Learning preferences, Trusted-circle prompts, Weekly insight summaries, Data used for personalization, and Reset suggestions.

The app should show what data personalization uses. For example: saved case categories, completed checks, selected protection profile, helper settings, and education topics. It should also show what it does not use if relevant, such as private message contents for unrelated advertising. The design brief should make clear that personalization should serve safety, not unrelated marketing.

The user should be able to turn off category emphasis. If the app keeps surfacing job scam guidance but the user no longer needs it, they should be able to reduce job-related suggestions. If they begin selling online, they should be able to add marketplace emphasis.

Personalization should not weaken critical protection. Even if a user says they are not interested in device safety, the app should still warn them if they say they installed a remote access app for a stranger. Preferences can shape routine guidance, but critical safety rules should still appear when relevant.

### Section 7 \- Accept Rules for Personalization and Family Protection

Personalization is acceptable when the user can understand why the app is showing certain examples, reminders, or suggestions. The user must be able to change the protection profile, switch safety modes, turn off insights, and reset suggestions. Personalization must improve relevance without hiding core safety guidance.

Safety modes are acceptable when Simple mode remains protective, Detailed mode remains clear, Quiet mode still shows critical warnings, Strong protection mode explains extra reminders, and Recovery mode prioritizes urgent recovery steps. No mode should make the app unsafe or unusable.

Vulnerable-user support is acceptable when the app uses respectful language, avoids labels that shame the user, provides easier helper access, supports simple explanations, and protects sensitive alerts. The app should assist without taking away user control.

Trusted-circle protection is acceptable when sharing is consent-based, roles are clear, helper invitations are understandable, sensitive info is hidden by default, helper activity is visible to the primary user, and adult users are not secretly monitored.

Caregiver support is acceptable when the primary user can accept, limit, pause, or remove support. Caregiver views should focus on active risks and requested help, not broad private surveillance. Temporary access should be supported for recovery situations.

Subscription boundaries are acceptable when the free tier remains useful for basic scam safety and paid tiers add depth, convenience, history, family tools, or enhanced checks. Upgrade prompts must be calm, transparent, and non-exploitative.

Offline behavior is acceptable when the app offers local stop-now guidance, saved education, saved cases, and limited review where possible. The app must clearly explain which features require internet and whether queued sensitive content will be uploaded later.

Cross-device continuity is acceptable when users understand sync, can limit sensitive syncing, can manage sessions where supported, and can use another device for recovery without exposing private case data unnecessarily.

Long-term safety history is acceptable when users can search, filter, protect, export, and delete case records. Pattern summaries must be factual, calm, optional, and tied to practical next steps.

### Section 7 completion note

Section 7 details the design brief with personalization principles, user profiles, safety modes, vulnerable-user support, family and trusted-circle protection, caregiver support, subscription boundaries, offline behavior, cross-device continuity, long-term safety history, personal safety insights, personalization settings, and accept rules while continuing to reserve the final area for later.

## Design Brief Section 8: Reporting Packages, Human Review Boundaries, Support Escalation, Abuse Prevention, Claim Limits, Reliability, and Trust Safeguards

### Detail pass purpose

This design section deepens the parts of Verivae that help the app behave professionally when a user needs to report a scam, ask for more help, challenge or clarify a result, recover from uncertainty, or understand what the app can and cannot promise. A scam safety app must be more than a scanner. It must help users create useful records, explain results honestly, avoid overclaiming, prevent misuse, and stay reliable when the user is stressed. The section also clarifies how reporting, help requests, result challenges, and uncertainty recovery connect into one coherent app experience. Harborwake remains the company name, and Verivae remains the temporary app name.

This detail also reinforces trust. Users may bring private messages, financial fear, identity concerns, romance pressure, blackmail threats, family worries, job hopes, and device concerns into Verivae. The app must respond with careful boundaries. It should help without pretending to be a bank, lawyer, police officer, therapist, antivirus company, or guaranteed fraud recovery service. The product should be useful because it is clear, honest, and action-oriented.

### Section 8 \- Reporting Package System

the app should include a reporting package system. A reporting package is a user-controlled summary of a scam case that can be copied, exported, or shared with a bank, payment app, marketplace, email provider, social platform, trusted helper, employer, school, or support team. The app should not automatically send reports without the user's confirmation. The purpose of a reporting package is to make the user's evidence easier to understand and easier to act on.

The reporting package should have a clear structure. It should include the case title, risk category, user summary, submitted messages or screenshots if selected, sender info if available, links if available, payment method if money was involved, amount if the user entered one, user actions already taken, app risk summary, recovery steps completed, unresolved steps, and helper comments if the user chooses to include them. The app should separate original evidence from app interpretation. Original evidence is what the user received or entered. App interpretation is the app's explanation of risk signs.

The reporting package should offer export levels. Summary only should include the case title, risk category, plain description, and advised next step. Summary plus evidence should include selected messages, screenshots, links, and sender details. Recovery package should include the recovery checklist and completed actions. Helper package should include helper comments and status. Full package should include everything the user selects. The app should preview each export before it is created.

The app should explain sensitive content before export. If a package includes private messages, payment amounts, identity info, phone numbers, email addresses, usernames, romance content, blackmail threats, personal photos, or family details, the app should warn the user and offer redaction. Redaction means hiding private details before sharing. The app should make redaction a normal privacy tool, not something only advanced users understand.

Reporting packages should be formatted for readability. A bank representative, platform support agent, trusted helper, or user under stress should be able to scan the package quickly. The top should contain a short summary. Details should be grouped by type. Long evidence should be collapsible in the app and organized in export. The package should avoid exaggerated claims such as "proven fraud" unless there is a direct user-entered confirmation. Safer wording is "risky scam pattern identified" or "the app found strong warning signs."

### Section 8 \- Report Destination Guidance

the app should help users understand where a case may need to be reported. Different scams require different reporting paths. A payment scam may need a bank or payment app. A fake marketplace seller may need the marketplace platform. A fake email may need an email provider. An account takeover may need the account service. A threatening message may need the platform and trusted human support. The app should organize these paths without pretending to guarantee outcomes.

The app should ask what happened before suggesting a report destination. Did the user send money? Did they enter a password? Did they share a code? Did they install an app? Did they receive threats? Was a marketplace listing involved? Was a job offer involved? Was a social media account involved? Was a phone number or email sender involved? These answers determine the most useful reporting path.

Reporting guidance should set expectations. The app can say that reporting creates a record, may help an institution investigate, and may help the user explain what happened. It should also say that reporting does not guarantee refunds, account recovery, or enforcement. This protects user trust by avoiding false hope.

The app should include destination-specific preparation. For a bank or card issuer, the app should help the user collect payment timing, amount, payment method, recipient details, messages, and whether credentials were shared. For a marketplace, it should collect listing details, seller or buyer username, payment request, shipping or pickup details, and screenshots. For an email provider, it should collect sender address, subject, link, attachment info, and message content. For a social platform, it should collect username, profile link if available, message screenshots, payment pressure, and account compromise signs.

The app should avoid giving legal instructions as if it were a legal authority. It can help organize evidence and suggest that users contact appropriate official or platform channels. It should not tell users that a specific agency will recover money or that a specific legal result will happen.

### Section 8 \- Human Review Boundaries

A future version of the app may include human review, expert review, community review, or support review. The design brief should define boundaries now so that future review features do not compromise privacy or create false authority. Human review means a person may look at selected case info to provide additional feedback. It should always require clear user consent.

If human review exists, the app should show what will be reviewed before submission. The user should choose whether to include message text, screenshots, links, payment details, sender details, account names, helper comments, and recovery notes. The default should minimize sensitive content while still providing enough context. The app should warn that removing too much context may reduce review quality.

Human review should not be presented as guaranteed fraud judgment. A reviewer can provide guidance, point out risk signs, suggest verification steps, and help organize recovery. They should not be framed as a judge, law enforcement agent, bank representative, or guaranteed recovery specialist unless the product truly has a verified partnership and clear legal authority. The default product language should be conservative.

Human review should have response categories that are easy to understand: Likely risky, Needs verification, Not enough info, No major scam signs found, Recovery advised, and Escalate to official support. These categories should be paired with written explanation. A human review result should still include uncertainty where appropriate.

Human review should have privacy controls. Users should be able to withdraw a request if it has not been reviewed, delete attached evidence where supported, and see whether the case has been viewed. The app should explain retention rules in plain text.

### Section 8 \- Support Escalation Paths

Support escalation means guiding the user from basic app guidance to a stronger help path when the situation is too serious, too unclear, or too emotionally intense for a normal scam result. the app should support escalation without making the user feel punished for needing help.

Escalation should be triggered by high-harm situations. Examples include active money movement, shared bank codes, remote access installation, suspected account takeover, blackmail threats, repeated harassment, large financial loss, ID doc exposure, or a user saying they feel unsafe. The app should present practical next steps at the top.

The first escalation path should be trusted helper support. The app can ask whether the user wants to share the case with someone they trust. The second path should be official verification or support, such as a bank, payment platform, marketplace, account provider, or device support channel. The third path should be emergency or urgent personal safety guidance when the user indicates immediate danger. The app should not overuse emergency language for ordinary scam checks.

Escalation screens should be short. In a serious situation, the user should see what to stop, who to contact, and what evidence to preserve. Longer explanations can be available below. For example, if a user shared a bank code during a call, the top actions could be: stop responding, contact the bank through official contact info, change account security where applicable, preserve the message or call details, and start the recovery checklist.

The app should include a "not ready" path. Some users may not be emotionally ready to act immediately. The app can let them save the case, set a reminder, or share with a helper. However, for critical risks, the app should still keep the urgent advised action visible.

### Section 8 \- Abuse Prevention and Misuse Resistance

the app should include abuse prevention because tools that review messages, links, and evidence can be misused. Someone might try to use the app to monitor another adult without consent, harass someone by labeling legitimate messages as scams, collect private evidence from a partner, or pressure a vulnerable person. The app should be designed to reduce these risks.

The app should not allow secret monitoring of another adult's messages or accounts. Consent should be explicit. Trusted-helper and family features should show who has access, what they can see, and how to remove them. The primary user should be able to review helper activity.

The app should discourage harassment. A user should not be encouraged to send aggressive accusations to someone based only on an app result. Safe reply templates should focus on pausing, verifying, declining, or stopping communication. They should not say "I know you are a criminal" or threaten retaliation. This protects users from escalation and keeps the product responsible.

The app should limit harmful exports. If a user exports evidence that contains private photos, ID docs, romance messages, or blackmail content, the app should provide a clear warning and redaction options. It should not make sensitive bulk sharing too easy by accident.

The app should protect helper invitations from impersonation. If a helper invite is sent, the recipient should see who invited them and what role is requested. If the invite seems unexpected, the app should advise verifying with the person through a separate known channel. This is important because scammers can imitate safety tools.

### Section 8 \- Claim Limits and Product Honesty

the app should have strict claim limits. Claim limits are boundaries around what the app says it can do. The app should not promise that it detects every scam, prevents all fraud, guarantees recovery, guarantees virus removal, guarantees account safety, or replaces official support. Overclaiming would harm users and weaken trust.

The app can honestly claim that it reviews risky messages, links, emails, screenshots, calls summaries, device signals where supported, and user-described situations. It can claim that it explains warning signs, suggests safer verification paths, helps organize evidence, supports recovery checklists, and helps users involve trusted helpers. It can also claim that some features depend on device permissions, platform support, internet access, and user-provided evidence.

Each high-stakes result should include uncertainty language when needed. If the app cannot verify sender identity, it should say so. If it cannot fully inspect a link or file, it should say so. If a device scan is limited by OS rules, it should say so. If recovery outcomes depend on a bank or platform, it should say so. This language should be plain and visible, not hidden in legal text.

The app should avoid pretending to be official support. It should not make users think they are chatting with their bank, the police, a government office, or a payment platform. It can help prepare what to say to those entities. It can guide users to official routes. It should not impersonate them.

### Section 8 \- Reliability and Service Failure Behavior

Reliability matters because users may open Verivae during a crisis. The app should behave clearly when analysis fails, a connection times out, an upload fails, the user is offline, a permission is missing, or a result cannot be generated. Failure should not look like safety.

If scam analysis fails, the app should say, "Review could not be completed," and give immediate safety basics: do not send money, do not share codes, do not enter passwords through unknown links, do not install apps at a stranger's request, and verify through official channels. The user should be able to retry, save the case, or use a limited manual checklist.

If a screenshot cannot be read, the app should say what went wrong. It can ask for a clearer screenshot, let the user type the message, or let the user crop the important part. It should not produce a confident result from unreadable evidence.

If a link check fails, the app should not say the link is safe. It should say that the link could not be checked and recommend opening the official app or typing the official website manually instead of using the risky link. If the user already clicked, it should offer post-click recovery questions.

If helper sharing fails, the app should show that the helper did not receive the case. It should offer retry, copy summary, or save draft. If export fails, the app should not delete the case. If device check fails, it should explain whether the issue was permission, OS limits, connection, or unknown failure.

### Section 8 \- System Status and User-Facing Confidence

the app should make system status understandable. Users should know whether a feature is linked, limited, offline, queued, reviewing, complete, or failed. Status should be visible at the point of action, not hidden in settings.

Analysis status labels should include Ready to review, Reviewing, Needs more info, Limited review, Review complete, Review failed, Saved, Shared, Waiting for helper, Helper responded, Recovery active, and Resolved. Each label should have a short explanation. For example, Limited review can mean the app reviewed what was available but could not inspect a missing sender, unreadable screenshot, inaccessible file, or dislinked service.

The app should show confidence without confusing users. Confidence should not be a fake precision percentage. A phrase such as Strong evidence, Some warning signs, Not enough info, or Limited by missing details is easier to understand. If the app uses an advanced confidence score internally, the beginner interface should translate it into plain text.

Confidence should not weaken urgent guidance. If the app has limited confidence but the user is being asked to share a login code, the app should still warn against sharing codes. Certain safety rules can be firm even when the full scam category is unknown.

### Section 8 \- Audit Trail for User Actions

An audit trail is a record of important actions inside a case. the app should use audit trails for user clarity, not surveillance. A case audit trail can help the user remember what happened, what they shared, what they exported, who reviewed it, and which recovery steps were completed.

The audit trail should include case created, evidence added, result generated, helper invited, case shared, helper viewed if available, helper commented, export created, recovery step completed, status changed, case archived, and case deleted. The user should be able to view this trail in simple language.

Audit trails should protect privacy. They should not expose full sensitive message content in the trail itself. The trail can say "Screenshot added" rather than displaying the screenshot. It can say "Case shared with helper" and show the helper name or label. It should show enough to support trust and accountability.

For caregiver or family support, the primary user should be able to see helper activity. If a helper marks a case risky, changes a status, or adds a note, that action should be visible. This protects the user's control and reduces hidden influence.

### Section 8 \- In-App Support and Help Center Behavior

the app should include in-app support that helps users understand features and resolve product problems. This support is different from scam recovery. Product support helps with account access, subscription questions, permissions, helper setup, export problems, app errors, and feature confusion.

The help center should be organized by user task. Useful sections include Check a risky message, Understand a result, Add a trusted helper, Run a device check, Use weekly check, Save or delete a case, Export evidence, Manage privacy, Manage subscription, Fix permissions, and Recover after clicking or paying. The help center should be searchable in plain text.

Support answers should be short first, then expandable. A stressed user should not have to read a long article to find the button they need. Each help answer should include a direct action and a plain explanation. Where the app cannot do something, it should say so clearly.

The app should separate product support from emergency help. A product support screen should not become the primary route for immediate threats, active financial harm, or self-safety concerns. Those situations should route to the appropriate escalation guidance inside the app.

### Section 8 \- Trust Safeguards for Paid Features

Paid features require special trust safeguards because the app operates in a fear-sensitive category. Users may be worried about losing money or protecting loved ones. the app must never use that fear to coerce payment.

Paid prompts should explain the benefit, not exploit the fear. A prompt can say, "Family case history is included in the family plan." It should not say, "Your family may be scammed unless you upgrade." A prompt can say, "Advanced weekly reports add more detail." It should not make the free result look incomplete when the free result already answered the user's basic safety question.

The app should prevent paywalls from blocking urgent safety steps. If a user is in a critical-risk flow, the app should not interrupt with an upgrade prompt before showing stop-now and recovery guidance. Paid features can appear after the urgent guidance if relevant, but they should not block the essential safety path.

Subscription status should be transparent. Users should know what plan they have, what features are included, what changes if they cancel, and where billing is managed. The app should not hide cancellation instructions or use confusing wording around renewals.

### Section 8 \- Accept Rules for Trust and Reporting Systems

The reporting package system is acceptable when users can create readable case summaries, choose what evidence to include, preview sensitive content, redact private info, separate original evidence from app interpretation, and export or copy the package without losing the original case.

Report destination guidance is acceptable when the app asks what happened, recommends relevant reporting paths, prepares destination-specific info, and sets honest expectations. It must not promise refunds, enforcement, account recovery, or legal outcomes.

Human review boundaries are acceptable when the user controls what is shared, review categories are understandable, privacy is protected, uncertainty is preserved, and human review is not presented as guaranteed authority.

Support escalation is acceptable when critical cases surface immediate action, trusted helper support, official verification guidance, and recovery flows. Escalation must stay calm, practical, and proportionate to the risk.

Abuse prevention is acceptable when the app resists secret monitoring, warns before sensitive exports, protects helper invitations, discourages harassment, and keeps adult consent central to family and trusted-circle features.

Claim limits are acceptable when Verivae avoids guarantees, avoids impersonating official support, explains platform and permission limits, and uses plain uncertainty language when evidence is incomplete.

Reliability behavior is acceptable when failures are visible, limited reviews are labeled, failed analysis does not look safe, retries and fallbacks are available, and urgent safety basics remain accessible during outages or errors.

System status is acceptable when users can understand whether a case is reviewing, limited, failed, saved, shared, waiting, resolved, or in recovery. Confidence language must be understandable and should not rely on fake precision.

Audit trails are acceptable when users can see major case actions, helper activity is transparent, sensitive content is not exposed unnecessarily, and the audit trail supports user control rather than hidden surveillance.

Paid trust safeguards are acceptable when upgrade prompts are calm, paid features add depth or convenience, urgent safety guidance is never blocked by payment, and subscription status is easy to understand.

### Section 8 completion note

Section 8 details the design brief with reporting packages, report destination guidance, human review boundaries, support escalation paths, abuse prevention, claim limits, reliability behavior, system status, confidence language, audit trails, in-app support behavior, paid feature trust safeguards, and accept rules while continuing to reserve the final area for later.

## Design Brief Section 9: Data Handling, Permission Transparency, Consent Records, Scam Library Maintenance, Localization, Accessibility Under Stress, and Content Quality Controls

### Detail pass purpose

This design section deepens the privacy, consent, language, accessibility, and content-management behavior of Verivae. The app handles sensitive material: messages, screenshots, payment worries, account concerns, device findings, family-helper relationships, recovery notes, and scam evidence. Because of that, privacy and clarity cannot be treated as legal afterthoughts. They must be visible product features inside the app. This section describes how the app should help users understand data use, manage permissions, review consent, maintain scam knowledge, work across languages, remain accessible under stress, and keep safety content clear and consistent.

This detail remains focused on the app itself. Harborwake remains the company name. Verivae remains the temporary app name. This section should be read as deeper design brief material for product, design, and engineering work: what the app should support, how the user experience should behave, and where safety boundaries need to remain clear.

### Section 9 \- Privacy Center Behavior

the app should include a Privacy Center that gives users one understandable place to see what the app knows, what it stores, what it shares, and what it can access. The Privacy Center should not be a dense legal page. It should be a practical control surface written for normal users. A user should be able to open it and quickly answer: What have I saved? What accounts or services are linked? What helpers can see? What device permissions are active? What can I delete? What will happen if I turn something off?

The Privacy Center should organize controls by user concern rather than technical category. Useful sections include Saved cases, Screenshots and attachments, Linked services, Device permissions, Trusted helpers, Weekly checks, Personalization, Exports and reports, Subscription data, and Delete my data. Each section should explain the purpose in plain text.

Saved cases should show whether the app stores case text, screenshots, links, notes, helper comments, risk results, recovery progress, and audit trail events. The user should be able to delete one case, delete selected evidence inside a case, archive a case, or clear all case history. The app should explain the difference between deleting a case and turning off future saving.

Linked services should show each service by name or category. For example: email review, message sharing, browser sharing, device check, alert permission, contacts for trusted helper invites, and cloud sync if available. Each connection should have a status such as Off, Linked, Limited, Permission missing, Needs review, or Dislinked. The user should not need to search through phone settings to understand what Verivae believes is linked.

The Privacy Center should include a plain data summary. Instead of saying only "Data processed according to policy," the app should say things like: "You have 12 saved cases," "Two helpers can see selected case summaries," "Weekly check is on," "Screenshots are saved only when you add them," or "Email review is manual only." These summaries make privacy tangible.

### Section 9 \- Data Handling and Storage Behavior

the app should distinguish between temporary review data, saved case data, exported report data, helper-shared data, device-local data, and account-level synced data. These categories matter because users need different controls for each one. The app should explain them simply.

Temporary review data is info the user provides for a single scam check that may not be saved unless the user chooses to save the result. The app should tell the user whether a manual check will be saved automatically or discarded after review. A privacy-friendly default is to let the user decide whether to save after seeing the result.

Saved case data is info stored so the user can return later. It may include message text, screenshots, links, call summaries, evidence notes, risk results, helper comments, recovery progress, report packages, and action history. Saved case data should be visible and manageable. The user should not have to wonder where their scam history went.

Exported report data is info the user creates to share outside the app. The app should treat exported data as leaving the app's normal privacy boundary. Before export, the app should remind the user that the exported file or copied text may be visible to whoever receives it. The app should encourage redaction of sensitive content.

Helper-shared data is info sent to a trusted helper. The app should show exactly what was shared, when it was shared, and whether the helper responded. The user should be able to stop future sharing. If the app cannot remove something already seen by a helper, it should explain that plainly.

Device-local data is info that stays on one device, such as some device check results, local settings, locally cached education, or offline queued reviews. Account-level synced data is info available across the user's devices when sync is enabled. The app should let users choose what syncs where possible, especially screenshots, attachments, sensitive case categories, and helper comments.

### Section 9 \- Permission Transparency

Permissions should be introduced only when the user reaches a feature that needs them. the app should not ask for many permissions immediately during onboarding. A beginner-friendly product should ask for permission at the moment it makes sense. For example, alert permission should be requested when the user turns on weekly checks or reminders. Contacts permission should be requested when the user wants to invite a trusted helper from contacts. Photo or file access should be requested when the user wants to add a screenshot or attachment.

Every permission request should answer four questions: what the permission allows, why the feature needs it, what happens if the user declines, and how to change it later. A good permission explanation might say, "Allow photo access so you can attach scam screenshots to a case. If you decline, you can still paste text manually." This reduces fear and confusion.

The app should avoid permission pressure. It should not say that protection is impossible unless a broad permission is granted when manual alternatives exist. If a permission improves convenience but is not required for core safety, the app should say so. For example, message sharing may make review easier, but the user can still paste text.

Permission status should be visible in settings and feature screens. If device check is limited because file access or system permission is off, the app should say exactly that. If weekly check cannot run because alerts are off, the app should explain the missing permission. If helper invites cannot use contacts, the app should offer manual email or phone entry where appropriate.

Permissions should have graceful fallback paths. Declining a permission should not punish the user. It should route them to manual entry, screenshot upload, copy-and-paste, guided summaries, or limited review. The app should preserve the user's sense of control.

### Section 9 \- Consent Records and User Control

Consent records are user-visible records of important permissions, sharing choices, and data decisions. the app should use consent records to increase transparency. Users should be able to see when they linked a service, enabled weekly checks, added a helper, shared a case, enabled sync, or agreed to save screenshots.

Consent records should be simple. They should not look like legal contracts. A record can say: "You turned on weekly checks," "You shared Case 14 with your helper," "You allowed selected screenshots to be saved," or "You linked email review in manual mode." Each record should include the feature, the choice, and a way to change or revoke the setting where possible.

The app should separate consent for different actions. Agreeing to save a case should not automatically mean agreeing to share it with helpers. Connecting a helper should not automatically mean sharing all future cases. Turning on weekly checks should not automatically mean sharing weekly summaries with a helper. Each meaningful privacy action should be its own choice.

Revocation should be visible. Revocation means taking back a permission or stopping future access. The app should use plain text such as Turn off, Stop sharing, Remove helper, Disconnect service, Delete case, Delete screenshots, or Stop syncing. If revocation cannot undo something already exported or already seen, the app should explain that clearly.

Consent records should support family and caregiver scenarios. If a caregiver or helper has access to a case, the primary user should see that. If temporary access expires, the app should record that. If a helper role changes, the app should show what changed. This protects trust between people.

### Section 9 \- Data Deletion and Retention Experience

the app should make deletion understandable. Users may want to delete a single embarrassing case, remove a screenshot, clear old scam history, disconnect a helper, or delete their entire account. The app should give clear choices and explain consequences.

Deleting a single case should remove the saved case from the user's case history. If the case had exports, the app should explain that files or copied summaries already shared outside the app cannot be pulled back by deleting the app case. If the case had helper comments, the app should explain whether those comments are removed from the user's view, helper view, or both depending on the product's rules.

Deleting evidence inside a case should allow the user to keep the case summary while removing sensitive attachments or message text. This is useful when a user wants to preserve recovery progress but no longer wants screenshots stored. The app should show what remains after evidence deletion.

Clearing history should be different from deleting the account. Clearing history removes saved cases and related case records. Deleting the account removes account-level info where supported. The app should avoid combining these into one confusing action. Users should be able to understand which action fits their goal.

Retention controls should be written plainly. Retention means how long the app keeps info. The app can offer options such as keep until I delete, auto-delete resolved cases after a chosen period, keep only summaries after a chosen period, or ask before deleting. If auto-delete is enabled, the app should warn before deleting important unresolved recovery cases.

### Section 9 \- Scam Library Maintenance Experience

The scam library is the app's organized knowledge of scam patterns, examples, warning signs, explanations, and safer actions. the app should treat this library as living product content. Scam patterns change, but the app should avoid presenting updates as mysterious or magical. Users should understand that examples and guidance may improve over time.

The scam library should include pattern categories, example messages, false-alarm comparisons, risk triggers, safe actions, recovery steps, and education snippets. It should support categories already described in the brief, including bank alerts, payment apps, marketplace scams, job scams, romance scams, family emergency impersonation, tech support, device compromise, delivery scams, fake invoices, investment pressure, account takeover, and blackmail threats.

The app should show when guidance was updated in a user-friendly way if that helps trust. For example, an education card can say, "This guidance was recently updated" without overwhelming the user. The app should not require users to understand model versions or content pipelines.

The scam library should support user feedback. If a user marks a result as helpful, not helpful, too scary, unclear, or possibly wrong, the app should capture that feedback in a way that can improve future content. The app should not make users feel responsible for training the product. Feedback should be optional and quick.

The scam library should include retired or changed guidance handling. If the product later changes guidance for a scam type, old saved cases should remain understandable. A case result generated earlier should not silently change without context. If a saved case is re-reviewed with newer guidance, the app should label that as a new review or updated review.

### Section 9 \- Content Quality and Review Controls

The safety content inside the app should follow clear quality controls. Content includes risk explanations, recovery steps, education cards, helper prompts, alert text, settings explanations, permission copy, paid feature prompts, and reporting package language. Because this app deals with sensitive decisions, inconsistent or careless wording can cause harm.

Every piece of safety content should pass a plain test. A non-technical user should understand it without searching the internet. If a technical term is necessary, the app should explain it nearby. For example, "remote access" can be explained as "an app or tool that lets someone else see or control your device."

Every piece of safety content should pass an action test. It should tell the user what to do, what not to do, or what info is missing. Content that only says "be careful" is not enough. The app should translate concern into a practical next step.

Every piece of content should pass a tone test. It should be calm, respectful, and nonjudgmental. It should not shame users for clicking, paying, trusting someone, or feeling confused. It should not use fear to push paid features.

Every piece of content should pass a boundary test. It should not claim legal, medical, financial, law-enforcement, or guaranteed recovery authority. It should say when the user needs official support, bank support, platform support, emergency help, or trusted human support.

### Section 9 \- Localization and Multilingual Behavior

the app should be designed for users who speak different languages or receive scam messages in different languages. Localization means adapting the app for another language and region in a way that remains clear and culturally appropriate. Translation alone is not enough. Scam wording, payment methods, institutions, and user expectations can differ by language and location.

The app should support message review when the user's app language and the scam message language differ. For example, a user may use Verivae in English but receive a risky message in Spanish. The app should be able to explain that the message appears to be in another language, review it if supported, and show the result in the user's preferred language.

The app should avoid overconfident results when language detection is uncertain. If a screenshot is blurry, slang is ambiguous, or translation is incomplete, the app should label the review as limited. The app should ask the user to confirm unclear text where needed.

Localized safety guidance should preserve tone. A warning that is calm and respectful in English should not become harsh, formal, or confusing in another language. The app should avoid idioms that do not translate well. It should use simple direct language.

The app should handle regional uncertainty carefully. It should avoid making claims about specific banks, agencies, laws, or reporting systems unless the product has accurate region-specific info. General guidance such as verify through official channels, do not share codes, and avoid unusual payment pressure can remain useful across regions.

### Section 9 \- Accessibility Under Stress

Accessibility should be evaluated not only for disability support but also for stress. Scam situations create panic, urgency, shame, and cognitive overload. A user may be shaking, tired, distracted, in public, or on a phone call. the app should be usable in those conditions.

Critical screens should use short headings, large primary actions, clear contrast, and minimal choices. A critical result should not bury the safest next step in paragraph five. The app should show the immediate action first, such as stop responding, do not share the code, contact your bank through official info, remove remote access, or save evidence.

The app should support larger text without breaking layouts. Buttons should still fit. Risk labels should not overlap. Helper prompts should remain readable. Recovery checklists should not become crowded. The design should anticipate accessibility text sizes from the start.

The app should support screen readers with meaningful labels. A risk badge should not be announced only as "red icon." It should be announced as "Risk" or "Critical risk." Buttons should clearly state actions, such as "Share this case with helper" or "Start recovery checklist." Screenshots and evidence attachments should have useful descriptions where possible.

The app should avoid motion that distracts or alarms. If animations exist, they should be subtle and reducible. A scam warning does not need dramatic flashing or shaking. Calm design supports better decisions.

### Section 9 \- Sensitive Category Handling

Some scam categories require extra privacy and tone controls. These include romance scams, blackmail or sextortion, family conflict, ID docs, financial hardship, job desperation, elder targeting, domestic-control concerns, and threats. the app should treat these categories as sensitive by design.

Sensitive cases should offer privacy controls at the time of saving and sharing. The app can ask whether the user wants to hide the case title, lock the case, remove sensitive preview text, hide details from alerts, or require confirmation before helper sharing. These controls should be easy to understand.

Sensitive case titles should avoid exposure. A lock-screen alert should not say "Blackmail case updated" or display private message content. It can say "A saved case needs attention." The app should let the user choose more discreet labels.

Sensitive category explanations should avoid moral judgment. In romance or blackmail cases, the app should focus on safety and control. It should not shame the user for trusting someone, sharing private content, or feeling attached. The app should provide practical evidence, reporting, and support guidance.

Sensitive categories should also have escalation options. If the user indicates immediate danger, coercion, threats, or self-safety concern, the app should surface urgent support guidance. It should do so carefully and proportionately.

### Section 9 \- Product Integrity Around AI and Automation

If Verivae uses automated analysis, AI review, or pattern matching, the app should be honest about automation. The user does not need technical model details, but they should understand whether a result is automated, human-reviewed, limited, or user-entered. This matters because users may overtrust a confident-looking result.

Automated results should be labeled in plain text where appropriate, such as "App-generated review" or "Automated safety review." If human review is added, human-reviewed results should be labeled separately. The app should not blur the two.

The app should avoid fake certainty in automated language. It should not say "This is definitely safe" based on limited evidence. It should say "No major warning signs found in the info provided" or "Strong scam signs found." These phrases are more honest.

Automation should not remove user control. Users should be able to add context, correct the app, mark a result as wrong, request a new review after adding evidence, or ignore a suggestion. The app should guide without pretending to control the user's choices.

Automation should not be used for hidden surveillance. If ongoing monitoring exists in future versions, it must be opt-in, explain what is monitored, and provide clear controls. Manual review should remain available for users who do not want ongoing monitoring.

### Section 9 \- Accept Rules for Privacy, Content, and Accessibility Systems

The Privacy Center is acceptable when users can understand saved cases, linked services, device permissions, helper access, weekly checks, personalization, exports, and deletion options from one clear place. It must be practical, not merely legal text.

Data handling is acceptable when the app distinguishes temporary review data, saved case data, exported report data, helper-shared data, device-local data, and synced account data. Users must be able to control these categories where meaningful.

Permission transparency is acceptable when permissions are requested at relevant moments, explained in plain text, paired with fallback options, and visible later in settings. Declining a permission must not unnecessarily block core manual checking.

Consent records are acceptable when users can see important privacy choices, sharing actions, helper access, linked services, and revocation paths. Consent for saving, sharing, syncing, helper access, and weekly checks must remain separate.

Deletion and retention are acceptable when users can delete cases, delete evidence, clear history, manage retention, and understand what cannot be pulled back after export or external sharing.

Scam library maintenance is acceptable when the app can update examples and guidance, keep saved cases understandable, collect optional feedback, and avoid silently rewriting old case conclusions without context.

Content quality controls are acceptable when all safety content is plain, actionable, calm, nonjudgmental, and honest about boundaries. Paid prompts must pass the same tone and trust tests.

Localization is acceptable when the app can handle multilingual inputs carefully, explain translation limits, preserve calm tone, and avoid unsupported region-specific claims.

Accessibility under stress is acceptable when critical screens prioritize immediate action, support larger text, work with screen readers, avoid alarming motion, and remain usable by stressed or distracted users.

Sensitive category handling is acceptable when sensitive cases receive stronger privacy controls, discreet alerts, respectful explanations, and appropriate escalation paths.

Automation integrity is acceptable when automated and human-reviewed results are clearly distinguished, uncertainty is visible, user correction is supported, and ongoing monitoring remains opt-in.

### Section 9 completion note

Section 9 details the design brief with privacy center behavior, data handling categories, permission transparency, consent records, deletion and retention controls, scam library maintenance, content quality controls, localization, accessibility under stress, sensitive category handling, automation integrity, and accept rules while continuing to reserve the final area for later.

## Design Brief Section 10: Cross-App Protection, Device Review, and Weekly Deep Check Detail

### Section 10 purpose

This detail deepens the app's linked protection layer. The app should not feel like a single-use checker that only works when the user remembers to paste a message into it. It should feel like a practical safety system that can help around the places where scams actually arrive: email, text messages, messaging apps, social messages, browser links, QR codes, attachments, payment requests, account warnings, and linked devices. The purpose of this section is to define how those linked protections should work inside the app experience, what the user should see, how the app should explain limits honestly, and how the layout should keep the user in control.

Every section below describes product behavior, screen structure, user-facing controls, risk handling, and functional expectations for Verivae. The focus is the app itself: what it should show, how it should guide users, and how each feature should behave under pressure.

### Section 10 \- Linked Protection Principle

the app should treat linked protection as permission-based assistance, not hidden surveillance. The app may help review emails, messages, links, attachments, device settings, and linked-device warning signs, but it should always make clear what it can see, what it cannot see, what it stores, and what the user can turn off. The safest version of this product is not the version that asks for the most access. The safest version is the one that asks for the minimum useful access, explains the benefit in plain text, and lets the user revoke access without punishment.

The linked protection area should be built around a simple idea: the user owns the phone, the accounts, the messages, the evidence, and the decision. the app is a protective assistant that reads only what the user allows, flags risks with clear reasons, and helps the user take safer next steps. It should not silently send private content to people. It should not create fear just to increase engagement. It should not imply that every unusual message is definitely a scam. It should separate strong evidence from weak signals and make uncertainty visible.

Inside the interface, linked protection should be represented as a main area called Protection Hub. This hub should show each linked source as its own row or tile: Email, Messages, Browser and Links, Attachments, Device Safety, Weekly Deep Check, Trusted Helper Review, and Reports. Each source should show one of several simple states: Not linked, Ready, Needs attention, Limited access, Recently checked, or Action required. These states should use plain wording instead of technical labels. A user should be able to understand the whole protection situation in less than a minute.

The Protection Hub should not overload the user with charts. Its main job is to answer three questions: what is being protected, what needs attention, and what can the user do next. The top of the hub should include a calm status summary, such as: No urgent scam risks found, Two risky messages need review, Weekly check is ready, or Email protection is limited until permission is restored. Beneath that summary, the app should show linked protection sources and direct actions.

The app should avoid using shame or blame language. If a user clicks something risky, receives a fake invoice, or responds to a scammer, the interface should not say they made a mistake. It should say what happened, what risk may exist, and what to do next. This matters because scam victims often delay getting help because they feel embarrassed. the app should be designed to reduce that delay.

### Section 10 \- Email Protection Layout

Email protection should help users review risky emails, fake invoices, account warnings, job offers, shipping notices, tax messages, bank alerts, subscription notices, and password reset emails. The email feature should support both manual and linked modes. Manual mode lets the user paste email text, upload a screenshot, or forward an email to a private review address if that option is supported later. Linked mode lets the user connect an email account and choose what the app may review.

The Email Protection screen should begin with a short status card that says whether email protection is active, limited, paused, or not linked. Under that, the app should show recent items that were reviewed or are waiting for review. Each email item should show sender name, sender address when available, subject, received time, risk level, and the main reason for the risk score. The app should avoid displaying large amounts of private email text on the main screen. The list should show enough to identify the message without exposing sensitive content to someone looking over the user's shoulder.

When the user opens an email result, the layout should split the info into layers. The first layer is the plain answer: Safe enough, Be careful, Risky, or Risk. The second layer explains why. The third layer lets the user inspect evidence. The fourth layer offers actions. This structure keeps the result understandable for beginners while still being useful for advanced users.

The email analysis should examine sender mismatch, risky domains, unusual reply-to addresses, urgent pressure, requests for payment, requests for gift cards, password reset tricks, fake security alerts, attachment risk, link destination mismatch, brand impersonation, grammar patterns, business email compromise signals, and unusual payment instructions. Each signal should be written in human language. For example, instead of saying SPF alignment failed, the app can say: This email claims to be from your bank, but the sending address does not match the bank's normal domain. Advanced details may still be available behind a Details button.

Email protection must also include a false-positive path. If the user says an email is safe, the app should ask why: I know the sender, I expected this email, I confirmed through another method, This is from my workplace, or Other. The app should not automatically train itself to trust everything from that sender forever. Instead, it should record a cautious preference and continue warning if stronger scam signs appear later.

The app should support privacy controls for email. The user should be able to choose one of three review levels. Basic review checks only selected emails or emails the user shares manually. Standard review checks risky-looking emails from linked inboxes when allowed by the provider. Sensitive review should be optional and should only be used when the user clearly understands what it means. The app should explain that linked email access can be removed at any time from both Verivae and the email provider's account settings.

For Gmail and similar providers, the design should assume provider rules may limit what the app can access. the app should not promise unlimited background scanning if the platform does not allow it. The interface should say what is active in practical terms: Manual email checks are available, Risky message review is available, Attachment scanning is available, or Background checks are limited by your email provider. Honest limits are part of a professional product.

### Section 10 \- Messages and Text Protection Layout

Message protection should cover SMS, MMS, iMessage-style content where allowed, Android messages where allowed, messaging-app screenshots, social DMs, marketplace messages, dating app messages, and copied chat text. Because phone platforms restrict message access differently, the design brief should separate direct integration from user-assisted review. Direct integration means the app can receive limited message data through approved platform features. User-assisted review means the user shares a screenshot, copies text, forwards a message, or uses a share menu.

The Messages Protection screen should include three main entry points: Check a message now, Review recent shared messages, and Set up message protection. Check a message now should open a simple input screen with options for text, screenshot, link, phone number, QR code, and attachment. Review recent shared messages should show items the user has already sent into Verivae. Set up message protection should explain which types of message monitoring are available on the user's current phone.

The message result screen should be optimized for fast decisions. Scam messages often create urgency, so the result should not require the user to read a long report before knowing what to do. The top should show a clear risk level and a advised first action, such as: Do not reply yet, Do not tap the link, Call the company using a number you already trust, Save this as evidence, or Block and report this sender. Beneath that, the app can show a more detailed breakdown.

The message analysis should detect payment pressure, romance scam progression, fake family emergency language, fake delivery updates, bank warning tricks, fake job offers, crypto investment pitches, refund scams, marketplace overpayment scams, login code theft, fake support chats, impersonation of known contacts, links with misleading previews, and requests to move the conversation to another app. The result should identify the pattern without making the user feel foolish. For example: This resembles a verification-code theft attempt because the sender is asking you to share a code that should stay private.

Message protection should also include conversation-level review. A single message may look harmless, but a sequence of messages can reveal grooming, pressure, emotional manipulation, or gradual financial requests. the app should allow the user to combine multiple screenshots or pasted messages into one case. The app should then show a conversation timeline, pressure changes, money requests, identity claims, and unresolved verification questions.

The layout for conversation review should show a left-to-right or top-to-bottom timeline depending on screen size. Each message group should include the detected tactic, the exact phrase that triggered concern when safe to display, and a plain explanation. Sensitive content should be collapsible so the user can hide private details when sharing the screen with a trusted helper.

Blocking and reporting should be treated as actions, not the whole solution. The app should offer options such as block sender, report spam, save evidence, check links, verify identity, contact bank, change password, and open recovery checklist. If the platform does not allow Verivae to block directly, the app should show guided steps for the user's phone instead of pretending it completed the action.

### Section 10 \- Browser, Link, and QR Code Protection Layout

Many scams begin with a link. The link may arrive through email, text, a social app, a QR code, a fake advertisement, a search result, or a fake login page. the app's link protection should help the user inspect a link before opening it, review a link after opening it, and understand whether a page is asking for dangerous info.

The Link Check screen should support pasted URLs, shared URLs from other apps, scanned QR codes, screenshots of links, and links found inside emails or messages. The screen should show the final destination, the visible link text, redirects when available, domain age if available, impersonation signs, risky characters, lookalike spelling, unusual country domains, URL shorteners, and whether the page requests sensitive info. The beginner version should show a simple answer. The advanced version should show the technical trail.

For QR codes, the app should not automatically open the destination. It should first decode the QR code, show the destination, and ask whether the user wants to check it. The QR result screen should include a clear warning if the QR code leads to a payment request, login page, file download, app install, crypto address, or shortened link. The app should explain that QR codes can hide a destination until scanned.

Browser protection should include an in-app safe preview where possible. A safe preview should load or summarize the destination in a controlled way without requiring the user to sign in or enter personal info. The preview should show warnings for fake login pages, brand impersonation, risky payment pages, cloned storefronts, download prompts, and fake support popups. The app should never ask the user to enter real passwords into a page being checked.

The link result layout should include: final domain, claimed brand, risk level, evidence, advised action, and alternatives. Alternatives matter because a user may still need to complete a real task. If the app warns about a bank login link, it should also say: Open your banking app directly or type the bank's address yourself. If it warns about a delivery link, it should say: Check tracking from the carrier's official app or website.

The app should also remember previously checked links inside case history. If the same risky link appears later, the app should be able to show that it has been seen before and connect the new event to the old case. This is useful for repeated scam campaigns and for users who receive the same message through multiple channels.

### Section 10 \- Attachment and File Review Layout

Attachment review should help with files attached to emails, downloaded from links, sent through messages, or uploaded manually. The app should support a cautious review flow for common file types such as PDFs, images, documents, compressed files, and installers where platform rules allow. The design should not promise full malware removal unless the product includes a real supported security engine. Instead, it should describe file review as risk analysis, risky behavior detection where supported, reputation checking, and safe handling guidance.

The Attachment Review screen should ask how the file was received: email, text message, social message, website download, QR code, USB or external device, or unknown. This context helps the app understand risk. A PDF invoice from a known vendor is different from a PDF sent by a stranger demanding immediate payment. The app should combine file traits with message context.

The file result should show: file name, file type, source, risk level, risky signs, what the file appears to be, what it may try to do, and what the user should do next. For images and screenshots, the app may analyze visible text for fake payment instructions, impersonation, QR codes, or support numbers. For documents, the app should warn about macros, password-protected content, unusual links, external downloads, or requests to enable editing. For compressed files, the app should warn that hidden contents can be risky and should be extracted only if the user understands the source.

The interface should include a Safe Handling section. This section should tell the user whether to delete the file, keep it as evidence, upload it for deeper analysis, open it only in a viewer, avoid enabling editing, avoid running installers, or ask a trusted helper. It should also explain when the app cannot safely inspect something because of encryption, password protection, damaged file structure, or platform limits.

Attachment review should connect to the Recovery Workspace. If a file is risk and the user opened it, the app should offer a path into device safety checks, password changes, account review, and bank monitoring. The app should avoid panic language but should make urgent steps visible.

### Section 10 \- Device Safety Overview Layout

Device safety should be designed carefully because the word virus means different things on different devices. On desktop computers and some Android devices, deeper malware scanning may be possible through supported permissions or security partners. On iPhones and iPads, apps usually cannot scan the whole OS like a traditional antivirus tool. the app should handle this honestly by offering a Device Safety Review that checks what it can and clearly explains what it cannot.

The Device Safety screen should show linked devices and their protection state. A device tile should include device name, device type, last check, protection status, attention items, and available actions. Statuses should be simple: Looks okay, Needs review, Limited check, Check failed, or Not linked. If the user connects multiple devices, the app should allow them to rename devices in plain text, such as My phone, Dad's laptop, Work tablet, or Old Android phone.

The Device Safety Review should include several categories. Account safety checks review whether important accounts may need password changes, two-factor auth, recovery email review, or sign-out from unknown sessions. App safety checks review risky app permissions, risky installed apps where allowed, outdated apps, sideloaded apps where applicable, and apps that may imitate banks or support tools. System safety checks review OS updates, screen lock, device encryption where visible, backup status, and security settings the platform exposes. File and download checks review recent risky attachments or downloads shared with Verivae. Link and browser checks review recently submitted risky links and fake login pages.

The app should not hide platform limitations. If a phone does not allow full device scanning, the screen should say: This device does not allow full virus scanning from third-party apps, but the app can still review risky links, risky files you share, unsafe settings, account warning signs, and scam-related behavior. That explanation keeps the product trustworthy and prevents future legal or support problems.

The Device Safety screen should include a Safety Score only if it is carefully explained. A score can be useful, but it can also mislead users into thinking they are completely safe. If used, the score should be labeled as a readiness score, not a guarantee. The app should say what affects the score: outdated software, risky permissions, recent risky scam contact, risky links opened, unknown account sessions, missing passcode, lack of two-factor auth, and unresolved recovery tasks.

### Section 10 \- Weekly Deep Check Layout

The Weekly Deep Check should be a guided review that runs on a regular rhythm chosen by the user. It should not be a vague scan animation that pretends to do more than the app can do. It should be a real checklist-based safety review that combines available automated checks, user-confirmed checks, account review prompts, device safety signals, and unresolved scam cases.

The Weekly Deep Check screen should open with a calm summary: Your weekly protection review is ready. The user should see estimated time, categories included, and whether anything urgent was already detected. The categories may include: Recent risky messages, email risk review, checked links, risky attachments, device settings, app permissions, account security, financial warning signs, open recovery tasks, trusted helper items, and education advices.

The weekly check should have two modes: Quick Review and Deep Review. Quick Review should take only a few minutes and focus on urgent items. Deep Review should be more thorough and include account and device prompts. The user should be able to pause and resume without losing progress. If the user is stressed or busy, the app should not force them through a long sequence before showing urgent risks.

The layout should show progress by category, not by artificial percentage alone. For example: Messages reviewed, Links reviewed, Device settings reviewed, Accounts reviewed, Recovery tasks reviewed. Each category should have a clear result: No issue found, Needs attention, Limited by permission, Skipped by user, or Could not check. This is more honest than a single green checkmark that hides missing coverage.

The Weekly Deep Check should create an understandable report at the end. The report should include what was checked, what could not be checked, what risks were found, what actions were taken, and what remains unresolved. The user should be able to save the report privately, share it with a trusted helper, or export it for personal records. Reports should avoid exposing full message contents unless the user chooses to include evidence.

The app should also support reminders without becoming annoying. A user should be able to choose weekly, every two weeks, monthly, or manual only. They should be able to turn reminders off. The reminder language should be calm: Time for your protection review, not Your device may be infected. Fear-based alerts would weaken trust.

### Section 10 \- Linked Device and Family Review Layout

Some users will want to protect more than one device. A parent may help a teenager. An adult child may help a parent. A person may want a trusted friend to review risky messages. the app should support linked-device and trusted-helper patterns without turning into a control tool.

The Linked Devices screen should show each device separately. The user should be able to see which device belongs to which person, what permissions are active, when it was last checked, and whether any items need attention. For privacy, the app should avoid showing sensitive message previews across devices by default. A helper should see risk summaries and action requests, not private content, unless the device owner explicitly shares it.

Trusted helper access should have clear permission levels. View alerts only means the helper can see that something needs review but not the private content. Review shared items means the helper can see specific messages or files the user shares. Help with recovery means the helper can view recovery checklist progress and suggested next steps. Manage protection settings should be a separate high-trust permission and should not be enabled by default.

For family and elder-support scenarios, the app should include respectful language. It should not describe older users as incapable. It should not assume parents want full access to a child's private life. The design should center consent, transparency, and limited sharing. Every person linked to the protection system should be able to see who has access and what they can view.

If a user receives a risky scam message, they should be able to tap Ask a trusted helper. The app should create a clean helper view with the risk summary, selected evidence, suggested questions, and advised next actions. The user should be able to hide private parts before sharing.
