The helper should not be able to change the original evidence unless explicitly allowed.

### Section 10 \- Alert and Alert Behavior

Alerts should be useful, limited, and plain. the app should avoid constant alarms. Too many warnings will train users to ignore the app. The alert system should prioritize urgent risks, unresolved recovery actions, and weekly review reminders.

There should be at least four alert levels. Infoal alerts tell the user about normal activity, such as weekly review available. Caution alerts tell the user a message or link deserves review. Risky alerts tell the user not to reply, pay, click, or share codes until the item is checked. Recovery alerts tell the user that action may be needed because money, passwords, identity info, or device safety may be involved.

Each alert should open to a specific screen, not a generic dashboard. If the alert is about a risky text, it should open the message result. If it is about a weekly check, it should open the review. If it is about a recovery task, it should open the exact task. This reduces confusion and makes the app feel dependable.

Alert wording should avoid fear. Examples of acceptable language include: Risky link found in a shared message, Review before replying, Weekly protection review is ready, A recovery task still needs attention, and Email protection needs permission. Examples to avoid include: You are hacked, Your phone is infected, Someone is stealing your money, or Open now or else. The app must earn trust through accuracy and clarity.

### Section 10 \- Permission, Privacy, and Control Layout

Every linked feature should have its own permission explanation screen. The explanation should answer: What will this access help with, what can the app see, what can the app not see, what is stored, how long it is kept, who can view it, and how to turn it off. This should be written for beginners.

The Permissions screen should show all linked sources in one place. Each row should include source name, status, last used, what access is active, and a manage button. When the user taps manage, the app should show choices such as pause, disconnect, delete stored items, change review level, and view recent access. The user should not have to search through hidden settings to understand what is linked.

The app should include a Privacy Receipt for important actions. A Privacy Receipt is a simple record showing what happened, such as: You shared one email for scam review, Verivae analyzed the sender, links, wording, and attachment name, the item was saved to Case 12, and no trusted helper received it. This helps users feel in control and helps support future trust.

If data is used to improve detection, the app should make that optional and separate from basic protection. Users should be able to use Verivae without donating private scam examples for model improvement. If they choose to contribute an example, the app should remove personal details when possible and show what is being shared.

### Section 10 \- Case Linking Across Apps

A professional scam safety app should connect related events into one case. A scam may begin with an email, continue by text, move to a phone call, send a fake website link, and end with a payment request. If each item is reviewed separately, the user may miss the full pattern. the app should support case linking across sources.

When a new item is checked, the app should ask whether it belongs to an existing case if it detects similar names, phone numbers, emails, domains, payment requests, or wording. The app should not merge cases automatically without user review. It can suggest: This may be related to your Bank Alert case because it uses the same phone number and asks for the same login code.

The Case Detail layout should show source tabs: Messages, Emails, Links, Files, Calls, Payments, Notes, Recovery, and Reports. Each tab should contain only that type of evidence. The Overview tab should summarize the pattern: who contacted the user, what they claimed, what they wanted, what risk exists, what actions were taken, and what remains unresolved.

Case linking should support duplicates and corrections. If the app incorrectly links two items, the user should be able to separate them. If the user later realizes two cases are related, they should be able to merge them. The app should preserve evidence history when cases are split or merged.

### Section 10 \- Functional Limits and Honest Safety Language

The design brief should require Verivae to be honest about what it can and cannot do. The app can reduce risk, guide decisions, detect warning signs, help preserve evidence, and support recovery. It cannot guarantee that every scam will be caught. It cannot guarantee that every safe-looking message is safe. It cannot always scan an entire phone for viruses. It cannot reverse payments by itself. It cannot replace a bank, police report, legal advice, tax advice, or medical advice.

Honest limits should appear in the right places, not only in legal text. If the app gives a result, it should say when confidence is limited. If a device check is limited by phone restrictions, it should say so near the result. If a link cannot be fully opened safely, it should say what was checked and what remains unknown. If an attachment is encrypted, it should say that the file could not be inspected fully.

This honesty is not a weakness. It is a product feature. Users who trust the app will be more likely to follow its advices, return for weekly reviews, and share the app with family members. Overpromising would create disappointment and risk.

### Section 10 \- Accept Rules

This detail is complete when the app has a clear design for linked email review, message review, link and QR code checking, attachment review, device safety review, weekly checks, linked-device support, trusted-helper support, alert behavior, permission controls, case linking, and honest platform-limit language.

The app should be able to guide a beginner from receiving a risky message to checking it, understanding the result, preserving evidence, asking for help, reviewing device safety, and completing recovery tasks. The app should also be able to explain what it checked, what it did not check, and what the user controls. The layout should keep risky actions visible without making the product feel frightening or complicated.

### Section 10 completion note

## Design Brief Section 11: Recovery Workspace, Evidence Vault, and Financial Damage Response Detail

### Section 11 purpose

This detail deepens the app's recovery experience. The app should not stop after saying something looks risky. A professional scam safety product needs to help the user understand what may have happened, preserve important evidence, decide what to do first, protect accounts, contact the right places, and track the situation until it is resolved. The recovery experience should be practical, calm, and specific enough that a beginner can follow it without feeling lost.

This section defines what the app should be capable of showing and doing when a user may have been exposed to a scam, lost money, shared private information, opened a risky file, installed something risky, or needs help documenting what happened. It keeps the product focused on in-app guidance, recovery organization, privacy-aware evidence handling, and safer next steps.

### Section 11 \- Recovery Workspace Principle

The Recovery Workspace should be the part of Verivae that turns fear into ordered action. A user may arrive there after a risky result, after opening a risky link, after sending money, after sharing a password, after sharing a login code, after installing an app, after downloading a file, after receiving a blackmail threat, after noticing unknown account activity, or after asking the app what to do next. The workspace should meet the user at the level of harm that may have happened.

The main principle is priority. The app should not give the user twenty tasks at once. It should sort recovery actions by urgency, reversibility, and likely damage. For example, if the user shared a banking password, changing the password and checking account sessions may come before writing a full summary. If the user sent money, contacting the payment provider may come before cleaning up low-risk account settings. If the user only received a risky text and did not interact, the recovery path may be brief and mostly focused on blocking, reporting, and learning.

The Recovery Workspace should always explain why a task matters. A beginner should not see a vague instruction like secure your account. The app should say: Change this sectionword because the scammer may try to log in before you do. The action is clearer, the reason is visible, and the user understands why it belongs near the top.

The Recovery Workspace should also show what the app cannot do directly. The app may guide the user, create summaries, organize evidence, suggest next steps, and open the correct external app or website when appropriate. It should not claim it can reverse a payment, force a bank refund, remove a criminal, guarantee account recovery, or make official reports on the user's behalf unless a real supported integration exists and the user explicitly confirms submission.

### Section 11 \- Recovery Home Layout

The Recovery Home screen should be organized around active cases. At the top, the user should see a calm status summary such as: One recovery case needs action, No urgent recovery tasks, Payment follow-up still unresolved, or Account protection tasks are complete. The summary should be plain and should not exaggerate the danger.

Below the summary, the screen should show active recovery cards. Each card should include the case name, risk type, last update, current status, next advised action, and urgency. Example case names may be user-created or app-suggested, such as Fake Bank Text, Marketplace Buyer Scam, Risky Invoice, Job Offer Scam, Romance Payment Request, or Unknown Login Warning. Since the app name is still Verivae, the case names should describe the incident, not the company.

The Recovery Home should include quick filters: Needs action, Waiting, Completed, Risk, Money involved, Account involved, Device involved, and Shared with helper. These filters help the user find the right case without scrolling through everything. The screen should also include a New recovery case button for users who know something happened but did not start from a scam check result.

Each case card should be compact. It should not display sensitive details like full account numbers, private message content, or financial amounts on the main Recovery Home unless the user chooses to show them. A privacy toggle can let the user blur sensitive summaries when they are in public or sharing their screen.

The Recovery Home should make unfinished tasks obvious. If a case has five advised tasks and two are complete, the card should show that progress clearly. It should also show whether any tasks are time-sensitive. The language should be direct: Contact payment provider, Change password, Save evidence, Review device, Ask trusted helper, or Confirm account activity.

### Section 11 \- Immediate Triage Screen

The Immediate Triage screen should appear when the app believes the user may need fast action. Triage means sorting the problem by what needs attention first. The screen should not be dramatic. It should ask a short set of questions that determine risk and priority.

The triage questions should be simple and answerable. Did you send money? Did you share a password? Did you share a login code? Did you share your Social Security number or similar identity number? Did you install an app or program? Did you open a file? Did you give remote access to your device? Did you provide bank or card info? Did the person threaten you? Are they still contacting you now? The user should be able to answer yes, no, not sure, or skip.

Based on those answers, the app should build a first-action list. The first-action list should be short, usually three to five items, and should focus on the most protective next steps. If money was sent, the app may prioritize contacting the payment provider, preserving transaction details, and avoiding further contact. If a password was shared, it may prioritize changing the password, signing out other sessions, enabling two-factor auth, and checking recovery details. If remote access was granted, it may prioritize disconnecting from the internet, reviewing installed remote-access tools, changing passwords from a different trusted device, and starting a device safety review.

The triage screen should include an Emergency Mode layout for serious cases. Emergency Mode should reduce the interface to the essentials: what happened, what to do first, who to contact, and what evidence to save. It should remove extra education panels, upsell prompts, long explanations, and nonessential animations. In a high-stress moment, clarity is more important than visual richness.

Triage should not require the user to know technical terms. If the app asks about remote access, it should explain: Did someone ask you to install an app so they could see or control your screen? If it asks about login codes, it should explain: Did someone ask you to read or send them a code that came by text, email, or authenticator app? These explanations should appear inline, not buried behind a help page.

### Section 11 \- Evidence Vault Layout

The Evidence Vault should be the private area where Verivae stores scam-related material that the user chooses to save. Evidence can include screenshots, message text, email headers where available, sender names, phone numbers, email addresses, URLs, QR code destinations, file names, payment receipts, transaction IDs, notes, call logs typed by the user, case summaries, and generated reports.

The Evidence Vault should be organized by case first, then by evidence type. A user should not have to remember whether something came from email or text. They should open the case and see everything linked to that situation. Inside a case, tabs can separate Messages, Emails, Links, Files, Payments, Calls, Notes, Device Events, Helper Comments, and Reports.

Each evidence item should have a clear card. The card should show what the item is, where it came from, when the user added it if known, whether it was analyzed, what risk it relates to, and whether it is included in exports. The user should be able to mark evidence as important, private, duplicate, unresolved, or no longer relevant. Deleting evidence should require confirmation because evidence may matter later.

The Evidence Vault should preserve original material and app-generated interpretation separately. If the user uploads a screenshot, the original screenshot should remain unchanged. The app can create extracted text, risk notes, and explanation summaries, but those should be clearly labeled as analysis. This distinction matters because official reports, banks, platforms, or trusted helpers may need to see the original evidence rather than only the app's interpretation.

The Evidence Vault should also support redaction. Redaction means hiding private parts before sharing. The user should be able to hide account numbers, addresses, phone numbers, names, private chat lines, personal photos, payment amounts, and other details they do not want to share. Redacted copies should not replace originals. The app should save the original privately and create a separate shareable version.

Evidence should include a chain-of-handling view in simple language. This does not need to be a legal evidence system at first, but the user should be able to see when something was added, edited, redacted, shared, exported, or deleted. This helps build trust and helps the user remember what happened.

### Section 11 \- Payment and Financial Damage Response Layout

The Payment Response section should activate when money, cards, bank accounts, payment apps, wire transfers, crypto, gift cards, checks, invoices, refunds, marketplace payments, subscriptions, or payroll info may be involved. The app should not act like every payment problem has the same recovery path. It should ask what kind of payment was involved and then show the most relevant actions.

The Payment Response screen should begin with a payment type selector. The choices should use normal words: debit card, credit card, bank transfer, payment app, wire transfer, crypto, gift card, check, cash, marketplace payment, invoice payment, subscription charge, payroll or direct deposit, and not sure. After the user chooses a type, the app should ask whether payment was completed, attempted, blocked, pending, or unknown.

The app should then create a task list. Examples include: contact your bank or payment provider, save transaction details, do not send more money, avoid communicating through the scammer's preferred channel, check recent account activity, change related passwords, turn on account alerts, and document who contacted you. These should be worded as user tasks, not guarantees. The app should not say the bank will refund you. It should say the provider may have its own dispute or fraud process and the app can help you prepare the info.

The Payment Response layout should include a Details to gather section. This section should ask for the payment date if the user knows it, amount, recipient name, recipient account or handle, transaction ID, payment app name, screenshot of receipt, reason the scammer gave, and any deadlines or threats used. The app should allow unknown answers. A stressed user may not know every detail immediately.

The app should create a Payment Summary that the user can read aloud, paste into a support chat, or use while calling a bank. The summary should be neutral and factual: I believe I may have sent money as part of a scam. The transaction was through this payment method. The recipient info I have is this. I have saved screenshots and messages. I am asking what fraud, dispute, reversal, freeze, or monitoring options are available. The wording should avoid blaming the user or making legal claims the app cannot verify.

For gift cards and crypto, the app should be especially clear that recovery may be difficult and quick action matters. It should still help the user preserve evidence, report through appropriate channels, and avoid additional payments. The app should not pretend there is an easy guaranteed recovery route.

### Section 11 \- Account Takeover Recovery Layout

Account takeover means someone may have access to one of the user's accounts. This can include email, banking, social media, cloud storage, shopping accounts, phone carrier accounts, work accounts, payment apps, or password manager accounts. The Account Recovery section should help users identify which accounts are at risk and what to do next.

The Account Recovery screen should start with a simple account selector. The user can choose the affected account type: email, bank, payment app, social media, shopping, phone carrier, cloud storage, workplace, school, password manager, crypto wallet, or other. The screen should ask what happened: shared password, shared login code, clicked login link, received unknown login alert, lost access, saw unfamiliar activity, installed remote-access app, or not sure.

The app should then build a recovery checklist. Common tasks may include changing the password from a trusted device, signing out other sessions, removing unknown devices, checking recovery email and phone number, turning on two-factor auth, reviewing recent activity, removing unknown forwarding rules for email accounts, checking payment methods, and saving proof of risky activity. Each task should explain why it matters.

The layout should distinguish between still have access and lost access. If the user still has access, the app can guide them through protective steps. If the user has lost access, the app should switch to an account recovery mode that helps them gather ownership proof, find the provider's recovery path, document dates and risky changes, and avoid scam recovery services that may target victims.

The Account Recovery area should also warn about repeating password use. If the user shared a password used on multiple accounts, the app should ask which other accounts may use the same password and create follow-up tasks. This should be framed practically: If this sectionword was reused, those accounts may also need new passwords.

### Section 11 \- Identity Info Response Layout

The Identity Info Response section should activate when the user may have shared identity details. This may include full name, address, date of birth, identity numbers, photos of IDs, tax info, insurance info, school info, workplace info, selfies, signatures, or answers to security questions. The app should handle this carefully and avoid providing jurisdiction-specific legal instructions unless the product has current official guidance for the user's region.

The screen should ask what info was shared. It should allow the user to select multiple categories without typing sensitive numbers into the app unless needed. For example, the user can mark Government ID shared without storing the actual ID number. If the user chooses to store details, the app should clearly label that as sensitive and explain how to delete it later.

The app should generate a risk explanation based on the type of info. Sharing a name and email address is different from sharing an identity number and a photo of an ID. The interface should show possible risks in plain text: someone may try to open accounts, reset passwords, impersonate you, pass identity checks, or target you with more convincing scams.

The next-step layout should include account monitoring prompts, password and recovery detail review, official-report preparation where appropriate, credit or identity monitoring reminders where available, and a personal record of what was exposed. Because identity response rules can vary by country and service, the app should label external actions as region-dependent and should update official destination links through verified current sources inside the product.

The app should also support a Sensitive Evidence Mode. In this mode, the app minimizes how much identity data appears on screen, hides details by default, and requires confirmation before exporting or sharing. This mode should be available for any case involving ID docs, minors, intimate images, threats, workplace accounts, or family safety.

### Section 11 \- Recovery Task Detail Layout

Every recovery task should open into a detail screen. The detail screen should not be just a checkbox. It should explain the task, why it matters, what the user needs before starting, what steps to follow, what to record afterward, and what to do if the task cannot be completed.

A task detail screen should include the following structure: task title, urgency label, plain purpose, before you start, steps, what to save as evidence, completion confirmation, blocked path, and related tasks. For example, a Change Password task should explain that the user should change the password from a trusted device, avoid using a link from the risky message, choose a new unique password, sign out other sessions when available, and save a note that the password was changed.

The app should support task statuses: Not started, In progress, Waiting, Blocked, Completed, Skipped, and No longer needed. Waiting is important because recovery often involves banks, platforms, family members, or official responses. Blocked is important because a user may not be able to access an account or may be unsure what info is required.

When a task is blocked, the app should ask why. Examples include: I cannot log in, I cannot reach support, I do not understand the instructions, I do not have the transaction ID, I am waiting for a response, I need a trusted helper, or I do not feel safe contacting the person. Based on the answer, the app should suggest a smaller next step.

The detail layout should include notes, attachments, and timestamps where useful, but it should not require the user to fill every field. Recovery needs to be flexible because real situations are messy.

### Section 11 \- Communication Helper Layout

The Communication Helper should help the user talk to banks, platforms, trusted helpers, employers, schools, marketplaces, or support teams. Many users know they need to contact someone but do not know what to say. the app should generate clear, factual, editable messages that the user controls.

The Communication Helper should offer message types such as bank fraud support, payment app support, marketplace support, email provider support, social account support, employer security team, school technology office, trusted family member, trusted friend, and official report preparation. Each message should be based on the case details the user chooses to include.

Before generating a message, the app should show an inclusion checklist. The user can choose whether to include their name, contact method, transaction amount, transaction ID, screenshots, sender info, timeline, and requested action. The app should not automatically include sensitive details without showing the user.

Generated messages should be calm and factual. They should avoid exaggeration, threats, accusations, or unsupported claims. A professional message helps the user get help faster. The app should also provide a shorter phone-call script for users who prefer calling. The script should include what to say first, what details to have ready, and what to ask for.

The Communication Helper should save the final message into the case if the user wants. It should let the user mark whether the message was sent, when they sent it, who they contacted, and what response they received. This turns communication into trackable recovery progress.

### Section 11 \- Report Builder and Export Layout

The Report Builder should let the user create a clear case report from saved evidence and recovery actions. The report should be useful for personal records, trusted helpers, banks, payment providers, platforms, employers, schools, or official reporting destinations. It should not force the user to share everything.

The Report Builder should start with a report purpose selector. The user can choose: personal record, bank or payment provider, account provider, marketplace or platform, trusted helper, employer or school, official report, or custom. The purpose should change the report structure. A bank report may focus on payment details and transaction evidence. A platform report may focus on account names, messages, links, and policy violations. A trusted helper report may focus on plain summary and next actions.

The report layout should include sections for summary, timeline, people or accounts involved, contact methods, links and domains, payment details if relevant, files or attachments, user actions already taken, unresolved risks, and evidence list. The user should be able to include original evidence, redacted evidence, or summary-only evidence.

Before export, the app should show a Review Before Sharing screen. This screen should highlight sensitive items included in the report. It should ask the user to confirm whether they want to include private messages, full receipts, identity info, addresses, phone numbers, account handles, or photos. This protects the user from oversharing while trying to get help.

Export formats should be practical. The app may support PDF, plain text, copied summary, email-ready message, support-chat summary, and printable view. If the product later supports direct submission to a partner or official destination, the app should require explicit confirmation and show exactly what will be sent.

### Section 11 \- Recovery History and Resolution Layout

The Recovery History screen should show what happened over time. It should include user actions, app analysis, evidence added, reports created, messages generated, helper reviews, completed tasks, skipped tasks, unresolved risks, and final resolution notes. This gives the user a reliable memory of the incident.

The history should be readable as a timeline. Each event should have a short title and optional details. Examples include: Risky message checked, Payment details added, Bank contact script created, Password changed, Evidence redacted, Helper reviewed case, Weekly check completed, Case marked resolved. The timeline should avoid technical logs unless the user opens advanced details.

Case resolution should be flexible. A case may end because it was confirmed safe, blocked before harm, money recovery was attempted, account was secured, evidence was saved, official reporting was completed, or the user chose to close it. The app should let the user mark a case resolved, unresolved but inactive, duplicate, false alarm, or archived.

When closing a case, the app should show a final review checklist. It should ask whether money was involved, accounts are secure, device safety was reviewed if needed, evidence has been saved, helper sharing is complete, and reminders are no longer needed. The app should not force the user to complete every task before closing, but it should make unresolved risks visible.

### Section 11 \- Emotional Safety and Anti-Shame Design

Recovery design must account for how users feel during and after scams. People may feel embarrassed, scared, angry, rushed, confused, or exhausted. A product that sounds judgmental can make them stop using it at the exact moment they need help. the app should use anti-shame design across the recovery experience.

Anti-shame design means the app uses neutral language. It says: This can happen to anyone. It says: Here is what to do next. It says: You are not required to handle this alone. It does not say: You should have known, You made a mistake, or This was obvious. The app can be serious without being cruel.

The recovery screens should include calm visual hierarchy. Urgent tasks can be prominent without using alarming colors everywhere. Red should be reserved for serious immediate warnings. Most recovery screens should use clear spacing, readable labels, and steady action buttons. The user should feel guided, not surrounded.

The app should also include a Safe Exit option for sensitive cases. If the user is being threatened, controlled, blackmailed, or watched by someone nearby, they may need to leave the screen quickly. Safe Exit should hide sensitive case details and return to a neutral screen. The design should be careful not to create more danger by sending obvious alerts or showing sensitive alerts on the lock screen.

### Section 11 \- Recovery Workspace Accept Rules

This detail is complete when the app has a clear recovery design that covers triage, active case cards, evidence storage, evidence redaction, payment response, account takeover response, identity info response, task detail screens, communication help, report building, export review, recovery history, case resolution, and anti-shame interface behavior.

The app should be able to help a beginner move from a scary moment to a short ordered action list. It should preserve evidence without exposing private content unnecessarily. It should help the user explain the situation to the right party. It should track progress over time. It should be honest about what it cannot guarantee. It should support high-stress use without becoming cluttered or frightening.

### Section 11 completion note

Section 11 details the design brief with case space behavior, immediate triage, evidence vault structure, payment response, account recovery, identity info response, task detail screens, communication helper tools, report builder controls, export review, recovery history, case resolution, and anti-shame design while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 12: Personalization, Risk Memory, and Adaptive Protection Layout Detail

### Section 12 purpose

This detail deepens how the app should personalize protection without becoming invasive. A scam safety app becomes more useful when it understands the user's normal communication patterns, preferred level of help, trusted contacts, common accounts, comfort with technical explanations, and unresolved scam history. At the same time, personalization can become risky if it quietly collects too much, makes hidden assumptions, or labels people and messages incorrectly. the app should use personalization to make protection clearer, faster, and more relevant while keeping the user in control.

This section defines how personalization, risk memory, user preferences, trusted entities, false-positive handling, explanation tuning, and adaptive interface behavior should work inside Verivae. The focus is the product experience: what the app remembers, what it should forget, how it adapts, and how the user stays in control.

### Section 12 \- Personalization Principle

The personalization principle for the app should be consent, clarity, and usefulness. The app should personalize only when personalization helps the user make safer decisions. It should not personalize just to collect more data. It should not make the product feel mysterious. The user should be able to see what the app has learned, correct it, delete it, pause it, or turn it off.

A beginner-friendly explanation should appear when personalization is introduced: Personalization means the app can remember safe patterns you approve, adjust warnings to your needs, and make future checks easier. It should also say: You control what is remembered. This language makes the concept understandable without technical vocabulary.

The app should avoid the feeling that it is spying. If Verivae learns that a user regularly receives invoices from a specific vendor, it should not say it is monitoring all business activity. It should say that the user marked that sender as familiar and that future emails from that sender may be reviewed with that context. Even then, the app should continue checking for unusual payment instructions, risky links, changed sender addresses, or risky attachments.

Personalization should never be a reason to hide a serious warning. If a trusted sender suddenly asks for gift cards, sends a strange login link, changes payment details, or uses a new risky domain, the app should still warn the user. Trust should be context-aware, not permanent. A trusted contact can be impersonated. A familiar company can have a compromised account. A normal-looking invoice can contain changed bank details. The app should explain this in practical language.

### Section 12 \- Personal Protection Profile Layout

The Personal Protection Profile should be the screen where users manage how Verivae adapts to them. This should not feel like a complicated settings page. It should feel like a simple profile for safety preferences. The top of the screen should show a short summary: Protection level, explanation style, linked sources, trusted helpers, trusted entities, and privacy status.

The profile should include a Protection Level control. Suggested levels can be Light, Balanced, and Strict. Light means fewer interruptions and mostly risky warnings. Balanced means warnings for clear risk and some risky patterns. Strict means more warnings and more review prompts. The app should explain the tradeoff in plain text: Strict may catch more risky activity but may show more false alarms. Light may interrupt less but may miss weaker warning signs.

The profile should include Explanation Style. Some users want short answers. Some users want detailed reasoning. Some users need simple stepwise guidance. The options can be Simple, Standard, Detailed, and Technical details available. Simple should use direct statements and short explanations. Standard should show the main evidence. Detailed should show multiple evidence points and possible alternatives. Technical details should reveal deeper info such as domain behavior, email routing details where available, redirect chains, file signals, and confidence factors.

The profile should include Stress Mode preference. Stress Mode is for risky situations where the user may be scared or rushed. When Stress Mode is active, the app should reduce optional text, show the safest next action first, increase button clarity, use fewer choices, and avoid distracting panels. The user should be able to turn Stress Mode on manually, and the app can suggest it after risky results.

The profile should include Privacy Defaults. The user can choose whether evidence previews are visible or blurred, whether reports include sensitive details by default, whether trusted helpers can see summaries only or selected evidence, and whether the app may remember approved safe patterns. These controls should be short and understandable.

### Section 12 \- Trusted Entities Layout

Trusted Entities are people, companies, services, phone numbers, email addresses, domains, payment handles, or accounts the user marks as familiar. This feature should make repeat reviews smarter, but it must be designed cautiously. A trusted entity is not automatically safe. It is a familiar reference point that helps the app notice when something is normal or abnormal.

The Trusted Entities screen should show categories: People, Companies, Email addresses, Phone numbers, Websites, Payment handles, Devices, and Other. Each entity should show why it is trusted, when it was added if known, what sources it is linked to, and whether it has any warnings. The user should be able to edit, pause, or remove trust at any time.

When adding a trusted entity, the app should ask how the user knows it. Choices can include: I know this person, I have used this company before, this is my bank or financial service, this is my workplace, this is a family member, this is a regular vendor, this is a school or organization, or other. The app should not require complex identity verification for every entry, but it should warn that scammers can imitate trusted names.

The layout should make impersonation visible. If an email claims to be from a trusted company but uses a different domain, the app should say: This message uses a name you recognize, but the sending address does not match the trusted entry. If a text claims to be from a trusted person but comes from a new phone number, the app should say: This may be someone using a familiar name. Verify through a contact method you already trust.

Trusted Entities should include trust boundaries. For example, the user may trust a company for normal receipts but not for payment change requests. The app can let users mark typical activity: sends receipts, sends invoices, sends appointment reminders, sends login alerts, sends delivery updates, or never asks for payment by text. These patterns help the app detect when a familiar sender does something unusual.

### Section 12 \- Risk Memory Layout

Risk Memory is the app's record of scam patterns, prior cases, risky senders, checked links, unresolved warnings, and user decisions. It should help the app connect new risks to old ones without creating a confusing surveillance log. The user should be able to open Risk Memory from the Protection Hub or from a case detail screen.

Risk Memory should be organized by pattern, not only by date or source. Categories can include repeated sender, repeated phone number, repeated link, repeated payment request, repeated impersonated brand, repeated phrase, repeated file name, repeated QR destination, repeated trusted-contact impersonation, and repeated recovery task. This helps the user understand that scams often arrive in clusters.

Each Risk Memory item should explain what was remembered. For example: Verivae remembered that this phone number appeared in a previous risky bank alert case. Or: This link destination was checked before and marked risky. Or: This sender used a payment change request that was previously flagged. The language should be concrete.

The user should be able to correct Risk Memory. If the app remembers something incorrectly, the user can mark it as not related, safe in this context, duplicate, no longer relevant, or mistaken. The app should then update the case connection and explain the effect. Corrections should not erase evidence unless the user chooses deletion.

Risk Memory should include expiration and cleanup controls. Some remembered items may remain useful for a long time, such as known scam domains or unresolved identity exposure. Other items may become outdated. The app should let the user clean old low-risk memory, archive resolved cases, delete selected remembered patterns, or keep important evidence. This supports privacy and keeps the app from becoming cluttered.

### Section 12 \- Adaptive Warning Behavior

Adaptive warnings should change how the app communicates, not whether serious risk exists. If a user chooses simple explanations, the app should still detect the same risky signs. If a user chooses strict protection, the app can show more caution prompts. If a user marks a sender as familiar, the app can reduce low-risk repetition but still flag risky changes.

The warning layout should include a Personal Context line when personalization affects the result. Examples include: You marked this sender as familiar, but the link is new. Or: This phone number is not in your trusted contacts. Or: This payment request is unusual for this sender. Or: You have seen a similar message before. This makes personalization visible instead of hidden.

Warnings should have adjustable depth. The first screen should show the risk level and next action. A Why this matters section should explain the main reason. A More detail section should show evidence. An Advanced detail section can show technical factors if the user wants them. The app should remember the user's preferred depth but still allow quick detail.

Adaptive warnings should avoid certainty when certainty is not justified. Instead of saying This is a scam every time, the app can say This has strong scam signs, This needs verification, This is unusual for this sender, or This cannot be confirmed as safe. This protects accuracy and credibility.

The app should support a quiet-warning pattern for low-risk items. A quiet warning may appear as a small caution label rather than a full interruption. For risky items, the app should interrupt more clearly. The distinction matters because users should not be trained to ignore constant warnings.

### Section 12 \- False Alarm and Missed Scam Feedback Layout

No scam detection system will be perfect. the app should include respectful feedback paths for false alarms and missed scams. A false alarm means the app warned about something the user believes was safe. A missed scam means the app failed to warn or did not warn strongly enough. Both types of feedback are valuable.

The Feedback screen should be available from every result. It should ask: Was this result helpful? The options can be Yes, Too cautious, Not cautious enough, Wrong explanation, I am not sure, and Report a problem. If the user selects Too cautious, the app should ask why: known sender, expected message, verified elsewhere, normal company behavior, or other. If the user selects Not cautious enough, the app should ask what happened: money requested, link was fake, account was compromised, sender impersonated someone, file was dangerous, or other.

The feedback flow should not make the user do a lot of work. It should take only a few taps unless the user wants to provide details. If the feedback affects a case, the app should ask whether to update the case result. For example, a message originally marked Caution may become Confirmed safe by user, or a message originally marked Low risk may become Suspected scam after user feedback.

The app should distinguish personal feedback from product improvement. Personal feedback updates the user's case and preferences. Product improvement feedback may help improve future detection, but only if the user allows sharing. The interface should not automatically use private evidence for broader improvement without clear permission.

Missed scam feedback should connect to recovery. If the user says the app missed a scam and money or account access was involved, the app should offer to open the Recovery Workspace. It should not simply say thank you for feedback and leave the user alone.

### Section 12 \- Personalized Education Layout

Education should adapt to what the user actually faces. A generic library is useful, but the app can be better if it recommends short lessons based on recent risks, unresolved cases, and user preferences. The education system should be practical and tied to real app behavior.

The Personalized Education screen should include Advised for You, Scam Types, Quick Lessons, Practice Checks, Saved Lessons, and Family or Helper Lessons. Advised for You can show topics related to recent cases, such as login code scams, fake bank texts, marketplace overpayment, romance scams, fake invoices, risky attachments, QR code risks, or account takeover recovery.

Each lesson should be short enough to complete without fatigue. The layout should include a simple explanation, a realistic example, what to look for, what to do, and a practice question. The app should avoid making lessons feel like school tests. The goal is confidence, not embarrassment.

Education should connect back to protection. After a lesson about fake delivery texts, the app can show a Check a message button. After a lesson about password reuse, the app can show an Account safety review button. After a lesson about gift cards, it can show Payment warning signs. This keeps education useful rather than separate from the app.

The user should be able to hide topics they do not want to see. For example, someone dealing with blackmail threats may not want repeated education prompts on that topic. The app should support emotional sensitivity. Useful protection should not repeatedly force the user to relive a stressful incident.

### Section 12 \- Personal Dashboard Adaptation

The Home screen should adapt based on the user's protection setup and current risk state. A new user should see setup steps, manual check options, and basic guidance. A user with linked email and message sharing should see recent reviewed items and protection source status. A user with an active recovery case should see the next recovery task near the top. A user with no urgent risks should see calm status and quick access to checks.

The adaptive dashboard should not rearrange everything unpredictably. Users need familiarity. The app should keep the same main areas: Check, Protection Hub, Cases, Recovery, Education, and Settings. What changes is priority and content inside those areas. The top module can adapt, but navigation should remain stable.

Dashboard modules can include: Check something now, Urgent item, Weekly check, Active recovery case, Recently checked, Protection status, Trusted helper request, Advised lesson, and Privacy reminder. Each module should have a clear purpose and one primary action. The dashboard should not become a wall of cards.

The app should include a Customize Home option. Users can choose whether to show education, recovery tasks, weekly check, recent items, or trusted helper requests. They should also be able to choose compact or detailed home layout. This helps different users make the app fit their habits.

The dashboard should have a calm empty state. If nothing needs attention, it should say something like: No urgent risks need action right now. It should then offer Check a message, Run weekly review, or Learn about a scam type. It should not create fake urgency just to fill space.

### Section 12 \- Accessibility Personalization

Accessibility personalization should be part of the product, not an afterthought. Scam protection often happens under stress, and people may need larger text, clearer contrast, voice-friendly guidance, simpler language, reduced motion, or fewer steps. the app should let users choose support that fits how they read and act.

The Accessibility Preferences screen should include text size, contrast, motion, reading level, button size, result detail, audio readout where supported, haptic alerts where supported, and screen privacy. These should be plain controls, not buried under technical settings.

The app should support Simplified Mode. Simplified Mode should reduce dense explanations, show one main action at a time, use larger buttons, and avoid technical details unless opened. This is useful for beginners, older adults, people under stress, and anyone who wants less clutter.

The app should support Detailed Mode for users who want more info. Detailed Mode can show evidence lists, advanced link details, sender analysis, case history, and technical explanations. The user should be able to switch between Simplified and Detailed without losing info.

Accessibility personalization should also apply to trusted helpers. A helper view should be easy to read, clear about what the helper can see, and structured around practical support. If the device owner uses Simplified Mode, shared helper views should still preserve the user's privacy choices.

### Section 12 \- Personalization Privacy Controls

Personalization requires strong privacy controls. The Privacy and Personalization screen should show exactly what is remembered. Categories can include trusted entities, user preferences, risk memory, case history, feedback, education progress, linked sources, and helper permissions. Each category should include View, Edit, Export, Pause, and Delete where appropriate.

The app should include a Pause Personalization control. Pausing personalization should stop new personal learning without deleting existing saved preferences. The user can later resume or delete. This is useful for people who want temporary privacy or who are helping someone else check a risky item.

The app should include a Delete Personal Memory option. This should explain what will be removed: trusted entities, personal warning adjustments, education progress, and remembered patterns. It should also explain what may remain if the user chooses to keep case evidence. Deleting personalization should not unexpectedly delete evidence unless the user chooses that too.

The app should include a Personalization Activity view. This view should show recent ways personalization affected results: trusted sender used, strict mode warning shown, similar prior case found, simple explanation selected, helper sharing limited by privacy setting. This makes the system understandable and auditable.

Privacy controls should be available before setup, during use, and during account deletion. A user should not have to contact support to understand or remove personal memory.

### Section 12 \- Multi-User Personalization Boundaries

If Verivae supports families, helpers, or multiple linked devices, personalization boundaries become especially important. The app should not mix one person's trusted contacts, risk memory, or preferences into another person's experience without permission. Each person should have their own protection profile.

A helper should not be able to silently train the device owner's app based on the helper's opinions. If a helper marks something safe, the app can record helper feedback in the case, but the device owner should control whether that affects future warnings. This prevents overreach and keeps the person being protected in control.

For shared devices, the app should include profiles or at least clear labels showing whose case and preferences are active. If the product does not support full profiles at first, it should warn users not to mix sensitive cases between people. The design should avoid accidental exposure of one person's private scam evidence to another person.

Family settings should be transparent. Each participant should see who can view alerts, who can review shared evidence, who can help with recovery, and who can manage settings. If permissions change, the app should show a clear notice inside the app.

### Section 12 \- Personalization Accept Rules

This detail is complete when the app has a clear design for personal protection profiles, protection levels, explanation styles, stress mode, trusted entities, risk memory, adaptive warnings, false alarm feedback, missed scam feedback, personalized education, adaptive dashboard modules, accessibility personalization, personalization privacy controls, and multi-user personalization boundaries.

The app should be able to become more helpful over time without becoming invasive. It should remember only what is useful, show what it remembers, let the user correct it, and avoid permanent trust that could hide real danger. It should make warnings more relevant while preserving serious protection. It should adapt the layout to the user's needs while keeping navigation stable and understandable.

### Section 12 completion note

Section 12 details the design brief with personal protection profiles, adaptive warning behavior, trusted entities, risk memory, feedback handling, personalized education, dashboard adaptation, accessibility preferences, personalization privacy controls, and multi-user boundaries while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 13: All-Area Functional Deepening and Layout Reinforcement

### Section 13 purpose

This detail strengthens every major area of the Verivae design brief at once. Instead of adding one isolated feature, this section reviews the app as a complete product and adds more detail to each major area so the design brief becomes more useful for future product decisions, interface design, user testing, and eventual development. The focus is still the app itself: what it does, how screens behave, how users move through it, how info is displayed, how warnings are explained, and how the app stays useful without becoming confusing.

This section defines app capability, user experience, and functional standards. It describes what Verivae should be able to show, guide, protect, organize, explain, and hand off when a user is dealing with suspicious messages, risky payment requests, account warnings, device concerns, evidence, recovery tasks, or trusted-helper review.

### Section 13 \- Area 1 Screen Experience Reinforcement

The screen-by-screen experience should make Verivae feel predictable from the first open. Every important screen should answer four basic user questions: Where am I, what does this screen do, what needs attention, and what can I do next? This matters because scam safety users may be anxious, embarrassed, rushed, or uncertain. The app should reduce the amount of thinking required before the user can take a safe action.

The Home screen should serve as the control center. It should not be a marketing page or a decorative welcome screen. It should show protection status, urgent items, manual check entry, weekly review status, active recovery cases, and privacy state. The first screen should make it clear that the user can check something immediately even if they have not linked email, messages, or devices. Manual checking must remain available because not every user will be comfortable connecting accounts.

The Check screen should remain one of the fastest paths in the app. The user should be able to check text, a screenshot, a link, a QR code, an email, a phone number, an attachment, a payment request, or a risky conversation. The layout should not require the user to know which scam type they are facing. Instead, the user should choose the form of evidence they have. The app can infer the likely scam category after analysis.

The Results screen should always lead with the plain result, then the reasoning, then the available actions. Users should not need to understand domain names, email auth, malware behavior, or fraud terminology before knowing whether to reply, click, pay, block, save, verify, or ask for help. The detailed evidence should be available, but it should not block the first decision.

The Cases screen should act like the user's scam notebook. It should store prior checks, linked evidence, recovery steps, helper comments, reports, and unresolved warnings. The user should be able to find a case by scam type, contact method, person or company name, link, phone number, payment method, or status. Search and filters should be visible enough for beginners.

The Settings screen should be understandable without technical language. It should contain privacy, personalization, linked accounts, trusted helpers, alerts, accessibility, data controls, and account deletion. It should not hide important controls under vague labels. If a setting changes what the app can see or remember, that effect should be explained beside the setting.

### Section 13 \- Area 2 Function Specification Reinforcement

Every function in the app should have a clear input, analysis behavior, result behavior, and next action. A function is not complete just because it can detect risk. It must also explain risk, handle uncertainty, preserve evidence when useful, connect to recovery when needed, and respect privacy settings.

Manual Scam Check should accept multiple evidence types and convert them into a common review structure. Whether the user pastes text, uploads a screenshot, scans a QR code, or shares a link, the result should be structured around claim, sender, requested action, urgency, money involvement, identity involvement, device involvement, evidence quality, confidence, and advised next step. This common structure makes the app easier to maintain and easier for the user to understand.

Automatic or linked checks should never make manual checks feel secondary. Linked checks can reduce effort, but manual checks give control. A professional app should support both because users have different comfort levels with permissions. The function specification should define each linked feature as optional and reversible.

Recovery functions should be triggered by risk context. A message asking for a login code should offer account protection steps. A payment request should offer payment response steps. A risky file should offer device safety review. A blackmail threat should offer privacy-first evidence handling and safe-exit behavior. The app should not show the same generic recovery checklist for every situation.

Reporting functions should transform messy evidence into clear summaries. The app should help users prepare info for banks, platforms, payment services, employers, schools, trusted helpers, and personal records. Reports should be editable, redaction-aware, and tied to cases. They should not include sensitive evidence by default without a review screen.

Education functions should be linked to real behavior. If a user repeatedly receives fake delivery texts, the app should suggest a short lesson on delivery scam patterns. If a user shared a login code, the app should explain why codes are sensitive. If a user receives fake investment messages, the app should explain pressure, unrealistic returns, and off-platform payment requests. Education should feel useful, not like filler content.

### Section 13 \- Area 3 User Flow and Edge Case Reinforcement

User flows should assume imperfect situations. Real users will upload blurry screenshots, paste incomplete messages, misunderstand prompts, abandon checks, deny permissions, accidentally delete evidence, receive conflicting info, or return to the app days later. The design brief should describe these imperfect paths so the app remains functional outside ideal conditions.

A risky-message flow should support a quick path and a detailed path. The quick path lets the user paste or share content, see a risk result, and choose a next action. The detailed path lets the user add sender info, screenshots, links, payment details, and conversation context. The app should not force the detailed path before giving basic guidance.

A money-loss flow should be more urgent. The app should ask what payment method was used, whether payment is pending or completed, whether the user has transaction details, and whether the scammer is still contacting them. It should create a recovery case immediately and show first actions before education content.

A shared-password flow should focus on account safety. The app should ask whether the password was unique, what account it belonged to, whether two-factor auth is enabled, whether the user still has access, and whether other accounts reuse the same password. The recovery checklist should adapt based on those answers.

A risky-file flow should distinguish between received, downloaded, opened, installed, and granted permissions. A file that was merely received may need deletion or evidence preservation. A file that was opened may require device review. An installed program or app may require stronger recovery steps. If remote access was granted, the app should treat that as risk and guide the user carefully.

Edge cases should include uncertainty. If the user is not sure whether they clicked, paid, shared, or installed something, the app should offer an Unsure path. The Unsure path should ask simple follow-up questions and choose cautious next steps without accusing the user of being careless.

### Section 13 \- Area 4 Interface Copy Reinforcement

The app's writing should be clear, calm, and specific. Scam protection copy must balance urgency with emotional safety. It should help the user act quickly when needed without using panic as a design tool. Every warning should explain what to do, why it matters, and what the user controls.

Risk labels should be consistent across the app. Suggested labels are Looks okay, Caution, Risky, Risk, and Could not fully check. Looks okay should not mean guaranteed safe. Caution should mean there are some warning signs or missing info. Risky should mean several scam signs are present. Risk should mean the user should stop before paying, replying, clicking, sharing codes, or entering info. Could not fully check should mean the app had limited evidence or platform restrictions.

Button copy should be action-based. Instead of vague buttons like Continue or Learn more, the app should use Check link, Save evidence, Open recovery steps, Ask trusted helper, Hide sensitive details, Review permissions, Mark as safe in this case, and Report a problem. Clear buttons reduce mistakes.

Explanations should avoid blame. The app should say: This message uses pressure, not You fell for pressure. It should say: This link may imitate your bank, not You clicked a fake bank link. It should say: Change this sectionword from a trusted device, not Your account is ruined. Language should preserve the user's dignity.

Legal and financial limits should be written plainly. The app should say it can guide, organize, and explain, but it cannot guarantee refunds, reverse payments, provide legal advice, or guarantee full device scanning on every platform. These limits should appear near relevant features, not only in terms and conditions.

### Section 13 \- Area 5 Visual Interface System Reinforcement

The visual system should communicate trust, clarity, and control. It should not look like a fear-based antivirus product filled with flashing danger signs. It should also not look overly playful, because users may be dealing with real money loss or identity risk. The visual tone should be calm, modern, readable, and practical.

Color should have a functional purpose. Green can represent no urgent issue. Yellow or amber can represent caution. Red should be reserved for risky moments. Blue or neutral colors can support info and guidance. The app should not rely on color alone because users may have color vision differences. Every status should also include text and icon cues.

Screen density should adapt to context. The Home screen can be moderately dense because users may check it repeatedly. Emergency recovery screens should be sparse and focused. Evidence Vault screens can be denser because they are used for reviewing details. Education screens should be comfortable and readable. Settings should be organized and direct.

Cards should be used for repeated objects such as cases, evidence items, linked sources, trusted entities, and tasks. Full page sections should not be turned into nested cards. The user should be able to scan repeated items without losing hierarchy. Important actions should remain visually stable across screen sizes.

Sensitive info should have visual privacy controls. The app should support blurred previews, hidden evidence, collapsed sensitive sections, and Safe Exit. When screen privacy is active, case cards should show broad labels instead of private details. This supports use in public spaces or around people the user does not want seeing the content.

### Section 13 \- Area 6 Privacy, Data, and Security Reinforcement

Privacy should be treated as a primary app feature. Users are sharing sensitive scam evidence, financial details, identity exposure, messages, emails, and device concerns. the app should make data handling understandable from inside the product. The user should not have to read a long legal policy to know what is stored.

Every evidence item should have a visible storage state. Examples include Not saved, Saved to case, Shared with helper, Included in report, Redacted copy created, or Deleted. This helps users understand what happened to their data. If the app reviews something temporarily without saving it, that should also be visible.

Data deletion should be granular. The user should be able to delete one evidence item, one case, all cases, personalization memory, linked account tokens, trusted helper access, or the entire account. Deletion screens should explain consequences clearly. For example, deleting evidence may remove it from future reports, while deleting personalization memory may not delete saved case evidence.

Linked permissions should be reviewed regularly. The app should show which services are linked, when access was last used, what purpose it serves, and how to disconnect. A permission should not remain mysterious. If email access is limited, expired, or dislinked, the app should show that clearly.

Security should also include account protection inside Verivae. The app should support strong auth, session review, device management, alert privacy, export controls, and sensitive-case locks. A scam safety app becomes a high-value target because it may contain evidence and private details. The design brief should assume the app itself must be protected carefully.

### Section 13 \- Area 7 Scam Detection Logic Reinforcement

Scam detection should be explainable. The app should not simply output a score and expect the user to trust it. Detection logic should turn signals into understandable reasons. A user should be able to see why something was flagged and what would make it safer or riskier.

Detection should combine content signals, context signals, behavior signals, technical signals, and user-provided context. Content signals include wording, urgency, threats, money requests, code requests, links, attachments, and impersonation claims. Context signals include whether the message was expected, whether the sender is known, whether the payment request matches normal behavior, and whether the user has seen similar messages before. Technical signals include link destination, redirects, sender domain, file type, and platform limits where available.

Confidence should be visible. A risky result with strong evidence should look different from a caution result based on limited evidence. The app should say when it has enough info and when it does not. If a screenshot is blurry, the app should say the review is limited. If a link cannot be safely opened, the app should say what was checked and what remains unknown.

The app should explain competing interpretations. A message may look like a normal delivery notice but include a risky short link. An invoice may be legitimate but include changed payment instructions. A person may be known to the user but using a new number. the app should show the key uncertainty rather than forcing a false yes-or-no answer.

Detection logic should include ongoing improvement controls. User feedback, trusted entities, missed scams, false alarms, and case outcomes can improve personalization, but private evidence should not automatically feed broad detection improvement without permission. This distinction should be written into the product behavior.

### Section 13 \- Area 8 Feature Specification Reinforcement

The feature set should feel linked. Manual checks, email review, message review, link checking, QR code checking, attachment review, device safety, weekly checks, cases, recovery, trusted helpers, reports, education, and personalization should not behave like unrelated tools. They should feed into a shared case model and a shared user experience.

A checked link should be able to become evidence in a case. A risky email should be able to open recovery steps. A weekly check should be able to find unresolved cases. A trusted helper review should be able to add comments to a case. A report should be able to include selected evidence and recovery actions. An education lesson should be able to connect back to checking or prevention.

Each feature should have a basic state and an advanced state. Basic state provides simple guidance for beginners. Advanced state reveals more detail for users who want it. This lets the same app serve users who want quick answers and users who want deeper investigation.

Features should also have failure states. If a provider connection fails, if a file cannot be scanned, if a message screenshot cannot be read, if a link times out, if a device check is limited, if evidence export fails, or if a helper invite expires, the app should show a useful explanation and a fallback action. A feature that only works in ideal conditions is not functionally complete.

The feature design should avoid dark patterns. The app should not hide basic protection behind confusing prompts. Paid options may exist later, but the core design should still define a useful free-first experience. The user should understand what is available, what is limited, and why.

### Section 13 \- Area 9 Scam Category Reinforcement

Scam categories should help the user recognize patterns without requiring them to label the scam correctly at the start. Categories can include bank impersonation, delivery scams, marketplace scams, romance scams, investment scams, job scams, fake invoices, tech support scams, account takeover attempts, login code theft, refund scams, gift card scams, crypto scams, charity scams, government impersonation, subscription scams, family emergency scams, blackmail threats, and malware delivery attempts.

Each category should have a consistent structure: what the scammer claims, what the scammer wants, common pressure tactics, evidence to preserve, risky actions to avoid, verification steps, recovery steps, and education prompts. This structure helps the app stay organized and helps future screens remain consistent.

Category pages should not overwhelm beginners. The first view should show a short explanation and common warning signs. Deeper views can show examples, variations, technical indicators, recovery guidance, and related categories. A category page should always include Check something now because education should connect back to action.

The app should support multi-category results. A scam may be both a job scam and a fake check scam. A romance scam may involve crypto. A bank impersonation scam may involve login code theft. the app should show primary and secondary categories instead of forcing one label.

Category handling should also support unknown and emerging scams. If the app does not recognize the exact category, it can still identify risky mechanics such as urgency, secrecy, money movement, impersonation, external links, remote access, or code sharing. The app should be useful even before it has a named category.

### Section 13 \- Area 10 Accessibility and Inclusive Design Reinforcement

Accessibility should shape every screen. Scam protection is not only for technical users. It should support beginners, older adults, disabled users, people under stress, people with limited literacy, people using small screens, people in noisy environments, people with color vision differences, and people who need help from someone they trust.

Text should be readable and scalable. Important warnings should not depend on tiny labels. Buttons should have clear targets. Critical actions should not be placed too close to destructive actions. Confirmation dialogs should be simple and specific. The app should avoid long dense paragraphs in high-stress screens.

The app should support plain explanations. Technical terms can exist behind detail panels, but the main path should use everyday language. If a technical term appears, the app should explain it. For example, domain can be explained as the website address a link goes to. Two-factor auth can be explained as an extra sign-in step, often a code or app approval.

The app should support assistive technology. Screen reader labels should describe buttons and status states clearly. Risk levels should be announced as text, not only color. Evidence lists should have meaningful item titles. Error messages should explain what happened and how to continue.

Inclusive design also means avoiding assumptions. The app should not assume every user has a bank account, a credit card, a printer, a second device, a trusted family member, paid antivirus software, or the confidence to call support. It should offer alternatives where possible.

### Section 13 \- Area 11 Screen States and Recovery Behavior Reinforcement

Every screen should define normal, empty, loading, limited, error, success, partial-success, offline, and privacy-protected states. These states are not cosmetic. They determine whether the app remains usable when something goes wrong.

A normal state shows available info and next actions. An empty state explains what can be done before the user has data. A loading state should be short and informative. A limited state should explain what could not be checked. An error state should provide a path forward. A success state should confirm what changed. A partial-success state should say what worked and what still needs attention.

Offline behavior matters. If the user has no internet, the app may still allow drafting notes, saving local evidence, viewing existing cases, reading downloaded education content, and preparing recovery tasks. It should clearly mark checks that require connection. Offline mode should not pretend analysis is current when it cannot reach needed services.

Privacy-protected states should be available on sensitive screens. If screen privacy is active, previews should be blurred, alerts should be discreet, and share views should hide private details by default. If the user uses Safe Exit, the app should return to a neutral screen and avoid showing sensitive recent history immediately.

Recovery behavior should account for interruptions. If the app closes during triage or report creation, it should save safe progress where appropriate. When the user returns, it should resume without losing context. It should also let the user discard a draft if they do not want it saved.

### Section 13 \- Area 12 Onboarding, Setup, Permissions, and Personalization Reinforcement

Onboarding should be short, optional where possible, and useful immediately. The app should not force the user to connect accounts before they can check a scam. The first-run experience should explain what the app does, what it needs permission for, and how the user stays in control.

The first setup should offer a simple path: Check something now, Set up protection, Learn how it works, or Invite a trusted helper. This lets users start from their real need. Someone who is actively worried about a message should not be forced through a long personalization wizard.

Permission screens should be feature-specific. Email access should explain email review. Message sharing should explain message checks. Alert permission should explain alerts. Device permission should explain device safety limits. Contacts access, if ever requested, should explain exactly why and should not be required for basic use. Permissions should be requested at the moment they become useful, not all at once during onboarding.

Personalization setup should be optional. The app can ask whether the user wants simple explanations, strict warnings, weekly reminders, screen privacy, and trusted helpers. The user should be able to skip and change these later. Skipping should not break the app.

Onboarding should include a trust-building privacy summary. It should say what the app can help with, what it will not do without permission, and where controls live. This should be short and visible. The app should earn permission rather than demand it.

### Section 13 \- Area 13 Complete App Blueprint Reinforcement

The complete app blueprint should tie every screen and function into one coherent system. The main navigation should remain stable: Home, Check, Protection Hub, Cases, Recovery, Education, and Settings. These names may change later, but the functional areas should remain distinct enough that users know where to go.

The Home area should summarize. The Check area should inspect. The Protection Hub should manage linked protection. The Cases area should organize evidence and history. The Recovery area should guide action after risk. The Education area should teach practical prevention. The Settings area should control privacy, personalization, accessibility, connections, and account management.

The blueprint should define how info moves. A message check can create a result. A result can create a case. A case can create recovery tasks. Recovery tasks can create notes and reports. Reports can include redacted evidence. Weekly checks can surface unresolved cases. Trusted helpers can review selected case items. Education can respond to repeated risk patterns. Personalization can adjust explanations and warning behavior while staying visible and controllable.

The blueprint should define what a professional first version must feel like. It must be useful without every advanced integration. It must support manual checks well. It must explain limits honestly. It must protect sensitive data. It must guide recovery clearly. It must not require the user to understand technical security concepts before taking safer action.

The blueprint should also define consistency standards. Similar screens should use similar layouts. Similar warnings should use similar labels. Similar evidence items should have similar cards. Similar recovery tasks should have similar statuses. Consistency will make the app easier to build, easier to test, and easier for users to trust.

### Section 13 \- Cross-Area Functional Cohesion

Across all areas, the app should use a shared object model in user-facing terms. The major objects are checks, results, cases, evidence, tasks, reports, trusted entities, helpers, devices, permissions, and lessons. Users do not need to know the technical database structure, but the product should behave as if these objects are linked.
