A check is the user's request to review something. A result is the app's answer. A case is a container for related scam activity. Evidence is material the user saves. A task is something the user may need to do. A report is a shareable summary. A trusted entity is something familiar. A helper is a person allowed to support the user. A device is a protected phone, tablet, or computer. A permission controls what the app can access. A lesson teaches a pattern.

When these objects are consistent, the app becomes easier to understand. For example, every evidence item should be able to belong to a case. Every result should be able to become evidence if the user chooses. Every recovery task should belong to a case or a device safety review. Every report should list exactly which evidence items it includes. Every helper access should show what case or evidence it applies to.

The app should avoid dislinked one-off screens. If a user checks a link from the Education area, that check should still appear in case history if saved. If a user starts recovery from a Result screen, the Recovery Workspace should know which evidence triggered it. If a user changes privacy settings, report sharing and helper views should respect those settings.

### Section 13 \- Cross-Area Beginner Friendliness

Beginner friendliness should be visible in every area. The app should not assume the user knows the difference between a phishing link, malware attachment, spoofed sender, remote access app, chargeback, account recovery, or identity monitoring. It should explain unfamiliar terms at the point of use.

A beginner-friendly app uses progressive detail. The first layer gives the answer. The second layer explains the reason. The third layer shows evidence. The fourth layer gives advanced details. This keeps the app usable for beginners without limiting advanced users.

The app should use examples carefully. Examples should be realistic and short. They should not copy actual private user evidence into education screens without permission. They should help users recognize patterns such as urgency, secrecy, money movement, identity requests, link tricks, and impersonation.

Beginner support should include undo, back, skip, not sure, ask for help, and save for later. These options reduce pressure. A user should not feel trapped by a question they cannot answer. The app can still provide cautious guidance when answers are incomplete.

### Section 13 \- Cross-Area Professional Success Standard

For Verivae to feel professional, every major function should meet a success standard: it must be understandable, actionable, honest, privacy-aware, recoverable from errors, and linked to the rest of the app. A feature should not be considered complete if it only produces a result but does not tell the user what to do next.

Understandable means the user knows what happened. Actionable means the user knows what to do. Honest means the app explains uncertainty and limits. Privacy-aware means sensitive info is protected by default. Recoverable means errors and interruptions have a path forward. Linked means the feature can link to cases, recovery, reports, education, or settings where appropriate.

This standard should apply to every area of the app: manual checks, email review, message review, link review, QR scanning, attachment review, device safety, weekly checks, trusted helpers, recovery tasks, evidence vault, report builder, education, onboarding, accessibility, and personalization.

### Section 13 completion note

Section 13 details the design brief across all major areas by reinforcing screen experience, function specifications, user flows, interface copy, visual system, privacy and security, scam detection logic, feature cohesion, scam categories, accessibility, screen states, onboarding, personalization, the complete app blueprint, beginner friendliness, and professional functional standards while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 14: Scenario-Based Function and Layout Deepening

### Section 14 purpose

This detail deepens Verivae by describing how the app should behave in real-world scam situations. A design brief becomes stronger when it does not only list features, but also explains how those features work together during specific user moments. People do not usually open a scam safety app thinking in product categories. They open it because a message scared them, a payment request feels strange, a loved one may be in trouble, an account warning looks urgent, a file may be unsafe, or they already did something and need help deciding what to do next.

This section defines what the app should show, ask, explain, save, and connect across common user scenarios. It focuses on the in-app experience: user prompts, result screens, recovery tools, privacy boundaries, and feature handoffs.

### Section 14 \- Scenario Design Principle

The scenario design principle is that the app should understand the user's situation before overwhelming them with features. A user should not have to decide whether they need the Evidence Vault, Recovery Workspace, Protection Hub, Link Checker, Education Library, or Trusted Helper flow. The app should infer the most useful next area based on what the user shares and what risk appears.

Every scenario should begin with one simple intake question: What are you worried about? The user can answer by choosing a plain option such as a message, email, link, payment request, account warning, file, phone call, person, device, or not sure. The app should then adapt the next screen to that concern. This keeps the experience beginner-friendly and reduces decision fatigue.

Scenario handling should avoid rigid paths. A fake bank text can involve a link, a login code, a payment request, and account takeover risk. A job scam can involve identity info, fake checks, bank details, and messaging outside the hiring platform. A romance scam can involve emotional pressure, money movement, crypto, private photos, and secrecy. the app should allow a case to evolve as more evidence is added.

The interface should show a scenario label only when it helps. For example, the app can say: This looks like a bank impersonation pattern. It should not force the user to choose a label before checking. The app should always prioritize the immediate decision: reply or not, click or not, pay or not, share or not, open or not, install or not, call or not, save evidence or not.

### Section 14 \- Fake Bank Alert Scenario

The fake bank alert scenario begins when the user receives a text, email, phone call, or push-style message claiming there is a problem with a bank account, card, payment, login, fraud alert, or frozen account. The app should assume this is a high-stress scenario because the user may fear losing money or being locked out.

The intake screen should ask what the message wants the user to do. Options can include tap a link, call a number, reply yes or no, share a code, confirm a transaction, move money, download an app, or not sure. This question is more useful than asking the user whether it is a scam because the requested action usually reveals the risk.

The result screen should clearly separate official-looking branding from verified safety. It should explain that a message can use a bank name, logo, or urgent wording without actually being from the bank. If the sender info or link does not match the trusted bank entry, the app should highlight that mismatch. If the user has not set a trusted bank entry, the app should still recommend verifying through the banking app or a number from the back of the card, not the risky message.

The layout should show a Stop Before You Do This panel when the message asks for codes, passwords, remote access, or money movement. The panel should say exactly which action is risky. For example: Do not share this login code with the sender. Codes are meant to prove it is you, and a scammer can use one to get into your account. The app should offer a safer action: open the banking app directly, call a known number, or check recent transactions from a trusted path.

If the user already clicked the link or shared info, the scenario should open a recovery path. It should ask whether the user entered login details, shared a code, made a payment, downloaded an app, or gave remote access. Based on the answer, the app should create account recovery tasks, payment response tasks, and device safety tasks as needed.

### Section 14 \- Fake Invoice or Business Payment Scenario

The fake invoice scenario covers emailed invoices, payment change requests, vendor impersonation, subscription renewals, business email compromise, fake purchase orders, payroll changes, and refund requests. This scenario matters because fake invoices can look professional and may not use obvious scam language.

The intake screen should ask whether the invoice or payment request was expected. The user can answer expected, unexpected, partly expected, or not sure. The app should also ask whether payment details changed, whether the sender is familiar, whether the amount matches expectations, whether urgency is present, and whether the message asks to keep the request secret or bypass normal approval.

The result layout should include an Invoice Consistency section. This section should compare the current request against known or user-provided expectations: sender, business name, payment destination, amount, timing, wording, attachment, and link. If the app does not have prior history, it should guide the user to verify through a known contact method.

The app should include a Payment Change Warning pattern. If an email asks the user to update bank details, wire money to a new account, pay through gift cards, use crypto, or send payment to a personal account, the app should treat that as a serious warning. The app should explain that payment changes are often used in business scams and should be verified outside the message thread.

The scenario should support workplace and small-business users without assuming they have a security team. The app can offer a verification checklist: confirm with the vendor using a known phone number, compare with past invoices, ask a second person to review, avoid using contact details from the risky message, and save evidence before deleting anything.

If money was sent, the app should open the Payment Response flow and create a report focused on invoice details, payment method, recipient info, transaction ID, sender address, attachments, and the reason the user believed the invoice might be legitimate.

### Section 14 \- Marketplace Buyer or Seller Scenario

Marketplace scams can involve fake buyers, fake sellers, overpayment, shipping tricks, fake escrow, fake payment screenshots, stolen listings, refund pressure, and requests to move off-platform. the app should treat marketplace scams as conversation-based and payment-based at the same time.

The intake screen should ask whether the user is buying, selling, renting, trading, or not sure. Then it should ask what the other person wants: pay outside the platform, receive a code, use a shipping service, accept overpayment, refund extra money, use a payment app, click a link, provide email or phone, or move to another app.

The result screen should show the marketplace pattern. For example: This resembles an overpayment scam because the other person claims they sent too much and asks you to return the difference. Or: This resembles a fake payment confirmation because the screenshot is not proof that money has cleared. The app should use plain examples.

The layout should include a Safe Transaction Checklist. It should recommend staying on-platform when possible, avoiding refunds for overpayment until funds are verified, not sharing login codes, checking payment status inside the actual payment app, avoiding shipping labels from unknown sources, and preserving the conversation.

Marketplace cases should support evidence from multiple sources: listing screenshots, user profile screenshots, message screenshots, payment screenshots, shipping labels, email confirmations, links, and notes. The app should let the user group these into one case with tabs for Listing, Messages, Payment, Shipping, Links, and Reports.

### Section 14 \- Romance, Friendship, or Emotional Pressure Scenario

Romance and emotional pressure scams require careful design because the user may feel attached, ashamed, defensive, or afraid. The app should avoid sounding dismissive. It should not tell the user that someone they care about is definitely fake unless evidence is strong. It should focus on patterns, requested actions, and safety.

The intake screen should ask what is happening in neutral terms: someone is asking for money, someone has an emergency, someone wants gift cards, someone wants crypto, someone asks for private photos, someone asks to keep the relationship secret, someone refuses video or in-person verification, someone wants to move conversations, or the user is unsure.

The result screen should use pattern-based language: This conversation includes emotional pressure and money requests, which are common in romance and friendship scams. The app should then show specific signals, such as urgency, secrecy, repeated emergencies, pressure to send money, refusal to verify identity, inconsistent stories, and requests for payment methods that are hard to recover.

The layout should include a Pause and Verify panel. This panel should encourage the user to slow down, avoid sending more money or private images, talk to a trusted person, preserve messages, and verify identity through safer methods. It should not mock the user or imply they are naive.

If threats, blackmail, intimate image abuse, self-harm claims, or coercion are involved, the app should switch into Sensitive Safety Mode. Sensitive Safety Mode should hide previews by default, make Safe Exit visible, avoid lock-screen alert details, and guide evidence preservation carefully. The app should be clear when external support may be needed, while staying within its role as an app that organizes and guides.

### Section 14 \- Job Offer and Work-from-Home Scenario

Job scams can be attractive because they look like opportunities. They may include fake recruiters, fake interviews, equipment checks, fake checks, identity requests, paid training, package forwarding, crypto tasks, or requests to buy supplies through a specific vendor. the app should help the user evaluate the offer without assuming every unusual job is fake.

The intake screen should ask where the job came from: job board, email, text, social media, messaging app, referral, company website, or unknown. It should ask whether the user had an interview, whether the company domain matches the claimed company, whether money or equipment is involved, whether the user was asked for ID docs early, and whether the user is being rushed.

The result layout should show a Hiring Legitimacy section. It should look at company identity, email domain, interview process, payment requests, check deposits, equipment purchases, job duties, salary claims, and communication channel. The app should explain if a request is unusual for a normal hiring process.

The app should include a Fake Check Warning. If the job asks the user to deposit a check and send money back, buy equipment, pay a vendor, or move funds before the check fully clears, the app should flag this as risk. The explanation should be simple: a deposited check can appear available before the bank determines it is fake, and the user may still be responsible if they send money out.

Job scam cases should support identity exposure review. If the user sent a resume, ID, Social Security number or similar identity number, bank details, direct deposit form, or tax form, the app should open the Identity Info Response flow and help the user track what was shared.

### Section 14 \- Remote Access and Tech Support Scenario

Remote access scams are risk because the scammer may see the user's screen, control the device, access accounts, install tools, or pressure the user while watching. The app should treat this scenario with clear urgency and direct steps.

The intake screen should ask whether someone told the user to install an app, share a screen, read a code, grant accessibility permissions, open a remote support tool, visit a support website, or move money for safety. It should ask whether the person claimed to be from a bank, tech company, government agency, delivery company, employer, or antivirus company.

If remote access may be active, the result screen should prioritize immediate safety. It can say: Stop interacting with the caller or sender. Do not enter passwords while they can see your screen. If you believe someone can control the device, use another trusted device for password changes. The app should then open device safety and account recovery steps.

The layout should include a Device Control Checklist. It should guide the user to disconnect risky remote access, review installed apps where possible, check permissions, restart if appropriate, change important passwords from another device, review bank and email activity, and save evidence. Exact steps may vary by platform, so the app should adapt to phone, tablet, desktop, Android, iOS, Windows, or Mac where applicable.

The scenario should be honest about scanning limits. If the app cannot fully scan a device, it should still help the user identify remote-access signs, risky apps, risky downloads, permission changes, account activity, and follow-up tasks.

### Section 14 \- QR Code and Public Poster Scenario

QR scams can appear on parking meters, restaurant menus, flyers, packages, event signs, mailers, fake notices, or payment requests. Users may scan a QR code without seeing the destination first. the app should make QR checking feel quick and safe.

The QR flow should begin with camera scan or screenshot upload. The app should decode the QR code without opening the destination automatically. The first result should show the destination domain, whether it is shortened, whether it redirects, what kind of action it appears to request, and whether it resembles a known brand or payment page.

The layout should include a Before Opening section. This section should say whether the QR code appears to lead to payment, login, download, contact form, map, menu, ticket, or unknown destination. If the QR code is attached to a payment request, the app should recommend verifying through the official website or app.

For public-place QR codes, the app should ask context: where did you see it? Options can include parking meter, restaurant, package, mail, sign, event, school, workplace, social post, or other. Context helps determine whether the destination makes sense.

If the user already opened the QR link and entered info, the app should ask what was entered and route to account recovery, payment response, identity response, or device review as needed.

### Section 14 \- Family Helper Scenario

A family helper scenario happens when one person is helping another review a risky item. This may involve a parent, adult child, spouse, sibling, friend, caregiver, or trusted coworker. The design must support help without taking control away from the person being helped.

The user should be able to share a single case or selected evidence with a helper. The helper view should show the risk summary, evidence the user chose to share, suggested questions, advised next actions, and privacy boundaries. The helper should not see unrelated cases or private app settings unless the user grants that access.

The app should include a Prepare for Helper Review screen. This screen lets the user choose what to share: summary only, selected screenshots, selected messages, payment details, recovery tasks, or full case. Sensitive details should be highlighted before sharing. The user should be able to redact info first.

Helper comments should appear inside the case as helper notes, not as app conclusions. If a helper says something is safe or unsafe, the app should show that as helper input while preserving the app's own risk analysis. This avoids confusion between personal opinion and detection result.

The app should include an end-helper-access control. The user should be able to remove helper access from a case or from the account. The app should show what access was removed and whether prior shared exports still exist outside the app.

### Section 14 \- Repeated Scam Campaign Scenario

Some users may receive repeated versions of the same scam. The messages may come from different numbers, emails, or accounts but use the same link, brand impersonation, wording, payment request, or threat. the app should help users see patterns across repeated events.

The repeated campaign layout should appear inside Cases or Risk Memory. It should say: Similar items have appeared before. Then it should show what is similar: phone number, domain, phrase, payment method, impersonated company, sender name, file name, QR destination, or requested action.

The app should let users group repeated items into one campaign case. This keeps the case list cleaner and helps the user avoid reviewing the same pattern from scratch every time. It should also allow separation if the app guessed incorrectly.

The repeated campaign screen should include bulk actions where appropriate: block or report related senders where platform support exists, save all related evidence, mark duplicates, add a trusted helper, create one report, or archive resolved items. If platform support does not allow direct blocking, the app should provide guided steps.

Education should adapt to repeated campaigns. If the user repeatedly receives fake bank texts, the app should suggest bank impersonation prevention. If the user repeatedly receives package texts, it should suggest delivery scam education. If the user repeatedly receives investment pitches, it should suggest investment scam warning signs.

### Section 14 \- Scenario Result Layout Standard

Every scenario result should use a consistent layout so the user does not have to relearn the app each time. The advised structure is: risk summary, immediate safe action, scenario pattern, evidence, uncertainty, next steps, save options, helper options, and related learning.

The risk summary should be one sentence. The immediate safe action should be visible without scrolling. The scenario pattern should explain what type of scam behavior the app sees. Evidence should show the specific signs. Uncertainty should explain what the app could not confirm. Next steps should be sorted by priority. Save options should let the user create or update a case. Helper options should let the user share selected details. Related learning should be optional and lower priority.

The app should not make every scenario look equally urgent. A risky link that was not opened is different from a remote access session that may still be active. A fake invoice not yet paid is different from a completed wire transfer. The layout should adapt urgency while keeping the structure familiar.

Scenario results should also support user correction. The user may say this is expected, this sender is known, this invoice is legitimate, I already verified it, I made a mistake in the details, or this is worse than shown. Corrections should update the case and personalization only with the user's knowledge.

### Section 14 \- Scenario Accept Rules

This detail is complete when the app has scenario-level design coverage for fake bank alerts, fake invoices, marketplace scams, romance or emotional pressure, job offers, remote access, QR codes, family helper review, repeated scam campaigns, and standard scenario result layouts.

The app should be able to move from a user's real-world concern into the correct combination of check, result, case, evidence, recovery, helper sharing, education, privacy control, and device review. The user should not need to understand the app's internal feature categories before getting useful help. Every scenario should preserve dignity, explain uncertainty, provide immediate next actions, and keep sensitive data under user control.

### Section 14 completion note

Section 14 details the design brief with scenario-based behavior for bank alerts, invoices, marketplaces, romance and emotional pressure, job offers, remote access, QR codes, family helper review, repeated scam campaigns, and consistent scenario result layouts while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 15: Full-System Functional Integration and Screen Behavior Deepening

### Section 15 purpose

This detail deepens Verivae as a complete app system. The goal is to make the brief more useful for a future app design and dev team by describing how the major features should connect, how screens should behave under real user pressure, how info should move from one area to another, and how the app should stay practical even when evidence is incomplete or platform permissions are limited. The app should feel like one coordinated protection system, not a collection of separate checkers.

This section stays within the app design scope: functions, screens, layout, user flows, safety behavior, privacy behavior, detection behavior, recovery behavior, accessibility, and user experience. Harborwake remains the company name. The app name remains Verivae.

### Section 15 \- Complete App System Principle

The complete system principle for the app is that every important user action should produce a useful next state. If the user checks a message, the app should not stop at a label. It should create a result, explain the evidence, offer next actions, allow saving to a case, offer helper review when appropriate, and open recovery if harm may have happened. If the user starts from recovery, the app should still connect back to evidence, reports, account safety, device safety, education, and privacy controls. If the user starts from a weekly check, the app should surface unresolved cases and risky patterns rather than act like a separate maintenance tool.

The app should be organized around a small number of stable concepts: checks, results, cases, evidence, tasks, reports, trusted entities, helpers, devices, lessons, permissions, and personal memory. A beginner does not need to know these as technical objects, but the interface should behave consistently around them. A check is something the user asks the app to review. A result is the app's answer. A case is a folder for related risk. Evidence is saved material. A task is something the user may need to do. A report is a shareable summary. A trusted entity is something familiar but not automatically safe. A helper is a person allowed to support the user. A device is a phone, computer, tablet, or linked system being reviewed. A lesson is practical learning attached to real risk. A permission controls what the app may access or remember.

The system should avoid dead ends. A result screen should not leave the user wondering what to do. A permissions screen should not just say access denied. A failed file review should still explain what the user can do next. A risky message should connect to recovery. A resolved case should connect to education or prevention if useful. A false alarm should let the user correct the result. A missed scam should let the user open recovery and give feedback without being blamed.

### Section 15 \- Navigation and Core Screen Integration

The main navigation should remain stable and should support repeated use. The advised main areas are Home, Check, Protection Hub, Cases, Recovery, Education, and Settings. These names can be refined later, but the functional separation should remain. Home summarizes what matters now. Check lets the user review something manually. Protection Hub manages linked sources and device safety. Cases stores evidence and history. Recovery guides action after risk. Education teaches prevention and pattern recognition. Settings controls privacy, permissions, accessibility, helpers, personalization, and account choices.

The Home screen should adapt without becoming unpredictable. Its top area should show the most important current state: no urgent risks, risky item waiting, weekly check ready, recovery task due, permission issue, or helper request. The main action should always be visible: Check something now. A user who opens the app while anxious should not have to hunt for the manual check. Below that, the Home screen can show active cases, protection source status, recent checks, weekly check status, and advised learning.

The Check screen should be the fastest path in the app. It should support text, screenshot, link, QR code, email, message, attachment, phone number, payment request, conversation, and not sure. The Not sure path matters because many beginners will not know what category they have. The Check screen should ask for the evidence form first, not the scam type. The app can identify the likely scam type after review.

The Protection Hub should show linked protection sources in one place. Email, messages, browser links, QR scanning, attachments, device safety, weekly checks, helpers, and reports should each have a state: ready, not linked, limited, paused, needs attention, or recently checked. The screen should explain what each source can do in plain text. It should also show when a platform limitation prevents full background monitoring or full device scanning.

The Cases screen should be a structured evidence and history area. A case should not be only a log. It should show overview, evidence, risk pattern, timeline, recovery tasks, helper activity, reports, and final status. A user should be able to search cases by sender, phone number, email, link, payment method, scam type, status, helper, or date-like relative period without needing technical search syntax.

### Section 15 \- Manual Scam Check Deepening

Manual Scam Check should be designed as the app's universal intake system. Even if linked integrations become advanced later, manual checking is the free-first and permission-light way for users to get help. The manual check should accept incomplete evidence and still provide a useful answer. It should not require account connection, paid setup, or technical knowledge.

The manual check layout should begin with evidence options. The user can choose Paste text, Upload screenshot, Check link, Scan QR code, Upload file, Describe what happened, Enter phone number, Enter email address, or Not sure. Each option should show a short explanation only when needed. For example, Upload screenshot can say: Use this if the message is in another app. Describe what happened can say: Use this if you already interacted and need next steps.

After intake, the app should create a review summary before showing a final result. The summary should show what the app understood: sender, claimed organization, requested action, money involvement, identity involvement, link or file involvement, urgency, and missing info. If the app misunderstood the evidence, the user should be able to correct it before saving the result. This is important because screenshots may be blurry, copied text may lose sender details, and users may omit context.

Manual check should support layered results. The first layer should be a clear risk label and safest next action. The second layer should show the main reasons. The third layer should show evidence details. The fourth layer should offer case saving, recovery, helper review, reporting, and learning. This layered structure keeps beginner use simple while preserving detail for deeper review.

Manual check should also support multiple items in one review. A scam often includes a message, link, screenshot, payment request, and follow-up text. The user should be able to add another item before or after the result. The app should then decide whether to update the same result, create a case, or suggest linking to an existing case.

### Section 15 \- Email and Gmail-Style Review Deepening

Email review should cover both manual and linked modes. Manual mode lets the user paste email text, upload screenshots, check a link, or upload an attachment. Linked mode, where allowed, lets the user connect an inbox and review selected risky items. The design should not assume unlimited email access. It should explain provider limits clearly.

The email result should separate identity, content, links, attachments, and requested action. Identity includes sender name, sender address, reply-to address, claimed organization, and domain match. Content includes urgency, threats, unusual tone, grammar, invoice language, account warning language, job offer language, or refund language. Links include visible text, destination, redirects, shorteners, brand impersonation, and login requests. Attachments include file type, file name, risky document behavior, and whether the file could be reviewed. Requested action includes pay, reply, call, share code, reset password, open file, download app, or move conversation.

For Gmail-style review, the app should present privacy choices before connection. Basic review can mean the user selects specific emails to check. Standard review can mean the app reviews risky items the user shares or flags. Deeper review should be optional and clearly explained. The interface should say what is reviewed, what is stored, and how to disconnect. If provider rules prevent a promised behavior, the app should show that limitation rather than hiding it.

Email review should include sender comparison against trusted entities. If a sender claims to be a familiar company but uses a new domain, the app should call out the mismatch. If an invoice claims to be from a known vendor but payment details changed, the app should show payment-change risk. If the user expected the email, the app should still check for link mismatch, attachment risk, and altered payment instructions.

Email review should support business and personal contexts without forcing the user into a business account. A user may check an invoice from a personal Gmail account, a professional Gmail account, or a small company inbox. The app should ask for context only when it changes guidance: personal purchase, workplace payment, vendor invoice, job offer, account warning, subscription notice, or unknown.

### Section 15 \- Message and Text Review Deepening

Message review should handle text messages, screenshots from messaging apps, social messages, marketplace chats, dating app conversations, family emergency messages, and copied conversation text. Because platform access varies, the app should support direct sharing, screenshots, copy-paste, and manual description. The product should be useful even when the OS does not allow direct message scanning.

The message review layout should show conversation context without exposing too much on screen. The first result should not display every private message by default. It should summarize the pattern and let the user expand specific evidence. Sensitive lines should be collapsible. If the user is sharing the screen with a helper, the app should offer a privacy view.

Message analysis should pay attention to progression. Many scams are not obvious in one message. The app should look for escalation: friendly opener, trust building, urgency, secrecy, emotional pressure, code request, payment request, link, file, remote access, or threat. A conversation timeline should show when the risk increased. This helps the user understand why something that started normally became dangerous.

Message results should include reply guidance. The app can recommend not replying, verifying through a trusted contact path, blocking, reporting, saving evidence, asking a helper, or moving to recovery. It should not generate aggressive replies that could escalate risk. In sensitive cases, it should recommend avoiding further contact and preserving evidence.

Message review should also handle known-contact impersonation. If a message claims to be from a family member, boss, friend, school, bank, marketplace buyer, or delivery service, the app should recommend verifying through a contact method already trusted by the user. It should explain that caller ID, display names, and message wording can be misleading.

### Section 15 \- Link and QR Checking Deepening

Link and QR checking should be designed around the idea that users often need to know whether to open something before they open it. The app should let users paste a URL, share a URL from another app, scan a QR code, upload a screenshot containing a URL, or check a link found inside an email or message. The app should not automatically open risky links as part of the user's normal browser session.

The link result should show the visible link, final destination, redirect chain when available, domain, claimed brand, page purpose, risk level, and safest next action. For beginners, this should be plain: This link says it is your bank, but it goes to a different website. For advanced users, the app can show redirects, domain age if available, unusual characters, shorteners, country-code domains, and technical notes.

QR checking should decode first and open later only if the user chooses. The screen should say where the QR code appears to go and what action it appears to request. A QR code leading to payment, login, app download, crypto address, or shortened link should get stronger warnings. The user should be able to save the QR result as evidence and add context such as parking meter, mail notice, restaurant, package, event, school, workplace, or social post.

Link checking should connect to trusted entities and risk memory. If the app has seen the same risky domain before, it should show that. If the link claims to be a trusted company but uses a different domain, it should show the mismatch. If the user previously marked a domain safe in one context, the app should still check new behavior instead of assuming permanent safety.

The link and QR screens should include safe alternatives. If a bank link is risky, the app should recommend opening the banking app directly or typing the bank's address manually. If a delivery link is risky, it should suggest checking the carrier's official app or website. If a payment QR is risky, it should suggest verifying through the official provider.

### Section 15 \- Attachment, File, and Device Safety Deepening

Attachment review should help the user decide whether a file is safe to open, whether it should be saved as evidence, and whether opening it may have created risk. The app should support screenshots, PDFs, documents, images, compressed files, installers, payment receipts, invoice files, and unknown files where platform support allows. It should be honest when it cannot fully inspect a file.

The attachment result should show file name, file type, source, context, visible content when safe, risk signs, limitations, and next action. It should warn about macros, password-protected documents, hidden links, executable installers, risky compressed files, fake invoice attachments, fake resume attachments, and files that ask the user to enable editing or bypass warnings.

Device safety should be framed as Device Safety Review rather than guaranteed virus removal. On some devices, full scanning may not be possible. The app should still review shared files, risky links, risky settings, recent scam interactions, installed-app concerns where available, account sessions, and recovery tasks. If the user expects a virus scan, the app should explain what it can check and what requires built-in system tools or a trusted security product.

Weekly Deep Check should combine device safety, linked sources, unresolved cases, recent risky links, risky attachments, account safety prompts, helper requests, education advices, and privacy review. It should not be a fake progress animation. It should be a guided review with visible categories and honest results: checked, needs attention, limited by permission, skipped, or could not check.

When device risk is linked to a scam case, the app should show the link. For example: This device review is advised because you opened a file from the Fake Invoice case. Or: This account review is advised because you shared a login code in the Bank Alert case. This makes safety tasks feel relevant instead of random.

### Section 15 \- Scam Result Screen Deepening

The scam result screen is one of the most important screens in the app. It should be designed for fast understanding under stress. The result should never be only a score. It should include a plain risk label, a one-sentence summary, the safest immediate action, key evidence, uncertainty, and next options.

The top of the result screen should include risk level and immediate advice. Examples include: Do not tap the link yet, Do not send money, Do not share this code, Verify through a known contact method, Save this as evidence, or Open recovery steps. The advice should match the actual risk. A low-confidence result should not sound certain. A risky result should not be vague.

The evidence section should show why the app reached the result. Evidence should be grouped by type: sender, link, wording, requested action, payment, identity, file, device, conversation pattern, trusted entity mismatch, or similar prior case. Each evidence item should explain its meaning. For example: The sender asks for a login code. Codes are usually meant to stay private and can be used to access an account.

The uncertainty section should be visible when needed. If the app cannot confirm the sender, cannot inspect a password-protected file, cannot access message metadata, cannot safely follow a link, or cannot scan the full device, it should say so. This makes the app more credible and helps the user know what to verify manually.

The result screen should always include next actions. Actions can include save to case, create new case, add to existing case, open recovery, ask trusted helper, report or block, check related link, check attachment, run device review, review account safety, learn about this scam type, mark as false alarm, or provide missed-scam feedback.

### Section 15 \- Evidence Vault and Case Continuity Deepening

The Evidence Vault should be designed as a user-controlled record of what happened. It should preserve original evidence, app analysis, user notes, helper comments, recovery actions, reports, and sharing history. Evidence should be organized by case because users think in situations, not databases.

Each evidence item should have a clear origin. The app should show whether it came from manual upload, screenshot, shared email, shared message, link check, QR scan, file review, device review, helper note, report, or user note. It should also show whether the item is original, extracted text, app analysis, redacted copy, or export version.

Case continuity means the app should remember the relationship between evidence and action. If a risky link created a recovery task, the case should show that link as the reason. If a payment report included a screenshot, the case should show that the screenshot was included. If a helper reviewed an item, the case should show which item they saw. This helps the user understand the chain of events.

The app should support evidence cleanup without breaking the case. If the user deletes an evidence item, reports that used it may need to show that the item was removed. If the user redacts evidence, the original should remain private unless deleted. If the user marks an item as duplicate, it should remain traceable but not clutter the main view.

Case views should have privacy modes. Standard view can show normal details. Private view can blur sensitive details. Helper view can show only selected evidence. Export review can show exactly what will leave the app. These modes should be consistent across the Evidence Vault, Recovery Workspace, and Report Builder.

### Section 15 \- Recovery Workspace Deepening

The Recovery Workspace should turn a risk result into a clear action path. It should not assume all scams require the same response. It should ask what happened, what was shared, whether money moved, whether accounts may be exposed, whether a file was opened, whether remote access was granted, and whether threats or emotional pressure are present.

Recovery should be built around triage. Triage means sorting actions by priority. The first tasks should reduce immediate harm. If money moved, contact payment provider and preserve transaction evidence. If a password was shared, change it from a trusted device and review sessions. If a login code was shared, secure the account quickly. If remote access was granted, stop screen control and use another trusted device for account changes. If identity info was shared, document what was exposed and prepare monitoring or official-report steps where appropriate.

Recovery tasks should have clear detail screens. Each task should explain why it matters, what the user needs, what steps to take, what evidence to save, what to do if blocked, and how to mark completion. Statuses should include not started, in progress, waiting, blocked, complete, skipped, and no longer needed.

The Recovery Workspace should also include communication helpers. The app should help users write bank support summaries, payment provider messages, platform reports, employer security notes, school technology office messages, and trusted-helper summaries. Every generated message should be editable and should show what evidence it includes.

Recovery should avoid shame. The app should say what to do next without blaming the user. It should handle sensitive cases with privacy controls, Safe Exit, hidden previews, and careful sharing. A user should be able to pause recovery, return later, and continue from the next task.

### Section 15 \- Payment and Account Recovery Deepening

Payment recovery should be specific to payment type. Debit card, credit card, bank transfer, wire transfer, payment app, marketplace payment, gift card, crypto, check, subscription charge, and cash all require different guidance. The app should ask what method was used and whether payment is pending, completed, blocked, or uncertain.

The Payment Response screen should collect details without forcing the user to know everything. Useful fields include payment method, amount if known, recipient name or handle, transaction ID, payment time if known, screenshot, reason given by the scammer, platform used, and whether the user has contacted the provider. Unknown should always be an accepted answer.

The payment flow should create a neutral summary for support conversations. The app should not promise a refund. It should prepare the user to ask about fraud review, dispute options, reversal options, account freeze, monitoring, and next steps. The summary should be factual and editable.

Account recovery should distinguish between still have access and lost access. If the user still has access, the app should guide password change, session sign-out, recovery email and phone review, two-factor auth, app permissions, forwarding rules for email accounts, payment method review, and risky activity checks. If access is lost, the app should help gather ownership proof and guide the user to provider recovery paths without pretending it can restore the account directly.

Account recovery should also handle reused passwords. If the user shared a password that may be used elsewhere, the app should create related tasks for other accounts. The app should explain that password reuse can spread risk across services.

### Section 15 \- Trusted Helper and Family Review Deepening

Trusted helper features should let users get support without giving away control. The app should support one-time sharing, case-specific sharing, summary-only sharing, selected-evidence sharing, recovery-task sharing, and full helper access only when the user clearly chooses it.

The helper invitation flow should show what the helper can see and do. It should use plain permission levels: view alert summary, review selected evidence, comment on case, help with recovery tasks, or manage selected settings. Manage settings should be treated as high trust and should not be the default.

The helper view should be designed for practical assistance. It should show the case summary, risk result, selected evidence, advised questions, suggested next actions, and privacy boundaries. It should not expose unrelated cases. It should not allow the helper to export private evidence unless the user grants that ability.

Helper comments should be clearly labeled as helper input. The app's risk analysis should remain separate. If the helper disagrees with the app, the user should see both views and decide what to do. The app can recommend additional verification when there is conflict.

Family support should be consent-based. The app should avoid language that treats older adults, teenagers, or less technical users as incapable. It should focus on respectful assistance. Every linked person should be able to see who has access and what level of access they have.

### Section 15 \- Personalization, Risk Memory, and Education Deepening

Personalization should make the app more useful without making it opaque. The user should know what Verivae remembers and why. The app can remember trusted entities, preferred explanation depth, privacy settings, accessibility settings, feedback, repeated scam patterns, and unresolved case context. The user should be able to edit, pause, or delete these memories.

Risk Memory should connect repeated scams. If the same domain, phrase, phone number, payment handle, sender name, QR destination, or impersonated brand appears again, the app should show the connection. It should not automatically merge cases without user confirmation. It should say why it thinks the items may be related.

Personalized education should respond to user risk patterns. A user dealing with fake bank alerts should see bank impersonation lessons. A user dealing with fake invoices should see payment change and invoice verification lessons. A user dealing with remote access should see screen-sharing and device safety lessons. Lessons should be short, practical, and linked back to checking, recovery, or prevention.

Education should not feel like punishment. If the user made a risky choice, the app should offer learning as support, not correction. The tone should be: Here is how to spot this next time. It should not be: You should have known.

Personalization should never suppress risky warnings. A trusted sender, familiar company, or expected message can still be compromised or imitated. The app should use personalization as context, not as an override.

### Section 15 \- Privacy, Permissions, and Safety Controls Deepening

Privacy controls should be visible and useful. The user should be able to see linked accounts, active permissions, saved evidence, shared helper access, personalization memory, reports, exports, and deletion options. A privacy screen should not be buried under vague account settings.

Each permission should explain what it helps with, what the app can see, what it cannot see, what is stored, and how to turn it off. Permissions should be requested when needed, not all at once. If the user denies permission, the app should offer manual alternatives.

Sensitive evidence should have extra controls. ID docs, intimate threats, blackmail messages, financial records, family cases, workplace cases, and minor-related cases should support hidden previews, Safe Exit, restricted sharing, redaction, export review, and discreet alerts.

The app should show Privacy Receipts for important actions. A Privacy Receipt explains what the user shared, what the app analyzed, whether it was saved, whether it was shared with a helper, and how to delete it. This makes privacy concrete instead of abstract.

Account deletion should be understandable. The app should explain the difference between deleting personalization memory, deleting cases, deleting evidence, revoking linked accounts, removing helper access, and deleting the entire account. The user should not accidentally lose evidence they intended to keep.

### Section 15 \- Accessibility, Stress, and Not Sure Paths Deepening

Accessibility should be built into every high-stress path. The app should support readable text, strong contrast, large tap targets, clear labels, screen reader support, reduced motion, simple language, and layouts that do not require precision under pressure.

Stress Mode should be available in risky situations. Stress Mode should reduce optional content, show one primary action at a time, increase clarity, and avoid unnecessary animations. It should be useful for users dealing with money loss, account compromise, remote access, threats, or active scammer contact.

The Not sure path should appear across the app. Users may not know if they clicked a link, entered a password, sent money, installed an app, shared a code, or exposed identity info. Not sure should not be treated as failure. The app should ask follow-up questions and choose cautious next steps.

Failure states should be understandable. If OCR cannot read a screenshot, the app should ask for a clearer image or pasted text. If a link check fails, the app should say whether the failure was connection, timeout, unsafe redirect, or unsupported format. If a device check is limited, the app should explain platform limits. If a report export fails, the app should preserve the draft and offer another format.

The app should support save for later. A user under stress may need to stop. Draft checks, recovery progress, report drafts, and evidence uploads should be resumable when privacy settings allow.

### Section 15 \- Alerts, Alerts, and Ongoing Protection Deepening

Alerts should be useful and restrained. Too many alerts will make users ignore the app. Alerts should focus on risky items, unresolved recovery tasks, weekly checks, permission problems, helper requests, and important privacy changes.

Alert text should be discreet. Lock-screen alerts should avoid showing private scam details unless the user allows it. Instead of showing the full message, the app can say: A shared item needs review, A recovery task needs attention, or Weekly protection review is ready. Sensitive cases should use even more private language.

Alert priority should match harm. A risky link that was not opened may need a caution alert. A shared login code may need a risky recovery alert. A permission expiration may need a mild settings alert. A helper comment may need a normal activity alert. The app should not treat every event as an emergency.

Ongoing protection should be transparent. The Protection Hub should show what is active, what is limited, what was checked recently, and what needs user action. The app should not imply that every app, message, email, and file is being scanned if that is not true.

Weekly Deep Check should act as the user's safety review. It should combine recent risky items, unresolved cases, device safety, account safety, linked permissions, helper access, education advices, and privacy reminders. It should produce a clear summary, not just a checkmark.

### Section 15 \- Feature Connection Map

The app should include internal product logic that connects features in user-visible ways. A manual message check can create a result. A result can create a case. A case can contain evidence. Evidence can trigger recovery tasks. Recovery tasks can create reports. Reports can include redacted evidence. Weekly checks can find unresolved tasks. Trusted helpers can review selected case items. Personalization can adjust explanation style. Education can respond to repeated patterns. Privacy settings govern what is saved and shared.

This connection map should be visible through the user experience. When the user is on a result screen, the app should show: Save this to a case. When the user is in a case, it should show: Open recovery tasks. When the user is in recovery, it should show: Build report. When the user is in a report, it should show: Review sensitive details before sharing. When the user is in education, it should show: Check something like this now.

The app should avoid duplicate work. If a user already uploaded a screenshot in a result, they should not have to upload it again for a report. If a payment task already collected transaction details, the Report Builder should reuse them with permission. If a helper already reviewed evidence, the case timeline should show that. The user should control reuse, but the app should reduce repetition.

The app should also support correction across linked features. If the user marks a result as false alarm, the case should update. If a helper access is removed, helper views should update. If evidence is deleted, reports should show that evidence is no longer included. If personalization is paused, future results should stop using new personal learning.

### Section 15 \- Professional Functional Acceptance Standard

This detail is complete when the app has a deeper, linked description of core navigation, manual checking, email review, message review, link and QR checking, attachment and file review, device safety, weekly checks, scam results, evidence vault, case space, payment recovery, account recovery, trusted helpers, personalization, privacy controls, accessibility, alerts, education, edge cases, failure states, and feature connections.

A future designer should be able to understand what screens exist, what each screen does, what the user sees first, what actions are available, what info is saved, and how the app handles stress, uncertainty, privacy, and follow-up. A future developer should be able to understand the major user-facing objects, how they relate, what states must be supported, and where the app must be honest about limits.

The app should remain free-first in spirit, useful without heavy setup, and practical before advanced integrations exist. It should help users check risky items, understand risk, preserve evidence, recover from harm, protect accounts and devices, involve trusted helpers, learn from patterns, and control their data.

### Section 15 completion note

Section 15 details the design brief with full-system integration detail across core screens, manual checks, email and Gmail-style review, messages, links, QR codes, attachments, device safety, weekly checks, results, evidence, recovery, payment and account response, trusted helpers, personalization, privacy, accessibility, alerts, education, edge cases, failure states, and feature connections while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 16: Screen Contracts, Functional Rules, and Acceptance Detail

### Section 16 purpose

This detail adds more functional depth to Verivae by defining screen contracts, decision rules, state expectations, and acceptance detail. A screen contract means a clear description of what a screen is responsible for, what info it must show, what actions it must support, what states it must handle, and how it connects to the rest of the app. This makes the design brief more useful because it turns broad ideas into practical product requirements without turning the document into code.

This section covers the app's functions, screens, layout, user flows, safety behavior, privacy behavior, detection behavior, recovery behavior, and user experience. Harborwake remains the company name. The app remains Verivae.

### Section 16 \- Universal Screen Contract Standard

Every major screen in the app should follow a consistent contract. The screen should have a clear purpose, a primary user question, a primary action, secondary actions, input requirements, output behavior, privacy behavior, error handling, and connection points to other app areas. This standard prevents screens from becoming vague or decorative. It also helps future designers and developers understand what each screen must accomplish.

The purpose describes why the screen exists. The primary user question describes what the user is trying to answer. On the Home screen, the question is: Is anything urgent, and what can I do now? On the Check screen, the question is: Can I review this risky item? On the Result screen, the question is: Is this risky, and what should I do next? On the Recovery screen, the question is: What action protects me first? On the Evidence Vault screen, the question is: What proof do I have, and where is it saved?

The primary action should be visible without hunting. If the screen is Check, the primary action is to submit or add evidence. If the screen is Result, the primary action depends on risk: do not click, save evidence, open recovery, verify safely, or ask helper. If the screen is Recovery, the primary action is the next advised task. If the screen is Privacy, the primary action may be manage access, pause personalization, delete data, or review sharing.

Secondary actions should never compete with urgent safety. A risky result should not show education, customization, or account upgrade prompts above the safety action. A recovery task should not bury the blocked path. A privacy screen should not hide delete or disconnect controls beneath unrelated settings. The hierarchy should match user safety.

Every screen should also define what happens when there is no data. Empty screens should be useful. An empty Cases screen can explain that saved checks will appear there and provide a Check something now action. An empty Evidence Vault can explain that evidence is saved only when the user chooses. An empty Trusted Helpers screen can explain helper sharing without pressuring the user to invite someone.

### Section 16 \- Home Screen Contract

The Home screen is the main control center for Verivae. It should summarize the current safety situation and offer immediate action. It must not become a marketing dashboard or a dense analytics page. Its job is to make the user feel oriented.

The Home screen should always include an immediate check entry. The entry should be labeled in beginner-friendly language, such as Check something risky. It should support text, screenshot, link, QR code, email, message, file, phone number, payment request, and not sure. This action should remain available even when no account is linked and even if permissions are denied.

The Home screen should include a current status area. Possible statuses include no urgent risks, risky item waiting, risky item needs action, recovery case active, weekly check ready, protection limited by permissions, helper request waiting, and privacy review advised. The status should be one short statement with a direct action. It should not use fear-based language.

The Home screen should include active modules but should limit clutter. Modules can include Active recovery case, Recent check, Weekly check, Protection source status, Trusted helper request, Advised lesson, Privacy reminder, and Device safety item. The app should show only the modules that matter. A user with no active recovery should not see a large empty recovery panel. A user with a risky case should see that before education advices.

The Home screen should support a compact mode and a detailed mode. Compact mode shows status and actions. Detailed mode shows more recent activity and protection source states. This supports users who want quick access and users who want ongoing oversight.

### Section 16 \- Check Screen Contract

The Check screen is the universal intake screen. It should accept evidence from many sources without requiring the user to understand scam categories. It should ask what the user has, not what the scam is. This keeps the experience accessible.

The Check screen should offer evidence-type options: pasted text, screenshot, link, QR code, email, message, file, phone number, payment request, conversation, and not sure. Each option should lead to the smallest useful input path. A link check should not ask for screenshots first. A screenshot check should not require the user to type a URL. A not sure path should ask simple questions and allow description.

After evidence is submitted, the Check screen should show an intake review when appropriate. The intake review should summarize what the app detected: possible sender, claimed company, link, requested action, urgency, money involvement, account involvement, identity involvement, file involvement, and missing details. The user should be able to correct obvious misunderstandings before saving the result.

The Check screen should support additional evidence. If the user checks a message and then adds a link from that message, the app should treat both as part of the same review unless the user chooses otherwise. If the user uploads multiple screenshots, the app should let them order them or identify conversation sequence when useful.

The Check screen should handle low-quality evidence gracefully. If a screenshot is blurry, the app should ask for a clearer image or pasted text. If a URL is incomplete, it should ask the user to confirm. If a file cannot be inspected, it should say why and provide safe handling guidance. If the user is not sure what happened, it should still provide cautious next steps.

### Section 16 \- Result Screen Contract

The Result screen should turn analysis into action. It should be one of the most carefully designed screens in the app because users may be making decisions about money, passwords, identity info, files, or contact with a scammer.

The Result screen should always show five elements near the top: risk label, short summary, safest immediate action, confidence or limitation note, and primary action button. The risk label should use consistent terms. The short summary should explain the main reason. The safest action should be specific. The confidence note should clarify whether the app had enough info. The primary action should match the risk.

The evidence area should use grouped reasoning. Instead of a long unstructured paragraph, evidence should be grouped into sender signals, wording signals, link signals, payment signals, identity signals, file signals, device signals, conversation signals, trusted entity mismatch, and previous-pattern signals. Each evidence item should explain why it matters.

The Result screen should include user correction controls. The user should be able to mark the result as helpful, too cautious, not cautious enough, wrong sender, expected message, verified elsewhere, related to existing case, or not related. Corrections should update the case and personalization only in transparent ways.

The Result screen should include safe alternatives. If a message tells the user to call a number, the app should recommend using a known number instead. If a link claims to be from a bank, the app should recommend opening the bank app directly. If a payment request appears risky, it should recommend verifying outside the message thread. These alternatives make warnings more useful.

### Section 16 \- Case Screen Contract

The Case screen is the long-term container for a scam situation. It should collect related checks, evidence, tasks, reports, helper reviews, and timeline events. A case may begin from a result, a recovery flow, a manual user entry, a weekly check, or a helper request.

The Case Overview should answer: what happened, what risk exists, what actions have been taken, what remains unresolved, and what evidence is saved. It should include a concise risk summary, current status, next action, evidence count, recovery progress, helper status, and report availability.

Case tabs should be consistent. Suggested tabs include Overview, Evidence, Timeline, Recovery, Reports, Helper, Education, and Settings. Evidence can include messages, emails, links, files, QR codes, payment records, device events, notes, screenshots, and generated summaries. Timeline should show events in order. Recovery should show tasks. Reports should show created or draft reports. Helper should show shared access and comments. Education should show lessons tied to the case. Settings should control privacy, sharing, archiving, and deletion for that case.

The Case screen should support merge and split. If two cases are related, the user should be able to merge them. If the app linked items incorrectly, the user should be able to split them. The app should preserve evidence history and explain what changes.

The Case screen should support final resolution without forcing perfection. A case may be resolved, unresolved but inactive, false alarm, duplicate, archived, or needs future monitoring. When the user closes a case, unresolved risks should be shown plainly, but the user should still control closure.

### Section 16 \- Evidence Vault Contract

The Evidence Vault should protect original evidence and make it useful. It should not mix original evidence with app interpretation in a way that confuses the user. Original screenshots, original message text, original files, and original payment records should remain clearly labeled. App analysis should be marked as analysis.

Each evidence item should include source, type, date-added inside the app, related case, privacy level, analysis status, export status, helper sharing status, and deletion controls. Evidence items should be searchable and filterable by type, case, risk level, source, shared status, and included-in-report status.

Redaction should be a first-class evidence function. The user should be able to create a redacted copy for sharing. The app should explain that redaction hides selected details in the shareable copy and does not change the original unless the user deletes the original. Redaction should support names, phone numbers, emails, addresses, account numbers, ID docs, private photos, payment amounts, and selected message lines.

Evidence export should require review. Before anything leaves the app, the user should see what is included. Reports, helper shares, copied summaries, and support messages should all respect privacy settings. The app should avoid accidental oversharing.

The Evidence Vault should support chain-of-handling in simple language. It should show when evidence was added, analyzed, redacted, shared, exported, deleted, or restored if restoration is supported. This helps the user understand what happened to sensitive material.

### Section 16 \- Recovery Workspace Contract

The Recovery Workspace should be organized around harm type and urgency. It should not show the same checklist for every situation. The app should ask what happened and then prioritize tasks based on money, account access, identity exposure, device risk, emotional threat, legal sensitivity, and ongoing contact.

Recovery intake should include yes, no, not sure, and skip answers. The app should ask whether the user sent money, shared a password, shared a login code, gave identity info, opened a file, installed an app, gave remote access, entered card or bank details, shared private images, or received threats. The user should not need to remember exact terms.

Recovery tasks should have priority labels. Immediate means act now before doing lower-priority tasks. Important means do soon. Evidence means save info. Waiting means a response is pending. Optional means useful but not urgent. The app should avoid showing everything as equally urgent.

Recovery should connect to communication helpers. If the user needs to contact a bank, platform, payment provider, employer, school, or trusted person, the app should generate a factual summary based on selected case details. The user should review and edit before sending.

Recovery should include blocked paths. If the user cannot complete a task, the app should ask why and offer a smaller step. Examples include cannot log in, cannot reach support, missing transaction ID, too overwhelmed, need helper, unsafe to continue, or not sure what happened.

### Section 16 \- Protection Hub Contract

The Protection Hub should show the user's protection setup and current coverage. It should include email, messages, links, QR codes, attachments, device safety, weekly checks, trusted helpers, permissions, privacy, and reports. Each source should show status and limits.

A linked source should show whether it is ready, limited, paused, dislinked, needs permission, or recently checked. The screen should explain what the app can review through that source and what it cannot review. This is especially important for email and device safety because platform rules may limit access.

The Protection Hub should include manual alternatives. If email connection is not active, the user can still paste email text or upload screenshots. If message scanning is not available, the user can still share screenshots or copied text. If device scanning is limited, the user can still review risky files, links, settings, and account safety.

The Protection Hub should support health checks. It can show permission status, alert status, weekly review schedule, helper access, privacy review, unresolved cases, and recent risky patterns. The goal is awareness, not fear.

Protection Hub should connect to Settings for permission changes, to Check for manual review, to Cases for unresolved items, to Recovery for harm response, and to Education for prevention lessons.

### Section 16 \- Privacy and Permission Contract

Privacy and permissions should be designed as user controls, not just legal compliance. The app should explain each permission before requesting it. The explanation should include what the access helps with, what the app can see, what it cannot see, what is stored, how long it is kept if known, who can view it, and how to turn it off.

The privacy dashboard should show categories: linked accounts, saved evidence, shared helpers, personalization memory, reports and exports, device records, alert privacy, data deletion, and account deletion. Each category should have view and manage controls.

Permission denial should not break the app. If the user denies email access, manual email checks should remain. If alerts are denied, in-app reminders should remain. If file access is limited, selected upload should remain. If contacts are denied, trusted helper entry by email or phone should remain if supported.

Privacy receipts should appear for sensitive actions. The receipt should say what was shared, what was analyzed, whether it was saved, whether it was added to a case, whether a helper could see it, and how to delete or change it.

The app should support privacy defaults. Users can choose blurred previews, discreet alerts, limited helper sharing, redaction reminders, local-only drafts where supported, and personalization pause.

### Section 16 \- Education and Learning Contract

Education should be practical, short, and linked to real risk. The app should not use education as filler. Every lesson should help the user make safer decisions, recognize a pattern, or recover from a specific situation.

A lesson should include what the scam looks like, what the scammer wants, warning signs, safe verification, what not to do, what evidence to save, and what app feature can help. Lessons should include practice checks only if they are respectful and useful. The goal is confidence, not testing or embarrassment.

Education should adapt to cases and risk memory. If the user has repeated marketplace cases, show marketplace lessons. If the user has a remote access case, show remote access lessons. If the user has payment change warnings, show invoice and payment verification lessons. If the user is in recovery, show only helpful recovery-adjacent learning, not distracting general material.

The Education screen should include browse, advised, saved, quick lessons, family/helper lessons, and practice examples. It should also include Check something now so learning can turn into action.

Education should respect emotional safety. Sensitive topics such as blackmail, intimate images, family exploitation, or major money loss should not be repeatedly pushed if the user hides or dismisses them. The app should allow the user to reduce or hide certain lesson prompts.

### Section 16 \- Accessibility and Stress Contract

Accessibility should apply to the whole app, not only a settings screen. Every major flow should support readable text, large tap targets, screen reader labels, color-independent status indicators, reduced motion, clear headings, and plain text.

Stress Mode should simplify risky flows. It should show one main action at a time, reduce optional content, keep exit and save controls visible, and avoid unnecessary animation. Stress Mode should be offered in risky results, recovery intake, remote access scenarios, payment loss, account takeover, identity exposure, threats, and sensitive cases.

Not sure should be a valid answer. Many users will not know whether they clicked a link, entered info, installed something, or sent money successfully. The app should use not sure answers to create cautious but not panic-driven guidance. It should ask follow-up questions in simple terms.

Accessibility should include helper support. If a trusted helper is involved, the helper view should be clear, structured, and respectful. The helper should see only what the user shared. If the user uses simplified explanations, helper views should still preserve privacy and evidence accuracy.

The app should support save and resume. Users under stress may need to stop. Checks, reports, triage flows, and recovery tasks should preserve progress when privacy settings allow. The app should explain what is saved.

### Section 16 \- Failure State and Edge Case Contract

Failure states should be treated as part of the product. A scam safety app cannot assume clean inputs and perfect integrations. It must handle blurry screenshots, partial links, dislinked email, denied permissions, unreadable files, expired helper links, conflicting user feedback, offline use, and abandoned recovery flows.

For blurry screenshots, the app should say it could not read everything and ask for a clearer image or pasted text. For partial links, it should ask the user to check the full address. For unreadable files, it should explain whether the issue is file type, password protection, corruption, size, or platform limits. For dislinked accounts, it should show reconnect and manual alternatives.

For conflicting evidence, the app should show uncertainty. If the sender looks familiar but the link is risky, say both. If the invoice was expected but the payment details changed, say both. If a helper marks something safe but the app sees risky signs, show the disagreement and recommend verification.

For offline use, the app should allow viewing saved cases, drafting notes, reviewing previous evidence, preparing questions, and reading downloaded lessons if available. It should mark live checks as unavailable until connection returns.

For abandoned flows, the app should preserve safe progress and provide a resume point. If the user leaves during recovery triage, the Home screen can later show Continue recovery triage. If the user leaves during report building, the report should remain a draft if the user allowed saving.

### Section 16 \- Accept Rules for Functional Completeness

This detail is complete when the design brief defines screen contracts for Home, Check, Results, Cases, Evidence Vault, Recovery Workspace, Protection Hub, Privacy, Education, Accessibility, and failure states.
