Alerts should use severity levels that map to user action. The app should avoid dramatic labels unless the risk is genuinely high. Suggested alert levels include “Review advised,” “Pause before acting,” “Risky warning,” and “Urgent account or payment risk.” These labels are plain enough for beginners and specific enough to guide behavior.

“Review advised” should appear when the app sees something mildly risky or incomplete. The user may not need to stop everything, but they should check before trusting the item. Examples include unknown sender with a link, vague delivery message, unfamiliar invoice, or brand claim that lacks verification. The alert should invite review without implying confirmed danger.

“Pause before acting” should appear when the content includes common scam pressure. Examples include urgent deadlines, account threats, secrecy requests, payment requests, personal info requests, or a link that appears unrelated to the claimed sender. This alert should tell the user not to click, pay, reply, or share info until the item is reviewed.

“Risky warning” should appear when multiple strong scam signals are present. Examples include gift card demands, crypto payment pressure, request for a one-time code, remote-access installation instructions, fake support contact, impersonation combined with urgency, or a risky payment page. The alert should lead to a result screen that prioritizes stop instructions and safer verification.

“Urgent account or payment risk” should appear when the user may already be in harm's way or an active compromise is possible. Examples include a shared code, submitted password, sent payment, installed remote-access app, opened risky attachment with risky behavior, or continued conversation after a risky warning. This alert should lead directly to case space options.

The alert system should avoid percentage scores in alerts. A percentage can imply precision the app may not have. The result screen can show detail, but the alert should remain action-focused. For example, “Pause before paying. This request has several scam warning signs” is better than “Scam risk 82 percent.”

### Section 20 \- Alert Timing and Interruption Rules

The timing of alerts matters. An alert is useful only if it arrives before the user takes the risky action or while recovery is still practical. the app should prioritize alerts before clicking links, before entering credentials, before sending money, before sharing one-time codes, before opening risky attachments, before installing software, and before replying to high-pressure messages.

For manual checks, timing is user-controlled. The user opens the app and asks for a review. For linked-source alerts, timing depends on platform permissions. If alert access is available, the app may detect risky text in a alert and warn quickly. If Gmail monitoring is available, the app may flag risky emails as they arrive or during periodic review. If only weekly review is available, the app should avoid presenting old alerts as urgent unless the risk is unresolved.

The app should avoid interrupting repeatedly for the same item. If a user has already reviewed a risky email and dismissed or saved it, the app should not keep sending the same warning unless new evidence appears or the situation becomes more dangerous. Repeated alerts can make users frustrated and less likely to use the app.

Alert timing should respect quiet hours and sensitive moments. The user may not want non-urgent alerts late at night. Risky account or payment risk can still appear when necessary, but lower-risk summaries can wait. The app should allow alert preferences without hiding critical protection entirely.

If the user is actively completing a recovery task, preventive alerts should be careful. For example, if the user is contacting their bank through an official channel, the app should not interrupt with generic payment education. It should only interrupt if it sees a new risky event, such as the scammer asking for another payment or the user opening a risky link from the scam conversation.

### Section 20 \- Alert Content Design

Alert content should be short, private, and action-oriented. Many alerts appear on lock screens. the app should avoid exposing sensitive details in a alert. Instead of showing the full risky message, the alert can say “Review before responding” or “This may involve payment pressure.” The user can open the app to view details after unlocking.

The alert should explain the action, not just the risk. A poor alert says “Scam detected.” A better alert says “Pause before sending money. This request has warning signs.” Another good alert says “Do not share a code until verified. This message asks for a security code.” The alert should help the user make a safer choice immediately.

When the user taps an alert, the destination screen should match the severity. A low-level alert can open the review result. A risky alert should open a stop-and-verify screen. An urgent account or payment risk alert should open the case space triage. The app should not send every alert to the same generic screen.

Alert content should include uncertainty when needed. If the app is not sure, the alert should not say the item is a scam. It can say “Review advised” or “This has warning signs.” The app should maintain trust by avoiding overconfident language.

The alert screen should include three core controls: review now, dismiss, and save for later. Risky alerts may also include “start recovery” or “ask trusted helper.” Dismissal should be allowed, but the app may ask for confirmation before dismissing urgent warnings. The confirmation should explain the risk in one sentence.

### Section 20 \- Protective Friction Before Risky Actions

Protective friction is one of the app's most important behaviors. It creates a safety pause when a user is about to do something risky. It should be designed carefully because too much friction makes the app annoying, while too little friction fails to protect the user.

The app can create protective friction in several ways. Before opening a risky link, it can show the destination and risk findings. Before sharing a one-time code, it can warn that codes should not be shared with someone who contacted the user. Before sending money based on a risky request, it can suggest verifying through an official channel or asking a trusted helper. Before installing an app after a support message, it can warn about remote-access scams. Before opening an unexpected attachment, it can recommend verifying the sender.

Protective friction should be strongest when the action is hard to reverse. Sending money, sharing a code, installing remote access software, entering a password, or sharing ID docs should trigger stronger pauses than reading a risky message. The app should map friction strength to potential harm.

The pause screen should include the reason for the pause, the safest next step, and a way to continue manually. the app should not lock the user out of their own decisions. It should make the danger clear and give safer choices. If the user continues anyway, the app can offer to save the event for follow-up or recovery.

Protective friction should support helper review. If a user has enabled trusted helper support, risky actions can show “Ask your helper before continuing.” This should be optional and user-controlled. The helper should receive the selected context, not broad access to the user's phone.

### Section 20 \- Weekly Safety Loop

The weekly safety loop should be a recurring review that keeps the app useful even when the user is not actively checking a scam. It should not be a generic newsletter. It should be a practical safety check inside the app. The weekly loop can summarize risky items reviewed, unresolved recovery tasks, permission health, device safety findings, evidence gaps, repeated risky senders, and education topics based on recent patterns.

The weekly safety summary should start with the most important status. Examples include “No urgent issues found,” “Two items need review,” “One recovery task is still open,” or “Device safety check found one setting to review.” The top summary should be short. Detailed sections can appear below.

The weekly loop should include a “what changed” section. If nothing changed, the app should say so. If a new permission was removed, a new risky sender appeared, a recovery case is still waiting, or a device setting changed, the app should highlight it. Users are more likely to pay attention to changes than repeated static info.

The weekly loop should also include positive closure. If the user handled a risky item, completed recovery tasks, improved device safety, or learned a scam pattern, the app can mark that progress. This should be practical rather than congratulatory. It helps the user understand that the app is helping them maintain safety.

The weekly loop should never claim complete protection. It should say what was reviewed and what was limited. If Gmail monitoring was off, the summary should not imply emails were checked. If device permissions were missing, the summary should not imply a full device review happened. Transparency protects trust.

### Section 20 \- Risk Memory in Everyday Protection

Risk memory should make Verivae more useful over time without becoming invasive. Risk memory means the app remembers selected safety-relevant patterns that the user allows it to remember. It can include trusted contacts, commonly used payment providers, expected accounts, previous false positives, repeated risky senders, common scam types the user encounters, and unresolved recovery risks.

Risk memory should improve context. If the user often receives legitimate emails from a school, employer, bank, or marketplace, the app can learn expected patterns. If a new message claims to be from that source but uses a strange address or asks for a code, the app can warn more clearly. If the user repeatedly receives fake delivery texts, the app can show education tailored to that pattern.

Risk memory should not become blind trust. Even if a sender is usually safe, a message asking for unusual money movement, secrecy, code sharing, or remote access should still be reviewed. The app should treat trust as context, not permission to ignore danger.

The user should be able to view and edit risk memory. A “Remembered safety patterns” screen can show trusted sources, repeated scam types, helper preferences, dismissed warning patterns, and active watch items. The user should be able to remove anything. If the user resets risk memory, the app should keep core function working with default rules.

Risk memory should be private by default. It may reveal personal habits, family relationships, payment providers, and account names. The app should not share it with helpers unless the user chooses. Helper review should receive case-specific context, not the full risk memory profile.

### Section 20 \- Preventive Protection Accept Rules

Preventive protection should pass functional review if manual review works without linked permissions, contextual review works through share, paste, screenshot, QR, and link entry, and proactive alerts work only when permissions allow. It should pass if alert severity maps to action. It should pass if alert content is private enough for lock screens. It should pass if risky alerts route to stop, verify, recovery, or helper options instead of a generic result.

The app should pass if it avoids repeating the same alert too often. It should pass if the weekly safety loop clearly says what was checked, what changed, what needs attention, and what was limited. It should pass if risk memory improves future review while remaining editable and private. It should pass if protective friction appears before high-impact actions like payments, code sharing, credential entry, remote-access installation, ID doc sharing, and risky file opening.

The app should fail if it floods the user with low-value warnings. It should fail if alerts expose private scam details on the lock screen. It should fail if it claims proactive protection is active when permissions are off. It should fail if users cannot dismiss or control non-urgent alerts. It should fail if risk memory silently treats risky future messages as safe only because a sender was trusted once.

### Section 20 completion note

Section 20 details the design brief with preventive protection models, alert severity levels, alert timing, alert content, protective friction, weekly safety loops, risk memory, everyday safety behavior, and preventive protection accept rules while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 21: Core Screen System, Navigation Behavior, and Everyday Use Layout

### Section 21 purpose

This detail defines the core screen system for Verivae. The app's function depends on screens that users can understand quickly, especially when they are scared, rushed, or unsure. A scam safety app cannot rely on beautiful screens alone. It needs screens that move users toward safer decisions with minimal confusion. Navigation should be simple, predictable, and linked to the app's protective purpose.

The screen system should help a first-time user check something risky within seconds, help a returning user continue an open recovery case, help a cautious user manage permissions, help a family member request review, and help a user who is not currently in crisis learn safer habits. Each screen should have a clear job. No screen should exist only because it looks complete. Every screen should support checking, understanding, protecting, recovering, learning, or managing privacy.

This section does not define visual polish in a marketing sense. It defines functional layout behavior. It explains what appears on the Home screen, how bottom navigation should work, what quick actions should do, how empty states should behave, how urgent states should appear, how screens should route users, and how the app should avoid burying important safety actions.

### Section 21 \- Main Navigation Model

the app should use a small main navigation structure. A likely first version can include Home, Check, Protection, Recovery, Vault, and Learn. If that is too many items for a phone bottom bar, the app can use Home, Check, Protection, Recovery, and More, with Vault and Learn inside More or Protection. The decision should be based on usability, not on making every feature equally visible.

Home should be the command center. It should show the most important next action for the user. If the user has no active issue, Home should make it easy to check a message, link, email, QR code, file, or risky situation. If the user has an urgent recovery case, Home should surface that case. If the weekly check found an issue, Home should show that. If the user has not set up any optional protections, Home can show a small setup suggestion without blocking use.

Check should be the fastest path to review. It should include manual check, message check, email check, link check, QR check, file check, and guided situation review. These can appear as large clear actions or as a single input area that adapts based on what the user provides. The Check area should minimize form fields. It should let users start with whatever they have.

Protection should show active safety coverage. It should include permission health, weekly checks, device safety, alert settings, risk memory, linked sources, and trusted helper options. This area should answer “what is protecting me right now?” It should not be a confusing settings dump. It should translate technical protections into plain safety coverage.

Recovery should show active and past recovery cases. It should prioritize open cases that need attention. It should show task progress and allow the user to resume recovery quickly. A person who just got off a bank call should be able to open the case, mark the bank-contact task done, add notes, attach new evidence, and see the next action.

Vault should store evidence and saved checks. It should not feel like a random history list. It should organize saved items by case, date, source, risk level, and type. If Vault is not a main navigation item, it should still be easy to reach from results, recovery cases, and Protection.

Learn should teach scam patterns in a practical way. It should not compete with urgent actions. When the user is in crisis, Learn content should appear as short explanations inside results and recovery tasks. The full Learn area is for calm browsing, pattern review, and building confidence.

### Section 21 \- Home Screen Functional Layout

The Home screen should adapt to the user's current safety state. The top of Home should answer the question “what needs attention now?” If nothing urgent is happening, the answer can be a calm status such as “Ready to check something risky.” If an urgent case exists, the answer should be “One recovery case needs attention.” If protection is limited by permissions, Home can show “Some protections are off” without making that the only focus.

Home should include a primary action area. The primary action should usually be “Check something risky.” This should open the Check flow with flexible input. Secondary quick actions can include “Scan QR,” “Check link,” “Review email,” “Review message,” “Check file,” and “I may have been scammed.” The exact visible actions can adapt based on usage and setup. A user who often checks texts may see message check more prominently. A user in recovery may see recovery tasks first.

Home should include an active issues area. This area should show urgent recovery cases, unresolved risky results, pending helper reviews, weekly check findings, and important device safety warnings. It should not show every low-risk saved item. Home is for action, not archive browsing.

Home should include a protection status summary. The summary should be small and scannable. It may show active manual check, active link check, Gmail selected review, message sharing status, weekly check status, and device safety status. Each item can lead to Protection Hub. The status summary should not use guilt-based language. It should say what works and what could be improved.

Home should include a privacy reminder only when relevant. For example, if the user has never saved evidence, it can say saved items stay private unless shared. If the user has linked Gmail, it can show a small “manage access” link. If the user has invited a helper, it can show who has access to what. These reminders should be useful, not constant banners.

### Section 21 \- Check Screen Functional Layout

The Check screen should be built around flexible input. The user may not know whether they are checking a message, email, link, QR code, file, phone call, payment request, or relationship situation. The interface should allow a user to start broadly and let Verivae classify the input.

The top of the Check screen should include a plain prompt such as “What do you want to check?” Below it, the app can show input options: paste text, add screenshot, enter link, scan QR, attach file, choose email, choose message, or answer guided questions. These actions should be visually distinct enough for beginners but not so large that the screen feels like a landing page.

If the user pastes or types content, the app should immediately detect visible objects such as links, phone numbers, email addresses, payment words, security-code requests, and urgency language. Before the user submits, the app can show small chips like “link found,” “money mentioned,” or “code request mentioned.” These chips should not be final judgments. They simply show what the app noticed.

If the input is incomplete, the Check screen should still allow review. For example, a user may not have the sender's email address or may only remember what a phone caller said. The app can mark the result as less certain and ask optional follow-up questions. It should not block the user with a required form.

The Check screen should include an exposure question when risk is detected. If the content includes a link, payment request, code request, file, or remote-access instruction, the app should ask whether the user already clicked, paid, replied, shared a code, downloaded something, or installed an app. This question determines whether the result should route to prevention or recovery.

### Section 21 \- Result Screen Functional Layout

The result screen should be one of the most carefully designed screens in Verivae. It should be fast to understand, calm in tone, and action-focused. The top area should show the risk level and the most important advice. For a risky result, the top action may be “Do not send money yet” or “Do not share this code.” For an unclear result, the top action may be “Verify through an official channel before acting.”

The result screen should include the main reasons for the assessment. Reasons should be ordered by importance. If the strongest reason is a gift card payment request, that should appear before weaker details such as grammar. If the strongest reason is a sender mismatch, that should appear before general urgency language. The app should avoid making users scroll past low-value details to find the real issue.

The result screen should include next actions. Low-risk results can show “continue carefully,” “save result,” and “learn why.” Medium-risk results can show “verify first,” “ask helper,” “save evidence,” and “check link.” Risky results can show “stop,” “save evidence,” “block/report,” “start recovery if you already acted,” and “ask trusted helper.” Active-compromise results should show “start recovery” as the main action.

The result screen should include expandable evidence detail. The top screen should not show every signal, but the user should be able to see more. Evidence detail can include sender data, links found, risky phrases, payment method, requested action, source reliability, file findings, device context, and what the app could not confirm.

The result screen should also include a correction path. The user can mark the result as helpful, not helpful, expected, risky, or needs more review. This feedback can improve risk memory, but it should not erase the original result or overrule strong safety warnings too quickly.

### Section 21 \- Protection Hub Layout

The Protection Hub should answer what is currently active, what is limited, and what the user can do next. The screen should be organized by protection areas: manual checking, linked sources, alerts, device safety, weekly checks, risk memory, helper review, and privacy controls. Each area should show status, benefit, and action.

Manual checking should always show as active because it does not require linked permissions. Linked sources should show whether Gmail, messages, files, browser share, and other sources are linked, partially active, or off. Alerts should show which alert types are active. Device safety should show the last check and any unresolved findings. Weekly checks should show schedule and last summary. Risk memory should show whether personalization is on. Helper review should show active helpers and their access.

Protection Hub should not hide limitations. If message background monitoring is unavailable, the app should say manual message review still works. If device scanning is limited, the app should say which safety checks are available. If Gmail background review is off, the app should say selected email review may still work. This makes the app honest and reduces false confidence.

Protection Hub should include a setup path, but setup should be modular. The user can enable one protection at a time. A single “turn on everything” button may be convenient, but it should not be the only path because users may want partial protection. Each setup step should explain why it matters.

### Section 21 \- Recovery Screen Layout

The Recovery screen should prioritize active cases. Open urgent cases should appear first. Each case card should show a short summary, urgency, next task, progress, and last updated time. The card should not expose sensitive details unnecessarily. The user should be able to tap into the case and continue from the next advised task.

Inside a recovery case, the layout should include overview, tasks, evidence, notes, helper, and history. Overview shows what happened and what may be at risk. Tasks show prioritized steps. Evidence shows saved items linked to the case. Notes allow the user to record calls, dates, provider responses, or personal reminders. Helper shows who has access. History shows completed tasks and major changes.

The Recovery screen should support stressful interruptions. If the user leaves during a task, the case should remember where they were. If the user comes back later, the app should resume with the next useful step. If the user marks a task waiting on provider, the app should move it out of urgent action and into waiting status.

Recovery should also support manual closure. The user may decide they are done. When closing, the app should show any remaining high-priority tasks and ask whether the user wants to keep evidence, delete evidence, or keep the case archived. The app should not delete important evidence accidentally.

### Section 21 \- Vault and Saved Items Layout

The Vault should organize saved items in a way that helps action. It should not be an endless chronological list unless that list is filtered. The user should be able to filter by case, source, risk level, item type, date, and shared status. Item types can include email, message, screenshot, link, QR result, file result, device finding, payment note, account note, helper comment, and app result.

Each saved item should have a summary card. The card should show what it is, when it was saved, why it matters, whether it is attached to a case, and whether it has been shared. The user should be able to open the item, add notes, redact a copy, attach it to a case, share it with a helper, export it, or delete it.

Vault should include privacy indicators. If an item contains sensitive data, the app can label it as sensitive. If an item was shared, the app should show with whom. If a helper can see it, the app should make that clear. If an item is private, the app should say so.

The Vault should support search, but search should be privacy-aware. The user can search by sender, case, date, risk type, or keyword. Search history should not expose sensitive terms on shared devices. The app can allow search history to be off by default.

### Section 21 \- Learn Screen Layout

The Learn screen should be organized around real situations rather than abstract categories. Users should be able to learn about bank impersonation, fake delivery texts, gift card scams, crypto scams, romance scams, job scams, marketplace scams, fake support calls, QR scams, phishing emails, identity theft, account takeover, and recovery scams. Each topic should explain warning signs, safe verification, what not to do, and how the app can help check that situation.

Learn content should connect to user activity without feeling invasive. If the user recently checked multiple delivery texts, the Learn screen can surface delivery scam education. If the user handled a payment scam, it can surface recovery scam warnings. If the user dismissed several warnings, it can surface safe verification habits.

The Learn screen should include quick practice examples. These examples can show a risky message and ask the user what warning signs they notice. The practice feature should be optional and simple. Its purpose is to strengthen user judgment, not to test or shame them.

Learn content should include “what to do now” links. A topic about fake bank texts should link to Check a Message and Check a Link. A topic about remote access scams should link to Device Safety Check. A topic about payment scams should link to Recovery Workspace. Education should connect to action.

### Section 21 \- Empty, Loading, and Error States

Every screen should have useful empty states. If there are no recovery cases, the Recovery screen should explain that cases will appear when the user starts recovery, and it should include a button for “I may have been scammed.” If the Vault is empty, it should explain that saved evidence will appear there and include a button to check something risky. If Protection Hub has no linked sources, it should show manual protection is active and explain optional setup.

Loading states should be specific. Instead of “loading,” the app can say “reviewing links,” “checking sender details,” “reading screenshot text,” “preparing recovery tasks,” or “reviewing device safety signals.” This helps the user understand progress without exposing technical complexity.

Error states should offer a next step. If an email cannot be loaded, the app can suggest pasting the email or uploading a screenshot. If a file cannot be scanned, the app can review source context and recommend safe handling. If a helper invite fails, the app can retry or copy an invite link. If a weekly check fails, the app can explain which part failed and reschedule.

### Section 21 \- Core Screen Accept Rules

The screen system should pass functional review if a user can start a check from Home within one or two taps. It should pass if urgent recovery work appears before low-priority content. It should pass if Protection Hub clearly explains active and limited protections. It should pass if the result screen gives a risk level, reasons, evidence detail, and next actions. It should pass if Recovery preserves task progress. It should pass if Vault makes saved evidence usable. It should pass if Learn connects education to checking and recovery.

The screen system should fail if the user has to understand technical permissions before checking anything. It should fail if urgent warnings are buried under generic cards. It should fail if the app has separate screens that do not share context. It should fail if the result screen explains risk but does not tell the user what to do. It should fail if privacy state is hidden from users. It should fail if empty states are dead ends.

### Section 21 completion note

Section 21 details the design brief with core screen systems, navigation behavior, Home layout, Check layout, result screen layout, Protection Hub layout, Recovery layout, Vault layout, Learn layout, empty states, loading states, error states, and screen accept rules while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 22: Detection Logic, Explainability, and Confidence Behavior

### Section 22 purpose

This detail defines how the app should explain its risk decisions. Users do not need to understand technical fraud systems, but they do need to understand why the app is warning them. If the app only says “dangerous” or “safe,” users may ignore it, distrust it, or misunderstand what to do. The app should make detection understandable without pretending that every answer is certain.

The detection system should be designed around signals, context, confidence, and action. A signal is something the app noticed, such as a link mismatch, a request for a one-time code, pressure to act quickly, or a risky payment method. Context is the surrounding situation, such as who sent it, whether money is involved, whether the user already acted, and whether the source can be verified. Confidence is how strongly the app can interpret the situation. Action is what the user should do next.

The user-facing result should never expose raw internal scoring as if it were perfect truth. Instead, the app should show practical reasoning. It should say what it found, why that matters, what it could not confirm, and what the user should do. This creates trust and makes the app more useful for beginners, families, and people under pressure.

### Section 22 \- Signal Categories

the app should organize scam detection into signal categories. These categories help the app produce consistent results across messages, emails, links, files, QR codes, device checks, and recovery cases. The main categories should include identity signals, pressure signals, payment signals, credential signals, link signals, file signals, device signals, relationship signals, platform signals, and history signals.

Identity signals involve who the sender claims to be and whether that identity appears consistent. The app should look for mismatches between display name and email address, claimed brand and domain, claimed family member and unknown number, claimed support agent and unofficial contact path, claimed employer and risky job setup, or claimed government agency and unusual payment demand. Identity signals are often important because scams rely on impersonation.

Pressure signals involve emotional or time-based manipulation. These include urgent deadlines, threats, secrecy, shame, fear, rescue stories, legal threats, account-lockout claims, limited-time investment pressure, romance pressure, and requests not to tell anyone. The app should explain that pressure is a warning sign because it reduces the user's ability to verify calmly.

Payment signals involve money movement. These include gift cards, crypto, wire transfer, bank transfer, payment app transfers, friends-and-family payment options, fake refund fees, fake taxes, fake shipping fees, fake overpayment, investment deposits, marketplace off-platform payment, and requests to send money before verifying identity. Payment signals should strongly affect risk because financial loss may be difficult to reverse.

Credential signals involve passwords, one-time codes, login links, account recovery links, security questions, ID docs, bank details, Social Security numbers, and private account data. The app should treat one-time code requests as especially risk when they come from a person who contacted the user. It should explain that sharing codes can let someone access or change an account.

Link signals involve where a link goes and how it is presented. The app should check shortened links, misspelled domains, unusual subdomains, unrelated destination domains, redirect chains, newly risky destinations, login pages, payment pages, fake brand pages, and links hidden behind friendly labels. The result should show the visible domain and explain mismatches plainly.

File signals involve file type, file name, source, attachment context, unexpected invoice behavior, executable or installer patterns, compressed archives, macro requests, password-protected files from unknown senders, and files linked to remote-access instructions. File signals should connect directly to device safety guidance when the user opened or installed something.

Device signals involve risky permissions, remote access tools, risky profiles, account sessions, disabled updates, browser alert abuse, and unusual changes found during quick or weekly checks. Device signals should be explained as practical risks, not technical accusations.

Relationship signals involve romance, family emergency, friendship, job opportunity, caregiving, marketplace trust, or authority relationships. Scammers often use relationships to make users act against their better judgment. The app should treat relationship pressure as a real risk signal, especially when combined with money, secrecy, or urgency.

History signals involve what the app already knows from the user's permission-controlled risk memory. These may include repeated sender patterns, prior false positives, trusted sources, previous scam cases, unresolved recovery tasks, or repeated scam categories. History should improve context, but it should not automatically override strong current risk signals.

### Section 22 \- Risk Level Decision Behavior

Risk levels should be action-based. A risk level should tell the user how cautious they should be and what kind of next step is appropriate. The app can use levels such as Low Concern, Review Advised, Pause Before Acting, High Risk, and Urgent Recovery Advised. These levels should be consistent across features.

Low Concern should mean the app did not find meaningful scam warning signs in the available info. It should not mean guaranteed safe. The result should say that the item appears lower risk based on what was reviewed and still encourage normal caution for money, passwords, or unfamiliar links.

Review Advised should mean the app found weak signals, missing context, or something unusual. The user should review before acting, but the app should not imply high danger. This may apply to unknown senders, incomplete screenshots, unclear links, or unusual wording without direct money or credential risk.

Pause Before Acting should mean the app found meaningful warning signs that could lead to harm if the user acts quickly. This may apply to urgency, links, payment requests, identity questions, or risky account claims. The result should make verification the main next step.

High Risk should mean strong scam patterns are present. These include code requests, gift-card demands, crypto payment pressure, remote-access instructions, fake support behavior, payment before verification, account threats with risky links, or multiple signals combined. High Risk should produce stop instructions and recovery options if the user already acted.

Urgent Recovery Advised should mean the user may already be exposed. The app should use this when the user says they paid, shared credentials, shared a one-time code, installed software, gave remote access, opened a risky file, or lost access to an account. This result should lead to the case space.

### Section 22 \- Confidence and Uncertainty Language

Confidence should be shown through plain text, not technical probability. The app can use phrases such as “several strong warning signs,” “some warning signs,” “not enough info,” “looks lower risk based on what was checked,” and “this needs verification before action.” These phrases help users understand the app's certainty without implying scientific precision.

The app should separate risk from confidence. A situation can be risk even if some details are missing. For example, a request for gift cards from someone claiming to be a family member is risk even if the app cannot verify the sender. A situation can be uncertain but still require caution. For example, an email may not have enough sender detail, but if it includes a login link and urgency, the app should still recommend verification.

When confidence is low because input is incomplete, the result should say what is missing. Missing info may include sender address, full screenshot, link destination, file source, whether the user already acted, or account involved. The app should ask for missing details only if they change the advice. It should not ask for extra data just to satisfy curiosity.

Uncertainty language should always include a safe next step. The worst result is “not sure” with no guidance. A better result says, “The app cannot confirm this sender from the screenshot alone. Before clicking the link, open the company's official app or website directly.” That gives the user practical safety.

The app should never use uncertainty to avoid warning. If strong scam patterns are present, the app should warn clearly even if it cannot verify every technical detail. It should say what it knows and what it does not know.

### Section 22 \- Explainability Screen Structure

Every result should include a “Why this result?” section. This section should be available from the main result screen and should be written for nontechnical users. It should list the main signals, explain why each one matters, and show what evidence the app used.

A strong explainability structure includes: main finding, evidence found, why it matters, what the app could not confirm, and safer action. For example, a code-sharing warning might say the main finding is that the message asks for a security code. The evidence is the phrase asking the user to read a code. The reason it matters is that codes can let someone access an account. The app could not confirm whether the sender is legitimate. The safer action is to avoid sharing the code and contact the service through the official app.

The explainability screen should avoid long technical labels at the top. Terms like phishing, spoofing, smishing, malware, social engineering, domain impersonation, and remote access can be included after a plain explanation. The app should teach terminology after it explains the practical meaning.

Explainability should include source limitations. If the user pasted text, the app should say sender details were not available. If the user uploaded a screenshot, it should say text was extracted from the image and may be incomplete. If the user shared a Gmail message, it can say sender details were available through linked review. If the file could not be scanned, it should say only file name and context were reviewed.

Explainability should also show disagreements between signals. A message may come from a known contact but request unusual money movement. A link may belong to a legitimate domain but be used in a risky context. A file may have a normal type but arrive with high-pressure instructions. The app should explain these mixed cases instead of collapsing them into a simple label.

### Section 22 \- Multi-Signal Combination Rules

the app should combine signals carefully. One weak signal should not always create a risky result. Multiple weak signals can become meaningful when they point in the same direction. One very strong signal can justify a strong warning. The app's output should reflect both signal strength and signal combination.

A single typo in a message should not make something risk. But a typo combined with an unknown sender, urgent bank threat, and login link should raise concern. An unfamiliar phone number alone may be normal. An unfamiliar number claiming to be a family member, requesting secrecy, and asking for money should be risk. A link shortener alone may be common. A link shortener inside a message demanding account verification should be more risky.

The app should recognize dangerous combinations. Urgency plus money is risky. Secrecy plus family emergency is risky. One-time code request plus impersonation is risk. Remote-access instruction plus tech support claim is risk. Gift card payment plus authority claim is risk. Crypto payment plus investment promise is risk. Attachment plus unexpected invoice plus pressure to open is risky.

The app should also recognize reducing context without fully trusting it. If the user selected an email from a known sender and the link goes to the expected domain, risk may be lower. If the message appears inside an official app and does not ask for private info, risk may be lower. But the app should still warn if the request includes unusual money movement, passwords, codes, or remote access.

Multi-signal rules should be reflected in the result explanation. The app should not simply show a final level. It should say that the result is risk because several warning signs appear together. This helps the user understand why the app is concerned.

### Section 22 \- False Positives and False Negatives

A false positive happens when the app warns about something that is actually legitimate. A false negative happens when the app misses a scam or underestimates risk. the app should be designed to handle both responsibly.

False positives should be easy to report. The user can mark a result as expected or not risky. The app should ask why only if it is useful. Options may include “I know this sender,” “I was expecting this,” “this came from the official app,” or “the warning did not match the situation.” The app can use this feedback to reduce future noise, but it should not blindly trust similar future messages.

False negatives should be taken seriously. If a user marks something as a scam after the app gave a low or unclear result, the app should ask what happened and whether the user wants to start recovery. It should allow evidence saving and case creation even if the original result was not risk. The app should also use this feedback to improve future reasoning where appropriate.

The app should not hide its mistakes. In history, the app can show the original result and later user outcome. For example, an item could say “Originally marked Review Advised. User later marked as scam.” This helps preserve evidence and makes recovery timelines more accurate.

Feedback should not require emotional labor from the user. If the user was harmed, the app should not make them fill out a long evaluation before getting help. Recovery should come first. Feedback can be collected later or through simple choices.

### Section 22 \- Detection Accept Rules

The detection system should pass functional review if each result shows a risk level, main advice, top signals, evidence used, source limitations, uncertainty if present, and next actions. It should pass if risky signals route to stop and recovery behavior. It should pass if incomplete inputs still produce safe guidance. It should pass if users can view why a result was reached. It should pass if false positives and false negatives can be reported without destroying original evidence.

The detection system should pass if signal categories are consistent across email, messages, links, QR codes, files, device checks, helper review, and recovery cases. It should pass if multi-signal combinations produce stronger explanations than isolated weak signals. It should pass if the app avoids saying something is definitely safe. It should pass if uncertain results still guide verification.

The detection system should fail if results are black boxes. It should fail if users see scores without explanations. It should fail if missing info is hidden. It should fail if weak signals create constant risky warnings. It should fail if strong signals are softened too much because the app cannot verify every detail. It should fail if feedback from users can erase serious warnings without trace.

### Section 22 completion note

Section 22 details the design brief with detection signal categories, risk level behavior, confidence language, uncertainty handling, explainability screens, multi-signal combination rules, false positive handling, false negative handling, and detection accept rules while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 23: Scenario Library, Edge Cases, and Functional Response Patterns

### Section 23 purpose

This detail adds a functional scenario library for Verivae. A scenario library describes realistic situations the app must handle. It helps future designers and developers understand not only the feature list, but the actual user moments the app must support. This is especially important for scam safety because scams do not arrive in neat categories. They arrive as confusing texts, emotional phone calls, fake emails, urgent payment requests, risky links, files, QR codes, and mixed situations where the user may already have acted.

The purpose of this section is to make Verivae more buildable. Each scenario should clarify what the user may bring into the app, what the app should notice, what the app should show, what decisions it should support, what evidence should be saved, and what recovery or prevention path should follow. These scenarios are not marketing examples. They are functional test cases for the app's behavior.

### Section 23 \- Scenario Pattern Standard

Every scenario in the app should be described through the same pattern. The pattern should include user situation, likely input, app detection focus, result behavior, advised actions, evidence behavior, recovery connection, helper connection, privacy considerations, and failure states. This structure prevents scenarios from becoming vague stories. It turns them into usable product requirements.

The user situation describes what is happening in real life. The likely input describes what the user can provide: pasted text, screenshot, forwarded email, shared message, link, QR scan, file, phone-call summary, payment receipt, device finding, or manual description. The detection focus describes what the app should look for. The result behavior describes what the user sees. Advised actions describe what the app asks the user to do next. Evidence behavior describes what can be saved. Recovery connection describes when a case should start. Helper connection describes when the user might involve another person. Privacy considerations describe what should not be exposed unnecessarily. Failure states describe what happens if the app cannot fully analyze the situation.

This pattern should apply across the whole app. It should apply to scams that are clearly risk and to situations that are ambiguous. It should apply to users who have not acted and users who already acted. It should apply when linked permissions are available and when the user only has a screenshot. Consistency makes the app easier to design and easier to test.

### Section 23 \- Bank Account Lockout Scenario

A common scenario is a message claiming that the user's bank account is locked, frozen, limited, or under fraud review. The message may arrive by text, email, or phone call. It often includes a link or phone number and asks the user to verify identity, enter a code, confirm card details, or log in quickly.

The likely input may be a pasted text message, a screenshot, a Gmail message, a link, or a phone-call summary. If the user provides a linked Gmail message, the app should inspect sender details and links. If the user provides only a screenshot, the app should extract visible text and show that sender verification is limited. If the user provides a phone-call summary, the app should treat the user's statement as context rather than verified evidence.

The app should focus detection on urgency, bank impersonation, login links, code requests, card-detail requests, sender mismatch, risky domain, and pressure to act immediately. It should also ask whether the user already clicked the link, entered a password, entered card details, or shared a security code.

The result should usually be Pause Before Acting or High Risk depending on the signals. The app should tell the user not to use the link or number from the message. The safest next step should be to open the bank's official app, type the bank's known website manually, or call the number printed on the card or statement. If the user already entered credentials or shared a code, the result should route to recovery.

Evidence should include the message, sender, link, timestamp, and any user notes about actions already taken. If recovery begins, the case should include account-security tasks, bank-contact tasks, password-change tasks if relevant, and device safety tasks if a file or app was involved.

### Section 23 \- Fake Delivery or Toll Payment Scenario

Another common scenario is a message claiming that a package, toll, parking fee, customs payment, or delivery issue requires immediate payment. These messages often include small dollar amounts to reduce suspicion. The scam may lead to a fake payment page that collects card details or personal info.

The likely input may be a text screenshot, pasted message, QR code from a fake notice, or link. The app should detect delivery language, toll language, small-fee payment pressure, risky link destination, deadline language, and requests for card details or identity info.

The result should explain that fake delivery and toll messages often use small amounts to make people act quickly. The app should recommend not using the link. The safer action is to check the official delivery carrier, toll agency, parking service, or account portal directly. If the user was not expecting a package or toll notice, the app can raise concern. If the user was expecting a package, the app should still recommend official verification rather than trusting the message.

If the user already paid or entered card details, the app should start recovery with payment-card steps. Evidence should include the link, message, payment page screenshot if available, transaction info if payment happened, and any receipt. Recovery tasks may include contacting the card issuer, monitoring for additional charges, and saving evidence.

### Section 23 \- One-Time Code Request Scenario

A one-time code request is one of the highest-risk situations the app must handle. The user may receive a call, text, email, or chat message from someone claiming to be support, a bank, a marketplace buyer, a family member, an employer, or a security team. The person asks the user to read or send a login code.

The likely input may be a pasted message, screenshot, call summary, or active guided review answer. The app should detect words like login code, security code, one-time passcode, confirmation number, login code, reset code, or two-factor code. The app should also detect the context: someone contacted the user and asked for the code.

The result should usually be High Risk. The app should explain that one-time codes are meant for the user's own login or confirmation process and should not be shared with someone who contacted them. The main action should be “Do not share the code.” If the user already shared it, the app should route to Urgent Recovery Advised.

Recovery tasks should depend on the affected account. If the user knows the account, the app should guide them to secure that account, review sessions, change password, contact official support, and check recovery settings. If the user does not know which account the code was for, the app should guide them to inspect recent messages, account alerts, and high-value accounts like email, bank, phone carrier, and payment apps.

Evidence should include the code-request message but should avoid saving the actual code unnecessarily after it expires. If the code appears in a screenshot, the app can offer redaction when sharing evidence with a helper. The app should avoid displaying the code prominently in alerts or case cards.

### Section 23 \- Remote Access Support Scenario

A remote-access support scam involves someone convincing the user to install an app, share a screen, enable accessibility permissions, grant device administrator access, or let someone control the device. The scammer may claim to be from a bank, computer company, phone company, payment app, government agency, or fraud department.

The likely input may be a phone-call summary, risky support email, text with installation link, downloaded file, installed app name, screenshot, or device safety finding. The app should detect remote access words, screen sharing, support desk, AnyDesk-like behavior without naming every possible product as malicious, installation pressure, refund claims, bank-transfer instructions, and directions to keep the call secret.

The result should be High Risk or Urgent Recovery Advised if the user installed the tool or granted access. The app should recommend stopping communication, avoiding new password entry on the affected device, using another trusted device for account security, removing risky remote-access apps, reviewing permissions, and contacting affected providers through official channels.

Device safety should connect directly. If the user says they installed an app, the app should start a device safety path and attach it to the recovery case. If the app can inspect installed apps or risky permissions, it should do so with user permission. If it cannot inspect directly, it should guide the user to check app lists and permissions manually.

Evidence should include the support message, link, app name, call notes, screenshots, payment request, and device findings. Helper review may be especially useful because remote-access situations can feel technically confusing. The app should allow the user to share a limited case view with a trusted helper.

### Section 23 \- Marketplace Buyer or Seller Scenario

Marketplace scams may involve fake buyers, fake sellers, overpayment, off-platform payment, shipping label tricks, fake escrow, fake pickup emergencies, or requests to verify through a code. The user may be buying or selling an item and may feel pressured to move quickly.

The likely input may be a marketplace message screenshot, pasted chat, payment request, link, email, or user description. The app should detect off-platform payment pressure, overpayment, fake confirmation emails, requests for codes, unusual shipping arrangements, escrow claims, courier claims, and pressure to use friends-and-family payment.

The result should explain the specific marketplace risk. If the issue is off-platform payment, the app should recommend keeping communication and payment inside the marketplace when possible. If the issue is overpayment, it should explain that scammers may ask for money back after a fake or reversible payment. If the issue is a code request, it should route to one-time code warnings. If the issue is a fake payment email, it should route to email review.

Evidence should include chat screenshots, payment screenshots, listing details, usernames, links, and app findings. Recovery should start if the user sent money, shipped an item after fake payment, shared a code, or gave account details. Helper review can be useful before shipping or accepting unusual payment.

### Section 23 \- Romance or Relationship Scam Scenario

Romance and relationship scams require careful tone. The user may be emotionally attached, embarrassed, defensive, or still communicating with the scammer. The app should not mock the relationship or dismiss the user's feelings. It should focus on behavior patterns and financial safety.

The likely input may be chat screenshots, payment requests, user descriptions, profile images, story summaries, or evidence of repeated emergencies. The app should detect money requests, secrecy, inability to meet, emergency stories, investment opportunities, gift cards, crypto, travel claims, medical emergencies, military claims, customs claims, and pressure to keep the relationship private.

The result should not say “this person is fake” unless there is strong evidence. It can say that the situation has serious scam warning signs, especially if money, secrecy, and repeated emergencies are involved. The main advice should be to pause payments, avoid sending more money, preserve evidence, and speak with a trusted person before continuing.

Recovery should start if the user sent money, shared ID docs, opened financial accounts, transferred crypto, or is being pressured for more. The app should warn about recovery scams because victims may be targeted again by people claiming they can recover lost money.

Helper review should be optional and sensitive. The user may be reluctant to share intimate conversations. The app should allow redaction and selected sharing. Privacy should be emphasized. Education content should explain manipulation patterns without blaming the user.

### Section 23 \- Job Offer and Check Deposit Scenario

Job scams often involve fake remote jobs, fake payroll setup, equipment purchases, fake checks, money forwarding, ID doc requests, or interviews conducted only through messaging. The user may be excited or financially vulnerable.

The likely input may be a job email, chat screenshot, offer letter, check image, payment request, link, or file. The app should detect too-good-to-be-true pay, rushed hiring, requests to buy equipment through a specific vendor, checks sent before work, requests to forward money, personal bank details, ID docs, risky company domains, and communication outside normal hiring channels.

The result should explain the specific risk. If the user receives a check and is asked to send money back or buy equipment, the app should warn that checks can appear to clear before later failing. If the user is asked to provide ID docs before verifying the employer, the app should recommend confirming the company through official channels.

Recovery should start if the user deposited a check, sent money, shared ID docs, gave bank details, or downloaded risky onboarding files. Evidence should include offer emails, chat messages, check images, payment receipts, file attachments, and company info. The app should avoid giving legal or employment advice, but it can guide safer verification.

### Section 23 \- Investment and Crypto Scenario

Investment and crypto scams may involve guaranteed returns, secret strategies, fake trading platforms, romance-investment crossover, celebrity claims, social media mentors, fake withdrawal fees, tax fees, account unlock fees, and recovery scams. These scenarios can cause major losses and repeated payments.

The likely input may be chat screenshots, website links, fake platform screenshots, wallet addresses, payment receipts, transaction hashes, email messages, social media profiles, or user descriptions. The app should detect guaranteed profit language, pressure to deposit more, withdrawal blocks, fees to unlock money, requests to move off-platform, and claims that only a specific person can help recover funds.

The result should usually be High Risk when guaranteed returns, withdrawal fees, or pressure to add money appear. The app should recommend not sending additional funds, saving evidence, and contacting relevant financial or platform support through official channels. It should explain that requests to pay more money to recover money are a major warning sign.

Recovery tasks should help the user organize transactions, wallet addresses, platform names, dates, messages, and payment methods. The app should be honest that recovery may be difficult. It should focus on stopping additional loss, preserving evidence, protecting accounts, and avoiding follow-up scams.

### Section 23 \- Family Emergency Scenario

Family emergency scams claim that a loved one is in trouble and needs money immediately. The scam may mention jail, accident, hospital, travel, phone loss, or danger. It may tell the user not to contact anyone else.

The likely input may be a text, call summary, voicemail transcript, chat screenshot, or payment request. The app should detect urgency, secrecy, emotional pressure, unknown number, request for immediate money, refusal to verify identity, and payment methods like gift cards, wire transfer, or payment apps.

The result should recommend pausing and verifying through another known contact method. The app can suggest calling the family member directly using a saved number, contacting another family member, asking a question only the real person would know, or refusing to use contact details provided in the risky message.

If the user already paid, recovery should start with payment steps and evidence capture. Helper review can be important here because family pressure can override caution. The app should make helper contact easy without exposing unnecessary private details.

### Section 23 \- Edge Case: Legitimate Message With Scam-Like Features

Some legitimate messages look risky. A real bank may send an account alert. A real delivery service may send a link. A real employer may request documents. A real family member may need help. the app must support these cases without teaching users to ignore all warnings.

The app should focus on safe verification. It can say that the message may or may not be legitimate, but the safest path is to verify through official channels. The app should not force a final scam label. It should help the user act safely even when the item is real.

The result should avoid false certainty. It may say, “This could be legitimate, but the link and urgency mean you should verify outside this message.” That is a useful answer. The app can teach that real companies will not be offended if users verify through official channels.

### Section 23 \- Edge Case: User Already Trusts the Sender

The user may trust the sender because it appears to be a friend, family member, employer, landlord, marketplace buyer, romantic partner, or known company. Trust can make warnings harder to accept. the app should handle this gently.

The app should explain that scams can come from impersonated accounts, compromised accounts, spoofed numbers, or manipulated relationships. It should not say the trusted person is bad. It should say the request has risky behavior and should be verified separately.

If the user marks the sender as trusted, the app should remember context carefully. It can reduce noise for normal messages, but it should still warn when a trusted sender asks for money, secrecy, codes, remote access, or ID docs. Trust should never disable risky protection.

### Section 23 \- Edge Case: User Has Only a Memory of the Event

Sometimes the user will not have evidence. They may remember a phone call, deleted message, lost screenshot, or vague payment request. The app should still help. It can run a guided review based on the user's memory, mark confidence as limited, and recommend safe next steps.

The app should ask simple questions: who contacted them, what was requested, whether money or info was shared, whether they clicked or installed anything, what account may be involved, and whether the person is still contacting them. These answers can create a recovery case even without original evidence.

The result should say that the app is using the user's description. It should not pretend to verify details it did not see. Evidence vault can store user notes as notes, not original evidence. This distinction matters for recovery timelines.

### Section 23 \- Edge Case: Multiple Scams in One Case

A user may face multiple linked scams. For example, a romance scam may turn into an investment scam. A fake bank text may lead to remote access. A fake job offer may lead to identity theft and a fake check. A crypto scam may lead to a recovery scam. the app should allow cases to contain multiple scam patterns.

The case summary should show the primary current risk and secondary related risks. The app should not force the user to create separate cases unless that helps organization. Evidence can be tagged with multiple categories. Recovery tasks should be prioritized by current exposure, not by the first category chosen.

The result explanation should show linked patterns. It can say that the situation includes both investment-risk signals and recovery-scam signals. This helps users understand why the app recommends stopping payments and preserving evidence.

### Section 23 \- Scenario Library Accept Rules

The scenario library should pass functional review if each major scam type maps to inputs, detection focus, result behavior, actions, evidence, recovery, helper review, privacy, and failure states. It should pass if ambiguous legitimate-looking messages still lead to safe verification rather than false certainty. It should pass if trusted-sender scenarios preserve caution. It should pass if memory-only cases can still receive guidance. It should pass if multi-scam cases can hold linked patterns without losing context.

The scenario library should fail if scenarios are only stories without app behavior. It should fail if the app gives the same generic advice for every scam. It should fail if recovery is not linked to exposure. It should fail if helper review ignores privacy. It should fail if edge cases are handled by forcing a yes-or-no scam label.

### Section 23 completion note

Section 23 details the design brief with a functional scenario library, bank lockout scenarios, delivery and toll scenarios, one-time code scenarios, remote-access support scenarios, marketplace scenarios, romance scenarios, job scenarios, investment and crypto scenarios, family emergency scenarios, legitimate-message edge cases, trusted-sender edge cases, memory-only event handling, multi-scam case behavior, and scenario accept rules while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 24: App Info Objects, Relationships, and Data Behavior

### Section 24 purpose

This detail defines the info objects inside Verivae. An info object is a major thing the app needs to understand and organize, such as a scam check result, saved evidence item, recovery case, task, linked source, permission, helper, device finding, risk memory item, or weekly check summary. Defining these objects makes the app more functional because every screen and flow needs to know what it is handling.

This section is not a database design and does not include code. It describes product behavior. It explains what each object represents, what info belongs to it, what actions can happen to it, and how it connects to other objects. This helps future designers understand screen content and helps future developers understand product relationships before implementation begins.

### Section 24 \- Scam Check Result Object

A scam check result is created whenever the user or app reviews risky content. The result can come from manual check, Gmail review, message review, link review, QR scan, file review, device safety check, weekly check, or guided review. The result should be treated as a meaningful object, not just a temporary screen.

A result should include source type, submitted content type, risk level, confidence language, top signals, evidence used, limitations, advised actions, user exposure answers, created time, and whether the result was saved. It may also include linked source metadata when permitted, such as sender email, sender phone number, link domain, file name, or QR destination.

The result should connect to other app objects. It can become a saved evidence item. It can start a recovery case. It can attach to an existing case. It can trigger a helper review. It can influence risk memory if the user allows personalization. It can appear in weekly checks if unresolved. It can be used as education context.

A result should have a user outcome state. The user may mark it helpful, not helpful, expected, risky, safe after verification, scam confirmed, or still unsure. This outcome should not erase the original result. The app should preserve both original assessment and later user outcome.

A result should have privacy behavior. If the result includes sensitive content, the app should avoid showing full details in alerts, Home cards, or shared helper views unless the user chooses. If a result is not saved, the app should explain whether it disappears after the session or remains in minimal history.

### Section 24 \- Evidence Item Object

An evidence item is any saved object that may help the user understand, report, recover from, or review a risky situation. Evidence can include screenshots, messages, emails, links, QR results, file findings, device findings, payment notes, transaction screenshots, account alerts, user-written notes, helper comments, and app-generated result summaries.

An evidence item should include type, title, source, created or captured time, saved time, related risk level, related case, sensitivity flag, shared status, redaction status, and notes. It should also include an original-content marker when applicable. Original content means content captured from a message, email, screenshot, file, or app result. User notes should be clearly separate from original content.

Evidence should have actions. The user can view, rename, add notes, attach to case, detach from case, redact a copy, share with helper, include in evidence package, export, delete, or mark as sensitive. Some actions may depend on the type. A payment note may not have the same preview as an image. A screenshot may support visual redaction. A link result may support re-checking.

Evidence should connect to recovery tasks. A task about contacting a payment provider can reference transaction evidence. A task about account recovery can reference risky login emails. A task about device cleanup can reference risky app findings. The user should not have to search the Vault manually during recovery.

Evidence should have clear deletion behavior. Deleting evidence should remove it from Vault and related case views, but the app may need to warn if the evidence is part of an open recovery case. If the user deletes a redacted copy, the original may remain. If the user deletes the original, redacted copies or exports that already left the app may not be recoverable or controllable. The app should explain this simply.

### Section 24 \- Recovery Case Object

A recovery case represents an organized risky event or harm event. It should group results, evidence, tasks, notes, helper activity, device findings, and status. A case can begin from a risky result, manual recovery start, evidence item, device finding, helper advice, or weekly check.

A case should include summary, primary risk type, secondary risk types, urgency level, status, exposure type, affected accounts, affected payment methods, related people or senders, evidence list, task list, notes, helper permissions, timeline, and last updated time. Not all fields must be filled. The app should tolerate incomplete cases.

A case should support multiple categories. A fake support case may include bank impersonation, remote access, payment risk, and device risk. A romance scam case may include relationship manipulation, payment loss, crypto transfer, and recovery scam risk. The app should not force one category when the situation crosses boundaries.

A case should have status changes. Status can move from needs attention to in progress, waiting on provider, monitoring, resolved as much as possible, or closed by user. Status changes should be based on task progress, user choices, and unresolved urgent items. The app should not automatically declare a case resolved just because time passed.

A case should have a timeline. The timeline should show when the risky item arrived, when the user acted, when the result was created, when evidence was saved, when tasks were completed, when helpers commented, and when status changed. The timeline helps the user remember what happened and supports recovery reports.

### Section 24 \- Recovery Task Object

A recovery task is an action the user can take to reduce harm, preserve evidence, secure accounts, contact providers, clean up devices, or monitor future risk. Tasks should be specific, plain, and tied to the user's exposure.

A task should include title, purpose, priority, related exposure, step list, required evidence, official-channel warning, status, due or reminder option, related case, related evidence, notes, and completion time. Status options can include not started, in progress, done, not applicable, waiting, needs help, and skipped by user.

Tasks should be generated based on exposure. Payment exposure creates provider-contact tasks. Password exposure creates account security tasks. Code exposure creates account takeover review tasks. Remote-access exposure creates device safety and trusted-device tasks. ID doc exposure creates identity-protection and monitoring tasks. Unknown exposure creates triage tasks.

Tasks should avoid generic overload. The app should not create forty tasks at once for every case. It should prioritize immediate tasks and allow additional tasks to appear after the user completes the first set. This supports users under stress.

Tasks should be linked to evidence and helper review. A helper may comment on a task or suggest that a user complete it. Evidence can be attached directly. The app should record task progress without exposing private task notes to helpers unless shared.

### Section 24 \- Linked Source Object

A linked source is any account, app, system, or input channel that the app can use for review. Sources may include Gmail, manual text input, message share, alert access, browser share, QR scanner, file picker, cloud file share, device safety permission, payment app evidence entered manually, or future companion apps.

A linked source should include source type, active status, permission level, last checked time, last successful review, limitations, user-facing benefit, privacy explanation, and disconnect action. It should also indicate whether the source supports selected review, background monitoring, or manual-only input.

Source status should be visible in Protection Hub. A source can be active, partially active, off, unavailable on this device, dislinked, permission expired, or needs attention. The app should explain what still works when a source is off.

Linked sources should not be treated as permanent. Permissions can expire, accounts can disconnect, devices can change, and users can revoke access. The app should detect this where possible and update the user. A dislinked source should not cause unrelated features to fail.

### Section 24 \- Permission Object

A permission object represents a specific access choice the user has made. Permissions should be visible, understandable, and reversible. They are central to trust because the app may handle sensitive messages, emails, screenshots, device signals, and recovery evidence.

A permission should include what it enables, why it is useful, whether it is required or optional, what data it may access, what it does not access, current status, where it can be changed, and what function remains without it. This should be expressed in plain text in the app.

Permissions should map to features. Gmail selected review may require one permission. Gmail monitoring may require a stronger or separate permission. Alert alerts may require alert access. Device safety checks may require settings or app-inspection access where supported. Evidence vault may require storage behavior. Helper review requires sharing permission for selected cases or items.

Permission changes should create app behavior changes. If the user turns off alert access, proactive message alerts pause. If Gmail access is removed, selected Gmail review becomes unavailable but manual email check remains. If evidence storage is disabled or cleared, recovery cases should explain missing evidence rather than breaking.

### Section 24 \- Trusted Helper Object

A trusted helper is a person the user chooses to involve. The helper object should include helper name, contact method, invitation status, accepted status, permission scope, shared cases, shared evidence, alert permissions, comments, and revocation status. The helper should not receive broad access by default.

Helper permissions should be scoped. A helper can view one result, one case, selected evidence, risky alerts, recovery tasks, or second-opinion requests. Each scope should be clear. The user should see who can access what. The helper should see only what was shared.

The helper object should support expiration. A user may want temporary review for one risky payment but not ongoing access. The app should allow access to expire after a case closes or after a selected period if the user chooses.

Helper activity should be recorded. If a helper comments, marks concern, suggests verification, or confirms that they reviewed an item, the app should show that in the case timeline. Helper comments should be distinguished from app findings.

### Section 24 \- Device Finding Object

A device finding is a safety signal from the current phone, linked device, account session review, or weekly check. Findings can include risky app permission, risky remote-access app, unknown configuration profile, browser alert abuse, unknown signed-in device, outdated system, weak lock screen, or unresolved risky download.
