A finding should include finding type, severity, explanation, source, what was checked, what was not checked, related case, advised action, status, and last checked time. It should always explain platform limits. If the app cannot remove a risky setting directly, it should guide the user to the correct phone settings path.

Device findings should connect to recovery. If a finding appears after a support scam, it should attach to that recovery case. If a weekly check finds a risky setting without a case, the app can create a standalone finding and recommend review. The user can dismiss, resolve, save, or start a case from a finding.

### Section 24 \- Risk Memory Object

Risk memory is a user-controlled set of remembered safety patterns. It may include trusted senders, expected accounts, repeated scam types, user-dismissed patterns, frequent payment providers, helper preferences, and unresolved watch items. It should improve context but remain editable.

A risk memory item should include type, label, reason remembered, source, created time, last used time, privacy level, and delete action. For example, a trusted sender memory may say it was created because the user marked a sender expected after verification. A scam-pattern memory may say the user has repeatedly checked fake delivery texts.

Risk memory should not create permanent trust. Every memory item should have boundaries. A trusted sender can still trigger warnings for money, secrecy, codes, ID docs, or remote access. A dismissed warning can reduce noise but should not disable future protection.

### Section 24 \- Weekly Deep Check Summary Object

A weekly check summary should record what the app reviewed during the scheduled safety loop. It should include date of check, protections active at the time, sources reviewed, sources unavailable, findings, unresolved cases, completed recovery tasks, permission changes, device changes, repeated patterns, and advised next actions.

The summary should be readable from Home, Protection Hub, and history. It should start with urgent items and then show details. If nothing urgent was found, it should still show what was checked. If permissions limited the check, it should say which checks were skipped.

The summary should connect to other objects. A finding can become a device finding. An unresolved case can be surfaced. A repeated risky sender can become risk memory. A missing permission can link to Permission Health. A risky item can become a result or recovery case.

### Section 24 \- Object Relationship Accept Rules

The app should pass functional review if a result can become evidence, a case, a helper review, a risk memory signal, or a recovery task trigger. It should pass if evidence can attach to cases and tasks. It should pass if cases can contain multiple results, evidence items, tasks, helper comments, and device findings. It should pass if permission changes update feature status without breaking manual flows.

The app should pass if linked sources show clear active, limited, or unavailable states. It should pass if helpers have scoped access. It should pass if device findings connect to actions. It should pass if risk memory is visible and editable. It should pass if weekly summaries connect to findings, cases, permissions, and education.

The app should fail if objects are isolated. It should fail if results disappear when the user needs recovery. It should fail if evidence is saved but cannot be used in tasks. It should fail if helper access is broad or unclear. It should fail if permission loss creates silent gaps. It should fail if risk memory cannot be reviewed or reset.

### Section 24 completion note

Section 24 details the design brief with app info objects, scam check result behavior, evidence item behavior, recovery case behavior, recovery task behavior, linked source behavior, permission behavior, trusted helper behavior, device finding behavior, risk memory behavior, weekly check summary behavior, and object relationship accept rules while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 25: Free Access, Paid Access, Account Behavior, and Ethical Monetization Inside the App

### Section 25 purpose

This detail defines how the app can support responsible in-app monetization while staying app-focused and user-safe. It describes the product behavior that would allow a free version, paid features, subscriptions, trials, account access, family helper access, and plan limitations to function without blocking urgent safety support.

Because Verivae deals with scams, money loss, account compromise, and user fear, monetization must be handled carefully. The app should never exploit panic. It should never hide urgent safety guidance behind a paywall when the user may already be at risk. It should never say “pay now or stay unsafe.” The product can still make money, but the free experience must remain genuinely useful and the paid experience must add convenience, depth, monitoring, storage, helper features, and extended protection.

### Section 25 \- Free-First Product Access

The free version of the app should provide meaningful protection. A free user should be able to manually check risky messages, links, QR codes, emails by paste or screenshot, and basic scam situations. The free user should receive plain risk results, basic next steps, safe verification guidance, and emergency recovery direction when they may already have acted.

The free version should not be a fake demo. If the free version only tells users to upgrade whenever risk appears, users will not trust the app. Basic scam checking should work. Basic risky warnings should work. Basic education should work. Basic recovery triage should work. This is especially important because the people most vulnerable to scams may not be ready to pay before they understand the product.

Free access can have limits, but the limits should be functional and fair. Examples of acceptable limits include a monthly number of manual checks, limited saved evidence storage, no background monitoring, no automatic Gmail monitoring, limited weekly check depth, limited helper seats, and basic recovery task lists instead of extended guided case spaces. These limits should be explained clearly before the user hits them where possible.

The app should allow a free user to complete an urgent safety action even if they hit a limit. For example, if the user has reached a free manual-check limit but enters an urgent recovery flow because they already shared a code, the app should still show core urgent safety guidance. The app may explain that advanced evidence packages or ongoing monitoring require paid access, but immediate harm-reduction guidance should remain visible.

### Section 25 \- Paid Feature Categories

Paid features should add meaningful value without removing core safety from free users. Strong paid categories may include background monitoring, advanced linked-source review, weekly checks, detailed evidence vault storage, trusted helper workflows, advanced case space tools, device safety scheduling, multi-device support, custom risk memory, detailed reports, family protection features, and priority review capacity if human or advanced review is ever added.

Background monitoring is a natural paid feature because it requires more infrastructure and provides ongoing convenience. Paid users may enable Gmail monitoring, alert-based risky alerts, repeated sender watch, risky link watch, and weekly protection summaries. Manual review should remain available for free.

Advanced evidence vault storage is another paid feature. Free users can save a small number of items or one active case. Paid users can save more evidence, create evidence packages, redact copies, organize more cases, and export reports. The app should clearly show storage limits and avoid surprising users when they need evidence.

Trusted helper workflows can have paid depth. A free user may be able to share one result or one case snapshot. Paid users may add multiple helpers, persistent family review, risky payment second opinions, helper comments, helper alerts, and shared recovery task progress. Helper access should always remain scoped and revocable.

Advanced case space features can be paid while urgent basics remain free. Free recovery can provide triage and essential steps. Paid recovery can provide deeper task organization, evidence packages, reminders, multi-account checklists, helper collaboration, and longer case history. The app should avoid paywalling the first urgent guidance after harm.

### Section 25 \- Paywall Placement Rules

Paywalls should appear at natural boundaries, not during panic moments. A natural boundary is a moment where the user is choosing an enhancement, not trying to stop immediate harm. Good paywall locations include enabling ongoing monitoring, increasing evidence storage, adding multiple helpers, scheduling deeper weekly checks, exporting detailed reports, or using advanced organization features.

Bad paywall locations include immediately after a risky warning, before showing basic recovery steps, before telling the user not to share a code, before warning about a risky payment, or before explaining that a link is risky. The app should not make the user pay to learn that they should stop a dangerous action.

When a paywall appears, it should explain the feature in plain terms. It should say what the paid feature adds, what remains free, and how the user can continue without upgrading. For example, a paywall for Gmail monitoring can say that manual email checks remain free, while automatic review of risky email patterns requires paid access.

Paywalls should never exaggerate risk to drive payment. The app should not use scare wording like “Upgrade or scammers can get you.” It can say “Paid monitoring can check for warning signs automatically, but you can still manually check risky items for free.”

### Section 25 \- Trial and Upgrade Behavior

If Verivae offers a free trial, the trial should be transparent. The app should show what features are included, when the trial ends, whether payment is required to start, how renewal works, and where cancellation is managed. The user should not be surprised by a charge.

Trial prompts should be tied to features. If the user tries to enable weekly checks, the app can offer a trial of advanced protection. If the user tries to add multiple helpers, it can explain paid family features. If the user tries to save more evidence than the free limit, it can offer detailed storage. The prompt should be contextual.

The app should preserve safety continuity when a trial ends. If advanced monitoring turns off, the app should show that status in Protection Hub. Existing recovery cases should not disappear. Existing evidence should not be deleted abruptly. If storage exceeds the free limit after a downgrade, the app should make items read-only or ask the user to choose what to keep rather than deleting evidence without warning.

Upgrade and downgrade behavior should be simple. The user should always know what plan is active, which features are available, what will change if they downgrade, and how to manage the subscription. Billing management should follow app store or platform requirements, but the app should still explain access status clearly.

### Section 25 \- Account Creation and Guest Behavior

the app should allow guest use for basic manual checks. A person who receives a risky message should not be forced to create an account before receiving basic help. Guest mode should support quick check, link check, QR check, basic education, and basic recovery triage.

Account creation becomes useful when the user wants saved evidence, recovery cases, linked Gmail review, helper sharing, risk memory, weekly checks, paid features, or multi-device continuity. The app should explain account creation as a way to save and protect info, not as a requirement for every check.

Guest mode should have clear limits. If the user wants to save evidence or start a case, the app can ask them to create an account so the info is not lost. If the user declines, the app can provide temporary guidance but should explain that unsaved info may not be available later.

Account security should be strong because the app may store sensitive scam evidence. The account should support secure sign-in, password reset, session review, and stronger auth where available. The app should never ask users to share their Verivae login code with anyone, and it can use its own education principles during account sign-in.

### Section 25 \- Plan State in the Interface

The app should show plan state without making the interface feel like an advertisement. Protection Hub is the best place for detailed plan state. It can show Free, Trial, Paid, Family, or expired states if those exist. It should show active features, unavailable features, and usage limits.

Feature screens can show small plan indicators when relevant. For example, Evidence Vault can show storage usage. Helper settings can show helper slots. Weekly check settings can show whether advanced scheduling is included. Gmail monitoring can show whether background review is included.

The app should avoid placing upgrade banners everywhere. Too many upgrade prompts can reduce trust. Upgrade prompts should appear when the user tries to use a paid feature or when a clear benefit relates to their current need. The prompt should never block basic safety guidance.

Plan state should also appear in weekly checks when paid protection changes. If a subscription expired and monitoring paused, the weekly summary can say background monitoring is off and manual checks remain available. This prevents false confidence.

### Section 25 \- Family and Helper Paid Access Behavior

Family or helper features may become one of the most valuable paid areas because scams often affect families. The app can support a family plan or helper seats, but the behavior should be designed around consent. A paying family member should not automatically get access to another user's private messages, evidence, or recovery cases.

Each protected user should control what is shared. A parent, adult child, spouse, sibling, caregiver, or trusted friend may be invited as a helper, but access should be scoped. Paid family features can make sharing easier, allow more helpers, support risky alerts, and preserve family review history. They should not remove user consent.

For vulnerable users who want more support, the app can support stronger optional sharing. For example, a user can choose to send risky payment warnings to a helper. This must be explicit. The app should make it easy to see and revoke.

Family paid access should include privacy boundaries. The account holder who pays should not automatically see private scam checks. Billing ownership and data access should be separate concepts. The app should explain this simply.

### Section 25 \- Monetization Safety Accept Rules

The app should pass functional review if free users can manually check risky content and receive useful safety guidance. It should pass if urgent warnings and basic recovery triage are not blocked by payment. It should pass if paid features add monitoring, storage, helper collaboration, deeper recovery tools, and convenience. It should pass if paywalls explain what remains free.

The app should pass if guest mode supports fast checking. It should pass if account creation is required only when persistence, sharing, linked sources, or paid access makes it necessary. It should pass if downgrades do not unexpectedly delete evidence or hide active recovery cases. It should pass if plan state is clear in Protection Hub.

The app should fail if it exploits fear to force payment. It should fail if a user must pay before learning not to share a code or send money. It should fail if subscription expiration silently disables protection. It should fail if family payment creates automatic access to private data. It should fail if free users cannot meaningfully understand scam risk.

### Section 25 completion note

Section 25 details the design brief with free-first access behavior, paid feature categories, paywall placement rules, trial and upgrade behavior, account and guest behavior, plan-state interface behavior, family and helper paid access behavior, and monetization safety accept rules while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 26: Accessibility, Plain-Language UX, and Support for Stressed or Vulnerable Users

### Section 26 purpose

This detail defines accessibility and beginner usability for Verivae. Scam protection is not only a technical problem. It is a human problem. The app must work for users who are stressed, older, visually impaired, distracted, embarrassed, overwhelmed, neurodivergent, new to smartphones, unfamiliar with banking terms, or uncertain about online safety. If the app is hard to read or hard to navigate, it will fail at the exact moment it is needed most.

Accessibility should be treated as core function. The user should be able to read warnings, understand next steps, use assistive technologies, complete recovery tasks, manage permissions, and share with helpers without needing technical confidence. The app should support people who are checking scams for themselves and people helping someone else.

### Section 26 \- Plain-Language Standard

the app should use plain text throughout the app. Plain language means short sentences, common words, clear actions, and explanations that do not require security knowledge. The app can teach terms like phishing, spoofing, malware, social engineering, and two-factor auth, but it should define the practical meaning first.

A result should not begin with “possible credential phishing due to domain mismatch.” It should begin with something like “This message asks you to sign in through a link that may not belong to the company it claims to be from.” The technical term can appear below as an explanation. This pattern helps beginners understand the risk without feeling excluded.

The app should avoid shame language. It should not say the user “fell for” a scam, “ignored obvious signs,” or “made a mistake.” It should say what happened and what can be done next. The app should assume the user is trying to protect themselves and needs calm guidance.

The app should avoid vague safety language. Words like risky, risky, and unsafe should be paired with reasons. “This is risky” is weaker than “This is risky because it asks for a security code after contacting you first.” Reasons help users learn and trust the warning.

### Section 26 \- Reading Level and Message Length

Core app copy should be written at a beginner-friendly reading level. The app should not use long paragraphs on urgent screens. Risky warnings should be brief at the top with more detail below. Users in crisis may only read the first few lines, so the top lines must carry the main action.

Result screens can use layered explanations. The first layer should be a short risk level and action. The second layer should show top reasons. The third layer can show detailed evidence and educational explanation. This keeps the app useful for both beginners and users who want more detail.

Recovery tasks should be broken into steps. A task should not say “secure your account” and stop there. It should say open the official app or website, change the password, sign out of other sessions, review recovery settings, and turn on stronger auth if available. Each step should be simple and checkable.

The app should avoid info overload in alerts. Alerts should be short and private. The detailed explanation belongs inside the app after the user opens it. A lock-screen alert should not show full scam content, personal messages, or sensitive evidence.

### Section 26 \- Visual Accessibility Behavior

The app should support readable text sizes. Users should be able to use system text-size settings without the layout breaking. Buttons should remain visible. Cards should not overlap. Long words like crypto, auth, verification, and impersonation should wrap cleanly.

Color should not be the only way to communicate risk. A risky result can use color, but it should also use text labels, icons, and clear action wording. Users with color vision differences should still understand whether something is low concern, needs review, risk, or urgent recovery.

Contrast should be strong enough for warnings, buttons, evidence labels, and task steps. The app should avoid faint gray text for important safety details. Secondary info can be visually quieter, but anything the user must act on should be easy to read.

Touch targets should be large enough for users with limited dexterity. Important buttons like Review, Stop and Verify, Start Recovery, Save Evidence, Call Official Provider, Ask Helper, and Done should be easy to tap. Destructive actions like Delete Evidence or Revoke Helper Access should require clear confirmation.

The app should support dark mode and light mode if feasible. Both modes should preserve contrast and risk meaning. Dark mode should not make risky warnings look decorative or reduce readability.

### Section 26 \- Screen Reader and Assistive Technology Behavior

the app should be usable with screen readers. Every important button, result label, risk level, icon, evidence item, and task control should have clear accessible names. A screen reader user should understand what a control does without seeing the screen.

Risk results should be announced in a useful order. The screen reader should read the risk level, main advice, top reason, and primary action before reading less important details. It should not read decorative elements first. The app's accessibility order should match the user's decision priority.

Evidence items should have accessible descriptions. A screenshot evidence item should be described by title, date, source, and risk relevance. If text was extracted from the screenshot, the user should be able to hear that text. If the image is unclear, the app should say that.

Task lists should be navigable. A screen reader user should be able to hear task status, priority, and next action. Completed tasks should be identified. Waiting tasks should be identified. Skipped tasks should be identified. Controls like done, not applicable, need help, and remind later should be easy to distinguish.

The app should support voice input where the OS allows it. Users should be able to dictate a scam description, recovery note, or helper message. The app should treat dictated text like typed text and allow editing before submission.

### Section 26 \- Cognitive Accessibility and Stress Support

Scam situations create cognitive load. The app should reduce that load. It should ask one important question at a time during guided review. It should avoid presenting a dozen equal choices when one action is urgent. It should remember previous answers inside a case so the user does not repeat themselves.

The app should use progressive disclosure. Progressive disclosure means showing the most important info first and hiding deeper detail behind expandable sections. For Verivae, the first view should show the advice and next action. The deeper view can show evidence, signal details, education, and source limitations.

The app should support “I am not sure” as a valid answer. Many users will not know whether they clicked, whether money was sent, whether the sender is real, or whether a file was opened. The app should not punish uncertainty. It should route uncertain answers to safe checks and explain what info would help.

The app should include pause moments. In risky payment or code-sharing situations, the app can display a short pause screen that says what not to do yet and what to verify. The pause should be calm, not dramatic. It should help the user slow down.

The app should support returning later. Users may need to call a bank, talk to family, find documents, or calm down. Recovery cases should save progress and show the next step when the user returns.

### Section 26 \- Older Adult and Family Support Behavior

the app should work well for older adults without stereotyping them. The app should avoid assuming older users are incapable. It should provide clear text, large touch targets, simple choices, helper support, and calm explanations. It should respect user control.

Family support should be consent-based. A helper can assist with review, but the user should choose what to share. The app should not quietly turn family support into surveillance. Older adults, parents, teenagers, and caregivers all need privacy boundaries.

The app should make it easy to ask for help. A result screen can include “Ask a trusted helper.” A recovery task can include “I need help with this step.” A helper invite should explain what will be shared. The user should be able to redact sensitive evidence before sharing.

The app should support phone-call scams, because many vulnerable users are targeted by calls rather than written messages. A user should be able to summarize a call, record notes after the call where legally and technically appropriate, or enter what the caller asked for. The app should not require perfect written evidence to provide guidance.

### Section 26 \- Multilingual and Translation Considerations

The app may eventually need multilingual support. Scam victims may receive messages in different languages or may be more comfortable reading safety guidance in a language other than English. The first version may not support every language, but the design should allow future translation.

Translation should preserve safety meaning. Risk labels, payment warnings, code-sharing warnings, and recovery tasks must be translated carefully. A literal translation that loses urgency or nuance can reduce safety. The app should avoid idioms that are difficult to translate.

If the user submits a message in another language, the app should identify that it may need translation before analysis. The result should say if translation quality may affect confidence. The app should still look for universal scam patterns like payment pressure, links, urgency, codes, and identity requests.

The interface should support longer translated text. Some languages take more space than English. Buttons and cards should allow wrapping without breaking layout. This is part of functional accessibility.

### Section 26 \- Accessibility in Recovery Tasks

Recovery tasks should be accessible under stress. A user should be able to complete one step, leave, and return. The app should not require memorizing instructions. Each task should provide clear status and next action.

Tasks should offer simpler explanations. A “what does this mean?” control can explain terms like password reset, signed-in devices, forwarding rules, remote access, charge dispute, identity alert, or two-factor auth. These explanations should be short and linked to the current task.

Tasks should support notes and reminders. A user may need to record who they called, what the provider said, what case number they received, or when to follow up. Notes should be easy to enter. Reminders should be optional.

Recovery tasks should avoid requiring the user to copy long strings manually when possible. If the app provides an evidence package summary, the user should be able to copy selected text. If the user must call a provider, the app should remind them to use official contact info from a card, statement, official app, or manually typed website.

### Section 26 \- Accessibility Accept Rules

The app should pass functional review if core scam checking works with large text settings, screen readers, plain text, and minimal required typing. It should pass if risk is communicated without relying only on color. It should pass if urgent screens show the main action first. It should pass if users can answer “not sure.” It should pass if recovery tasks are stepwise and resumable.

The app should pass if helper sharing is understandable and consent-based. It should pass if evidence cards have accessible descriptions. It should pass if alerts avoid exposing sensitive content. It should pass if translated text can fit without breaking the interface. It should pass if users who only remember a phone call can still get help.

The app should fail if warnings are hard to read. It should fail if screen reader order hides the main action. It should fail if users must understand technical terms before acting. It should fail if risky screens overwhelm users with too many equal choices. It should fail if accessibility is treated as a later polish item instead of core function.

### Section 26 completion note

Section 26 details the design brief with accessibility behavior, plain standards, reading-level expectations, visual accessibility, screen reader behavior, cognitive accessibility, stressed-user support, older adult and family support, multilingual considerations, recovery task accessibility, and accessibility accept rules while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 27: Platform Feature Boundaries and Device-Specific Behavior

### Section 27 purpose

This detail defines how the app should behave across different platforms and permission environments. Users may expect the app to connect with Gmail, messages, links, files, QR codes, phone settings, and linked devices. The app should support those goals where possible, but it must be honest about what each platform allows. The product should not promise that it can read every message, scan every file, remove every virus, or inspect every linked device unless the platform and user permission actually allow that behavior.

Platform feature boundaries should be visible in the product. If a feature works differently on iPhone, Android, desktop, browser, or web, the app should explain the difference in plain text. The user should not need to understand operating-system policy. They only need to know what protection is active, what is limited, and what they can do manually.

### Section 27 \- Platform-Aware Product Principle

The central platform principle for the app should be “best available protection with honest limits.” This means the app uses the strongest available review method on the user's device while keeping manual paths available. If linked review is possible, the app uses it. If linked review is blocked, the app supports paste, share, screenshot, scan, and guided questions. If deep device checks are limited, the app provides safe setting review and guided cleanup.

The app should never hide platform limits in small legal text. It should explain them at the feature level. A message review screen can say that automatic text-message monitoring may not be available on this device, but the user can still paste or screenshot risky messages. A device safety screen can say that the app can review certain safety settings, but cannot guarantee a complete virus scan. A Gmail screen can say that selected email review is active, while background monitoring is off.

Platform-aware design also means avoiding one-size-fits-all setup. iPhone users, Android users, web users, and future desktop users may see different setup choices. The interface should adapt without making any user feel punished for using a certain device. The app should focus on what is possible.

### Section 27 \- iPhone Behavior

On iPhone, the app should assume stronger privacy boundaries around messages, app inspection, file system access, and device scanning. The product should still be useful through manual checks, share-sheet flows, screenshots, QR scanning, Gmail integration, browser sharing, file picker access where available, evidence vault, case space, helper review, and education.

For message review on iPhone, the primary path may be copy and paste, screenshot upload, or share when supported. The app should not depend on full background access to iMessage or SMS content. If alert-based review is not available or is limited, the app should say manual review remains available.

For Gmail on iPhone, linked Gmail review can provide selected email analysis and possibly monitoring depending on granted account access. The app should make Gmail connection separate from Apple Mail access. If the user uses Apple Mail but does not connect Gmail or another supported provider, they can still paste or screenshot emails.

For links and QR codes on iPhone, the app should support paste, share-sheet entry, QR scan inside the app, screenshot reading, and safe preview before opening. The app should not automatically open QR destinations. It should show the decoded link, risk findings, and action choices first.

For file review on iPhone, the app should accept files through the file picker or share action where available. It should explain when full file inspection is limited. If a file cannot be scanned, the app can still review file name, file type, source context, surrounding message, and user actions.

For device safety on iPhone, the app should focus on guided safety checks and available signals. It can guide users to review installed apps, remove risky profiles if present, check VPN settings, review browser alerts, update the OS, use a strong passcode, check account sessions from official services, and secure accounts from a trusted device. It should avoid claiming full antivirus scanning if not possible.

### Section 27 \- Android Behavior

On Android, the app may have different opportunities depending on device version, manufacturer, permissions, and user choices. Android may allow richer sharing, alert access, SMS-related features in some contexts, installed-app visibility in limited ways, file access, and deeper device-safety guidance. The app should still be careful, permission-based, and transparent.

For message review on Android, the app can support paste, screenshot, share action, and possibly alert-based risky alerts if the user grants permission. If SMS access is considered in a future version, the app should use the narrowest useful permission and explain exactly what it does. It should not silently read private messages for broad purposes.

For alert-based protection, Android may allow the app to detect risky phrases from alerts. The app should limit use to scam and safety warning signs. It should avoid storing alert content unless the user chooses to save it as evidence. Lock-screen alerts should remain private.

For device safety on Android, the app may guide users through installed apps, app permissions, accessibility access, alert access, device administrator apps, unknown app install settings, VPN profiles, browser alert abuse, and OS updates. If the app can inspect some signals directly, it should show what was checked. If it cannot, it should provide guided review.

For file review on Android, the app may support file picker, shared files, downloads, and attachment review. It should be careful with risky files. If full scanning is not available, it should explain limits and still provide context-based warnings.

Android behavior should account for variation. A feature may work on one Android phone and not another. The app should detect feature at runtime where possible and show device-specific setup. It should not assume all Android users have the same permissions or settings.

### Section 27 \- Web App Behavior

A web version of Verivae, if created, should focus on manual checks, account access, evidence review, education, helper review, and case space. It may not have deep device integration. The web app can still be valuable because users may want to paste risky content from a computer, review a Gmail message, organize evidence, or work through recovery tasks on a larger screen.

The web version should allow users to paste emails, messages, links, file details, and situation descriptions. It can allow file upload when safe and permitted. It can show saved cases, evidence, tasks, helper comments, and weekly summaries. It can provide account security guidance and official-channel reminders.

The web version should not pretend to monitor phone messages or scan phone apps unless linked companion features exist. If the user asks why mobile protections are missing, the web app should explain that phone-level alerts and device checks require the mobile app.

The web version may be especially useful for recovery. Users often need a larger screen to collect evidence, read task steps, export summaries, and organize provider contact notes. Case space should be comfortable on web while preserving the same privacy controls.

### Section 27 \- Browser Extension Behavior

A future browser extension could provide link and page checking inside a desktop browser. This would be different from the mobile app. The extension could warn before the user enters credentials on a risky page, opens a risky download, visits a fake support site, or follows a risky redirect. This should be considered a future feature, not a required first version.

The extension should use clear permission boundaries. It should explain whether it checks only pages the user asks it to review, checks risky pages automatically, or monitors all browsing for scam signs. The least invasive useful mode should be preferred.

A browser extension result should connect to the same app objects. A risky page result can become evidence, attach to a case, trigger recovery, or inform risk memory. If the user signs into the app, extension findings should appear in the Vault or case history with permission.

The extension should avoid reading or storing unrelated browsing content. Its purpose is scam and money-safety review. Any background checking should be limited, transparent, and controllable.

### Section 27 \- Desktop Companion Behavior

A future desktop companion could help review downloaded files, risky emails, browser pages, and desktop security settings. This is more advanced than the first mobile app but should be described as a possible feature. The desktop companion should not be assumed in the first version.

If a desktop companion exists, it should connect to the user's Verivae account and show which device it represents. The Protection Hub can display the desktop as a linked device with clear status. It should show what the companion can check and when it last checked.

Desktop file review may be more capable than mobile file review depending on operating-system permissions. Still, the app should avoid saying a file is completely safe. It can say no known threat or risky indicators were found, or that risk indicators exist.

Desktop companion findings should connect to recovery cases. If a user downloaded a file from a risky email on a computer, the file finding should attach to the email result and recovery case. If a browser warning appears on desktop, it should be saved as a result if the user chooses.

### Section 27 \- Linked Device List Behavior

The linked device list should distinguish between physical devices, account sessions, and protected sources. A phone with the app installed is a device. A Gmail account session shown by Google is an account session. A browser extension is a linked tool. A trusted helper's phone is not automatically a protected device unless the helper separately uses Verivae.

Each linked device card should show device name, platform, connection type, last active time, protection status, available checks, limitations, and disconnect action. If the device has unresolved findings, the card should show them. If the device has not checked in recently, the card should say so.

The app should not imply that it controls devices it only knows through account info. For example, if Gmail shows a signed-in laptop, the app can guide the user to review that session, but it cannot scan that laptop unless a companion app is installed. The interface should make this distinction plain.

Linked devices should be privacy-sensitive. A helper should not see the user's full device list unless the user shares it. Device names may reveal personal info. The app should avoid exposing them unnecessarily in alerts or helper views.

### Section 27 \- Platform Limits in Weekly Deep Checks

Weekly checks should adapt to platform feature. On iPhone, the weekly check may review app permissions available to the app, linked Gmail status, recent risky results, unresolved recovery tasks, evidence gaps, and guided device-safety reminders. On Android, the weekly check may include additional permission or alert findings if granted. On web, the weekly check may focus on account, evidence, and recovery status.

The weekly summary should say what was checked on the current platform. It should not use the same wording for all devices if the actual checks differ. A summary can say “Manual checks, saved cases, Gmail selected review, and recovery tasks were reviewed. Full message monitoring is not active on this device.” That is honest and useful.

If the user has multiple devices, the weekly summary should separate them. It can show phone checks, desktop companion checks, browser extension checks, and linked account checks. Each should have a status and limitation. The user should be able to drill into details.

### Section 27 \- Platform-Specific Failure States

Platform-specific failure states should be designed. If iPhone message sharing is unavailable, the app should offer screenshot and paste. If Android alert permission is disabled, the app should show manual review and explain how to turn alerts back on. If Gmail permission expires, the app should request reconnection. If a browser extension cannot inspect a page, it should explain and provide manual link checking. If a file cannot be accessed, the app should review context and recommend safe handling.

The app should not show generic errors like “feature unavailable” without alternatives. Every platform limitation should lead to a manual fallback, explanation, or guided setting path. The user should always have a next step.

When a platform update changes feature, the app should update its explanation. If a phone OS removes or adds permission options, the app should reflect that. The design should expect platform behavior to change over time.

### Section 27 \- Platform Feature Accept Rules

The app should pass functional review if iPhone, Android, web, browser extension, and desktop companion behaviors are described with realistic limits. It should pass if every unavailable linked feature has a manual fallback. It should pass if device checks distinguish between actual device inspection and account-session review. It should pass if weekly checks state what was checked and what was limited by platform.

The app should pass if permissions are platform-specific and understandable. It should pass if linked device cards do not overclaim control. It should pass if platform failure states provide next actions. It should pass if future features can connect to existing result, evidence, case, helper, and risk memory objects.

The app should fail if it promises full phone, file, message, or virus scanning everywhere. It should fail if platform differences are hidden. It should fail if users cannot manually check risky content when integration is unavailable. It should fail if linked account sessions are presented as fully scannable devices. It should fail if weekly checks imply protections that were not active.

### Section 27 completion note

Section 27 details the design brief with platform feature boundaries, iPhone behavior, Android behavior, web behavior, browser extension behavior, desktop companion behavior, linked device list behavior, weekly check platform limits, platform-specific failure states, and platform feature accept rules while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 28: Alerts, Reminders, Background Review, and Attention Management

### Section 28 purpose

This detail defines how the app should communicate with users outside active app sessions. Scam protection often needs to intervene before a user clicks, pays, replies, shares a code, or ignores an unresolved recovery step. At the same time, the app must not become noisy. If Verivae sends too many alerts, users will disable alerts or stop trusting the product. The alert and reminder system should be precise, private, respectful, and tied to real safety value.

This section covers alert categories, reminder logic, background review behavior, quiet hours, lock-screen privacy, alert fatigue prevention, recurring deep-check communication, recovery reminders, helper alerts, and alert accept rules. It is app-only function. It does not define marketing emails, launch campaigns, or business outreach.

### Section 28 \- Alert Philosophy

The alert philosophy should be “interrupt only when the interruption helps safety.” the app should not send alerts just to increase engagement. Every alert should have a reason linked to scam prevention, recovery progress, permission health, helper review, device safety, or user-requested reminders.

Alerts should be grouped by urgency. Urgent alerts involve active payment risk, code sharing, account compromise, remote access, or unresolved recovery tasks that are time sensitive. Important alerts involve risky risky items, helper review responses, device safety findings, or weekly check issues. Low-priority alerts involve education suggestions, non-urgent summaries, or optional setup reminders.

The app should give users control over alert categories. A user may want risky alerts but not education reminders. A user may want recovery task reminders but not weekly summaries. A user may want helper alerts only for urgent cases. Alert controls should use plain text rather than technical categories.

Alerts should be private by default. The app should assume that a phone may be visible to family, coworkers, partners, helpers, or strangers. Alerts should avoid showing full risky messages, payment amounts, account names, ID doc details, or private recovery notes unless the user chooses a more detailed alert mode.

### Section 28 \- Alert Categories

the app should define several alert categories. Risky scam alerts warn about risky messages, emails, links, QR scans, or linked-source findings. Recovery reminders help users continue urgent or waiting tasks. Device safety alerts report risky settings or deep-check findings. Helper alerts tell the user when a trusted helper reviewed or commented. Permission health alerts warn when a protection has turned off or expired. Weekly summary alerts invite the user to review the latest safety check.

Risky scam alerts should be rare and meaningful. They should appear when the app has a strong reason to believe the user should pause before acting. These alerts should open the relevant result screen or stop-and-verify screen. They should not open a generic Home screen.

Recovery reminders should be tied to tasks. If the user sets a reminder to call a provider, the alert should open that task. If a task is waiting on provider, the app can remind the user to follow up only when the user selected a follow-up date or when the task is clearly time sensitive. Recovery reminders should not shame the user for unfinished tasks.

Device safety alerts should describe the category of issue without exposing sensitive details. For example, “One device safety setting needs review” is better than listing a risky app name on the lock screen. The detailed finding should appear inside the app.

Helper alerts should respect shared scope. If a helper comments on a shared case, the user can receive a alert. If the helper marks concern about a risky item, the alert should open that case or result. The helper should not be able to trigger unlimited alerts to the user.

Permission health alerts should be limited. If a critical protection turns off, the user should know. If a low-priority permission is off by choice, the app should not nag constantly. The app should distinguish between unexpected permission loss and user-selected disabled features.

### Section 28 \- Background Review Behavior

Background review should only happen when the user has clearly enabled it and the platform allows it. Background review may include Gmail monitoring, alert-based risky pattern checks, repeated sender watch, link watch, weekly checks, device safety checks, and recovery case follow-up. Each background review area should be visible in Protection Hub.

Background review should not create silent judgments. If Verivae flags something in the background, the user should be able to see why. The result should say what source was reviewed, which signals were found, what was unavailable, and what action is advised. Background results should follow the same explainability rules as manual checks.

Background review should be conservative about storage. The app should not automatically save every reviewed email, alert, or message as evidence. It can create a minimal alert record or risk event, then ask the user whether to save full evidence. For risky events, it can recommend saving evidence but should explain what will be saved.

Background review should avoid broad personal surveillance. Its purpose is scam and money-safety detection. The app should not analyze unrelated personal content for non-safety reasons. User-facing privacy language should make this clear.

Background review should support pause controls. The user may pause monitoring for a source, pause alerts temporarily, disable a category, or turn off all proactive protection while keeping manual checks. Pausing should be easy to reverse.

### Section 28 \- Reminder Logic

Reminders should be user-supportive, not controlling. The app can remind users about recovery tasks, weekly checks, unresolved risky results, permission reconnection, helper responses, and saved items needing organization. Reminders should have clear purpose and direct routing.

A recovery task reminder should include the task name and open that task directly. It should not make the user search through a case. If the task involves contacting a provider, the reminder can say “Follow up with your payment provider through an official channel.” It should not include sensitive payment details on the lock screen.

An unresolved risky result reminder should be used carefully. If the user dismissed a risky warning, the app may offer one follow-up reminder if the item involved money, codes, credentials, remote access, or ID docs. It should not repeatedly challenge the user. A single follow-up can ask whether they want to save evidence, verify, or start recovery if they acted.

A weekly check reminder should happen on the schedule the user selected. If the weekly check found no urgent issues, the alert can be calm. If it found urgent issues, it should say that something needs review without exposing details.

Permission reminders should be event-based. If Gmail access expires unexpectedly, the app can notify. If the user intentionally disabled Gmail monitoring, the app should not repeatedly ask. It can show status inside Protection Hub instead.

### Section 28 \- Quiet Hours and Sensitivity Settings

the app should support quiet hours for non-urgent alerts. Users should be able to choose times when low-priority reminders and summaries are held. Risky active scam warnings may still need to appear, but the app should make this behavior clear.

The app can include a sensitivity setting for proactive alerts. A cautious user may want more warnings. A user who feels overwhelmed may want only risky alerts. The sensitivity setting should not disable urgent recovery warnings without clear explanation. It should adjust non-urgent alert frequency.

Alert privacy settings should be separate from alert sensitivity. A user can choose to receive risky alerts while still hiding details on the lock screen. Privacy settings should include options like private alerts, brief alerts, or detailed alerts if the platform allows.

The app should avoid alert guilt. It should not show streaks, shame, or fear-based language. Scam protection reminders should be direct: what needs attention, why, and where to go.

### Section 28 \- Alert Fatigue Prevention

Alert fatigue happens when users see too many warnings and stop responding. the app should actively prevent this. The app should combine related low-priority findings into summaries, suppress repeated alerts for the same item, prioritize high-impact risks, and learn from user feedback.

If the same sender sends multiple similar low-risk messages, the app can summarize instead of alerting each time. If the same risky scammer continues messaging, the app can warn strongly once and then show updates inside the case unless new risk appears. If the user has already started recovery, repeated scam messages can attach to the case instead of creating new alerts.

The app should track alert outcomes. If users repeatedly dismiss a category as expected, the app can reduce low-priority alerts for that pattern while preserving risky warnings. If users mark dismissed items as scams later, the app can adjust.

Alert fatigue prevention should be transparent. Protection Hub can show that some low-risk alerts are summarized to reduce noise. The user should still be able to review full history if they want.

### Section 28 \- Helper Alert Behavior

Trusted helpers need their own alert rules. A helper should receive alerts only for items the user shared or categories the user explicitly allowed. A helper should not receive private scam checks by default. The user should control helper alert scope.

Helper alerts may include “review requested,” “risky payment review requested,” “recovery task help requested,” or “new evidence shared.” The alert should open the helper view with only the shared context. It should not expose private message content on the helper's lock screen.

The user should be able to see helper alert status. If the helper has not accepted, alerts should not be assumed active. If the helper turns off alerts, the app can show that helper review may be delayed. If a helper is removed, future alerts stop.

Helper alert behavior should avoid pressure. A helper can support the user, but the app should not let helpers flood the user with alerts or override the user's choices. Helper comments and concerns should appear in the case, with priority based on user settings.

### Section 28 \- Alert Routing

Every alert should route to the most useful screen. A risky email alert routes to the email result. A risky link alert routes to the link result. A code-sharing alert routes to the stop-and-verify screen. A recovery reminder routes to the task. A device finding routes to the finding details. A helper comment routes to the shared case. A permission issue routes to the relevant permission screen.

Alerts should not dump the user on Home unless Home is the right context. Direct routing saves time and reduces confusion. If the target object was deleted, resolved, or unavailable, the app should show a graceful message and offer the closest available context.

If the user opens a alert on a different device, the app should respect device feature. For example, opening a mobile device safety alert on web may show the summary and explain that full phone settings must be reviewed on the phone.

### Section 28 \- Alert Accept Rules

The alert system should pass functional review if every alert category has a safety purpose, privacy behavior, routing destination, and user control. It should pass if urgent alerts are action-focused and low-priority alerts can be summarized. It should pass if background review is visible and permission-based. It should pass if reminders open the exact task or result they reference.

The alert system should pass if quiet hours affect non-urgent alerts. It should pass if lock-screen privacy is preserved. It should pass if helpers only receive alerts within shared scope. It should pass if repeated alerts are suppressed or summarized. It should pass if permission loss is communicated without nagging.

The alert system should fail if it sends engagement alerts unrelated to safety. It should fail if it exposes sensitive scam content on lock screens by default. It should fail if alerts lead to generic screens. It should fail if the user cannot control categories. It should fail if background monitoring happens without clear permission. It should fail if repeated warnings make the app noisy and easy to ignore.

### Section 28 completion note

Section 28 details the design brief with alert philosophy, alert categories, background review behavior, reminder logic, quiet hours, sensitivity settings, alert fatigue prevention, helper alert behavior, alert routing, and alert accept rules while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

## Design Brief Section 29: Privacy, Data Retention, Security States, and User Control

### Section 29 purpose

This detail defines deeper privacy and data-retention behavior for Verivae. The app may handle risky messages, emails, screenshots, links, payment notes, ID doc references, account compromise details, device findings, helper comments, and recovery task notes. These are sensitive. The app's privacy behavior must be clear inside the product, not only in a policy outside the product.

This section focuses on what users see and control: what is saved, what is temporary, what is shared, what is deleted, what is redacted, what is included in recovery cases, what appears in alerts, what helpers can see, and what happens when permissions or subscriptions change. Strong privacy is part of the app's function.

### Section 29 \- Data Visibility Model

the app should have a data visibility model with clear states. Content can be temporary, saved privately, attached to a case, shared with a helper, exported by the user, or deleted. The app should show these states in plain text. A user should not have to guess whether a screenshot, message, result, or note is stored.

Temporary content is used for a review but not saved afterward unless the user chooses. Saved privately means the item is in the user's Vault and visible only to them. Attached to a case means the item appears inside a recovery case. Shared with a helper means a selected helper can see it. Exported means the user created a copy outside the app. Deleted means the app no longer shows it in active storage, though exported copies outside the app cannot be controlled by Verivae.

Every result screen should include a clear save state. If the item is not saved, the app can show “Not saved yet.” If the user saves it, the app can show “Saved privately.” If the user shares it, the app can show who can see it. If the user exports it, the app should explain that exported copies leave the app's control.

### Section 29 \- Temporary Review Behavior

Temporary review should support privacy-conscious users. A user may want to check a risky text or link without storing it. the app should allow this for basic checks. After the result, the app can offer to save the item if it may be useful for recovery, reporting, helper review, or future reference.

Temporary review should have limits. If the user closes the app or leaves the session, the result may not be recoverable unless saved. The app should explain this when the user is reviewing a risky item. It can say that saving evidence may help if the user needs to contact a provider or ask a helper.

Temporary review should not weaken safety. Even if the user does not save the content, the app should still provide risk findings and safer next steps. Saving should be optional unless a feature inherently requires persistence, such as recovery case tracking or helper collaboration.

### Section 29 \- Evidence Retention Behavior

Evidence retention should be user-controlled. The user should decide what evidence stays in the Vault and for how long when possible. The app can recommend saving evidence for active recovery, but it should not silently store everything.

Evidence items should show retention status. An item can be saved indefinitely until deletion, saved while a case is active, scheduled for deletion, or archived. If automatic deletion options exist, the app should show when deletion will happen. If the user changes retention settings, the app should explain what will be affected.

The app should avoid deleting evidence unexpectedly. If a user downgrades from a paid plan, evidence should not vanish without warning. If storage limits change, the app can make older items read-only, ask the user to choose what to keep, or prevent new saves until storage is managed. It should not remove recovery evidence during an active case without user confirmation.

Evidence deletion should include confirmation for sensitive or case-attached items. The confirmation should say what will happen: the item will be removed from the Vault and any attached cases, but exported copies or helper copies already shared may remain outside the app's control.

### Section 29 \- Redaction Behavior

Redaction lets the user hide sensitive parts before sharing evidence. the app should support redaction for screenshots, message text, emails, notes, and evidence summaries where feasible. Redaction should be easy enough for nontechnical users.

The user should be able to redact account numbers, addresses, identity numbers, codes, personal names, unrelated conversation, payment amounts, or other private info. The app can suggest sensitive areas, but the user should control final redaction. Suggested redaction should not replace user review.

Redacted copies should be separate from originals. The original can remain private while the redacted copy is shared with a helper or included in an evidence package. The app should label which copy is original and which is redacted. This avoids confusion during recovery.

If the user shares evidence without redaction, the app can show a gentle warning when sensitive data is detected. The warning should not block sharing unless there is a strong safety reason. It should help the user make an informed choice.

### Section 29 \- Helper Sharing Privacy

Helper sharing must be scoped and visible. The user should know exactly what a helper can see. A helper can view a result, case, evidence item, task list, or risky alert only if the user shared that scope. The helper should not see all Vault items or linked sources by default.

The sharing screen should summarize access before sending. It can say “This helper will see this case summary, selected evidence, current tasks, and your notes marked as shared.” If notes are private, it should say that private notes are not included. If evidence is redacted, it should show that the helper sees the redacted copy.

The user should be able to revoke helper access. Revoking access should stop future viewing inside Verivae, but the app should explain that screenshots or exported copies already saved by the helper cannot be pulled back. This should be plain and non-alarming.

Helper comments should have visibility states. A helper comment may be visible only to the user and helper inside a shared case. If the user exports an evidence package, they should choose whether helper comments are included.

### Section 29 \- Account and Session Security Behavior

Because the app may store sensitive evidence, account security is part of the product design. The app should support secure sign-in, session review, device list review, sign-out from other devices, password reset, and stronger auth where available. The exact technical implementation can be decided later, but the user-facing behavior should be defined.

The user should be able to see active Verivae sessions. A session card can show device type, approximate location if available, last active time, and sign-out action. If the user sees an unknown session, the app should guide them to sign it out and change password.

The app should protect recovery content if account security is uncertain. If the app detects risky account access, it can recommend securing the Verivae account before exporting evidence or sharing helper access. It should not lock the user out of urgent safety guidance.

Sensitive actions should require confirmation. Deleting evidence, exporting evidence packages, adding a helper, changing helper access, disabling recovery storage, or signing out all devices should not happen accidentally.

### Section 29 \- Privacy Status in Screens

Privacy status should appear where useful. Vault items should show private, shared, redacted, exported, or attached-to-case status. Recovery cases should show helper access and evidence visibility. Protection Hub should show linked sources and permission status. Results should show whether the reviewed item is saved.

The app should avoid cluttering every screen with privacy labels, but sensitive areas need clear markers. If a user is about to share, export, delete, or save, privacy status should be explicit. If a user is simply checking a message temporarily, privacy status can be compact.

Privacy explanations should be written in user terms. Instead of “data retention policy,” the app can say “Choose what stays saved.” Instead of “third-party disclosure,” it can say “Who can see this.” Instead of “revocation,” it can say “Remove helper access.”

### Section 29 \- Data Retention Accept Rules

The app should pass functional review if users can tell whether content is temporary, saved, shared, exported, or deleted. It should pass if users can manually save evidence after a review. It should pass if users can delete evidence with clear confirmation. It should pass if redacted copies are separate from originals. It should pass if helper access is scoped and revocable.

The app should pass if active recovery evidence is not deleted unexpectedly after plan changes. It should pass if session review exists for the user's Verivae account. It should pass if privacy status appears in Vault, Recovery, Protection Hub, and Result screens. It should pass if exported content is clearly described as outside the app's control.

The app should fail if it silently saves everything. It should fail if users cannot tell who can see evidence. It should fail if helper sharing exposes unrelated private items. It should fail if deletion behavior is vague. It should fail if redaction overwrites originals. It should fail if privacy controls are hidden in settings only.

### Section 29 completion note

Section 29 details the design brief with privacy behavior, data visibility states, temporary review behavior, evidence retention, redaction, helper sharing privacy, account and session security behavior, privacy status across screens, and data retention accept rules while keeping the document focused only on the app's app functions and layout.

Design Brief Section 30: Quality and Readiness Rules

Section 30 purpose  
Quality rules define how the app proves each feature works before release. The app must be calm, clear, private, and useful under stress.

Section 30 \- Test Areas  
Test manual check, email review, text review, link check, QR check, file check, device check, weekly check, result screen, proof vault, case space, payment recovery, account recovery, helper review, privacy settings, alerts, and education.

Section 30 \- Readiness  
A feature is ready when the user knows what happened, sees risk level, sees why, has one next action, can save proof, can undo or correct, can handle not sure, and can keep privacy control.

Section 30 \- Failure  
Failures need safe fallback. If scan fails, explain. If source permission is off, show how to turn it on. If offline, save draft. If app is unsure, say unsure and give safe verify steps.

Section 30 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when every feature has success, empty, loading, error, offline, permission, not sure, and recovery states; each state has clear text and a safe action.

Design Brief Section 31: UI Components and States

Section 31 purpose  
Reusable UI parts keep the app clear across checks, cases, proof, helper review, alerts, and settings.

Section 31 \- Components  
Core parts include risk badge, source chip, proof chip, task row, case card, warning bar, safe route button, helper chip, permission row, redaction tag, file card, link preview, QR preview, device tile, and privacy toggle.

Section 31 \- States  
Common states are empty, loading, scanning, safe, risky, not sure, blocked, offline, permission off, helper waiting, action needed, done, skipped, expired, and error. Each state needs one next action.

Section 31 \- Interaction  
Primary actions should be short: check, save, stop, verify, recover, ask, redact, share, pause, clear, and done. Destructive actions need confirm text. Risk actions need plain why text.

Section 31 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when the same components can support every major feature, state names are clear, and no screen leaves the user without a safe next action.

Design Brief Section 32: Feature Tiers and Product Boundaries

Section 32 purpose  
Feature tiers define what the app must do first and what can stay advanced. Boundaries keep the product useful, clear, and buildable.

Section 32 \- Core  
Core includes manual check, link check, QR check, file check, email review, text review, result screen, proof vault, case space, pay recovery, account recovery, helper review, privacy controls, alerts, and education.

Section 32 \- Advanced  
Advanced includes deeper device checks, weekly review, richer pattern memory, family mode, wider source links, proof packs, and premium recovery aids. Advanced work must not break core safety.

Section 32 \- Boundaries  
The app is not a bank, lawyer, police, device OS, or money sender. It guides, checks, saves proof, warns, and routes to safe provider paths. It must say when outside help is needed.

Section 32 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when designers can tell what belongs in the first useful product, what can wait, what must never be promised, and how later features connect without changing the core idea.

Design Brief Section 33: Product Decision Rules

Section 33 purpose  
Decision rules keep the app steady when facts conflict, data is missing, or risk is unclear. The app should prefer safe action over false certainty.

Section 33 \- Risk Choice  
If proof is strong, app gives a clear risk result. If proof is mixed, app says not sure and gives safe verify steps. If proof is weak, app explains what is missing.

Section 33 \- Conflict  
If message, email, link, file, helper, and user memory disagree, app shows each source label. It does not hide conflict. It asks the user to verify through a safe route.

Section 33 \- Priority  
Money loss, account access, remote access, ID exposure, and active pressure outrank low-risk education. Recovery tasks outrank long reading. Stop tasks outrank reports.

Section 33 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when the app avoids false certainty, names missing facts, chooses safer next steps, explains conflict, and keeps the user moving without panic.

Design Brief Section 34: Scam Education and Action Learning

Section 34 purpose  
Education must help the user act now, not feel tested. Lessons should appear beside real checks, cases, warnings, and recovery tasks.

Section 34 \- Lesson Types  
Lesson types include link risk, QR risk, file risk, code risk, pay risk, crypto risk, ID risk, remote access risk, fake job, fake market, romance, bank claim, tax threat, and recovery scam. Each lesson has signs, safe action, and one example.

Section 34 \- Placement  
Lessons appear after result, inside case tasks, in weekly check, in settings, and after user asks why. They stay short during high stress. Full lessons are optional.

Section 34 \- Personal Fit  
App can suggest lessons based on user cases, skipped warnings, linked sources, pay methods, and helper notes. User can hide topics or turn off personal lesson tips.

Section 34 \- Test and Recall  
Mini checks ask what the user would do next. Wrong answer gives calm correction. App never blocks use because a lesson was skipped.

Section 34 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when learning helps action, connects to real app flows, avoids shame, supports repeated scams, and stays optional unless needed to explain a safety warning.

Design Brief Section 35: Risk Flows and Mistake Recovery

Section 35 purpose  
Risk flows guide the user when harm may be active. The app must slow unsafe action, explain the risk, and give a next step that can be done now.

Section 35 \- High Risk Triggers  
High risk includes pay now, gift card, crypto wallet, login code, password, remote access, ID upload, bank claim, law threat, romance ask, fake job fee, refund scam, file install, QR pay, and urgent secrecy. Each trigger opens a result with stop, verify, save proof, and recover options.

Section 35 \- Friction  
For risky sends, app uses friction: pause screen, plain warning, safe contact route, helper option, proof save, and action checklist. It must not shame user. It says what could go wrong and what to do instead.

Section 35 \- Mistake Recovery  
If user clicked, paid, shared code, sent ID, installed app, opened file, scanned QR, or gave remote access, app asks what happened and starts recovery. It never hides the check because harm already happened.

Section 35 \- Escalation  
Escalation routes to bank, card, pay app, email provider, phone carrier, device cleanup, ID protection, market support, crypto exchange, or formal report. App gives safe route rules and proof pack links.

Section 35 \- Edge Cases  
If risk is unclear, app says not sure and gives safe verify steps. If user dismisses warning, app can save a quiet note and remind later. If user is under pressure, app shows one first action only.

Section 35 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when risky moments get a clear stop path, mistakes become recovery cases, warnings stay calm, proof is saved, helper can join, and the user always has a safe next action.

Design Brief Section 36: Recovery Cases and Task Library

Section 36 purpose  
Case space turns a scare into clear work. User needs one place for facts, proof, tasks, status, and next step. It must avoid panic text and show only what helps recovery.

Section 36 \- Case Types  
Case types include pay loss, bank risk, card risk, account take over, email risk, phone/SIM risk, ID exposure, remote access, device malware risk, fake job, fake market deal, crypto, romance, tax, rental, charity, and not sure. User can change type later.

Section 36 \- Case Header  
Header shows case name, risk level, open money risk, open account risk, open device risk, next task, proof count, helper state, and last check. It has buttons for add proof, ask helper, call safe route, mark done, and pause.

Section 36 \- Task Library  
Tasks are grouped by stop, secure, contact, report, monitor, learn, and close. Each task has plain goal, why it matters, needed info, safe contact route, proof link, done state, skipped state, and not sure state.

Section 36 \- Recovery Flow  
App asks what happened, what was shared, what money moved, what accounts were touched, what device access occurred, and what proof exists. It then builds task order. Urgent stop tasks come before reports. Device and account safety come before long forms.

Section 36 \- Provider Tasks  
Provider tasks cover bank, card, pay app, crypto exchange, email provider, phone carrier, marketplace, employer platform, tax portal, and ID service. App gives safe route advice and warns user not to call numbers from the risky message.

Section 36 \- States  
Task states are to do, doing, blocked, not sure, done, skipped, waiting, and expired. Blocked asks why. Not sure opens helper or plain guide. Done can attach proof. Skipped asks if risk remains.

Section 36 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when user can start any case, see the next safest task, save proof, recover accounts, protect money, ask helper, track state, pause without losing work, and close only when major risks are addressed.

Design Brief Section 37: Proof Packs, Redaction, and Share

Section 37 purpose  
Proof is useful only when user can save it, sort it, redact it, and share the right part with the right person. App must keep raw proof private, build short packs, and avoid over sharing.

Section 37 \- Proof Types  
Proof types are text, email, link, QR, file, device, account, pay, ID, helper note, and user note. Each item has source, case, risk, private flag, share state, and notes. Original, excerpt, summary, redacted copy, and note are labeled.

Section 37 \- Vault  
Vault shows recent proof, active case proof, unlinked proof, private proof, and draft packs. Filters are case, source, type, risk, private, date, and share state. Item view shows content, source, risk, links, redaction, and share history.

Section 37 \- Packs  
Pack starts with case, audience, and goal. Audience may be bank, pay app, market, device help, helper, formal report, or personal record. App suggests proof and says why. User can add, remove, redact, and preview.

Section 37 \- Redaction  
Redaction hides card numbers, SSN, address, full ID, private chat, child data, medical data, unrelated names, codes, and account data. Raw stays private if user keeps it. Shared copy is flattened. If redaction fails, share is blocked.

Section 37 \- Timeline  
Timeline shows what happened, what user did, what app checked, what proof exists, what tasks are done, and what is still open. It marks confirmed fact, user memory, helper note, and app summary.

Section 37 \- Export and Share  
Export has cover summary, short timeline, proof index, selected proof, redaction note, user actions, and open issues. Sharing needs user approval. Helper share can be summary only. App shows share history.

Section 37 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when user can save proof from any feature, attach it to case, redact it, build audience pack, preview it, share only by choice, see share history, and keep proof useful for recovery.

Design Brief Section 38: Helper Review and Consent

Section 38 purpose  
Helper review lets user ask a trusted person for aid without losing control. It must be consent first, case scoped, private by default, and useful in risk moments.

Section 38 \- Invite  
User can invite helper from result, case, proof pack, pay warning, remote access warning, ID exposure, or settings. Invite shows what helper sees before send. It warns user not to invite a person suggested by a risky sender.

Section 38 \- Access Levels  
Levels are summary only, selected proof, task help, and case review. Summary hides raw proof. Selected proof shows only chosen items. Task help lets helper see chosen tasks. Case review adds comments. Full access is not default.

Section 38 \- Helper Screen  
Helper sees case summary, risk signs, first action, open question, shared proof, and task ask. Helper can suggest: stop, verify safe route, add proof, call provider, ask bank, secure account, remove remote access, or not sure.

Section 38 \- Safety Limits  
Helper cannot take over account, export all proof, invite others, change user facts, contact provider, or message scammer by default. User can remove helper. Removal stops future live access but cannot recall downloaded data.

Section 38 \- Family Mode  
Family or caregiver mode is separate from one time review. It can share selected alerts, weekly summary, and case status only by user choice. Private areas stay off by default.

Section 38 \- Alerts and Conflict
