Helper alerts use neutral text unless user allows detail. If helper and app disagree, app shows both and asks for safe route check. Helper approval never cancels app risk warning.

Section 38 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when user can invite, preview, share limited data, get notes, revoke access, hide private proof, keep case control, and keep urgent recovery moving even if helper does not reply.

Design Brief Section 39: Weekly Check and Recurring Review

Section 39 purpose  
Weekly check is a repeat safety review. It looks at open cases, source review, device risk, proof gaps, account tasks, pay tasks, helper state, and user memory. It must be useful with no links set up, better with linked sources, and honest about OS limits.

Section 39 \- Home  
Weekly home shows last check, next check, due state, linked modules, missing access, open risk, and start button. It says what will be checked and what will not be checked. If urgent case is open, that case appears first.

Section 39 \- Modules  
Modules are messages, Gmail, links, QR, files, device access, apps, browser, accounts, pay review, proof vault, ID watch, helper, alerts, and education. Each module state is checked, skipped, not ready, limited, needs review, or manual only. Quick check reviews urgent items. Full check reviews all set modules.

Section 39 \- Source Review  
Weekly source review groups risk: code asks, pay asks, fake bank, delivery link, job pitch, market ask, romance pressure, investment pitch, remote tool, and recovery scam. It shows group count, source, risk reason, and next step. If source is off, it gives paste, share, screenshot, or manual check.

Section 39 \- Device Review  
Device review checks apps, access, profiles, VPN, extensions, downloads, remote tools, alerts, and recent file events where OS allows. It marks known, risky, unknown, or not ready. It asks user if app is known before calling it bad.

Section 39 \- Incident Trigger  
File opened, remote access, password typed, code shared, ID sent, or pay sent can trigger a focused deep check. App says why check is advised and starts with highest risk. If user dismisses it, case keeps reminder.

Section 39 \- Account and Pay Review  
Account review tracks email, bank, pay app, carrier, cloud, social, work, school, and shop accounts. States include not reviewed, password changed, sessions checked, recovery info checked, 2FA on, risk found, or not needed. Pay review tracks charges, cards, pay apps, gift cards, subscriptions, disputes, and repeat pay asks.

Section 39 \- Proof Review  
Proof review finds active cases with no proof, proof not linked to case, private proof not redacted, draft pack not done, and provider pack not sent. It can suggest link proof, redact proof, build pack, or keep private.

Section 39 \- Result and Alerts  
Result shows status, next action, modules checked, modules skipped, modules not ready, and open items. Alerts are private by default. User sets day, time, style, and helper share. If user ignores checks, app offers shorter check, new time, or manual only.

Section 39 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when weekly check is opt in, modular, honest, linked to cases, tied to proof, linked to device check, and useful without full access. It must never imply full virus or account scan when access or OS blocks that.

Design Brief Section 40: Link, QR, File, and Attachment Check

Section 40 purpose  
Links, QR codes, files, and mail or chat attachments are core scam paths. App must let user check first, open later. It must show source, risk, what was checked, what was not checked, and next step. It must not auto open risky links or files.

Section 40 \- Link Intake  
User can paste link, share link, pick link from Gmail, pick link from text, scan QR, upload screenshot, or choose link from proof. App shows true domain, shown text, full link view, source, and case link. If user already opened it, app asks what happened: login, pay, code, ID, file, remote app, wallet, or none.

Section 40 \- Link Check  
Link check looks at domain, look alike spelling, sender match, redirect, short link, path text, odd top level domain, risky form, pay ask, login ask, code ask, wallet ask, file ask, and remote app ask. Result says why. A safe looking link can still be risky if message asks for money, code, ID, or password.

Section 40 \- QR  
QR flow decodes first and opens only if user chooses. It shows target, source, risk, and action. Source can be parking sign, invoice, package note, table card, email, poster, market post, or pay request. If image has many QR codes, app lets user pick one. If none is found, app offers retry or paste.

Section 40 \- Files and Attachments  
File check stores file name, type, source, claimed use, user action, and risk. It asks if file was received, downloaded, opened, macro enabled, app installed, or used before login. It flags installers, scripts, macro docs, zip files, browser add ons, profiles, password zip files, remote tools, and odd file types.

Section 40 \- Safe Preview  
Safe preview shows domain, file facts, QR target, sender, and risk before user opens anything. It does not load risky active content by default. If user chooses to open outside app, app reminds: do not enter password, code, card, bank data, ID, wallet seed, or install app until verified by safe route.

Section 40 \- Result Labels  
Labels are low concern, caution, risky, high risk, critical, cannot inspect, and needs more context. Each result has reason, checked items, missing items, and next step. Cannot inspect is not safe. Needs more context asks only useful questions.

Section 40 \- Follow Up  
Follow up asks short, high value questions: Did you pay? share code? enter password? upload ID? install app? open file? connect wallet? give remote access? If yes, app opens the right case path. If not sure, app suggests safer check and proof save.

Section 40 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when user can check links, QR codes, files, and attachments before action; see why risk was found; save proof; ask helper; start case; open device safety; and use manual path when OS or file limits block scan.

Design Brief Section 41: Gmail, Text, and Linked Source Review

Section 41 purpose  
Linked source review gives app context. A link, code, file, pay ask, or ID ask is riskier when it comes from an odd sender, fake bank, fake job, fake market buyer, fake helper, or repeat scam source. Source review must be opt in, clear, and easy to turn off.

Section 41 \- Source Setup  
Source setup lists Gmail, texts, screenshots, pasted text, shared links, files, and future apps. Each card says what it helps check, what access it needs, what app reads, what app skips, and how to pause or remove it. If OS blocks text access, app says so and offers paste, share, screenshot, or manual check.

Section 41 \- Gmail  
Gmail review looks for risky senders, domain mismatch, reply-to mismatch, bad links, QR images, risky files, login alerts, password reset mail, pay receipts, market mail, job mail, fake invoices, delivery claims, and case updates. It groups findings by risk type. It marks real security alerts as real alerts that may still need action.

Saved Gmail proof keeps sender, subject, excerpt, links, file names, risk result, and case link. It does not share full inbox with helper. User can redact, save, attach, or delete.

Section 41 \- Text and Chat  
Text review checks code asks, pay asks, urgent threats, delivery links, fake bank alerts, market code asks, romance pressure, job tasks, crypto pitches, family claims, and remote access steps. It may use direct text access, pasted text, shared chat, screenshot text, or manual entry. If OCR is used, user can fix bad text.

Review shows risky line, sender, nearby context if needed, why app cares, and next step. Full thread is hidden by default. User can expand if needed.

Section 41 \- Sender Rules  
Saved contact is not always safe. A known name can be spoofed or hacked. App checks sender name, email domain, reply-to, phone, handle, short code, first seen time, prior case link, and claimed org. It says why: unknown sender, domain mismatch, reply-to mismatch, new sender with pay ask, or sender linked to old risk.

Section 41 \- Queue  
Review queue groups source findings. Urgent: pay ask, login code ask, remote app ask, password reset, login alert, active case match. Lower risk: spam, old item, already handled item. Each card can save proof, create case, attach to case, ask helper, mark safe, mark scam, or learn why.

Section 41 \- Privacy  
Connecting Gmail or text does not share it. Helper sees only what user shares. Source data can be paused, removed, or kept as proof. Settings show source state: on, off, paused, limited, needs reconnect, or not ready. If source fails, app says manual checks still work.

Section 41 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when user can see linked sources, know what app reads, know what it skips, review findings, save proof, attach cases, disconnect sources, and use manual options. Gmail and text review must link to manual check, proof vault, cases, helper review, weekly check, and education.

Design Brief Section 42: Device Safety and Linked Device Review

Section 42 purpose  
Device safety is app help for phone, tablet, browser, account sessions, files, remote tools, and linked devices. It must aid virus and risk checks while being honest: some OS rules block full file scans. App must say what it checked, what it could not check, and what user can do next.

Section 42 \- Home  
Device home shows state: no urgent issue, review due, risky app found, remote access risk, browser issue, check limited, or action needed. It lists last check, next weekly check, open device case, missing access, and quick actions: quick check, deep check, app review, access review, remote access review, browser review, downloads review, linked device review.

Section 42 \- Quick Check  
Quick check is for fast risk. It checks recent risky file events, remote tools, risky access, device profiles, VPNs, alert access, downloads, browser signs, and open cases. Result gives one next step first. If remote access may be live, stop access is first. If account data may be seen, use safe device for password change.

Section 42 \- Deep Check  
Deep check is longer. It has modules: apps, access, remote tools, profiles, VPN, browser, downloads, files, accounts, proof, and follow up. Each module has state: checked, needs review, not ready, skipped, or manual check needed. Deep check can run by user choice or weekly check. It saves a device report when tied to a case.

Section 42 \- Linked Device Review  
Linked device review separates three ideas: this phone, another device, and account sessions. User can say concern is phone, laptop, tablet, child device, family device, work device, or unknown signed in device. App routes to device check, account session tasks, helper review, or manual list.

For account sessions, app guides review of email, bank, pay app, social, cloud, shop, carrier, work, and school accounts. App does not need passwords. It stores task state, not secrets.

Section 42 \- Remote Access  
Remote access review checks remote desktop apps, screen share apps, support tools, device profiles, accessibility access, screen recording, and install context where OS allows it. It asks if caller told user to install app, share screen, read login codes, open bank, or keep call secret. Result gives stop access, remove tool, review device, secure accounts, save proof.

Section 42 \- Browser  
Browser review checks unknown extensions, fake pop ups, changed search, changed home page, site alerts, redirects, wallet add ons, and risky downloads where possible. If app cannot inspect directly, it gives a manual path. Actions include remove extension, turn off site alerts, reset search, clear risky download, and avoid numbers shown in pop ups.

Section 42 \- Result  
Device result shows urgent item, first action, checked areas, limited areas, case links, proof save, helper ask, follow up check, and account tasks. It must not say "hacked" unless proof supports that. Better text is exact: "screen share app was installed near risky call." State can be complete, partial, blocked by OS, waiting on user, waiting on helper, or unresolved.

Section 42 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when user can run quick check, run deep check, review apps, review access, review remote tools, review browser, link findings to cases, save proof, and understand OS limits. It works when file events, remote access, password entry, risky link, and weekly check can all open device safety.

Design Brief Section 43: Risk Memory and User Control

Section 43 purpose  
Risk memory lets app link new risk to old risk. It must help, not spy. It tracks safe facts that aid scam checks: sender, domain, pay handle, wallet, phone, link, file, QR, ID risk, device flag, open case, skipped task, helper note, and user choice. It must not store more private text than needed. User can view, edit, clear, pause, or turn off memory.

Section 43 \- Memory Sources  
Memory can come from manual check, Gmail review, text review, link check, QR check, file check, device check, weekly check, proof vault, case space, helper review, alert tap, user note, and user feedback. Each memory item needs a source label, a plain reason, a case link if any, and a clear state: active, off, cleared, stale, user confirmed, helper noted, or app inferred.

App stores small safety facts first. Store "this sender asked for gift cards" before storing a full chat. Store "ID doc shared" before storing the doc. Store "remote access was used" before storing full device data. Full proof stays in vault only if user saved it.

Section 43 \- User Controls  
User needs direct controls: see memory, clear one item, clear one source, clear one case link, pause memory, reset all memory, keep proof but clear memory, keep case but clear future use, and turn off personal tips. Each control says what will change. If memory is off, manual check still works.

Controls must be shown in privacy settings, result screens, case detail, proof detail, helper settings, and weekly check settings. User must never wonder why app linked two events. Any link has an explain and clear action.

Section 43 \- Pattern Rules  
Pattern links may use same sender, close sender, same domain, short link, same QR target, same pay handle, same wallet, same fake job story, same romance ask, same gift card ask, same login code ask, same remote app, same file source, same ID ask, same bank claim, same market seller, or same recovery scam pitch.

If app is sure, it says "This matches a past case." If app is not sure, it says "This may match a past case." If user says no, app drops the link. If user says yes, app links proof, case, risk reason, and next task.

Section 43 \- Risk Profile  
User risk profile is a safety profile, not a score on the person. It can hold warning tone, helper choice, alert style, access needs, top account types, used pay methods, source links, device check choice, weekly check cadence, scam types user wants extra help with, and education progress.

Profile can make app more useful. A market buyer sees market risk tips. A job seeker sees fake job risk. User with ID exposure gets future ID alerts. User with remote access history gets device prompts. User with stress needs gets shorter steps.

Section 43 \- Helper Boundary  
Helper input is not app truth. Helper notes stay labeled. Helper approval does not cancel app warning. Helper memory is used only if user allows it. Helper cannot see memory, proof, cases, or source data outside the share level user chose.

Section 43 \- Clear and Reset  
Clear one item means app forgets that item for future risk. Clear proof means saved proof is gone if user confirms. Clear case means case is removed if allowed. Clear memory but keep proof is allowed. Clear all memory is allowed. Reset must warn that repeat-pattern help will be weaker.

Section 43 \- Accept Rules  
This area works when user can see why a result is personal, what old fact was used, where it came from, how to clear it, and how to keep using app with memory off. It also works when app keeps small safety facts, avoids needless private text, treats helper notes as helper notes, and gives clear repeat-pattern warnings.

Appendix A: Functional Requirement Matrix and Rule Index

Appendix purpose  
This appendix turns the app's safety behavior into a practical reference for product, design, engineering, QA, privacy review, and support. It is not a separate plan. It is an app-only map of signals, risks, screens, and responses. Each requirement should be read as a product rule: when the app sees a signal or user reports a situation, the app should provide the matching response with clear consent, privacy limits, and recovery support.

How to read the matrix  
Each row in this appendix follows six fields: signal, risk, app response, user screen, recovery action, and priority. Signal means the thing the user submits or the app observes. Risk means the possible harm. App response means what the product should do. User screen means where the response appears. Recovery action means the next safe step if harm may have occurred. Priority means whether the behavior belongs in the first version, a near-term advanced version, or a later specialized version.

Priority definitions  
Core means the first useful version should include it. Advanced means the feature is valuable but can wait until the core product is stable. Specialist means the product should support the idea only after legal, security, privacy, and platform constraints are understood.

Signal: payment request. Risk: user may send money to a scammer. App response: pause the user, ask what is being requested, check for urgency, secrecy, unusual payment method, identity claim, and pressure. User screen: Quick Check, Result, Case Space. Recovery action: save proof, contact bank or payment app through a safe route, and track follow-up. Priority: Core.

Signal: gift card request. Risk: irreversible loss. App response: warn that gift cards are a major scam signal, ask who requested the card, and advise not sharing card numbers or photos. User screen: Manual Check, Pay Warning, Result. Recovery action: save receipt, contact card issuer, document request, and start case. Priority: Core.

Signal: crypto wallet request. Risk: high-loss irreversible transfer. App response: show a strong warning, ask whether the sender is known offline, check for investment, romance, job, recovery, or urgent-fee patterns, and advise safe verification before any transfer. User screen: Manual Check, Payment Review, Result. Recovery action: save wallet address, transaction hash if any, conversation proof, and exchange support path. Priority: Core for warning; Advanced for wallet analytics.

Signal: login code request. Risk: account takeover. App response: warn that real support teams do not need the user's one-time code, explain the risk in plain text, and advise changing passwords if a code was shared. User screen: Manual Check, Text Review, Email Review, Result. Recovery action: secure account, revoke sessions, update recovery email and phone, and save proof. Priority: Core.

Signal: password request. Risk: account theft and identity misuse. App response: block any suggestion that sharing a password is safe, ask what account is involved, and route user to official password reset. User screen: Manual Check, Email Review, Result. Recovery action: change password, turn on two-step sign-in, check active sessions, and monitor account. Priority: Core.

Signal: remote access request. Risk: device takeover, bank theft, and data exposure. App response: warn strongly, ask whether remote software was installed, and place device safety tasks before long reports. User screen: Manual Check, Device Safety, Case Space. Recovery action: disconnect network if needed, remove remote tool, change passwords from another trusted device, contact bank, and run device check. Priority: Core for warning; Advanced for device inspection.

Signal: suspicious link. Risk: phishing, credential theft, malware, or fake payment page. App response: preview destination, explain mismatch, check for short links and lookalike domains, and advise opening known sites directly instead of tapping the submitted link. User screen: Link Check, Result. Recovery action: save link, mark source, start account recovery if credentials were entered. Priority: Core.

Signal: QR code. Risk: hidden link or payment redirection. App response: decode and preview before opening, show domain or payment target, and require user confirmation before leaving the app. User screen: QR Check, Result. Recovery action: save QR image, save decoded target, and start payment or account case if used. Priority: Core.

Signal: file attachment. Risk: malware, credential theft, malicious document, or fake invoice. App response: show file type, source, risk signs, and safe-open guidance. The app should not promise full malware certainty unless it uses a trusted scanning method. User screen: File Review, Result. Recovery action: quarantine or delete if possible, save file metadata, and start device check if opened. Priority: Core for metadata and warning; Advanced for deeper scan.

Signal: email claiming to be a known contact. Risk: compromised contact account or impersonation. App response: check unusual request, money ask, link, attachment, tone shift, and sender details. User screen: Gmail Review, Result. Recovery action: advise contacting the person through another known channel and saving proof. Priority: Advanced because email permissions require careful privacy design.

Signal: text from unknown number. Risk: phishing, smishing, fake delivery, fake bank, fake support, or payment pressure. App response: check sender, link, urgency, request type, and whether the message asks for money or identity. User screen: Text Review, Result. Recovery action: block or report where supported, save proof, and start case if user acted. Priority: Core for manual paste; Advanced for direct message integration.

Signal: user already clicked. Risk: account, device, or money harm may already be active. App response: skip blame, ask what happened, and open recovery-first flow. User screen: Already Acted, Case Space. Recovery action: secure account, contact provider, run device check, save proof, and monitor. Priority: Core.

Signal: user already paid. Risk: financial loss and repeat targeting. App response: ask payment method, amount, recipient, time, and proof; warn against recovery scams; build recovery tasks. User screen: Payment Recovery, Case Space. Recovery action: contact bank or payment app through official route, save proof, and monitor follow-up. Priority: Core.

Signal: user shared ID. Risk: identity theft and account fraud. App response: ask what ID was shared, with whom, and where; explain risk without panic; start identity exposure case. User screen: ID Exposure, Case Space. Recovery action: save proof, consider credit freeze guidance, monitor accounts, and avoid paying fake recovery services. Priority: Advanced.

Signal: user installed an app. Risk: spyware, remote access, credential theft, or unwanted subscription. App response: ask app name, install source, permission grants, and whether money or accounts were accessed after install. User screen: Device Safety, Case Space. Recovery action: remove app, review permissions, change passwords from a trusted device, and contact bank if needed. Priority: Advanced.

Signal: weekly safety review. Risk: unresolved cases and missed follow-up. App response: summarize open tasks, unresolved proof, device checks due, risky sources, and accounts needing review. User screen: Weekly Check. Recovery action: reopen tasks, remind user, and ask helper if consent exists. Priority: Advanced.

Signal: trusted helper request. Risk: user may share too much or invite the wrong person. App response: show exactly what helper can see before sending, prevent scammer-suggested helper choices, and use limited access by default. User screen: Helper Review, Permission Preview. Recovery action: revoke helper access, save helper notes, and keep user in control. Priority: Advanced.

Signal: family or caregiver mode. Risk: privacy loss or overreach. App response: require consent, use narrow sharing, and separate one-time review from ongoing care. User screen: Helper Settings, Privacy Settings. Recovery action: remove access, limit alerts, and keep private proof hidden unless user shares it. Priority: Advanced.

Signal: evidence item. Risk: proof may be lost, overshared, or hard to use. App response: let user save, label, redact, connect to case, and share only by choice. User screen: Evidence Vault, Proof Pack. Recovery action: build provider-ready pack with timeline, selected proof, and redaction note. Priority: Core.

Signal: redaction needed. Risk: private data may leak during help or reporting. App response: detect common private fields, let user hide them, and require preview before sharing. User screen: Redaction Preview, Proof Pack. Recovery action: share flattened redacted copy, not raw proof, when possible. Priority: Core.

Signal: app is unsure. Risk: false confidence. App response: say not sure, name what is missing, show safer verification steps, and avoid declaring safe. User screen: Result, Manual Check, Case Space. Recovery action: save proof, ask helper, or contact official provider route. Priority: Core.

Signal: user dismisses warning. Risk: harm may continue. App response: allow dismissal without shame, offer save-for-later, and optionally remind if risk is high. User screen: Result, Alert. Recovery action: reopen case if user returns or reports harm. Priority: Core.

Signal: permission denied. Risk: integration cannot work. App response: explain what permission enables, what stays private, and how to use manual check instead. User screen: Permission Screen, Settings. Recovery action: no recovery needed unless user already acted. Priority: Core.

Signal: offline state. Risk: user cannot complete scan or save cloud data. App response: allow manual note, local draft, and retry when online; do not pretend a scan completed. User screen: Any Check, Case Space. Recovery action: preserve user notes locally if privacy settings allow. Priority: Core.

Signal: false positive. Risk: user loses trust. App response: let user mark as safe, explain that this does not train blindly, and keep risk logic cautious. User screen: Result Feedback. Recovery action: update memory only with consent. Priority: Core.

Signal: false negative report. Risk: user was harmed after low warning. App response: let user report what happened, start recovery, and mark the case for model or rule review. User screen: Result Feedback, Case Space. Recovery action: save proof and escalate to recovery tasks. Priority: Core.

Signal: sensitive data storage. Risk: privacy breach. App response: minimize saved data, keep proof optional, make deletion clear, and separate memory from raw proof. User screen: Privacy Settings, Evidence Vault. Recovery action: delete, export, or clear memory by user choice. Priority: Core.

Signal: premium feature prompt. Risk: user may feel exploited during a crisis. App response: keep core safety free, never block urgent warnings behind payment, and show paid options only after immediate safety steps. User screen: Recovery Workspace, Settings. Recovery action: free route remains available. Priority: Core policy; Advanced monetization.

Signal: competitor overlap. Risk: product may feel generic. App response: focus on guided scam decision support, proof capture, recovery workspace, and helper review rather than only identity monitoring or antivirus. User screen: Product-wide. Recovery action: not applicable. Priority: Core positioning.

Signal: professional handoff. Risk: design and engineering may misread intent. App response: keep the master brief, scope boundaries, feature sections, privacy rules, and appendices aligned. User screen: Document structure. Recovery action: not applicable. Priority: Core documentation.

Appendix acceptance rules  
This appendix is useful when each app feature can be traced to a signal, risk, response, screen, recovery path, and priority. If a future feature cannot be placed in this structure, the feature is not ready to design. If a row asks for data access that the app does not need, the privacy design should reject or narrow that access. If a row creates a warning without a next step, the user experience is incomplete. If a row creates a recovery task without proof capture, the recovery experience is incomplete.

Appendix B: Screen-by-Screen Product Specification

This appendix describes the major screens that should exist inside Verivae and the functional purpose of each screen. The point of this section is to make the product easier to design and build by reducing ambiguity. A future designer should be able to use these descriptions to create wireframes, and a future developer should be able to understand which information each screen needs, which actions the user can take, and which follow-up screens are triggered by those actions. The app should feel calm, practical, and protective. It should avoid dramatic language unless a threat is genuinely urgent. Its interface should behave like a patient assistant that slows risky decisions down, not like a panic alarm that overwhelms the person who is already under pressure.

B1. Home screen

The home screen is the user's starting point and should answer one question immediately: what can I safely do next? The top of the screen should show the current protection status in simple language. Examples include "No urgent issues found," "One item needs review," or "Protection paused for messages." The status should be useful without requiring the user to understand security terms. Under the status, the screen should provide fast entry points into Manual Scam Check, Recent Alerts, Evidence Vault, Recovery Workspace, Weekly Deep Check, Connected Accounts, and Trusted Helper review. The home screen should not be crowded with every feature in the product. It should prioritize the actions most likely to matter in a stressful moment.

The primary action on the home screen should be Manual Scam Check because this is the feature a user will reach for when they are unsure about a text, email, call, link, QR code, file, payment request, job offer, marketplace buyer, romantic message, or account warning. The action should be large enough to find quickly, but the surrounding design should stay restrained. The user should not feel as if the app is selling fear. A secondary action should show "Review latest alerts" when the app has found something that deserves attention. If nothing needs review, that space can show a short safety summary and a clear path into the weekly check.

The home screen should show connection health for major permission-based features. This should include email review if connected, message review if supported and permitted, file review if enabled, device safety checks if supported by the operating system, and notifications if allowed. Each connection should use normal language: "Gmail connected," "Messages not connected," "Device checks ready," or "Notifications off." Tapping a connection should open a short explanation of what that permission does, what it does not do, and how to turn it off. The home screen should never hide a missing permission behind vague status text. If the user thinks the app is watching for email scams but Gmail is disconnected, the home screen must make that clear.

The home screen should also provide a safe path for confused users. A visible "I need help now" action should open a guided triage screen that asks what happened: "I received a suspicious message," "I clicked a link," "I sent money," "I shared a code," "I installed something," "I gave login information," or "I am not sure." This action matters because many victims do not know which technical category their problem belongs to. The app should meet them at the level of their situation, then translate their answer into the right product flow.

B2. Manual Scam Check screen

Manual Scam Check is the central input screen for anything the user wants the app to review on demand. It should support pasted text, screenshots, copied links, email forwarding, uploaded attachments, QR code scanning, sender details, payment instructions, bank names, marketplace listings, profile screenshots, and short descriptions written by the user. The screen should not ask for all of this at once. It should start with a simple prompt such as "What do you want checked?" and then offer input choices: paste text, add screenshot, scan link, scan QR code, upload file, describe situation, or import from connected account.

The manual check should explain that the more context the user gives, the better the result can be. It should also explain that the user can remove private information before submitting if they prefer. If the app can analyze locally, it should state when information stays on the device. If information must be sent to a server for a stronger review, the app should ask clearly and explain what is sent. This is especially important for screenshots, bank names, payment details, email bodies, and attachments. Trust is part of the product, not a decoration layered on afterward.

The screen should allow the user to add optional context without turning the flow into paperwork. Optional questions might include: "Is this person asking for money?" "Are they asking you to act quickly?" "Did they ask for a code, password, gift card, crypto transfer, wire, bank login, remote access, or ID document?" "Do you personally know this person?" "Have you already clicked, paid, or replied?" Each answer should improve the result and recovery instructions. The user should be able to skip questions, but skipped context should cause the app to use cautious language when confidence is limited.

The manual check screen should include a visible privacy reminder near upload controls. It should say in plain language that the user should avoid adding more personal information than necessary. When the user uploads a screenshot, the app should offer automatic redaction suggestions for account numbers, full addresses, Social Security numbers, bank balances, medical details, and unrelated conversations. Redaction should be optional because the user may need the exact evidence later, but the app should help them reduce exposure whenever possible.

B3. Scam result screen

The result screen is one of the most important screens in the product because it determines whether the user understands the risk and knows what to do. It should not simply say "scam" or "safe." It should provide a clear result level, a plain-language explanation, the specific evidence found, recommended next steps, and a confidence statement. Result levels should include likely safe, caution, suspicious, likely scam, urgent risk, and not enough information. These levels should be visually distinct but not theatrical. Color can help, but the text must carry the meaning for users with color vision differences.

The top of the result screen should give the user the immediate answer: "Do not pay yet," "Do not click the link," "Do not share the code," "This looks like a fake support request," or "This looks normal, but review the sender before acting." Below that, the app should explain why. Evidence should be concrete: urgency language, payment method, mismatched sender, suspicious link, request for verification code, unusual attachment, impersonation pattern, known scam phrase, remote access request, pressure to keep the conversation secret, or request to move communication off platform. The app should avoid vague claims such as "AI detected risk" without showing useful reasons.

The result screen should include a "What to do now" area. For a likely scam, this area should suggest not replying, blocking the sender, saving evidence, reporting the message, contacting the real company through a known official path, and starting recovery steps if the user already interacted. For a caution result, the app should ask the user to verify independently before taking action. For a likely safe result, it should still give a small reminder not to share passwords, verification codes, or payment details outside trusted channels. For a not-enough-information result, the app should ask for the missing context instead of pretending to know.

The screen should include a path into Evidence Vault and Recovery Workspace. If the user has not lost money or shared sensitive information, the app should offer to save the item for future reference. If the user has already clicked, paid, installed software, shared a code, or gave account access, the app should show a recovery prompt immediately. Recovery should not feel like punishment. The language should be practical: "Let's secure the account," "Let's document what happened," or "Let's reduce further risk." The user may already feel embarrassed. The product should reduce shame because shame makes people hide evidence and delay action.

B4. Evidence Vault screen

The Evidence Vault should collect scam-related items in a way that is organized, searchable, and useful for reports or recovery. It should not be a generic file cabinet. Each saved item should have a case, a source, a date captured by the system, a description, related people or accounts, risk level, and linked recovery tasks. The user should be able to save screenshots, emails, message text, links, files, sender details, phone numbers, payment instructions, transaction notes, support conversations, and app-generated results. The vault should preserve original evidence while also allowing redacted copies for sharing.

The vault should support case grouping. A case might be "fake bank text," "marketplace buyer," "romance request," "job offer," "crypto investment," or "unknown suspicious contact." When the same sender, link, phone number, payment handle, email address, or story appears multiple times, the app should suggest linking items into one case. The user should be able to accept or decline that suggestion. This matters because scam attempts often unfold over several messages and platforms. A single suspicious text might become a phone call, then a payment request, then a fake refund offer.

Each evidence item should show a chain of custody in simple app terms: when it was added, where it came from, whether it was edited, whether a redacted copy exists, whether it was shared with a trusted helper, and whether it was included in a report. The app should not overpromise legal-grade evidence handling, but it should preserve enough detail to help users explain what happened. Any edits to notes should be recorded as notes, not changes to the original captured item. The product must make a clear distinction between original evidence, user notes, app analysis, and shareable summaries.

The vault should include search and filters because large scam cases can become messy. Filters should include risk level, source type, sender, payment method, case, saved date, recovery status, and whether the evidence has been shared or reported. Search should find words inside saved text and user notes, but sensitive data should be handled carefully. If cloud sync exists, the user should know whether vault search happens locally or remotely. If offline mode is enabled, the vault should remain usable even when the app cannot reach external services.

B5. Recovery Workspace screen

The Recovery Workspace should appear when the user may have already been harmed or exposed. It should be task-based, not article-based. The user should not be forced to read a long help page while panicked. The workspace should ask what happened, create a recovery checklist, and connect each checklist item to the evidence and result that caused it. Example situations include: clicked a suspicious link, entered login details, shared a one-time code, sent a payment, gave bank information, installed remote-access software, downloaded a suspicious file, gave identity documents, or allowed someone to control a device.

Recovery tasks should be grouped by urgency. Immediate tasks might include disconnecting remote access, changing passwords from a safe device, contacting a bank, freezing or locking cards, enabling stronger account security, saving evidence, and stopping communication. Next tasks might include reporting the scam, monitoring accounts, reviewing device apps, checking forwarding rules in email, reviewing connected devices, updating recovery email and phone settings, and notifying trusted people. Longer-term tasks might include credit monitoring, identity theft reports, password manager cleanup, or recurring weekly checks.

Each task should explain why it matters in one short sentence and then provide precise action instructions. The app should not say "contact your bank" and stop there. It should tell the user what to ask: report fraud, stop pending transfers if possible, replace compromised cards, review recent transactions, change online banking password, remove unknown payees, and ask about dispute or chargeback options when appropriate. For account recovery, it should guide the user to official account recovery pages by telling them to type the address themselves or use saved official links, not links from suspicious messages.

The workspace should track task status. Status choices should be not started, in progress, done, not applicable, waiting, and need help. Users should be able to add notes, attach evidence, and assign a task to themselves or a trusted helper. The app should never pressure the user to finish everything at once. Recovery is often emotionally difficult. The workspace should surface the next most important action and keep the remaining work organized.

B6. Connected account review screen

The Connected Accounts screen should list services the user has authorized Verivae to review, such as Gmail, email accounts, message sources supported by the operating system, cloud storage, device safety features, browser sharing, and helper accounts. Each connection should show what is connected, what permission was granted, when it was connected, what the app can review, what the app cannot review, and how to disconnect it. This screen is the user's control center for trust.

For Gmail review, the screen should explain whether Verivae can scan new mail automatically, review only selected messages, or review messages the user forwards into the app. It should distinguish subject line, sender, link, attachment, and body review. It should also show whether the app stores copies of reviewed messages or only stores risk findings and user-saved evidence. The user should be able to pause Gmail review without deleting existing evidence. If permission expires, the app should say so clearly and offer reconnect steps.

For message review, the screen should explain platform limitations. Some phone systems may not allow full automatic scanning of texts or third-party messages. The app should be honest: it can review messages shared into the app, screenshots, notifications if permission allows, or selected conversations if the operating system provides a safe integration. It should not imply that it can read every private message in the background unless that is actually supported and permitted. Clear limitation language protects the user and protects the product.

B7. Link and QR review screens

The Link Review screen should accept pasted links, links shared from another app, links found inside emails or messages, and links captured from screenshots. It should show the visible link, the real destination when detectable, any redirects, the domain age or reputation when available, brand impersonation signals, suspicious characters, shortened link behavior, and whether the link asks for login, payment, downloads, remote access, wallet connection, or identity information. The screen should not automatically open suspicious links in the user's normal browser. If the app uses safe previewing, it should do so in a controlled way that does not expose the user to active content.

The QR Review screen should open the camera or image picker and decode QR content before the user visits anything. The result should show whether the QR code contains a website, payment address, Wi-Fi credentials, contact card, calendar invite, app store link, crypto wallet address, or plain text. If the QR code leads to a payment or login page, the app should warn before the user continues. QR scams often exploit physical trust, such as stickers on parking meters or posters. The app should allow the user to add context like "parking meter," "restaurant menu," "package label," "flyer," or "email attachment" because context changes risk.

Both link and QR review should provide a safe next step. If the item claims to be from a bank, delivery service, payment app, government agency, employer, school, marketplace, or social network, Verivae should recommend using the official app or typing the official website manually. If the link appears to be harmless but shortened, the app should still show the expanded destination. If the app cannot inspect a destination because the site blocks automated checks or requires login, the result should say that and ask the user to verify through a trusted route.

B8. Attachment and file review screen

The Attachment and File Review screen should accept files shared from email, browser downloads, cloud storage, and local device storage. The app should inspect file name, extension, declared type, actual type when detectable, size, source, embedded links, macros when supported, scripts, executable behavior, archive contents where safe, and mismatch signals such as a file that appears to be a PDF but behaves like an executable. The screen should explain what was checked and what was not checked. Users should not be told that a file is safe simply because one basic check passed.

The app should handle dangerous files with a strict safety model. It should avoid opening files in ways that execute code or reveal the user's environment. If deeper analysis requires cloud scanning or a sandbox, the app should ask for permission and explain the tradeoff. If a file is password-protected, encrypted, too large, corrupted, or unsupported, the result should say this plainly and recommend caution. A common scam pattern is an attachment that asks the user to enable macros, sign in to view a document, pay an invoice, install an app, or call fake support. The file result should surface these patterns in normal language.

B9. Device Safety screen

The Device Safety screen should focus on what Verivae can realistically check on the user's device. It should not pretend to replace the operating system's built-in security features. Its job is to help the user notice risky settings, suspicious apps, recent downloads, unsafe permissions, remote-access tools, browser notification spam, profile or configuration changes, unknown connected devices where visible, and signs that a scammer may still have access. Device safety should be framed as "risk review" rather than a guaranteed virus removal promise unless the app truly includes certified antivirus scanning.

The screen should separate quick checks from deeper checks. A quick check can review recent downloads, suspicious permissions, known remote-access app names, notification settings, browser pop-ups, app install recency, device lock status, operating system update status, and whether weekly checks are enabled. A deeper check can inspect more categories if the user grants permission and the platform allows it. The app should explain that some checks are different on iPhone and Android because the operating systems expose different capabilities. This prevents the product from promising the same behavior everywhere when platform rules differ.

If the app detects a likely remote-access tool, risky profile, suspicious notification permission, or unknown app installed around the time of a scam, it should give action steps immediately. These might include disconnecting from the internet temporarily, removing remote-access apps, revoking permissions, restarting the device, changing important passwords from another trusted device, reviewing account sessions, and saving evidence before deleting anything if evidence may matter. The app should avoid telling the user to delete everything blindly because recovery sometimes depends on preserving proof.

B10. Weekly Deep Check screen

The Weekly Deep Check should be a recurring protective review that helps the user catch problems they missed. It should not be noisy. The screen should show the date of the last completed check, the next scheduled check, the categories included, and whether any permissions are needed. The check should review saved suspicious items, unresolved recovery tasks, account connection health, email risk trends, message risk trends where available, newly detected risky links, suspicious attachments, device safety signals, app permissions, notification settings, and evidence cases that have not been closed.

The weekly check should produce a summary that is short at the top and detailed underneath. The top should say something like "No urgent action needed," "Two items need review," or "One recovery task is still waiting." The detail area should group findings by urgency. The app should not bury a critical bank-account recovery reminder under low-risk education items. The weekly check should also avoid alert fatigue. If the same unresolved item appears every week, the app should show progress and next action rather than repeating the same warning with no new value.

B11. Trusted Helper screen

The Trusted Helper screen should let a user invite a family member, friend, caregiver, or advisor to help review suspicious situations or recovery tasks. This feature must be built with privacy limits from the beginning. The user should control what the helper can see. Sharing options should include a single scam result, a redacted evidence item, a case summary, a recovery checklist, or ongoing alerts for high-risk events. The helper should not automatically receive all messages, all emails, or all evidence unless the user deliberately chooses a broad sharing mode with clear explanation.

The screen should support helper roles. A review-only helper can give advice but cannot change settings. A recovery helper can view selected tasks and mark assigned tasks complete. A family safety helper can receive certain alerts if the user enables that. A user should be able to remove a helper at any time. The app should show when a helper last accessed shared material and whether they downloaded or copied anything if that is trackable. For users who are being manipulated by a scammer, the helper feature can be valuable because scams often rely on isolation and secrecy.

B12. Privacy and permission settings screen

Privacy settings should be written like a control panel, not a legal document. The screen should show data categories in plain language: messages shared for review, connected email data, uploaded screenshots, links checked, files scanned, device safety signals, saved evidence, helper sharing, analytics, and notification preferences. For each category, the app should show whether it is on, what it is used for, where it is processed, how long it is kept, and how the user can delete it. If the app offers local-only mode for some checks, this screen should make that option visible.

The user should be able to export or delete their data. Deleting data should explain consequences clearly: saved evidence and recovery history may be removed, but reports already sent to external organizations may not be retractable through the app. If the app keeps minimal security logs to prevent abuse or protect the service, the screen should say so in understandable terms. Trust requires honesty even when the answer is not perfectly simple.

B13. Scam education screen

The education screen should be practical and tied to real product behavior. It should not become a generic blog. Lessons should be short, scenario-based, and connected to what the user has actually encountered when personalization is enabled. Examples include fake bank warnings, package delivery links, romance money requests, marketplace overpayment, job scams, gift card pressure, crypto investment promises, refund scams, remote support scams, and verification code theft. Each lesson should show the pattern, the warning signs, the safe alternative, and what Verivae would look for during a scan.

Education should also appear inside results and recovery tasks. If the app flags a gift-card scam, it should briefly explain why gift cards are risky in that context. If it flags a fake login page, it should explain domain mismatch and urgency language without asking the user to learn technical vocabulary first. The dedicated education screen can go deeper, but moment-of-need education is what changes behavior when the user is about to act.

B14. Alerts and notifications screen

The alerts screen should collect warnings, reminders, recovery nudges, permission issues, and weekly check summaries. Alerts should be grouped by urgency and source. The product should distinguish urgent safety alerts from ordinary reminders. Urgent alerts might include likely scam payment requests, suspicious account access, recovery tasks after money was sent, dangerous file results, or remote-access risk. Ordinary reminders might include weekly check completion, evidence case review, education suggestions, or permission renewal. The app should let users tune notification frequency so protection does not become noise.

Every alert should have a destination. Tapping an alert should open the exact result, recovery task, evidence item, connection setting, or weekly check summary that explains it. Alerts should never drop the user onto a generic home screen with no context. If an alert was generated because of connected Gmail or messages, the alert should show a privacy-respecting summary rather than exposing sensitive content on the lock screen by default. The user should be able to choose private notification previews.

B15. Search screen

The search screen should allow the user to search across saved scam results, evidence cases, links, phone numbers, emails, payment handles, recovery tasks, and education topics. Search should be helpful but privacy-aware. It should not surface sensitive content in full unless the user has unlocked the app. Search results should be grouped by type so the user can distinguish a saved evidence item from a lesson or recovery task. If the user searches for a phone number or email address, the app should show matching evidence, matching alerts, and related cases.

Search should also help the user answer questions like "Where did I save that bank text?" or "Did this email appear before?" A professional app brief should account for this because scam protection becomes more valuable over time as the app builds memory. Search should include a "not found" state that suggests next actions: run a manual check, check connected account status, or create a new evidence note.

B16. Empty states and first-use states

Empty states should teach without turning into marketing copy. When the user first opens Evidence Vault and has no items, the screen should say what can be saved and offer a simple action to run a check. When Recovery Workspace has no active tasks, it should state that no recovery tasks are currently open and provide a path for users who already clicked, paid, or shared information. When Gmail is not connected, the screen should explain the benefit of connecting it and the privacy controls involved. These states should reduce confusion rather than decorate emptiness.

First-use setup should be skippable. The app can ask whether the user wants to connect Gmail, enable notifications, turn on weekly checks, add a trusted helper, and set privacy preferences, but it should not force all of this before Manual Scam Check works. A person who is actively worried about a scam needs fast access. Setup can continue later. The product should prioritize immediate usefulness over perfect configuration.

B17. Error states and uncertain states

Professional app behavior depends heavily on what happens when something fails. Verivae should have clear error states for unavailable network, expired account permission, unsupported file, blocked link inspection, message import failure, camera permission denied, helper invitation failure, evidence save failure, and recovery task sync conflict. Each error should explain what happened, what the user can do, and whether safety is affected. The app should never show a bare technical error message for a protection feature.

Uncertain states are equally important. If the app cannot tell whether something is safe, it should say so. It should explain what information is missing and recommend a cautious next step. The product should treat uncertainty as a responsible result, not a failure. A result like "Not enough information" should still be useful: it can ask for sender details, full link, screenshot, payment request wording, account name, or whether the user already interacted.

B18. Cross-feature continuity

All major screens should connect to each other through cases and tasks. A manual check can create a result. A result can save evidence. Evidence can belong to a case. A case can create recovery tasks. Recovery tasks can reference evidence. Weekly checks can reopen unresolved tasks. Trusted helpers can review selected evidence or tasks. Privacy settings can control what data these flows use. Education can explain the scam pattern found in the result. This continuity is what makes the app feel like one coherent product instead of a bundle of unrelated tools.

The app should remember enough context to prevent the user from repeating themselves, but it should never feel like it is secretly watching everything. If the user shares a suspicious email into the app and later uploads a screenshot from the same sender, Verivae can suggest that they may be related. The suggestion should be editable and dismissible. The user remains in control of what gets linked, saved, shared, or deleted.

Appendix B acceptance standard

Appendix B is satisfied when every major screen has a clear purpose, a primary user action, visible state behavior, privacy expectations, and a connection to the rest of the product. A designer should be able to turn the section into wireframes without inventing the product from scratch. A developer should be able to identify the main data objects each screen needs. A tester should be able to understand which screen states require verification. The screen model is incomplete if any major safety decision has no visible user path, if permissions are hidden behind vague labels, if scam results do not explain evidence, or if recovery work is separated from the events that caused it.

Appendix C: User Flow Library and Real-World Scenario Behavior

This appendix describes how Verivae should behave in realistic scam situations. A user flow is the path a person takes through the app from the moment they notice a problem to the moment the app gives them a useful next step. These flows matter because scam protection is not one single feature. The same detection engine, evidence vault, recovery workspace, helper review, privacy controls, and education system must work together across many different situations. A professional product brief should not only define features in isolation; it should also define how those features behave when a real user is rushed, scared, distracted, embarrassed, or unsure.

C1. Suspicious bank text flow

The user receives a text that claims to be from a bank and says a payment was declined or an account will be locked. The message includes a link and asks the user to verify immediately. The user opens Verivae and chooses Manual Scam Check. They paste the text or share a screenshot. The app extracts the sender number, visible link, claimed institution, urgency language, requested action, and whether the message asks for login information. If the screenshot includes a shortened link or a link with a bank-like name, the app checks the real destination where possible without opening the page in the user's normal browser.

The result should focus on the action the user is about to take. The app should say not to click the link yet, explain that banks generally do not ask users to verify through random text links, identify the suspicious indicators, and recommend opening the official banking app or typing the known website address manually. If the user says they already clicked the link but did not enter information, the app should create a recovery task to close the page, avoid entering information, check browser downloads, and monitor for follow-up contact. If the user entered banking credentials, the app should move the user into account recovery immediately, with tasks for changing the password from a safe route, contacting the bank, reviewing recent transactions, and saving evidence.

C2. Fake package delivery flow

The user receives an email or text saying a delivery failed and a small fee is needed. The app should recognize that package scams often use familiar delivery brands and small payment amounts to reduce suspicion. The manual or connected review should inspect the sender, domain, link destination, fee request, grammar, tracking-number format when visible, and whether the message creates urgency. The result should recommend going to the delivery company's official site or app and entering the tracking number manually. If no tracking number exists, the app should treat that as a risk signal.

If the user paid the small fee, the app should not treat the damage as small. The recovery flow should ask what payment method was used. A card payment should create tasks to contact the card issuer, watch for additional charges, replace the card if needed, and avoid future messages using the same story. If the user entered an address, phone number, or email, the app should explain that personal information may be reused for follow-up scams. If the user downloaded a delivery app from a link, the app should trigger device safety review and file/app review.

C3. Marketplace buyer or seller flow

Marketplace scams are context-heavy, so Verivae should ask a few targeted questions after the user uploads a conversation. The app should ask whether the user is buying or selling, whether the other person wants to move off the marketplace, whether they offered overpayment, whether they requested a verification code, whether they sent a check image, whether they want courier pickup, whether they ask for a deposit, and whether payment is being requested through unusual channels. The app should identify red flags such as payment screenshots that cannot be verified, claims of pending payment, pressure to refund accidental overpayment, requests to ship before confirmed funds, or links that imitate marketplace login pages.

The result should give role-specific next steps. If the user is selling, the app should recommend staying on-platform, waiting for confirmed payment, refusing overpayment refunds, not sharing verification codes, and meeting safely if local pickup is involved. If the user is buying, it should recommend avoiding off-platform deposits, verifying seller history, using protected payment methods, and not trusting screenshots as proof of payment. If the user has already shipped an item or sent money, the app should create evidence and recovery tasks tied to the payment provider, shipping carrier, platform report, and communication history.

C4. Job offer and employment scam flow

The user receives a job offer that may involve remote work, equipment checks, personal documents, direct deposit setup, training fees, or messaging through a chat app. The app should inspect whether the company domain matches the real organization, whether the recruiter uses a free email account, whether the interview process is suspiciously short, whether the job asks the applicant to deposit a check, buy equipment, pay for training, install software, provide identity documents too early, or receive and resend money. The app should ask whether the user applied for the job, how contact started, and whether any documents or banking details were already shared.

The result should separate ordinary hiring steps from risky timing. A real employer may ask for identity and payment details after a legitimate hiring process, but a scam may ask before trust is established. The app should advise verifying the company through its official website, contacting HR through a known address, and refusing checks or money movement tasks. If the user has deposited a check or bought equipment with promised reimbursement, the recovery workspace should explain check-clearing risk, bank contact steps, evidence collection, and account monitoring.

C5. Gift card or crypto pressure flow

The user receives a message asking them to buy gift cards, send crypto, transfer through a payment app, or use a wire service. The scammer may claim to be a boss, family member, romantic partner, government agency, tech support worker, investment advisor, or urgent helper. The app should treat gift cards, crypto, wires, and irreversible payment methods as high-risk when paired with urgency, secrecy, emotional pressure, threats, or impersonation. The result should be direct: do not buy, send, photograph, or share the code or payment details.

The app should show the specific manipulation pattern. It might say that the message asks for an irreversible payment method, creates pressure to act quickly, and discourages independent verification. It should recommend calling the real person through a known phone number if the request claims to come from someone the user knows. If the user already sent codes or crypto, the recovery flow should focus on evidence preservation, platform reporting, contacting the payment provider where possible, and warning the user that recovery scammers may appear next. The app should explicitly flag follow-up messages promising to recover lost money for a fee.

C6. Romance or friendship money request flow

Romance and friendship scams require careful, non-shaming language. The app should not mock the relationship or assume the user is foolish. If a user asks the app to review a money request from someone they met online, Verivae should inspect the story, urgency, payment method, refusal to video chat, repeated emergencies, isolation language, requests for secrecy, inconsistent identity details, and requests to move communication to private channels. The app should ask whether the user has met the person in real life, whether money has been sent before, and whether the person becomes angry or affectionate when questioned.

The result should be compassionate but clear. It should explain that the request has common romance-scam patterns and recommend pausing payments, talking to a trusted person, preserving conversations, and verifying identity outside the scammer's control. If the user wants help but is not ready to label it a scam, the app should offer a "pause and verify" plan rather than forcing a harsh conclusion. Trusted Helper sharing can be especially important here. The user should be able to share a redacted case summary with someone they trust without exposing every private message.

C7. Fake technical support and remote access flow

The user sees a pop-up, receives a call, or gets an email saying their device is infected, account is compromised, or refund is available. The scammer asks the user to call a number, install remote-access software, share a screen, log in to a bank, or move money to a safe account. Verivae should detect this as one of the highest-risk flows because remote access can combine device compromise, financial theft, and account manipulation. The app should ask whether remote-access software was installed, whether the user gave control, whether banking information was shown, whether files were downloaded, and whether money was moved.

If remote access may still be active, the recovery screen should prioritize disconnecting safely, removing remote-access tools, changing important passwords from a trusted device, contacting financial institutions, reviewing account sessions, and saving evidence. The app should avoid instructions that require the user to keep interacting with the scammer. If the user is on a call, the app should say to end the call and use known official contact channels. If the user is unsure whether software was installed, Device Safety should open with a guided list of common signs and supported checks.

C8. Verification code theft flow

The user receives a request to share a code sent by text, email, authenticator app, or account recovery system. The app should treat one-time codes as highly sensitive. It should detect language like "send me the code," "prove you are real," "I accidentally sent a code to your phone," "verify your account," or "read the number back." The result should explain that codes are like temporary keys and should not be shared with another person. The app should recommend stopping the conversation and checking the relevant account directly.

If the user already shared a code, the recovery workspace should ask which account was involved. Tasks should include changing the password, signing out of other sessions, checking recovery email and phone settings, enabling stronger authentication, reviewing recent activity, and saving the suspicious conversation. If the app cannot identify the account, it should ask what service sent the code and provide a generic account-security checklist.

C9. Tax, government, or legal threat flow

The user receives a message claiming to be from a government agency, court, police department, tax office, immigration office, or benefits program. It may threaten arrest, fines, deportation, benefit loss, license suspension, or legal action. The app should inspect sender identity, payment method, urgency, threats, grammar, links, attachments, and whether the message asks for gift cards, crypto, wire transfers, prepaid cards, remote access, or personal documents. The result should explain that official agencies usually provide verifiable contact paths and do not demand unusual payments through threatening messages.

The safe next step should be to contact the agency through an official website or known phone number, not through the suspicious message. If the user shared identity documents, the recovery workspace should focus on identity protection and evidence. If money was sent, it should create payment-specific tasks. The app should be careful with legal language and avoid pretending to be a lawyer. It can provide safety steps and suggest official reporting or professional advice when appropriate.

C10. QR code payment or login flow

The user scans a QR code from a parking meter, restaurant table, poster, event sign, email, package, or flyer. Verivae should decode the QR content before opening it. If the code leads to a payment page, login page, app install, crypto wallet, or unknown shortened link, the app should show a caution result and recommend verifying the source. For physical QR codes, the app should allow the user to add context and optionally capture a photo of the surrounding sign or sticker for evidence.

If the QR appears to be a sticker placed over a legitimate code, the app should let the user save the image and location note. The app should avoid using exact location unless the user permits it and understands why. If the QR code is safe or low risk, the result should still show the destination in readable form so the user knows where they are going.

C11. Suspicious attachment flow

The user receives an invoice, resume, shared document, voicemail file, tax file, package form, or image attachment. Verivae should review the file without executing it. It should inspect name, extension, type mismatch, embedded links, macro or script indicators where detectable, password protection, and whether the message around the file creates pressure. If the file claims to be from a known company but uses an unusual sender or asks the user to enable features, the result should explain that pattern.

If the file cannot be fully checked, the app should not give a confident safe result. It should say that inspection is limited and recommend verifying the sender through a known channel. If the user already opened the file or installed something, the flow should connect to Device Safety and Recovery Workspace. Evidence Vault should save the original file only if storage is safe and permitted; otherwise, it can save metadata, screenshots, and the app result.

C12. Unknown or mixed situation flow

Many users will not know what category applies. The app should always support "I am not sure." In this flow, Verivae should ask broad, simple questions: Did someone ask for money? Did they ask for a code? Did they send a link? Did you enter a password? Did you install anything? Did they ask you to keep it secret? Did they threaten you? Did they claim to be from a bank, company, government agency, employer, friend, or romantic partner? Did you already do anything?

Based on answers, the app should route to the right checks and recovery tasks. If multiple risks exist, the app should prioritize the highest-risk action first. For example, if the user installed remote-access software and also sent money, the first task may be stopping access and securing accounts, followed by bank contact and evidence. The app should not force the user to classify the scam before getting help. It should classify the risk behind the scenes and show the next safest action.

C13. Repeated scammer and linked-case flow

If the same phone number, email, domain, payment handle, name, script, or attachment pattern appears again, Verivae should suggest linking the new item to an existing case. The suggestion should be phrased gently: "This may be related to a saved case." The user can link it, keep it separate, or ignore the suggestion. Linking should improve recovery and evidence organization, but it should never automatically expose more information to a helper or report destination without permission.

Linked cases should show a timeline of events inside the case view, but the document should not treat this as a development timeline or company plan. It is a user-facing event history. The event history helps the user and any helper understand how the scam progressed: first contact, suspicious link, payment request, user action, result, evidence saved, recovery tasks created, reports submitted, and case closed. Each event should connect back to the original item.

C14. False positive and user disagreement flow

The app must handle cases where the user disagrees with the result. If Verivae flags something as risky and the user believes it is legitimate, the result screen should allow them to provide more context, mark the result as incorrect, or save the item as trusted with limits. The app should avoid letting one user action permanently whitelist dangerous patterns. A better design is to trust a specific sender, domain, or context only after clear confirmation, and to continue warning about high-risk requests such as verification codes, gift cards, crypto transfers, or remote access.

If the app says something is likely safe and the user still feels unsure, the app should support that too. The user can request a deeper review, ask a trusted helper, save the evidence, or follow independent verification steps. Trustworthy products do not force confidence. They help the user make a careful decision.

C15. Flow handoff rules

Every scenario flow should end in one of several clear destinations: safe to proceed with caution, verify independently, do not interact, save evidence, ask a trusted helper, begin recovery, or continue review because information is missing. These destinations should be consistent across the app. A user should not see a completely different safety vocabulary on the email screen than they see on the link screen or file screen. Consistency is a functional requirement because people rely on repeated patterns when stressed.

The app should also preserve context across handoffs. If a suspicious email has a link and an attachment, the user should not have to manually re-upload the same material in three places. The email review should send the link to Link Review, the file to File Review, and the overall situation to the result screen while keeping everything tied to the same case. If a result creates recovery tasks, those tasks should remember the triggering evidence. If a helper reviews a case, the helper should see the exact item the user chose to share.

Appendix C acceptance standard

Appendix C is satisfied when the app has defined behavior for common scam situations, uncertain situations, already-harmed situations, repeated-contact situations, and disagreement situations. The scenario library is incomplete if it only describes ideal cases where the user has not clicked or paid yet. The app must support prevention, detection, evidence, recovery, and helper review across the same real-world flows.

Appendix D: Acceptance Criteria and Quality Behavior

This appendix defines how Verivae should be judged when a feature is designed, built, or tested. Acceptance criteria are plain-language conditions that tell the team when a feature works well enough to be considered complete. They are not code, and they are not a schedule. They are product rules. For a scam-protection app, acceptance criteria matter because the cost of vague behavior is high. A confusing button, weak warning, missing recovery task, or overconfident result can cause a user to click, pay, share, install, or ignore a problem.

D1. Core result acceptance criteria

Every scam check result should include a result level, a short answer, supporting evidence, confidence language, and next steps. The result level tells the user how risky the item appears. The short answer tells the user what to do immediately. The supporting evidence explains which signals caused the result. The confidence language explains how certain the app is. The next steps tell the user what action to take or avoid. A result is incomplete if it only gives a score with no explanation, if it explains risk without a recommended action, or if it gives a confident answer when important information is missing.

The app should support at least six result outcomes: likely safe, caution, suspicious, likely scam, urgent risk, and not enough information. These outcomes should be used consistently across manual checks, email review, message review, link review, QR review, file review, device safety, and weekly checks. If one feature uses "high risk" and another uses "dangerous" for the same severity, users may not understand the system. Consistent language is a quality requirement.

The result screen should never shame the user. It should not say "you were tricked" or "this is obvious." It should say what happened and what to do next. A professional app should treat mistakes as normal events that need recovery, not as personal failures. This matters especially for older adults, people under financial pressure, people new to digital tools, and people manipulated by emotional scams.

D2. Manual Scam Check acceptance criteria
