Manual Scam Check is complete when the user can submit text, screenshots, links, QR codes, files, and a written situation description without needing to understand technical categories. The app should accept partial information and ask for missing context only when it improves the result. If the user submits a screenshot, the app should extract visible text where possible and still allow the user to correct or add context. If text extraction fails, the app should explain that it could not read the image and ask the user to paste the text or retake the screenshot.

The check should identify common risk categories such as payment pressure, credential request, verification code request, suspicious link, suspicious attachment, impersonation, secrecy pressure, remote-access request, refund or recovery promise, government or legal threat, investment promise, job-equipment scheme, and marketplace overpayment. The app does not need perfect detection to be useful, but it must show what it found and what it did not find. A manual check should not claim full certainty from a tiny sample.

The manual check should include a safe cancellation path. If the user starts a check and decides not to submit personal information, they should be able to back out without saving the draft. If the user does submit information and then chooses to save the result, the app should ask whether to save the original material, a redacted copy, or only the summary. This criterion connects manual checking to privacy and the Evidence Vault.

D3. Email review acceptance criteria

Email review is complete when the app can explain how it receives email content, what parts it reviews, and what the user controls. If Gmail is connected, the app should distinguish between automatic review, selected-message review, and manual sharing. It should not blur those modes. The user should be able to pause review, disconnect the account, delete saved evidence, and understand whether the app keeps email copies or only risk findings.

The email review should inspect sender identity, display-name mismatch, reply-to mismatch, link destinations, attachments, urgency language, payment requests, credential requests, and brand impersonation signals. It should also check for a common pattern where a message appears safe because the sender name looks familiar but the actual address is unrelated. The result should show sender details in a way normal users can understand: "The name says Bank Support, but the address is not from the bank's domain." If technical headers are used, the app should translate the finding into plain language.

Email review should support reporting and recovery paths. If a user marks an email as suspicious, they should be able to save it to the Evidence Vault, create a case, block or report using available provider actions where supported, and open recovery if they already clicked, paid, replied, downloaded a file, or shared information. If a connected email permission fails, the app should show a clear connection issue and avoid pretending that email protection is still active.

D4. Message and text review acceptance criteria

Message review is complete when Verivae can review messages the user shares into the app, screenshots of conversations, and any supported direct message integration. The app must be honest about platform limits. If the operating system does not allow full automatic scanning, the product should say so plainly. A user should not believe they are protected from every text when the app only reviews shared messages.

The message review should inspect sender identity, phone number or handle, message content, links, payment requests, secrecy pressure, impersonation claims, code requests, emotional manipulation, and attempts to move the conversation to another channel. Conversation-level context matters. A single message may not be enough to detect a scam, but a series of messages may show escalation from friendly contact to urgent money request. The app should let users provide multiple screenshots or message snippets in order.

Message review should support helper sharing because texts are often personal and stressful. The user should be able to share a redacted conversation summary with a trusted helper. The helper should see enough to advise, but not more than the user chooses to reveal. If the app recommends calling a real person to verify an emergency request, it should specify that the user should use a known phone number, not the number provided inside the suspicious message.

D5. Link and QR acceptance criteria

Link review is complete when the app shows the visible link, the real destination where detectable, redirect behavior when safe to inspect, domain mismatch, suspicious spelling, shortened-link resolution, brand impersonation cues, and the type of action requested by the page. The app should avoid opening risky links in the user's ordinary browser as part of detection. If safe preview is used, the product should isolate that process and avoid sending user credentials to the destination.

QR review is complete when the app decodes QR content before taking action. The result should explain whether the code contains a web address, payment address, contact card, Wi-Fi network, calendar item, app link, crypto wallet, or plain text. If the code triggers a payment or login path, the app should require a warning screen before the user proceeds. If the QR code is physical, the user should be able to save a context photo or note when helpful.

Both features should include a "verify another way" path. For banks, government agencies, delivery companies, payment apps, marketplaces, schools, and employers, the app should recommend opening the official app or typing the known address manually. The app should not tell users to trust a link simply because it loads successfully.

D6. Attachment and file acceptance criteria

File review is complete when the app can inspect supported files without executing unsafe content and can clearly describe inspection limits. It should check file name, extension, actual type when possible, size, source, embedded links, macro/script indicators where supported, archive contents where safe, password protection, and suspicious mismatch. The result should not overstate safety. A file can be "no obvious risk found" without being guaranteed safe.

If a file is unsupported, too large, encrypted, corrupted, or password-protected, the app should provide cautious next steps. It should ask the user to verify the sender through a known route and avoid enabling macros, installing viewers, logging into unknown document portals, or calling numbers inside the file. If the surrounding email or message is suspicious, the file result should include that context rather than analyzing the file in isolation.

D7. Device Safety acceptance criteria

Device Safety is complete when the app gives realistic checks based on platform permission and operating-system rules. It should identify risky apps, remote-access tools, suspicious recent downloads, risky notification permissions, outdated operating system status where visible, unlocked or weak device security where visible, suspicious browser behavior, and unresolved recovery risks. The screen should clearly separate supported checks from unavailable checks.

Weekly deep checks should not promise full virus removal unless the product truly includes qualified antivirus capability. Instead, the app can say it reviews device safety signals and helps the user find common scam-related risks. If an actual malware scanning engine is used, the brief should later specify the engine, update method, scan scope, quarantine behavior, and user consent flow. Until then, language should stay accurate: risk review, file scanning, permission review, and device safety guidance.

D8. Recovery Workspace acceptance criteria

Recovery Workspace is complete when every harmful user action can create a useful recovery path. Harmful actions include clicking a link, entering a password, sharing a one-time code, sending money, buying gift cards, sending crypto, wiring money, sharing identity documents, installing software, allowing remote access, downloading a file, or continuing a suspicious relationship. The workspace should ask what happened and create tasks that match the user's situation.

Each task should have a title, reason, action, status, optional due reminder, evidence connection, and optional helper assignment. The task should not be vague. "Secure account" is not enough by itself. A better task says which account, what to check, how to verify through a trusted route, and what evidence to save. The workspace should also support "not applicable" because not every task will fit every user.

D9. Evidence Vault acceptance criteria

Evidence Vault is complete when saved items preserve source, capture time, user notes, app result, case association, sharing status, and redaction status. The user should be able to tell the difference between original evidence, redacted evidence, app analysis, and personal notes. Deleting or redacting a share copy should not secretly alter the original unless the user chooses to delete the original too.

The vault should support case grouping, search, filters, export, helper sharing, and recovery linkage. A user dealing with a long scam should be able to collect the full story without losing track of what was sent, received, clicked, paid, or reported. The vault is incomplete if evidence exists as scattered screenshots with no case structure.

D10. Trusted Helper acceptance criteria

Trusted Helper is complete when the user can invite, limit, review, and remove a helper. The user should choose what the helper can see and what the helper can do. Sharing a single result should not automatically share the user's full vault. A helper should not receive private email or message content unless the user deliberately shares it. The app should show helper access in plain language so the user understands the privacy consequences.

The helper flow should include safety protections against coercion. If someone pressures the user to add them as a helper, the app should include warnings around broad access. Helper permissions should be easy to revoke. The product should assume that helpers are often good, but permissions must still be explicit.

D11. Monetization acceptance criteria

Monetization is complete only if it does not weaken user safety. Core protection should remain useful without payment. The app may offer paid features such as advanced monitoring, family/helper features, larger evidence storage, deeper scans, or premium recovery organization, but it should not block urgent scam warnings, basic manual checks, basic evidence saving, or immediate recovery guidance behind a paywall. If the user is in an urgent risk state, the app should never interrupt them with an upgrade screen before showing the safety action.

Paid offers should be clear, calm, and reversible. The app should not use fear-based countdowns, fake scarcity, or pressure language. Pricing should be presented separately from scam results unless a paid feature is directly relevant and the free path remains visible. Trust is part of the business model. A scam-protection app that monetizes through panic will damage its own credibility.

D12. Privacy acceptance criteria

Privacy is complete when every sensitive input has a defined purpose, retention behavior, deletion path, and permission explanation. Users should know whether checks happen on the device, on Harborwake-controlled servers, or through a third-party service. They should know when data is saved, when it is temporary, and when it is shared. The app should use the least amount of data needed for the feature. That means manual check can work before the user connects Gmail, helper review can share one case instead of the whole account, and device checks can request only the permissions needed for the chosen scan.

The app should not collect sensitive material simply because it might be useful later. If a feature can operate on redacted text or metadata, the app should prefer that when it does not harm safety. If full content is needed, the app should explain why. A user must be able to revoke permissions and still use the basic app where possible.

D13. Accessibility acceptance criteria

Accessibility is complete when the app can be used by people with low vision, color vision differences, motor limitations, cognitive overload, and limited technical knowledge. Result levels should not depend on color alone. Buttons should be large enough to tap. Text should be readable. Alerts should be understandable without jargon. Important flows should work with screen readers. Screens should avoid dense walls of text during urgent decisions, even if the full design brief is detailed.

The app should provide simple language without removing important meaning. It should explain terms like domain, redirect, attachment, permission, two-factor code, recovery email, and remote access when they appear. It should allow users to slow down, save progress, ask a helper, or return later. Accessibility is not only visual; it is emotional and cognitive too.

D14. Failure-state acceptance criteria

Failure states are complete when every major failure tells the user what happened, whether safety is affected, and what they can do. Examples include no internet, expired Gmail permission, denied camera permission, unsupported file, blocked link inspection, failed OCR, failed evidence save, failed helper invite, and sync conflict. The app should not leave the user in silence after a failed scan. A failed check should still provide cautious general guidance when possible.

If the app cannot provide a reliable answer, it should say "not enough information" or "unable to complete this check" and offer next steps. It should not guess confidently to look smart. Responsible uncertainty is a feature.

Appendix D acceptance standard

Appendix D is satisfied when each major capability has a clear testable standard for completeness, privacy, user understanding, and safe failure behavior. The product is not ready for design handoff if important features are described only as ideas without result states, limits, recovery paths, and privacy behavior.

Appendix E: Privacy, Permissions, and Data Handling Matrix

This appendix defines how Verivae should request, use, explain, store, and delete sensitive information. Scam protection requires trust at the same time that it asks for unusually sensitive access. A user may want the app to review Gmail messages, text conversations, screenshots, files, links, QR codes, device safety signals, payment-related notes, identity-document exposure, and recovery progress. The app therefore needs privacy behavior that is visible, specific, and practical. Privacy should not live only in a policy page. It should appear at the moment a permission is requested, at the moment sensitive content is uploaded, at the moment evidence is saved, at the moment information is shared with a helper, and at the moment the user wants to delete or export their data.

E1. Permission purpose rule

Every permission should have a clear purpose written in ordinary language. The app should not ask for broad access before the user understands why. For example, Gmail permission should be explained as: "This lets Verivae review selected email or enabled email categories for scam signs such as fake senders, suspicious links, risky attachments, and payment requests." Camera permission should be explained as: "This lets Verivae scan QR codes before you open them." File access should be explained as: "This lets Verivae review files you choose to share or upload." Notifications should be explained as: "This lets Verivae warn you about urgent results and remind you about recovery tasks."

The permission prompt should appear near the feature that needs it. A person who chooses QR Review can be asked for camera access at that point. A person who never uses QR Review does not need to see that prompt on first launch. This keeps setup lighter and reduces distrust. The product should avoid a first-run wall of permissions because that feels invasive and prevents urgent manual checks.

E2. Least-access behavior

Verivae should use the least access that still makes the feature work. If a user wants to check one suspicious email, the app should support sharing or selecting that email without requiring full mailbox monitoring. If a user wants to check one screenshot, the app should accept that screenshot without requiring full photo-library access. If a user wants to scan one QR code, the camera can be used for that scan without requiring location data. If a user wants a trusted helper to review one case, the helper should not receive the whole Evidence Vault.

The app can offer stronger protection through broader access, but stronger access should be optional and explained. For instance, ongoing Gmail review may detect threats faster than manual forwarding, but it requires more trust. The app should make that tradeoff plain. A user should be able to start free and narrow, then grant more access later when they understand the value.

E3. Gmail and email data handling

When Gmail or another email account is connected, Verivae should define exactly what it reviews. Possible scopes include sender address, display name, reply-to address, subject, body text, links, attachments, and message metadata. The app should explain whether review happens only after user selection, in certain risky categories, or automatically for new messages. It should also explain whether messages are stored, temporarily processed, summarized, or ignored after analysis.

A careful design would avoid saving full email bodies by default. Instead, the app can store a risk result, extracted suspicious signals, user-approved evidence, and recovery tasks. If the user chooses to save an email as evidence, the app should ask whether to save the full email, a redacted copy, or a summary. If the email includes unrelated personal conversation, the app should suggest redaction before sharing with a helper. The same rules should apply when an email is forwarded, imported, or selected through a connected account.

Email deletion should be understandable. If a user deletes a saved email item from Evidence Vault, the app should remove its stored copy or summary from Verivae. It should not claim to delete the original email from Gmail unless the app has that permission and performs that specific provider action. Product language should distinguish deleting from the app, deleting from the user's email account, and deleting a shared copy.

E4. Message and conversation data handling

Messages can be more personal than email. The app should treat shared texts, chat screenshots, and conversation snippets as highly sensitive. The default should be user-initiated review: the user shares a message, screenshot, or selected conversation into Verivae. If any operating-system integration allows automatic review, the app should explain the exact scope and limitations. It should not imply complete background reading if the platform does not permit it.

Conversation review should support selective capture. A user may want to share only the suspicious part of a conversation. The app should allow cropping, redaction, or text-only entry. If the user uploads several screenshots, the app should order them where possible and ask the user to correct the sequence if uncertain. The app should not share raw conversations with helpers by default. A helper share should default to a summary plus selected evidence, with full conversation sharing as an explicit choice.

E5. Screenshot and image data handling

Screenshots can contain account balances, names, addresses, phone numbers, private messages, profile photos, order numbers, bank details, and one-time codes. Before saving or sending screenshots for cloud review, Verivae should offer redaction suggestions. Redaction targets should include full account numbers, full addresses, government ID numbers, card numbers, one-time passcodes, unrelated contacts, unrelated messages, and visible children or bystanders in photos where relevant. The app should explain that redaction can reduce exposure but may remove details needed for evidence.

The app should keep original and redacted images distinct. If the user saves an original screenshot and creates a redacted helper copy, the vault should label them clearly. Sharing a redacted copy should not expose the original. If the user deletes the original, the app should explain whether redacted copies remain. The user should never have to guess which version is being sent.

E6. Link, domain, and QR data handling

Link and QR review can often work with less sensitive information than email or screenshots. The app may need to send the URL, decoded QR content, redirect chain, domain, or page metadata to a reputation service or Harborwake server. The app should explain that checking a link may reveal the link being checked. If the link contains a personal token, tracking code, password reset token, invitation code, or account-specific identifier, the app should warn the user before cloud analysis when possible.

The product should avoid automatically visiting suspicious links as the user. It should not load a suspicious page in a way that logs the user in, sends cookies, or executes risky downloads. If a safe preview or sandbox is used, the app should describe the protection in simple language: "We check the destination without opening it in your normal browser." If the destination cannot be checked safely, the app should say so and recommend independent verification.

QR codes should be decoded first and acted on second. The app should never take the user straight from camera scan to external payment, login, or app install without showing the decoded destination and a safety result. If the QR contains Wi-Fi credentials, contact cards, calendar items, or payment addresses, the app should show that content before asking the user to proceed.

E7. Attachment and file data handling

Files should be handled with extra caution because review itself can create risk if the product opens or executes content carelessly. Verivae should inspect files in a non-executing manner wherever possible. It should check metadata, file extension, actual type, embedded links, macro indicators, archive contents where safe, and suspicious mismatch. If cloud scanning is needed, the app should ask permission before upload and explain what leaves the device.

The app should not store every uploaded file forever by default. A better default is temporary analysis plus a prompt asking whether to save the file as evidence. If the file may be dangerous, the app should prefer saving metadata and screenshots unless saving the original is important and safe. If an original file is saved, the vault should label it as potentially risky and avoid opening it casually. Exporting or sharing risky files should require an extra warning.

E8. Device safety data handling

Device safety checks should collect only the signals needed for the check. These may include installed-app names where the platform allows, recent download names, operating system update status, risky permission settings, remote-access app indicators, notification permission settings, browser notification settings, and evidence-linked timestamps. The app should not collect full device inventories without explaining why. It should not claim to inspect protected areas that the operating system does not expose.

If weekly deep checks include device safety, the user should know which categories are included. A weekly check might review permission changes, newly installed risky apps, suspicious download history where allowed, unresolved recovery tasks, and connected-account health. The user should be able to turn off device safety checks without losing manual scam check functionality.

E9. Evidence Vault retention

Evidence retention should be controlled by the user. The app should define default retention behavior: saved evidence remains until deleted by the user, temporary analysis material is deleted after a short processing window unless saved, and recovery tasks remain until the case is closed or deleted. If legal, compliance, fraud-prevention, or abuse-prevention logs are kept separately, the app should explain them without burying the detail. The explanation can be simple: "Some basic service logs may remain for security and abuse prevention, but they do not include your full evidence unless required for a specific support or safety reason."

The vault should support case deletion and item deletion separately. Deleting a case should ask whether to delete all evidence, keep evidence unassigned, or export before deletion. Deleting one item should not break recovery tasks without warning; if a task references deleted evidence, the task should show that the evidence was removed. This matters because users may delete sensitive material and later need to know why a recovery note no longer has proof attached.

E10. Helper sharing data handling

Trusted Helper sharing should be explicit, narrow, and revocable. The user should choose whether to share a result, a single evidence item, a redacted evidence item, a case summary, selected recovery tasks, or ongoing high-risk alerts. The app should show exactly what will be shared before sending. It should also show whether the helper can comment, mark tasks, download evidence, invite others, or only view.

The user should be able to revoke helper access. Revocation should stop future access inside the app, but the app should be honest about any content already downloaded, copied, screenshotted, or sent outside the app. If the app cannot prevent copies, it should not imply that revocation erases what the helper already saw. Clear limits are safer than comforting fiction.

E11. Analytics and product improvement data handling

Analytics should be minimal and separate from sensitive content. The app may need to know which features are used, where users get stuck, whether scans fail, and whether alerts are opened. It should not collect raw email bodies, message text, screenshots, files, payment details, or identity documents as ordinary analytics. If users opt in to share anonymized scam examples to improve detection, that should be a separate setting with a clear explanation and a way to opt out.

The app should avoid analytics during urgent recovery if analytics create risk or confusion. It should also avoid using user-submitted scam content for model training unless the user has clearly agreed and the data is handled according to the privacy policy. Because the product deals with scams, users will be sensitive to hidden data use. Product improvement cannot come at the cost of user trust.

E12. Notification privacy

Notifications should protect sensitive content by default. A lock-screen notification should not reveal a suspicious message, sender, bank name, payment amount, identity issue, or helper comment unless the user enables detailed previews. A safer default is "A scam check needs your attention" or "One recovery task is urgent." Inside the unlocked app, the alert can show more detail. This matters because people may share devices, live with others, or be targeted by someone nearby.

Notification settings should include urgent alerts, weekly check summaries, recovery reminders, helper activity, permission problems, and education reminders. The user should be able to reduce noise without disabling urgent warnings entirely. If notification permission is off, the app should show that protection is limited because reminders and urgent warnings may not appear outside the app.

E13. Data export and deletion

The app should give users control over their material. Export should allow a user to create a case summary with selected evidence, results, timestamps, notes, and recovery tasks. Export formats can be decided later, but the brief should specify the behavior: export should be understandable, organized by case, and safe to share. Redacted export should be available when the user wants help without exposing every private detail.

Deletion should be clear and reversible only when technically true. If the app has a short undo window, it should say so. If deletion is immediate and permanent, it should say that. If cloud backups or synced devices may take time to remove data, the app should explain the delay. The deletion screen should avoid scary language but should prevent accidental loss of important evidence.

E14. Child, elder, caregiver, and family privacy

The app may be used by people helping parents, grandparents, teens, partners, or friends. The design should avoid assuming that helper access is always harmless. A family member may be trusted, but the primary user still owns their data. The app should support assistance without turning into surveillance. A helper should only see what the user shares or what the user has explicitly authorized as an alert category.

For older adults or people who want extra protection, the app can offer stronger helper alerts, but those settings should be deliberate. The app should explain what events trigger helper notices, such as likely scam payment requests, remote-access risk, or urgent recovery tasks. The user should be able to pause or revoke the arrangement. If guardianship, caregiver authority, or enterprise management ever becomes relevant, that should be treated as a separate product design problem, not quietly folded into normal helper sharing.

E15. Privacy acceptance standard

Appendix E is satisfied when every sensitive data category has a defined purpose, consent point, processing location, storage rule, deletion path, sharing rule, and user-facing explanation. The privacy model is incomplete if the app asks for broad access without a narrow alternative, stores full sensitive content by default without clear reason, shares private material with helpers too broadly, hides platform limitations, or uses urgent safety moments to push users into permissions they do not understand.

Appendix F: Threat Model and Abuse Prevention

This appendix describes what Verivae should protect against, what can go wrong inside the product itself, and how the app should reduce harm. A threat model is a structured way of asking, "Who might try to harm the user, what are they trying to get, how could they misuse the app or the user's data, and what protections should exist?" For Verivae, the threat model must cover outside scammers, malware or risky files, impersonators, manipulative contacts, malicious helpers, accidental user mistakes, misleading results, overbroad permissions, and privacy failures. The app is not only fighting scam messages; it is also responsible for not becoming a new source of risk.

F1. Protected assets

The app should treat certain user assets as especially sensitive. These include passwords, one-time verification codes, bank accounts, payment cards, crypto wallets, identity documents, Social Security numbers or equivalent government identifiers, tax information, home addresses, phone numbers, private messages, email bodies, account recovery settings, device access, remote-control permission, evidence files, and trusted helper relationships. The app should also protect less obvious assets such as user confidence, family trust, and the user's willingness to ask for help. Scam victims often stop seeking help when they feel judged or exposed. That emotional asset matters because the product's effectiveness depends on the user returning before the next risky decision.

Every high-sensitivity asset should have related interface protections. A one-time code should trigger direct warning language. A bank credential should trigger account recovery guidance. A payment action should trigger irreversible-payment warnings. A remote-access clue should trigger device-safety steps. An identity-document exposure should trigger identity-protection guidance. Evidence containing private messages should trigger redaction and sharing controls. The app should not treat all content as equal text. The meaning of the content determines the product response.

F2. External attacker types

The app should assume scammers use many identities. They may impersonate banks, payment apps, delivery services, government agencies, employers, technical support teams, online marketplaces, romantic partners, friends, relatives, schools, charities, investment advisors, law enforcement, tax agencies, subscription services, or refund departments. The attacker may communicate by email, text, phone call, social media, messaging app, dating app, marketplace chat, fake website, QR code, attachment, or remote-access tool. A good product does not only look for one channel. It looks for the behavior pattern.

The app should also assume attackers adapt. If Verivae becomes popular, scammers may tell users not to use it, may claim the app is wrong, may pressure users to disable protections, may imitate Harborwake or Verivae, may create fake support pages for the app, or may send screenshots designed to confuse automated review. This is not paranoia; it is normal product thinking for a protection tool. The app should have anti-impersonation guidance inside its own support surfaces and should warn users that no Harborwake representative will ask for their passwords, verification codes, gift cards, crypto, or remote access through unsolicited contact.

F3. Manipulation patterns

Scams often work because they manipulate emotion, timing, and authority. Verivae should detect and explain pressure patterns such as urgency, secrecy, fear, romance, embarrassment, greed, helpfulness, obedience, scarcity, refund hope, sunk cost, and social proof. The app should not only identify technical indicators like suspicious domains. A perfectly spelled message from a real-looking sender can still be dangerous if it asks for gift cards, verification codes, crypto, remote access, or secret payment.

The result screen should explain manipulation patterns in a way users can accept. Instead of saying "This is emotional manipulation," the app might say, "This message pressures you to act quickly and keep the request private. That combination is common in scams." Instead of saying "The scammer is exploiting greed," it might say, "The promised return is unusually high and the payment method would be hard to reverse." Language matters. The app should be firm without sounding accusatory.

F4. Product misuse by scammers

Scammers may try to use Verivae against users. They could ask a user to upload only a harmless portion of a conversation so the app gives a low-risk result. They could send fake proof that "a scam checker approved this." They could instruct the user to ignore warnings. They could claim to be a trusted helper. They could create fake Harborwake emails or fake Verivae support agents. They could use the app's education material to learn what warning signs to avoid.

To reduce misuse, Verivae should make results context-aware. A result should say when the review is based on limited information. If only one message is uploaded, the app can say that more context may change the result. Shareable result images or summaries should include clear wording that they are based on the reviewed material and should not be treated as universal proof that a person or offer is safe. The app should avoid creating easy-to-fake "certified safe" badges. It can provide a shareable summary, but the summary should include enough context and limitations to prevent misuse.

F5. Malicious or unsafe helper behavior

Trusted Helper is powerful and therefore sensitive. A helper might be genuinely supportive, careless, nosy, controlling, or malicious. The app should protect the primary user's privacy even when a helper is involved. Helper access should be scoped, visible, revocable, and logged where possible. A helper should not be able to silently expand their access. A helper should not be able to delete evidence unless the user gave that specific permission, and even then the product should think carefully before allowing it. Evidence deletion by helpers can create risk if the helper is part of the harm.

The app should also help users avoid adding scammers as helpers. If a new helper invitation is created immediately after a suspicious conversation, payment request, or remote-access event, the app should display a warning: "Only add someone you already trust outside this conversation." If the person asking to become a helper is part of the suspicious situation, the app should recommend not granting access. Helper names, email addresses, or phone numbers should be verified through the user's own trusted contact method where possible.

F6. False positive risk

A false positive happens when the app marks a legitimate item as risky. False positives can annoy users, damage trust, or delay real action. But in scam protection, some false positives are acceptable if the app explains uncertainty and provides safe verification steps. The app should avoid extreme language unless the risk evidence is strong. It should allow the user to provide more context, mark a result as incorrect, or trust a specific sender with limits. However, high-risk request types should remain cautious even when the sender is trusted. A real friend can have a compromised account. A real employer can be impersonated. A real-looking bank email can contain a fake link.

The product should distinguish between "this source is trusted" and "this action is safe." A known contact asking for a one-time code is still dangerous. A familiar email address asking for gift cards may indicate account compromise. The app should explain that trust in a person does not automatically make every request safe.

F7. False negative risk

A false negative happens when the app misses a scam. This is the most dangerous detection failure. The app should reduce false negatives by combining signals: content, sender, link, file, payment method, urgency, context, history, known scam patterns, user answers, and connected-account evidence where permitted. The product should avoid claiming that likely safe means guaranteed safe. It should use careful language such as "No obvious scam signs found" when evidence is limited.

For high-impact situations, the app should use safety floor rules. Even if most signals look normal, the app should warn strongly about sharing passwords, one-time codes, remote access, gift cards, crypto transfers, wires, and unusual payment instructions. These categories deserve extra caution because harm can be immediate and hard to reverse.

F8. Data exposure risk

The app itself can create privacy risk if it stores too much, shares too broadly, or sends sensitive material to third parties unnecessarily. To reduce exposure, Verivae should prefer local analysis for simple checks where feasible, temporary processing for unsaved material, redaction before sharing, clear retention rules, and minimal analytics. Sensitive evidence should not be mixed with ordinary product analytics. Helper sharing should default to summaries or redacted evidence. Cloud processing should be explained before upload when the material is sensitive.

The app should also protect data at rest and in transit when it stores or sends information. The brief does not need to define code-level encryption details yet, but it should require secure storage, secure transmission, access controls, audit awareness for helper access, and deletion behavior that matches the user interface. A future technical specification can define exact implementation methods.

F9. Account takeover risk

Because Verivae may store evidence, recovery tasks, connected account status, and sensitive scam history, the user's Verivae account becomes important. The app should support strong login protection, recovery options, session review, and suspicious-login alerts. If a scammer gets into the user's Verivae account, they might see evidence, learn what the user knows, delete helpful material, or manipulate helper settings. The app should treat its own account security as part of scam protection.

Account recovery for Verivae should avoid becoming a scam path. Support agents should not ask users for passwords, one-time codes, full bank details, or remote access. The app should teach users how real Harborwake support communicates. If in-app support exists, it should happen through authenticated app channels where possible.

F10. Detection bypass and adversarial content

Attackers may format messages to bypass detection. They may use images instead of text, misspell brand names, split links across lines, use homoglyph characters, encode links in QR codes, use URL shorteners, hide text in attachments, or tell the user to read instructions over the phone. The app should handle screenshots, OCR, link extraction, QR decoding, and context questions because scams are not always machine-readable text. When the app cannot inspect content, it should say what it could not inspect and ask for another input form.

The app should also watch for attempts to hide the important request. A conversation may look friendly for many messages, then include a payment request in a screenshot or voice call. If the user describes a phone call, Verivae should still ask structured questions and create recovery tasks. The product should not fail simply because the scam did not arrive as copyable text.

F11. Harmful advice risk

A protection app can cause harm if it gives advice that is too broad, too confident, or legally/financially inaccurate. Verivae should separate general safety guidance from official financial, legal, medical, or law-enforcement advice. It can recommend contacting a bank, payment provider, account provider, local authorities, or official reporting channel, but it should avoid guaranteeing refunds, legal outcomes, account recovery, or malware removal. It should not tell users to confront scammers or continue risky conversations to collect evidence unless professional guidance supports that situation.

Recovery instructions should prioritize reducing harm. If the user is on a call with a suspected scammer, the app should recommend ending the call and using a trusted channel. If remote access is active, it should focus on stopping access and securing accounts. If money was sent, it should focus on fast contact with the relevant institution. If identity documents were shared, it should focus on identity-protection steps and monitoring.

F12. Abuse reporting and feedback

The app should include a way for users to report missed scams, incorrect warnings, confusing results, unsafe content, helper abuse, or impersonation of Harborwake. Feedback should not require the user to share full private evidence unless needed. The app should allow a redacted report or a description. If a user reports a serious failure, the product should guide them to immediate safety actions rather than simply collecting feedback.

Feedback should improve the app carefully. User-submitted examples can help detection, but they may contain sensitive data. The app should separate support, product feedback, detection improvement, and evidence storage. A user who reports a missed scam should know whether the report is saved to their vault, sent to Harborwake, both, or neither.

F13. Threat model acceptance standard

Appendix F is satisfied when the product considers attackers, victims, helpers, platform limits, privacy risks, detection failures, harmful advice, account security, and misuse of app-generated results. The threat model is incomplete if it only lists scam types without explaining how the app itself could be misused or how the app should behave when its confidence is limited.

Appendix G: Recovery Playbooks

This appendix defines recovery playbooks for the most important harm situations in Verivae. A recovery playbook is a guided set of app screens and tasks for a specific situation after the user may have already interacted with a scam. The product should not treat recovery as a generic help article. It should turn the user's situation into a small set of prioritized actions, connect those actions to evidence, and keep the user moving without requiring them to understand every technical detail immediately.

G1. Recovery intake screen

The recovery intake screen should ask what happened in plain language. The choices should include: I clicked a link, I entered a password, I shared a verification code, I sent money, I bought or shared gift cards, I sent crypto, I sent a wire or bank transfer, I shared bank or card information, I shared identity documents, I installed an app or file, someone controlled my device, I replied to a suspicious message, I gave personal information, and I am not sure. The user should be able to choose more than one answer because scams often involve several events. For example, a fake support scam may include a phone call, remote access, bank login, and money movement.

After the user chooses events, the app should ask only the most important follow-up questions. It should not turn recovery into a long survey. Useful follow-up questions include which account was involved, which payment method was used, whether the user is still in contact with the person, whether remote access may still be active, whether the user used the same password elsewhere, and whether they want to involve a trusted helper. The app should build the recovery workspace from those answers.

G2. Clicked link playbook

If the user clicked a suspicious link but did not enter information, the app should first reduce anxiety and then check for follow-up risk. The result can say that clicking alone does not always mean the account is compromised, but the user should avoid entering information, close the page, avoid downloads, and check whether anything was installed. Tasks should include saving the original message, reviewing browser downloads, checking whether the page requested login or payment, and using the official app or website if the user still needs to handle the real issue.

If the user clicked a link and entered information, the flow should escalate based on the type of information. Password entry should trigger account recovery. Card entry should trigger payment-card recovery. Bank login should trigger bank recovery. Identity details should trigger identity protection. The app should not treat all link clicks the same. The harm depends on what happened after the click.

G3. Entered password playbook

If the user entered a password on a suspicious site, the app should ask which account the password belongs to and whether the same password is used elsewhere. Immediate tasks should include changing the password through the official app or website, signing out of other sessions where supported, checking recent account activity, updating recovery email and phone settings, turning on stronger authentication, and watching for password-reset emails. If the same password is used on other accounts, the app should create additional tasks to change those passwords too.

The app should explain password reuse in simple terms: if one password was given away, any account using that same password may be at risk. The app should not ask the user to type the compromised password into Verivae. It only needs to know where the password was used. If the user does not know, the app can create a general password-cleanup task and suggest starting with email, banking, payment apps, cloud storage, phone provider, social media, and work or school accounts.

G4. Shared verification code playbook

If the user shared a one-time code, the app should treat it as urgent because the code may have allowed a scammer to log in, reset a password, add a device, or authorize a payment. The first question should be which service sent the code. If the user knows, the app should create account-specific tasks: open the official app or website, change the password, review active sessions, remove unknown devices, check recovery settings, check recent payments or changes, and enable stronger login protection. If the user does not know, the app should ask them to search recent texts or emails for the code sender, without sharing more private content than necessary.

The result should explain that a one-time code is not harmless just because it expires. It may already have been used. The app should avoid blaming language. It should simply say that the safest next step is to secure the related account now.

G5. Sent card payment playbook

If the user entered card information or made a card payment, the app should ask whether the card was credit, debit, prepaid, or unknown. Tasks should include contacting the card issuer, reporting possible fraud, reviewing recent transactions, replacing the card if advised by the issuer, changing account passwords connected to the payment site, saving the receipt or transaction record, and watching for follow-up charges. If the card was connected to a digital wallet, the app should include wallet review steps.

The app should not guarantee a refund. It should say that the user should contact the issuer quickly because options may depend on payment type, timing, issuer rules, and local law. The recovery screen should help the user prepare what to say: when the payment happened, who requested it, how contact occurred, amount, merchant name, link used, and evidence saved. This makes the user's phone call or chat with the bank more effective.

G6. Sent bank transfer or wire playbook

Bank transfers and wires can be harder to reverse, so the app should prioritize speed. The first task should be contacting the bank or transfer provider through a trusted phone number or official app. The app should help the user gather details: amount, recipient, time sent, confirmation number, bank name, routing or account information if known, message thread, sender contact, and any promise or threat used. The app should recommend asking whether the transfer can be stopped, recalled, disputed, or flagged as fraud.

The app should also create tasks to secure online banking. These tasks may include changing the banking password from the official app or site, reviewing recent transactions, checking payees or recipients, removing unknown linked accounts, reviewing alerts, and checking whether the scammer saw bank information through screen sharing. If remote access was involved, the flow should include device safety before password changes on the same device.

G7. Sent gift card playbook

If the user bought or shared gift card numbers, the app should ask which brand, amount, store, whether codes were photographed or typed, and whether the cards were already redeemed if known. Tasks should include saving receipts, saving card images if available, contacting the gift card issuer, contacting the store where purchased if relevant, reporting the scam, and preserving the conversation. The app should explain that gift card recovery is difficult but quick reporting can still matter.

The app should also warn about recovery scams. After gift card loss, scammers may contact the user claiming they can recover money for a fee. The app should flag this pattern and tell the user not to pay anyone who promises guaranteed recovery. This warning should also appear after crypto, wire, and payment-app losses.

G8. Sent crypto playbook

If the user sent cryptocurrency, the app should ask which wallet, exchange, asset, address, amount, transaction hash if known, and how the scammer contacted the user. Tasks should include saving the transaction record, contacting the exchange if one was used, reporting the wallet address where appropriate, preserving the conversation, securing exchange accounts, changing passwords, reviewing connected wallets, and watching for recovery scams. The app should not promise that crypto can be reversed.

The app should translate crypto terms for beginners. It can explain that a wallet address is like the destination for the transfer and a transaction hash is the public receipt-like identifier for the transaction. The product should not require the user to understand blockchain concepts before saving evidence.

G9. Installed app, file, or remote access playbook

If the user installed software, opened a suspicious file, or allowed remote control, recovery should start with access containment. Tasks should include ending the remote session, disconnecting from the internet if remote access seems active, removing remote-access tools, restarting the device, running supported device safety checks, reviewing recently installed apps, checking downloads, and changing important passwords from a trusted device. If the user logged into banking or email while the scammer could see the screen, the app should create account recovery tasks for those accounts.

The app should be careful about evidence. Deleting suspicious software may be necessary, but preserving names, screenshots, install times, and messages may help reporting. The app should suggest saving evidence before removal when doing so does not increase risk. If the app cannot inspect the device deeply because of platform limits, it should explain that limitation and still provide practical steps.

G10. Shared identity documents playbook

If the user shared an ID, Social Security number, tax document, passport, driver's license, bank statement, utility bill, selfie, or other identity proof, the app should create identity-protection tasks. These may include saving what was shared, noting where and when it was shared, contacting relevant institutions, monitoring accounts, considering credit freezes or fraud alerts where appropriate, updating account security, and watching for follow-up impersonation. The app should be careful with jurisdiction-specific advice and should point users toward official resources when needed.

The app should distinguish between shared photo ID, shared government number, shared financial statement, and shared login credentials. Each creates a different risk. The intake screen should not require the user to know the exact consequences. It should ask what was shared and build the right recovery path.

G11. Ongoing contact playbook

If the user is still talking to the suspected scammer, Verivae should help them stop safely. The app should recommend pausing communication, not sending money or codes, not installing anything, not clicking new links, not warning the scammer about evidence collection if that could escalate pressure, and contacting a trusted person. The product should not encourage dramatic confrontation. It should focus on reducing risk.

If the scam involves emotional manipulation, the app should support a softer "pause and verify" path. The user may not be ready to block the person. The app can suggest waiting before acting, asking a trusted helper, verifying identity outside the conversation, and saving evidence. The goal is to interrupt the scam's momentum.

G12. Report preparation playbook

Reporting should be organized but optional. The app should help the user prepare a report summary: what happened, who contacted them, how they contacted them, what was requested, what the user did, payment amount if any, accounts involved, links, phone numbers, email addresses, screenshots, files, transaction records, and recovery steps already taken. The app should not automatically submit sensitive evidence anywhere without user review.

Report preparation should support redaction. The user may need to share enough detail to be useful while hiding unrelated private information. The app should provide a plain-language preview before export or submission. If official reporting links are included in a future build, they should be verified, maintained, and presented as official external destinations.

G13. Recovery status and closure

The app should allow a recovery case to be open, paused, waiting, completed, or archived. Closing a case should not delete evidence automatically. The close screen should ask whether the user wants to keep evidence, export evidence, remove helper access, turn on future monitoring, or add a reminder. The app should also support reopening a case if new messages arrive or if the user discovers another compromised account.

A closed case can still feed personalization if the user allows it. For example, if the user was targeted by a fake package scam, the app can be more alert to similar package messages later. This should be explained as risk memory and controlled in privacy settings.

Appendix G acceptance standard

Appendix G is satisfied when each major harm event creates a clear recovery path, the path is prioritized by urgency, and the tasks connect to evidence, account safety, payment recovery, device safety, helper review, and reporting where appropriate. The recovery system is incomplete if it gives generic advice without asking what happened, if it fails to distinguish payment types, if it ignores remote access, or if it leaves users with no next step after serious exposure.

Appendix H: Monetization, Trust, and Upgrade Boundaries

This appendix defines how Verivae can support paid features without weakening its safety promise. The app can be profitable, but it should not profit by making frightened users feel trapped. A scam-protection product must earn money in a way that increases trust, not in a way that imitates the pressure tactics it is designed to protect against. The product should therefore separate urgent safety help from optional convenience, advanced monitoring, storage, family tools, deeper analysis, and professional-grade organization.

H1. Free core principle

The free version should be genuinely useful. A user should be able to run basic manual scam checks, receive a clear result, see the main evidence behind that result, save a limited amount of evidence, and access immediate recovery guidance for serious events. The free product does not need to include every advanced feature, but it must not withhold the basic warning that something looks dangerous. If a user is about to send gift cards, share a verification code, enter a bank password, install remote-access software, or send irreversible payment, the app should show the safety warning before any upgrade prompt.

The free core should also include basic education and basic privacy controls. Users should be able to delete their data, disconnect accounts, and understand what the app is doing without paying. Privacy controls are not premium features. They are part of user safety.

H2. Paid feature categories

Paid features should be positioned as extra protection, organization, convenience, or family support rather than the only path to safety. Good paid categories may include expanded evidence storage, deeper weekly checks, broader connected-account monitoring where permitted, advanced link and attachment review, family or trusted-helper dashboards, multi-device protection, premium recovery organization, advanced case export, longer history, priority support, and business or family plans. These features can create value without blocking urgent warnings.

The app should define each paid feature by user benefit, not by vague premium language. Instead of "unlock advanced AI," the app can say "review more saved evidence per month," "monitor connected email for suspicious links," "share selected recovery tasks with family," or "create a detailed case export." Clear feature naming reduces the chance that users misunderstand what they are buying.

H3. No crisis paywall rule

The app should never interrupt an urgent safety flow with a paywall before showing the immediate protective action. If the result is urgent risk, the user should see what not to do and what to do next. A paid upgrade can be offered later, after the safety-critical step is complete. For example, if a user already sent money, the free flow should tell them to contact the payment provider quickly and save evidence. A paid feature might offer expanded case organization or helper coordination, but the first recovery steps must not be hidden.

The app should also avoid countdowns, fake scarcity, threatening copy, or emotional pressure around upgrades. A product that protects people from manipulation should not manipulate them. This is both an ethical rule and a practical trust rule.

H4. Upgrade placement

Upgrade prompts should appear in places where the user is calm enough to make a decision. Good locations include the settings screen, account screen, evidence storage limit screen, weekly check configuration, trusted-helper setup, and feature comparison page. Risk-result screens can mention paid features only if the free safety guidance remains complete and the upgrade is clearly optional. For example, after a result says not to click a link and explains why, the screen could offer deeper monitoring as an optional next step, but it should not blur the urgent recommendation.

Upgrade prompts should explain what changes immediately after purchase. If a user pays for expanded storage, the app should say how much storage or how many saved items are included. If a user pays for family features, it should say how many helpers or family members are included and what they can do. If a user pays for advanced monitoring, it should say which integrations are supported and which platform limits still apply.

H5. Subscription cancellation and downgrade behavior

If Verivae uses subscriptions, cancellation and downgrade behavior should be designed from the start. A user who cancels should not lose access to urgent safety warnings. If they exceed the free evidence storage limit after downgrade, the app should not delete evidence automatically without clear notice. A safer design is read-only retention with prompts to export, delete, or upgrade before adding more. Recovery tasks tied to saved evidence should remain visible even if some advanced organization features become unavailable.

The app should make cancellation and plan management easy to find. A user should not feel trapped. Trustworthy downgrade behavior can actually support revenue because users are more willing to subscribe when they know they will not be punished unfairly for canceling.

H6. Family and helper monetization

Family plans can be a strong paid path because scam protection often involves families helping each other. Paid family features might include multiple protected users, helper alerts, shared recovery workspaces, selected case sharing, and family safety summaries. However, family monetization must not become surveillance. The person being protected should understand what is shared and should have control where appropriate.

The app should support different relationship models. An adult helping a parent, a parent helping a teen, a partner helping a partner, and a caregiver helping a vulnerable person are not identical situations. The product should use roles and permissions rather than one broad family access switch. Paid family features should increase coordination while keeping privacy boundaries explicit.

H7. Evidence storage monetization

Evidence storage is a natural paid feature because large cases can include many screenshots, emails, files, notes, exports, and recovery records. The free version can include limited storage so users can save the most urgent material. Paid tiers can add more storage, longer retention, case export options, and richer organization. The app should avoid locking the user out of existing evidence during a crisis. If a storage limit is reached, the app should offer choices: delete unneeded items, export a case, save a summary instead of the full item, or upgrade.

Storage prompts should be factual. They should not say "Your evidence will disappear unless you pay" unless that is literally true and unavoidable. A better pattern is: "You can still view existing saved evidence. To save more full-size items, free up space, export a case, or upgrade." This keeps the tone protective.

H8. Advanced monitoring monetization

Advanced monitoring can include broader email review, more frequent checks, larger attachment limits, additional device-safety categories, more helper alerts, and stronger suspicious-pattern memory. The app should be careful to explain platform limits. A paid plan should not promise to monitor messages or apps that the operating system does not allow it to access. If iPhone and Android capabilities differ, the plan description should say so clearly.

Monitoring should also be tunable. Paying users should not be forced into noisy alerts. They should be able to decide whether they want only high-risk warnings, weekly summaries, helper alerts, or detailed review notifications. Good monetization increases control rather than increasing interruptions.

H9. Premium recovery organization

Premium recovery features can include expanded recovery playbooks, advanced case export, helper task assignment, reminder schedules, provider-specific call preparation, saved contact notes, document checklists, and richer progress tracking. The free flow should still include immediate safety steps. The paid version can make recovery more organized and less lonely.

The product should not imply that paid recovery guarantees refunds, legal outcomes, account restoration, or malware removal. It can help users act faster, stay organized, and communicate clearly with institutions. That is valuable enough without making promises the app cannot control.

H10. Support monetization

If premium support is offered, it must be framed carefully. Support can help users navigate the app, organize evidence, understand result explanations, and prepare for contact with banks or platforms. It should not pretend to be legal counsel, financial advice, law enforcement, or guaranteed recovery. Support agents should follow strict rules: never ask for passwords, one-time codes, full card numbers, unnecessary identity documents, gift cards, crypto, or remote access unless a future specialized support model is legally and operationally designed for it. Even then, the safer default is no remote access.

The app should teach users how to identify real support. Official support should happen through the app or verified channels. Users should be warned that scammers may impersonate support teams, especially after a reported loss.

H11. Advertising boundary

If the app ever includes advertising, it should avoid ads in urgent risk, recovery, evidence, or privacy screens. Ads for financial products, crypto, debt relief, antivirus tools, legal services, or recovery services could create conflicts of interest and user confusion. A scam-protection app must be very careful about what it promotes. If ads are included at all, they should be clearly separated from safety results and never look like recommended recovery actions.

A cleaner trust model may be subscription-first, family-plan-first, or storage-and-monitoring-first rather than advertising-first. The brief does not need to decide final pricing, but it should define that monetization must not weaken safety, privacy, or clarity.

H12. Upgrade comparison screen

The upgrade comparison screen should compare free and paid features in plain language. It should show what is included, what is limited, what platform restrictions may apply, and what remains free forever. It should avoid security jargon and vague promises. Users should be able to understand the difference between manual checks, connected monitoring, weekly checks, evidence storage, helper sharing, and recovery organization.

The comparison screen should include a trust statement: urgent warnings, basic manual checks, basic recovery guidance, privacy controls, and data deletion are available without payment. If any of these boundaries change later, the design brief should be updated before implementation. The product promise must stay explicit.

H13. Monetization acceptance standard

Appendix H is satisfied when the app has a clear free core, clear paid feature categories, safe upgrade timing, honest platform-limit language, cancellation behavior, storage-limit behavior, helper/family permission boundaries, and support boundaries. The monetization model is incomplete if it hides urgent safety advice behind payment, uses fear-based upgrade prompts, weakens privacy controls for free users, or presents paid features as guarantees of recovery.

Appendix I: App Data Objects and Feature Connections

This appendix defines the main information objects that Verivae should understand. This is still a design brief section, not code. The goal is to make the app's behavior clearer by naming the things the product handles: scam checks, results, evidence items, cases, recovery tasks, permissions, helpers, alerts, and user risk memory. When these objects are defined clearly, screens can connect cleanly and the product is less likely to become a pile of separate tools.

I1. Scam check object

A scam check is any review the user or app starts to decide whether something is risky. A scam check can come from pasted text, screenshot, email, message, link, QR code, file, device safety signal, weekly review, or helper-submitted item. Each check should know its source, user-provided context, extracted signals, analysis status, result, and whether it is connected to a case. It should also record whether the user chose to save the check, discard it, share it, or begin recovery from it.

A check should have a status. Useful statuses include draft, submitted, analyzing, needs more information, complete, failed, saved, and discarded. Draft means the user started entering material but has not submitted it. Needs more information means the app cannot responsibly decide without more context. Failed means the review could not complete because of a technical or permission issue. Complete means the app produced a result. Saved means the user chose to keep it in the Evidence Vault or case history.

I2. Result object

A result is the app's answer to a check. It should include level, short answer, evidence summary, detailed findings, confidence, recommended actions, optional recovery trigger, optional helper sharing option, and education link. The result should also remember what the app could not check. For example, if a file was password-protected or a link destination blocked safe inspection, that limitation should remain attached to the result.

Results should not be treated as permanent truth. A result can be updated if the user adds context, if a link reputation changes, if the same sender appears in a later case, or if the user marks the result as incorrect. Result history should show meaningful changes. If the app changes a result from caution to likely scam because the user added payment details, that change should be understandable.

I3. Evidence item object

An evidence item is saved material that may help the user understand, report, or recover from a scam. Evidence can include screenshots, copied text, emails, message snippets, sender details, links, QR images, files, transaction notes, receipts, account-change notes, call notes, app results, and helper comments. Each evidence item should have a type, source, saved time, case link, sensitivity level, original version, redacted version if created, notes, related result, and sharing history.

Evidence should support sensitivity labels. A low-sensitivity item might be a public website link. A medium-sensitivity item might be a suspicious message with a phone number. A high-sensitivity item might contain bank names, account details, identity documents, private conversations, or one-time codes. Sensitivity should affect how the app previews, shares, exports, and deletes the item. High-sensitivity evidence should not appear in lock-screen notifications or broad helper shares by default.

I4. Case object

A case is a group of related scam checks, evidence items, results, alerts, and recovery tasks. Cases help the user understand events that unfold across time and channels. A case should have a title, risk level, status, summary, related contacts, related links, related payment methods, evidence list, recovery tasks, helper access, report status, and event history. The case title can be user-written or suggested by the app, such as "fake package delivery," "marketplace buyer," or "unknown bank text."

Case status should be simple: open, watching, recovery active, waiting, closed, and archived. Open means the user is still reviewing. Watching means the app should keep an eye out for related items. Recovery active means there are tasks after harm or exposure. Waiting means the user is waiting on a bank, platform, helper, or official response. Closed means no current action is needed. Archived means the case remains saved but is not active.

I5. Recovery task object

A recovery task is a specific action the app recommends after risk or harm. Each task should include title, reason, instructions, urgency, status, related evidence, related account or payment method, optional reminder, optional helper assignment, and completion note. The task should avoid vague labels. A task called "Call bank" should specify why, what to ask, and what information to have ready. A task called "Change password" should specify which account if known and remind the user to use the official app or site.

Task statuses should include not started, in progress, done, waiting, skipped, not applicable, and need help. Skipped and not applicable are not the same. Skipped means the user chose not to do it. Not applicable means the task does not fit the situation. Need help should suggest trusted helper sharing or support options where appropriate.

I6. Permission object

A permission is a user-approved access path that allows Verivae to perform a feature. Permissions can include Gmail or email access, message sharing, camera, files, notifications, device safety signals, contacts for helper invitations, and cloud sync. Each permission should have a feature purpose, current status, granted date when available, last successful use, limitation note, and revoke action. The app should show permission status in both settings and feature screens.

Permission status should be more specific than on or off. Useful statuses include not requested, requested and denied, enabled, enabled with limited scope, expired, paused, unavailable on this device, and error. This helps users understand why a feature is not working. If Gmail review is paused, the app should not simply say Gmail is disconnected. If message scanning is unavailable on a platform, the app should not make the user hunt for a missing setting.

I7. Helper object

A helper is a person the user chooses to involve. The helper object should include display name, contact method, relationship label chosen by the user, role, permissions, invite status, last access if trackable, shared cases, shared tasks, and removal status. Helper roles should include review-only, recovery helper, family safety helper, and emergency helper if such a role is later designed carefully. The app should not assume every helper can see everything.

Helper permissions should be attached to specific content where possible. A helper can be allowed to view one result, comment on one case, mark assigned tasks, receive urgent alerts, or view selected evidence. Broad access should require a clear confirmation screen. Removing a helper should stop future access and remove them from active shares, with honest language about anything they may already have seen.

I8. Alert object

An alert is an app notice that requires attention or awareness. Alerts can come from scam results, connected account review, weekly checks, recovery tasks, helper activity, permission problems, device safety findings, or repeated-case matches. Each alert should have urgency, source, title, summary, destination screen, privacy preview setting, status, and created time. Alert status can be unread, read, dismissed, snoozed, resolved, or expired.

Alerts should always open to context. A payment-risk alert should open to the relevant result or recovery task. A permission alert should open to the permission settings screen. A helper alert should open to the shared case or comment. No alert should drop the user into a generic home screen without explaining why it appeared.

I9. Risk memory object

Risk memory is the user's personalized safety context. It can remember patterns the user has chosen to keep: trusted senders, suspicious senders, past scam categories, known payment methods involved in cases, repeated domains, helper preferences, and education topics already completed. Risk memory should improve protection without becoming hidden surveillance. The user should be able to view, edit, pause, or delete meaningful memory entries.

Risk memory should be careful with trust. Marking a sender as trusted should not silence warnings for high-risk requests such as verification codes, gift cards, crypto, wires, remote access, or password entry. Marking a domain as familiar should not silence warnings if a page asks for unusual information. Risk memory should provide context, not blind permission.

I10. Education object

An education item is a short lesson connected to a scam pattern, result, recovery task, or user question. It should include topic, short explanation, example pattern, warning signs, safe action, related app feature, and completion state. Education should be surfaced at the moment it helps. A result about gift cards can link to gift-card scam education. A recovery task about one-time codes can link to a short explanation of why codes should not be shared.

Education should avoid overwhelming the user. The app can offer deeper learning, but urgent flows should show only what the user needs right now. A beginner-friendly explanation is not a watered-down explanation; it is a carefully ordered explanation.

I11. Cross-object connection rules

A scam check can produce a result. A result can create evidence. Evidence can belong to a case. A case can create recovery tasks. Recovery tasks can produce alerts. Alerts can return the user to a result, task, case, permission, helper item, or weekly check. Helpers can view selected cases, evidence, or tasks. Permissions determine which checks can run. Risk memory can suggest links between new items and old cases. Education explains patterns found by results and tasks.

These connections should be visible enough that the user understands the app's logic. If a weekly check reopens a recovery task, the app should show which case caused it. If a helper comments on a case, the comment should appear inside that case. If a suspicious link from an email is checked separately, it should still connect back to the original email evidence. The app should not make users repeat work because different modules cannot talk to each other.

I12. Data object acceptance standard

Appendix I is satisfied when the product has clear definitions for the main objects that screens and features use: checks, results, evidence, cases, tasks, permissions, helpers, alerts, risk memory, and education. The object model is incomplete if features cannot share context, if recovery tasks are detached from evidence, if helper access is too broad, if alerts have no destination, or if privacy settings cannot explain what data each feature uses.

Appendix J: Platform Reality and Operating System Boundaries

This appendix defines how Verivae should behave across different phones, email providers, message apps, browsers, and app-store rules.
