The app should be ambitious, but it must not promise access that iPhone, Android, Gmail, messaging services, or app stores may not allow. Platform reality is not a weakness in the product. It is part of professional design. A user can trust Verivae more when it clearly explains which protections are automatic, which protections require permission, which protections require manual sharing, and which protections are not available on a specific device.

J1. Platform honesty principle

Verivae should tell users what is active instead of implying invisible protection. If Gmail is connected, the app can say Gmail review is active or paused. If message review only works when the user shares a message into the app, the app should say that. If automatic text-message scanning is unavailable on a device, the app should say that without hiding the limitation. If device safety checks differ between iPhone and Android, the app should say the available checks depend on the phone and permissions. This is a core trust requirement because users may make risky decisions if they believe protection is broader than it really is.

The app should use three simple labels for protection coverage: automatic, assisted, and manual. Automatic means the app can check something after the user has granted permission and enabled the feature. Assisted means the app can help when the user takes a small action, such as sharing a message, forwarding an email, uploading a screenshot, or scanning a QR code. Manual means the user must paste, describe, upload, or select the item directly. These labels should appear in connection settings, onboarding, home-screen status, and feature screens.

J2. iPhone capability boundaries

On iPhone, Verivae should expect stricter privacy boundaries. The app may support manual scam checks, screenshot review, QR review through camera permission, file review for files the user shares, email review through supported account permissions, notifications, evidence storage, recovery tasks, helper sharing, and education. However, it should not assume it can freely read every text message, inspect every app, access full call history, scan every installed file, or monitor all device activity in the background. If a feature depends on system APIs, the interface should clearly explain what the user must enable and what remains outside the app's view.

The iPhone version should be designed so the app remains useful even when automatic message monitoring is unavailable. The user should be able to share suspicious texts, screenshots, links, QR codes, files, and emails into Verivae. The home screen should show message protection as "manual sharing available" or "limited by device settings" rather than pretending it is fully automatic. This keeps the product honest while still useful.

J3. Android capability boundaries

On Android, Verivae may have more integration possibilities in some areas, but it still must respect permission rules and app-store restrictions. Text-message or call-log access is highly sensitive and should only be used if it is absolutely necessary for a core feature and allowed by policy. The app should prefer safer alternatives when possible, such as user-shared messages, notification-based review where permitted, SMS Retriever-style approaches for specific verification flows, screenshots, manual paste, and connected email review. If full SMS access is not approved or not appropriate, the app should not design the entire product around it.

Android device safety checks may support different signals than iPhone, such as installed-app review or permission review depending on available APIs. The app should still avoid overclaiming. It should say it reviews visible safety signals, risky permissions, known remote-access indicators, suspicious recent apps, and supported file risks. It should not say it can guarantee a device is free of malware unless a qualified scanning engine and supported operating-system behavior make that claim true.

J4. Email provider boundaries

Gmail and other email providers may allow connected review through approved permissions, but the app should treat email access as sensitive. Verivae should support several levels of email participation: forwarding one email, sharing one email into the app, selecting specific messages, connecting an account for limited review, and enabling broader monitoring where supported and approved. The user should be able to start with a narrow mode and later choose a broader mode.

The email screen should show provider status clearly. Possible statuses include not connected, connected for selected review, connected for monitoring, paused, permission expired, permission limited, and error. If the app cannot review attachments because a provider blocks access or a file type is unsupported, the result should say so. If an email was reviewed through a forwarded copy rather than a connected account, the app should avoid claiming it verified provider-level details that were not included.

J5. Messaging app boundaries

Many conversations happen outside ordinary SMS: WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, TikTok, Discord, dating apps, marketplace chats, school apps, and work chat tools. Verivae should not assume direct access to these services. The universal fallback should be sharing text, uploading screenshots, using system share sheets where available, or writing a short situation description. The app should make this path feel normal, not like a downgrade. A user should not feel they failed setup just because a private messaging app does not allow background review.

When screenshots are used, the app should support OCR, sequence correction, sender context, and redaction. It should also ask targeted follow-up questions because screenshots may omit earlier context, profile details, payment instructions, or the link destination. The result should say when it is based on partial conversation evidence.

J6. Browser and link boundaries

The app should avoid opening suspicious links in a risky way. When possible, it should inspect links through safe resolution, reputation checks, redirect analysis, and controlled previews. If a link requires login, blocks automated checking, hides behind a shortener, or contains a personal token, the app should explain the limitation and recommend independent verification. The user should not be encouraged to test a suspicious link by visiting it in their ordinary browser.

J7. Store review and policy boundary

Verivae should be designed with app-store review in mind from the beginning. It should request only necessary permissions, explain each permission in context, provide a privacy policy, allow users to revoke access, avoid misleading claims, avoid fear-based monetization, and accurately describe subscription features. App-store review is not just an external gate; it is a useful design discipline. If a feature sounds impressive but depends on a permission that is unlikely to be approved or accepted by users, the product should have a manual or assisted fallback.

J8. Platform reality acceptance standard

Appendix J is satisfied when every major protection mode has a realistic access path, a user-facing explanation, a fallback when automatic review is not available, and a clear status label. The platform model is incomplete if the app promises automatic coverage that the operating system may not allow, hides permission failures, treats iPhone and Android as identical, or designs message protection with no useful fallback.

Appendix K: Security Standards and Mobile Safety Requirements

This appendix translates professional mobile-security expectations into product behavior for Verivae. It does not define implementation code, but it does define the security outcomes the app should require. Because Verivae handles scam evidence, emails, messages, files, links, payment recovery notes, helper sharing, and device safety information, it should be designed like a sensitive security product from the beginning. Security should not be something added after the interface is finished.

K1. Secure storage requirement

Sensitive saved material should be protected when stored. Evidence items, case notes, screenshots, email content, message content, files, recovery tasks, helper-sharing records, and account information should not be stored casually. The app should use platform-supported secure storage for tokens and sensitive keys. Highly sensitive vault material should be encrypted at rest where practical. The brief should require that local storage, cloud storage, backups, logs, and cached previews are all considered during technical design.

The user interface should reflect storage sensitivity. High-sensitivity evidence should have stronger preview controls, private notification behavior, redaction suggestions, and clear delete/export options. The app should not show bank details, private messages, identity documents, or scam evidence on a lock screen or in a casual widget. Security is partly technical and partly visible.

K2. Secure communication requirement

Any communication between the app, Harborwake-controlled services, email providers, reputation services, file-scanning services, helper accounts, or cloud sync should use secure network communication. The app should not send sensitive scam evidence or tokens over insecure channels. If a check requires cloud analysis, the app should explain what is being sent and why. If a third-party service is used for link reputation, file scanning, analytics, support, or crash reporting, the product should treat that service as part of the security and privacy surface.

K3. Authentication and session requirement

The Verivae account should be protected because it may contain evidence, recovery tasks, helper settings, and connected-account information. The app should support strong login, session expiration, secure token storage, device session review, and sign-out from other devices where applicable. Sensitive operations should require re-authentication or an equivalent platform check. Sensitive operations include viewing high-sensitivity evidence, exporting a case, deleting a case, changing helper permissions, connecting email, changing account recovery settings, and viewing payment-related recovery notes.

The app should avoid asking users to type sensitive passwords into Verivae for unrelated accounts. If a user says they entered a bank password into a suspicious site, Verivae should ask which account was involved, not ask for the password. This rule should be visible in support guidance too: Harborwake support should never ask for passwords, one-time codes, gift cards, crypto, or unnecessary identity documents.

K4. Logging and analytics requirement

Logs should not contain private evidence, full message text, email bodies, payment details, one-time codes, passwords, identity documents, or full files unless there is a narrow, justified, user-approved support process. Ordinary analytics should measure feature health, not private content. Useful analytics might include scan completion, feature usage, permission errors, crash events, and alert interaction. Sensitive content should be separated from analytics and protected by stricter rules.

The app should also prevent accidental leakage through crash reports, background screenshots, clipboard handling, notifications, debug logs, and support transcripts. If a user copies a suspicious message into the app, the app should not keep clipboard content longer than needed. If the app moves to the background while showing evidence, it should consider hiding sensitive content from app switcher previews where the platform allows.

K5. File and attachment safety requirement

Files should be inspected without unsafe execution. The app should never run an attachment simply to check it. It should analyze metadata, extension, type mismatch, embedded links, macros or scripts where detectable, archive contents where safe, and known risky patterns. If deeper analysis requires a sandbox or cloud scan, the app should ask permission and explain what leaves the device.

Potentially dangerous files should be handled with special warnings in Evidence Vault. A saved suspicious file should not open casually when tapped. The app should show a safe summary first and ask before export or sharing. If a file is too large, encrypted, password-protected, corrupted, or unsupported, the result should say the app could not fully inspect it and recommend caution.

K6. Platform interaction requirement

The app should interact safely with the phone and other apps. It should not abuse accessibility permissions, VPN permissions, notification permissions, SMS permissions, or device administration features to collect more data than needed. If any powerful platform permission is ever considered, the design should require a separate explanation, a strong user benefit, a narrow use, a fallback where possible, and policy review before implementation.

The app should also guard against unsafe deep links and external intents. If another app sends content into Verivae, the app should treat it as untrusted until checked. If Verivae opens another app or website, it should tell the user why and avoid sending sensitive information unintentionally.

K7. Tampering and impersonation requirement

Scammers may impersonate Verivae or Harborwake. The app should include clear in-app support identity rules, official communication guidance, and warnings against fake support. The app should avoid easy-to-forge "safe certificate" screens that scammers could screenshot and reuse. Shareable summaries should include context and limitations so they cannot be used as universal proof that an offer is safe.

Future technical design should also consider app tampering, malicious clones, fake websites, fake support emails, and copied branding. This belongs in the security model because the product itself may become a target once users trust it.

K8. Security standards acceptance rule

Appendix K is satisfied when the product requires secure storage, secure communication, strong account protection, careful logs, safe file handling, safe platform interaction, and anti-impersonation behavior. The security model is incomplete if it focuses only on detecting scams while ignoring the sensitive evidence and permissions the app itself controls.

Appendix L: Risk Scoring Logic and Result Decision Rules

This appendix defines how Verivae should decide what result level to show. The exact scoring formula can be decided later, but the product behavior must be clear now. A scam-protection app should not feel random. Users, designers, developers, and testers should understand why one item is marked likely safe, another is marked caution, and another becomes urgent risk. The app should combine technical signals, behavioral signals, user context, historical patterns, and platform limits.

L1. Result levels

Verivae should use these result levels consistently: likely safe, caution, suspicious, likely scam, urgent risk, and not enough information. Likely safe means no obvious scam signals were found in the available material, but it should not mean guaranteed safe. Caution means something deserves verification before the user acts. Suspicious means multiple signals suggest the user should not proceed without independent confirmation. Likely scam means the pattern strongly matches known scam behavior. Urgent risk means the user may be about to suffer immediate harm or may already have exposed money, credentials, device access, or identity information. Not enough information means the app cannot responsibly decide yet.

Each result level should control the interface. Likely safe can show calm confirmation plus basic safety reminders. Caution can show verification steps. Suspicious can recommend pausing and asking for more context. Likely scam can recommend not interacting, saving evidence, blocking or reporting, and verifying through official channels. Urgent risk should prioritize immediate recovery or prevention actions. Not enough information should ask for the missing input and give cautious interim guidance.

L2. High-risk triggers

Certain signals should strongly raise risk regardless of other context. These include requests for one-time codes, passwords, bank login, remote access, gift cards, crypto, wire transfers, payment-app transfers to unknown people, account recovery actions, identity documents, secrecy, threats, urgent deadlines, "safe account" money movement, refund fees, job equipment checks, marketplace overpayment, romance emergencies, investment guarantees, and instructions to ignore warnings. These triggers do not always prove a scam alone, but they are serious enough to require caution or stronger.

The app should treat irreversible actions with special weight. Gift cards, crypto, wires, and some peer-to-peer payments may be difficult or impossible to reverse. If these appear with urgency, secrecy, impersonation, or emotional pressure, the result should often be likely scam or urgent risk. The app should explain that the payment method is part of the risk, not just the message wording.

L3. Technical signals

Technical signals include sender mismatch, suspicious domain, lookalike spelling, URL shortener, unusual redirect chain, newly created or low-reputation domain where known, executable attachment, mismatched file extension, embedded suspicious link, unsafe QR destination, suspicious app install, risky permission, remote-access app indicator, expired email permission, and blocked analysis. Technical signals should support the result, but the app should translate them into ordinary language. The user should not have to know what a redirect or domain mismatch means.

Technical limits should also affect confidence. If a link cannot be safely inspected, a file is encrypted, OCR failed, or the user submitted only a cropped screenshot, the app should avoid overconfidence. Missing technical evidence is not proof of safety.

L4. Behavioral signals

Behavioral signals are the scam story patterns. These include urgency, secrecy, isolation, threats, love-bombing, authority claims, fake refund promises, guaranteed profits, pressure to move off platform, refusal to verify identity, request to keep a call open, request to install software, request to pay before receiving money, and instructions that normal safety steps are unnecessary. Behavioral signals matter because many scams are technically simple but psychologically powerful.

The app should explain behavioral risk without insulting the user. It can say, "This request pressures you to act before verifying," or "This person asks you to keep the payment private," or "The message combines an urgent threat with a link to a login page." Those explanations are useful and respectful.

L5. User context signals

User context can raise or lower confidence, but it should not erase high-risk warnings. If the user says they know the sender personally, the app can adjust impersonation risk, but it should still warn about verification codes, gift cards, crypto, wires, and remote access. If the user says they already paid, the result should shift toward recovery. If the user says they only received the message and took no action, the result can focus on prevention. If the user is unsure what happened, the app should ask clarifying questions and keep guidance cautious.

The app should remember user-approved risk memory carefully. A trusted sender or familiar domain can reduce some warnings, but it should not silence serious danger categories. Risk memory should be a context helper, not an override switch.

L6. Confidence behavior

Every result should have confidence language. High confidence means the app found strong, relevant signals and enough context. Medium confidence means the app found meaningful signals but still has missing context. Low confidence means the app lacks enough material or could not complete key checks. Confidence should affect wording. A low-confidence suspicious result might say, "This needs caution because the visible link and payment request are risky, but more context would improve the review." A high-confidence likely scam result can be firmer.

The app should also separate confidence from severity. A low-confidence urgent-risk result can still require immediate caution if the possible harm is severe. For example, if the user may have shared a bank password but the app lacks full details, the safest result is urgent recovery guidance with honest uncertainty.

L7. Result override and learning behavior

Users should be able to correct results, add context, and mark false positives or missed scams. The app should treat this feedback as useful but not blindly obey it. If a user marks a gift-card request as safe because the sender is familiar, the app should still warn that familiar accounts can be compromised. If many users report a pattern as a missed scam, Harborwake may review detection logic, but raw private evidence should only be used according to the user's privacy choices.

The app should keep result history when a result changes. If an item moves from caution to likely scam after the user adds a screenshot or payment detail, the case should show that the new context changed the result. This helps the user understand the app and helps future testing.

L8. Risk scoring acceptance standard

Appendix L is satisfied when each result level has a clear meaning, high-risk triggers are defined, technical and behavioral signals are combined, user context is considered carefully, confidence is shown responsibly, and result changes are explainable. The scoring model is incomplete if it gives unexplained scores, treats missing information as safety, silences serious warnings because a sender is familiar, or fails to route urgent exposure into recovery.

Appendix M: Official Reporting and Recovery Resource Behavior

This appendix defines how Verivae should guide users toward official reporting and recovery resources without pretending to be a bank, law firm, law-enforcement agency, credit bureau, app store, phone carrier, or government office. The product should help users organize what happened, understand which type of organization may be relevant, and prepare evidence before they leave the app. It should not promise a refund, account restoration, arrest, malware removal, identity repair, or legal outcome. The app's responsibility is to make official recovery paths easier to understand and harder to confuse with scammer-controlled paths.

M1. Official-resource principle

When Verivae recommends outside help, it should direct the user toward official channels and teach them not to trust contact details provided by the suspicious message. If a message claims to be from a bank, the app should recommend using the bank's official app, the number on the back of the card, or the bank website typed manually. If a message claims to be from a delivery company, marketplace, school, employer, tax office, court, or government agency, the app should recommend independently finding the official contact route. The product should avoid one-tap links during urgent scam situations unless the destination is maintained, verified, and clearly labeled as external.

The app should separate "report this scam" from "recover from harm." Reporting helps others and may support investigations. Recovery helps the user reduce immediate damage. The same evidence can support both, but the user may need different next steps. Someone who only received a suspicious text may report and block. Someone who sent money may need to call a bank first. Someone who shared identity documents may need identity-protection steps. Someone who installed remote-access software may need device safety before changing passwords.

M2. Report preparation screen

The Report Preparation screen should help the user assemble a clear summary before contacting an outside organization. It should collect what happened, how contact started, who the scammer claimed to be, what was requested, what the user did, payment method if any, accounts involved, links, phone numbers, email addresses, usernames, QR codes, attachments, receipts, transaction identifiers, screenshots, and relevant dates already captured by the app. The screen should distinguish confirmed facts from user notes and app analysis.

The user should be able to preview the report before exporting or submitting it. The preview should show selected evidence, redacted evidence, result summaries, and recovery actions already completed. The user should be able to remove private details that are not needed. This keeps reporting useful without carelessly exposing unrelated private information.

M3. Payment-provider routing

If money was involved, Verivae should help the user identify the payment route. Categories should include credit card, debit card, bank transfer, wire, payment app, gift card, crypto, check, cash, and unknown. Each route should produce different guidance. Card payments may involve a card issuer. Bank transfers may involve a bank fraud department. Payment apps may involve in-app support and transaction reporting. Gift cards may involve the issuer and purchase receipt. Crypto may involve an exchange, wallet, transaction record, and wallet address. Checks may involve bank contact and warning about fake-check clearing delays.

The app should phrase this as preparation, not guarantee. It should say that options depend on timing, provider rules, payment type, and local law. It should emphasize speed where relevant because some institutions can act only before a transaction fully settles.

M4. Identity-theft routing

If identity information was shared, Verivae should create a different recovery path. The app should ask what was exposed: photo ID, government number, tax document, bank statement, utility bill, account login, address, phone number, selfie, or full identity packet. The result should create tasks for saving evidence, monitoring accounts, changing related account security, considering credit protection steps where appropriate, and using official identity-theft resources. The app should be careful not to offer jurisdiction-specific certainty without verified local guidance.

For U.S. users, the app should be designed to recognize FTC consumer reporting and identity-theft resources as important official destinations. In other countries, the app should later support country-specific official resources. The interface should avoid assuming every user is in the same legal system.

M5. Recovery-scam warning

After a user reports losing money, the app should warn about refund and recovery scams. A person who has already lost money may be contacted by someone promising to recover it for a fee, asking for more personal information, or claiming to represent an official agency. Verivae should flag upfront-fee recovery promises as high risk. This warning should appear in recovery playbooks for gift cards, crypto, wires, payment apps, fake investments, marketplace losses, romance scams, and technical-support scams.

M6. Official reporting acceptance standard

Appendix M is satisfied when Verivae can help users prepare evidence, choose the right external category, avoid scammer-provided contact details, distinguish reporting from recovery, and understand that outside outcomes are not guaranteed. The reporting model is incomplete if it sends users to random links, treats every scam the same, promises refunds, or shares sensitive evidence externally without user review.

Appendix N: App Store Review Readiness and Claim Boundaries

This appendix defines how Verivae should be shaped so the app can pass major app-store expectations and maintain user trust. This is not a launch checklist. It is a product-behavior section that affects permissions, privacy, subscriptions, claims, screenshots, descriptions, and in-app explanations. App stores care about whether an app accurately describes what it does, asks for data responsibly, avoids hidden behavior, and treats subscriptions and sensitive permissions clearly. Users care about the same things, even if they do not call it app review.

N1. Accurate description rule

The app's public description, screenshots, onboarding, and in-app settings should match the actual product. If Verivae only supports manual text-message review through sharing or screenshots, the store listing should not claim automatic full-message monitoring. If device safety checks review visible risk signals but do not perform full antivirus removal, the app should not claim complete virus removal. If Gmail review is optional, the product should not imply that email scanning is mandatory. Accurate description prevents rejection risk and prevents user distrust.

N2. Privacy policy readiness

The app should have a privacy policy that explains what data is collected, how it is collected, why it is used, which third parties receive it, how long it is kept, how users delete it, and how users revoke permission. The in-app Privacy and Permission settings should mirror those ideas in simpler language. A user should not have to read a legal page to understand whether a screenshot, email, file, link, or case note is saved.

If the app uses AI services, link reputation services, file scanning, analytics, crash reporting, cloud storage, payment processing, or support tools, those services should be represented honestly in the privacy model. Sensitive content should not be routed through third parties without a clear purpose and user understanding.

N3. Permission explanation rule

Every permission request should be tied to a visible feature. Camera access supports QR review. Notification access supports urgent alerts and reminders. Email access supports selected or enabled email review. File access supports chosen file review. Contacts access, if ever used, should support helper invitations or trusted contact selection and should not be required for basic scam checking. Broad file access, SMS access, call-log access, accessibility access, VPN behavior, and notification-listener access are especially sensitive and should require separate product justification before implementation.

The app should also provide fallback paths. If the user denies camera access, they can upload a QR screenshot. If they do not connect Gmail, they can forward or paste email content. If automatic message access is unavailable, they can share screenshots or text. A denied permission should reduce a specific feature, not break the whole app.

N4. Subscription and purchase clarity

If Verivae offers paid plans, it should state what the user gets for the price before purchase. Paid features should have clear names and limits, such as evidence storage, advanced monitoring, family/helper access, premium recovery organization, deeper file review, or larger history. The app should not trick users into subscriptions, hide cancellation behavior, or use fear-based prompts during urgent scam situations. The free core should continue to provide basic warnings, basic manual checks, basic recovery guidance, data deletion, and privacy controls.

N5. Security and safety claim boundaries

The app should avoid claims it cannot prove. It should not say "guaranteed scam protection," "complete malware removal," "full phone protection," "refund guaranteed," "official recovery service," or "law enforcement reporting completed" unless those statements are technically, legally, and operationally true. Better language is specific: "checks selected messages for scam signs," "reviews links before you open them," "helps organize recovery tasks," "helps prepare evidence," or "reviews supported device safety signals." Specific claims are more professional and safer.

N6. App-store readiness acceptance standard

Appendix N is satisfied when the app's claims, permissions, subscriptions, privacy controls, sensitive-data use, and safety language match what the product actually does. The review-readiness model is incomplete if impressive marketing language outruns the real feature, if permissions are requested before the user understands them, if payment blocks urgent safety help, or if the app hides how sensitive content is processed.

Appendix O: Detection Evaluation, Human Review, and Continuous Safety Quality

This appendix defines how Verivae should judge whether its scam detection is working well. Detection quality is not just whether the app catches obvious scam examples. It must handle confusing cases, partial screenshots, new scam scripts, platform limits, real user mistakes, and high-stakes false negatives. The product should be built around responsible uncertainty: it should say what it knows, what it does not know, and what the safest next step is.

O1. Detection-quality goals

Verivae should optimize for useful safety decisions, not just impressive scores. A useful decision tells the user whether to proceed, pause, verify, save evidence, ask a helper, or begin recovery. The app should measure whether results include clear evidence, correct severity, appropriate confidence, and relevant next steps. A result that says "82 percent risky" but gives no reason is worse than a result that says "Do not share this code; one-time codes can let someone into your account."

O2. False negative handling

A false negative means the app fails to flag a real scam. This is especially dangerous when money, identity, passwords, one-time codes, remote access, or irreversible payments are involved. The app should use safety floor rules for these categories. Even when confidence is limited, it should warn users not to share verification codes, passwords, gift-card numbers, crypto transfers, wire transfers, or remote access with unverified people. Missing information should not become a quiet safe result.

When a user reports that the app missed a scam, Verivae should support feedback without forcing the user to expose more than necessary. The user should be able to share a redacted example, attach evidence from the vault, or describe what happened. The app should connect serious missed-scam feedback to recovery guidance immediately.

O3. False positive handling

A false positive means the app warns about something legitimate. False positives can frustrate users, but respectful caution is acceptable when harm could be severe. The app should allow users to add context, correct a result, mark a source as trusted with limits, and request a deeper review. It should not allow one correction to silence high-risk request categories forever. A trusted sender can still be compromised, and a legitimate-looking message can still include a dangerous action.

The product should track which warnings users dismiss, but it should interpret that signal carefully. Dismissal does not always mean the app was wrong. A user may dismiss a warning because they are under pressure from a scammer. The app should use feedback to improve clarity and calibration, not to blindly weaken safety.

O4. Test scenario library

The app should maintain a scenario library for evaluation. This library should include fake bank texts, package delivery scams, marketplace overpayment, job-equipment checks, romance money requests, gift-card requests, crypto investment promises, refund and recovery scams, fake support remote access, one-time code theft, suspicious QR codes, malicious attachments, account takeover attempts, and ambiguous legitimate messages. Each scenario should define the expected result level, evidence explanation, confidence behavior, and next-step destination.

The scenario library should also include partial and messy inputs: cropped screenshots, blurry QR images, shortened links, incomplete conversations, screenshots without sender details, forwarded emails missing headers, unsupported attachments, and user descriptions of phone calls. Real people will not always give perfect input. The app must still fail gracefully.

O5. Human review behavior

Some situations should support human or trusted-helper review. The app should offer helper review when the user is unsure, emotionally pressured, dealing with a relationship-based scam, facing a large payment request, or handling identity exposure. If Harborwake later offers professional support, the support scope should be narrow and clearly explained. Human review should not require unnecessary access to the user's entire email, message history, or vault.

Human review should also respect urgency. If the user may be about to pay or share a code, the app should show the immediate warning before waiting for a human. Human review is an additional layer, not a replacement for fast safety guidance.

O6. Evaluation privacy

Testing and improvement should protect user privacy. The app should not automatically use private user evidence to improve detection unless the user has clearly agreed. Redacted examples should be preferred. Sensitive categories such as identity documents, bank details, private messages, passwords, and one-time codes should be excluded from ordinary model-improvement workflows unless a future policy and consent model explicitly allows a narrow use. Product improvement cannot quietly consume the very evidence the app promises to protect.

O7. Continuous safety acceptance standard

Appendix O is satisfied when Verivae defines how detection quality is evaluated, how false positives and false negatives are handled, how messy real-world inputs are tested, how human review fits safely, and how improvement protects private evidence. The detection model is incomplete if it focuses only on a score, ignores confidence, treats missing information as safety, or learns from sensitive user content without clear permission.

# Appendix P: Official Reporting Assistant and Source Verification

Verivae should include an Official Reporting Assistant that helps users understand where a scam, identity theft event, account takeover, suspicious payment, impersonation attempt, or device-abuse event may need to be reported. This feature should not make the app feel like a government agency, police service, bank, lawyer, or recovery company. Its purpose is narrower and safer: organize the user's information, explain which official channels may be relevant, help the user prepare a clean report, and remind the user to submit reports only through official websites, official phone numbers, verified account portals, or other trusted paths. The app should keep the user in control of every report. It should never submit a report silently, never sign the user's name without approval, never claim that a report guarantees recovery, and never imply that Harborwake or Verivae can investigate crimes directly.

The Reporting Assistant should appear as a calm workspace rather than an emergency form. A user may reach it from a scam result screen, an Evidence Vault case, a recovery task, a payment-risk result, an account takeover warning, a device-safety result, or the Already Acted flow. The entry point should change the starting context. If the user arrives from a suspicious text message, the assistant should begin with communication evidence: sender, phone number, message content, link, requested payment method, and screenshots. If the user arrives from a payment case, it should begin with transaction evidence: amount, date, merchant or recipient, payment rail, confirmation number, bank or app name, and whether the payment was authorized or unauthorized. If the user arrives from identity theft, it should begin with the personal-information exposure: what was shared, when, to whom, and what accounts may now be at risk.

The first screen should separate reporting destinations into plain-language categories: report fraud or scam attempt, report identity theft, report internet crime, report payment problem, report account takeover, report platform impersonation, and report unsafe device access. Each category should explain what it is for in simple language. A beginner should not need to know the difference between fraud, identity theft, cybercrime, and account abuse before they can start. The app can ask a few routing questions: Did money leave an account? Did someone use your identity? Did someone access your email, phone, bank, or social account? Was there a cryptocurrency transfer, wire transfer, gift card, payment app transfer, or bank transfer? Did someone pretend to be a government agency, bank, shipping company, employer, family member, romantic partner, tech-support worker, or investment adviser?

The assistant should recommend possible reporting destinations without pretending there is one universal answer. For many users, the safest starting points will be official consumer-fraud reporting, identity-theft recovery resources, the user's bank or payment provider, the relevant platform where the scam occurred, and internet-crime reporting when the event involved online fraud. The app should present these as options with explanations: why this destination may matter, what information the user may need, what the destination can and cannot do, and whether the user should act quickly. The app should include a warning that search results can contain ads, lookalike pages, or impersonation pages. Whenever the app points to a reporting destination, it should encourage users to use verified official links inside the app, bookmarked official sites, or contact information they independently confirm.

A professional Reporting Assistant should include a Report Preparation Checklist. This checklist should adapt to the case. For a payment-app scam, it should ask for the payment app name, account handle, recipient information, linked card or bank, transfer amount, transfer time, dispute status, screenshots, and communication that pressured the payment. For a gift-card scam, it should ask for card brand, card number if safe to record, receipt, store location, activation time, photo of the card, and instructions from the scammer. For a cryptocurrency scam, it should ask for exchange name, wallet address, transaction hash, coin type, amount, date, blockchain network, and any website or chat that led to the transfer. For identity theft, it should ask what personal information was shared or stolen, which accounts are affected, whether new accounts were opened, whether mail or email changed, and whether the user has placed fraud alerts or account locks.

The assistant should include a Plain-Language Report Builder that helps the user write a factual timeline. Many people freeze when asked to describe what happened. The app should offer prompts like: How did the contact begin? What did the other person claim? What did they ask you to do? What did they say would happen if you did not act? What money or information was requested? What steps did you take? What evidence do you have? What have you already reported? What are you still worried about? The generated report summary should be editable. It should avoid emotional exaggeration, speculation, accusations beyond the evidence, and legal conclusions. It should use clear facts: dates, times, names, handles, links, amounts, payment methods, account names, and screenshots.

The reporting workspace should connect tightly to the Evidence Vault. When a case is opened in Reporting Assistant, the app should show available evidence grouped by type: messages, email headers or sender details, links, screenshots, files, payment records, account alerts, device-safety findings, call notes, trusted-helper notes, and recovery tasks already completed. The user should be able to select which items belong in a report packet. The app should warn before including sensitive personal information, especially Social Security numbers, full account numbers, passwords, recovery codes, private keys, seed phrases, full card numbers, or identification images. If a reporting destination specifically warns users not to include certain information in narrative fields, the app should reflect that with a careful warning and a safer field mapping.

The assistant should include a Report Packet Preview. This is not a submitted report. It is a clean view showing what the user plans to share. The preview should label every included item, show whether the item contains sensitive information, and provide a short explanation of why it may help. A screenshot of a payment request may show pressure language, the requested method, and the recipient handle. A transaction ID may help a bank or platform locate the event. A suspicious URL may help a platform or agency identify an impersonation page. A call note may help the user remember what was said even if the call was not recorded. The preview should include a final confirmation that the app is helping prepare information, and that the user is responsible for choosing where to submit it and checking that the destination is official.

The app should support Save, Export, and Continue Later behavior. Reporting is stressful, and users may not have everything ready. If the user pauses, the case should remain in the Recovery Workspace and Evidence Vault with a visible status such as Not started, preparing, ready to submit, submitted by user, waiting for response, follow-up needed, or closed. The status should never imply that a government agency, bank, or platform has accepted a report unless the user records that outcome or the integration can verify it. The app should let the user add confirmation numbers, dates, contact names, notes, and next-step reminders after submitting a report.

The assistant should include source-verification behavior. If the user types or pastes a reporting website, the app should check whether the domain appears to be official, whether it uses HTTPS, whether it has misleading spelling, whether it uses pressure language, whether it asks for upfront payment, and whether it asks for unnecessary sensitive data. The app should teach users that official reporting resources do not normally require payment to file a consumer fraud report. It should warn about recovery scams that impersonate official agencies, nonprofits, law firms, cybersecurity firms, or refund processors. If a page claims to guarantee recovery, asks for crypto, gift cards, wire transfer, payment-app payment, or upfront fees to recover money, Verivae should mark that as a high-risk recovery-scam sign.

The assistant should be careful with geography and legal variation. Reporting destinations vary by country, state, bank, payment method, and platform. If the app does not know the user's location, it should avoid pretending that a single reporting route is complete. It can ask the user to choose a country or region and explain why. It should still provide general app behavior even when exact local resources are not configured. For the United States, the assistant can support common official reporting paths, but it should phrase them as reporting options, not guarantees. For other regions, the app should either provide region-specific official resources once verified or state that the user should use official local consumer protection, police, banking, and platform channels.

The Reporting Assistant is successful when a stressed user can understand where to report, gather useful evidence, avoid fake reporting pages, prepare a factual summary, export or copy the right information, and track what they did. It fails if it guarantees recovery, sends reports without consent, confuses reporting with investigation, pushes the user into paid help during an emergency, hides official resources behind payment, stores sensitive evidence without clear permission, or makes the user feel blamed for needing help.

# Appendix Q: Recovery Scam Protection Mode

Verivae should include a Recovery Scam Protection Mode for users who have already lost money, shared private information, opened a risky file, installed remote-access software, or contacted a fake support agent. This mode matters because people who have already been harmed are often targeted again. A user who is embarrassed, scared, angry, or desperate to get money back is more likely to believe someone who says they can fix everything quickly. The app should treat this as a high-risk emotional state and give the user stronger protection against anyone offering refunds, asset recovery, crypto tracing, fake legal help, fake government paperwork, fake bank recovery, or fake cybersecurity cleanup in exchange for upfront payment or sensitive information.

The entry point should appear whenever a case changes to Already Acted, Money Sent, Information Shared, Account Access Given, Remote Access Given, or Device Risk Found. The app should not wait for the user to know the term recovery scam. It should say something plain, such as: After a scam, another scammer may contact you pretending they can recover your money. Before paying anyone or sharing more information, check the offer here. The screen should be calm and direct. It should not shame the user. It should make the next safe action obvious: check the new contact, save the message, avoid paying upfront, and contact official institutions using verified channels.

The mode should detect common recovery-scam patterns across messages, email, phone notes, web pages, ads, social messages, and comments. Warning signs include promises to recover all money, demands for upfront fees, claims of special government access, claims of being from a secret investigation unit, requests for crypto wallet access, requests for seed phrases, instructions to install remote-control software, claims that the user must pay taxes or clearance fees before a refund, claims that the app or service can put the user's name on a priority refund list, and requests to keep the process secret. The app should also watch for fake law firms, fake cybersecurity vendors, fake asset-recovery companies, fake blockchain tracing companies, fake exchange support, fake bank fraud teams, and fake agency employees.

The user flow should begin with a simple question: Is someone offering to recover money, reverse a payment, unlock funds, trace cryptocurrency, clean your device, restore an account, or file official paperwork for you? If yes, the app should ask what they want from the user: money, banking details, identity documents, account passwords, authentication codes, remote access, crypto wallet details, or silence from family. Each answer should produce clear risk reasoning. If the offer requires money first, the app should mark it as high risk. If the offer requires seed phrases, private keys, passwords, or authentication codes, the app should mark it as critical risk. If the offer uses official-looking badges, logos, seals, or names, the app should say that logos are not proof and should guide the user to verify through official channels.

Recovery Scam Protection Mode should include a Safe Verification Checklist. The user should be guided to ask: Did I contact this organization first using a verified number or official website? Is this person asking for payment before helping me? Are they asking for sensitive information that an official resource would not need in this channel? Are they pressuring me to act quickly? Are they asking me to use gift cards, crypto, wire transfer, payment apps, cash, or unusual payment methods? Are they telling me not to talk to my bank, family, or law enforcement? Are they using fear, embarrassment, secrecy, or urgency? Have I independently confirmed the person's identity? If the user answers yes to multiple risk questions, the app should recommend stopping contact and saving evidence.

The mode should have a Recovery Offer Result Screen. Instead of a generic scam score, it should use labels like Likely recovery scam, high-risk recovery offer, unverified recovery offer, proceed only after independent verification, or low evidence. The screen should show the top reasons in plain language. It should separate what is known from what is unknown. For example: Known: the person contacted you unexpectedly; they say they can recover crypto; they want a tracing fee; they ask for wallet details. Unknown: whether the company is legally registered; whether you contacted them first; whether their website is official. Safer next step: do not pay upfront, do not share wallet secrets, contact your exchange or bank through official channels, and save the message.

This feature should connect to the Evidence Vault. Recovery scams often happen after the original scam, so the app should let the user link a recovery offer to the original case. The case timeline should show Original Scam, Money Sent, Recovery Offer Received, Recovery Offer Checked, Evidence Saved, and Safer Action Chosen. This makes it easier for a bank, platform, helper, or official report to understand the full chain. The app should not mix the recovery scam with the original scam so completely that the user loses track of what happened when. It should show them as connected but distinct events.

The app should protect against exploitative monetization in this mode. If Verivae later has paid features, Recovery Scam Protection Mode should keep core safety checks free. The app should not create fear and then immediately sell the solution. Paid features could include advanced case organization, family plan dashboards, longer retention, business invoice review, or deeper report formatting, but the basic warning that an upfront-fee recovery offer is dangerous should remain free. A professional safety product earns trust by refusing to charge for urgent warnings that prevent additional harm.

The mode should include a Trusted Helper handoff. Users who have already been scammed may need another person to help them slow down. The app should allow the user to send a privacy-limited recovery-offer summary to a trusted helper. The helper should see the offer text, risk signs, requested payment or information, and recommended safe next steps. The helper should not automatically see unrelated evidence, full financial details, identity documents, or private messages unless the user chooses to share them. The helper view should include a script: I am worried this may be another scam. Please do not pay or share more information until we verify it through official channels.

The feature should include a fake-helper defense. A scammer may try to become the user's trusted helper or pressure the user to add them as a helper. The app should warn users not to add someone they only met through the suspicious situation. If a newly added helper immediately asks for evidence, money, codes, remote access, or identity documents, the app should treat that behavior as suspicious. Trusted helper access should be revocable at any time, and the app should have an emergency revoke button that immediately removes helper access from active cases.

The mode should support aftercare without pretending to be therapy, legal advice, or financial advice. It can remind the user that scams are designed to manipulate smart people, that quick action can still help, and that the safest next step is to slow down and contact real institutions. It can offer a private checklist for bank contact, account password changes, two-factor authentication, device checks, identity-theft reporting, credit monitoring options, and evidence organization. It should avoid telling the user that everything will be fine, because that may be untrue. It should instead say what can be done next and which actions are time-sensitive.

Recovery Scam Protection Mode is successful when it helps a harmed user avoid a second loss. It should be judged by whether it catches upfront-fee recovery claims, fake official contact, fake crypto tracing, fake refund processors, fake tech-support cleanup, and pressure to keep secrets. It fails if it treats every recovery service as automatically legitimate, encourages users to pay unknown helpers, hides warnings behind paid features, or makes absolute promises about recovering funds. The product should remain firm: do not pay more money to someone who unexpectedly claims they can recover money already lost.

# Appendix R: Payment-Specific Recovery and Prevention Playbooks

Verivae should include payment-specific playbooks because the safest next step after a scam depends heavily on how money moved. A user who paid by credit card needs a different flow than someone who bought gift cards, sent cryptocurrency, wired money, used a payment app, mailed a check, authorized a bank debit, scanned a QR code, or gave banking credentials. A generic recovery screen is not enough. The app should identify the payment type early, explain why it matters, and provide a tailored checklist for prevention, immediate response, evidence capture, and follow-up. The app should avoid refund promises and instead help the user act quickly through the correct institution or platform.

The payment flow should begin with the question: Did money move, or are you being asked to send money? If money has not moved yet, the app should enter Before You Pay mode. If money has moved, the app should enter Already Acted mode. If the user is not sure, the app should ask whether they entered card details, shared bank login, clicked a payment confirmation link, approved a push notification, read out a code, sent a screenshot, bought a gift card, scanned a payment code, mailed a check, sent cryptocurrency, or gave remote access. The app should assume uncertainty is normal. It should not require the user to know banking terms before it can help.

For credit-card and debit-card payments, the app should focus on contacting the card issuer quickly, identifying whether the transaction is pending or posted, gathering merchant information, saving the receipt or confirmation, and asking about dispute or fraud options. The app should explain that the card issuer is the authority on whether a charge can be reversed. It should ask whether the user authorized the transaction, whether the merchant was fake, whether the card number was stolen, whether recurring charges may continue, and whether the card needs to be replaced. It should include follow-up tasks: monitor statements, change account passwords, check for saved card use on suspicious sites, and save the case number from the bank.

For bank transfers and account debits, the app should ask whether the user initiated the transfer, whether account login was compromised, whether there was an unauthorized debit, whether the recipient account is known, whether the transfer is pending, and whether the bank has been contacted. It should urge fast contact with the bank through verified channels. It should include evidence fields for transfer amount, date, recipient name, account details shown to the user, confirmation number, device used, and any messages that pressured the transfer. The app should distinguish unauthorized account access from authorized-but-manipulated payments because the bank's process may differ. It should not make legal conclusions about liability.

For wire transfers, the app should emphasize urgency. Wire transfers may be difficult to reverse, but a fast report may still matter. The app should gather sending bank, receiving bank if known, wire reference number, amount, date and time, recipient name, routing or account details if visible, branch or online channel, and any fraud department contact. The app should recommend contacting the sending institution immediately using a verified phone number or in-person branch. If the user was told to lie to the bank, say the payment was for a home project, avoid mentioning investment, or keep the transfer secret, the app should mark those as scam-pressure indicators.

For payment apps, the app should separate peer-to-peer payments, merchant payments, linked-card payments, linked-bank payments, and account takeover. It should ask which app was used, what handle or phone number received the money, whether the payment was labeled as friends and family, goods and services, instant transfer, business payment, or unknown, and whether the app's support flow has been used. The app should remind users to report through the payment app's official support path and, if a linked card or bank funded the payment, also contact that card issuer or bank. The app should capture screenshots of the transaction, profile, messages, QR code, and any request to move the conversation off-platform.

For gift-card scams, the app should treat the payment method as a strong warning sign. It should ask for card brand, store where purchased, receipt, card packaging, activation time, card numbers or photos if the user can store them safely, amount, and whether the scammer asked for pictures of the codes. The app should guide the user to contact the gift-card issuer quickly and preserve the physical card and receipt. The app should warn that gift cards are for gifts, not official payments, fines, taxes, bail, grants, refunds, tech support, romance emergencies, job fees, or account protection. If someone demands gift cards as the only payment method, the app should show a high-risk result before the user buys or sends the card.

For cryptocurrency payments, Verivae should be especially careful. The app should explain that crypto payments are often difficult or impossible to reverse unless the recipient cooperates or a platform can intervene before funds move further. It should not promise blockchain recovery. The app should capture exchange or wallet used, coin or token type, network, amount, date, transaction hash, receiving wallet address, destination tag or memo if any, screenshots, website involved, and messages. It should warn users never to share seed phrases, private keys, recovery words, wallet passwords, or one-time codes. It should treat any recovery service asking for wallet secrets or upfront payment as critical risk.

For checks, the app should support fake-check scams and check-payment recovery. It should ask whether the user deposited a check, mailed a check, used mobile deposit, was told to send back extra money, or was told the check cleared. The app should explain that a bank making funds available does not always mean the check is valid. The app should capture check image, sender name, bank shown on check, mailing details, deposit confirmation, withdrawal or onward payment, and messages. If the user mailed a check recently, the app should suggest contacting the bank and mail carrier or delivery service as appropriate through official channels. It should avoid promising stop-payment success.

For QR-code payments, the app should merge link checking and payment checking. The app should scan or receive the QR code, identify whether it points to a website, payment address, payment app profile, crypto wallet, Wi-Fi network, app download, or login page, and explain the risk before the user proceeds. If the QR code appears on a parking meter, restaurant table, flyer, email, package, invoice, marketplace listing, or event page, the app should ask whether the user expected it, whether there is a verified alternative, and whether the payment destination matches the real business. The app should warn when a QR code hides the true destination or pushes payment outside a trusted app.

The playbooks should connect directly to prevention. Before money moves, the app should identify high-risk payment instructions: pay only by gift card, crypto, wire transfer, payment app, bank transfer, cash, gold, courier pickup, or unusual split payments; keep the payment secret; hurry because an account will close or a loved one will be harmed; lie to bank staff; test a small amount first; or download an app before paying. The app should show a strong warning when payment instructions are paired with urgency, secrecy, impersonation, romance, investment promises, fake jobs, fake rentals, fake support, or government threats.

Each playbook should have an evidence minimum. The app should show a case completeness bar, but the bar should not punish the user. It should say: More evidence may help, but you can still act now. The minimum for a payment case should include payment type, amount, date or approximate date, recipient or merchant if known, account or service used, screenshots or receipts if available, and communication that led to the payment. If the user does not have all of this, the app should still create a case and help them proceed. A professional product handles imperfect records because real victims rarely have perfect documentation.

The payment playbooks should include follow-up reminders. After contacting a bank, payment app, exchange, gift-card issuer, or platform, the user should be able to save case numbers, contact dates, staff names, next deadline, document requests, and outcome. The app should remind the user to check statements, watch for new charges, change passwords if credentials were shared, remove suspicious devices from accounts, revoke payment authorizations, enable alerts, and check for related scams. It should also warn the user that scammers may recontact them pretending to be from the bank or recovery department after they report the issue.

The payment-specific playbooks are successful when users can choose a payment method and immediately see relevant next steps, evidence needs, risk signs, and recovery boundaries. They fail if every payment method gets the same advice, if the app promises refunds, if it ignores unauthorized account access, if it treats crypto like card payments, if it hides urgent contact steps, or if it cannot tell the difference between prevention before payment and recovery after payment.

# Appendix S: AI Impersonation, Deepfake, and Synthetic-Trust Checks

AI impersonation protection is necessary because many modern scams use familiar voices, realistic images, polished videos, copied writing styles, fake profiles, and stolen accounts. Verivae should treat this as a trust-verification problem, not only a media-analysis problem. The app should help the user answer: is this person really who they claim to be, and is the action they want safe?

The main entry point should be an "Is this really them?" path inside Manual Scam Check. The user should be able to start from a message, email, phone call note, voicemail, screenshot, profile, image, video clip, payment request, or suspicious social conversation. The app should ask who the contact claims to be, how they reached the user, what they want the user to do, whether money or account access is involved, whether urgency or secrecy is being used, and whether the user has another trusted way to contact the person.

For voice, family-emergency, workplace, celebrity, romance, investment, and support impersonation, Verivae should prioritize behavior and verification over appearance. A familiar voice, realistic photo, verified-looking profile, or convincing writing style should not be treated as proof. The safer action should be to stop, avoid using contact details supplied inside the suspicious request, and verify through a known-safe contact method the user already trusted before the suspicious interaction began.

If the app analyzes audio, images, or video, it must explain the limits plainly. It can check for suspicious signs, reuse patterns, inconsistencies, and context risk, but it should not promise to prove that media is real or fake. When evidence is incomplete, the result should say so directly and recommend independent verification before the user sends money, shares codes, installs software, grants remote access, or provides private information.

This capability should connect to the Evidence Vault when the user chooses to save material. Screenshots, call notes, profile names, payment instructions, phone numbers, email addresses, links, attachments, and user observations should be grouped into one case. The user should be able to keep the check temporary, save it privately, or share selected evidence with a trusted helper.

AI impersonation protection is successful when it slows down high-pressure decisions, gives the user a safe verification route, explains uncertainty honestly, and connects identity claims to money, account, device, and recovery risks. It fails if it treats realistic media as proof, promises perfect deepfake detection, ignores emotional pressure, dismisses possible emergencies, or makes users feel foolish for being targeted.
